The relational model, SQL, PostgreSQL internals, indexing, transactions, ORMs, scaling, migrations, compatibility and NoSQL modelling.

Part 16 — Databases and the Relational Model

16.1 Why databases exist

Most backend developers meet the database as "the place where the ORM puts things". That is like meeting an aircraft engine as "the place where the noise comes from". This part goes underneath. By the end you should be able to look at any table in your system and explain why every column has the type it has, why every constraint is there, and what breaks if it were removed.

We will use one realistic e-commerce schema for the whole of Part 16 and Part 17: users, addresses, products, categories, inventory, orders, order items, payments, shipments, reviews and notifications. It is defined in full in section 16.3, and every later example refers back to it.

16.1.1 What a database guarantees that a file or a Map does not

Concept

A database is not "a smarter file". It is a piece of software that makes a set of promises about your data and keeps those promises under concurrency, crashes and partial failures. The promises are: durability (once it says "committed", the data survives a power cut), atomicity (a group of changes happens entirely or not at all), isolation (concurrent users do not see each other's half-finished work), consistency (declared rules are never violated, no matter which code path wrote the data), and efficient lookup at scale (find one row among a billion in a few milliseconds).

A JavaScript Map, a JSON file on disk, or an in-memory array gives you none of these unless you build them yourself. And building them yourself is roughly the work of writing a database.

Why does it exist?

Imagine you write an order service that keeps orders in a Map<string, Order>. It works in development. Then:

  • The process restarts on deploy. Every order is gone. So you write the map to orders.json after each change.
  • Two requests arrive at once. Both read the file, both modify it, both write it back. One order silently disappears. So you add a mutex.
  • The process is killed halfway through writing the file. The file is now half-written and unparseable. So you write to a temp file and rename atomically.
  • The file reaches 4 GB. Reading it to find one order takes 30 seconds. So you build an index: a second file mapping orderId to byte offset.
  • You add a second server behind the load balancer. The mutex no longer works across machines.
  • Finance asks for "total revenue by category last month". You write a script that loads 4 GB into memory and crashes with an out-of-memory error.

Each of these problems has been solved, carefully, in PostgreSQL over thirty years. The write-ahead log solves durability and crash recovery. MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) solves isolation without a global mutex. B-tree indexes solve lookup. The query planner solves "revenue by category" in one declarative statement. That is why databases exist: to stop every team from re-solving these problems badly.

Mental model

Imagine a bank vault versus a shoebox under your bed. Both "store money". The vault has a ledger of every deposit and withdrawal (write-ahead log), a rule that a withdrawal either completes or is fully reversed (atomicity), separate counters so two tellers do not overwrite each other's work (isolation), locked drawers with rules like "this drawer can never go negative" (constraints), and a catalog that tells you which drawer holds account 4471 without opening every drawer (indexes). The shoebox is faster to open, right up to the moment you need any of those things.

How it works

At the highest level, when your NestJS service runs INSERT INTO orders ... and then COMMIT, PostgreSQL does the following:

  1. Parses the SQL and checks it against the catalog (does the table exist, do the types match).
  2. Plans how to execute it (which index to use, which join algorithm).
  3. Acquires the necessary locks (a row lock on the row being written, a light table lock that blocks DROP TABLE but not other writers).
  4. Writes a new row version into a data page in shared memory, marked with the current transaction id.
  5. Writes a WAL (write-ahead log) record describing the change.
  6. On COMMIT, forces the WAL record to disk with fsync. Only after the disk confirms does the client get "COMMIT" back. This single step is what makes durability real. On a typical SSD it costs 0.5 to 2 ms, which is why a transaction commit is never "free".
  7. The dirty data page is written to disk later, lazily, by the background writer or checkpointer. If the server crashes before that, recovery replays the WAL and rebuilds the page.
  8. Constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, foreign keys) are checked before the row is accepted. A violation aborts the statement and, by default, the whole transaction.

Part 20 (Database Transactions) and Part 21 (PostgreSQL Internals) go deeper into WAL and MVCC. Here the point is: every one of those steps is a guarantee that a file does not give you.

Practical example

A POST /orders request in a food-delivery app must (a) create the order, (b) create three order items, (c) reserve stock for each product, and (d) record an initial payment attempt. If step (c) fails for the third product because it just sold out, steps (a) and (b) must vanish as if they never happened. In a database this is one BEGIN ... COMMIT block; the failure triggers ROLLBACK. In a file-based store you would need to write compensating code for every partial-failure combination.

NestJS example

The database-backed version is short because the database does the hard work. The important lines are the transaction boundary and the fact that the stock check is a database constraint, not just an if in application code.

// orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { CreateOrderDto } from './dto/create-order.dto';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async placeOrder(userId: string, dto: CreateOrderDto): Promise<{ orderId: string }> {
    // One transaction: all-or-nothing across four tables.
    return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const [order] = await manager.query(
        `INSERT INTO orders (user_id, status, currency)
         VALUES ($1, 'pending', 'INR') RETURNING id`,
        [userId],
      );

      for (const item of dto.items) {
        // CHECK (quantity_reserved <= quantity_on_hand) in the DB rejects oversell.
        const result = await manager.query(
          `UPDATE inventory
              SET quantity_reserved = quantity_reserved + $2
            WHERE product_id = $1
            RETURNING quantity_on_hand - quantity_reserved AS available`,
          [item.productId, item.quantity],
        );
        if (result.length === 0) {
          throw new ConflictException(`Product ${item.productId} not found`);
        }
        await manager.query(
          `INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, product_name)
           SELECT $1, p.id, $2, p.price, p.name FROM products p WHERE p.id = $3`,
          [order.id, item.quantity, item.productId],
        );
      }
      return { orderId: order.id };
    });
    // If any statement throws (including a CHECK violation), TypeORM issues ROLLBACK.
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

This is the guarantee in its rawest form. Run it in psql, kill the server between the two statements, and the first insert is gone on restart.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, status) VALUES ('7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7', 'pending');
-- crash here: nothing persisted, nobody else ever saw the row
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, product_name)
VALUES (currval_of_something, ...);
COMMIT;
-- only now is the WAL fsynced and the data durable

Production scenario

A mid-size e-commerce backend handles around 300 orders per minute at peak, 5 writes per order, so roughly 25 write transactions per second plus 2,000 to 3,000 reads per second. A single PostgreSQL instance on a 4-vCPU machine with NVMe storage handles this comfortably: commit latency 1 to 3 ms, indexed point reads under 1 ms, 99th percentile API latency dominated by network and application code, not the database. The database becomes the bottleneck far later than most teams expect, and usually because of a missing index or a bad query, not because of raw volume.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call engineer was paged: "orders.json is corrupt". A legacy internal tool had stored purchase-order drafts in a JSON file, guarded by an in-process lock. The night before, the tool had been scaled to two replicas to handle a busy period. Both replicas wrote the file. The last write won, then a pod was OOM-killed mid-write, leaving a truncated file. Twelve hours of drafts were lost. The fix was a one-table PostgreSQL schema with a primary key and a jsonb column, done in a morning. The lesson was not "JSON files are bad"; it was that the tool had silently taken on durability, atomicity and isolation responsibilities that it could not meet.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Durability is only as good as fsync. With synchronous_commit = off, a crash can lose the last few hundred milliseconds of "committed" transactions. Know your setting.
  • Durability on one machine is not durability across a data-center failure. That needs replication (Part 22 — Replication and High Availability).
  • A database guarantees the rules you declared. If you never declare CHECK (quantity > 0), a negative quantity is perfectly valid to the database.
  • Connection exhaustion: every guarantee is behind a connection, and PostgreSQL connections are expensive processes. Pooling is mandatory (Part 21).
  • A transaction that is left open (application bug, forgotten await) holds locks and blocks vacuum. The database keeps its promises, but at a cost to everyone else.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior question is never "SQL or NoSQL". It is: "Which guarantees does this data need, and which system gives them at the lowest operational cost?" For orders, payments and inventory the answer is almost always a relational database, because money and stock need atomicity and constraints. For a session cache, Redis is right because losing it costs nothing. For an append-only clickstream, a log system is right. Seniors also refuse to reimplement database guarantees in application code: if you find yourself writing a mutex to protect a counter, you have found a place where the database should be doing the work.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the database as dumb storage and enforcing every rule in the service layer. Application code has bugs, races and multiple entry points (admin tools, migrations, scripts). The database is the only place every write must pass through.
  • Using synchronous_commit = off globally "for performance" without telling anyone.
  • Building a "simple" file-backed store for "just internal use", then scaling it to two replicas.

Interview questions

  1. What does COMMIT actually do in PostgreSQL, and why is it not free? Expected: it fsyncs the WAL; the client only gets an acknowledgement after the disk confirms; typically 0.5 to 2 ms on SSD. Follow-up: what does synchronous_commit = off change?
  2. Why can a Map protected by a mutex not replace a database, even for a small service? Expected: no durability, no crash atomicity, no cross-process isolation, no efficient lookup at scale.
  3. Which guarantee would you give up first for a session store, and why?
  4. If the application already validates everything, why add database constraints? Expected: multiple write paths, races, future bugs; constraints are the last line of defense.

Practical exercise

Build a tiny key-value store on a JSON file in Node.js. Then write a test that spawns two processes writing 1,000 keys each concurrently, and a test that kills the process mid-write. Document exactly which guarantees broke. Acceptance criteria: you can name which of durability, atomicity and isolation failed in each test and which PostgreSQL mechanism would have prevented it.

16.2 The relational model

16.2.1 Relations, tuples and set semantics

Concept

A relation is what we casually call a table. Formally it is a set of tuples (rows) that all share the same attributes (columns). Three properties of the formal model matter in daily work:

  1. A relation is a set. Sets have no order and no duplicates. This is why SELECT * FROM orders without ORDER BY returns rows in whatever order is cheapest for PostgreSQL today, and a different order tomorrow.
  2. Every attribute has a domain: a data type plus the constraints on it. price numeric(12,2) CHECK (price >= 0) is a domain, not just a type.
  3. Operations on relations produce relations. A JOIN, a WHERE, a GROUP BY each take one or more relations and produce a new one. This is why SQL composes: any query result can be treated as a table and queried again.

Why does it exist?

Before the relational model (Codd, 1970), databases were hierarchical or network-shaped. To find "all orders for products in category X" you wrote a navigation program that walked pointers. Changing the physical layout broke every program. The relational model separated the logical view (tables, relationships expressed as shared values) from the physical layout (pages, indexes, pointers). You describe what you want; the database decides how to fetch it. That separation is what lets you add an index without changing a single query.

Mental model

Imagine a spreadsheet where every sheet has a strict header row, no merged cells, no colors, no "notes" column that sometimes holds a number and sometimes a date. Now imagine a rule that says two sheets can only be related by having a column with the same values (an order_id in the items sheet that matches an id in the orders sheet), never by a hand-drawn arrow. That is the relational model. The strictness is the point: it is what makes the sheets combinable by a machine.

How it works

The relational operators you use every day map to the algebra:

Algebra operation SQL What it produces
Selection WHERE Subset of rows
Projection SELECT a, b Subset of columns
Cartesian product CROSS JOIN Every row combined with every row
Join JOIN ... ON Product filtered by a condition
Union / intersection / difference UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT Set combinations
Rename AS Same data, new name
Aggregation (extension) GROUP BY One row per group

Because the model is set-based, two things surprise people:

  • Duplicate rows are legal in SQL tables without a primary key (SQL relaxed the pure model into "bags"). PostgreSQL will happily store two identical rows. Without a key you cannot even delete just one of them cleanly. This is the practical reason every table gets a primary key.
  • DISTINCT and UNION (without ALL) are expensive because they must re-impose set semantics by sorting or hashing every row.

PostgreSQL example

-- A relation with no key: legal, and a trap.
CREATE TABLE audit_scratch (event text, at timestamptz);
INSERT INTO audit_scratch VALUES ('login', now()), ('login', now());
-- Two identical rows may now exist. "Delete one of them" is not expressible cleanly.

-- Set semantics: the same query, two runs, potentially different order.
SELECT id, status FROM orders LIMIT 5;
-- Adding ORDER BY is the only way to make order part of the contract.
SELECT id, status FROM orders ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id LIMIT 5;

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors treat "rows have no order" and "results are relations" as tools. Need a report? Build it as a chain of relations: filter, join, aggregate, join again. Need a fast path? Materialize one of those intermediate relations as a table or materialized view. The algebra also explains the planner: since WHERE then JOIN equals JOIN then WHERE mathematically, the planner is free to reorder, and does.

Interview questions

  1. Why can the same SELECT return rows in a different order tomorrow? Expected: relations are sets; physical order changes with updates, vacuum, and plan changes.
  2. Why is DISTINCT expensive? Expected: must sort or hash all rows to remove duplicates.

16.2.2 NULL and three-valued logic

Concept

NULL means "unknown" or "not applicable", not zero and not empty string. Because it is unknown, any comparison with it is also unknown. SQL therefore has three truth values: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE; UNKNOWN rows are dropped, silently.

Why does it exist?

Real data has holes. An order that has not shipped has no shipped_at. A user who never gave a phone number has no phone. The alternative to NULL is sentinel values (0, '', '1970-01-01'), which are worse because they look like real data and corrupt aggregates. NULL is a deliberate marker that says "do not treat this as a value".

Mental model

Imagine a form where one field is blank. If someone asks "is the phone number 555-1234?", the honest answer is not "no", it is "I don't know". If they ask "is the phone number different from 555-1234?", the answer is still "I don't know". Only "is the field blank?" gets a yes. That is IS NULL.

How it works

The rules, which you must know cold:

Expression Result
NULL = NULL UNKNOWN (not TRUE)
NULL <> 5 UNKNOWN
NULL IS NULL TRUE
NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 5 TRUE (null-safe comparison)
NULL AND FALSE FALSE
NULL AND TRUE UNKNOWN
NULL OR TRUE TRUE
NOT NULL (the boolean) UNKNOWN
5 + NULL NULL
'a' || NULL NULL
COUNT(col) counts non-null values only
COUNT(*) counts rows
SUM(col) over all-null NULL, not 0
AVG(col) ignores nulls (divides by non-null count)
x IN (1, NULL) where x = 2 UNKNOWN
x NOT IN (1, NULL) never TRUE for any x
UNIQUE constraint multiple NULLs allowed by default

The last three are where production bugs live. NOT IN against a list or subquery that contains even one NULL returns no rows at all, because x <> NULL is UNKNOWN and UNKNOWN AND anything is never TRUE. Part 17 returns to this with the safe alternative, NOT EXISTS.

PostgreSQL example

-- Which orders are NOT cancelled? Wrong version drops orders with NULL cancelled_reason.
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE cancel_reason <> 'fraud';        -- excludes NULL reasons
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE cancel_reason IS DISTINCT FROM 'fraud';  -- includes them

-- Aggregates and NULL
SELECT count(*), count(shipped_at), sum(discount), avg(discount)
FROM orders;
-- count(*) = 1000, count(shipped_at) = 640 (360 not yet shipped),
-- sum(discount) treats NULL as absent, avg divides by non-null count.

-- Make NULL explicit in output
SELECT id, coalesce(shipped_at::text, 'not shipped') AS shipped FROM orders;

-- Unique with NULLs: both rows are accepted
CREATE TABLE demo_unique (a int UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO demo_unique VALUES (NULL), (NULL);   -- succeeds
-- PostgreSQL 15+: treat nulls as equal
ALTER TABLE demo_unique DROP CONSTRAINT demo_unique_a_key;
ALTER TABLE demo_unique ADD CONSTRAINT demo_unique_a_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (a);

TypeORM example

ORMs hide NULL semantics and then surprise you. In TypeORM, { where: { cancelReason: null } } generates IS NULL correctly, but Not(null) generates <> NULL, which matches nothing. Use IsNull() and Not(IsNull()).

import { IsNull, Not } from 'typeorm';

// Correct
const shipped = await orderRepo.find({ where: { shippedAt: Not(IsNull()) } });

// Silent bug: generates "shipped_at <> NULL" which is UNKNOWN for every row
const wrong = await orderRepo.find({ where: { shippedAt: Not(null as any) } });

Sequelize example

import { Op } from 'sequelize';

// Correct null checks
const shipped = await Order.findAll({ where: { shippedAt: { [Op.ne]: null } } });
// Sequelize translates {[Op.ne]: null} to "IS NOT NULL", and {[Op.eq]: null} / null to "IS NULL".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders) where any user_id is NULL returns zero rows. It looks like "no users without orders" when the truth is "the query is broken".
  • WHERE status <> 'cancelled' silently excludes rows where status is NULL. Make status NOT NULL with a default so the question cannot arise.
  • ORDER BY shipped_at DESC puts NULLs first in PostgreSQL (nulls are considered larger). Use NULLS LAST when that is not what the UI wants.
  • Concatenation with NULL yields NULL: first_name || ' ' || last_name is NULL when either is missing. Use concat_ws(' ', first_name, last_name), which skips nulls.
  • SUM() over zero rows or all-null rows is NULL; coalesce(sum(x), 0) when the report needs a number.
  • JSON: payload->>'phone' is NULL both when the key is missing and when it is JSON null. Distinguish with payload ? 'phone'.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors minimize NULL at the schema level. Every column gets NOT NULL unless "unknown" is genuinely a business state. Status columns are always NOT NULL DEFAULT. Timestamps like shipped_at are allowed to be null because "not yet shipped" is a real state, and that nullability is documented. When they review a query with NOT IN, <>, or != against a nullable column, they ask "what happens to the nulls?" every time.

Common mistakes

  • Using = NULL in hand-written SQL. It is always UNKNOWN.
  • Storing empty strings to avoid nulls. Now '' and NULL both mean "no value", and UNIQUE treats them differently.
  • Assuming COUNT(column) counts rows.

Interview questions

  1. What does WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t) return if any y is NULL? Expected: no rows. Why: x <> NULL is UNKNOWN. Follow-up: rewrite it safely (NOT EXISTS).
  2. Why does UNIQUE allow multiple nulls, and how do you change that? Expected: nulls are not equal to each other; UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT in PG15+, or a partial unique index.
  3. What is the difference between <> and IS DISTINCT FROM?

Practical exercise

Take the orders table from section 16.3. Write five queries, each using a different nullable column with <>, NOT IN, string concatenation, SUM, and ORDER BY. Predict the output on paper, then run them. Acceptance criteria: you correctly predicted the null behavior of all five before running.

16.3 The reference schema

Everything in Part 16 and Part 17 uses this schema. Read it once carefully; the design decisions are explained in the following sections (types in 16.4, keys in 16.5, constraints in 16.6, normalization in 16.7, relationships in 16.9).

erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ ADDRESSES : has
    USERS ||--o{ ORDERS : places
    USERS ||--o{ REVIEWS : writes
    USERS ||--o{ NOTIFICATIONS : receives
    CATEGORIES ||--o{ CATEGORIES : "parent of"
    CATEGORIES ||--o{ PRODUCTS : contains
    PRODUCTS ||--|| INVENTORY : "stocked as"
    PRODUCTS ||--o{ ORDER_ITEMS : "appears in"
    PRODUCTS ||--o{ REVIEWS : "reviewed in"
    ORDERS ||--|{ ORDER_ITEMS : contains
    ORDERS ||--o{ PAYMENTS : "paid by"
    ORDERS ||--o{ SHIPMENTS : "shipped as"
    ADDRESSES ||--o{ ORDERS : "ships to"
-- PostgreSQL 15+. gen_random_uuid() is built in since PG13.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id            uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email         text        NOT NULL,
  password_hash text        NOT NULL,
  full_name     text        NOT NULL,
  phone         text,
  status        text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                            CHECK (status IN ('active', 'suspended', 'deleted')),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at    timestamptz
);
-- Case-insensitive uniqueness on email, excluding soft-deleted users.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_lower_uidx ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE addresses (
  id           uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id      uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  label        text,
  line1        text        NOT NULL,
  line2        text,
  city         text        NOT NULL,
  state        text,
  postal_code  text        NOT NULL,
  country_code char(2)     NOT NULL,
  is_default   boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX addresses_user_id_idx ON addresses (user_id);
-- At most one default address per user.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX addresses_one_default_uidx ON addresses (user_id) WHERE is_default;

CREATE TABLE categories (
  id         bigint      GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id  bigint      REFERENCES categories(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  name       text        NOT NULL,
  slug       text        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CHECK (parent_id IS DISTINCT FROM id)
);
CREATE INDEX categories_parent_id_idx ON categories (parent_id);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          uuid          PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  sku         text          NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        text          NOT NULL,
  description text,
  category_id bigint        NOT NULL REFERENCES categories(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  price       numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  currency    char(3)       NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR',
  attributes  jsonb         NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,   -- color, size, material...
  tags        text[]        NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  is_active   boolean       NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  created_at  timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX products_category_id_idx ON products (category_id);
CREATE INDEX products_attributes_gin ON products USING gin (attributes);
CREATE INDEX products_tags_gin ON products USING gin (tags);

CREATE TABLE inventory (
  product_id        uuid        PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  quantity_on_hand  integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (quantity_on_hand >= 0),
  quantity_reserved integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (quantity_reserved >= 0),
  reorder_level     integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 10,
  updated_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CHECK (quantity_reserved <= quantity_on_hand)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id                  uuid          PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  order_number        bigint        GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY UNIQUE,
  user_id             uuid          NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status              text          NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
                                    CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped','delivered','cancelled','refunded')),
  shipping_address_id uuid          REFERENCES addresses(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  subtotal            numeric(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (subtotal >= 0),
  discount            numeric(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (discount >= 0),
  total               numeric(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total >= 0),
  currency            char(3)       NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR',
  placed_at           timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at          timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  cancelled_at        timestamptz,
  cancel_reason       text,
  version             integer       NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);
CREATE INDEX orders_user_id_placed_at_idx ON orders (user_id, placed_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX orders_placed_at_idx ON orders (placed_at);
CREATE INDEX orders_open_status_idx ON orders (status, placed_at) WHERE status IN ('pending', 'paid');
CREATE INDEX orders_shipping_address_id_idx ON orders (shipping_address_id);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  id           bigint        GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id     uuid          NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id   uuid          NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  quantity     integer       NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price   numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),  -- price snapshot at order time
  product_name text          NOT NULL,                          -- name snapshot at order time
  UNIQUE (order_id, product_id)
);
CREATE INDEX order_items_product_id_idx ON order_items (product_id);

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id                  uuid          PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  order_id            uuid          NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  provider            text          NOT NULL,          -- 'razorpay', 'stripe'
  provider_payment_id text,
  idempotency_key     text          NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  amount              numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
  currency            char(3)       NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR',
  status              text          NOT NULL DEFAULT 'initiated'
                                    CHECK (status IN ('initiated','authorized','captured','failed','refunded')),
  attempt_no          integer       NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at          timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at          timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX payments_order_id_created_at_idx ON payments (order_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX payments_one_captured_per_order_uidx ON payments (order_id) WHERE status = 'captured';

CREATE TABLE shipments (
  id              uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  order_id        uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  carrier         text        NOT NULL,
  tracking_number text,
  status          text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'created'
                              CHECK (status IN ('created','in_transit','delivered','returned')),
  shipped_at      timestamptz,
  delivered_at    timestamptz,
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CHECK (delivered_at IS NULL OR shipped_at IS NOT NULL)
);
CREATE INDEX shipments_order_id_idx ON shipments (order_id);

CREATE TABLE reviews (
  id         bigint      GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  user_id    uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  rating     smallint    NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  title      text,
  body       text,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (product_id, user_id)          -- one review per user per product
);
CREATE INDEX reviews_user_id_idx ON reviews (user_id);

CREATE TYPE notification_channel AS ENUM ('email', 'sms', 'push');

CREATE TABLE notifications (
  id           bigint               GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id      uuid                 NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  channel      notification_channel NOT NULL,
  template     text                 NOT NULL,
  payload      jsonb                NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  status       text                 NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
                                    CHECK (status IN ('pending','sent','failed')),
  attempts     integer              NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  scheduled_at timestamptz          NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at      timestamptz,
  created_at   timestamptz          NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX notifications_user_id_idx ON notifications (user_id);
-- The job-queue index: only pending rows, ordered by when they are due.
CREATE INDEX notifications_pending_idx ON notifications (scheduled_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

A few design decisions to notice now, because they recur throughout:

  • users, addresses, products, orders, payments, shipments use uuid primary keys because those ids are exposed in URLs and generated by multiple services. categories, order_items, reviews, notifications use bigint identity because they are internal, high-volume, and benefit from sequential keys. Section 16.4 explains the cost of each.
  • Money is numeric(12,2). Never float. Section 16.4 explains why with an actual rounding failure.
  • Every timestamp is timestamptz.
  • Status columns are text with a CHECK constraint, except notification_channel, which is a real ENUM. Section 16.4 compares them.
  • order_items snapshots unit_price and product_name because an invoice must not change when the catalog changes. This is deliberate, controlled denormalization (section 16.8).
  • Every foreign key column has an index. PostgreSQL does not create these for you (section 16.5).
  • Business rules such as "one default address per user" and "one captured payment per order" are partial unique indexes, not application code (section 16.6).

16.4 Choosing data types in PostgreSQL

A column's type is the cheapest constraint you will ever add and the most expensive one to change later. Changing integer to bigint on a 500-million-row table rewrites the table and every index that includes the column, under an exclusive lock, for hours. Choosing right the first time is a senior skill. This section covers each decision the reference schema had to make.

16.4.1 Primary key type: uuid vs bigint identity

Concept

A surrogate key is an identifier with no business meaning, generated by the system. The two mainstream choices in PostgreSQL are a 64-bit sequential integer (bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY) and a 128-bit UUID (uuid). They differ in size, generation location, index behavior and what they leak.

Why does it exist?

Sequential integers are compact and fast to index, but they must be generated by the database, so the application cannot know the id before the insert, they reveal how many rows exist (/orders/10432 tells competitors your volume), and they are guessable (/orders/10433). UUIDs can be generated by any service without coordination, are unguessable, and are safe to expose. The cost is 16 bytes instead of 8 and, for random UUIDs, a badly behaved index.

Mental model

Imagine a library that shelves books in the order they arrive. A new book always goes at the end of the last shelf: fast, no reshuffling. That is a sequential key in a B-tree. Now imagine the shelving rule is "shelve by a random number stamped on the spine". Every new book goes to a random place in the building; the shelf there is full, so half its books move to a new shelf. Every insert touches a random page, and the whole building must stay in memory to be fast. That is a random UUID (v4) in a B-tree.

How it works

A B-tree index stores keys in sorted order across 8 KB pages. When you insert:

  1. With sequential keys, every new key is larger than all existing keys. It goes to the rightmost leaf page. That page is hot in cache. Page splits happen only at the right edge and PostgreSQL optimizes this case (it fills the split pages asymmetrically so the right page has room).
  2. With random keys, the new key belongs on a random leaf page. If that page is not in shared_buffers, it is read from disk. If it is full, it splits 50/50, and both halves are now half-empty. Over time the index runs at roughly 50 to 70 percent fill instead of 90 percent, so it is bigger, and the working set is the entire index rather than its right edge.
  3. WAL volume increases because every insert dirties a random page plus its full-page image after each checkpoint.

Concrete numbers from a typical benchmark on a 100-million-row table: a bigint primary key index is about 2.1 GB; a random uuid index is about 3 GB before bloat and closer to 4.5 GB after sustained inserts; insert throughput with random UUIDs drops 20 to 40 percent once the index exceeds RAM. A sorted UUID removes almost all of that penalty.

UUIDv7 (RFC 9562, 2024) solves the problem: the first 48 bits are a millisecond Unix timestamp, the rest is random. Keys generated in the same instant are still unique and unguessable, but they sort by creation time, so inserts land on the right edge of the index. PostgreSQL 18 includes uuidv7() natively; on earlier versions you generate it in the application (uuid npm package v10+ has v7()) or with a small SQL function.

-- UUIDv7 generator for PostgreSQL 13 to 17 (PG18 has uuidv7() built in)
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION uuid_generate_v7() RETURNS uuid AS $$
SELECT encode(
  set_bit(set_bit(
    overlay(uuid_send(gen_random_uuid())
            placing substring(int8send((extract(epoch from clock_timestamp()) * 1000)::bigint) from 3)
            from 1 for 6),
    52, 1), 53, 1),
  'hex')::uuid;
$$ LANGUAGE sql VOLATILE;

Practical example

In the reference schema, orders.id is a UUID because the order id appears in URLs, emails, webhooks from the payment provider, and support tickets. orders.order_number is a separate bigint identity because customer support and finance want a short, human-readable number. order_items.id is bigint because nobody outside the database ever sees it and there will be five to ten times more of them than orders.

PostgreSQL example

-- Both patterns, side by side
CREATE TABLE orders_v1 (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, placed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
CREATE TABLE orders_v2 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),           placed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
CREATE TABLE orders_v3 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v7(),           placed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());

-- Measure index size after 10 million inserts
INSERT INTO orders_v1 (placed_at) SELECT now() FROM generate_series(1, 10000000);
INSERT INTO orders_v2 (placed_at) SELECT now() FROM generate_series(1, 10000000);
INSERT INTO orders_v3 (placed_at) SELECT now() FROM generate_series(1, 10000000);

SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid))
FROM pg_class WHERE relname LIKE 'orders_v%_pkey';
-- orders_v1_pkey  214 MB   (bigint, sequential)
-- orders_v2_pkey  428 MB   (uuid v4, random; bloated after splits)
-- orders_v3_pkey  301 MB   (uuid v7, near-sequential)

TypeORM example

import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, PrimaryColumn, Column } from 'typeorm';
import { v7 as uuidv7 } from 'uuid';

@Entity({ name: 'orders' })
export class Order {
  // Let PostgreSQL generate: DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')
  id!: string;

  // Human-friendly sequence, generated by DB, never written by the app
  @Column({ type: 'bigint', generated: 'identity', insert: false, update: false })
  orderNumber!: string; // bigint arrives as string in node-postgres
}

@Entity({ name: 'payments' })
export class Payment {
  // Generate UUIDv7 in the application so the id is known before insert
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid')
  id: string = uuidv7();
}

Note the bigint as string detail: node-postgres returns bigint as a string because JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53. TypeORM follows that. Do not declare bigint columns as number in TypeScript unless you configure a parser and accept the risk.

Sequelize example

import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class Order extends Model {
  declare id: string;
  declare orderNumber: string;
}

Order.init(
  {
    id: { type: DataTypes.UUID, primaryKey: true, defaultValue: DataTypes.UUIDV4 },
    // For UUIDv7, use defaultValue: () => uuidv7() instead of DataTypes.UUIDV4
    orderNumber: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, autoIncrement: true, unique: true, field: 'order_number' },
  },
  { sequelize, tableName: 'orders', underscored: true },
);

Production scenario

A marketplace at 50 million orders with random UUIDv4 keys on orders, order_items and payments had 14 GB of primary-key indexes on 9 GB of table data. shared_buffers was 8 GB. Insert p99 latency was 40 ms and rising. Migrating new rows to UUIDv7 (old rows stayed v4; both are valid uuid) brought the right-edge inserts back into cache, and p99 fell to 6 ms within a week as the hot region of the index shrank.

Failure scenario

"At 02:14 the on-call got paged: integer out of range on INSERT INTO events." The events.id column was serial (32-bit). It reached 2,147,483,647 after four years. Every insert failed; the ingestion pipeline backed up; the fix (ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint) rewrote a 900 GB table and took eleven hours with the table locked. The senior lesson: never use serial or integer for a primary key. bigint costs 4 extra bytes per row and removes the question forever.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Integer overflow at 2^31 with serial/integer PKs. Use bigint.
  • Sequences are not transactional: a rolled-back insert consumes the number. Gaps in order_number are normal, and any process that assumes no gaps is wrong.
  • Random UUID as a clustered ordering: ORDER BY id is meaningless for v4 and only "roughly by time" for v7. Always order by a timestamp column with a tiebreaker.
  • UUIDs as strings: storing a UUID in text or varchar(36) costs 37 bytes instead of 16, compares byte-by-byte instead of as two 64-bit integers, and allows invalid values. Always use the uuid type.
  • Passing a UUID parameter typed as text (WHERE id = $1 with $1::text) can defeat the index. Part 17 covers implicit casts.
  • Exposing sequential ids in public URLs leaks volume and enables enumeration attacks. If you must, add a separate public slug.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The decision table they use:

Situation Choice Why
Id exposed in URLs / to third parties uuid (v7 if possible) unguessable, no volume leak, client can pre-generate
Id generated by multiple services or offline clients uuid no central coordination
Internal, high-volume child table (items, events, logs) bigint identity 8 bytes, dense index, fast joins
Human-readable reference needed bigint identity as a second unique column keep uuid as PK
Existing integer PK approaching 1.5 billion migrate to bigint now, not at 2.1 billion rewriting is the only fix

They also refuse serial (legacy, creates an implicit sequence with odd ownership semantics) in favor of GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, which is SQL-standard and prevents accidental explicit ids.

Common mistakes

  • varchar(36) for UUIDs.
  • integer PKs "because we'll never have 2 billion rows". Events tables do.
  • Random UUIDv4 on a 10-billion-row time-series table, then wondering why the index is larger than the data.
  • Using the UUID for ordering.

Interview questions

  1. Why do random UUIDs hurt B-tree insert performance? Expected: every insert lands on a random leaf page; cache misses, 50/50 splits, index bloat, WAL growth. Follow-up: how does UUIDv7 fix this?
  2. When would you still pick a bigint identity? Expected: internal high-volume tables where compactness and join speed matter.
  3. What happens when a serial column overflows, and how long does the fix take?
  4. Why does node-postgres return bigint as a string?

Practical exercise

Create the three orders_v* tables above, insert 5 million rows each, and compare index size, insert time, and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for a point lookup. Acceptance criteria: a table of measurements and a one-paragraph recommendation for your team.

16.4.2 Money: numeric vs float

Concept

numeric(precision, scale) stores exact decimal numbers. real and double precision (float) store binary approximations. Money must be exact. numeric(12,2) holds up to 10 digits before the decimal point and exactly 2 after, which covers 9,999,999,999.99, enough for order totals in any currency with two minor units.

Why does it exist?

Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Multiply that by a million transactions and your ledger does not balance. Auditors do not accept "floating point" as an explanation.

How it works

numeric is stored as a variable-length array of base-10,000 digits with a sign and a scale. Arithmetic is done in software, so it is roughly 3 to 10 times slower than float arithmetic, which is irrelevant for order totals and highly relevant for scientific computation. Comparison and indexing work normally. Division produces as many digits as needed up to an internal limit, so always round explicitly when storing results of division.

PostgreSQL example

SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8;          -- 0.30000000000000004
SELECT 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric;        -- 0.3

-- Tax computation: round explicitly, at the boundary you control
SELECT round(1999.99 * 0.18, 2) AS gst;    -- 360.00 (exactly 359.9982 rounded)

-- Sum of a million 0.1 values
SELECT sum(0.1::float8) FROM generate_series(1, 1000000);   -- 100000.00000133288
SELECT sum(0.1::numeric) FROM generate_series(1, 1000000);  -- 100000.0

TypeORM example

TypeORM returns numeric as a string, to preserve exactness. Convert with a decimal library, never parseFloat.

import { Column, Entity } from 'typeorm';
import Big from 'big.js';

@Entity({ name: 'order_items' })
export class OrderItem {
  @Column({ type: 'numeric', precision: 12, scale: 2 })
  unitPrice!: string; // "1999.99" - keep as string until arithmetic is needed

  lineTotal(quantity: number): string {
    return new Big(this.unitPrice).times(quantity).toFixed(2);
  }
}

An alternative many payment teams prefer: store minor units as bigint (amount_paise bigint). Integer arithmetic in JavaScript is exact up to 2^53, no library needed, and the type makes "this is not a float" impossible to get wrong. The reference schema uses numeric(12,2) because it reads naturally in reports; either is correct, mixing them is not.

Sequelize example

unitPrice: { type: DataTypes.DECIMAL(12, 2), allowNull: false, field: 'unit_price',
  get() { return this.getDataValue('unitPrice'); } }, // returns string; do not parseFloat

Edge cases & failure modes

  • parseFloat("1999.99") * 3 in JavaScript gives 5999.969999999999. The string from the driver is exact until someone parses it.
  • Currency with three minor units (KWD, BHD) or zero (JPY): numeric(12,2) is wrong there. If you go multi-currency, store numeric(14,4) or minor units plus a currency code.
  • Rounding rules: banker's rounding vs half-up differ in the last cent. Decide once, implement in the database with round(), and test it.
  • money type in PostgreSQL: locale-dependent formatting, fixed two decimals, painful to cast. Avoid.

Interview questions

  1. Why not store prices as double precision? Expected: 0.1 is not representable; sums drift; audits fail.
  2. numeric(12,2) or bigint minor units? Expected: both exact; minor units avoid driver string handling; numeric reads naturally. Pick one.

16.4.3 Time: timestamptz vs timestamp

Concept

timestamptz ("timestamp with time zone") stores an absolute instant in UTC and converts to the session's time zone on output. timestamp ("without time zone") stores a wall-clock reading with no idea which zone it was read in. Despite the name, timestamptz does not store a time zone; it stores a point on the global timeline, which is exactly what you want for "when did this happen".

Why does it exist?

An order placed at "14:30" is meaningless without a zone. Was that Mumbai or Frankfurt? With timestamp, the answer depends on the server's TimeZone setting at insert time, which changes when you move to a new cloud region or a developer runs the migration from a laptop. With timestamptz the instant is unambiguous forever.

How it works

Both types are 8 bytes (microseconds since 2000-01-01). The difference is purely in conversion: timestamptz input is interpreted in the session TimeZone (or the explicit offset in the literal) and stored as UTC; output is converted back. timestamp input and output are stored and shown verbatim.

SET TimeZone = 'Asia/Kolkata';
SELECT '2026-03-01 14:30'::timestamptz;           -- 2026-03-01 14:30:00+05:30
SELECT '2026-03-01 14:30'::timestamptz AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';  -- 2026-03-01 09:00:00 (timestamp)
SELECT '2026-03-01 14:30+00'::timestamptz;        -- 2026-03-01 20:00:00+05:30

-- Comparing timestamptz with a date literal: the literal is interpreted in session zone
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01';   -- midnight in session TZ

Production scenario

Node's Date is an absolute instant, so it maps cleanly to timestamptz. Set the session zone to UTC from the application (options: '-c TimeZone=UTC' in the connection string, or SET TIME ZONE 'UTC' on connect) so every DATE-literal comparison and date_trunc in raw SQL behaves the same in every environment. Do reporting in the customer's zone explicitly: date_trunc('day', placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata').

Failure scenario

A daily revenue report for "yesterday" showed a 4-hour hole every day. The report used placed_at::date = current_date - 1 on a timestamp column. Production had migrated from a server in Europe/Berlin to one in UTC; old rows were stored as Berlin wall-clock, new rows as UTC wall-clock, and no row carried enough information to tell which. It took a week of forensics using payment-provider timestamps to rebuild. The fix was timestamptz and a UTC session zone, but the old data could only be corrected approximately.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Daylight saving: timestamp + interval '1 day' across a DST boundary in timestamptz context yields the same wall-clock time next day (23 or 25 hours later). If you need exactly 24 hours, add interval '24 hours'.
  • now() is the transaction start time, constant within a transaction. clock_timestamp() is the real current time. Long transactions inserting now() rows all carry the same timestamp.
  • Index on date(placed_at) vs placed_at::date: the cast of timestamptz to date depends on the session zone, so it is not immutable and cannot be indexed directly. Index (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date or a range predicate instead.
  • Storing "date of birth" or "delivery slot 9 to 11 AM local" is wall-clock data, and date or timestamp plus a zone column is correct there. timestamptz is for instants.

Interview questions

  1. Does timestamptz store the time zone? Expected: no, it stores UTC instants and converts on I/O.
  2. Why set the session time zone to UTC from the application?
  3. What is the difference between now() and clock_timestamp()?

16.4.4 Text: text vs varchar(n) vs char(n)

Concept

In PostgreSQL, text, varchar, and varchar(n) share one storage format and one performance profile. varchar(n) only adds a length check. char(n) pads with spaces to exactly n characters and is almost never what you want.

Why does it exist?

varchar(n) exists for SQL-standard compatibility and for one legitimate purpose: a hard length limit that should be enforced at the database (a two-letter country code, a 3-letter currency code). For everything else, text is idiomatic PostgreSQL.

How it works

Values up to about 2 KB live inline in the row. Larger values are compressed and, if still large, moved out of line into a TOAST table (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique), transparently. A text column can hold up to 1 GB. varchar(255) is not faster than text; it is a MySQL habit.

-- Length rule as a CHECK: change it without a type rewrite
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_full_name_len CHECK (length(full_name) BETWEEN 1 AND 200);

-- Changing varchar(50) to varchar(100) on PG is a metadata-only change (fast), but
-- changing varchar(100) to varchar(50) rescans the table to validate. A CHECK can be added NOT VALID and validated later.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • char(2) with a one-character value stores 'A ' and comparisons ignore trailing spaces, which surprises string functions and JSON output. The reference schema uses char(2) and char(3) for ISO codes only because they are always exactly that length.
  • Collation: sorting and LIKE depend on the database collation. en_US.UTF-8 sorts case-insensitively-ish but compares with case; C collation is byte-order and enables LIKE 'abc%' to use a plain B-tree index. If you need LIKE prefix search on a non-C collation, create the index with text_pattern_ops.
  • Case-insensitive uniqueness: index lower(email) (as the reference schema does) or use the citext extension.

Interview questions

  1. Is varchar(255) faster than text in PostgreSQL? Expected: no; identical storage; the limit is a check.
  2. When is varchar(n) justified? Expected: hard domain limits like ISO codes.

16.4.5 jsonb: when it is right and when it is a smell

Concept

jsonb stores JSON in a decomposed binary format that can be indexed and queried with operators (->, ->>, @>, ?, jsonb_path_query). json (without b) stores the raw text and is only useful for preserving exact formatting. Use jsonb.

Why does it exist?

Some data is genuinely schema-less or varies per row: product attributes (a phone has ram_gb, a shoe has size_eu), a webhook payload from a third party, a notification template's variables. Forcing that into columns means either hundreds of nullable columns or an entity-attribute-value table that is painful to query. jsonb gives you a document inside a relational row, with the row still carrying the relational guarantees.

Mental model

Imagine a well-organized filing cabinet (the table) where each folder (row) has labeled tabs (columns) and one pocket in the back where you can drop any loose notes (jsonb). The pocket is useful. A cabinet that is all pockets and no tabs is a pile of paper.

How it works

  1. On write, the JSON text is parsed, keys are deduplicated (last wins), and the object is stored as a binary tree. Key order is not preserved. Whitespace is dropped.
  2. Operators: -> returns jsonb, ->> returns text. @> is containment ("does this document contain this sub-document"). ? tests key existence.
  3. A GIN index on the column makes @>, ?, ?|, ?& and jsonb_path_ops queries fast (tens of milliseconds on millions of rows). A B-tree index on an expression (attributes->>'brand') makes equality and range queries on that one key fast.
  4. Updating one key rewrites the whole value (PostgreSQL rows are immutable versions; MVCC). A 50 KB jsonb document updated 100 times per day generates 5 MB of dead tuples per day for that one row.

PostgreSQL example

-- Products with attributes: legitimate jsonb use
INSERT INTO products (sku, name, category_id, price, attributes)
VALUES ('PHN-001', 'Phone X', 3, 49999.00,
        '{"brand": "Acme", "ram_gb": 8, "colors": ["black", "blue"]}');

-- Containment query: uses products_attributes_gin
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"brand": "Acme"}';

-- Key extraction with a targeted expression index
CREATE INDEX products_attr_brand_idx ON products ((attributes->>'brand'));
SELECT id FROM products WHERE attributes->>'brand' = 'Acme';

-- Range on a numeric key: cast in the index expression
CREATE INDEX products_attr_ram_idx ON products (((attributes->>'ram_gb')::int));
SELECT id FROM products WHERE (attributes->>'ram_gb')::int >= 8;

-- Guard against garbage: CHECK on shape
ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT products_attributes_is_object
  CHECK (jsonb_typeof(attributes) = 'object');

When jsonb is a schema-avoidance smell

The red flags a senior looks for:

  • You JOIN on a value inside jsonb (ON o.meta->>'user_id' = u.id::text). That is a foreign key hiding in a document, with no referential integrity and a text comparison instead of a uuid comparison.
  • You need a NOT NULL or UNIQUE on a key inside the document.
  • Every row has the same keys. That is a table with extra steps.
  • The document is updated frequently in small pieces (counters, statuses). Each update rewrites the whole document.
  • Reports group by a jsonb key. It works, but it is slower than a column and the planner has poor statistics for it.

The decision table:

Data Column(s) jsonb
Queried by equality/range often, filtered in WHERE, joined yes no
Sparse, per-row-varying attributes no yes
Third-party payload kept for audit no yes
Needs UNIQUE / FK / NOT NULL yes no
Updated in small pieces frequently yes no
Read as a whole, written as a whole either yes

TypeORM example

@Column({ type: 'jsonb', default: () => "'{}'::jsonb" })
attributes!: Record<string, unknown>;

// Query with containment (raw operator; TypeORM has no typed jsonb operators)
const acme = await productRepo
  .createQueryBuilder('p')
  .where('p.attributes @> :filter', { filter: JSON.stringify({ brand: 'Acme' }) })
  .getMany();

Sequelize example

attributes: { type: DataTypes.JSONB, allowNull: false, defaultValue: {} },

// Sequelize supports nested key queries on JSONB for PostgreSQL:
const acme = await Product.findAll({ where: { 'attributes.brand': 'Acme' } });
// Generates: WHERE ("attributes"#>>'{brand}') = 'Acme'  (expression index needs to match this form)

Failure scenario

A notification service stored delivery attempts inside notifications.payload as an array that grew on every retry. Retries ran every minute for failed rows. After a month, some documents were 2 MB, each update rewrote 2 MB, the table had 60 GB of dead tuples, autovacuum could not keep up, and SELECT ... WHERE status = 'pending' slowed from 2 ms to 900 ms because the partial index pointed at bloated heap pages. The fix was a separate notification_attempts table with one narrow row per attempt. jsonb was not the problem; unbounded growth of a value that is rewritten on each change was.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • NULL vs JSON null vs missing key are three different states. ->> returns SQL NULL for the last two.
  • Numbers in JSON are arbitrary precision in jsonb, but ->> returns text; cast explicitly and expect cast errors on bad data.
  • GIN index maintenance is expensive on write-heavy tables (fastupdate pending list helps; tune gin_pending_list_limit).
  • jsonb columns bigger than 2 KB go to TOAST; reading any key decompresses the whole document.
  • Duplicate keys are silently collapsed on insert.

Interview questions

  1. When is jsonb the right choice? Expected: sparse, per-row-varying, read-whole/write-whole data; not for keys you join, constrain, or update in pieces.
  2. What index do you add for attributes @> '{"brand":"Acme"}', and for attributes->>'brand' = 'Acme'? Expected: GIN on the column; B-tree on the expression.
  3. Why is updating one key in a large jsonb document expensive? Expected: MVCC rewrites the whole row version.

16.4.6 Arrays

Concept

PostgreSQL columns can be arrays of any type (text[], int[], uuid[]). They are indexable with GIN and support operators like @> (contains), && (overlaps), and = ANY(...).

Why does it exist?

Small, unordered sets of scalar values that belong to a row, are queried by membership, and never need their own attributes or foreign keys: product tags, allowed roles, a list of applied coupon codes. Modeling those as a join table is correct in pure normalization terms and often over-engineering.

PostgreSQL example

-- Tags on products: text[] with a GIN index (already in the reference schema)
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE tags @> ARRAY['sale'];        -- contains 'sale'
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE tags && ARRAY['sale', 'new']; -- overlaps either

-- Passing a list parameter: ANY beats IN for prepared statements (one parameter, any length)
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE id = ANY($1::uuid[]);

-- Unnest to rows when you need to aggregate per tag
SELECT tag, count(*) FROM products, unnest(tags) AS tag GROUP BY tag ORDER BY 2 DESC;

When not to use arrays

If the elements need attributes (when was the tag added, by whom), a foreign key (tags must exist in a tags table), or you need to find "all products with tag X" in a way that must stay fast at 100 million rows with heavy writes, use a join table. Arrays of foreign keys (category_ids bigint[]) have no referential integrity and are the most common array misuse.

Interview questions

  1. tags text[] or a product_tags join table? Expected: array when tags are simple labels queried by membership; table when they need attributes, FK integrity, or high-cardinality reverse lookups.

16.4.7 Enums vs lookup tables vs CHECK constraints

Concept

Three ways to restrict a column to a fixed set of values:

  1. CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM — a real type with an ordered, named set of labels stored as 4-byte OIDs.
  2. text with CHECK (status IN (...)) — plain text, validated by a constraint.
  3. A lookup table with a foreign key — values are rows, can have attributes, can be added by an INSERT.

How it works and the tradeoffs

Property ENUM text + CHECK Lookup table + FK
Storage 4 bytes length of text ('pending' = 8 bytes) 4 or 8 bytes FK
Add a value ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE (cannot run inside a transaction block before PG12; new value not usable in same transaction) ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT then ADD CONSTRAINT (validates whole table unless NOT VALID) INSERT INTO statuses
Remove/rename a value Rename yes; remove: not supported (recreate type) Replace constraint DELETE (if no FK references)
Ordering By declaration order (ORDER BY status follows enum order) Alphabetical By a sort column you add
Extra attributes (label, description, is_terminal) no no yes
ORM friendliness TypeORM enum type works; migrations awkward trivial join or cache needed
Readability in psql good good needs join

The reference schema uses text + CHECK for orders.status, payments.status, shipments.status because order statuses change as the business evolves (a "returned" state gets added, "refunded" gets split into partial and full) and constraint replacement is a fast, transactional, rollback-able migration. It uses a real ENUM for notification_channel because the set (email, sms, push) is tiny, stable, and used in a high-volume table where 4 bytes versus 5 to 8 bytes per row matters slightly.

PostgreSQL example

-- Evolving a CHECK-constrained status safely, without a full-table scan blocking writers
ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_status_check;
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_check
  CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped','delivered','cancelled','refunded','returned')) NOT VALID;
-- Existing rows are trusted; new writes are validated. Validate later, with only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock:
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_status_check;

-- Evolving an ENUM
ALTER TYPE notification_channel ADD VALUE IF NOT EXISTS 'whatsapp';
-- PG12+: allowed inside a transaction, but the new value cannot be used until that transaction commits.
-- Removing 'sms' later: no ALTER TYPE DROP VALUE. You must create a new type, cast the column, drop the old type.

TypeORM example

export enum OrderStatus { Pending = 'pending', Paid = 'paid', Shipped = 'shipped',
  Delivered = 'delivered', Cancelled = 'cancelled', Refunded = 'refunded' }

@Column({ type: 'text' })                 // DB enforces via CHECK; TS enum for the app
status!: OrderStatus;

// If you use a real PG enum:
@Column({ type: 'enum', enum: NotificationChannel, enumName: 'notification_channel' })
channel!: NotificationChannel;

Failure scenario

A team ran ALTER TYPE order_status ADD VALUE 'returned' inside their migration framework, which wraps each migration in a transaction. On PostgreSQL 11 it failed outright ("ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE cannot run inside a transaction block"). After upgrading to PG12 it succeeded, but the same migration then ran UPDATE orders SET status = 'returned' WHERE ... and failed with "unsafe use of new value". The migration had to be split into two deploys. With text + CHECK this would have been one transactional migration.

Interview questions

  1. Enum or CHECK for an order status? Expected: CHECK for evolving sets (transactional changes, removals); enum for tiny stable sets in huge tables.
  2. What is the operational cost of removing an enum value? Expected: not supported directly; recreate the type and rewrite the column.
  3. Why add a CHECK constraint as NOT VALID first? Expected: avoids a full-table validation scan under a heavy lock; validate later with a weaker lock.

Practical exercise

Take the orders.status column and implement it three ways in three copies of the table. For each, write the migration that adds a returned state and the migration that removes refunded. Time each on a 10-million-row table and note which locks are taken (SELECT * FROM pg_locks from a second session). Acceptance criteria: a decision matrix with your own measured numbers.

16.5 Keys: primary keys and foreign keys

16.5.1 Primary keys

Concept

A primary key (PK) is the column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and can never be NULL. Every table gets exactly one. PostgreSQL implements it as a unique B-tree index plus a NOT NULL constraint on each column. Other tables refer to a row by its primary key value.

Two philosophies exist. A natural key is a real-world identifier that already exists: an email, an ISBN, a SKU, a country code. A surrogate key is a meaningless system-generated identifier: a bigint sequence or a UUID. A composite key is a PK made of more than one column, common in join tables ((order_id, product_id)).

Why does it exist?

Without a primary key, a table is a bag of rows with no reliable way to address one of them. UPDATE ... WHERE email = ... works until two rows share the email. Replication systems (logical replication, Debezium, CDC pipelines) need a key to describe "which row changed". ORMs need a key to implement save() and identity maps. And most importantly, foreign keys need something stable to point at.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital. A patient's name is a natural key: real, meaningful, and a disaster the day two "Priya Sharma"s are admitted, or when one patient changes her name. The hospital assigns a patient number that never changes and means nothing. That is a surrogate key. The name is still stored, still unique-ish, still searched, but nothing points at it.

How it works

  1. PRIMARY KEY (col) creates a unique index named <table>_pkey and marks col NOT NULL.
  2. Every insert probes that index for a duplicate; a duplicate raises 23505 unique_violation.
  3. Foreign keys from other tables reference this index to validate that the parent row exists.
  4. Logical replication uses the PK as the row identity (REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT). A table without a PK cannot have its UPDATEs and DELETEs replicated logically unless you set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, which sends the whole old row.

Natural vs surrogate decision table:

Property Natural key (email, SKU) Surrogate key (bigint, uuid)
Stability Changes (email changes, SKU renumbered) Never changes
Size in child tables Text copied into every child row (email is ~25 bytes) 8 or 16 bytes
Meaning in logs and debugging Readable Opaque
Uniqueness truly guaranteed? Often no (two products, one SKU after a merger) Yes, by construction
Cascading updates when the key changes ON UPDATE CASCADE rewrites every child row Not needed
Recommended for Reference data that is itself the value (country_code, currency) Every entity table

The reference schema uses surrogate keys on every entity table and keeps natural identifiers (email, sku, slug) as UNIQUE columns. That gives you both: fast stable references and business uniqueness.

Practical example

products.sku is unique and meaningful, so why not make it the PK? Because a SKU gets reassigned when a supplier changes, because order_items would then carry a text SKU in millions of rows, and because the day merchandising decides SKUs are case-insensitive you would need to rewrite every child table. products.id uuid as PK and sku text UNIQUE costs 16 bytes per product and removes every one of those problems.

PostgreSQL example

-- Composite primary key in a join table with no other identity
CREATE TABLE product_tags_v2 (
  product_id uuid   NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id     bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id)     ON DELETE CASCADE,
  added_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (product_id, tag_id)
);
-- The PK index covers lookups by product_id (leading column).
-- Lookups by tag_id need their own index:
CREATE INDEX product_tags_v2_tag_id_idx ON product_tags_v2 (tag_id);

-- Identity column semantics
CREATE TABLE demo_ident (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, note text);
INSERT INTO demo_ident (id, note) VALUES (5, 'x');
-- ERROR: cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"  (ALWAYS protects you)
INSERT INTO demo_ident (id, note) OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (5, 'x');  -- explicit override
-- GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY allows explicit values silently; prefer ALWAYS.

In the reference schema, order_items has a surrogate bigint id plus UNIQUE (order_id, product_id), rather than a composite PK. Both are valid; the surrogate makes ORMs and API URLs (/order-items/123) simpler, and the unique constraint still enforces the business rule.

TypeORM example

import { Entity, PrimaryColumn, ManyToOne, JoinColumn, CreateDateColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'product_tags_v2' })
export class ProductTag {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid', { name: 'product_id' })
  productId!: string;

  @PrimaryColumn('bigint', { name: 'tag_id' })
  tagId!: string;

  @ManyToOne(() => Product, { onDelete: 'CASCADE' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'product_id' })
  product!: Product;

  @CreateDateColumn({ name: 'added_at', type: 'timestamptz' })
  addedAt!: Date;
}
// Two @PrimaryColumn decorators produce PRIMARY KEY (product_id, tag_id).

Sequelize example

ProductTag.init(
  {
    productId: { type: DataTypes.UUID, primaryKey: true, field: 'product_id' },
    tagId: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, primaryKey: true, field: 'tag_id' },
  },
  { sequelize, tableName: 'product_tags_v2', underscored: true, timestamps: false },
);
// Sequelize supports composite PKs in init(); some helpers (findByPk) expect a single PK,
// so use findOne({ where: { productId, tagId } }) for composite keys.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A table with no PK: logical replication of updates fails, ORMs misbehave, duplicates are unremovable. Add one even to log tables.
  • Natural key that turns out not to be unique (national ID reused, email shared by a family). Surrogate keys make this a data-quality issue instead of a schema rewrite.
  • GENERATED BY DEFAULT lets an application insert an explicit id and later collide with the sequence. Use ALWAYS.
  • Composite PK with a leading column that is never queried alone: the index cannot serve lookups on the second column.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

"Every entity table gets a surrogate PK. Every natural identifier gets a UNIQUE constraint. Join tables get a composite PK unless they need their own identity." They also think about what the PK will be used for beyond the table: replication identity, sharding key later, cache key in Redis, path parameter in URLs. That is why they prefer UUIDs for anything that leaves the database.

Common mistakes

  • Making email the PK on users, then handling an email change with ON UPDATE CASCADE across nine tables.
  • Composite natural PK (country_code, postal_code, line1) on addresses. Addresses are not unique; two users live at the same address.
  • Forgetting the second-column index on a composite PK join table.

Interview questions

  1. Natural or surrogate key for users? Expected: surrogate; email changes, and it gets copied into every child row. Follow-up: where does the email uniqueness live? (UNIQUE index, case-insensitive, excluding soft-deleted rows.)
  2. What does GENERATED ALWAYS prevent that BY DEFAULT does not?
  3. What happens to logical replication of a table with no primary key?

16.5.2 Foreign keys

Concept

A foreign key (FK) is a column (or columns) in a child table whose values must exist as a primary or unique key in a parent table. order_items.order_id must match an orders.id. The database enforces this on every insert and update of the child, and on every delete and key-update of the parent. The ON DELETE clause says what happens to children when the parent goes away.

Why does it exist?

Without FKs, an order item can point at an order that was deleted, a payment can reference a non-existent order, and a report that joins them silently drops or duplicates rows. These orphans are the most common form of data corruption in systems that "enforce it in the application", because the application has many write paths (API, admin tool, migration script, support engineer in psql) and only some of them remember the rule. The FK is the one rule that every path must obey.

Mental model

Imagine a library where each borrowing slip must name a real book on the catalog. The FK is the librarian who refuses to file a slip for a book that does not exist, and who, when a book is removed from the catalog, either refuses (RESTRICT), shreds the slips too (CASCADE), or blanks the book field on the slips (SET NULL).

How it works

  1. On INSERT or UPDATE of the child's FK column, PostgreSQL looks up the parent key in the parent's unique index. Missing parent raises 23503 foreign_key_violation. It also takes a FOR KEY SHARE lock on the parent row so the parent cannot be deleted or have its key changed until the child transaction ends.
  2. On DELETE (or key UPDATE) of a parent row, PostgreSQL must find all child rows referencing it. This is where the index matters: with an index on the child FK column it is an index scan; without one it is a sequential scan of the entire child table, per deleted parent row, while holding locks.
  3. The referential action then runs: RESTRICT / NO ACTION (error if children exist; NO ACTION is the default and is checked at end of statement or, if deferred, at commit), CASCADE (delete or update children, recursively), SET NULL, SET DEFAULT.
  4. Constraint timing: by default FKs are checked immediately at the end of each statement. DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED moves the check to COMMIT, which lets you insert a child before its parent within one transaction, or swap two rows' keys.
flowchart LR
    D["DELETE FROM users WHERE id = X"] --> L{"Index on addresses.user_id?"}
    L -->|yes| I["Index scan: find children in ms"]
    L -->|no| S["Seq scan of addresses: full table per parent row"]
    I --> A["Apply ON DELETE action"]
    S --> A
    A --> C{"CASCADE / RESTRICT / SET NULL"}

Choosing the ON DELETE action

Relationship Action in reference schema Reason
addresses.user_id CASCADE Address has no meaning without its user; deleting a user removes their address book
orders.user_id RESTRICT Orders are financial records. A user with orders cannot be hard-deleted; soft-delete or anonymize instead
order_items.order_id CASCADE Items are part of the order document
order_items.product_id RESTRICT A product that was ever sold cannot vanish; deactivate it instead
orders.shipping_address_id SET NULL If the address is deleted, the order still exists; the snapshot of the address should live elsewhere (a shipping_address jsonb snapshot is common)
payments.order_id RESTRICT Money records never cascade
reviews.user_id CASCADE Product decision: user deletion removes their reviews (GDPR-friendly)
categories.parent_id RESTRICT Deleting a parent with children is a mistake, not an intent

The senior default is RESTRICT. CASCADE is opt-in, only for true composition (children that are part of the parent's document). SET NULL is rare and requires the column to be nullable.

PostgreSQL example

-- Missing FK index demonstration: this is the single most common schema mistake in production.
CREATE TABLE audit_events (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  event text NOT NULL,
  at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- 50 million rows, no index on user_id.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 'a4c3...';
-- Delete on users  (actual time=0.05..0.06 rows=0 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan using users_pkey on users  (actual time=0.03..0.03 rows=1 loops=1)
-- Trigger for constraint audit_events_user_id_fkey: time=48211.331 calls=1
-- Execution Time: 48211.5 ms
-- The trigger time is the cascade scanning 50 million rows. During those 48 seconds the
-- session holds a ROW EXCLUSIVE lock on audit_events and a row lock on the user.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY audit_events_user_id_idx ON audit_events (user_id);
-- Same delete: Trigger ... time=1.2 calls=1

-- Find all FKs without a supporting index (run this in every code review of a migration)
SELECT c.conrelid::regclass AS child_table, a.attname AS fk_column
FROM pg_constraint c
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = ANY (c.conkey)
WHERE c.contype = 'f'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i
    WHERE i.indrelid = c.conrelid
      AND i.indkey[0] = a.attnum          -- FK column is the leading index column
  )
ORDER BY 1, 2;

Deferrable constraints:

-- Two-way reference: orders.current_shipment_id -> shipments, shipments.order_id -> orders
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN current_shipment_id uuid;
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_current_shipment_fkey
  FOREIGN KEY (current_shipment_id) REFERENCES shipments(id) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED;

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, current_shipment_id) VALUES ('o1', 'u1', 's1');  -- s1 does not exist yet: allowed, check deferred
INSERT INTO shipments (id, order_id, carrier) VALUES ('s1', 'o1', 'delhivery');
COMMIT;  -- both FKs are validated here

-- Deferring an existing immediate constraint for one transaction:
BEGIN;
SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED;   -- only works for constraints declared DEFERRABLE
...
COMMIT;

TypeORM example

import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, ManyToOne, JoinColumn, Index } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'order_items' })
@Index('order_items_product_id_idx', ['productId'])   // FK index: TypeORM does NOT add it for you
export class OrderItem {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn({ type: 'bigint' })
  id!: string;

  @Column('uuid', { name: 'order_id' })
  orderId!: string;

  @ManyToOne(() => Order, (o) => o.items, { onDelete: 'CASCADE', nullable: false })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'order_id' })
  order!: Order;

  @Column('uuid', { name: 'product_id' })
  productId!: string;

  @ManyToOne(() => Product, { onDelete: 'RESTRICT', nullable: false })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'product_id' })
  product!: Product;
}

Declaring both the scalar orderId column and the order relation on the same column is a deliberate pattern: you can insert with just the id (no extra SELECT to load the parent) and still navigate the relation when needed.

Sequelize example

Order.hasMany(OrderItem, { foreignKey: 'orderId', as: 'items', onDelete: 'CASCADE' });
OrderItem.belongsTo(Order, { foreignKey: 'orderId', as: 'order' });
OrderItem.belongsTo(Product, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'product', onDelete: 'RESTRICT' });

// Sequelize's sync() will create the FK; it will NOT create the FK index. Add it in the model:
OrderItem.init({ /* ... */ }, {
  sequelize, tableName: 'order_items', underscored: true,
  indexes: [{ fields: ['product_id'] }],
});

Production scenario

A support engineer runs DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ... for a GDPR request. users is referenced by eight tables. Six have FK indexes; two (audit_events, 50 million rows, and email_opens, 200 million rows) do not. The delete takes 3 minutes. During those 3 minutes: the user row is locked (harmless), audit_events and email_opens are each under a ROW EXCLUSIVE lock (other writers proceed, but CREATE INDEX and ALTER TABLE block), and the sequential scans evict hot pages from shared_buffers, so unrelated queries get 5 to 10 times slower. Nobody notices the delete itself; they notice the p99 spike on GET /products.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged for "checkout latency p99 > 5 s". pg_stat_activity showed 40 sessions waiting on Lock: relation behind one ALTER TABLE order_items ADD COLUMN gift_note text that was itself waiting behind a DELETE FROM products WHERE is_active = false AND created_at < '2020-01-01' started by a cleanup job. The delete had RESTRICT on order_items.product_id and had to scan order_items for every one of 12,000 candidate products, because the FK index had been dropped a month earlier during an "unused index cleanup" that mistook a rarely-read index for an unused one.
