FK indexes are used by the cascade machinery, which does not show up as normal index reads until a delete happens. The team restored the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and added the "FK without index" query to their CI.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No index on the FK column: parent deletes and key updates scan the child table; locks are held for the duration.
  • CASCADE on the wrong relationship: deleting one category cascades to products, which cascades to inventory, reviews, and (if someone had set it) order items. A cascade chain is a data-loss chain. Audit every CASCADE for reachability.
  • Adding an FK to an existing large table validates every row under a SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE lock (blocks writes). Use ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (which takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE).
  • FK to a non-unique column is not allowed; the parent column must have a unique index. This means FK to a partial unique index is not allowed either.
  • The FOR KEY SHARE lock on the parent row means heavy child inserts under one parent (many order items for one order) briefly serialize with any UPDATE of the parent's key columns. Non-key updates of the parent (orders.status) use FOR NO KEY UPDATE and do not conflict. This is why PostgreSQL distinguishes the two lock modes.
  • Cross-database FKs do not exist. Once you split into microservices, referential integrity across services is your problem, not PostgreSQL's.
  • FKs across partitions: supported from PG12 for references to partitioned tables; check version.
  • Bulk loads with FKs on: each row is validated; for very large loads, drop the FK, load, re-add with NOT VALID + VALIDATE.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask three questions for every FK: (1) What happens on parent delete, and is that the business intent? (2) Is there an index on the child column? (3) Will this ever need to be deferred? They default to RESTRICT, add the index in the same migration as the constraint, and put the "FK without index" catalog query in CI. When someone proposes "we'll drop FKs for performance", they ask for the benchmark; FK validation is one index probe per insert, typically 20 to 50 microseconds, and never the bottleneck it is blamed for.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the index. PostgreSQL never creates it. MySQL does, which is why people assume.
  • ON DELETE CASCADE everywhere "so deletes just work".
  • Adding an FK with validation on a 100-million-row table at 2 PM.
  • Relying on the ORM's synchronize to create constraints in production (see section 16.10).

Interview questions

  1. Does PostgreSQL index foreign key columns automatically? Expected: no. Why it matters: parent deletes scan the child table. Follow-up: write the query that finds FKs without indexes.
  2. What lock does inserting a child row take on the parent row, and why? Expected: FOR KEY SHARE; prevents the parent key from changing or the row being deleted while the child references it; does not block non-key updates.
  3. How do you add an FK to a 200 GB table without blocking writes? Expected: NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT.
  4. When is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED needed? Expected: circular references, swapping keys, inserting child before parent in one transaction.
  5. Which relationships in an e-commerce schema should never cascade? Expected: orders, payments, anything financial.

Practical exercise

Add a product_images table referencing products without an FK index. Load 5 million rows. Time DELETE FROM products WHERE id = <one id> and observe pg_locks from another session. Add the index and repeat. Then write a CI check (a Jest test that runs the catalog query against the test database) that fails if any FK lacks an index. Acceptance criteria: before/after timings recorded, CI check passing on the reference schema and failing when you drop one FK index.

16.6 Constraints: the last line of defense

16.6.1 NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK

Concept

A constraint is a rule the database enforces on every write, no matter where the write comes from. NOT NULL says a value must be present. UNIQUE says no two rows may share a value (or combination of values). CHECK says an expression over the row's own columns must be true. Together they turn "the application should never write bad data" into "the database cannot store bad data".

Why does it exist?

Application validation runs in one process, on one code path, on one version of the code. The database sees every write from every version of every service, every migration, every script, and every concurrent transaction. Two requests that each pass application validation can together violate a rule (two users registering the same email in the same millisecond). Only the database, which serializes conflicting writes on the unique index, can reject the second. That is what "last line of defense" means: constraints catch the bugs you did not know you had and the races you cannot prevent in code.

Mental model

Imagine an airport. The airline's app checks your passport when you book (application validation). The gate agent checks it again (DTO validation in the controller). Immigration checks it at the border, and immigration does not care which airline you flew or what their app said (the constraint). If every airline were perfect, immigration would be unnecessary. It is not unnecessary.

How it works

  1. NOT NULL is checked when the tuple is formed, before it is written. It is nearly free.
  2. CHECK is evaluated as an expression against the new row on every insert and update. It can only reference the row's own columns (no subqueries, no other tables). Cost is the expression's cost, typically microseconds.
  3. UNIQUE creates a unique B-tree index. On insert, the index is probed; if an equal key exists and its transaction is committed, 23505 is raised. If an equal key exists from an uncommitted transaction, the insert waits for that transaction to finish. This wait is what makes unique constraints race-proof: two concurrent inserts of the same email serialize, the first commits, the second gets an error. Not a duplicate, not a "both succeed", an error.
  4. Violations abort the current statement and, unless you are using savepoints, the whole transaction. The client receives an error with SQLSTATE 23502 (not null), 23505 (unique), 23514 (check), 23503 (foreign key).

Practical example

The reference schema encodes business rules directly:

  • inventory: CHECK (quantity_on_hand >= 0) and CHECK (quantity_reserved <= quantity_on_hand). No code path, no race, no retry storm can oversell. An UPDATE that would breach it fails, and the service returns 409 Conflict to the client.
  • reviews: UNIQUE (product_id, user_id). One review per user per product, even if the "Submit" button is clicked twice and both requests reach different pods.
  • payments: idempotency_key text NOT NULL UNIQUE. The payment provider's webhook retry, the client's retry, and the queue's redelivery all collapse into one row.
  • shipments: CHECK (delivered_at IS NULL OR shipped_at IS NOT NULL). Cannot be delivered before being shipped.

NestJS example

The application still validates (fast feedback, good error messages), and the constraint catches what validation cannot. Map the SQLSTATE to an HTTP status in one place.

// common/filters/database-exception.filter.ts
import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';
import { QueryFailedError } from 'typeorm';
import { Response } from 'express';

interface PgError { code?: string; constraint?: string; detail?: string }

@Catch(QueryFailedError)
export class DatabaseExceptionFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  catch(exception: QueryFailedError, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const pg = exception.driverError as PgError;

    switch (pg.code) {
      case '23505': // unique_violation: duplicate email, duplicate review, duplicate idempotency key
        return res.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).json({ error: 'already_exists', constraint: pg.constraint });
      case '23503': // foreign_key_violation: referenced product/user does not exist
        return res.status(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY).json({ error: 'invalid_reference', constraint: pg.constraint });
      case '23514': // check_violation: oversell, negative price, bad status
        return res.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).json({ error: 'rule_violated', constraint: pg.constraint });
      case '23502': // not_null_violation
        return res.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST).json({ error: 'missing_field', detail: pg.detail });
      default:
        return res.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR).json({ error: 'database_error' });
    }
  }
}

Naming your constraints (CONSTRAINT inventory_no_oversell CHECK (...)) is what makes pg.constraint useful in that filter and in logs.

PostgreSQL example

-- Named constraints: you will thank yourself when reading logs
ALTER TABLE inventory DROP CONSTRAINT inventory_check;
ALTER TABLE inventory ADD CONSTRAINT inventory_no_oversell
  CHECK (quantity_reserved <= quantity_on_hand);

-- CHECK across columns for state consistency
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_cancel_consistency
  CHECK ((status = 'cancelled') = (cancelled_at IS NOT NULL));
-- cancelled  <=> cancelled_at set. Both directions enforced by one boolean equality.

-- CHECK on totals
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_total_math
  CHECK (total = subtotal - discount);

-- The race: two sessions, same email
-- Session A: INSERT INTO users (email, ...) VALUES ('a@x.com', ...);   -- not yet committed
-- Session B: INSERT INTO users (email, ...) VALUES ('A@X.COM', ...);   -- blocks on users_email_lower_uidx
-- Session A: COMMIT;
-- Session B: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_email_lower_uidx"

Edge cases & failure modes

  • UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs. UNIQUE (order_id, coupon_code) with a nullable coupon lets one order have many null-coupon rows. Use NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PG15+) or make the column NOT NULL with a sentinel.
  • CHECK cannot see other rows. "Total of items equals order total" is not expressible as a CHECK; it needs a trigger or application logic.
  • CHECK with a volatile function (now()) is allowed but is a bug: the constraint is checked at write time only, so CHECK (expires_at > now()) passes at insert and is meaningless later.
  • Adding NOT NULL to a large existing column scans the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. From PG12, if a validated CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) already exists, SET NOT NULL skips the scan. Pattern: add CHECK ... NOT VALID, VALIDATE, then SET NOT NULL.
  • Unique violation inside a transaction aborts the transaction. If you want to "try insert, fall back to select" you need a savepoint or ON CONFLICT (next section).
  • Constraint errors are the wrong tool for expected user input errors (validate in the DTO), but the right tool for concurrency and cross-service invariants.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the constraint first and the validation second. For every column: "Can this be null? Why?" For every table: "Which combination of columns must be unique?" For every state machine: "Which column combinations are impossible?" They see a constraint violation in production logs as a success ("the database caught a bug") and add a test that reproduces the path. They also know when a constraint is too expensive: a unique index on a 500-byte text column on a 1-billion-row write-heavy table costs real I/O, and a hash of the value might be the better unique key.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping NOT NULL "to make inserts easier", then discovering nulls in 30 percent of rows two years later.
  • Using unnamed constraints and then parsing detail strings in error handlers.
  • Validating in code, not in the database, and then discovering duplicates created by a data-import script.

Interview questions

  1. Why add database constraints when the DTO already validates? Expected: many write paths, races, future bugs; unique indexes serialize conflicting writes.
  2. What does a unique index do when two uncommitted transactions insert the same key? Expected: the second waits for the first to commit or roll back, then errors or proceeds.
  3. Can a CHECK constraint reference another table? Expected: no; use FKs, triggers, or exclusion constraints.
  4. How do you add NOT NULL to a large table without a long lock? Expected: CHECK ... NOT VALID, VALIDATE, SET NOT NULL.

16.6.2 Partial unique indexes and unique constraints vs unique indexes

Concept

A partial index has a WHERE clause and only contains rows matching it. A partial unique index enforces uniqueness only among those rows. This expresses rules like "one default address per user" (unique on user_id where is_default), "one captured payment per order", "one active subscription per customer", or "unique email among non-deleted users".

A unique constraint (ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE) and a unique index (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX) both create a unique B-tree index. The differences: a constraint can be referenced by a foreign key and appears in information_schema; an index can be partial, can use expressions (lower(email)), and can be built CONCURRENTLY. ON CONFLICT works with either, as long as the conflict target matches.

Why does it exist?

Many real uniqueness rules are conditional. "Only one default address" cannot be a plain UNIQUE (user_id, is_default) because that would also allow only one non-default address. Application-side enforcement ("unset the old default, then set the new one") races: two concurrent requests both unset the old default and both set themselves, and the user ends up with two defaults. The partial unique index makes the second commit fail.

How it works

  1. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX addresses_one_default_uidx ON addresses (user_id) WHERE is_default;
  2. On insert or update, PostgreSQL evaluates the predicate for the new row. If it is true, the row's user_id is inserted into the index, and the uniqueness check applies. If false, the index is untouched.
  3. Rows with is_default = false never enter the index, so any number of them per user is fine.
  4. The index is also much smaller than a full index (only default rows), so it is cheap to maintain.

PostgreSQL example

-- One default address per user (reference schema)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX addresses_one_default_uidx ON addresses (user_id) WHERE is_default;

-- Switching the default atomically: both statements in one transaction.
BEGIN;
UPDATE addresses SET is_default = false WHERE user_id = $1 AND is_default;
UPDATE addresses SET is_default = true  WHERE id = $2 AND user_id = $1;
COMMIT;
-- If two transactions race, one of them fails on the unique index at its second UPDATE.
-- The application retries once; the retry sees the other's committed default and succeeds.

-- One captured payment per order
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX payments_one_captured_per_order_uidx ON payments (order_id) WHERE status = 'captured';

-- Unique email among live users (soft delete friendly), case-insensitive
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_lower_uidx ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- Unique constraint vs unique index: FK can only reference the constraint (or a full unique index)
ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT products_sku_key UNIQUE (sku);   -- FK-referenceable
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX products_sku_uidx ON products (sku);            -- also FK-referenceable (full, non-expression)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_lower_uidx ON users (lower(email)); -- NOT FK-referenceable (expression)

TypeORM example

import { Entity, Index, Column } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'addresses' })
@Index('addresses_one_default_uidx', ['userId'], { unique: true, where: '"is_default"' })
export class Address {
  @Column('uuid', { name: 'user_id' }) userId!: string;
  @Column('boolean', { name: 'is_default', default: false }) isDefault!: boolean;
}

TypeORM's @Index with where supports partial indexes on PostgreSQL. Expression indexes (lower(email)) are not expressible via decorators; write them in a migration with queryRunner.query(...).

Sequelize example

Address.init({ /* ... */ }, {
  sequelize, tableName: 'addresses', underscored: true,
  indexes: [
    { name: 'addresses_one_default_uidx', unique: true, fields: ['user_id'], where: { is_default: true } },
  ],
});

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A partial unique index cannot be the target of a foreign key.
  • ON CONFLICT with a partial unique index must repeat the predicate: ON CONFLICT (user_id) WHERE is_default DO ....
  • Changing the predicate means dropping and recreating the index; build the new one CONCURRENTLY before dropping the old.
  • Soft delete plus a full (non-partial) unique index means a deleted user's email can never be reused. The partial index is the fix; see section 16.9 for the full soft-delete discussion.

Interview questions

  1. How do you enforce "only one default address per user" without races? Expected: partial unique index on (user_id) WHERE is_default; application retries on conflict.
  2. What can a unique constraint do that a unique index cannot, and vice versa? Expected: constraint is FK-referenceable and standard; index can be partial, expression-based, and built concurrently.

16.6.3 EXCLUDE constraints

Concept

An EXCLUDE constraint generalizes UNIQUE: instead of "no two rows have equal values", it says "no two rows have values that satisfy operator X". With the && (overlaps) operator on a range, that becomes "no two rows have overlapping ranges", which is the correct way to prevent double bookings: delivery slots, warehouse dock reservations, coupon validity windows, or flash-sale price schedules for a product.

Why does it exist?

"Check for overlap, then insert" in application code races exactly like "check for duplicate, then insert". Two requests both see no overlap, both insert, and a delivery slot is double-booked. A UNIQUE cannot express overlap. EXCLUDE USING gist can, and it is enforced with the same serialize-then-reject mechanism as unique indexes.

How it works

  1. The constraint is backed by a GiST index (B-trees cannot index "overlaps").
  2. Each row contributes its range (tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at)) and, optionally, an equality column (resource_id WITH =), which needs the btree_gist extension so GiST can handle scalar equality.
  3. On insert or update, the index is searched for existing rows where all operators are satisfied (same resource AND overlapping range). If one exists, 23P01 exclusion_violation is raised.

PostgreSQL example

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

-- Delivery slots: a courier cannot be booked for overlapping windows
CREATE TABLE delivery_slots (
  id         bigint      GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  courier_id uuid        NOT NULL,
  order_id   uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  window     tstzrange   NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT delivery_slots_no_overlap
    EXCLUDE USING gist (courier_id WITH =, window WITH &&)
);

INSERT INTO delivery_slots (courier_id, order_id, window)
VALUES ('c1', 'o1', tstzrange('2026-03-01 10:00+05:30', '2026-03-01 11:00+05:30', '[)'));
INSERT INTO delivery_slots (courier_id, order_id, window)
VALUES ('c1', 'o2', tstzrange('2026-03-01 10:30+05:30', '2026-03-01 11:30+05:30', '[)'));
-- ERROR: conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "delivery_slots_no_overlap"

-- Product price schedules: one active price per product at any instant
CREATE TABLE product_prices (
  product_id uuid          NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  price      numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  valid      tstzrange     NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, valid WITH &&)
);
-- Query the price at a point in time; the GiST index serves this too:
SELECT price FROM product_prices WHERE product_id = $1 AND valid @> now();

Bound notation: '[)' means inclusive start, exclusive end. Two slots [10:00, 11:00) and [11:00, 12:00) do not overlap. Always use half-open ranges for time.

TypeORM example

TypeORM has no decorator for exclusion constraints. Write it in a migration:

import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class DeliverySlots1709000000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  async up(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist`);
    await qr.query(`
      CREATE TABLE delivery_slots (
        id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
        courier_id uuid NOT NULL,
        order_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
        "window" tstzrange NOT NULL,
        CONSTRAINT delivery_slots_no_overlap EXCLUDE USING gist (courier_id WITH =, "window" WITH &&)
      )`);
  }
  async down(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`DROP TABLE delivery_slots`);
  }
}

In the entity, map the range column as @Column({ type: 'tstzrange' }) window!: string; and parse the [...,...) string in a value transformer, or query it with raw SQL. Sequelize has DataTypes.RANGE(DataTypes.DATE) with native range parsing for PostgreSQL.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GiST index maintenance is slower than B-tree; fine for bookings (hundreds per second), not for millions of inserts per hour.
  • Unbounded ranges ([now, )) overlap everything after them; "current price" rows must be closed when a new one starts, ideally in one transaction.
  • Empty ranges never overlap anything and slip through; add CHECK (NOT isempty(valid)).
  • Exclusion constraints cannot be deferred to accommodate "move slot A to B while B moves to A" unless declared DEFERRABLE, which they can be.

Interview questions

  1. How do you prevent overlapping bookings for the same resource without races? Expected: EXCLUDE USING gist (resource WITH =, range WITH &&) with btree_gist.
  2. Why [) bounds for time ranges?

16.6.4 Race-proof "insert if not exists" with ON CONFLICT

Concept

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (target) DO NOTHING inserts a row unless a unique constraint or index on target already holds an equal key, in which case it does nothing and no error is raised. DO UPDATE SET ... turns it into an upsert. The conflict target must match a unique index or constraint exactly (same columns, same expression, same partial predicate).

Why does it exist?

The naive pattern is SELECT ... WHERE email = $1; if not found, INSERT. Between the select and the insert, another request can insert. Both selects saw nothing; one insert succeeds, one fails with a unique violation, and the whole transaction is aborted. ON CONFLICT resolves this inside the insert itself: PostgreSQL attempts the index insert, detects the conflict (waiting for a concurrent uncommitted insert if needed), and follows the DO clause. No error, no aborted transaction, one round trip.

How it works

  1. The row is formed and the unique index is probed ("speculative insertion").
  2. If no conflict: normal insert.
  3. If a conflict with a committed row: DO NOTHING skips, DO UPDATE locks the existing row and updates it using EXCLUDED.column for the proposed values.
  4. If a conflict with an uncommitted row from another transaction: wait. When that transaction commits, treat as conflict; if it rolls back, retry the insert.
  5. RETURNING returns the inserted or updated row. With DO NOTHING, nothing is returned on conflict; to always get the id, use the DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col trick on a harmless column, or a follow-up select.

PostgreSQL example

-- Idempotent payment attempt creation: the client retries with the same idempotency key.
INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider, idempotency_key, amount, status)
VALUES ($1, 'razorpay', $2, $3, 'initiated')
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;
-- First call: returns the new id. Retry: returns zero rows. The service then SELECTs by key.

-- Always return the row (insert or existing), one round trip:
INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider, idempotency_key, amount, status)
VALUES ($1, 'razorpay', $2, $3, 'initiated')
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO UPDATE SET updated_at = now()   -- harmless touch
RETURNING id, status, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;
-- xmax = 0 is true for a freshly inserted row, false for an updated one.

-- Partial unique index as conflict target: predicate must be repeated
INSERT INTO addresses (user_id, line1, city, postal_code, country_code, is_default)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, 'IN', true)
ON CONFLICT (user_id) WHERE is_default DO NOTHING;

-- Expression index as conflict target
INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash, full_name) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;

NestJS example

// payments/payments.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

interface AttemptRow { id: string; status: string; inserted: boolean }

@Injectable()
export class PaymentsRepository {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /** Creates a payment attempt or returns the existing one for this idempotency key. */
  async createOrGetAttempt(orderId: string, key: string, amount: string): Promise<AttemptRow> {
    const rows = await this.ds.query<AttemptRow[]>(
      `INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider, idempotency_key, amount, status)
       VALUES ($1, 'razorpay', $2, $3, 'initiated')
       ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO UPDATE SET updated_at = now()
       RETURNING id, status, (xmax = 0) AS inserted`,
      [orderId, key, amount],
    );
    return rows[0];
  }
}

TypeORM example

// Repository API: orIgnore / orUpdate
await paymentRepo
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .insert()
  .into(Payment)
  .values({ orderId, provider: 'razorpay', idempotencyKey: key, amount, status: 'initiated' })
  .orIgnore()                                  // ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (no target; any unique index)
  .execute();

await inventoryRepo
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .insert()
  .into(Inventory)
  .values({ productId, quantityOnHand: 100 })
  .orUpdate(['quantity_on_hand'], ['product_id'])   // ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity_on_hand = EXCLUDED.quantity_on_hand
  .execute();

TypeORM's orUpdate cannot express partial-index predicates or WHERE clauses on the update; drop to query() for those.

Sequelize example

// upsert() uses ON CONFLICT on the primary key or a unique constraint it can detect
const [payment, created] = await Payment.upsert(
  { orderId, provider: 'razorpay', idempotencyKey: key, amount, status: 'initiated' },
  { conflictFields: ['idempotency_key'], returning: true },
);
// bulkCreate with updateOnDuplicate for multi-row upserts:
await Inventory.bulkCreate(rows, { updateOnDuplicate: ['quantityOnHand', 'updatedAt'] });

Failure scenario

A "get or create user by email" endpoint used findOne then save. Under a marketing campaign, the same email arrived from the mobile app and the web app within 50 ms. findOne returned null in both pods; both called save; one hit the unique index and threw; TypeORM's transaction was aborted; the controller returned 500; the mobile app retried; now it found the row and succeeded. Users saw a flash of "something went wrong" and support got 200 tickets. The fix was one statement with ON CONFLICT (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL DO UPDATE SET updated_at = now() RETURNING id, which turned a race into a no-op.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Conflict target mismatch: ON CONFLICT (email) when the index is on lower(email) raises "there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification".
  • ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE bumps the row version and generates a dead tuple even when nothing changes. Under extreme write rates, DO NOTHING plus a select is cheaper.
  • ON CONFLICT does not work on a table with multiple candidate unique indexes unless you name the target (or use ON CONSTRAINT name).
  • Inside DO UPDATE, WHERE can restrict the update: DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status WHERE payments.status <> 'captured' (never downgrade a captured payment).
  • ON CONFLICT is per-row for multi-row inserts, but a multi-row insert that conflicts with itself twice (same key twice in VALUES) raises an error: "ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time". Dedupe the input first.
  • Identity sequences are consumed even when the insert is skipped. Gaps are expected.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

"Every idempotent create is an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT." They model the idempotency key as a unique column, not a Redis check. They decide explicitly what "conflict" means for each endpoint (return the existing, update it, or reject with 409) and encode that in the DO clause. They avoid orIgnore() without a target on tables with several unique indexes, because it hides which rule fired.

Common mistakes

  • SELECT then INSERT. It is a race every time.
  • Catching the unique violation and retrying in a loop inside the same transaction. The transaction is already aborted; every subsequent statement fails with "current transaction is aborted".
  • Using ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET everything and silently overwriting a captured payment with initiated.

Interview questions

  1. Why is SELECT then INSERT unsafe, and what is the fix? Expected: race between the two; ON CONFLICT handles it inside the insert with speculative insertion.
  2. How does ON CONFLICT behave when the conflicting row is from an uncommitted transaction? Expected: waits for it, then either conflicts or retries.
  3. How do you tell whether the RETURNING row was inserted or updated? Expected: (xmax = 0) AS inserted.
  4. Why must the conflict target repeat a partial index's predicate?

Practical exercise

Implement POST /reviews so that submitting the same review twice (same user, same product) returns 200 with the existing review id on the second call, using a single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Load-test it with 50 concurrent identical requests. Acceptance criteria: exactly one row in reviews, zero 500 responses, and a Jest test that asserts both.

16.7 Normalization

16.7.1 Why normalize: update anomalies

Concept

Normalization is the process of organizing tables so that each fact is stored exactly once. A normal form (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) is a checklist of what "exactly once" means at increasing levels of strictness. The practical goal is to eliminate three kinds of anomaly:

  • Update anomaly: the same fact lives in many rows, so changing it means changing many rows, and missing one leaves the data contradictory.
  • Insert anomaly: you cannot record a fact because it is stuck inside a row that requires other facts you do not have yet.
  • Delete anomaly: deleting one fact accidentally deletes another that was stored in the same row.

Why does it exist?

Imagine the pre-normalization version of our orders data, the kind that comes out of an exported spreadsheet:

orders_flat
order_id | customer_email | customer_name | customer_city | product_sku | product_name | category | price   | qty
1001     | ravi@x.com     | Ravi Kumar    | Pune          | PHN-001     | Phone X      | Phones   | 49999   | 1
1001     | ravi@x.com     | Ravi Kumar    | Pune          | CBL-77      | USB-C Cable  | Cables   | 499     | 2
1002     | ravi@x.com     | Ravi Kumar    | Pune          | PHN-001     | Phone X      | Phones   | 47999   | 1
1003     | meera@y.com    | Meera Iyer    | Chennai       | CBL-77      | USB-C Cable  | Cables   | 499     | 3

Every anomaly is visible:

  • Ravi moves to Mumbai. Update anomaly: three rows must change. A bug updates two. Reports now show Ravi in two cities.
  • A new product is created but has not sold yet. Insert anomaly: there is nowhere to put it, because every row needs an order.
  • Order 1003 is cancelled and deleted. Delete anomaly: Meera's customer record disappears with it.
  • "Phone X" costs 49999 in one row and 47999 in another. Is that a price change, a discount, or a typo? The flat table cannot say.

Normalization is the systematic method for splitting this into tables where none of those can happen.

Mental model

Imagine a company where every employee keeps their own copy of the phone directory. When someone's number changes, HR emails everyone, and half of them do not update their copy. Normalization is putting one directory on the wall and having everyone refer to it by name. The cost is that looking up a number now takes a walk to the wall (a join). The benefit is that there is exactly one truth.

How it works: the normal forms in plain language

The forms build on each other. Each is defined in terms of functional dependencies: "A determines B" (written A -> B) means that whenever two rows have the same A, they have the same B. sku -> product_name because a SKU always has one name.

flowchart TB
    F["orders_flat: one wide row per line item"] --> N1["1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups, a key"]
    N1 --> N2["2NF: no column depends on only part of a composite key"]
    N2 --> N3["3NF: no column depends on another non-key column"]
    N3 --> B["BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key"]
    N1 -.->|"split: orders + order_lines"| N2
    N2 -.->|"split: products out of order_lines"| N3
    N3 -.->|"split: customers out of orders, categories out of products"| B

1NF — First normal form. Every column holds one atomic value, there are no repeating groups (no product_1, product_2, product_3 columns and no comma-separated lists in a cell), and every row is identifiable by a key. Our flat table already fails this if someone stored "PHN-001, CBL-77" in one cell. Fix: one row per order line, with a key of (order_id, product_sku).

A note on arrays and jsonb: strictly they violate 1NF. Pragmatically, tags text[] is fine when the elements are simple labels never referenced elsewhere (section 16.4.6). Purity is a tool, not a religion.

2NF — Second normal form. 1NF, plus: no non-key column depends on only part of a composite key. In orders_flat with key (order_id, product_sku), customer_email depends only on order_id (partial dependency), and product_name depends only on product_sku. Both must move out: customer_email to an orders table keyed by order_id, product_name to a products table keyed by sku. What remains in order_lines is only what depends on the whole key: qty and the price at the time of that order.

3NF — Third normal form. 2NF, plus: no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency). In orders, customer_name and customer_city depend on customer_email, not on order_id. order_id -> customer_email -> customer_city is transitive. Move customer columns to a users table. In products, category is a name that other products share and that could be renamed; sku -> category_id -> category_name is transitive, so categories becomes its own table.

The one-sentence memory aid: every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

BCNF — Boyce-Codd normal form. 3NF, plus: every determinant (left side of any dependency) is a candidate key. The difference from 3NF only shows up with overlapping candidate keys. Example in our domain: a table warehouse_stock (warehouse_id, product_sku, product_id, qty) where both sku and product_id identify a product. product_sku -> product_id holds, but product_sku is not a candidate key of this table (it needs warehouse_id too). 3NF allows this; BCNF does not. The fix is the same as always: keep exactly one product identifier in the child table, and let products own the sku <-> id mapping. In practice, if you use surrogate keys consistently and put each natural identifier in its owning table, you land in BCNF without thinking about it.

Higher forms (4NF, 5NF) concern multi-valued and join dependencies. They matter for tables like (product_id, supplier_id, region_id) where suppliers and regions are independent facts about a product. The practical rule: if two independent many-to-many facts are in one table, split them into two join tables.

Practical example: the normalized result

orders_flat becomes the reference schema: users (name, city via addresses), products (name, price, category_id), categories, orders (user_id, placed_at), order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price snapshot). Each fact once. Ravi's city change is one row. A product can exist before it sells. Cancelling an order does not delete Meera.

The one deliberate exception is order_items.unit_price and product_name. Those look like a 3NF violation (product_id -> name), but they are not: the dependency is (order_id, product_id) -> unit_price_at_that_time, which is a different fact from product_id -> current_price. An invoice is a historical record. This is the pattern for every "snapshot" column: it is normalized if it records a fact about the row itself (the price this customer was charged), and denormalized if it merely caches a fact owned elsewhere (the product's current price).

PostgreSQL example

-- Migrating a flat table into the normalized schema (idempotent, batched approach shown in Part 26 - Migrations)
INSERT INTO categories (name, slug)
SELECT DISTINCT category, lower(category) FROM orders_flat
ON CONFLICT (slug) DO NOTHING;

INSERT INTO products (sku, name, category_id, price)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (f.product_sku) f.product_sku, f.product_name, c.id, f.price
FROM orders_flat f JOIN categories c ON c.slug = lower(f.category)
ORDER BY f.product_sku, f.order_id DESC          -- latest price seen wins as "current"
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO NOTHING;

INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash, full_name)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (lower(customer_email)) customer_email, 'MIGRATED', customer_name
FROM orders_flat ORDER BY lower(customer_email), order_id DESC
ON CONFLICT (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL DO NOTHING;
-- orders and order_items follow the same pattern, joining back by email and sku.

Production scenario

A normalized schema at 10 million orders and 30 million order items handles "order detail page" in one query with three joins, roughly 1 to 3 ms with proper indexes. The joins are not the cost people fear: a nested loop over indexed foreign keys touches a handful of 8 KB pages. The cost of the flat alternative shows up differently: a product rename becomes a 30-million-row update, and the analytics team can never trust which of the four spellings of "Phone X" is current.

Failure scenario

A team stored customer_name directly on orders "for faster listing pages". A customer changed her name after marriage. Support updated users.full_name. Six months later, a legal request required all documents for that customer; half the orders showed the old name, half the new, and nobody could prove which was correct at which time. The fix was not "never store names on orders". It was to store it deliberately, as a snapshot with a clear name (recipient_name, meaning "the name on the shipping label"), and to derive the display name from users everywhere else.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Over-normalization: a phone_number_types table with three rows, joined into every user query. Reference data with fewer than ten stable values is often better as a CHECK constraint.
  • Under-normalization disguised as "performance": duplicated columns that then drift.
  • Historical facts mistaken for denormalization: snapshots on order_items, shipments.address_snapshot jsonb, and payments.amount are correct.
  • Normalizing the wrong axis: splitting users into users and user_profiles 1:1 for no reason adds a join to every request and no benefit unless the profile columns are huge or rarely read.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They normalize by default to 3NF, think about BCNF only when two natural keys overlap, and then denormalize deliberately, in named places, with a plan for keeping the copy consistent (next section). They separate "cached copy of a current fact" (dangerous) from "recorded historical fact" (correct). When asked "isn't a join slow?", they answer with a number from EXPLAIN ANALYZE, not an opinion.

Common mistakes

  • Comma-separated ids in a text column (category_ids = '3,7,12'). Unindexable, unjoinable, unconstrained.
  • Storing the current product price on order items without realizing it is the right thing, then "fixing" it to a join, and changing historical invoices when prices change.
  • Repeating groups: address_line_1, address_line_2, second_address_line_1....

Interview questions

  1. Explain 3NF in one sentence and give an example of a transitive dependency in an orders schema. Expected: every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, nothing but the key; order_id -> user_id -> user_city.
  2. Is order_items.unit_price a normalization violation? Expected: no; it records the price charged, a fact about the order item, not a cache of the product's price.
  3. What is an update anomaly, and which normal form removes it? Expected: same fact in many rows; 2NF/3NF splits it into the owning table.
  4. When would you stop at 3NF and not bother with BCNF? Expected: when there are no overlapping candidate keys, which is the common case with surrogate keys.

Practical exercise

Take the orders_flat table above, add 20 realistic rows including two price changes and a customer city change, and write the migration into the reference schema. Then write the query that reconstructs orders_flat from the normalized tables. Acceptance criteria: the reconstructed output matches the input except where the input was contradictory, and you can list each contradiction.

16.8 Denormalization

16.8.1 When and how to denormalize

Concept

Denormalization is storing a derived or duplicated value so that reads do not have to compute it. Examples: orders.total (derivable from order_items), products.review_count and products.avg_rating (derivable from reviews), a daily_revenue table (derivable from orders), or a materialized view of "top 100 products this week". It trades write complexity and consistency risk for read speed.

Why does it exist?

Some reads are too frequent or too heavy to compute on demand. A product listing page that shows average rating for 40 products would need to aggregate potentially millions of reviews per request. A dashboard of revenue per category per day over two years would scan every order. At 3,000 reads per second, computing from source is not an option; caching the answer somewhere is. The question is only where and how fresh.

Mental model

Imagine a shop that counts its cash drawer. The normalized way is to add up every receipt each time someone asks "how much is in the drawer". The denormalized way is a running total on a whiteboard, updated with every sale. The whiteboard is fast to read and wrong the moment someone forgets to update it, so the shop reconciles it against the receipts every night.

How it works: the four mechanisms

Mechanism Freshness Write cost Consistency guarantee Best for
Same-transaction update in application code Immediate One extra UPDATE per write Only as good as every write path remembering Totals owned by one service, few write paths
Database trigger Immediate Trigger executes on every write Strong: every path is covered, including scripts Counters, totals, updated_at, audit rows
Materialized view (REFRESH) Stale until refreshed Full recompute on refresh Snapshot-consistent at refresh time Reports, leaderboards, aggregates over millions of rows
Asynchronous read model (queue + worker) Seconds of lag Event publish + consumer write Eventual; needs reconciliation Cross-service views, search indexes, analytics

Each has a place. The senior approach is to pick the weakest mechanism that meets the freshness requirement, and to always have a reconciliation job that recomputes from source and alerts on drift.

PostgreSQL example

Cached order total, kept correct by a trigger:

-- orders.total is derived from order_items; keep it correct on every item change.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION recompute_order_totals() RETURNS trigger AS $$
DECLARE
  target_order uuid := coalesce(NEW.order_id, OLD.order_id);
BEGIN
  UPDATE orders o
     SET subtotal = s.subtotal,
         total    = s.subtotal - o.discount,
         updated_at = now()
    FROM (SELECT coalesce(sum(quantity * unit_price), 0) AS subtotal
            FROM order_items WHERE order_id = target_order) s
   WHERE o.id = target_order;
  RETURN NULL;   -- AFTER trigger: return value ignored
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER order_items_recompute_totals
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON order_items
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION recompute_order_totals();

Counter cache with a race-safe increment (never read-then-write):

-- products.review_count and avg_rating maintained incrementally
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN review_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
                     ADD COLUMN rating_sum   integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
-- avg_rating is computed at read time as rating_sum::numeric / nullif(review_count, 0)

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION reviews_counter_cache() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
    UPDATE products SET review_count = review_count + 1, rating_sum = rating_sum + NEW.rating WHERE id = NEW.product_id;
  ELSIF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN
    UPDATE products SET review_count = review_count - 1, rating_sum = rating_sum - OLD.rating WHERE id = OLD.product_id;
  ELSIF NEW.rating <> OLD.rating THEN
    UPDATE products SET rating_sum = rating_sum - OLD.rating + NEW.rating WHERE id = NEW.product_id;
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER reviews_counter_cache_trg
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF rating OR DELETE ON reviews
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION reviews_counter_cache();

review_count = review_count + 1 is atomic under row locking: two concurrent inserts both increment correctly, because the second UPDATE waits for the first to commit and then reads the new value. A read-then-write in application code (count = await get(); await set(count + 1)) loses one of them.

Materialized view for a heavy report:

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_category_revenue AS
SELECT date_trunc('day', o.placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS day,
       c.id   AS category_id,
       c.name AS category_name,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue,
       count(DISTINCT o.id)            AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN categories c   ON c.id = p.category_id
WHERE o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped', 'delivered')
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
WITH DATA;

-- A unique index is required for REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX daily_category_revenue_uidx ON daily_category_revenue (day, category_id);

-- Refresh without blocking readers (takes a while, but SELECTs keep working on the old data)
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_category_revenue;

Reconciliation job that catches drift regardless of mechanism:

-- Run nightly; alert if any rows return
SELECT o.id, o.total, s.computed
FROM orders o
JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT coalesce(sum(quantity * unit_price), 0) - o.discount AS computed
  FROM order_items WHERE order_id = o.id
) s ON true
WHERE o.total <> s.computed
LIMIT 100;

NestJS example

The asynchronous read-model variant, using an event emitter to update a denormalized "customer summary" outside the write transaction:

// orders/orders.service.ts (excerpt)
import { EventEmitter2 } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';

async markPaid(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
  await this.dataSource.transaction(async (m) => {
    await m.query(`UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', updated_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'pending'`, [orderId]);
    // Outbox row in the same transaction guarantees the event is not lost (see Part 29 - Messaging)
    await m.query(`INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, type, payload) VALUES ($1, 'order.paid', $2)`,
      [orderId, JSON.stringify({ orderId })]);
  });
}

// customers/customer-summary.listener.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OnEvent } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';

@Injectable()
export class CustomerSummaryListener {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  @OnEvent('order.paid')
  async onOrderPaid(evt: { orderId: string }): Promise<void> {
    // Idempotent: recompute from source for this one customer rather than incrementing blindly.
    await this.ds.query(`
      INSERT INTO customer_summary (user_id, lifetime_value, order_count, last_order_at)
      SELECT o.user_id, sum(o.total), count(*), max(o.placed_at)
      FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE id = $1) AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
      GROUP BY o.user_id
      ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO UPDATE
        SET lifetime_value = EXCLUDED.lifetime_value, order_count = EXCLUDED.order_count, last_order_at = EXCLUDED.last_order_at`,
      [evt.orderId]);
  }
}

Recomputing per customer rather than incrementing is a deliberate choice: an event delivered twice produces the same result, so duplicate delivery is harmless.

Production scenario

A product listing with 40 items per page at 2,000 requests per second: computing avg(rating) per product from a 20-million-row reviews table would be roughly 40 index scans per request, each touching tens of pages, roughly 15 to 40 ms and 80,000 index scans per second. With the counter cache it is zero extra work: the numbers are on the product row already. The trigger costs about 50 microseconds per review write, and reviews arrive at maybe 5 per second. This is the classic asymmetric trade: reads outnumber writes by 400 to 1, so moving work to the write side wins.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call got paged: "Order totals mismatch: 1,204 orders". The nightly reconciliation had found orders whose total did not equal the sum of their items. Root cause: a new "bulk edit line items" admin feature bypassed the service layer and updated order_items with a raw multi-row statement, while the total was maintained in application code, not a trigger. Nobody had broken a rule; there simply was a new write path. The fix was the AFTER trigger above, which covers every path. The reconciliation job was what turned a silent data corruption into a next-morning fix instead of a next-quarter audit finding.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Counter drift from failed transactions: a trigger runs inside the same transaction, so a rollback undoes both. Application-side increments outside the transaction drift.
  • Hot row: a counter on a single row (site_stats.total_orders) becomes a lock serialization point at high write rates. Shard it (N rows, sum on read) or move it to Redis with periodic flush.
  • REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW without CONCURRENTLY takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; readers block for the whole refresh.
  • REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and does a diff, which is slower than a plain refresh on large changes.
  • Async read models lag; the UI must tolerate "your order is not in your history yet" for a few seconds, or read-your-writes must be handled explicitly.
  • Denormalized copies across services (a product_name in the orders service) go stale when the owning service changes it; decide whether that is a snapshot (fine) or a cache (needs an event).
  • Triggers are invisible in application code; document them, test them, and include them in migrations under version control.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Before denormalizing, they ask: "What is the read rate, what is the write rate, what is the acceptable staleness, and how will I detect drift?" They prefer triggers for in-database derived values because they are the only mechanism that cannot be bypassed. They prefer materialized views for reports with minute-level staleness. They reach for async read models only when the data crosses a service boundary. Every denormalized value gets a reconciliation query and an alert. They can explain to a product manager: "The product rating you see is exact but updates within one transaction; the revenue dashboard is exact as of the last five-minute refresh."

Common mistakes

  • Read-modify-write counters in application code (count + 1 in TypeScript).
  • Denormalizing before measuring; adding orders.item_count for a page that gets 10 requests per day.
  • No reconciliation. Drift is discovered by finance.
  • Triggers with business logic sprawling into hundreds of lines; keep triggers to derived-value maintenance.

Interview questions

  1. How would you show average rating on a product listing at 2,000 RPS? Expected: counter cache (rating_sum, review_count) maintained by trigger; explain why increment is race-safe in SQL.
  2. Trigger vs application code for a cached total: which and why? Expected: trigger covers every write path; application code misses admin tools and scripts.
  3. How do you refresh a materialized view without blocking readers? Expected: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY with a unique index.
  4. How do you detect drift in a denormalized value? Expected: periodic recompute-from-source comparison with alerts.
  5. When does a counter become a hot-row problem, and what do you do? Expected: single row updated hundreds of times per second; shard the counter or move to Redis.

Practical exercise

Add products.review_count and products.rating_sum with the trigger above. Write a Jest integration test that inserts 200 reviews concurrently across 10 connections, then asserts the counters match SELECT count(*), sum(rating) FROM reviews. Then write the reconciliation query and schedule it with @nestjs/schedule. Acceptance criteria: test passes under concurrency; reconciliation query returns zero rows; deleting a review decrements correctly.

16.9 Designing schemas and modeling relationships

16.9.1 The schema design process for a new feature

Concept

Schema design is not "draw boxes for the nouns in the requirements". It is a sequence: requirements, entities, access patterns, schema, indexes, constraints, migration. The order matters. Access patterns before schema, because the queries you will run decide which columns live together. Constraints before migration, because adding them later means validating existing bad data.

Why does it exist?

Schemas designed from nouns alone produce tables that are correct and slow: every page needs six joins and there is no index for the one query that runs 2,000 times per second. Schemas designed from access patterns alone produce fast tables that cannot answer next quarter's question. The process balances both and, critically, makes the migration safe, because you thought about the 200-million-row table before writing ALTER TABLE.

How it works

Take a concrete feature: "Customers can save products to named wishlists and share a wishlist by link."

  1. Requirements. A user has many wishlists. A wishlist has a name, is private by default, can be shared by an unguessable link. A product can be in many wishlists. Show "in your wishlist" on the product page. Notify the user when a wishlisted product drops in price.
  2. Entities. wishlists (user, name, visibility, share token). wishlist_items (wishlist, product, added time). Nothing else; "price drop notification" reuses notifications.
  3. Access patterns, with expected rates:
    • List a user's wishlists: WHERE user_id = ? — 50 per second.
    • Show a wishlist with products: WHERE wishlist_id = ? join products — 200 per second.
    • Open a shared link: WHERE share_token = ? — 20 per second.
    • "Is product X in any of this user's wishlists?" on every product page — 2,000 per second. This is the one that drives the index design.
    • Price-drop job: "all users who wishlisted product X" — batch, once per price change.
  4. Schema. Because pattern four is hot, wishlist_items gets user_id denormalized onto it, so the check is a single index probe without a join through wishlists.
  5. Indexes. wishlists (user_id), wishlists (share_token) UNIQUE, wishlist_items (user_id, product_id) for the hot check, wishlist_items (product_id) for the price-drop job, and the PK (wishlist_id, product_id) for the detail page.
  6. Constraints. share_token unique and generated; UNIQUE (wishlist_id, product_id); wishlist_items.user_id must equal the wishlist's user_id (enforced by a composite FK, shown below); name length check.
  7. Migration. Two new tables, no rewrite of existing tables, no locks beyond the trivial. Ship behind a feature flag.
CREATE TABLE wishlists (
  id          uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  name        text        NOT NULL CHECK (length(name) BETWEEN 1 AND 80),
  is_public   boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  share_token text        NOT NULL UNIQUE DEFAULT encode(gen_random_bytes(16), 'hex'),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (id, user_id)    -- lets children reference the pair, enforcing same-owner
);
CREATE INDEX wishlists_user_id_idx ON wishlists (user_id);

CREATE TABLE wishlist_items (
  wishlist_id uuid        NOT NULL,
  user_id     uuid        NOT NULL,     -- denormalized for the hot "is in wishlist" check
  product_id  uuid        NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  added_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (wishlist_id, product_id),
  -- Composite FK: the (wishlist_id, user_id) pair must exist, so user_id can never disagree with the wishlist's owner
  FOREIGN KEY (wishlist_id, user_id) REFERENCES wishlists (id, user_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
CREATE INDEX wishlist_items_user_product_idx ON wishlist_items (user_id, product_id);
CREATE INDEX wishlist_items_product_id_idx ON wishlist_items (product_id);

The composite foreign key is the senior touch: the denormalized user_id cannot drift, because the database refuses any row whose (wishlist_id, user_id) pair does not exist in wishlists.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the access patterns down with rates before they write DDL. They design for the top two or three queries and accept that the rest will be "fine". They ask "what is the biggest table this touches and what lock will the migration take?" before approving. They check the FK-index rule, the NOT NULL rule, and the naming convention in every review. And they ask the product manager the question that changes the schema most often: "Will this ever need to be per-tenant, per-region, or per-currency?"

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through designing the schema for wishlists. Expected: entities, access patterns with rates, hot path drives the denormalized user_id and its index, composite FK to keep it honest.
  2. Why access patterns before schema? Expected: the queries decide co-location and indexes; nouns alone give correct-but-slow schemas.

16.9.2 One-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many

Concept

  • 1:1 — each row in A has at most one row in B and vice versa. Modeled by putting B's primary key as a foreign key to A (or by merging the tables). inventory.product_id is both the PK and an FK to products.
  • 1:N — one row in A has many rows in B. Modeled by an FK in B pointing at A. orders.user_id, order_items.order_id.
  • M:N — rows in A relate to many rows in B and vice versa. Modeled by a join table with two FKs and, usually, extra columns. order_items is the join table between orders and products, and it carries quantity and unit_price.

Why does it exist?

Relational databases do not have pointers or lists. Every relationship is expressed as "these two rows share a value". The three shapes are the only three ways two tables can share values with cardinality constraints, and each has an idiomatic physical layout.

How it works

1:1 (products and inventory): use the parent's key as the child's PK. This enforces "at most one" for free, and the join is a PK-to-PK nested loop, effectively free. Why a separate table at all? When the child's columns are updated far more often than the parent's (stock levels change per order; product names change per year), splitting keeps the hot updates from rewriting the wide product row and bloating its indexes. When the child is optional for most rows (a seller_profiles table for the 2 percent of users who sell), splitting avoids nulls in 98 percent of rows.

1:N (users and orders): FK on the many side, indexed, usually with a sort column for the common "latest N for this parent" query: orders (user_id, placed_at DESC).

M:N (orders and products via order_items): join table. Composite PK or surrogate plus unique pair. Index on the second FK column. Extra columns on the join table are normal and expected; a join table with no extra columns is a hint that an array might have been simpler, if the elements are simple.

TypeORM example

// 1:1 with shared primary key
@Entity({ name: 'inventory' })
export class Inventory {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid', { name: 'product_id' })
  productId!: string;

  @OneToOne(() => Product, (p) => p.inventory, { onDelete: 'CASCADE' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'product_id' })       // JoinColumn goes on the owning side (the one with the FK)
  product!: Product;

  @Column('integer', { name: 'quantity_on_hand', default: 0 })
  quantityOnHand!: number;
}

// 1:N
@Entity({ name: 'orders' })
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;

  @Column('uuid', { name: 'user_id' }) userId!: string;
  @ManyToOne(() => User, (u) => u.orders, { onDelete: 'RESTRICT' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'user_id' }) user!: User;

  @OneToMany(() => OrderItem, (i) => i.order, { cascade: ['insert'] })
  items!: OrderItem[];   // cascade insert: saving an order saves its items in one transaction
}

// M:N with extra columns: model the join table as its own entity. Do NOT use @ManyToMany,
// which cannot hold quantity/unit_price.
@Entity({ name: 'order_items' })
export class OrderItem {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn({ type: 'bigint' }) id!: string;
  @ManyToOne(() => Order, (o) => o.items, { onDelete: 'CASCADE' }) @JoinColumn({ name: 'order_id' }) order!: Order;
  @ManyToOne(() => Product, { onDelete: 'RESTRICT' }) @JoinColumn({ name: 'product_id' }) product!: Product;
  @Column('integer') quantity!: number;
  @Column('numeric', { precision: 12, scale: 2, name: 'unit_price' }) unitPrice!: string;
}

@ManyToMany with @JoinTable is fine for a pure join table with no attributes (products <-> tags). The moment the relationship has its own data, promote it to an entity.

Sequelize example

// 1:1
Product.hasOne(Inventory, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'inventory', onDelete: 'CASCADE' });
Inventory.belongsTo(Product, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'product' });

// 1:N
User.hasMany(Order, { foreignKey: 'userId', as: 'orders' });
Order.belongsTo(User, { foreignKey: 'userId', as: 'user' });

// M:N with extra columns: `through` a real model
Order.belongsToMany(Product, { through: OrderItem, foreignKey: 'orderId', otherKey: 'productId', as: 'products' });
Product.belongsToMany(Order, { through: OrderItem, foreignKey: 'productId', otherKey: 'orderId', as: 'orders' });
// Also declare the direct associations so you can query OrderItem rows with their columns:
Order.hasMany(OrderItem, { foreignKey: 'orderId', as: 'items' });
OrderItem.belongsTo(Product, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'product' });

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A "1:1" that is really "1:0..1" needs the child to be optional; a "1:1" that is mandatory both ways is a circular dependency at insert time and usually means one table.
  • 1:N where N is unbounded (a user with 5 million notifications): the (user_id, created_at) index and keyset pagination are mandatory; OneToMany eager loading is a memory bomb.
  • M:N join tables with a surrogate id but no UNIQUE (a, b): duplicates creep in.

Interview questions

  1. How do you model 1:1 in PostgreSQL, and when is a separate table worth it? Expected: child PK = parent FK; worth it for hot-update columns or optional/sparse data.
  2. Why not @ManyToMany for order items? Expected: the relationship has attributes; model the join table as an entity.

16.9.3 Self-referencing relationships: the category tree

Concept

A self-referencing (recursive) relationship is a table whose FK points at itself: categories.parent_id -> categories.id. It models trees and hierarchies: categories, org charts, comment threads, folder structures.

How it works: three models

Model Storage Get children Get all descendants Move a subtree Notes
Adjacency list (parent_id) One FK Index probe Recursive CTE One UPDATE Simplest; recursion cost grows with depth
Materialized path (path text like '1.4.17' or ltree) Path string per row Prefix match Prefix match (path <@ '1.4' with ltree) Rewrite paths of all descendants Fast reads; ltree extension has GiST index
Closure table (ancestor_id, descendant_id, depth) One row per ancestor-descendant pair depth = 1 All rows for ancestor Delete and reinsert pairs Fastest queries; most rows; most write logic

The reference schema uses adjacency list because category trees are small (hundreds to low thousands of rows), shallow (three to five levels), and rarely restructured. The recursive CTE for "all products under Electronics" is in Part 17. For a comment system with millions of threads and deep nesting, ltree is usually the better choice.

PostgreSQL example

-- Adjacency list (reference schema) plus a guard against self-parenting
-- CHECK (parent_id IS DISTINCT FROM id) is already there. Cycles deeper than one level need a trigger or the CYCLE clause on read.

-- ltree alternative
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS ltree;
ALTER TABLE categories ADD COLUMN path ltree;
CREATE INDEX categories_path_gist ON categories USING gist (path);
-- Electronics = '1', Phones = '1.4', Accessories = '1.4.17'
SELECT * FROM categories WHERE path <@ '1.4';         -- Phones and everything under it
SELECT * FROM categories WHERE path ~ '1.*{1}';       -- direct children of Electronics

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cycles: A.parent = B, B.parent = A. An adjacency list cannot forbid this with a CHECK. Use a BEFORE UPDATE trigger that walks up from the new parent, or accept it and use CYCLE detection in the reading CTE (Part 17).
  • Deleting a parent with RESTRICT (correct) means the application must re-parent or delete children first.
  • Depth limits: put a CHECK (nlevel(path) <= 6) on ltree paths, or a trigger on adjacency lists, so a bug cannot create a 10,000-level chain that makes every recursive query crawl.

Interview questions

  1. Adjacency list, materialized path or closure table for a product category tree? Expected: adjacency for small, shallow, stable trees; ltree when descendant queries dominate; closure for maximum read speed with heavy write logic.

16.9.4 Polymorphic associations: the trap and the alternatives

Concept

A polymorphic association is a column pair like (commentable_type, commentable_id) that points at "either a product or an order or a review". Rails popularized it; ORMs make it look easy. In a relational database it is a trap, because a foreign key cannot reference "one of several tables". You lose referential integrity, you cannot join without a CASE, and commentable_id must be a type wide enough for all targets (which breaks when one target uses uuid and another bigint).

The alternatives

  1. Separate tables per target: product_comments, order_comments. Full integrity, boring, best when the targets have different attributes anyway.
  2. Exclusive-arc FKs: one nullable FK per target with a CHECK that exactly one is set. Full integrity, one table, the planner can use each FK's index.
  3. Supertype table: an attachable parent table with a PK that both products and orders reference 1:1 (each product row has a corresponding attachable row); comments reference attachable.id. Full integrity, general, extra join.
-- Exclusive-arc: a notification is about exactly one of an order, a shipment or a payment
ALTER TABLE notifications
  ADD COLUMN order_id    uuid REFERENCES orders(id)    ON DELETE CASCADE,
  ADD COLUMN shipment_id uuid REFERENCES shipments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  ADD COLUMN payment_id  uuid REFERENCES payments(id)  ON DELETE CASCADE,
  ADD CONSTRAINT notifications_exactly_one_subject CHECK (
    (order_id IS NOT NULL)::int + (shipment_id IS NOT NULL)::int + (payment_id IS NOT NULL)::int = 1
  );
CREATE INDEX notifications_order_id_idx    ON notifications (order_id)    WHERE order_id IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX notifications_shipment_id_idx ON notifications (shipment_id) WHERE shipment_id IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX notifications_payment_id_idx  ON notifications (payment_id)  WHERE payment_id IS NOT NULL;

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

If the number of target types is small and known, exclusive arcs. If the targets share a lot of behavior (all "attachable things"), a supertype table. Never (type, id) pairs in a database that supports foreign keys. When an ORM offers polymorphic relations, they read the generated DDL first; TypeORM has no first-class polymorphic relations, and Sequelize's scoped associations (constraints: false) explicitly disable the FK, which is the problem itself.

Interview questions

  1. Why is (commentable_type, commentable_id) a problem in PostgreSQL? Expected: no FK possible, no integrity, mixed id types, awkward joins. Follow-up: give two alternatives.

16.9.5 Soft delete

Concept

Soft delete marks a row as deleted (deleted_at timestamptz) instead of removing it. The row stays for audit, undo, and referential integrity with historical data (orders keep pointing at "deleted" products).

Consequences you must handle

  1. Every query must filter deleted_at IS NULL. Miss one and deleted users appear in reports. ORMs help: TypeORM @DeleteDateColumn makes find filter automatically and softRemove set it; Sequelize paranoid: true does the same. Raw SQL and views do not, so a live_users view is a common safety net.
  2. Unique constraints break. A deleted user's email cannot be reused unless the unique index is partial: WHERE deleted_at IS NULL (the reference schema does this). UNIQUE (email, deleted_at) does not work because NULL values are distinct from each other.
  3. Foreign keys still hold. A soft-deleted product with ON DELETE RESTRICT is not deleted at all, so nothing cascades; that is usually what you want, but "delete a user" then means soft-deleting their addresses in application code.
  4. Indexes fill with dead-forever rows. Partial indexes WHERE deleted_at IS NULL on hot columns keep the live index small.
  5. Privacy law: "delete my account" often requires actual removal or anonymization. Soft delete plus a scheduled purge or an anonymize_user() procedure that scrubs PII while keeping the row.
-- Live view for raw SQL safety
CREATE VIEW live_users AS SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- Anonymize instead of delete, keeping orders intact (RESTRICT FK on orders.user_id)
UPDATE users
   SET email = 'deleted+' || id || '@example.invalid',
       full_name = 'Deleted User', phone = NULL,
       status = 'deleted', deleted_at = now()
 WHERE id = $1;

TypeORM example

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @DeleteDateColumn({ name: 'deleted_at', type: 'timestamptz', nullable: true })
  deletedAt?: Date | null;
}
// userRepo.softRemove(user) sets deleted_at; userRepo.find() adds WHERE deleted_at IS NULL automatically;
// userRepo.find({ withDeleted: true }) includes them; createQueryBuilder().withDeleted() likewise.

Sequelize example

User.init({ /* ... */ }, { sequelize, tableName: 'users', paranoid: true, deletedAt: 'deleted_at', underscored: true });
// User.destroy({ where }) sets deleted_at; User.findAll() excludes them; { paranoid: false } includes them.

Interview questions

  1. What breaks when you add soft delete to users? Expected: unique email, every raw query, FK cascade semantics, privacy deletion; fixes: partial unique index, view or ORM filter, explicit child handling, anonymization.

16.9.6 Audit columns and audit tables

Concept

Audit columns are created_at, updated_at, created_by, updated_by on every table. An audit table records every change as a row (who, when, what changed, old and new values).

created_at and updated_at are cheap and universally useful for debugging, incremental exports, and support. Keep updated_at correct with a trigger, not with application code, so bulk scripts cannot forget:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN NEW.updated_at = now(); RETURN NEW; END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

For a full audit trail, a generic trigger writing jsonb old/new rows into audit_log (table_name, row_id, op, old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb, actor, at) is the standard pattern. It costs one insert per write and a lot of storage; partition audit_log by month and drop old partitions (Part 22 — Partitioning). TypeORM's @CreateDateColumn, @UpdateDateColumn and @VersionColumn and Sequelize's timestamps: true set the columns from the application, which is fine as a convenience but not as the source of truth.

16.9.7 Multi-tenancy

Concept

Multi-tenancy is one deployment serving many customers (tenants) whose data must never mix. Three PostgreSQL strategies:

Strategy Isolation Cost per tenant Cross-tenant queries Migrations Noisy neighbor Best for
Shared tables with tenant_id column Logical only; a missing WHERE leaks data Near zero Trivial One migration Shared everything SaaS with thousands of small tenants
Schema per tenant Strong; separate tables Catalog bloat beyond a few thousand schemas Awkward (UNION across schemas) One migration per schema Shared instance Tens to hundreds of mid-size tenants
Database per tenant Strongest; separate everything Connection pools per DB; ops overhead Impossible in SQL One per database Isolated if separate instances Few large tenants, regulatory isolation

Row-level security for the shared-table model

The shared-table model's risk is one forgotten WHERE tenant_id = ?. Row-level security (RLS) makes the database add it for you. The policy is enforced on every statement regardless of which application code issued it.

ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tenant_id uuid NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX orders_tenant_id_placed_at_idx ON orders (tenant_id, placed_at DESC);

ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE orders FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;   -- applies to the table owner too

-- The app sets the tenant per transaction; the policy reads it.
CREATE POLICY orders_tenant_isolation ON orders
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)          -- rows visible for SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);   -- rows allowed for INSERT/UPDATE

-- The application role must not be a superuser or BYPASSRLS
CREATE ROLE app_user LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOBYPASSRLS;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON orders TO app_user;
// A NestJS interceptor or a repository wrapper sets the tenant for the transaction:
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (m) => {
  // SET LOCAL is scoped to this transaction; safe with connection pooling
  await m.query(`SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)`, [tenantId]);
  return m.query(`SELECT id, total FROM orders ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20`);  // RLS adds the tenant filter
});

Costs: every query gets an extra predicate (cheap with the tenant_id-leading index), EXPLAIN shows the filter, and the planner sometimes chooses worse plans because the policy expression is opaque. current_setting(..., true) returns NULL when unset, so with no tenant set the policy matches nothing, which is the safe failure.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Connection pooling with SET (not SET LOCAL): the tenant setting leaks to the next request that reuses the connection. Always SET LOCAL inside a transaction, or set_config(..., true).
  • Superuser or table owner without FORCE bypasses RLS. Migrations should run as a different role than the application.
  • Shared-table unique constraints must include tenant_id: UNIQUE (tenant_id, sku), not UNIQUE (sku).
  • Schema-per-tenant with 5,000 schemas: pg_dump, autovacuum and the catalog all slow down; connection pool per schema in PgBouncer becomes a problem.
  • A tenant that is 80 percent of the data in a shared table skews planner statistics for everyone else; consider partitioning by tenant or moving that tenant out.

Interview questions

  1. How do you guarantee tenant isolation in a shared-table model? Expected: RLS with a per-transaction setting, non-bypass role, SET LOCAL; tenant-leading indexes and tenant-including unique constraints.
  2. When would you move from shared tables to schema-per-tenant? Expected: regulatory isolation, per-tenant backup/restore, or a tenant so large it hurts others.

Practical exercise

Add tenant_id and RLS to orders and order_items. Write an integration test that opens two connections with different tenant settings and asserts that neither can read or update the other's rows, and that an unset tenant sees nothing. Acceptance criteria: tests pass; EXPLAIN shows the tenant index used; a SET (non-local) variant of the test demonstrates the leak.

16.10 Mapping the schema in TypeORM and Sequelize

16.10.1 TypeORM entities for the core schema

Concept

An ORM entity is a TypeScript class whose decorators describe a table. TypeORM reads the decorators to build SQL for find, save, and relations. The entity is a mapping, not a schema authority: the schema lives in migrations, and the entity must agree with it.

Why does it exist?

Mapping rows to typed objects removes boilerplate (rows.map(r => new Order(r))), gives you IDE completion, and lets the ORM manage simple relations. What it does not do is design your schema or optimize your queries. Treat the ORM as a convenience layer over SQL you already understand.

TypeORM example

The core entities, with the column types matching the DDL exactly:

// users/user.entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, OneToMany, CreateDateColumn, UpdateDateColumn, DeleteDateColumn, Index } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from '../orders/order.entity';
import { Address } from './address.entity';

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;

  @Column('text') email!: string;               // uniqueness enforced by the expression index in the migration
  @Column('text', { name: 'password_hash', select: false }) passwordHash!: string;  // never returned by default
  @Column('text', { name: 'full_name' }) fullName!: string;
  @Column('text', { nullable: true }) phone?: string | null;
  @Column('text', { default: 'active' }) status!: 'active' | 'suspended' | 'deleted';

  @CreateDateColumn({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz' }) createdAt!: Date;
  @UpdateDateColumn({ name: 'updated_at', type: 'timestamptz' }) updatedAt!: Date;
  @DeleteDateColumn({ name: 'deleted_at', type: 'timestamptz', nullable: true }) deletedAt?: Date | null;

  @OneToMany(() => Address, (a) => a.user) addresses!: Address[];
  @OneToMany(() => Order, (o) => o.user) orders!: Order[];
}
// products/product.entity.ts
@Entity({ name: 'products' })
export class Product {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column('text', { unique: true }) sku!: string;
  @Column('text') name!: string;
  @Column('text', { nullable: true }) description?: string | null;

  @Column('bigint', { name: 'category_id' }) categoryId!: string;
  @ManyToOne(() => Category, { onDelete: 'RESTRICT', nullable: false })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'category_id' }) category!: Category;

  @Column('numeric', { precision: 12, scale: 2 }) price!: string;   // string: exact decimal
  @Column('char', { length: 3, default: 'INR' }) currency!: string;
