  @Column('jsonb', { default: () => "'{}'::jsonb" }) attributes!: Record<string, unknown>;
  @Column('text', { array: true, default: () => "'{}'" }) tags!: string[];
  @Column('boolean', { name: 'is_active', default: true }) isActive!: boolean;

  @OneToOne(() => Inventory, (i) => i.product) inventory?: Inventory;
}
// orders/order.entity.ts
@Entity({ name: 'orders' })
@Index('orders_user_id_placed_at_idx', ['userId', 'placedAt'])
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column('bigint', { name: 'order_number', generated: 'identity', insert: false, update: false }) orderNumber!: string;

  @Column('uuid', { name: 'user_id' }) userId!: string;
  @ManyToOne(() => User, (u) => u.orders, { onDelete: 'RESTRICT', nullable: false })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'user_id' }) user!: User;

  @Column('text', { default: 'pending' }) status!: OrderStatus;
  @Column('uuid', { name: 'shipping_address_id', nullable: true }) shippingAddressId?: string | null;
  @Column('numeric', { precision: 12, scale: 2, default: 0 }) subtotal!: string;
  @Column('numeric', { precision: 12, scale: 2, default: 0 }) discount!: string;
  @Column('numeric', { precision: 12, scale: 2, default: 0 }) total!: string;
  @Column('timestamptz', { name: 'placed_at', default: () => 'now()' }) placedAt!: Date;
  @Column('timestamptz', { name: 'cancelled_at', nullable: true }) cancelledAt?: Date | null;

  @VersionColumn() version!: number;   // optimistic locking: UPDATE ... WHERE version = ? (Part 20)

  @OneToMany(() => OrderItem, (i) => i.order, { cascade: ['insert'] }) items!: OrderItem[];
  @OneToMany(() => Payment, (p) => p.order) payments!: Payment[];
}

The DataSource configuration that goes with it:

// database/data-source.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  entities: [__dirname + '/../**/*.entity.{ts,js}'],
  migrations: [__dirname + '/migrations/*.{ts,js}'],
  synchronize: false,                  // ALWAYS false outside a throwaway local DB
  migrationsRun: false,                // run migrations as a deploy step, not at app boot
  logging: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' ? ['query', 'error'] : ['error'],
  extra: { max: 20, statement_timeout: 10_000, options: '-c TimeZone=UTC' },
});

Pitfalls

  • synchronize: true in production. TypeORM diffs entities against the live schema and applies ALTER TABLE at boot, including DROP COLUMN for anything it does not recognize. A renamed property becomes a dropped column. There is no confirmation, no review, no rollback. It is fine for a local database you can recreate; it is never fine anywhere data matters. Use migrations (typeorm migration:generate to draft, then read and edit the SQL before committing).
  • Bidirectional relations and eager loading. @OneToMany(..., { eager: true }) on User.orders plus @ManyToOne(..., { eager: true }) on Order.user creates a loop that TypeORM refuses at runtime, or, when only one side is eager, silently loads thousands of rows on every findOne. Keep eager: false (the default) and load relations explicitly per query with relations: [...] or leftJoinAndSelect.
  • cascade: true on both sides. Saving an order with a loaded user that has loaded orders re-saves everything. Limit cascades to ['insert'] on true composition (order to items) and never on the many-to-one side.
  • Numeric and bigint arrive as strings. Declaring them as number compiles and then silently produces "1999.99" + 1 = "1999.991".
  • @Column({ type: 'enum' }) creates a PostgreSQL enum type per entity per column in migrations, with generated names like orders_status_enum. If you want CHECK constraints instead (section 16.4.7), declare the column as text and put the CHECK in the migration.
  • find() with no take on an unbounded relation. Always paginate.
  • Entity property renames. @Column({ name: 'placed_at' }) decouples the TypeScript name from the column name. Without it, renaming placedAt to createdAt changes the column name in the generated migration.
  • Two DataSources in tests and production drifting. Generate the test schema from the same migrations, never from synchronize.

16.10.2 Sequelize models for the core schema

// models/order.model.ts
import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize, InferAttributes, InferCreationAttributes, CreationOptional } from 'sequelize';

export class Order extends Model<InferAttributes<Order>, InferCreationAttributes<Order>> {
  declare id: CreationOptional<string>;
  declare orderNumber: CreationOptional<string>;
  declare userId: string;
  declare status: CreationOptional<'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled' | 'refunded'>;
  declare subtotal: CreationOptional<string>;
  declare discount: CreationOptional<string>;
  declare total: CreationOptional<string>;
  declare placedAt: CreationOptional<Date>;
  declare version: CreationOptional<number>;
}

export function initOrder(sequelize: Sequelize): void {
  Order.init(
    {
      id: { type: DataTypes.UUID, primaryKey: true, defaultValue: DataTypes.UUIDV4 },
      orderNumber: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, autoIncrement: true, unique: true, field: 'order_number' },
      userId: { type: DataTypes.UUID, allowNull: false, field: 'user_id' },
      status: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false, defaultValue: 'pending',
        validate: { isIn: [['pending','paid','shipped','delivered','cancelled','refunded']] } },  // app-level; DB CHECK is the real guard
      subtotal: { type: DataTypes.DECIMAL(12, 2), allowNull: false, defaultValue: 0 },
      discount: { type: DataTypes.DECIMAL(12, 2), allowNull: false, defaultValue: 0 },
      total: { type: DataTypes.DECIMAL(12, 2), allowNull: false, defaultValue: 0 },
      placedAt: { type: DataTypes.DATE, allowNull: false, defaultValue: DataTypes.NOW, field: 'placed_at' },
      version: { type: DataTypes.INTEGER, allowNull: false, defaultValue: 1 },
    },
    {
      sequelize, tableName: 'orders', underscored: true,
      createdAt: false, updatedAt: 'updated_at',   // placed_at plays the role of created_at
      version: true,                                // optimistic locking on the version column
      indexes: [{ fields: ['user_id', { name: 'placed_at', order: 'DESC' }] }],
    },
  );
}
// models/associations.ts
export function associate(): void {
  User.hasMany(Address, { foreignKey: 'userId', as: 'addresses', onDelete: 'CASCADE' });
  User.hasMany(Order, { foreignKey: 'userId', as: 'orders', onDelete: 'RESTRICT' });
  Order.belongsTo(User, { foreignKey: 'userId', as: 'user' });
  Order.hasMany(OrderItem, { foreignKey: 'orderId', as: 'items', onDelete: 'CASCADE' });
  Order.hasMany(Payment, { foreignKey: 'orderId', as: 'payments', onDelete: 'RESTRICT' });
  OrderItem.belongsTo(Product, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'product', onDelete: 'RESTRICT' });
  Product.hasOne(Inventory, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'inventory', onDelete: 'CASCADE' });
  Product.belongsTo(Category, { foreignKey: 'categoryId', as: 'category', onDelete: 'RESTRICT' });
  Category.hasMany(Category, { foreignKey: 'parentId', as: 'children' });
  Category.belongsTo(Category, { foreignKey: 'parentId', as: 'parent' });
}

Pitfalls

  • sequelize.sync({ alter: true }) is Sequelize's synchronize: true. Same danger, same rule: migrations only (sequelize-cli or Umzug), never sync outside local development.
  • DataTypes.DECIMAL returns strings; DataTypes.BIGINT returns strings. Same handling as TypeORM.
  • include with hasMany produces a joined result set that Sequelize deduplicates in memory; with limit it generates a subquery that is often slow, and with two hasMany includes it produces a Cartesian product (Part 17 covers row explosion). Use separate: true on hasMany includes to issue a second query instead.
  • paranoid: true (soft delete) adds deleted_at IS NULL to model queries but not to sequelize.query raw SQL.
  • Association aliases (as) must match in include, or you get "is not associated" at runtime, not compile time.
  • Validators (validate: { isIn }) run only through the model; bulkCreate skips them unless validate: true is passed. The database CHECK is the real guard.

16.10.3 Keeping entity, migration and database in agreement

The three artifacts must agree: the migration (source of truth for the schema), the entity/model (what the ORM believes), and the live database (what actually exists). Drift between any two causes "column does not exist" at 3 AM. The senior practices:

  1. Migrations are hand-reviewed SQL, committed, run in CI against a fresh database, then run as a deploy step before the new application version starts.
  2. A CI test boots the ORM against the migrated schema and asserts zero pending schema changes (typeorm schema:log prints nothing; for Sequelize, compare queryInterface.describeTable output against the model attributes).
  3. Application startup fails fast if the migrations table shows unapplied migrations, rather than silently running with a mismatched schema.

16.11 Edge cases & failure modes: data modeling

A consolidated list, each with the mechanism and the fix. Most of these have already appeared in context; this is the checklist form.

  • NULL in unique columns. UNIQUE (order_id, coupon_code) with nullable coupon_code allows unlimited null-coupon rows per order. Mechanism: nulls are distinct. Fix: NOT NULL with a sentinel, UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PG15+), or a partial index.
  • FK without index locks the parent delete. DELETE FROM users scans every child table without an FK index, holding ROW EXCLUSIVE on each. Fix: index every FK column; CI check for FKs without indexes.
  • Cascading deletes wipe data. categories -> products -> inventory, reviews chained CASCADE means deleting a category removes stock and reviews. Fix: RESTRICT by default; CASCADE only for true composition; review the cascade graph in every migration.
  • Enum ALTER TYPE and locking. ADD VALUE is fast but the new value is unusable in the same transaction; removing a value requires recreating the type and rewriting the column under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Fix: text plus CHECK for evolving sets.
  • jsonb growing unbounded. Appending to an array inside a document rewrites the whole document each time; dead tuples pile up; autovacuum falls behind. Fix: one row per event in a normal table; keep jsonb for bounded, read-whole documents.
  • Integer PK overflow at 2,147,483,647. Inserts fail; the fix is a full table rewrite. Fix: bigint from day one; monitor serial columns above 50 percent with a query against pg_sequences.
  • Timezone bugs. timestamp without zone stores wall-clock ambiguity; comparing timestamptz to a date literal depends on session zone; DST makes + interval '1 day' not equal to 24 hours. Fix: timestamptz everywhere, session zone UTC, explicit AT TIME ZONE in reports.
  • Money rounding. float drifts; parseFloat in JavaScript drifts; division without explicit rounding creates 1999.9982. Fix: numeric(12,2) or integer minor units, string handling in the app with a decimal library, round(..., 2) at every division.
  • Random UUID index bloat. v4 keys land on random pages; index size doubles, cache hit rate drops. Fix: UUIDv7 or bigint identity for high-volume tables.
  • Soft delete breaks uniqueness. A deleted user's email cannot be reused with a full unique index. Fix: partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.
  • Polymorphic (type, id) columns. No FK, orphans accumulate, joins require CASE. Fix: exclusive-arc FKs or a supertype table.
  • Hot counter row. UPDATE site_stats SET orders = orders + 1 at 500 per second serializes on one row lock. Fix: sharded counters, or Redis with periodic flush, or accept eventual counts from a materialized view.
  • synchronize: true or sync({ alter: true }) in production. A renamed property drops a column. Fix: migrations, reviewed and run as a deploy step.
  • Adding NOT NULL or a validated FK to a huge table. Full scan under a heavy lock during business hours. Fix: NOT VALID then VALIDATE; CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) then SET NOT NULL.
  • Denormalized copy without reconciliation. Totals drift through a new write path. Fix: triggers for in-DB derived values; nightly recompute-and-compare with alerting.
  • Unbounded 1:N without pagination. user.notifications eager-loads 3 million rows and the pod is OOMKilled. Fix: never eager-load collections; keyset pagination with (user_id, created_at) index.
  • Multi-tenant leak through pooled SET. A non-local SET app.tenant_id persists on the pooled connection into the next request. Fix: SET LOCAL or set_config(..., true) inside a transaction.
  • serial vs identity. serial creates a loosely owned sequence and allows silent explicit ids. Fix: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY.
  • Case-sensitive email uniqueness. Ravi@x.com and ravi@x.com become two accounts. Fix: unique index on lower(email) or citext.
  • CHECK with now(). Passes at insert, meaningless afterwards. Fix: enforce time-based validity in queries, not constraints.

Senior Checklist — Part 16

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain what PostgreSQL guarantees (durability, atomicity, isolation, constraints) that a file or in-memory store does not, and what COMMIT costs
  • I can predict the result of any expression involving NULL, including NOT IN, <>, COUNT(col) and UNIQUE
  • I choose uuid (v7) vs bigint identity per table with a reason, and never serial or integer for a PK
  • I store money as numeric(12,2) or integer minor units, never float, and handle it as strings or a decimal library in TypeScript
  • I use timestamptz, set the session zone to UTC, and can explain the DST and date-literal traps
  • I can say when jsonb and arrays are appropriate and when they are schema avoidance
  • I can compare enum, text + CHECK and lookup tables and pick one for a given column
  • I index every foreign key column and can write the catalog query that finds unindexed FKs
  • I choose ON DELETE actions deliberately, defaulting to RESTRICT
  • I can add a constraint to a large table without blocking writes (NOT VALID then VALIDATE)
  • I can express "one active X per Y" as a partial unique index and "no overlapping ranges" as an EXCLUDE constraint
  • I write idempotent creates as INSERT ... ON CONFLICT and know how xmax = 0 tells insert from update
  • I can normalize a flat table to 3NF and explain each anomaly it removes
  • I denormalize deliberately, choose trigger vs application vs async vs materialized view, and always add a reconciliation query
  • I design new features from access patterns with rates before writing DDL
  • I can model 1:1, 1:N, M:N with attributes, trees, and the alternatives to polymorphic associations
  • I know what soft delete breaks and how to fix uniqueness, queries and privacy deletion
  • I can implement row-level security for shared-table multi-tenancy without leaking through connection pools
  • I never run synchronize: true or sync({ alter: true }) outside a disposable local database

Part 16 — Key Takeaways

  • A database is a set of kept promises: durability, atomicity, isolation and constraints. A file or a Map keeps none of them, and rebuilding them yourself is rebuilding a database badly.
  • NULL means unknown. Every comparison with it is unknown. NOT IN with a null, <> on a nullable column, and COUNT(col) are where production bugs hide.
  • Types are constraints. bigint identity or UUIDv7 for keys, numeric for money, timestamptz for instants, text for strings, jsonb only for genuinely per-row-varying data.
  • PostgreSQL does not index foreign keys. You do. The parent delete that scans a 50-million-row child table under lock is the most common self-inflicted outage in schema design.
  • Constraints are the last line of defense against application bugs and races. Unique indexes serialize conflicting writes; partial unique indexes and EXCLUDE express real business rules; ON CONFLICT makes creates idempotent.
  • Normalize to 3NF by default so every fact lives once. Snapshots of historical facts (the price charged) are not denormalization; cached copies of current facts (the product's price) are.
  • Denormalize deliberately: trigger for in-database derived values, materialized view for reports, async read model across services. Every copy gets a reconciliation query.
  • Design from access patterns with rates. The hottest query decides which columns live together and which index is mandatory.
  • RESTRICT is the default delete action. CASCADE is a data-loss chain you must trace to the leaves.
  • Polymorphic (type, id) columns throw away referential integrity; use exclusive-arc FKs or a supertype table.
  • Soft delete changes uniqueness, every query and privacy deletion; plan the partial index, the view, and the anonymization procedure with it.
  • The ORM maps the schema; it does not own it. Migrations are the source of truth, reviewed as SQL, run as a deploy step. synchronize: true in production is a dropped column waiting to happen.

Part 17 — SQL Mastery for Backend Engineers

SQL is the one language every backend engineer writes that runs on someone else's execution engine, against data they cannot see, with a cost that scales with a table they do not control. Writing it well means knowing what the planner will do with it. This part teaches the SQL a senior engineer uses daily, on the e-commerce schema defined in Part 16 (section 16.3): users, addresses, categories, products, inventory, orders, order_items, payments, shipments, reviews, notifications. Every query here runs against that schema unchanged.

Query tuning in depth (indexes, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, statistics) is Part 19. Here we introduce enough plan reading to know whether a query is sane.

17.1 SELECT and WHERE: writing predicates the planner can use

17.1.1 Sargable predicates

Concept

A predicate is a condition in WHERE. A sargable predicate ("search-argument-able") is one the planner can turn into an index range: col = value, col > value, col BETWEEN a AND b, col IN (...), col LIKE 'prefix%', col IS NULL. A non-sargable predicate wraps the column in a function or expression, so the index on the raw column is useless: lower(email) = ... when the index is on email, placed_at::date = ..., price * 1.18 > 1000, LIKE '%cable%'.

Why does it exist?

A B-tree index is sorted by the column's value. The planner can find placed_at >= '2026-03-01' by descending the tree to that value and scanning right. It cannot find date(placed_at) = '2026-03-01' that way, because the tree is sorted by placed_at, not by date(placed_at). To satisfy the function form it must read every row, compute the function, and compare. The query is correct both ways; one costs 0.1 ms, the other 4 seconds on 10 million orders.

Mental model

Imagine a phone book sorted by surname. "Find everyone whose surname is Sharma" is a page flip (sargable). "Find everyone whose surname, spelled backwards, is Amrahs" requires reading every entry and reversing it (non-sargable), even though it is the same set of people.

How it works

  1. The planner looks at each predicate and asks: is the left side a bare indexed column (or an indexed expression that matches exactly), and is the operator one the index supports?
  2. If yes, it estimates how many rows the range covers using statistics, and considers an index scan.
  3. If no, the only options are a sequential scan with a filter, or an index scan on some other predicate followed by filtering.
  4. Rewriting the predicate so the column is bare (move the function to the constant side) restores option 2.
Non-sargable Sargable rewrite Notes
date(placed_at) = '2026-03-01' placed_at >= '2026-03-01' AND placed_at < '2026-03-02' Range on the raw column
lower(email) = 'x' Keep, but index lower(email) (expression index) The index must match the expression exactly
price * 1.18 > 1000 price > 1000 / 1.18 Move arithmetic to the constant
sku LIKE '%77' Not rewritable; use a trigram index (pg_trgm) or reversed column Suffix and infix search need a different index type
status <> 'cancelled' status IN ('pending','paid',...) Inequality rarely uses an index; enumerating does
coalesce(cancelled_at, '9999-01-01') > now() (cancelled_at IS NULL OR cancelled_at > now()) Splitting removes the function
id::text = '...' id = '...'::uuid Cast the parameter, not the column
extract(year FROM placed_at) = 2026 placed_at >= '2026-01-01' AND placed_at < '2027-01-01' Range

PostgreSQL example

-- Orders placed on a given day (IST). Non-sargable: index on placed_at is ignored.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total FROM orders
WHERE (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date = '2026-03-01';
-- Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..412876.00 rows=48000 width=24) (actual time=0.031..3812.114 rows=41932 loops=1)
--   Filter: (((placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'))::date = '2026-03-01'::date)
--   Rows Removed by Filter: 9958068
--   Buffers: shared hit=112000 read=180876
-- Execution Time: 3818.902 ms

-- Sargable: compute the day's boundaries as timestamptz constants.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total FROM orders
WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01 00:00+05:30' AND placed_at < '2026-03-02 00:00+05:30';
-- Index Scan using orders_placed_at_idx on orders  (cost=0.43..2310.55 rows=41800 width=24) (actual time=0.028..14.302 rows=41932 loops=1)
--   Index Cond: ((placed_at >= '2026-03-01 00:00:00+05:30') AND (placed_at < '2026-03-02 00:00:00+05:30'))
--   Buffers: shared hit=1418
-- Execution Time: 16.011 ms

The Rows Removed by Filter: 9958068 line is the tell: the database read ten million rows to return forty thousand.

LIKE:

-- Prefix: index-usable if the index has text_pattern_ops (or the DB uses C collation)
CREATE INDEX products_sku_prefix_idx ON products (sku text_pattern_ops);
SELECT id FROM products WHERE sku LIKE 'PHN-%';        -- Index Scan (Index Cond: sku ~>=~ 'PHN-' AND sku ~<~ 'PHN.')

-- Infix: needs a trigram GIN index
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm_idx ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%cable%';  -- Bitmap Index Scan on products_name_trgm_idx

TypeORM example

// Sargable range from a day in IST
const start = DateTime.fromISO(day, { zone: 'Asia/Kolkata' }).startOf('day');
const rows = await orderRepo
  .createQueryBuilder('o')
  .select(['o.id', 'o.total'])
  .where('o.placedAt >= :start AND o.placedAt < :end', { start: start.toJSDate(), end: start.plus({ days: 1 }).toJSDate() })
  .getMany();

// Repository find(): Between is inclusive on both ends; prefer explicit range for time
import { MoreThanOrEqual, LessThan, Like } from 'typeorm';
await orderRepo.find({ where: { placedAt: MoreThanOrEqual(start.toJSDate()) /* and */ } });
await productRepo.find({ where: { sku: Like('PHN-%') } });  // prefix LIKE

Sequelize example

import { Op } from 'sequelize';
const rows = await Order.findAll({
  attributes: ['id', 'total'],
  where: { placedAt: { [Op.gte]: start.toJSDate(), [Op.lt]: start.plus({ days: 1 }).toJSDate() } },
});
await Product.findAll({ where: { sku: { [Op.like]: 'PHN-%' } } });
await Product.findAll({ where: { name: { [Op.iLike]: '%cable%' } } }); // needs the trigram index to be fast

Edge cases & failure modes

  • WHERE id = $1 with $1 bound as text against a uuid or bigint column: node-postgres sends untyped parameters, and PostgreSQL infers the column's type, so this is usually fine. But WHERE id::text = $1 or WHERE id = $1::text forces a cast on the column side and kills the index. Section 17.21 covers implicit casts.
  • Parameterized LIKE: sku LIKE $1 where $1 = 'PHN-%' is planned generically after five executions and may lose the prefix optimization; sku LIKE 'PHN-' || '%' style concatenation in SQL with a plain parameter usually keeps it. Check the plan for prepared statements.
  • OR across different columns (email = $1 OR phone = $2) can use a BitmapOr of two indexes; OR mixing an indexed and unindexed column forces a sequential scan.
  • Functions marked STABLE or VOLATILE on the constant side (now()) are fine; the planner evaluates them once per query.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the predicate with the column bare, and if the business rule needs a function, they add the matching expression index or reshape the predicate into a range. They know the six lines of an EXPLAIN that matter (Seq Scan vs Index Scan, Filter vs Index Cond, Rows Removed by Filter) and look at them before shipping any query that runs more than once per second.

Common mistakes

  • WHERE DATE(created_at) = CURRENT_DATE. Universal, and always a sequential scan.
  • WHERE LOWER(email) = LOWER($1) without the expression index.
  • LIKE '%term%' on a B-tree index and wondering why it is slow.
  • SELECT * in a hot path: reads every column including TOASTed jsonb, breaks when a column is added, and prevents index-only scans. Name your columns.

Interview questions

  1. Why does WHERE date(placed_at) = '2026-03-01' not use the index on placed_at? Expected: the index is sorted by placed_at, not by date(placed_at); rewrite as a range or add an expression index. Follow-up: what about timezone?
  2. How do you make LIKE '%cable%' fast? Expected: pg_trgm GIN index.
  3. What does Rows Removed by Filter tell you?

Practical exercise

Write the "orders for a customer in a date range, most recent first" query three ways: with date() casts, with a range, and with an expression index. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a 5-million-row table. Acceptance criteria: you can point to the line in each plan that shows whether the index was used and explain the buffers difference.

17.2 JOINs

17.2.1 Join types

Concept

A join combines rows from two tables based on a condition. The types differ in what happens to rows that have no match:

  • INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides.
  • LEFT JOIN: all rows from the left, plus matching rows from the right; unmatched right columns are NULL.
  • RIGHT JOIN: the mirror. Rarely used; rewrite as LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped for readability.
  • FULL JOIN: all rows from both sides; unmatched columns NULL on either side.
  • CROSS JOIN: every row of the left with every row of the right (Cartesian product). Useful for generating grids (every product for every day).
  • LATERAL join: the right side is a subquery that can reference the left row, evaluated per left row. The SQL way to say "for each order, the latest payment".
flowchart LR
    subgraph InnerJoin
      A1["orders with a payment"] --- B1["payments with an order"]
    end
    subgraph LeftJoin
      A2["ALL orders"] --- B2["matching payments or NULL"]
    end
    subgraph FullJoin
      A3["ALL orders"] --- B3["ALL payments"]
      A3 -.-> N3["NULL where no match either side"]
    end
    subgraph CrossJoin
      A4["every order"] --- B4["every day in series"]
    end

Why does it exist?

Normalization put customers in users, their orders in orders, and the items in order_items. Any page that shows an order with the customer's name needs both tables. Joins are how the relational model reassembles what normalization separated, on demand, and only for the rows you asked for.

Mental model

Imagine two stacks of index cards: orders and payments, each order card labeled with an order id, each payment card labeled with the order id it paid. INNER JOIN pairs cards that share an id and discards the rest. LEFT JOIN keeps every order card, attaching a payment card where there is one and a blank card otherwise. FULL JOIN keeps every card from both stacks. CROSS JOIN pairs every order card with every payment card regardless of label.

How it works

The logical definition: CROSS JOIN, then filter by the ON condition, then (for outer joins) add back the unmatched rows with NULLs. The planner never actually does the Cartesian product; it picks one of three algorithms (next section) that produce the same result. What you must internalize is the difference between ON and WHERE for outer joins:

  • A condition in ON decides which right-side rows match. Unmatched left rows survive with NULLs.
  • A condition in WHERE filters the final result. WHERE p.status = 'captured' after a LEFT JOIN payments p discards every order with no payment (because NULL = 'captured' is unknown), silently turning the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

PostgreSQL example

-- INNER: orders that have at least one captured payment (duplicates if more than one; see 10.3)
SELECT o.id, o.total, p.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id AND p.status = 'captured';

-- LEFT: every order, with its captured payment if any. The status filter MUST be in ON.
SELECT o.id, o.total, p.amount
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id AND p.status = 'captured';

-- Same query with the filter in WHERE: silently becomes INNER
SELECT o.id, o.total, p.amount
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE p.status = 'captured';       -- drops unpaid orders

-- Orders with NO captured payment (anti-join via LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL; NOT EXISTS is clearer, see 10.5)
SELECT o.id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id AND p.status = 'captured'
WHERE p.id IS NULL;

-- FULL: reconcile our payments with the provider's settlement file loaded into a temp table
SELECT p.id AS our_id, s.provider_payment_id, p.amount AS ours, s.amount AS theirs
FROM payments p
FULL JOIN settlement_lines s ON s.provider_payment_id = p.provider_payment_id
WHERE p.id IS NULL OR s.provider_payment_id IS NULL OR p.amount <> s.amount;

-- CROSS: a calendar grid, every day x every category, for a report with zeros
SELECT d::date AS day, c.id AS category_id
FROM generate_series('2026-03-01'::date, '2026-03-31'::date, interval '1 day') d
CROSS JOIN categories c;

-- LATERAL: for each order, the latest payment attempt (top-1 per group)
SELECT o.id, o.total, lp.status AS latest_payment_status, lp.created_at
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT p.status, p.created_at
  FROM payments p
  WHERE p.order_id = o.id
  ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
  LIMIT 1
) lp ON true
WHERE o.user_id = $1
ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Uses payments_order_id_created_at_idx: one index probe per order, 20 probes total.

LATERAL deserves attention. It is the right tool whenever you need "the top N related rows per parent" in one query, and it is efficient because the inner subquery uses the parent's key as an index probe. Without LATERAL you would need a window function over all payments (fine for reports, wasteful for a 20-order page) or N+1 queries.

TypeORM example

// LEFT JOIN with the condition in ON
const orders = await orderRepo
  .createQueryBuilder('o')
  .leftJoinAndSelect('o.payments', 'p', 'p.status = :status', { status: 'captured' })
  .where('o.userId = :userId', { userId })
  .orderBy('o.placedAt', 'DESC')
  .take(20)
  .getMany();

// LATERAL is not expressible in QueryBuilder relations; use raw SQL:
const rows = await dataSource.query(
  `SELECT o.id, o.total, lp.status AS latest_payment_status
   FROM orders o
   LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT status FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1) lp ON true
   WHERE o.user_id = $1 ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC LIMIT 20`,
  [userId],
);

take(20) with a joined collection makes TypeORM run two queries (ids first, then the join) to keep the limit on orders rather than on joined rows. That is correct and worth knowing when you see two statements in the log.

Sequelize example

const orders = await Order.findAll({
  where: { userId },
  include: [{ model: Payment, as: 'payments', required: false, where: { status: 'captured' } }],
  order: [['placedAt', 'DESC']],
  limit: 20,
});
// required: false keeps the LEFT JOIN. required: true (the default when `where` is present) makes it INNER.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Filter in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN becomes INNER. Reviewers should look for this in every outer join.
  • LEFT JOIN on a 1:N relation multiplies the left rows. Summing o.total after joining order_items overcounts (section 17.3).
  • CROSS JOIN on two large tables is a row explosion: 10,000 x 10,000 = 100 million rows.
  • FULL JOIN with a WHERE on one side's column also loses rows; use IS NULL checks or coalesce.
  • USING (order_id) merges the join column into one output column and is convenient but breaks when the column is ambiguous elsewhere; ON is explicit.

Interview questions

  1. Where does a filter on the right table go in a LEFT JOIN, and why? Expected: in ON; in WHERE it removes unmatched left rows.
  2. When would you use LATERAL? Expected: top-N per parent, per-row subquery that uses the parent's key.
  3. How does TypeORM handle take() with a joined collection?

17.2.2 Join algorithms and join order

Concept

PostgreSQL has three physical join algorithms: nested loop, hash join, and merge join. The planner picks one per join based on estimated row counts, available indexes, sort order, and memory. Knowing which one you are looking at in a plan tells you immediately whether the query is going to scale.

flowchart TB
    Q["JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id"] --> P{"Planner estimates"}
    P -->|"few outer rows + index on inner"| NL["Nested Loop: for each outer row, index probe inner"]
    P -->|"large unsorted inputs, fits work_mem"| HJ["Hash Join: build hash of smaller input, probe with larger"]
    P -->|"both inputs sorted or sortable on join key"| MJ["Merge Join: walk both sorted inputs together"]
    NL --> C1["Cost grows with outer rows x probe cost"]
    HJ --> C2["Cost grows with both sizes, memory for hash"]
    MJ --> C3["Cost grows linearly, may need Sort nodes"]

How it works

Nested loop. For each row of the outer input, scan the inner input for matches. With an index on the inner join column, each "scan" is an index probe of a few pages. Cost is roughly outer_rows x probe_cost. This is the winner when the outer side is small (a page of 20 orders) and the inner side has an index (order_items (order_id)). It is the loser when the outer side is large and the inner side has no index, where it degrades to outer_rows x inner_rows page reads.

Hash join. Read the smaller input entirely, build an in-memory hash table on the join key, then stream the larger input and probe the hash. Cost is roughly linear in both sizes. Needs the hash table to fit in work_mem; if it does not, the join spills to disk in batches, which is still correct but several times slower. Winner for large joins with no useful index or when most rows on both sides will match (a report joining all orders to all users).

Merge join. Both inputs are sorted on the join key (either already, via an index scan, or with an explicit Sort node), then walked together like merging two sorted lists. Cost is linear once sorted. Winner when both sides come pre-sorted from indexes or when the outputs must be sorted anyway. Explicit sorts are expensive, so the planner uses merge join mostly when sort order is free.

The planner also chooses join order. For three tables, there are several orders and it evaluates most of them (up to join_collapse_limit, default 8 tables; beyond that it uses a genetic algorithm). The general shape it prefers: start from the most selective table (the one where WHERE leaves the fewest rows), nested-loop into indexed children, and hash-join when it has to combine large intermediate results.

PostgreSQL example

-- Small outer, indexed inner: nested loop
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, oi.product_id, oi.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.user_id = 'a1b2...' AND o.placed_at > now() - interval '30 days';
-- Nested Loop  (cost=0.99..312.44 rows=38 width=40) (actual time=0.041..0.412 rows=41 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan using orders_user_id_placed_at_idx on orders o  (rows=12 loops=1)
--         Index Cond: ((user_id = 'a1b2...') AND (placed_at > (now() - '30 days'::interval)))
--   ->  Index Scan using order_items_order_id_product_id_key on order_items oi  (rows=3 loops=12)
--         Index Cond: (order_id = o.id)
-- Execution Time: 0.480 ms
-- "loops=12": the inner index scan ran once per outer row. 12 probes, 41 rows. Ideal.

-- Large report: hash join
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT u.id, u.email, count(o.id), sum(o.total)
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.placed_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY u.id, u.email;
-- HashAggregate  (actual time=2210.114..2298.402 rows=412880 loops=1)
--   ->  Hash Join  (actual time=180.221..1710.330 rows=2104411 loops=1)
--         Hash Cond: (o.user_id = u.id)
--         ->  Index Scan using orders_placed_at_idx on orders o  (rows=2104411 loops=1)
--         ->  Hash  (actual time=178.902..178.903 rows=1200000 loops=1)
--               Buckets: 2097152  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 98304kB
--               ->  Seq Scan on users u  (rows=1200000 loops=1)
-- Execution Time: 2335.120 ms
-- "Batches: 1" means the hash fit in work_mem. "Batches: 8" would mean it spilled to disk.

-- Forcing the issue to see the alternative (never in production code; useful in tuning sessions)
SET enable_hashjoin = off;
-- Re-run: the planner now picks Merge Join with two Sort nodes, or Nested Loop with 2.1 million probes.
RESET enable_hashjoin;

Joining on unindexed columns

Joining order_items to orders without order_items (order_id) indexed forces the planner into a hash join even for "one order's items", because a nested loop would be a sequential scan of order_items per order. For a single order that is a 30-million-row scan for 3 rows. The rule from Part 16 applies with force: every join column that is a foreign key gets an index, and any non-FK column you regularly join on (a provider_payment_id reconciliation join) needs one too.

Also watch for type mismatches on join columns. Joining orders.id uuid to a text column holding UUID strings makes the planner cast one side, which disables the index on that side and often forces a hash join with a cast per row. Fix the schema.

Production scenario

An order-detail endpoint at 400 requests per second joins orders, order_items, products, and the latest payments row. With all FK indexes present, the plan is nested loops all the way down: 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 index probes, roughly 25 buffer hits, 0.5 ms. A reporting query for "revenue by product last quarter" joins 2 million order items to 50,000 products: a hash join with the small products side hashed, 1.8 seconds, run once a day from a replica. Same tables, different algorithms, both correct choices.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call got paged for database CPU at 100 percent. pg_stat_statements showed a query joining notifications to users with Nested Loop and loops=3400000. A new "resend failed notifications" job had been deployed. Its query filtered notifications.status = 'failed' (no index: the partial index only covered pending), so the planner estimated few rows (statistics said failures were rare) and chose a nested loop into users. In reality a provider outage had produced 3.4 million failures overnight. Each was a users probe: fine individually, catastrophic in aggregate, and the estimate was wrong because statistics were stale. The fixes: ANALYZE notifications, a partial index for status = 'failed', and batching the job by id ranges of 10,000. The senior lesson is that the join algorithm the planner chooses is only as good as its row estimates.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Nested loop with a huge outer side because of a bad estimate: loops= in the millions.
  • Hash join spilling: Batches > 1 in the plan; increase work_mem for that session or reduce the input.
  • Merge join adding a Sort of millions of rows: check whether an index could provide the order.
  • Join order forced by LEFT JOIN chains: outer joins restrict reordering, so a long chain of LEFT JOINs may be planned in the order written.
  • More than 8 tables: join_collapse_limit and from_collapse_limit cap the search; the genetic optimizer (geqo) takes over and may produce a poor plan. Consider CTEs to fix the shape.
  • Correlated data (all big orders come from one region) fools the planner's independence assumption; CREATE STATISTICS (Part 19) helps.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read the join node names first. Nested Loop with small loops and index scans underneath is a healthy OLTP plan. Hash Join with Batches: 1 is a healthy report plan. Nested Loop with loops=2000000 or Hash Join with Batches: 16 is a bug in either the index set, the statistics, or the query shape. They ask "what is the outer side, how many rows, and is the inner side indexed on the join key?" for every join in a hot path.

Common mistakes

  • Joining on a column with no index and blaming "joins are slow".
  • Joining columns of different types.
  • Writing a ten-table join and expecting the planner to find the best order.
  • Treating a hash join as an error. It is the right choice for large inputs.

Interview questions

  1. Describe the three join algorithms and when the planner picks each. Expected: nested loop for small outer plus indexed inner; hash join for large unsorted inputs; merge join for pre-sorted inputs.
  2. What does loops=12 under an inner index scan mean? Expected: the inner side executed 12 times, once per outer row.
  3. What does Batches: 8 in a Hash node mean, and what do you do about it? Expected: hash spilled to disk; raise work_mem or shrink the input.
  4. Why does joining uuid to text hurt? Expected: cast on one side disables its index and adds per-row cost.

Practical exercise

Run the order-detail join with and without the order_items (order_id) index on a 10-million-row order_items table, capture both plans, and compute the difference in buffers and time. Then write the "revenue by product" report and identify the hash build side. Acceptance criteria: for each plan you can name the join algorithm, the outer and inner sides, and the reason the planner chose it.

17.3 GROUP BY and HAVING

17.3.1 Grouping, HAVING, FILTER and grouping sets

Concept

GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same values in the listed columns into one row per group, and aggregate functions (count, sum, avg, min, max, and many more) compute a value per group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, the way WHERE filters rows before it. FILTER (WHERE ...) restricts which rows feed one aggregate without affecting the others. GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE compute several groupings in one pass, producing subtotals and grand totals.

Why does it exist?

Every dashboard, report and summary is a grouping: orders per day, revenue per category, reviews per rating. Without GROUP BY you would pull millions of rows into the application and aggregate in JavaScript, which is slower, uses memory, and moves the work to the least scalable tier. HAVING exists because you cannot filter on an aggregate in WHERE (the aggregate does not exist yet when WHERE runs). FILTER exists to avoid the older sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN ... END) idiom. Grouping sets exist so that "by category with subtotals per parent and a grand total" is one scan instead of three queries unioned together.

Mental model

Imagine sorting a box of receipts into piles by month. Each pile is a group. Writing the total on top of each pile is sum(). Throwing away piles under 1,000 rupees is HAVING. Counting only the receipts marked "refund" while still keeping the pile total is FILTER. Adding a grand total slip on top of all piles is ROLLUP.

How it works

  1. FROM and JOIN produce the input rows; WHERE filters them.
  2. Rows are grouped, either by sorting on the group columns (GroupAggregate, used when the input is already sorted or the output must be sorted) or by hashing (HashAggregate, used when the number of groups fits in work_mem).
  3. Aggregates accumulate per group. FILTER clauses are evaluated per row per aggregate.
  4. HAVING drops groups.
  5. SELECT computes the output columns. Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY, or be functionally dependent on a grouped primary key (PostgreSQL allows SELECT u.email when you GROUP BY u.id because id is the PK).
  6. ORDER BY, LIMIT apply last.

Order of evaluation, which explains every "column must appear in GROUP BY" and "aggregates not allowed in WHERE" error: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

PostgreSQL example

-- Orders and revenue per day for March, only days with at least 100 orders
SELECT date_trunc('day', placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS day,
       count(*)                                      AS orders,
       sum(total)                                    AS revenue,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled')  AS cancelled,
       sum(total) FILTER (WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')) AS realized_revenue,
       avg(total)                                    AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01 00:00+05:30' AND placed_at < '2026-04-01 00:00+05:30'
GROUP BY 1
HAVING count(*) >= 100
ORDER BY 1;
--     day     | orders |  revenue   | cancelled | realized_revenue | avg_order_value
-- 2026-03-01  |  41932 | 61240187.50|      1204 |    58119904.00   | 1460.46
-- ...

-- Review distribution per product with the PK-dependency rule
SELECT p.id, p.name,                        -- p.name allowed because p.id is the PK and grouped
       count(r.id)                          AS reviews,
       round(avg(r.rating), 2)              AS avg_rating,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.rating = 5) AS five_star
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id
HAVING count(r.id) >= 10
ORDER BY avg_rating DESC, reviews DESC
LIMIT 50;
-- Note count(r.id), not count(*): with LEFT JOIN, a product with no reviews yields one row with r.id NULL; count(*) would say 1.

-- ROLLUP: revenue by parent category and child category, with subtotals and a grand total
SELECT coalesce(parent.name, 'ALL')  AS parent_category,
       coalesce(child.name, 'ALL')   AS category,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o     ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
JOIN products p   ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN categories child  ON child.id = p.category_id
LEFT JOIN categories parent ON parent.id = child.parent_id
WHERE o.placed_at >= '2026-03-01' AND o.placed_at < '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY ROLLUP (parent.name, child.name)
ORDER BY parent.name NULLS LAST, child.name NULLS LAST;
-- parent_category | category    | revenue
-- Electronics     | Cables      |  2410500.00
-- Electronics     | Phones      | 48120000.00
-- Electronics     | ALL         | 50530500.00     <- subtotal
-- Home            | Kitchen     |  9100200.00
-- Home            | ALL         |  9100200.00
-- ALL             | ALL         | 59630700.00     <- grand total

-- GROUPING SETS: two independent breakdowns in one scan (by day, and by status)
SELECT date_trunc('day', placed_at)::date AS day, status, count(*)
FROM orders
WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01' AND placed_at < '2026-03-08'
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((day), (status))
ORDER BY day NULLS LAST, status NULLS LAST;
-- CUBE (a, b) is shorthand for all combinations: (a,b), (a), (b), ().
-- Use GROUPING(col) to tell a real NULL from a subtotal row: GROUPING(parent.name) = 1 means "subtotal over parents".

GROUPING() is worth remembering: coalesce(name, 'ALL') breaks if a real name is NULL. CASE WHEN GROUPING(parent.name) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE parent.name END does not.

The row-multiplication trap: aggregating after a join

This is the most common wrong number in production reports. Joining orders to order_items produces one row per item. sum(o.total) then counts each order's total once per item. An order with three items is tripled.

-- WRONG: revenue tripled for three-item orders
SELECT u.id, sum(o.total) AS lifetime_value
FROM users u
JOIN orders o      ON o.user_id = u.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id     -- multiplies o rows
GROUP BY u.id;

-- RIGHT (a): aggregate the child first, then join
SELECT u.id, sum(o.total) AS lifetime_value, sum(oi.items) AS items
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
JOIN (SELECT order_id, count(*) AS items FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY u.id;

-- RIGHT (b): do not join what you do not need
SELECT u.id, sum(o.total) FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.id;

-- RIGHT (c): count distinct parents when the join is unavoidable (slower; forces dedup)
SELECT u.id, count(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders FROM users u JOIN orders o ON ... JOIN order_items oi ON ... GROUP BY u.id;

The rule: aggregate each 1:N child to the parent's grain before joining it to anything else. Two hasMany includes in Sequelize or two leftJoinAndSelect collections in TypeORM produce exactly this multiplication (orders x items x payments), and the ORM deduplicates entities in memory, which hides the problem until you add count() or sum().

TypeORM example

const rows = await dataSource
  .getRepository(Order)
  .createQueryBuilder('o')
  .select("date_trunc('day', o.placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date", 'day')
  .addSelect('count(*)', 'orders')
  .addSelect('sum(o.total)', 'revenue')
  .addSelect("count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled')", 'cancelled')
  .where('o.placedAt >= :from AND o.placedAt < :to', { from, to })
  .groupBy('day')
  .having('count(*) >= :min', { min: 100 })
  .orderBy('day')
  .getRawMany<{ day: string; orders: string; revenue: string; cancelled: string }>();
// getRawMany, not getMany: aggregates do not map to entities. All numbers arrive as strings.

Sequelize example

import { fn, col, literal } from 'sequelize';
const rows = await Order.findAll({
  attributes: [
    [literal(`date_trunc('day', "placed_at" AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date`), 'day'],
    [fn('count', col('id')), 'orders'],
    [fn('sum', col('total')), 'revenue'],
    [literal(`count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled')`), 'cancelled'],
  ],
  where: { placedAt: { [Op.gte]: from, [Op.lt]: to } },
  group: ['day'],
  having: literal('count(*) >= 100'),
  order: [[literal('day'), 'ASC']],
  raw: true,
});

Production scenario

A "daily sales" dashboard query over 10 million orders with the placed_at range index: index scan of 1.3 million rows for the month, HashAggregate into 31 groups, about 400 ms. Acceptable once a minute, unacceptable per page view. Materialize it (Part 16, section 16.8) or aggregate incrementally into a daily_sales table from a trigger or job. The senior instinct: any GROUP BY over more than a few hundred thousand rows on a request path is a materialization candidate.

Failure scenario

Finance reported that the "lifetime value" column in the admin panel was 2.7 times the sum of actual invoices. The query joined orders to order_items and payments "to show item count and payment status" and summed o.total. Each order was counted items x payments times. The numbers had been wrong for four months; nobody noticed because they were consistently wrong. The fix was pre-aggregating items and taking the latest payment via LATERAL. The senior lesson: any aggregate after a join must be defended with a comment saying why the join does not multiply, or restructured so it cannot.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • count(*) vs count(col) after LEFT JOIN: a parent with no children counts as 1 with count(*) and 0 with count(child.id).
  • avg() of an integer column returns numeric; avg() on numeric returns numeric with many digits; round for display.
  • sum() of an empty group is NULL; wrap with coalesce(sum(x), 0) when the report needs zeros.
  • HashAggregate with millions of groups spills to disk when work_mem is exceeded (PG13+ spills gracefully; earlier versions could OOM). Watch Disk Usage in the plan.
  • GROUP BY on an expression must repeat the expression exactly or use its alias (PostgreSQL allows the output alias and positional GROUP BY 1).
  • Grouping by jsonb or text keys is slower than by integers; group by ids and join names in afterwards.
  • DISTINCT inside aggregates (count(DISTINCT user_id)) forces a sort per group and can be 5 to 10 times slower than a plain count; for approximate counts at scale, hyperloglog extensions or pre-aggregation.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They check the grain of every table in the FROM clause and make sure the aggregate runs at the grain of the thing being summed. They write FILTER instead of CASE for readability. They reach for ROLLUP when the UI needs subtotals, instead of three round trips. They know that a GROUP BY on a request path over a large range is a signal to materialize. And they keep count(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) in their toolkit as the cheapest way to produce five metrics in one scan.

Common mistakes

  • Filtering aggregates in WHERE (does not parse) or filtering rows in HAVING (parses, but scans everything before filtering; put row conditions in WHERE).
  • SELECT o.status, count(*) ... GROUP BY o.user_id: error, or silently wrong if the column is functionally dependent in a way you did not intend.
  • Summing after joining 1:N children.
  • count(DISTINCT ...) everywhere, because it "feels safer". It hides join multiplication and costs a sort.

Interview questions

  1. Why does WHERE count(*) > 5 fail, and what is the fix? Expected: aggregates do not exist when WHERE runs; use HAVING.
  2. A report sums orders.total joined to order_items and is too high. Why? Expected: row multiplication; pre-aggregate the child or drop the join.
  3. What does FILTER (WHERE ...) do and what did people write before it? Expected: per-aggregate row filter; sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE 0 END).
  4. What is the difference between count(*) and count(r.id) after a LEFT JOIN?
  5. What does ROLLUP (a, b) produce? Expected: groups by (a,b), (a), and (); subtotals and grand total.

Practical exercise

Build the "revenue by parent category with subtotals" query with ROLLUP, then produce the same output with three UNION ALL queries, compare plans and timings on 5 million order items. Then introduce a deliberate join to payments and show the multiplied numbers, then fix it with LATERAL. Acceptance criteria: identical output between ROLLUP and UNION ALL, and a written explanation of the multiplication factor you observed.

17.4 ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET and pagination

17.4.1 Sorting and the cost of deep offsets

Concept

ORDER BY sorts the result. LIMIT n returns the first n rows. OFFSET m skips the first m rows. Together they are the naive pagination pattern: page 500 of 20 rows is LIMIT 20 OFFSET 9980. The problem is that OFFSET does not skip; it reads and discards. Page 500 reads 10,000 rows to return 20. Page 50,000 reads a million.

Keyset pagination (also called cursor or seek pagination) replaces OFFSET with a WHERE that starts after the last row of the previous page: WHERE (placed_at, id) < (:last_placed_at, :last_id) ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. It reads exactly 20 rows regardless of page depth, provided an index exists on the sort columns.

Why does it exist?

Sorting is expensive: O(n log n) in memory when the input fits work_mem, and an external merge sort on disk when it does not. An index on the sort columns is already sorted, so an index scan can produce ordered rows without a Sort node at all, and LIMIT stops the scan after n rows. That combination (index-provided order plus early termination) is the difference between 0.2 ms and 2 seconds. OFFSET breaks early termination: the scan must produce OFFSET + LIMIT rows before stopping. Keyset pagination restores it.

Mental model

Imagine a bookshelf sorted by date. "Give me the 20 newest" is taking books off one end. "Give me books 9,981 to 10,000" means counting 9,980 books first, every time. "Give me the next 20 after the one dated March 3rd, id 1234" is opening the shelf at that point (index seek) and taking 20.

How it works

  1. The planner checks whether an index matches the ORDER BY columns and direction (an index on (user_id, placed_at DESC) matches WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY placed_at DESC, and also ORDER BY placed_at ASC by scanning backward).
  2. If yes, an Index Scan (or Index Scan Backward) produces rows in order, and Limit stops it after OFFSET + LIMIT rows.
  3. If no, all matching rows are collected and a Sort node sorts them. For LIMIT, PostgreSQL uses a top-N heapsort that keeps only OFFSET + LIMIT rows in memory, which is faster than a full sort but still reads every input row.
  4. If the sort exceeds work_mem (default 4 MB), it becomes an external sort using temp files; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Sort Method: external merge Disk: 84512kB.
  5. OFFSET is applied by the Limit node discarding rows.

PostgreSQL example

-- Order history page 1: index-ordered, early termination
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, order_number, status, total, placed_at
FROM orders WHERE user_id = 'a1b2...'
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Limit  (actual time=0.031..0.058 rows=20 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan using orders_user_id_placed_at_idx on orders  (actual time=0.029..0.052 rows=20 loops=1)
--         Index Cond: (user_id = 'a1b2...')
--   Buffers: shared hit=6
-- Execution Time: 0.081 ms

-- Admin "all orders" page 5,000 with OFFSET: reads 100,020 rows
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, total, placed_at FROM orders
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
-- Limit  (actual time=212.884..212.905 rows=20 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan Backward using orders_placed_at_idx on orders  (actual time=0.026..201.114 rows=100020 loops=1)
--   Buffers: shared hit=98211
-- Execution Time: 212.930 ms
-- 100,020 rows visited, 98,211 buffers, to return 20 rows. Page 50,000 would be 10x worse.

-- Keyset: constant cost at any depth. Client sends the last row's (placed_at, id).
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, total, placed_at FROM orders
WHERE (placed_at, id) < ('2026-02-11 09:14:02.118+05:30', '9f1c...')
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Limit  (actual time=0.040..0.071 rows=20 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan Backward using orders_placed_at_id_idx on orders  (actual time=0.038..0.066 rows=20 loops=1)
--         Index Cond: (ROW(placed_at, id) < ROW('2026-02-11 09:14:02.118+05:30', '9f1c...'))
--   Buffers: shared hit=7
-- Execution Time: 0.094 ms
-- Requires: CREATE INDEX orders_placed_at_id_idx ON orders (placed_at, id);
-- The row-value comparison (a, b) < (x, y) is the correct "strictly after this row" predicate and is index-usable.

-- A sort that does not fit work_mem
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 100;
-- Limit
--   ->  Sort  (actual time=1890.221..1890.240 rows=100 loops=1)
--         Sort Key: total DESC
--         Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 33kB      <- LIMIT keeps only 100 rows in memory
--         ->  Index Scan using orders_placed_at_idx  (rows=2104411)
-- Without LIMIT: Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 61440kB  (spilled; consider SET work_mem = '256MB' for this session)

The tie-breaker column (id) in ORDER BY is not optional. Two orders in the same microsecond have the same placed_at; without a unique tiebreaker, the order between them is undefined, and keyset pagination can skip or repeat rows. Every ORDER BY used for pagination ends in a unique column.

NestJS example

// orders/dto/list-orders.dto.ts
import { IsOptional, IsString, IsInt, Min, Max } from 'class-validator';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';

export class ListOrdersDto {
  @IsOptional() @IsString() cursor?: string;         // opaque base64 of {placedAt, id}
  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(100) limit = 20;
}

// orders/orders.service.ts (excerpt)
interface OrderRow { id: string; status: string; total: string; placed_at: Date }

async listForUser(userId: string, dto: ListOrdersDto): Promise<{ items: OrderRow[]; nextCursor: string | null }> {
  const cursor = dto.cursor ? decodeCursor(dto.cursor) : null;   // { placedAt: string; id: string }
  const rows = await this.ds.query<OrderRow[]>(
    `SELECT id, status, total, placed_at
       FROM orders
      WHERE user_id = $1
        AND ($2::timestamptz IS NULL OR (placed_at, id) < ($2::timestamptz, $3::uuid))
      ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
      LIMIT $4`,
    [userId, cursor?.placedAt ?? null, cursor?.id ?? null, dto.limit + 1],   // fetch one extra to know if there is a next page
  );
  const hasMore = rows.length > dto.limit;
  const items = hasMore ? rows.slice(0, dto.limit) : rows;
  const last = items[items.length - 1];
  return { items, nextCursor: hasMore && last ? encodeCursor({ placedAt: last.placed_at.toISOString(), id: last.id }) : null };
}

Fetching limit + 1 rows is the standard trick to know whether a next page exists without a separate count(*). The cursor is opaque to the client so you can change its contents later.

TypeORM example

const qb = orderRepo.createQueryBuilder('o')
  .where('o.userId = :userId', { userId })
  .orderBy('o.placedAt', 'DESC').addOrderBy('o.id', 'DESC')
  .take(limit + 1);
if (cursor) qb.andWhere('(o.placedAt, o.id) < (:placedAt, :id)', { placedAt: cursor.placedAt, id: cursor.id });
const rows = await qb.getMany();

take()/skip() are TypeORM's LIMIT/OFFSET; when relations are joined, TypeORM turns them into a two-query pattern (ids first). For keyset pagination with joined collections, fetch the page of parent ids first, then load children WHERE order_id = ANY($1).

Sequelize example

const rows = await Order.findAll({
  where: {
    userId,
    ...(cursor ? { [Op.and]: [literal(`("placed_at", "id") < (:placedAt, :id)`)] } : {}),
  },
  order: [['placedAt', 'DESC'], ['id', 'DESC']],
  limit: limit + 1,
  replacements: cursor ? { placedAt: cursor.placedAt, id: cursor.id } : undefined,
});

Production scenario

A marketplace admin panel offered "jump to page N" over 40 million orders. Page 1 took 2 ms; page 200,000 (which a CSV-exporting script actually requested, iterating page by page) took 6 seconds and read 4 million rows per request. The script's total cost was quadratic: it read 40 million x 20,000 / 2 rows over its run and saturated the replica's I/O for two hours. Switching the script to keyset pagination made the whole export read each row once: 40 million rows in eleven minutes. The admin UI kept OFFSET for the first 100 pages (where it is fine) and switched to "next/previous" cursors beyond that.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • LIMIT without ORDER BY returns arbitrary rows, different between runs, and different after a VACUUM or plan change. Never paginate without a total order.
  • ORDER BY without a unique tiebreaker makes pagination skip or duplicate rows at page boundaries.
  • Keyset with a nullable sort column: NULL comparisons break the predicate. Use coalesce in both the index expression and the query, or exclude nulls.
  • Keyset cannot jump to page N; it only moves forward and backward. Offer "jump" only for shallow pages.
  • Deleted or inserted rows between pages: keyset handles them gracefully (no skips, no duplicates); OFFSET shifts the window and repeats or skips.
  • ORDER BY random() sorts the whole table. For "a random product", use TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1) or a random id range probe.
  • ORDER BY on a computed column or a joined column may prevent index use; sort on the driving table's indexed column.
  • work_mem is per sort operation per session; raising it globally with 200 connections and several sorts per query can exhaust RAM. Raise it per session for known heavy reports.
  • Index direction: (placed_at DESC, id DESC) and (placed_at ASC, id ASC) are the same index scanned in opposite directions; (placed_at DESC, id ASC) is a different index.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Every list endpoint gets a total order ending in a unique column, an index that provides that order under the endpoint's filter, and keyset pagination by default. OFFSET is allowed for small bounded pages (an admin table capped at 100 pages) and never for exports or infinite scroll. They check the plan for a Sort node on a hot path and treat it as a missing index. They explain to the product manager that "page 4,000 of 20" is not a feature anyone uses and "next page" is.

Common mistakes

  • LIMIT 20 OFFSET :page * 20 for infinite scroll.
  • ORDER BY placed_at without id.
  • Sorting on a column from a joined table when the driving table's index could have provided the order.
  • Running count(*) for total pages on every request over a million-row filter.

Interview questions

  1. Why is OFFSET 1000000 slow, and what replaces it? Expected: reads and discards a million rows; keyset pagination with a composite index and row-value comparison.
  2. Why must a pagination ORDER BY end in a unique column?
  3. How does LIMIT change the sort algorithm? Expected: top-N heapsort keeping only OFFSET + LIMIT rows.
  4. What is work_mem and why is raising it globally risky?
  5. What does LIMIT without ORDER BY return?

Practical exercise

Implement GET /orders?cursor=&limit= with keyset pagination on (placed_at, id), and a comparison endpoint using OFFSET. Seed 5 million orders. Measure both at page 1, page 1,000 and page 100,000. Then delete 50 rows in the middle of the range while paging through both and record which one skips or repeats. Acceptance criteria: plans captured for both, keyset shows constant buffers at any depth, and the deletion test documents the OFFSET anomaly.

17.5 EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN: semi-joins and anti-joins

Concept

Three ways to ask "orders that have a captured payment":

  • JOIN payments p ON ... AND p.status = 'captured': returns one row per match. Two captured payments (impossible with our partial unique index, but possible on other tables) would duplicate the order.
  • WHERE o.id IN (SELECT order_id FROM payments WHERE status = 'captured'): returns each order at most once. A semi-join.
  • WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id AND p.status = 'captured'): same result as IN, a semi-join, and the form that handles NULL correctly and reads naturally for correlated conditions.

The negatives: NOT IN (subquery) and NOT EXISTS (...) both ask "orders with no captured payment", an anti-join. They differ in one crucial way: NOT IN returns nothing at all if the subquery produces even one NULL.

Why does it exist?

A join is for combining columns from two tables. When you only need to check whether a related row exists, joining is the wrong tool: it multiplies rows and forces you to DISTINCT them back. EXISTS and IN express the intent "filter by existence" and let the planner use semi-join and anti-join strategies, which stop scanning the inner side as soon as one match is found.

Mental model

Imagine checking which customers on a list have ever placed an order. Joining is stapling every one of their orders to their name, then removing the duplicates. EXISTS is looking in the orders file, finding the first order with their name, and ticking the box. The tick is all you wanted.

How it works

  1. PostgreSQL rewrites IN (subquery) and EXISTS (subquery) into a Semi Join node when the subquery is uncorrelated or simply correlated. NOT EXISTS becomes an Anti Join. Both use the same physical algorithms (nested loop, hash, merge) but stop probing after the first match.
  2. NOT IN (subquery) cannot be turned into an anti-join if the subquery column is nullable, because the semantics differ: x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is UNKNOWN for every x, never TRUE. The planner uses a hashed subplan with special null handling and the result is an empty set the moment a NULL appears.
  3. IN (list of constants) with many values is rewritten to = ANY(ARRAY[...]) and can use an index; a very long list (thousands) is better passed as an array parameter.
  4. A correlated EXISTS with an index on the inner side's correlation column is a nested loop semi-join: one index probe per outer row, stopping at the first hit.

PostgreSQL example

-- Semi-join: customers who have placed at least one paid order, no duplicates
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered'));
-- Hash Semi Join  (actual rows=412880)  or  Nested Loop Semi Join with an index probe per user

-- Equivalent with IN
SELECT u.id, u.email FROM users u
WHERE u.id IN (SELECT o.user_id FROM orders o WHERE o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered'));

-- Anti-join, safe: users with no orders at all
SELECT u.id, u.email FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
-- Hash Anti Join

-- The NOT IN bug: orders.shipping_address_id is nullable.
-- "Addresses that are not used as a shipping address on any order":
SELECT a.id FROM addresses a
WHERE a.id NOT IN (SELECT o.shipping_address_id FROM orders o);
-- Returns ZERO rows as soon as one order has shipping_address_id = NULL. Not an error, just wrong.

-- Safe versions:
SELECT a.id FROM addresses a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.shipping_address_id = a.id);

SELECT a.id FROM addresses a
WHERE a.id NOT IN (SELECT o.shipping_address_id FROM orders o WHERE o.shipping_address_id IS NOT NULL);

-- EXISTS with a LIMIT inside is redundant; EXISTS already stops at the first row.
-- JOIN + DISTINCT: correct but does more work
SELECT DISTINCT u.id, u.email FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;  -- Hash Join then HashAggregate over 2M rows

Decision table:

Need Use Why
Columns from the related table JOIN Only joins return the other table's columns
Existence check, related table 1:N EXISTS No duplication; stops at first match; null-safe
Existence check against a small constant list IN (...) / = ANY($1) Index-usable; simplest to read
Non-existence NOT EXISTS Null-safe anti-join; NOT IN is a trap with nullable subquery columns
Existence with a condition on the related row EXISTS (... WHERE ...) Condition stays inside; nothing leaks into the outer filter

TypeORM example

// EXISTS via a subquery in QueryBuilder
const users = await userRepo.createQueryBuilder('u')
  .where((qb) => {
    const sub = qb.subQuery().select('1').from(Order, 'o')
      .where('o.user_id = u.id').andWhere("o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')").getQuery();
    return `EXISTS ${sub}`;
  })
  .getMany();

// NOT EXISTS
const idle = await userRepo.createQueryBuilder('u')
  .where((qb) => `NOT EXISTS ${qb.subQuery().select('1').from(Order, 'o').where('o.user_id = u.id').getQuery()}`)
  .getMany();

// IN with an array parameter (becomes = ANY)
import { In } from 'typeorm';
const some = await productRepo.find({ where: { id: In(ids) } });

Sequelize example

const buyers = await User.findAll({
  where: literal(`EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = "User"."id" AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered'))`),
});
// Or an include with required: true, which is an INNER JOIN and will duplicate unless you add distinct/attributes: []
const buyers2 = await User.findAll({
  include: [{ model: Order, as: 'orders', required: true, attributes: [], where: { status: ['paid','shipped','delivered'] } }],
  // Sequelize deduplicates parent instances in memory, but count() would be wrong without { distinct: true }
});

Failure scenario

A cleanup job "delete addresses not used by any order" ran DELETE FROM addresses WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT shipping_address_id FROM orders). It deleted nothing, for a year, because one order in 2023 had a NULL shipping address. Then a data fix set that one order's address, the subquery no longer contained NULL, and the next nightly run deleted 1.8 million "unused" addresses, including every address of every customer who had never checked out. The query was not wrong that night; it had been wrong all along, and the NULL had been masking it. NOT EXISTS would have behaved correctly on every run.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • NOT IN with a nullable subquery column: empty result.
  • IN with a subquery returning millions of rows: hashed, fine; with a correlated subquery: evaluated per row, can be O(n squared) without an index.
  • EXISTS with SELECT * vs SELECT 1: identical; 1 is convention.
  • JOIN + DISTINCT to fake a semi-join: correct, more expensive, and DISTINCT hides multiplication bugs elsewhere.
  • Semi-join with LIMIT on the outer query: the planner may pick a nested loop and stop early, which is good; without an inner index it is a sequential scan per outer row.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

EXISTS for existence, NOT EXISTS for absence, JOIN only when they need columns. They flag NOT IN (subquery) in every code review, and they flag DISTINCT as a symptom to investigate.

Common mistakes

  • NOT IN on nullable columns.
  • JOIN then DISTINCT on the request path.
  • IN with a 50,000-element literal list; use an array parameter or a temp table.

Interview questions

  1. NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS: which is safe and why? Expected: NOT EXISTS; NOT IN returns nothing when the subquery has a NULL.
  2. What is a semi-join and how does the planner execute it? Expected: existence check that stops at the first match; Semi Join node using nested loop, hash, or merge.
  3. When is JOIN better than EXISTS? Expected: when you need the related table's columns.

17.6 UNION vs UNION ALL

Concept

UNION combines two result sets and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL combines them and keeps everything. INTERSECT returns rows present in both; EXCEPT returns rows in the first but not the second. All require the same number of columns with compatible types.

Why does it exist?

Sometimes the rows you want come from different tables or different conditions that cannot be expressed as one WHERE: "all activity for a user" from orders, reviews and notifications into one timeline; "products in category A priced under 500 or in category B priced over 5000" when different indexes serve each half better than one OR.

How it works

  1. Each branch is planned and executed independently.
  2. UNION ALL is an Append node: rows stream through with no extra work.
  3. UNION adds a HashAggregate or Sort + Unique over the combined rows to remove duplicates, which reads and hashes every row. On a million rows that is hundreds of milliseconds and work_mem pressure for nothing, if the branches were already disjoint.
  4. ORDER BY and LIMIT at the end apply to the combined result; to limit each branch, wrap it in parentheses.

PostgreSQL example

-- User activity timeline: branches are disjoint by construction, so UNION ALL
SELECT 'order' AS kind, id::text AS ref, placed_at AS at FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'review', id::text, created_at FROM reviews WHERE user_id = $1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'notification', id::text, created_at FROM notifications WHERE user_id = $1
ORDER BY at DESC
LIMIT 50;
-- Limit -> Sort -> Append -> three Index Scans. The Sort is over at most (rows per branch), bounded by the user's activity.

-- Same with UNION: adds a HashAggregate over all rows for no reason
-- UNION when you genuinely want set semantics: emails that appear in both marketing lists
SELECT email FROM newsletter_subscribers
INTERSECT
SELECT email FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- OR split into UNION ALL so each half uses its own index (the planner often does this itself via BitmapOr)
SELECT id FROM products WHERE category_id = 3 AND price < 500
UNION ALL
SELECT id FROM products WHERE category_id = 7 AND price > 5000;
-- If a product could satisfy both, UNION ALL duplicates it; here the categories differ so it cannot.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • UNION silently deduplicates rows that are legitimately identical (two identical order lines in an export). Use UNION ALL unless you have a reason.
  • Type mismatch between branches: id uuid in one branch and id bigint in another needs an explicit ::text on both.
  • Column names come from the first branch; aliases in later branches are ignored.
  • ORDER BY inside a branch without parentheses is a syntax error or applies to the whole union.

Interview questions

  1. UNION or UNION ALL for a timeline from three tables? Expected: UNION ALL; branches are disjoint, and UNION would hash every row to remove duplicates that cannot exist.

17.7 Common Table Expressions

17.7.1 WITH for readability, and materialization vs inlining

Concept

A CTE (common table expression) is a named subquery declared with WITH name AS (...) and then used like a table in the main query. It makes multi-step queries readable: filter first, aggregate second, join third, each step named. Since PostgreSQL 12, a CTE that is referenced once and has no side effects is inlined into the main query by default, so the planner can push predicates into it and choose indexes; before 12, every CTE was an optimization fence, always materialized. You can force either behavior with MATERIALIZED or NOT MATERIALIZED.

Why does it exist?

Nested subqueries three levels deep are unreadable and unreviewable. CTEs turn them into a pipeline you read top to bottom. Materialization exists because sometimes you want the fence: an expensive subquery used twice should run once, and a subquery with a volatile function must not be duplicated.

How it works

  1. The parser registers each CTE by name. A CTE can reference earlier CTEs in the same WITH.
  2. Planning (PG12+): if the CTE is non-recursive, referenced exactly once, and contains no volatile functions or data-modifying statements, it is inlined as if you had written a subquery. The planner then treats it like any subquery: predicates from the outer query can be pushed down, join order can be changed.
  3. If referenced more than once, or marked MATERIALIZED, it is executed once into a temporary result (in memory up to work_mem, then temp file), and each reference scans that result. Outer predicates cannot be pushed into it.
  4. NOT MATERIALIZED forces inlining even when referenced multiple times (the subquery is duplicated at each reference).
  5. Data-modifying CTEs (WITH moved AS (DELETE ... RETURNING *) INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM moved) always run exactly once and see the same snapshot.

PostgreSQL example

-- Readable pipeline: active customers in March, their order stats, joined to their default address
WITH march_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, id, total
  FROM orders
  WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01' AND placed_at < '2026-04-01'
    AND status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
),
per_user AS (
  SELECT user_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM march_orders
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.email, pu.orders, pu.revenue, a.city
FROM per_user pu
JOIN users u ON u.id = pu.user_id
LEFT JOIN addresses a ON a.user_id = u.id AND a.is_default
WHERE pu.revenue > 10000
ORDER BY pu.revenue DESC
LIMIT 100;
-- PG12+: march_orders and per_user are each referenced once, so both are inlined; the planner sees one query.

-- The materialization fence in action: a predicate that should be pushed down
WITH recent AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= now() - interval '90 days'   -- 1.5M rows materialized
)
SELECT * FROM recent WHERE user_id = 'a1b2...';   -- scans the 1.5M-row temp result; cannot use orders_user_id_placed_at_idx
-- Without MATERIALIZED (PG12+ default) the user_id predicate is pushed into the CTE and the index is used: 0.1 ms vs 400 ms.

-- Legitimate MATERIALIZED: expensive subquery used twice
WITH stats AS MATERIALIZED (
