  SELECT product_id, count(*) AS n, avg(rating) AS avg_rating FROM reviews GROUP BY product_id   -- 20M rows aggregated once
)
SELECT p.name, s.avg_rating FROM products p JOIN stats s ON s.product_id = p.id WHERE s.n >= 100
UNION ALL
SELECT 'AVERAGE OF ALL', avg(avg_rating) FROM stats;

-- Data-modifying CTE: archive and delete in one statement, one snapshot
WITH archived AS (
  DELETE FROM notifications
  WHERE status = 'sent' AND sent_at < now() - interval '180 days'
  RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO notifications_archive SELECT * FROM archived;

TypeORM example

// TypeORM QueryBuilder supports CTEs via addCommonTableExpression
const rows = await dataSource.createQueryBuilder()
  .addCommonTableExpression(
    `SELECT user_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
       FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= :from AND placed_at < :to GROUP BY user_id`,
    'per_user',
  )
  .select(['u.email AS email', 'pu.orders AS orders', 'pu.revenue AS revenue'])
  .from('per_user', 'pu')
  .innerJoin('users', 'u', 'u.id = pu.user_id')
  .where('pu.revenue > :min', { min: 10000 })
  .orderBy('pu.revenue', 'DESC')
  .limit(100)
  .setParameters({ from, to })
  .getRawMany();
// Beyond two CTEs, raw SQL via dataSource.query() is usually more readable than the builder.

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no CTE API; use sequelize.query with replacements and a model for mapping if needed:

const [rows] = await sequelize.query(
  `WITH per_user AS (SELECT user_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders
                     WHERE placed_at >= :from AND placed_at < :to GROUP BY user_id)
   SELECT u.email, pu.orders, pu.revenue FROM per_user pu JOIN users u ON u.id = pu.user_id
   WHERE pu.revenue > :min ORDER BY pu.revenue DESC LIMIT 100`,
  { replacements: { from, to, min: 10000 }, type: QueryTypes.SELECT },
);

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Upgrading from PG11 to PG12+ changes CTE behavior; queries that relied on the fence (to avoid a bad plan or to run an expensive subquery once) may regress. Audit with MATERIALIZED.
  • A CTE referenced twice is materialized, and its temp result may spill to disk if larger than work_mem.
  • CTEs cannot be indexed. A CTE producing a million rows joined to a big table is a hash join at best.
  • Data-modifying CTEs all see the same snapshot: a WITH d AS (DELETE ...) SELECT count(*) FROM target still counts the deleted rows.
  • Deeply nested CTE chains are hard for the planner: join_collapse_limit applies to the inlined result.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

CTEs for readability by default, trusting PG12+ inlining. MATERIALIZED when a subquery is expensive and reused, or when the plan without it is demonstrably worse. They check the plan after adding a CTE, because "it reads better" and "it runs the same" are different claims.

Interview questions

  1. What changed about CTEs in PostgreSQL 12? Expected: single-reference, side-effect-free CTEs are inlined; before, always materialized as an optimization fence.
  2. When would you write MATERIALIZED explicitly? Expected: expensive subquery used multiple times; or to deliberately fence a bad plan.
  3. What does a data-modifying CTE see? Expected: all statements in the query share one snapshot; later parts do not see earlier parts' modifications.

17.8 Recursive CTEs

Concept

A recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) is a query that refers to its own result. It has an anchor (the starting rows) and a recursive term (how to get the next rows from the current ones), combined with UNION or UNION ALL. It is how SQL walks trees and graphs: the category tree, an org chart, a bill of materials, "who can this user reach through friends of friends", and "which orders are transitively linked to this one through returns and exchanges".

Why does it exist?

Adjacency lists (parent_id) are the simplest way to store a tree, but "all descendants of Electronics" has no fixed depth, so no fixed number of self-joins answers it. The recursive CTE loops until no new rows are produced.

Mental model

Imagine finding every folder under "Projects" on a disk. You start with "Projects" (anchor). You list its subfolders (one recursive step). For each of those, you list their subfolders (next step), until there are no more. The recursive CTE does exactly this, one level per iteration, and returns everything it visited.

flowchart TB
    A["Anchor: categories WHERE slug = 'electronics'"] --> W0["Working set 0: Electronics"]
    W0 --> R1["Recursive term: children of working set"]
    R1 --> W1["Working set 1: Phones, Cables, Audio"]
    W1 --> R2["Recursive term again"]
    R2 --> W2["Working set 2: Accessories, Cases, Chargers"]
    W2 --> R3["Recursive term again"]
    R3 --> W3["Working set 3: empty"]
    W3 --> D["Done: result = union of all working sets"]

How it works

  1. Evaluate the anchor term. Its rows go into the result and into a working table.
  2. Evaluate the recursive term with the CTE name bound to the working table (only the previous iteration's rows, not the whole result so far).
  3. With UNION ALL, append the new rows; with UNION, discard rows already in the result (which also stops cycles for exactly-duplicate rows).
  4. Replace the working table with the new rows. Repeat from step 2 until the working table is empty.
  5. Depth, path and cycle detection are added by carrying extra columns (depth + 1, path || id) or with the CYCLE clause (PG14+).

Each iteration is one query execution; a tree of depth 5 is 6 executions. With an index on parent_id, each execution is a set of index probes. Cost is proportional to the number of nodes visited, not the size of the table.

PostgreSQL example

-- All descendants of Electronics with their depth and path (category tree)
WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 0 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path
  FROM categories WHERE slug = 'electronics'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, s.depth + 1, s.path || c.id
  FROM categories c
  JOIN subtree s ON c.parent_id = s.id
  WHERE s.depth < 10                          -- hard depth limit as a safety net
)
SELECT repeat('  ', depth) || name AS tree, depth, path FROM subtree ORDER BY path;
-- tree               | depth | path
-- Electronics        | 0     | {1}
--   Phones           | 1     | {1,4}
--     Accessories    | 2     | {1,4,17}
--   Cables           | 1     | {1,6}

-- Products in a category OR any descendant (the query every category page needs)
WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
  SELECT id FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id FROM categories c JOIN subtree s ON c.parent_id = s.id
)
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price
FROM products p
WHERE p.category_id IN (SELECT id FROM subtree) AND p.is_active
ORDER BY p.name
LIMIT 40;

-- Ancestors: breadcrumb for a category (walk up instead of down)
WITH RECURSIVE ancestors AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 0 AS depth FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, a.depth + 1 FROM categories c JOIN ancestors a ON c.id = a.parent_id
)
SELECT string_agg(name, ' > ' ORDER BY depth DESC) AS breadcrumb FROM ancestors;

-- Cycle protection with the CYCLE clause (PG14+): a corrupt parent_id loop will not run forever
WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name FROM categories c JOIN subtree s ON c.parent_id = s.id
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT * FROM subtree WHERE NOT is_cycle;
-- Before PG14: carry path ARRAY and add "WHERE NOT c.id = ANY(s.path)" to the recursive term.

-- Bill of materials: total quantity of each leaf component for one bundle product
-- (product_components: parent_product_id, child_product_id, qty)
WITH RECURSIVE bom AS (
  SELECT child_product_id AS product_id, qty::bigint AS total_qty, 1 AS level
  FROM product_components WHERE parent_product_id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT pc.child_product_id, b.total_qty * pc.qty, b.level + 1
  FROM product_components pc JOIN bom b ON pc.parent_product_id = b.product_id
  WHERE b.level < 20
)
SELECT product_id, sum(total_qty) AS required
FROM bom
WHERE product_id NOT IN (SELECT parent_product_id FROM product_components)  -- leaves only
GROUP BY product_id;

-- Graph traversal: users reachable within 3 hops via a referrals table (referrer_id, referred_id)
WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
  SELECT referred_id AS user_id, 1 AS hops, ARRAY[$1::uuid, referred_id] AS path
  FROM referrals WHERE referrer_id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT r.referred_id, rc.hops + 1, rc.path || r.referred_id
  FROM referrals r JOIN reach rc ON r.referrer_id = rc.user_id
  WHERE rc.hops < 3 AND NOT r.referred_id = ANY(rc.path)     -- manual cycle check
)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) user_id, hops FROM reach ORDER BY user_id, hops;

TypeORM example

// Recursive CTEs: raw SQL is the right tool. Keep it in a repository method with typed output.
interface CategoryNode { id: string; name: string; depth: number }

async subtree(rootId: string): Promise<CategoryNode[]> {
  return this.ds.query<CategoryNode[]>(
    `WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
       SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path FROM categories WHERE id = $1
       UNION ALL
       SELECT c.id, c.name, s.depth + 1, s.path || c.id
       FROM categories c JOIN subtree s ON c.parent_id = s.id WHERE s.depth < 10
     )
     SELECT id, name, depth FROM subtree ORDER BY path`,
    [rootId],
  );
}

TypeORM has a TreeRepository with @Tree('closure-table' | 'materialized-path' | 'nested-set' | 'adjacency-list') decorators, which manage the storage strategy for you. It is convenient for small trees; for anything with custom columns or performance needs, the raw recursive CTE is more predictable.

Production scenario

A category page on a 40,000-product catalog: the recursive CTE over a 900-row category table takes about 0.3 ms (three iterations, each a handful of index probes on categories_parent_id_idx), and the products query then uses products_category_id_idx with = ANY over the 12 resulting ids. Total under 2 ms. Caching the subtree id list in Redis for 10 minutes removes even that; categories change rarely.

Failure scenario

A data import set categories.parent_id = id for one row (self-parent) before the CHECK (parent_id IS DISTINCT FROM id) existed. The category page's recursive CTE ran forever, or rather until it exhausted temp disk at 200 GB and the query was killed after 40 minutes, having pinned one CPU core the whole time. Since then the CTE carries WHERE s.depth < 10, the CHECK exists, and PG14's CYCLE clause is in place for multi-node loops. Recursion without a depth guard is an outage waiting for one bad row.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Infinite recursion on cycles: always a depth limit and, on PG14+, CYCLE.
  • UNION vs UNION ALL: UNION deduplicates complete rows and thereby stops simple cycles, but costs a hash per iteration; carrying depth makes rows distinct so UNION no longer stops cycles.
  • Recursive term must reference the CTE exactly once and cannot use aggregates, ORDER BY, or LIMIT on the CTE reference.
  • Wide recursion (a node with 100,000 children) produces a large working table; fine, but memory-bound.
  • Deep recursion (a 10,000-level chain) is 10,000 query executions; use ltree or a closure table for very deep structures.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Recursive CTE for trees under a few thousand nodes and graphs with bounded hops. Always a depth guard. Cache the result when the tree is read-mostly. Move to ltree or a closure table when the read pattern is "descendants of X" at high volume on a large tree.

Common mistakes

  • No depth limit.
  • Using the recursive CTE to walk 10 million rows when a single self-join or a materialized path would do.
  • Forgetting that the recursive term sees only the previous iteration's rows.

Interview questions

  1. How does a recursive CTE execute? Expected: anchor, then repeated recursive term over the previous iteration's rows until empty.
  2. How do you protect against cycles? Expected: depth column with a limit; path array with NOT = ANY; CYCLE clause in PG14+.
  3. When is a recursive CTE the wrong tool for a tree? Expected: very deep or very large trees read at high volume; use ltree or a closure table.

Practical exercise

Build a 5-level category tree with 2,000 nodes. Implement GET /categories/:id/products using the recursive CTE, then implement the same with ltree. Insert a cycle deliberately and verify both the depth guard and the CYCLE clause stop it. Acceptance criteria: both implementations return identical product sets; the cycle test terminates in under 100 ms; plans captured for each.

17.9 Window functions

17.9.1 What a window function is

Concept

A window function computes a value for each row using a set of related rows (the "window") without collapsing them into one row the way GROUP BY does. sum(total) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at) gives every order row its customer's running total up to that order. row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) numbers each order's payments from newest to oldest, so = 1 picks the latest. The row stays; a new column appears.

The pieces of an OVER clause:

  • PARTITION BY splits rows into groups (like GROUP BY, but rows are kept).
  • ORDER BY orders rows within each partition and defines "before" and "after".
  • The frame (ROWS BETWEEN ... AND ... or RANGE ...) says which rows around the current one feed the function. The default, when ORDER BY is present, is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which is why sum() OVER (ORDER BY x) is a running total.

Why does it exist?

Before window functions, "rank each product within its category by revenue", "the previous order's date for each order", or "running balance" required self-joins, correlated subqueries, or application code looping over sorted rows. Those are slow (O(n squared) for the correlated form) and unreadable. Window functions do it in one sorted pass per partition.

Mental model

Imagine a spreadsheet of orders sorted by customer and date. For each row, you look at a sliding highlighted region: "all rows above me for this customer" (running total), "the one row above me" (LAG), "all rows for this customer" (partition total for a percentage). You write the answer into a new column on the same row. The rows do not merge; the highlight moves.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Partition_user_A
      R1["order 1  total 500"] --> R2["order 2  total 300"] --> R3["order 3  total 700"] --> R4["order 4  total 200"]
    end
    F["Frame for row 3 with ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW = rows 2 and 3, sum 1000"]
    R3 -.-> F
    G["Frame for row 3 with default RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING = rows 1..3, running sum 1500"]
    R3 -.-> G

How it works

  1. The planner adds a WindowAgg node. Rows are sorted by PARTITION BY then ORDER BY (using an index if one matches, otherwise a Sort).
  2. For each partition, rows are processed in order. The function sees the frame and computes the value.
  3. Functions like row_number, rank, lag, lead are cheap (constant state). Aggregates over frames (sum, avg) are incremental for growing frames and can be more expensive for sliding frames.
  4. Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, and before ORDER BY and LIMIT. You cannot filter on a window result in the same SELECT; wrap it in a subquery or CTE.
  5. Multiple windows with the same PARTITION BY/ORDER BY share one sort. Different orderings need separate sorts; name windows with WINDOW w AS (...) to make sharing explicit.

Function reference:

Function Meaning Typical use
row_number() 1, 2, 3... within partition, no ties top-N per group, dedup
rank() 1, 1, 3 (gaps after ties) leaderboards where ties share a rank
dense_rank() 1, 1, 2 (no gaps) "top 3 distinct scores"
lag(col, n) / lead(col, n) value n rows before/after time since previous order; next status
first_value / last_value / nth_value value at frame edge first purchase date per customer
sum/avg/count/min/max ... OVER aggregate over the frame running totals, moving averages, partition totals
ntile(n) bucket rows into n groups quartiles of customers by spend
percent_rank, cume_dist relative position percentile of a product's price in its category

PostgreSQL example

-- Running total and partition total per customer, plus share of lifetime spend
SELECT user_id, id, placed_at, total,
       sum(total) OVER w                                        AS running_total,
       sum(total) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id)                   AS lifetime_total,
       round(100.0 * total / sum(total) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id), 1) AS pct_of_lifetime
FROM orders
WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at, id)
ORDER BY user_id, placed_at;

-- Days since the customer's previous order (LAG), and whether this is a repeat purchase
SELECT id, user_id, placed_at,
       placed_at - lag(placed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at, id) AS since_previous,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at, id) > 1        AS is_repeat
FROM orders;

-- Top 3 products per category by revenue (top-N per group)
WITH product_revenue AS (
  SELECT p.category_id, p.id AS product_id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o   ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.placed_at >= now() - interval '90 days'
  GROUP BY p.category_id, p.id, p.name
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *, dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk
  FROM product_revenue
)
SELECT category_id, product_id, name, revenue, rnk
FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY category_id, rnk;

-- Dedup: keep the newest row per email among a messy import (users_import has duplicates)
DELETE FROM users_import
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(email) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
    FROM users_import
  ) t
  WHERE rn > 1
);

-- Moving 7-day average of daily revenue with an explicit frame
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', placed_at)::date AS day, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered') GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT day, revenue,
       avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_7d,
       revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day)                                AS delta_vs_yesterday
FROM daily ORDER BY day;

-- Gaps and islands: contiguous runs of days on which a user placed at least one order
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, date_trunc('day', placed_at)::date AS day FROM orders
),
numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, day, day - (row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day))::int AS grp
  FROM days
)
SELECT user_id, min(day) AS streak_start, max(day) AS streak_end, count(*) AS streak_days
FROM numbered
GROUP BY user_id, grp
HAVING count(*) >= 3
ORDER BY streak_days DESC;
-- The trick: for consecutive days, "day minus row_number" is constant, so it identifies the island.

-- Frame semantics that bite: last_value with the default frame returns the CURRENT row, not the last in the partition
SELECT user_id, placed_at, total,
       last_value(total) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at)   AS wrong_last,   -- equals total (frame ends at current row)
       last_value(total) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at
                               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS real_last
FROM orders;

RANGE vs ROWS: RANGE groups peers (rows with equal ORDER BY values) into the frame together; ROWS counts physical rows. With a unique ORDER BY they agree; with ties, sum() OVER (ORDER BY placed_at) using the default RANGE includes all rows sharing the same timestamp in each of their running totals. Add a unique tiebreaker or use ROWS when you want strict one-row steps. GROUPS mode (PG11+) frames by peer groups.

TypeORM example

// Window functions are raw SQL territory. Keep them behind a typed repository method.
interface RankedProduct { category_id: string; product_id: string; name: string; revenue: string; rnk: number }

async topProductsPerCategory(days: number, n: number): Promise<RankedProduct[]> {
  return this.ds.query<RankedProduct[]>(
    `WITH product_revenue AS (
       SELECT p.category_id, p.id AS product_id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
       FROM order_items oi
       JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
       JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
       WHERE o.placed_at >= now() - ($1 || ' days')::interval
       GROUP BY p.category_id, p.id, p.name)
     SELECT * FROM (
       SELECT *, dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk FROM product_revenue
     ) r WHERE rnk <= $2 ORDER BY category_id, rnk`,
    [days, n],
  );
}

QueryBuilder can express a window via addSelect('row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)', 'rn') inside getRawMany, but the wrapping subquery for WHERE rn = 1 is awkward; raw SQL reads better and is easier to review.

Sequelize example

const [rows] = await sequelize.query(
  `SELECT id, user_id, placed_at, total,
          sum(total) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at, id) AS running_total
   FROM orders WHERE user_id = :userId ORDER BY placed_at`,
  { replacements: { userId }, type: QueryTypes.SELECT },
);

Production scenario

A "your spending this year" widget for 2 million customers is computed nightly into a summary table by one query with sum() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY placed_at) over 12 million orders: one sort using the (user_id, placed_at) index (no Sort node), one WindowAgg pass, about 40 seconds on a replica. The alternative, a correlated subquery per order, would be 12 million index scans.

Failure scenario

A leaderboard used rank() for "top 100 sellers" and paginated with WHERE rnk BETWEEN 101 AND 200. Ties at rank 100 (three sellers with identical revenue) meant ranks 100, 100, 100, 103; page two started at 103 and the two tied sellers were never shown on any page. Switching to row_number() with a deterministic tiebreaker (ORDER BY revenue DESC, seller_id) made pagination complete, and dense_rank() was shown to the user as the displayed rank. Use row_number() to paginate and rank()/dense_rank() to display.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • last_value and the default frame (see example): almost always needs UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
  • Non-deterministic order: row_number() OVER (ORDER BY placed_at) with ties gives different numbering on different runs; add a unique tiebreaker.
  • A window over a huge unindexed partition sorts on disk; check for Sort Method: external merge under WindowAgg.
  • PARTITION BY on a low-cardinality column with millions of rows per partition is fine for row_number, but sliding-frame aggregates (ROWS BETWEEN 1000 PRECEDING) are recomputed per row and can be slow.
  • Filtering on a window result requires a subquery; WHERE row_number() OVER (...) = 1 is a syntax error.
  • Window functions cannot be nested and cannot appear in GROUP BY or HAVING.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Top-N per group, dedup, running totals, deltas versus the previous row, and cohort math are window problems. They reach for LATERAL when the outer set is small (a page of 20 orders) and the window when the set is large (a nightly report over every order). They always add a unique tiebreaker to every window ORDER BY, and they know the last_value trap by heart.

Common mistakes

  • rank() for pagination.
  • Missing tiebreakers.
  • last_value without a frame.
  • Using a correlated subquery for "previous row" when lag() exists.

Interview questions

  1. Difference between row_number, rank, and dense_rank? Expected: 1,2,3 vs 1,1,3 vs 1,1,2.
  2. How do you select the latest payment per order with a window function, and when is LATERAL better? Expected: row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) = 1 in a subquery; LATERAL when the outer set is small.
  3. Why does last_value return the current row by default? Expected: default frame ends at CURRENT ROW.
  4. Explain gaps and islands with row_number. Expected: day - row_number() is constant within a contiguous run.
  5. What is the difference between ROWS and RANGE frames?

Practical exercise

Write four queries on the reference schema: running spend per customer, top 3 products per category, deduplicate a users_import table keeping newest, and 7-day moving average revenue. For each, capture the plan and confirm whether the WindowAgg is fed by an index scan or a Sort. Acceptance criteria: all four correct on a seeded dataset with deliberate ties, and at least one query rewritten to avoid a disk sort by adding an index.

17.10 CASE: conditional logic, conditional aggregation and pivoting

Concept

CASE WHEN cond THEN a WHEN cond2 THEN b ELSE c END is SQL's if/else. It appears in SELECT (derive a label), ORDER BY (custom sort order), WHERE (rarely; usually a smell), and, most importantly, inside aggregates to compute several conditional metrics in one pass (conditional aggregation), which is how you pivot rows into columns.

Why does it exist?

Reports want "count of orders by status as columns", not as rows. Sort orders want "pending first, then paid, then the rest". Labels want "small / medium / large basket". Doing these in application code means pulling all rows over the wire; CASE does it in the database in the same scan.

PostgreSQL example

-- Labeling and custom sort order
SELECT id, total,
       CASE WHEN total < 500 THEN 'small' WHEN total < 5000 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'large' END AS basket_size
FROM orders
ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'pending' THEN 0 WHEN 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 2 END, placed_at DESC;

-- Pivot: order counts per status as columns, per day (conditional aggregation)
SELECT date_trunc('day', placed_at)::date AS day,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending')   AS pending,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') AS delivered,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
       sum(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_value   -- older idiom, same result
FROM orders
WHERE placed_at >= now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- Rating distribution per product as columns (the "stars histogram")
SELECT product_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE rating = 5) AS five,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE rating = 4) AS four,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE rating = 3) AS three,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE rating = 2) AS two,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE rating = 1) AS one,
       round(avg(rating), 2)              AS avg_rating
FROM reviews GROUP BY product_id;

-- CASE in an UPDATE: bulk status transitions in one statement
UPDATE shipments
   SET status = CASE
                  WHEN delivered_at IS NOT NULL THEN 'delivered'
                  WHEN shipped_at   IS NOT NULL THEN 'in_transit'
                  ELSE status
                END
 WHERE status = 'created';

-- Dynamic pivots (unknown number of columns) need crosstab() from the tablefunc extension or application-side pivoting.

FILTER is preferred over sum(CASE ...) for readability; both plan identically. CASE is still needed when the conditional value is not a simple filter (different expressions per branch).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CASE returns the type of the first branch; mixing text and integer errors. Cast explicitly.
  • No ELSE returns NULL; sum() ignores it, count() ignores it, but array_agg includes it.
  • CASE in WHERE (WHERE CASE WHEN $1 = 'x' THEN a = 1 ELSE b = 2 END) prevents index use; write the branches as OR conditions or two queries.
  • CASE on a column inside ORDER BY needs a Sort node; you cannot index a custom status order unless you use an expression index on the same CASE.

Interview questions

  1. How do you get order counts per status as columns? Expected: conditional aggregation with FILTER or sum(CASE ...).
  2. When does CASE in WHERE hurt? Expected: it hides sargable predicates; the planner cannot use indexes.

17.11 Subqueries: scalar, correlated and derived tables

Concept

A subquery is a SELECT inside another statement. Three shapes:

  • Scalar subquery: returns exactly one value; usable anywhere an expression is. (SELECT count(*) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = o.id) as a column.
  • Correlated subquery: references a column from the outer query, so it is logically evaluated once per outer row. The scalar example above is correlated. This is where O(n squared) hides.
  • Derived table: a subquery in FROM, used as a table. FROM (SELECT ... GROUP BY ...) t. Always planned as a normal join input; PG inlines or materializes as appropriate.

Why does it exist?

Subqueries let you compute an intermediate result inline without a CTE or a temp table. Derived tables are how you aggregate a child to the parent's grain before joining (the fix for row multiplication in section 17.3). Correlated subqueries express "for this row, look up something" naturally, and the planner turns many of them into joins.

How it works

  1. A scalar uncorrelated subquery ((SELECT max(placed_at) FROM orders)) is an InitPlan: executed once, its value cached.
  2. A correlated subquery in SELECT or WHERE becomes a SubPlan: executed per outer row, unless the planner can decorrelate it (it often can for EXISTS/IN, rarely for scalar aggregates in SELECT). With an index on the correlation column, each execution is an index probe: fine for 20 outer rows, painful for 2 million (loops=2000000 in the plan).
  3. A derived table in FROM is planned like a CTE that is inlined: predicates from the outer query are pushed into it when safe, and it participates in join ordering.
  4. A subquery returning more than one row where a scalar is expected raises "more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression". Add LIMIT 1 with an ORDER BY, or use an aggregate.

PostgreSQL example

-- Scalar correlated subqueries in SELECT: fine for a single order page
SELECT o.id, o.total,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = o.id)                       AS item_count,
       (SELECT status FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1) AS latest_payment
FROM orders o
WHERE o.id = $1;
-- Plan: Index Scan on orders; SubPlan 1 (loops=1); SubPlan 2 (loops=1). Total < 0.3 ms.

-- The same shape over a report: SubPlan loops = number of orders
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
SELECT o.id, (SELECT count(*) FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = o.id) AS item_count
FROM orders o WHERE o.placed_at >= '2026-01-01';
-- Index Scan using orders_placed_at_idx on orders o (rows=2104411)
--   SubPlan 1
--     ->  Aggregate (loops=2104411)
--           ->  Index Only Scan using order_items_order_id_product_id_key on order_items oi (loops=2104411)
-- Execution Time: 41210 ms   <- 2.1 million index scans

-- Rewrite as a derived table (aggregate once, join once): hash join, ~2 seconds
SELECT o.id, coalesce(ic.item_count, 0) AS item_count
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, count(*) AS item_count FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) ic ON ic.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.placed_at >= '2026-01-01';

-- Uncorrelated scalar as InitPlan: computed once
SELECT id, total, total - (SELECT avg(total) FROM orders) AS vs_average FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1;

-- Derived table for "customers whose average order is above 2000"
SELECT u.email, s.avg_total
FROM (SELECT user_id, avg(total) AS avg_total FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING avg(total) > 2000) s
JOIN users u ON u.id = s.user_id;

-- Row-returning subquery with ANY/ALL
SELECT id, price FROM products p
WHERE price > ALL (SELECT price FROM products WHERE category_id = p.category_id AND id <> p.id);  -- most expensive in its category
-- Clearer as a window: rank() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY price DESC) = 1

Decision table for "per-parent computed value":

Outer row count Child indexed on FK Best tool
1 to a few hundred yes Correlated scalar subquery or LATERAL
thousands to millions yes or no Derived table (GROUP BY then join) or window function
need top-1 child with several columns yes LATERAL ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1
need top-N children per parent over a large set any Window function with row_number()

TypeORM example

// Derived-table join in QueryBuilder
const rows = await orderRepo.createQueryBuilder('o')
  .select(['o.id AS id', 'coalesce(ic.item_count, 0) AS item_count'])
  .leftJoin(
    (qb) => qb.select('oi.order_id', 'order_id').addSelect('count(*)', 'item_count').from(OrderItem, 'oi').groupBy('oi.order_id'),
    'ic', 'ic.order_id = o.id',
  )
  .where('o.placedAt >= :from', { from })
  .getRawMany();

// Scalar subquery as a selected column
const withCount = await orderRepo.createQueryBuilder('o')
  .addSelect((qb) => qb.select('count(*)').from(OrderItem, 'oi').where('oi.order_id = o.id'), 'item_count')
  .where('o.id = :id', { id })
  .getRawOne();

Sequelize example

const rows = await Order.findAll({
  attributes: {
    include: [[literal(`(SELECT count(*) FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = "Order"."id")`), 'itemCount']],
  },
  where: { id },
});
// For reports, use sequelize.query with the derived-table form instead of a literal per row.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: the "orders export" job was at 100 percent CPU for its fourth hour. The export selected every order of the year with three scalar subqueries per row (item count, latest payment status, shipment status). Each was an index probe, 40 microseconds; three per row over 2.1 million rows was 250 seconds of pure probing per subquery, and the Aggregate above each probe added more. Rewriting as three derived tables joined once brought the job to 90 seconds. The plan had said loops=2104411 from the first run; nobody had looked.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Scalar subquery returning more than one row: runtime error, often only in production data.
  • Scalar subquery returning zero rows: NULL, silently; coalesce.
  • Correlated subquery on an unindexed column: sequential scan per outer row. Catastrophic.
  • Derived table with ORDER BY and no LIMIT: the order is not guaranteed to survive the outer join.
  • Predicate pushdown into a derived table is blocked by window functions, DISTINCT ON, or LIMIT inside it; the derived table is then computed in full first.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They look for SubPlan with a large loops count in any report plan and rewrite it as a derived table or window. They keep scalar subqueries for single-row lookups where they are the clearest expression. They never write a correlated subquery against a column without an index.

Interview questions

  1. What is a correlated subquery and what is its cost model? Expected: references the outer row; evaluated per outer row; loops=N in the plan; needs an index or a rewrite.
  2. Rewrite SELECT o.id, (SELECT count(*) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = o.id) FROM orders o for 2 million orders. Expected: derived table aggregated once, joined.
  3. What is an InitPlan versus a SubPlan? Expected: uncorrelated, run once, vs correlated, run per row.
  4. What happens when a scalar subquery returns two rows?

Practical exercise

Take the orders export query with three scalar subqueries, run it over 1 million orders, and capture the plan showing loops. Rewrite with derived tables, then with LATERAL for the top-1 payment, and compare the three plans and timings. Acceptance criteria: a table of timings and a one-paragraph rule for when each form is appropriate.

17.12 Aggregation functions beyond SUM and COUNT

Concept

PostgreSQL's aggregates go well past the basic five. The ones a backend engineer uses weekly:

  • count(*) counts rows; count(col) counts non-null values; count(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-null values.
  • array_agg(col ORDER BY ...) collects values into an array; string_agg(col, ', ' ORDER BY ...) joins them into text.
  • jsonb_agg(expr) and jsonb_object_agg(key, value) build JSON; combined with jsonb_build_object they return nested documents in one query, which is the SQL answer to N+1.
  • bool_or(cond) / bool_and(cond) ("any child is X", "all children are X").
  • min/max on any orderable type, including timestamps and text.
  • percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col) for medians and other percentiles (interpolated); percentile_disc for the nearest actual value; mode() for the most common value.
  • every() is an alias of bool_and.
  • filter (WHERE ...) applies to all of them.

Why does it exist?

An API that returns an order with its items has two choices: one query for the order plus one per item collection (N+1, or 2 queries with = ANY), assembling JSON in TypeScript; or one query that returns the JSON already nested. jsonb_agg makes the second possible. Percentiles exist because averages lie: the average delivery time is dragged by a few stuck shipments, and p50/p90 tell the truth. bool_or exists so "does this order have any failed payment" is a group predicate, not a join and a DISTINCT.

Mental model

Imagine a clerk summarizing a folder of receipts for one customer. count(*) is the number of receipts. array_agg is writing the receipt numbers on a list. string_agg is writing them as one comma-separated line. jsonb_agg is photocopying the receipts into one bound booklet. bool_or(is_refund) is ticking "has at least one refund". percentile_cont(0.5) is finding the receipt in the middle when they are sorted by amount.

How it works

  1. Aggregates run inside HashAggregate or GroupAggregate (sorted input), one accumulator per group per aggregate.
  2. ORDER BY inside an aggregate (array_agg(x ORDER BY y)) forces the group's rows to be sorted first; it makes the output deterministic and costs a sort per group.
  3. count(DISTINCT col) needs a sort or hash per group to find distinct values; it is markedly more expensive than count(col). Two count(DISTINCT a), count(DISTINCT b) in one query each need their own de-duplication.
  4. Ordered-set aggregates (percentile_cont ... WITHIN GROUP) sort the group's values and pick or interpolate. Cost is a sort per group; for huge groups consider a sampled or approximate approach.
  5. jsonb_agg builds the JSON in memory per group. A group with 100,000 rows produces a 100,000-element array; it is a tool for bounded child sets (items of an order), not unbounded ones (all events for a user).

PostgreSQL example

-- COUNT variants on one table: the difference is nulls and distinctness
SELECT count(*)                       AS orders,
       count(cancelled_at)            AS cancelled,           -- non-null cancelled_at only
       count(DISTINCT user_id)        AS distinct_customers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE shipping_address_id IS NULL) AS no_address
FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01';

-- Order with items as nested JSON, one query, no N+1
SELECT o.id, o.order_number, o.status, o.total, o.placed_at,
       jsonb_build_object('id', u.id, 'email', u.email, 'name', u.full_name) AS customer,
       coalesce(items.items, '[]'::jsonb) AS items
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT jsonb_agg(
           jsonb_build_object('productId', oi.product_id, 'name', oi.product_name,
                              'quantity', oi.quantity, 'unitPrice', oi.unit_price,
                              'lineTotal', oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
           ORDER BY oi.id
         ) AS items
  FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = o.id
) items ON true
WHERE o.id = $1;
-- Result: one row with a `customer` object and an `items` array; node-postgres parses jsonb into JS objects.

-- List page: 20 orders each with their items nested, still one query
SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total,
       (SELECT coalesce(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('name', oi.product_name, 'qty', oi.quantity) ORDER BY oi.id), '[]')
          FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = o.id) AS items
FROM orders o
WHERE o.user_id = $1
ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- 20 correlated subqueries, each an index probe: fine. Do not do this over 2 million rows (section 10.11).

-- array_agg and string_agg: tags of products in a category, and a CSV of skus per order
SELECT o.id, string_agg(oi.product_name, ', ' ORDER BY oi.id) AS summary,
       array_agg(oi.product_id) AS product_ids
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.user_id = $1
GROUP BY o.id;

-- bool_or / bool_and: order-level flags derived from children
SELECT o.id,
       bool_or(p.status = 'failed')     AS had_failed_attempt,
       bool_or(p.status = 'captured')   AS is_paid,
       bool_and(s.status = 'delivered') AS fully_delivered,
       max(p.created_at)                AS last_payment_activity
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p  ON p.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.placed_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY o.id;
-- Note: joining two 1:N children multiplies rows, but bool_or/bool_and/max are immune to duplication. sum/count are not.

-- Percentiles: delivery time distribution per carrier (avg would mislead)
SELECT s.carrier,
       count(*)                                                                         AS shipments,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY s.delivered_at - s.shipped_at)      AS p50,
       percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY s.delivered_at - s.shipped_at)      AS p90,
       percentile_cont(ARRAY[0.5, 0.9, 0.99]) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY s.delivered_at - s.shipped_at) AS p50_90_99,
       avg(s.delivered_at - s.shipped_at)                                               AS mean,
       mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY date_part('dow', s.delivered_at))                  AS most_common_delivery_dow
FROM shipments s
WHERE s.delivered_at IS NOT NULL AND s.shipped_at >= now() - interval '90 days'
GROUP BY s.carrier ORDER BY p90;
--  carrier   | shipments |   p50    |   p90    |  mean
--  delhivery |    48211  | 2 days   | 4 days   | 2 days 9 hours
--  bluedart  |    22104  | 1 day    | 3 days   | 1 day 14 hours

-- jsonb_object_agg: settings as a map
SELECT jsonb_object_agg(channel, cnt) FROM (SELECT channel, count(*) AS cnt FROM notifications GROUP BY channel) t;
-- {"email": 120400, "push": 88210, "sms": 3011}

NestJS example

Returning nested JSON straight from the query removes the mapping layer:

// orders/orders.repository.ts
export interface OrderDetail {
  id: string; order_number: string; status: string; total: string; placed_at: Date;
  customer: { id: string; email: string; name: string };
  items: Array<{ productId: string; name: string; quantity: number; unitPrice: string; lineTotal: string }>;
}

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async findDetail(orderId: string): Promise<OrderDetail | null> {
    const rows = await this.ds.query<OrderDetail[]>(
      `SELECT o.id, o.order_number, o.status, o.total, o.placed_at,
              jsonb_build_object('id', u.id, 'email', u.email, 'name', u.full_name) AS customer,
              coalesce((SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
                          'productId', oi.product_id, 'name', oi.product_name, 'quantity', oi.quantity,
                          'unitPrice', oi.unit_price, 'lineTotal', oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) ORDER BY oi.id)
                        FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = o.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS items
       FROM orders o JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
       WHERE o.id = $1`,
      [orderId],
    );
    return rows[0] ?? null;
  }
}

One round trip, roughly 0.4 ms, versus TypeORM relations: ['user', 'items'] which is either one join with row duplication deduplicated in memory, or two queries. Both are acceptable at low volume; the SQL version is the one that stays fast.

TypeORM example

// relations: two round trips (TypeORM issues a second query for the collection when take() is used)
const order = await orderRepo.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { user: true, items: true } });

// Or a QueryBuilder with joins and in-memory entity assembly:
const order2 = await orderRepo.createQueryBuilder('o')
  .leftJoinAndSelect('o.user', 'u')
  .leftJoinAndSelect('o.items', 'i')
  .where('o.id = :id', { id })
  .getOne();
// Rows returned = number of items; TypeORM hydrates one Order with items[]. Fine for one order; multiply by a page of 20 with 2 collections and you have 20 x items x payments rows.

Sequelize example

const order = await Order.findByPk(id, {
  include: [
    { model: User, as: 'user', attributes: ['id', 'email', 'fullName'] },
    { model: OrderItem, as: 'items', separate: true, order: [['id', 'ASC']] },  // separate: second query, no row multiplication
  ],
});

Edge cases & failure modes

  • jsonb_agg over zero rows returns NULL, not []; wrap with coalesce(..., '[]'::jsonb).
  • array_agg of a nullable column includes NULL elements; add FILTER (WHERE col IS NOT NULL).
  • string_agg without ORDER BY returns elements in arbitrary order; two runs differ.
  • count(DISTINCT a, b) is not valid; use count(DISTINCT (a, b)) with a row constructor.
  • Huge JSON documents (thousands of items) built per row blow up memory and response size; paginate the children instead.
  • percentile_cont on interval works; on text it does not (no interpolation); use percentile_disc.
  • Numeric aggregates over numeric columns return numeric with many digits; round for the API.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They return nested documents from SQL when the child set is bounded (items of an order, addresses of a user) and use two queries with = ANY($ids) when it is not. They report percentiles, never just averages, for anything time-like. They use bool_or to derive flags rather than joining and de-duplicating.

Common mistakes

  • count(col) when count(*) was meant, or the reverse.
  • jsonb_agg without coalesce, producing null items arrays in the API.
  • Averages of delivery times.
  • count(DISTINCT ...) on every column "to be safe" on a report that runs every minute.

Interview questions

  1. How do you return an order with its items as nested JSON in one query? Expected: jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(...)) in a LATERAL or scalar subquery with coalesce.
  2. Why is count(DISTINCT x) expensive? Expected: per-group sort or hash to de-duplicate.
  3. Why report p50 and p90 instead of the mean for delivery time? Expected: skewed distributions; a few outliers move the mean.
  4. What does bool_or give you that a join does not? Expected: a group-level flag without row multiplication or DISTINCT.

Practical exercise

Implement GET /orders/:id with the single-query JSON approach and with TypeORM relations. Benchmark both at 200 requests per second for an order with 8 items. Then implement GET /users/:id/orders with items nested for 20 orders per page. Acceptance criteria: identical JSON output, latency comparison recorded, and the page endpoint shows exactly one query in the log.

17.13 Querying jsonb

Concept

jsonb columns are queried with operators and functions: -> (get JSON value by key or index), ->> (get as text), #> / #>> (by path), @> (contains), <@ (is contained by), ? (key exists), ?| / ?& (any/all keys exist), jsonb_path_query / @? / @@ (SQL/JSON path language), jsonb_array_elements (unnest an array into rows), jsonb_each (unnest an object). A GIN index on the column accelerates @>, ?, ?|, ?&, @? and @@. A B-tree expression index on (col->>'key') accelerates equality and range on that one key.

Why does it exist?

products.attributes holds per-product properties that differ by category. The catalog must still filter by them ("8 GB RAM phones under 20,000"), facet them ("count by brand"), and index them. The operators and index types are how PostgreSQL makes a document column behave like columns when you need it to.

How it works

  1. -> returns jsonb, so you can chain: attributes->'dimensions'->>'height'. ->> returns text, the end of a chain. Cast text results to compare numerically: (attributes->>'ram_gb')::int.
  2. @> asks "does the left document contain the right document as a subset" and is the workhorse for equality filters on one or more keys, because it is GIN-indexable with the default jsonb_ops opclass.
  3. jsonb_path_ops is a smaller, faster GIN opclass that supports only @>, @? and @@, not ? key-existence. Choose it when you only need containment.
  4. Range queries (ram_gb >= 8) cannot use GIN containment. Use an expression B-tree index on the cast, or jsonb_path_ops with a path predicate @? '$.ram_gb ? (@ >= 8)' (which GIN supports in a limited way, often falling back to recheck).
  5. Statistics on jsonb are poor: the planner does not know how selective @> '{"brand":"Acme"}' is. Expect mediocre row estimates and check plans.

PostgreSQL example

-- Extraction
SELECT id, name,
       attributes->>'brand'                    AS brand,
       (attributes->>'ram_gb')::int            AS ram_gb,
       attributes->'colors'                    AS colors_json,      -- jsonb array
       attributes#>>'{dimensions,height_mm}'   AS height_mm
FROM products WHERE id = $1;

-- Containment (GIN index products_attributes_gin from the reference schema)
SELECT id, name, price FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"brand": "Acme", "5g": true}' AND is_active
ORDER BY price LIMIT 40;
-- Bitmap Heap Scan on products
--   Recheck Cond: (attributes @> '{"5g": true, "brand": "Acme"}'::jsonb)
--   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on products_attributes_gin

-- Array containment inside the document: products available in blue
SELECT id FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"colors": ["blue"]}';   -- array containment is subset semantics

-- Key existence
SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE attributes ? 'warranty_months';

-- Range on a key: expression index
CREATE INDEX products_attr_ram_idx ON products (((attributes->>'ram_gb')::int)) WHERE attributes ? 'ram_gb';
SELECT id FROM products WHERE (attributes->>'ram_gb')::int >= 8 AND attributes ? 'ram_gb';

-- SQL/JSON path
SELECT id FROM products WHERE attributes @? '$.colors[*] ? (@ == "blue")';
SELECT jsonb_path_query(attributes, '$.dimensions.*') FROM products WHERE id = $1;   -- all dimension values as rows
SELECT id FROM products WHERE jsonb_path_exists(attributes, '$.ram_gb ? (@ >= 8 && @ <= 16)');

-- Faceting: count products per brand within a category (unnest not needed; ->> on a scalar key)
SELECT attributes->>'brand' AS brand, count(*) FROM products
WHERE category_id = $1 AND is_active
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Unnesting arrays to rows: how many products offer each color
SELECT color, count(*)
FROM products, jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes->'colors') AS color
WHERE category_id = $1 GROUP BY color ORDER BY 2 DESC;

-- Updating a document: set one key, delete one key, append to an array
UPDATE products SET attributes = attributes || '{"warranty_months": 24}' WHERE id = $1;
UPDATE products SET attributes = attributes - 'discontinued_reason' WHERE id = $1;
UPDATE products SET attributes = jsonb_set(attributes, '{colors}', (attributes->'colors') || '"red"') WHERE id = $1;
-- Every one of these rewrites the whole row version (MVCC). Fine at catalog write rates; not for counters.

-- Aggregating notification payloads: the "template variables" report
SELECT template, jsonb_object_keys(payload) AS key, count(*)
FROM notifications WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '1 day'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 3 DESC;

TypeORM example

// Containment with a parameter (send the filter as a JSON string; pg casts it to jsonb)
const acme5g = await productRepo.createQueryBuilder('p')
  .where('p.attributes @> :f::jsonb', { f: JSON.stringify({ brand: 'Acme', '5g': true }) })
  .andWhere('p.isActive = true')
  .orderBy('p.price').limit(40)
  .getMany();

// Range on a key
const highRam = await productRepo.createQueryBuilder('p')
  .where(`(p.attributes->>'ram_gb')::int >= :min`, { min: 8 })
  .andWhere(`p.attributes ? 'ram_gb'`)
  .getMany();

Sequelize example

const acme = await Product.findAll({ where: { attributes: { [Op.contains]: { brand: 'Acme', '5g': true } } } });
const highRam = await Product.findAll({ where: literal(`(attributes->>'ram_gb')::int >= 8 AND attributes ? 'ram_gb'`) });

Edge cases & failure modes

  • ->> returns NULL for a missing key and for JSON null; ? distinguishes presence.
  • Comparing attributes->>'price' > '100' compares text: '20' > '100' is true. Cast.
  • @> with a number: '{"ram_gb": 8}' matches 8 but not "8" (string). JSON types matter.
  • GIN index bloat under heavy updates; fastupdate pending list and gin_pending_list_limit.
  • Large documents are TOASTed; extracting one key decompresses the whole document; keep documents small (under a few KB) for hot paths.
  • A parameter typed as text compared with @> fails: cast $1::jsonb explicitly.

Interview questions

  1. Which index for attributes @> '{"brand":"Acme"}' and which for (attributes->>'ram_gb')::int >= 8? Expected: GIN on the column; B-tree expression index on the cast.
  2. jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops? Expected: path_ops is smaller and faster for containment only; no key-existence support.
  3. Why is attributes->>'price' > '100' wrong?

17.14 Dates, times and generating series

Concept

timestamptz arithmetic uses interval: now() - interval '30 days', placed_at + interval '2 hours'. date_trunc('day' | 'week' | 'month' | 'hour', ts) snaps to a boundary. AT TIME ZONE converts between timestamptz and wall-clock timestamp for a zone. generate_series(start, end, step) produces rows for every day (or hour, or minute), which is how reports get zero-filled rows for days with no orders. age(), extract(), date_part(), make_interval(), to_char() round out the toolkit.

Why does it exist?

Every report has a time axis. "Orders per day for March" must show zero for March 15 if there were none, and GROUP BY alone does not produce rows that do not exist. Time zones exist because the customer in Kolkata and the warehouse in Frankfurt disagree about which day it is, and finance wants the report in one of them, consistently.

How it works

  1. date_trunc on timestamptz truncates in the session time zone. To truncate in a specific zone regardless of the session: date_trunc('day', placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata') returns a wall-clock timestamp in that zone; convert back with AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata' if you need an instant. PG12+ also accepts date_trunc('day', placed_at, 'Asia/Kolkata') directly.
  2. interval arithmetic with months and days is calendar-aware: '2026-01-31'::date + interval '1 month' is 2026-02-28. Hours are exact.
  3. generate_series with timestamptz and interval '1 day' respects DST in the session zone (a day can be 23 or 25 hours); with date it steps calendar days.
  4. Range predicates on the raw column stay sargable (section 17.1); date_trunc on the column in WHERE does not.

PostgreSQL example

-- Daily orders and revenue for a month, zero-filled, in IST
WITH days AS (
  SELECT d::date AS day
  FROM generate_series('2026-03-01'::date, '2026-03-31'::date, interval '1 day') d
),
daily AS (
  SELECT (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS day, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01 00:00+05:30' AND placed_at < '2026-04-01 00:00+05:30'   -- sargable
    AND status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT days.day, coalesce(daily.orders, 0) AS orders, coalesce(daily.revenue, 0) AS revenue
FROM days LEFT JOIN daily ON daily.day = days.day
ORDER BY days.day;

-- Hourly heatmap of order placement for capacity planning
SELECT extract(dow FROM placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::int  AS dow,
       extract(hour FROM placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::int AS hour,
       count(*)
FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= now() - interval '8 weeks'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;

-- Week-over-week: current week vs previous week, aligned by weekday
SELECT date_trunc('week', placed_at)::date AS week_start, count(*) AS orders,
       count(*) - lag(count(*)) OVER (ORDER BY date_trunc('week', placed_at)) AS delta
FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= now() - interval '12 weeks'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- Age and SLA checks
SELECT id, now() - placed_at AS age
FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND placed_at < now() - interval '48 hours';   -- paid but not shipped in 2 days

-- Month buckets that respect calendar months
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'), 'YYYY-MM') AS month, sum(total)
FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- Business days between two dates (skip weekends)
SELECT count(*) FROM generate_series('2026-03-02'::date, '2026-03-13'::date, '1 day') d
WHERE extract(isodow FROM d) < 6;   -- 10

-- Epoch conversions for clients that send unix seconds
SELECT to_timestamp(1772323200);                       -- timestamptz
SELECT extract(epoch FROM placed_at)::bigint FROM orders LIMIT 1;

NestJS example

// Reports controller: accept a zone and a month, compute sargable bounds in the app
import { DateTime } from 'luxon';

@Get('daily-revenue')
async dailyRevenue(@Query() q: DailyRevenueDto) {
  const start = DateTime.fromISO(q.month + '-01', { zone: q.zone ?? 'Asia/Kolkata' }).startOf('month');
  const end = start.plus({ months: 1 });
  return this.reports.dailyRevenue(start.toJSDate(), end.toJSDate(), q.zone ?? 'Asia/Kolkata');
}
// The SQL then uses $1/$2 as timestamptz bounds and $3 for AT TIME ZONE, keeping the predicate index-friendly.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • date_trunc('day', ts) in WHERE kills the index; put the truncation in SELECT/GROUP BY and use a range in WHERE.
  • generate_series with timestamptz across DST: days are 23 or 25 hours in zones with DST; India has no DST, but Europe and the US do.
  • now() is fixed for the transaction; a long batch that stamps now() on rows produces identical timestamps.
  • interval '1 month' from January 31 lands on February 28; monthly billing must decide on "same day or last day" explicitly.
  • extract(dow) is 0 (Sunday) to 6; isodow is 1 (Monday) to 7. Mixing them off-by-ones weekly reports.
  • Comparing timestamptz to a date literal uses the session zone's midnight; set the session zone to UTC in the pool and pass explicit offsets in literals.
  • to_char output is locale-influenced for month names; use numeric formats for machine consumption.

Interview questions

  1. How do you get a zero-filled daily report? Expected: generate_series for the axis, LEFT JOIN the aggregate, coalesce.
  2. Why put date_trunc in SELECT but a range in WHERE? Expected: sargability.
  3. What is the difference between AT TIME ZONE on a timestamptz and on a timestamp? Expected: timestamptz AT TIME ZONE gives wall-clock timestamp in that zone; timestamp AT TIME ZONE interprets the wall-clock as that zone and gives a timestamptz.
  4. What is now() inside a transaction?

Practical exercise

Build GET /reports/daily-revenue?month=2026-03&zone=Asia/Kolkata with zero-filled days and a week-over-week delta column, using one query. Verify the day boundaries by inserting orders at 23:59 and 00:01 IST and confirming they land on the right days. Acceptance criteria: 31 rows always returned, boundaries correct, EXPLAIN shows the placed_at index range scan.

17.15 Data modification: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE done properly

17.15.1 INSERT with RETURNING, multi-row inserts and upserts

Concept

INSERT ... RETURNING writes rows and returns any columns of what was written, including database-generated values (id, order_number, created_at), in one round trip. A multi-row INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), (...) or INSERT ... SELECT writes many rows in one statement. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is the upsert: insert, or if a unique key already exists, update that row instead. Part 16 introduced ON CONFLICT as the race-proof "insert if not exists"; this section covers its full update semantics.

Why does it exist?

Without RETURNING, creating an order means INSERT then SELECT ... WHERE id = ? (two round trips, and you need to know the id, which the database generated). Without multi-row inserts, importing 10,000 products is 10,000 round trips at roughly 0.5 ms each, five seconds of mostly network. Without upserts, "set this product's inventory to 40" is a SELECT, a branch, and either an INSERT or an UPDATE, with the race in between.

How it works

  1. RETURNING evaluates the listed expressions against the inserted row after defaults, triggers (BEFORE), and generated columns have been applied. It works for UPDATE and DELETE too (returning the new and the old row respectively).
  2. A multi-row VALUES list is parsed into one plan; rows are inserted in order; constraints are checked per row; the whole statement is atomic. node-postgres has a parameter limit of 65,535 per statement, so batch inserts in chunks (for example 1,000 rows x 10 columns = 10,000 parameters).
  3. ON CONFLICT (target) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col locks the conflicting row and updates it. EXCLUDED is the row you tried to insert. The SET list decides which columns are overwritten; unlisted columns keep their existing values. An optional WHERE on the DO UPDATE decides whether to update at all.
  4. Triggers fire for the path taken: INSERT triggers on insert, UPDATE triggers on the conflict-update path.
  5. With RETURNING, the upsert returns the row as it exists after the statement, whichever path it took.

PostgreSQL example

-- Create an order and get everything the API response needs, one round trip
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, shipping_address_id, currency)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'INR')
RETURNING id, order_number, status, placed_at;

-- Multi-row insert of items with per-row price snapshots from the catalog, and RETURNING for the response
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, product_name)
SELECT $1, p.id, v.qty, p.price, p.name
FROM (VALUES ($2::uuid, $3::int), ($4::uuid, $5::int), ($6::uuid, $7::int)) AS v(product_id, qty)
JOIN products p ON p.id = v.product_id AND p.is_active
RETURNING id, product_id, quantity, unit_price;
-- If a product is inactive it is silently skipped; compare returned count to requested count in the service and roll back if they differ.

-- Bulk import with unnest: one parameter per column, any number of rows
INSERT INTO products (sku, name, category_id, price)
SELECT * FROM unnest($1::text[], $2::text[], $3::bigint[], $4::numeric[]);

-- Upsert: inventory sync from the warehouse system. Set absolute stock; never lower reserved below current.
INSERT INTO inventory (product_id, quantity_on_hand, reorder_level, updated_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, now())
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
   SET quantity_on_hand = EXCLUDED.quantity_on_hand,
       reorder_level    = EXCLUDED.reorder_level,
       updated_at       = now()
 WHERE inventory.quantity_on_hand IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.quantity_on_hand   -- skip no-op updates (no dead tuple)
    OR inventory.reorder_level    IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.reorder_level
RETURNING product_id, quantity_on_hand, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;

-- Upsert that must never regress state: payment webhook that may arrive out of order
INSERT INTO payments (id, order_id, provider, idempotency_key, amount, status, provider_payment_id)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'razorpay', $3, $4, $5, $6)
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO UPDATE
   SET status = EXCLUDED.status, provider_payment_id = EXCLUDED.provider_payment_id, updated_at = now()
 WHERE payments.status NOT IN ('captured', 'refunded')            -- terminal states win
RETURNING id, status;
-- Zero rows returned means the update was refused by the WHERE (already terminal): treat as success, idempotently.

NestJS example

// inventory/inventory.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class InventoryService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /** Bulk stock sync in chunks of 500 to stay under the parameter limit and keep lock time short. */
  async syncStock(rows: Array<{ productId: string; onHand: number; reorderLevel: number }>): Promise<number> {
    let changed = 0;
    for (const chunk of chunked(rows, 500)) {
      const res = await this.ds.query<Array<{ product_id: string }>>(
        `INSERT INTO inventory (product_id, quantity_on_hand, reorder_level, updated_at)
         SELECT * FROM unnest($1::uuid[], $2::int[], $3::int[]) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(product_id, on_hand, reorder_level, ord), now()
         ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
            SET quantity_on_hand = EXCLUDED.quantity_on_hand, reorder_level = EXCLUDED.reorder_level, updated_at = now()
          WHERE inventory.quantity_on_hand IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.quantity_on_hand
             OR inventory.reorder_level IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.reorder_level
         RETURNING product_id`,
        [chunk.map((r) => r.productId), chunk.map((r) => r.onHand), chunk.map((r) => r.reorderLevel)],
      );
      changed += res.length;
    }
    return changed;
  }
}

TypeORM example

// RETURNING via the insert builder
const result = await orderRepo.createQueryBuilder().insert().into(Order)
  .values({ userId, shippingAddressId, currency: 'INR' })
  .returning(['id', 'orderNumber', 'status', 'placedAt'])
  .execute();
const created = result.raw[0];   // { id, order_number, status, placed_at }

// Multi-row insert
await orderItemRepo.createQueryBuilder().insert().into(OrderItem).values(items).execute();

// Upsert with orUpdate: columns to overwrite, conflict target
await inventoryRepo.createQueryBuilder().insert().into(Inventory)
  .values({ productId, quantityOnHand, reorderLevel })
  .orUpdate(['quantity_on_hand', 'reorder_level', 'updated_at'], ['product_id'], { skipUpdateIfNoValuesChanged: true })
  .execute();
// The Repository.upsert(entityOrEntities, ['product_id']) shortcut exists too; neither supports a DO UPDATE ... WHERE guard. Use query() for that.

Sequelize example

const order = await Order.create({ userId, shippingAddressId, currency: 'INR' }, { returning: true });
await OrderItem.bulkCreate(items, { returning: ['id', 'productId', 'quantity', 'unitPrice'] });
await Inventory.bulkCreate(rows, { updateOnDuplicate: ['quantityOnHand', 'reorderLevel', 'updatedAt'], conflictAttributes: ['product_id'] });

Edge cases & failure modes

  • RETURNING reflects BEFORE triggers but not AFTER triggers that modify other rows.
  • Multi-row insert with one bad row fails the whole statement (good: atomic), but the error message names only the first failure.
  • Upsert SET lists that overwrite everything downgrade state; always ask "which columns may this source legitimately change".
  • ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE on a partitioned table requires the conflict target to include the partition key.
  • Parameter limit (65,535) in node-postgres; unnest with array parameters sidesteps it.
  • INSERT ... SELECT from a large table without ORDER BY and with a unique index: fine; with a serial id and expectations of order: no order is guaranteed.

Interview questions

  1. Why RETURNING instead of insert-then-select? Expected: one round trip; database-generated values; consistent snapshot.
  2. How do you bulk insert 100,000 rows from Node without hitting the parameter limit? Expected: chunking, unnest arrays, or COPY.
  3. How do you make an upsert never regress a terminal state? Expected: DO UPDATE ... WHERE existing.status NOT IN (terminal).

17.15.2 UPDATE ... FROM and DELETE ... USING

Concept

UPDATE target SET ... FROM other WHERE join_condition updates rows in target using values from other (a table, a VALUES list, or a subquery), joined in the same statement. DELETE FROM target USING other WHERE ... deletes rows in target that match rows in other. Both replace the correlated-subquery form (SET x = (SELECT ... WHERE ...)) with a join, which is faster and clearer.

How it works

  1. The planner joins target with the FROM/USING sources like a normal query.
  2. Each target row that appears in the join output is updated or deleted once. If a target row matches multiple source rows, PostgreSQL updates it with one of them, arbitrarily; this is a silent bug when the join is not 1:1. Ensure the source is unique per target row (pre-aggregate or DISTINCT ON).
  3. Row locks are taken on target rows as they are found; a large UPDATE ... FROM holds many locks until commit. Batch by key range for large tables.

PostgreSQL example

-- Re-price order items in pending orders from the current catalog (a business decision; shown for the syntax)
UPDATE order_items oi
   SET unit_price = p.price
  FROM products p, orders o
 WHERE p.id = oi.product_id AND o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status = 'pending' AND oi.unit_price <> p.price;

-- Apply a VALUES list of corrections in one statement
UPDATE products p
   SET price = v.new_price, updated_at = now()
  FROM (VALUES ('PHN-001', 47999.00), ('CBL-77', 449.00)) AS v(sku, new_price)
 WHERE p.sku = v.sku;

-- Mark orders as shipped from a shipments batch, with RETURNING for the notification job
UPDATE orders o
   SET status = 'shipped', updated_at = now()
  FROM shipments s
 WHERE s.order_id = o.id AND s.shipped_at >= now() - interval '1 hour' AND o.status = 'paid'
RETURNING o.id, o.user_id, s.tracking_number;

-- The multi-match trap: an order with two shipments matches twice; the update still happens once, with an arbitrary s.tracking_number in RETURNING.
-- Fix with DISTINCT ON in a subquery:
UPDATE orders o SET status = 'shipped'
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ON (order_id) order_id, tracking_number FROM shipments ORDER BY order_id, shipped_at DESC) s
 WHERE s.order_id = o.id AND o.status = 'paid';

-- DELETE ... USING: purge notifications of deleted users
DELETE FROM notifications n
 USING users u
 WHERE u.id = n.user_id AND u.deleted_at < now() - interval '30 days';

-- Batched delete for large purges: bounded lock time, vacuum can keep up
DELETE FROM notifications
 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM notifications WHERE status = 'sent' AND sent_at < now() - interval '180 days' LIMIT 5000);
-- Loop in the application until 0 rows affected, sleeping 50 ms between batches.

TypeORM example

// UPDATE ... FROM is not expressible in QueryBuilder's update(); use query():
await ds.query(
  `UPDATE products p SET price = v.new_price, updated_at = now()
     FROM unnest($1::text[], $2::numeric[]) AS v(sku, new_price)
    WHERE p.sku = v.sku`,
  [skus, prices],
);
// Simple updates are fine in the builder:
await productRepo.createQueryBuilder().update(Product).set({ isActive: false }).where('categoryId = :c', { c }).execute();

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Multiple source matches per target row: arbitrary pick, silent.
  • UPDATE without WHERE updates every row (section 17.21) and locks the whole table's rows until commit.
  • UPDATE on the same row twice in one statement is not possible; PostgreSQL updates once and ignores the second match.
  • Large updates create a dead tuple per row; a 50-million-row update doubles the table until vacuum; batch it.

Interview questions

  1. What happens when UPDATE ... FROM joins one target row to two source rows? Expected: updated once with an arbitrary source; de-duplicate the source.
  2. Why batch large deletes? Expected: bounded locks, WAL, and bloat; vacuum can keep up; replication lag stays small.

17.16 Locking reads: FOR UPDATE, SKIP LOCKED, FOR NO KEY UPDATE

Concept

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads rows and locks them as if you were about to update them, so no other transaction can update, delete, or lock them FOR UPDATE until you commit. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is a slightly weaker lock that still blocks concurrent updates but does not block other transactions inserting child rows that reference the row (foreign key KEY SHARE locks). FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE are read locks that block writers but not other readers. SKIP LOCKED makes the select skip rows that are already locked instead of waiting; NOWAIT makes it error immediately. Together, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the PostgreSQL job-queue pattern: many workers, each claims different rows, none waits.

Why does it exist?

"Read the stock, check it, decrement it" is a race: two transactions read 5, both see enough for 3, both decrement, stock is negative (or the CHECK fails for one after it has done other work). FOR UPDATE serializes the read-check-write on that row. Job queues in the database exist because a table with status = 'pending' plus SKIP LOCKED gives you a transactional queue with no extra infrastructure, exactly-once processing within a transaction, and visibility via SQL, up to a few thousand jobs per second.

Mental model

Imagine a library with one copy of a popular book. FOR UPDATE is taking the book to your desk: anyone else who wants it waits. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is the same, except people are still allowed to add the book to their reading list (insert a child row) while you have it. SKIP LOCKED is walking along a shelf of pending returns and picking up the first book that nobody else is holding.

How it works

  1. The SELECT finds rows normally, then for each row takes a row-level lock by writing the transaction id into the tuple header (xmax) with a lock-mode flag. Row locks live in the heap, not in a lock table, so locking a million rows does not exhaust memory (but does dirty a million pages).
  2. A conflicting locker waits (default), errors (NOWAIT), or skips (SKIP LOCKED).
  3. Locks are released at transaction end. Holding them across an HTTP call or a sleep is how you create lock queues.
  4. FOR UPDATE conflicts with FOR KEY SHARE, which foreign key checks take on the parent row. So locking an orders row FOR UPDATE blocks inserting order_items for that order in another transaction. FOR NO KEY UPDATE does not, and is what UPDATE of non-key columns takes by default. Prefer FOR NO KEY UPDATE unless you intend to change the key or delete.
  5. SKIP LOCKED with LIMIT and an index on the queue predicate gives each worker a disjoint batch. The lock is the claim; the UPDATE ... SET status = 'processing' makes the claim visible to non-locking readers and survives the worker's transaction commit.
  6. Deadlocks: two transactions locking rows in opposite order. PostgreSQL detects after deadlock_timeout (1 s) and aborts one. Always lock in a consistent order (by primary key) when locking several rows. Part 20 (Transactions) covers this in depth.

PostgreSQL example

-- Reserve stock safely: read-check-write under a row lock
BEGIN;
SELECT quantity_on_hand - quantity_reserved AS available
  FROM inventory WHERE product_id = $1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
-- application checks available >= requested; if not, ROLLBACK and return 409
UPDATE inventory SET quantity_reserved = quantity_reserved + $2, updated_at = now() WHERE product_id = $1;
COMMIT;
-- Or skip the select entirely and let the CHECK constraint decide (Part 16): a single UPDATE with RETURNING is both atomic and race-free.

-- Lock several rows in a deterministic order to avoid deadlocks
SELECT product_id FROM inventory WHERE product_id = ANY($1::uuid[]) ORDER BY product_id FOR NO KEY UPDATE;

-- The job queue: claim up to 10 due notifications, skipping ones other workers hold
WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id
    FROM notifications
   WHERE status = 'pending' AND scheduled_at <= now()
   ORDER BY scheduled_at
   LIMIT 10
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE notifications n
   SET status = 'processing', attempts = attempts + 1
  FROM claimed
 WHERE n.id = claimed.id
RETURNING n.id, n.user_id, n.channel, n.template, n.payload;
-- Uses notifications_pending_idx (partial, on scheduled_at WHERE status = 'pending').
-- Workers commit this claim, do the send, then UPDATE ... SET status = 'sent' | 'failed' in a second transaction.
-- If a worker dies after claiming, the row stays 'processing'; a reaper resets rows in 'processing' older than N minutes.

-- NOWAIT for "try to lock, fail fast" (admin actions)
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;   -- ERROR 55P03 lock_not_available if someone holds it

-- Seeing who holds what
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';
SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, left(blocking.query, 60)
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid));

NestJS example

A worker using the claim pattern with @nestjs/schedule:

// notifications/notification-worker.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

interface Job { id: string; user_id: string; channel: 'email' | 'sms' | 'push'; template: string; payload: Record<string, unknown> }

@Injectable()
export class NotificationWorker {
  private readonly log = new Logger(NotificationWorker.name);
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly sender: NotificationSender) {}

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_5_SECONDS)
  async tick(): Promise<void> {
    // 1. Claim in a short transaction; locks are released at commit so other workers proceed immediately.
    const jobs = await this.ds.transaction(async (m) =>
      m.query<Job[]>(
        `WITH claimed AS (
           SELECT id FROM notifications
            WHERE status = 'pending' AND scheduled_at <= now()
            ORDER BY scheduled_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
         UPDATE notifications n SET status = 'processing', attempts = attempts + 1
           FROM claimed WHERE n.id = claimed.id
         RETURNING n.id, n.user_id, n.channel, n.template, n.payload`,
      ),
    );

    // 2. Do the slow work outside any transaction; no locks held while calling the provider.
    for (const job of jobs) {
      try {
        await this.sender.send(job);   // has its own timeout (Part 30 - Resilience)
        await this.ds.query(`UPDATE notifications SET status = 'sent', sent_at = now() WHERE id = $1`, [job.id]);
      } catch (err) {
        this.log.warn(`notification ${job.id} failed: ${(err as Error).message}`);
        // 3. Retry with backoff up to 5 attempts, then park as failed.
        await this.ds.query(
          `UPDATE notifications
              SET status = CASE WHEN attempts >= 5 THEN 'failed' ELSE 'pending' END,
                  scheduled_at = now() + make_interval(secs => least(600, 10 * power(2, attempts)))
            WHERE id = $1`,
          [job.id],
        );
      }
    }
  }
}

TypeORM example

// Pessimistic locks in QueryBuilder
const inv = await manager.getRepository(Inventory).createQueryBuilder('i')
  .setLock('pessimistic_write')            // FOR UPDATE ; 'pessimistic_partial_write' -> FOR NO KEY UPDATE
  .where('i.productId = :id', { id })
  .getOne();

// SKIP LOCKED
const jobs = await manager.getRepository(Notification).createQueryBuilder('n')
  .setLock('pessimistic_write')
  .setOnLocked('skip_locked')              // or 'nowait'
  .where("n.status = 'pending' AND n.scheduledAt <= now()")
  .orderBy('n.scheduledAt').limit(10)
  .getMany();
// These must run inside a transaction (manager from dataSource.transaction), or the lock is released immediately.

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const inv = await Inventory.findOne({ where: { productId }, lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE, transaction: t });   // FOR UPDATE
  const jobs = await Notification.findAll({
    where: { status: 'pending', scheduledAt: { [Op.lte]: new Date() } },
    order: [['scheduledAt', 'ASC']], limit: 10,
    lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE, skipLocked: true, transaction: t,
  });
});
