// Sequelize has LOCK.UPDATE, LOCK.SHARE, LOCK.KEY_SHARE, LOCK.NO_KEY_UPDATE.

Production scenario

A notification queue in PostgreSQL with 8 workers, each claiming 10 rows every 5 seconds, sustains about 1,500 sends per minute with average claim latency of 1 ms and zero duplicate sends. The partial index keeps the claim query fast even with 50 million historical rows, because only pending rows are in it. At around 5,000 jobs per second the pattern starts to strain (index contention on the hot left edge, vacuum of the churned rows), and a dedicated broker (Part 27 — Messaging) becomes the better tool.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call got paged: checkout p99 at 12 seconds. pg_stat_activity showed 60 sessions waiting on a row lock in inventory. The blocking session was a "reserve stock" transaction that did SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then called the fraud-check API (p99 8 s, and it was having a bad night), then updated. Every other checkout for that popular product queued behind the API call. The fix was to move the external call before the transaction and shrink the locked region to the read-check-write only, roughly 2 ms. The rule: never hold a row lock across a network call.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lock held across an external call or a sleep: lock queue; everything for that row waits.
  • FOR UPDATE on a parent row blocks child inserts (FK KEY SHARE conflict); use FOR NO KEY UPDATE.
  • SKIP LOCKED without ORDER BY and an index: workers scan the table; with a partial index they read only pending rows.
  • A crashed worker leaves rows in processing; a reaper with a timeout is mandatory.
  • FOR UPDATE with LIMIT and a join can lock more rows than returned in some plans; keep the locking query simple (single table, indexed predicate).
  • FOR UPDATE cannot be used with GROUP BY, DISTINCT, window functions, or in a view with aggregates.
  • Under REPEATABLE READ, a FOR UPDATE on a row updated by a concurrent committed transaction fails with a serialization error; retry the transaction.
  • Deadlocks from inconsistent lock order; always ORDER BY primary key when locking multiple rows.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They lock the minimum rows, for the minimum time, in a consistent order, and never across I/O. They prefer a single atomic UPDATE with a CHECK constraint to a SELECT FOR UPDATE followed by a decision in code, when the rule can be expressed in SQL. They use SKIP LOCKED queues for moderate volumes and value their simplicity: one system, transactional, observable with SELECT.

Common mistakes

  • FOR UPDATE outside a transaction (locks released immediately; TypeORM setLock without transaction is a no-op protection).
  • Forgetting the reaper for stuck processing rows.
  • Locking the parent order FOR UPDATE while inserting items in another transaction.
  • Polling the queue with SELECT count(*) on a table with 50 million rows.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED job queue. Expected: claim in a short transaction with LIMIT, mark as processing, release locks, do the work, mark done; reaper for stuck rows; partial index on pending.
  2. FOR UPDATE vs FOR NO KEY UPDATE? Expected: the latter does not block FK child inserts; use it unless deleting or changing the key.
  3. Why is holding a row lock across an HTTP call dangerous?
  4. How does PostgreSQL store row locks? Expected: in the tuple header (xmax and flags), not a central lock table.
  5. When should the PostgreSQL queue give way to a broker? Expected: thousands of jobs per second, fan-out to many consumers, or replay requirements.

Practical exercise

Implement the notification worker with SKIP LOCKED, run four instances against a table with 100,000 pending rows, and verify with a sent_count per id that no notification is sent twice. Kill one worker mid-batch and verify the reaper recovers its rows. Acceptance criteria: zero duplicates, all rows reach sent or failed, claim latency under 5 ms measured from the worker.

17.17 COPY, TRUNCATE and a first look at EXPLAIN

17.17.1 COPY for bulk load and export

COPY streams rows between a table and a file or the client connection in text, CSV or binary form. It bypasses per-row statement overhead and is the fastest way to load data: 100,000 to 500,000 rows per second on ordinary hardware, versus 5,000 to 20,000 with batched inserts.

-- Server-side file (requires superuser or pg_read_server_files; the file is on the DB server)
COPY products (sku, name, category_id, price) FROM '/imports/products.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true);

-- Client-side via psql (\copy reads the local file and streams it)
\copy products (sku, name, category_id, price) FROM 'products.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)

-- Export a report to CSV
\copy (SELECT id, order_number, total, placed_at FROM orders WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01') TO 'march_orders.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)

From Node, the pg-copy-streams package pipes a readable stream into COPY ... FROM STDIN:

import { from as copyFrom } from 'pg-copy-streams';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';

const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('BEGIN');
  const ingest = client.query(copyFrom(`COPY products_staging (sku, name, category_id, price) FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)`));
  await pipeline(createReadStream('products.csv'), ingest);
  // Validate and merge from staging with ON CONFLICT; constraints on the real table stay on.
  await client.query(`INSERT INTO products (sku, name, category_id, price)
                      SELECT sku, name, category_id, price FROM products_staging
                      ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, price = EXCLUDED.price`);
  await client.query('COMMIT');
} catch (e) { await client.query('ROLLBACK'); throw e; } finally { client.release(); }

Load into a staging table first: COPY fails the whole statement on the first bad row, and merging from staging lets you validate, de-duplicate and upsert with normal SQL. For very large loads, drop non-unique indexes on the staging table, load, then create them.

17.17.2 TRUNCATE

TRUNCATE table removes all rows instantly by replacing the table's data files, instead of deleting row by row. It is transactional in PostgreSQL (can be rolled back), takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (blocks everything on that table, briefly), resets nothing unless you say RESTART IDENTITY, and refuses to run if another table references this one by foreign key unless you add CASCADE (which truncates the referencing tables too; read that twice). It does not fire DELETE triggers. Use it for staging and test tables; never on a table with foreign-key children in production without checking what CASCADE would reach.

TRUNCATE products_staging;
TRUNCATE order_items, orders RESTART IDENTITY;    -- both at once, sequence reset
-- TRUNCATE orders;  -> ERROR: cannot truncate a table referenced in a foreign key constraint

17.17.3 Reading EXPLAIN, the minimum

Part 19 is the deep dive. For now, the five things to read in every plan:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, o.total FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = $1 ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Limit  (cost=0.56..45.21 rows=20 width=24) (actual time=0.031..0.062 rows=20 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan using orders_user_id_placed_at_idx on orders o  (cost=0.56..312.40 rows=140 width=24) (actual time=0.029..0.055 rows=20 loops=1)
--         Index Cond: (user_id = 'a1b2...'::uuid)
--   Buffers: shared hit=6
-- Planning Time: 0.140 ms
-- Execution Time: 0.085 ms
  1. The scan type on each table. Index Scan / Index Only Scan / Bitmap Heap Scan are index-driven; Seq Scan reads the whole table, which is right for small tables or big reports and wrong for a point lookup.
  2. Index Cond versus Filter. Index Cond is what the index answered; Filter is what was checked row by row afterwards. Rows Removed by Filter in the thousands means the index did not cover the predicate.
  3. rows= estimated versus actual rows=. A 10x mismatch means stale statistics or a predicate the planner cannot estimate (jsonb, correlated columns), and every decision downstream (join algorithm, sort strategy) was made on wrong information.
  4. loops=. A node with loops=100000 ran 100,000 times; multiply its time by loops.
  5. Buffers: shared hit / read. Hit is from memory, read is from disk. read in the tens of thousands on an OLTP query means the working set does not fit or the query touches far more than it needs.
  6. Then the join nodes (section 17.2) and Sort Method (section 17.4): external merge means a disk sort.

EXPLAIN alone shows the plan without running it (safe for UPDATE/DELETE). EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement; wrap data-modifying statements in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.

17.18 The query-writing process a senior follows

Concept

A senior engineer does not write a query and ship it. They write it for correctness, check the plan, add or confirm the index, and verify it against production-sized data. The four steps take ten minutes and prevent most of the database incidents in this book.

Why does it exist?

Queries behave differently at 1,000 rows and 100 million rows. Development databases have 1,000 rows. Every query works in development. The planner picks different algorithms based on row counts and statistics, so a query that runs in 2 ms on a laptop can run in 40 seconds in production with the identical plan shape but different inputs, or with a completely different plan. The process exists to make the production behavior visible before production.

How it works

Step 1: Write for correctness. Name the grain of every table in FROM. State in a comment which rows you want and what could duplicate them. Handle NULLs explicitly. Use EXISTS, not NOT IN. Put outer-join filters in ON. Add a unique tiebreaker to every ORDER BY used for pagination. Return only the columns you need.

Step 2: Check the plan. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) against a database with realistic row counts (a masked production snapshot, or a seeded table with the right cardinality). Look for: Seq Scan on a large table in an OLTP query, Rows Removed by Filter large, loops= large, Sort Method: external, Batches > 1, and estimated-vs-actual mismatches. For parameterized queries, test with representative parameters, including the worst case (the customer with 50,000 orders, the category with 200,000 products).

Step 3: Add the index, or reshape the query. If the plan shows a filter that should have been an index condition, add the index (composite, in the right column order, with the right direction, partial if the predicate is fixed). If the plan shows row explosion, pre-aggregate. If it shows OFFSET, switch to keyset. If it shows a correlated SubPlan with a big loop count, use a derived table or window. Re-run step 2.

Step 4: Verify with real volume and real concurrency. Run the query at production data size, then run it under the expected concurrency (a small load test), and watch pg_stat_statements for mean and p99 time, rows, and shared_blks_read. Confirm the index is actually used in production plans (auto_explain for slow queries). Add the query's expected latency to the endpoint's SLO.

Then, and only then, wrap it in the ORM or repository method, with the raw SQL preserved in a comment or a .sql file so the next engineer can run it in psql.

Practical example

Request: "Show a customer's 20 most recent orders with item count and latest payment status."

Step 1 draft:

-- Grain: one row per order. Items pre-aggregated; latest payment via LATERAL (top-1). No 1:N join at order grain.
SELECT o.id, o.order_number, o.status, o.total, o.placed_at,
       coalesce(ic.n, 0) AS item_count,
       lp.status         AS latest_payment_status
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = o.id) ic ON true
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT status FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1) lp ON true
WHERE o.user_id = $1
ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC
LIMIT 20;

Step 2 plan (production snapshot, a customer with 3,000 orders):

Limit (actual rows=20 loops=1)
  -> Nested Loop Left Join (actual rows=20 loops=1)
       -> Nested Loop Left Join (actual rows=20 loops=1)
            -> Index Scan using orders_user_id_placed_at_idx on orders o (actual rows=20 loops=1)
                 Index Cond: (user_id = $1)
            -> Aggregate (actual rows=1 loops=20)
                 -> Index Only Scan using order_items_order_id_product_id_key on order_items oi (actual rows=3 loops=20)
       -> Limit (actual rows=1 loops=20)
            -> Index Scan Backward using payments_order_id_created_at_idx on payments p (actual rows=1 loops=20)
Buffers: shared hit=112
Execution Time: 0.412 ms

Twenty outer rows, each side a small indexed probe, 112 buffers, sub-millisecond. The LIMIT stops the outer scan at 20 rows regardless of how many orders the customer has, because the index provides the sort order. Ship it.

Contrast the naive version, LEFT JOIN order_items and LEFT JOIN payments at order grain with count(DISTINCT oi.id) and max(p.created_at), which has to read all 3,000 orders and all their children before it can LIMIT, and multiplies rows on the way.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask the mantra questions of every query: Can it become slow (what is the largest parameter value in production)? Can it return a wrong response (nulls, duplicates, outer-join filters)? Can it partially succeed (multi-statement without a transaction)? Can it lock (does it hold rows across I/O)? They know that "works on my machine" is a statement about row counts, not correctness.

Common mistakes

  • Testing only against the seed data.
  • Reading the plan without ANALYZE (estimates only) or without BUFFERS (no I/O visibility).
  • Adding an index for the wrong column order and never checking whether it was used.
  • Shipping the ORM query without ever seeing the SQL it generates.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through how you would take a new query from draft to production. Expected: correctness, plan on realistic data, index or reshape, verify under volume and concurrency, monitor.
  2. What is the worst-case parameter for a query, and why test it? Expected: the customer or category with the most rows; plans change with cardinality.

17.19 SQL through the ORMs, and when to go raw

17.19.1 TypeORM: QueryBuilder and raw queries

Concept

TypeORM offers three levels: the Repository API (find, findOne, save, update), the QueryBuilder (a fluent SQL builder that still maps to entities or raw rows), and dataSource.query() (raw SQL with positional parameters). Each level down gives more control and less mapping.

How it works

  • Repository.find({ where, relations, order, take, skip, select }) generates a SELECT with LEFT JOINs for relations. With take and a joined collection, TypeORM issues two queries (ids first) to keep the limit on the root entity.
  • createQueryBuilder('alias') builds SQL piece by piece. getMany() hydrates entities (and de-duplicates joined collections); getRawMany() returns rows as the driver gives them (use for aggregates and computed columns); getRawAndEntities() returns both.
  • Parameters are named (:name) in the builder and positional ($1) in query(). Never interpolate values into strings; always use parameters.
  • query() returns plain rows; column names are as PostgreSQL returns them (snake_case), and numeric/bigint are strings.
// Repository level: simple, readable, limited
const orders = await orderRepo.find({
  where: { userId, status: In(['paid', 'shipped']) },
  order: { placedAt: 'DESC', id: 'DESC' },
  take: 20,
  select: { id: true, orderNumber: true, status: true, total: true, placedAt: true },
});

// QueryBuilder level: joins with conditions, aggregates, subqueries
const rows = await orderRepo.createQueryBuilder('o')
  .select(['o.id AS id', 'o.total AS total'])
  .addSelect((qb) => qb.select('count(*)').from(OrderItem, 'oi').where('oi.order_id = o.id'), 'item_count')
  .leftJoin('o.payments', 'p', "p.status = 'captured'")
  .addSelect('p.amount', 'captured_amount')
  .where('o.userId = :userId', { userId })
  .orderBy('o.placedAt', 'DESC').addOrderBy('o.id', 'DESC')
  .limit(20)                      // limit() is raw SQL LIMIT; take() is entity-aware pagination
  .getRawMany<{ id: string; total: string; item_count: string; captured_amount: string | null }>();

// Seeing the SQL before it runs
const sql = orderRepo.createQueryBuilder('o').where('o.userId = :userId', { userId }).getSql();
// Or enable logging: ['query'] in the DataSource for development.

// Raw level: anything PostgreSQL can do
const detail = await dataSource.query(
  `SELECT o.id, jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('name', oi.product_name, 'qty', oi.quantity) ORDER BY oi.id) AS items
     FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.id = $1 GROUP BY o.id`,
  [orderId],
);

// Raw inside a transaction, sharing the connection
await dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  await manager.query(`UPDATE inventory SET quantity_reserved = quantity_reserved + $2 WHERE product_id = $1`, [productId, qty]);
  await manager.getRepository(OrderItem).insert({ orderId, productId, quantity: qty, unitPrice, productName });
});

Pitfalls specific to TypeORM SQL generation:

  • take()/skip() with joins produce the two-query pattern and a DISTINCT subquery that can be slow; for large pages, fetch ids with a raw keyset query and then load entities WHERE id IN (...).
  • leftJoinAndSelect of two collections multiplies rows before hydration. Load the second collection with a separate query or relationLoadStrategy: 'query'.
  • find({ where: { relation: { field } } }) generates a join; check the SQL, it is not always the join you expect.
  • save() on an entity with relations issues a SELECT first (to diff) and then the writes; for hot paths, use insert()/update() which do not.
  • Entity hydration for 10,000 rows is slow (milliseconds per thousand); use getRawMany for reports and exports.

17.19.2 Sequelize: findAll with include, literal, and raw query

Concept

Sequelize's findAll with include generates joins; attributes with fn/col/literal inserts expressions; sequelize.query runs raw SQL with named replacements or bind parameters and can map results to a model.

// Include with conditions, attributes, and pagination
const orders = await Order.findAll({
  where: { userId, status: { [Op.in]: ['paid', 'shipped'] } },
  attributes: ['id', 'orderNumber', 'status', 'total', 'placedAt'],
  include: [
    { model: Payment, as: 'payments', required: false, where: { status: 'captured' }, attributes: ['amount'] },
    { model: OrderItem, as: 'items', separate: true, attributes: ['productName', 'quantity'] },   // second query; no multiplication
  ],
  order: [['placedAt', 'DESC'], ['id', 'DESC']],
  limit: 20,
  subQuery: false,   // avoid the wrapped subquery Sequelize generates for limit + hasMany include; verify the SQL
});

// Aggregates with fn/col/literal
const perDay = await Order.findAll({
  attributes: [
    [fn('date_trunc', 'day', col('placed_at')), 'day'],
    [fn('count', col('id')), 'orders'],
    [fn('sum', col('total')), 'revenue'],
    [literal(`count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled')`), 'cancelled'],
  ],
  where: { placedAt: { [Op.gte]: from, [Op.lt]: to } },
  group: [fn('date_trunc', 'day', col('placed_at'))],
  order: [[literal('day'), 'ASC']],
  raw: true,
});

// Raw with replacements (escaped and interpolated) or bind (true parameters; preferred)
const [rows] = await sequelize.query(
  `SELECT o.id, lp.status AS latest_payment_status
     FROM orders o
     LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT status FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1) lp ON true
    WHERE o.user_id = $userId ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC LIMIT $limit`,
  { bind: { userId, limit: 20 }, type: QueryTypes.SELECT },
);

// Raw mapped to a model
const mapped = await sequelize.query(`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 LIMIT 20`, { bind: [userId], model: Order, mapToModel: true });

// Seeing the SQL
const sql = await Order.findAll({ where: { userId }, logging: console.log });

Pitfalls specific to Sequelize:

  • limit with a hasMany include and the default subQuery: true wraps the parent query in a subquery with the limit, which is correct but often slow; separate: true on the include is usually the better fix.
  • Two hasMany includes without separate produce a Cartesian product; count() with includes needs distinct: true.
  • replacements escape and interpolate into the SQL string; bind sends real parameters. Prefer bind.
  • raw: true returns flat objects with dotted keys for included models ('items.productName') unless nest: true.
  • paranoid filtering does not apply to raw queries.

17.19.3 When raw SQL is simply better

Decision table:

Need ORM API Raw SQL
CRUD by primary key, simple filters, entity hydration yes no need
Simple joins for a detail page yes (relations / include) fine either way
Aggregates and reports builder with getRawMany / fn + literal usually clearer
Window functions awkward (literal in a subquery) yes
Recursive CTEs not supported yes
LATERAL joins not supported yes
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE guards partial (orUpdate, updateOnDuplicate) yes for guards
UPDATE ... FROM, DELETE ... USING no yes
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with LIMIT and RETURNING in one statement partial (setLock + setOnLocked) yes
jsonb_agg nested documents via addSelect with raw expression yes
COPY no yes (pg-copy-streams)
Keyset pagination with row-value comparison via where with raw expression yes

The rule that keeps teams sane: the ORM is for the 80 percent of queries that are boring, and raw SQL lives in repository classes with typed result interfaces, unit-tested against a real database, for the 20 percent that are not. Nobody scatters query() calls across controllers; nobody forces a recursive CTE through a query builder.

Production scenario

A NestJS service with 140 endpoints: 110 use Repository/Model APIs, 20 use the builder for filtered lists with aggregates, 10 use raw SQL in repository classes (order detail JSON, category subtree, job claim, keyset lists, upserts with guards, a cohort report). The raw queries are the ones that appear in pg_stat_statements as the most executed; they are the ones worth the extra care, and the ones that were tuned with EXPLAIN before shipping.

Failure scenario

A team standardized on "never write SQL; the ORM will handle it". The order-list page used find({ relations: ['items', 'payments', 'shipments'], take: 20 }). In development it was fine. In production, a customer with 800 orders, 3 items each, 2 payments each, 1 shipment each made TypeORM generate a join returning 800 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 4,800 rows, then a DISTINCT subquery for the two-query pagination, then hydration of thousands of entities to return 20. Two seconds per page load and 40 MB of heap per request. The fix was one raw query with LATERAL and jsonb_agg, 3 ms, written by an engineer who read the generated SQL first.

Interview questions

  1. When do you drop from the ORM to raw SQL? Expected: window functions, recursive CTEs, LATERAL, guarded upserts, UPDATE ... FROM, SKIP LOCKED claims, nested JSON; anywhere the builder obscures the plan.
  2. What does TypeORM do with take() plus a joined collection? Expected: two queries, ids first with a DISTINCT subquery.
  3. What is the difference between Sequelize replacements and bind? Expected: string interpolation with escaping vs true bind parameters.
  4. How do you keep raw SQL maintainable in a NestJS codebase? Expected: repository classes, typed result interfaces, integration tests against a real database, SQL visible in psql.

Practical exercise

Take the order-list endpoint with items and latest payment. Implement it three ways: Repository.find with relations, QueryBuilder with getRawMany, and raw SQL with LATERAL and jsonb_agg. Log the generated SQL for each, capture plans, and load-test at 100 requests per second for a customer with 1,000 orders. Acceptance criteria: identical JSON from all three; a table of p50/p99 latency and rows transferred; a written recommendation.

17.20 SQL cookbook: production queries on the e-commerce schema

Each recipe is a query you will actually need, written the way a senior would write it, with two or three lines on why. All run against the reference schema (Part 16, section 16.3). Two recipes (wallet balance, cohort retention) add a small table or use users.created_at; the DDL is included where needed.

17.20.1 Top 10 customers per month by realized revenue

WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS month,
         o.user_id,
         sum(o.total) AS revenue,
         count(*)     AS orders
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
    AND o.placed_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00+05:30' AND o.placed_at < '2026-07-01 00:00+05:30'
  GROUP BY 1, 2
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY revenue DESC, user_id) AS rn
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT r.month, r.rn, u.email, r.revenue, r.orders
FROM ranked r JOIN users u ON u.id = r.user_id
WHERE r.rn <= 10
ORDER BY r.month, r.rn;

Aggregate first at (month, user) grain, then rank inside each month with row_number and a deterministic tiebreaker, then join users only for the 60 rows that survive. Joining users before aggregating would hash 1.2 million users for nothing.

17.20.2 Revenue by category with parent subtotals and a grand total

SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(parent.name) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE coalesce(parent.name, child.name) END AS parent_category,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(child.name)  = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE child.name END                          AS category,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue,
       count(DISTINCT o.id)             AS orders
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o          ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
JOIN products p        ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN categories child  ON child.id = p.category_id
LEFT JOIN categories parent ON parent.id = child.parent_id
WHERE o.placed_at >= '2026-03-01' AND o.placed_at < '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY ROLLUP (parent.name, child.name)
ORDER BY GROUPING(parent.name), parent.name, GROUPING(child.name), child.name;

ROLLUP produces leaf rows, per-parent subtotals and the grand total in one scan. GROUPING() distinguishes a subtotal row from a real NULL parent (a top-level category). Revenue is computed from order_items (the invoice grain), not orders.total, so discounts and multi-category orders are attributed correctly.

17.20.3 An order with its items, customer and latest payment as one JSON document

SELECT o.id, o.order_number, o.status, o.total, o.currency, o.placed_at,
       jsonb_build_object('id', u.id, 'email', u.email, 'name', u.full_name)                 AS customer,
       (SELECT jsonb_build_object('line1', a.line1, 'city', a.city, 'postalCode', a.postal_code, 'country', a.country_code)
          FROM addresses a WHERE a.id = o.shipping_address_id)                                  AS shipping_address,
       coalesce((SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('productId', oi.product_id, 'name', oi.product_name,
                                                     'quantity', oi.quantity, 'unitPrice', oi.unit_price,
                                                     'lineTotal', oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) ORDER BY oi.id)
                   FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id = o.id), '[]'::jsonb)               AS items,
       (SELECT jsonb_build_object('status', p.status, 'amount', p.amount, 'provider', p.provider, 'at', p.created_at)
          FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 1)          AS latest_payment
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.id = $1;

One round trip returns the whole document; each scalar subquery is a single index probe, so this is about 0.3 ms. coalesce turns a missing items array into [] rather than null.

17.20.4 Latest payment per order for a batch of orders

-- Small batch (a page of orders): LATERAL, one probe per order
SELECT o.id, lp.*
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT p.id AS payment_id, p.status, p.amount, p.created_at
  FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 1
) lp ON true
WHERE o.id = ANY($1::uuid[]);

-- Whole table (a report): DISTINCT ON, one pass
SELECT DISTINCT ON (p.order_id) p.order_id, p.id AS payment_id, p.status, p.amount, p.created_at
FROM payments p
ORDER BY p.order_id, p.created_at DESC;

LATERAL wins when the outer set is small because it probes payments_order_id_created_at_idx per order. DISTINCT ON wins over millions of rows because it is a single sorted pass (and that index provides the sort). Both are top-1-per-group; pick by outer cardinality.

17.20.5 Inventory at or below reorder level, with pending demand

SELECT p.sku, p.name, i.quantity_on_hand, i.quantity_reserved,
       i.quantity_on_hand - i.quantity_reserved AS available,
       i.reorder_level,
       coalesce(pd.pending_qty, 0)              AS pending_demand
FROM inventory i
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id AND p.is_active
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT sum(oi.quantity) AS pending_qty
  FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE oi.product_id = i.product_id AND o.status = 'pending'
) pd ON true
WHERE i.quantity_on_hand - i.quantity_reserved <= i.reorder_level
ORDER BY available, p.sku;

The filter runs on inventory first (small table, one row per product), and the pending-demand lookup only runs for products that are already low. An expression index on (quantity_on_hand - quantity_reserved) would help if the inventory table were large; at catalog sizes it is a fast sequential scan.

17.20.6 Abandoned checkouts: pending orders with no payment attempt in 24 hours

SELECT o.id, o.user_id, u.email, o.total, o.placed_at,
       now() - o.placed_at AS age
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id AND u.deleted_at IS NULL
WHERE o.status = 'pending'
  AND o.placed_at < now() - interval '24 hours'
  AND o.placed_at > now() - interval '7 days'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id AND p.created_at > now() - interval '24 hours')
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM notifications n WHERE n.user_id = o.user_id AND n.template = 'abandoned_checkout'
                    AND n.created_at > now() - interval '7 days')
ORDER BY o.placed_at
LIMIT 500;

orders_open_status_idx (partial on status IN ('pending','paid')) makes the driving scan tiny. Both anti-joins are NOT EXISTS (null-safe). The second one prevents nagging a customer more than once a week, and the LIMIT bounds the batch for the reminder job.

17.20.7 Cohort retention: percent of each signup month's users who ordered in months 0, 1, 2, 3

WITH cohorts AS (
  SELECT id AS user_id, date_trunc('month', created_at)::date AS cohort_month
  FROM users WHERE created_at >= '2025-09-01'
),
activity AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT o.user_id, date_trunc('month', o.placed_at)::date AS active_month
  FROM orders o WHERE o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
),
joined AS (
  SELECT c.cohort_month, c.user_id,
         (extract(year FROM a.active_month) - extract(year FROM c.cohort_month)) * 12
         + (extract(month FROM a.active_month) - extract(month FROM c.cohort_month)) AS month_offset
  FROM cohorts c JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = c.user_id AND a.active_month >= c.cohort_month
),
sizes AS (SELECT cohort_month, count(*) AS cohort_size FROM cohorts GROUP BY 1)
SELECT s.cohort_month, s.cohort_size,
       round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT j.user_id) FILTER (WHERE j.month_offset = 0) / s.cohort_size, 1) AS m0,
       round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT j.user_id) FILTER (WHERE j.month_offset = 1) / s.cohort_size, 1) AS m1,
       round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT j.user_id) FILTER (WHERE j.month_offset = 2) / s.cohort_size, 1) AS m2,
       round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT j.user_id) FILTER (WHERE j.month_offset = 3) / s.cohort_size, 1) AS m3
FROM sizes s LEFT JOIN joined j ON j.cohort_month = s.cohort_month
GROUP BY s.cohort_month, s.cohort_size
ORDER BY s.cohort_month;

Cohort by signup month, activity as distinct (user, month) pairs, offset in months, then conditional count(DISTINCT) per offset pivoted into columns. Cohort size comes from a separate CTE so cohorts with zero activity still appear with 0 percent.

17.20.8 Deduplicate users by email, keeping the newest, and repoint children

BEGIN;
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, lower(email) AS email_key,
         row_number()  OVER (PARTITION BY lower(email) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn,
         first_value(id) OVER (PARTITION BY lower(email) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS keeper_id
  FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
),
dupes AS (SELECT id AS dupe_id, keeper_id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1)
UPDATE orders o SET user_id = d.keeper_id FROM dupes d WHERE o.user_id = d.dupe_id;
-- repeat for addresses, reviews, notifications (reviews may hit UNIQUE (product_id, user_id); handle with ON CONFLICT or delete the dupe's review)
UPDATE users u SET deleted_at = now(), status = 'deleted', email = 'merged+' || u.id || '@example.invalid'
FROM (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(email) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
                      FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) r WHERE rn > 1) d
WHERE u.id = d.id;
COMMIT;

row_number picks the keeper; first_value carries the keeper's id onto every duplicate row so children can be repointed. The merge is one transaction: either every child moves and the duplicates are retired, or nothing changes. Soft-deleting with a rewritten email keeps the partial unique index happy.

17.20.9 Claim pending jobs with SKIP LOCKED

WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id FROM notifications
  WHERE status = 'pending' AND scheduled_at <= now()
  ORDER BY scheduled_at
  LIMIT 10
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE notifications n
   SET status = 'processing', attempts = attempts + 1
  FROM claimed
 WHERE n.id = claimed.id
RETURNING n.id, n.user_id, n.channel, n.template, n.payload;

Workers never wait on each other; the partial index notifications_pending_idx keeps the scan to due rows; the claim and its visibility (processing) happen in one statement so a crash between "lock" and "mark" is impossible. Pair it with a reaper: UPDATE notifications SET status = 'pending' WHERE status = 'processing' AND updated_at < now() - interval '10 minutes'.

17.20.10 Running balance per wallet from a ledger

CREATE TABLE wallet_entries (
  id         bigint        GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    uuid          NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  amount     numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount <> 0),        -- positive credit, negative debit
  reason     text          NOT NULL,
  ref_id     uuid,                                               -- order or payment id
  created_at timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX wallet_entries_user_id_created_at_idx ON wallet_entries (user_id, created_at, id);

-- Statement with running balance
SELECT id, created_at, reason, amount,
       sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at, id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS balance_after
FROM wallet_entries
WHERE user_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;

-- Current balance for everyone (report) and a guard against negative balances
SELECT user_id, sum(amount) AS balance FROM wallet_entries GROUP BY user_id HAVING sum(amount) < 0;

A ledger is append-only, so the balance is a running sum; ROWS with an id tiebreaker makes it exact even when two entries share a timestamp. For the "current balance" hot path, keep a wallets.balance column maintained by a trigger on wallet_entries (Part 16, section 16.8) and reconcile against this sum nightly.

17.20.11 Products never ordered, per category

SELECT c.name AS category, p.sku, p.name, p.created_at
FROM products p
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
WHERE p.is_active
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)
ORDER BY c.name, p.created_at;

Anti-join with NOT EXISTS; order_items_product_id_idx makes each probe cheap, and the planner may turn it into a Hash Anti Join over the whole catalog. NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items) would be equivalent here only because product_id is NOT NULL; NOT EXISTS does not depend on that.

17.20.12 Daily revenue, zero-filled, with 7-day moving average

WITH days AS (
  SELECT d::date AS day FROM generate_series(current_date - 59, current_date, interval '1 day') d
),
daily AS (
  SELECT (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS day, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
    AND placed_at >= (current_date - 59)::timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT days.day,
       coalesce(daily.revenue, 0) AS revenue,
       round(avg(coalesce(daily.revenue, 0)) OVER (ORDER BY days.day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_7d
FROM days LEFT JOIN daily ON daily.day = days.day
ORDER BY days.day;

generate_series supplies the axis so quiet days show as zero, and the moving average is a ROWS frame over the zero-filled series, which is the only way it is correct on days with no orders.

17.20.13 Delivery time percentiles per carrier and per week

SELECT date_trunc('week', s.shipped_at)::date AS week, s.carrier,
       count(*) AS shipments,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY s.delivered_at - s.shipped_at) AS p50,
       percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY s.delivered_at - s.shipped_at) AS p90,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.delivered_at - s.shipped_at > interval '5 days') AS late
FROM shipments s
WHERE s.delivered_at IS NOT NULL AND s.shipped_at >= now() - interval '12 weeks'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

Medians and p90 on interval values with percentile_cont; a late count via FILTER in the same pass. The mean is deliberately absent.

17.20.14 Churn risk: customers whose last order was 90 to 180 days ago

SELECT u.id, u.email, last.last_order_at, last.lifetime_orders, last.lifetime_value
FROM users u
JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT max(o.placed_at) AS last_order_at, count(*) AS lifetime_orders, sum(o.total) AS lifetime_value
  FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')
) last ON true
WHERE u.deleted_at IS NULL
  AND last.last_order_at BETWEEN now() - interval '180 days' AND now() - interval '90 days'
  AND last.lifetime_orders >= 2
ORDER BY last.lifetime_value DESC
LIMIT 1000;

Correct but, over 1.2 million users, it is one aggregate per user (loops=1200000). For a nightly job that is acceptable (a few minutes on a replica). For anything more frequent, maintain customer_summary (Part 16, section 16.8) and query that: WHERE last_order_at BETWEEN ... on an indexed column.

17.20.15 Rating histogram and average per product, pivoted

SELECT p.id, p.name,
       count(r.id)                                    AS reviews,
       round(avg(r.rating), 2)                        AS avg_rating,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.rating = 5)           AS star5,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.rating = 4)           AS star4,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.rating = 3)           AS star3,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.rating = 2)           AS star2,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.rating = 1)           AS star1
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.id = ANY($1::uuid[])
GROUP BY p.id;

FILTER pivots the rating distribution into columns in one pass; count(r.id) (not count(*)) returns 0 for products with no reviews after the LEFT JOIN. The FILTER counts are zero for those products because NULL = 5 is unknown.

17.20.16 Top 3 products per category by units sold in the last 30 days

WITH sold AS (
  SELECT p.category_id, p.id AS product_id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o   ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered') AND o.placed_at >= now() - interval '30 days'
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY p.category_id, p.id, p.name
)
SELECT category_id, product_id, name, units
FROM (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY units DESC, product_id) AS rn FROM sold) t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category_id, rn;

Aggregate to (category, product) grain first, then row_number per category. dense_rank would return more than three rows on ties; row_number with a tiebreaker returns exactly three.

17.20.17 Order status funnel for a period

SELECT count(*)                                                     AS placed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status <> 'cancelled')                AS not_cancelled,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered')) AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status IN ('shipped','delivered'))    AS shipped,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered')                 AS delivered,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') / nullif(count(*), 0), 1) AS delivered_pct
FROM orders
WHERE placed_at >= $1 AND placed_at < $2;

Five funnel stages in one index range scan; nullif guards the division when the period has no orders.

17.20.18 Catalog search by attributes, tags and price, with facets

-- Results page
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price, p.attributes->>'brand' AS brand
FROM products p
WHERE p.is_active
  AND p.category_id = ANY($1::bigint[])                       -- subtree ids from the recursive CTE, cached
  AND p.attributes @> $2::jsonb                                -- e.g. {"brand":"Acme","5g":true}
  AND p.tags && $3::text[]                                     -- any of the requested tags
  AND p.price BETWEEN $4 AND $5
ORDER BY p.price, p.id
LIMIT 40;

-- Brand facet counts for the same filter (without the brand condition)
SELECT p.attributes->>'brand' AS brand, count(*)
FROM products p
WHERE p.is_active AND p.category_id = ANY($1::bigint[]) AND p.tags && $3::text[] AND p.price BETWEEN $4 AND $5
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;

The GIN indexes on attributes and tags combine with the B-tree on category_id through a BitmapAnd. Facets are the same predicate minus the facet's own dimension. Beyond a few hundred thousand products with many facets, this moves to a search engine; below that, PostgreSQL is enough.

17.20.19 Reconcile payments against a provider settlement file

-- settlement_lines loaded with COPY: (provider_payment_id text, amount numeric, settled_at timestamptz)
SELECT coalesce(p.provider_payment_id, s.provider_payment_id) AS provider_payment_id,
       p.id AS our_payment_id, p.amount AS our_amount, s.amount AS their_amount,
       CASE WHEN p.id IS NULL THEN 'missing_in_db'
            WHEN s.provider_payment_id IS NULL THEN 'missing_in_settlement'
            WHEN p.amount <> s.amount THEN 'amount_mismatch' END AS issue
FROM (SELECT * FROM payments WHERE status = 'captured' AND created_at >= $1 AND created_at < $2) p
FULL JOIN settlement_lines s ON s.provider_payment_id = p.provider_payment_id
WHERE p.id IS NULL OR s.provider_payment_id IS NULL OR p.amount <> s.amount
ORDER BY 1;

FULL JOIN surfaces rows missing on either side; the payments side is pre-filtered in a derived table so the outer join keeps unmatched settlement lines. An index on payments (provider_payment_id) makes the join a merge or hash on two sorted inputs.

17.20.20 Category breadcrumb and subtree ids

-- Breadcrumb (walk up)
WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 0 AS depth FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, up.depth + 1 FROM categories c JOIN up ON c.id = up.parent_id WHERE up.depth < 10
)
SELECT string_agg(name, ' > ' ORDER BY depth DESC) AS breadcrumb, array_agg(id ORDER BY depth DESC) AS id_path FROM up;

-- Subtree ids (walk down), cached in Redis for 10 minutes by the service
WITH RECURSIVE down AS (
  SELECT id FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id FROM categories c JOIN down ON c.parent_id = down.id
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT array_agg(id) AS ids FROM down WHERE NOT is_cycle;

Two recursive CTEs, one up, one down; the depth guard and CYCLE clause protect against corrupt trees; the subtree array feeds recipe 18 as $1::bigint[].

17.20.21 Customers with a failed payment and no successful retry (support follow-up)

SELECT o.id AS order_id, u.email, o.total, f.last_failure_at, f.failures
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT max(created_at) AS last_failure_at, count(*) AS failures
  FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id AND p.status = 'failed'
) f ON f.failures > 0
WHERE o.status = 'pending'
  AND o.placed_at > now() - interval '3 days'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id AND p.status IN ('authorized','captured'))
ORDER BY f.last_failure_at DESC
LIMIT 200;

The LATERAL with a condition in ON (f.failures > 0) acts as an inner join that also computes the aggregate; the NOT EXISTS excludes orders that later succeeded. Driven by the partial index on open orders.

17.20.22 Monthly active customers and new vs returning split

WITH first_order AS (
  SELECT user_id, min(placed_at) AS first_at FROM orders WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered') GROUP BY user_id
),
monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.placed_at)::date AS month, o.user_id,
         bool_or(date_trunc('month', o.placed_at) = date_trunc('month', f.first_at)) AS is_new
  FROM orders o JOIN first_order f ON f.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status IN ('paid','shipped','delivered') AND o.placed_at >= now() - interval '12 months'
  GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT month,
       count(*)                          AS active_customers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_new)    AS new_customers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT is_new) AS returning_customers
FROM monthly GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

First-order month per customer once, then per (month, customer) a bool_or flag, then the split with FILTER. count(*) at (month, customer) grain is the MAU because that CTE already collapsed multiple orders per customer per month.

17.21 Edge cases & failure modes in SQL

Every item here has caused a real incident. For each: what goes wrong, why, and the fix.

  • NULL comparisons. WHERE cancel_reason <> 'fraud' drops rows where cancel_reason IS NULL; = NULL never matches. Why: three-valued logic; UNKNOWN rows are filtered out. Fix: IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM, coalesce, and NOT NULL columns wherever "unknown" is not a real state.

  • NOT IN (subquery) with a NULL. WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT shipping_address_id FROM orders) returns zero rows the moment one shipping_address_id is NULL, and starts returning rows (or deleting them) the day the NULL disappears. Fix: NOT EXISTS.

  • Implicit casts disabling indexes. WHERE order_number = '12345' on a bigint column is fine (the literal is coerced), but WHERE order_number::text = $1 or a parameter explicitly typed as text compared to uuid/bigint forces a cast on the column side and a sequential scan. Also WHERE created_at::date = $1. Fix: cast the parameter, never the column; bind parameters with the column's type ($1::uuid); check the plan for Filter on a cast expression.

  • Join row explosion. Joining two 1:N children at parent grain (orders x items x payments) multiplies rows; sums and counts inflate; ORMs hide it by de-duplicating entities in memory while still transferring every row. Fix: aggregate each child to parent grain before joining; LATERAL for top-1; separate: true / second query in ORMs; count(DISTINCT parent.id) only as a diagnostic.

  • LEFT JOIN turned INNER by WHERE. LEFT JOIN payments p ... WHERE p.status = 'captured' removes orders without payments. Fix: right-side conditions go in ON; only IS NULL checks on the right side go in WHERE.

  • SELECT *. Reads and transfers every column (including TOASTed jsonb and text), prevents index-only scans, breaks INSERT INTO ... SELECT * and positional code when a column is added or reordered, and leaks new sensitive columns (password_hash) into API responses. Fix: name columns; in TypeORM use select or select: false on sensitive columns.

  • OFFSET 1000000. Reads and discards a million rows per request; export scripts that page with OFFSET are quadratic; concurrent inserts and deletes shift the window so rows are skipped or repeated. Fix: keyset pagination on an indexed (sort_col, id) with a row-value comparison.

  • LIMIT without ORDER BY. Returns whichever rows are cheapest today; a different set after VACUUM, a plan change, or a replica switch. "Get any 10 pending jobs" looks fine until the same 10 rows are returned forever because they sit at the start of the heap. Fix: ORDER BY with a unique tiebreaker; for random sampling, TABLESAMPLE.

  • String concatenation SQL injection. `WHERE email = '${email}'` lets ' OR 1=1 -- through; TypeORM where(\... ${value}`)and Sequelizeliteralwith interpolated input are the same hole, as is buildingORDER BY ${column} from a request without an allowlist. Fix: parameters everywhere ($1, :name, bind), allowlisted identifiers for dynamic column and direction, and quote_ident` if you must build identifiers in SQL.

  • UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE. Every row changes, every row is locked until commit, every other writer on that table queues, replication lag spikes, and the fix is a restore. Fix: transactions with an explicit ROLLBACK habit in psql (BEGIN; UPDATE ...; SELECT count(*) ...; COMMIT), statement_timeout, a linter rule for ORM update() without where, and no DELETE in production without a row-count check.

  • Long-running reporting queries holding back vacuum. A 40-minute report on the primary keeps its snapshot open; VACUUM cannot remove tuples deleted after the snapshot started; hot tables bloat; n_dead_tup climbs; every query on those tables slows. Fix: run reports on a replica (with hot_standby_feedback considerations, Part 22), set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and materialize heavy reports.

  • Lock waits from a wide UPDATE. UPDATE products SET is_active = false WHERE category_id = 7 on 2 million products locks 2 million rows for the transaction's duration and blocks every checkout touching those products. Fix: batch by primary key range (5,000 rows per transaction), short transactions, lock_timeout on interactive sessions.

  • Correlated subquery in a report. (SELECT count(*) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = o.id) over 2 million orders is 2 million index scans (loops=2000000). Fix: derived table or window function.

  • DISTINCT as a bandage. Added to hide join multiplication; the plan gains a sort or hash over the inflated set, and the underlying bug remains for the next aggregate. Fix: fix the join grain.

  • ORDER BY without a unique tiebreaker. Ties are ordered arbitrarily; pagination skips and repeats; row_number() differs between runs. Fix: always end with the primary key.

  • rank() for pagination. Gaps after ties cause missing rows. Fix: row_number() to paginate, rank()/dense_rank() to display.

  • last_value() with the default frame. Returns the current row. Fix: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

  • date_trunc or ::date on the column in WHERE. Sequential scan. Fix: half-open range on the raw column; truncation in SELECT/GROUP BY.

  • Session time zone drift. The same WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01' means different instants on a developer laptop (Asia/Kolkata) and a server (UTC). Fix: UTC session zone from the pool; explicit offsets in literals; AT TIME ZONE in reports.

  • now() in a long transaction. All rows get the transaction start time; SLA calculations off by minutes. Fix: clock_timestamp() when the actual time matters.

  • Upsert that regresses state. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status lets a late initiated webhook overwrite captured. Fix: WHERE existing.status NOT IN (terminal states).

  • ON CONFLICT target mismatch. Index on lower(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, ON CONFLICT (email): error at runtime, only when a conflict first happens. Fix: match the expression and predicate exactly; test the conflict path.

  • Multi-row insert conflicting with itself. Two identical keys in one VALUES list with DO UPDATE: "cannot affect row a second time". Fix: dedupe input.

  • Row lock held across I/O. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then an HTTP call, then UPDATE: every request for that row waits for the slowest external dependency. Fix: I/O before or after the transaction; lock for milliseconds.

  • FOR UPDATE on a parent while children insert. Blocks FK KEY SHARE; order_items inserts wait on an orders FOR UPDATE. Fix: FOR NO KEY UPDATE.

  • Queue rows stuck in processing. A worker crash after claim; the row never returns. Fix: reaper by timestamp; attempts cap.

  • Recursive CTE without a depth guard. One self-referencing row and the query runs until temp disk is full. Fix: depth limit, CYCLE clause, CHECK (parent_id IS DISTINCT FROM id).

  • CTE fence surprise across a major upgrade. A query that depended on PG11 materialization to avoid a bad plan changes plan on PG12. Fix: MATERIALIZED explicitly where the fence was load-bearing; re-check plans after upgrades.

  • Parameter limit and huge IN lists. 70,000 ids in IN (...) exceeds node-postgres's 65,535 parameters, or produces a plan the parser chokes on. Fix: = ANY($1::uuid[]) with one array parameter, or a temp table.

  • jsonb text comparisons. attributes->>'price' > '100' compares strings. Fix: cast, and index the cast expression.

  • Hash join spilling. Batches: 16 in the plan; the join runs from disk. Fix: session-level work_mem for the report, or reduce the input with a tighter predicate.

  • Stale statistics after a bulk load. A 20-million-row import, no ANALYZE, and the planner still believes the table has 1,000 rows; every plan is wrong until autovacuum catches up. Fix: ANALYZE table after bulk loads (Part 19).

  • Replica reads after writes. Insert on the primary, immediately read on a replica: not found. Fix: read-your-writes routing (Part 22).

  • Unbounded results. SELECT ... FROM notifications WHERE user_id = $1 with no LIMIT for a user with 3 million rows: the pod is OOMKilled assembling the array. Fix: every list query has a LIMIT; stream with a cursor for exports.

  • Returning numeric/bigint as JavaScript numbers. Precision loss above 2^53 and float drift on money. Fix: strings from the driver, a decimal library, integer minor units.

  • TRUNCATE ... CASCADE. Truncates every table that references the target, transitively. Fix: never CASCADE a TRUNCATE on a table with production children; list the dependents first.

  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a data-modifying statement. It runs the statement. Fix: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK;.

Senior Checklist — Part 17

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I write sargable predicates: no functions or casts on the column side, ranges instead of date_trunc, expression indexes when a function is unavoidable
  • I know which LIKE patterns use a B-tree, which need text_pattern_ops, and which need pg_trgm
  • I put right-side filters of a LEFT JOIN in ON, and I can explain why WHERE turns it into an inner join
  • I can identify nested loop, hash join and merge join in a plan, say why the planner chose each, and spot loops= and Batches problems
  • I aggregate 1:N children to parent grain before joining, and I can explain the row-multiplication trap to a junior in one sentence
  • I use FILTER, ROLLUP/GROUPING SETS and GROUPING() for multi-metric and subtotal reports in one pass
  • I paginate with keyset on (sort_col, id) and a row-value comparison, and I never ship OFFSET for deep pages or exports
  • I use EXISTS/NOT EXISTS for existence checks and I flag NOT IN (subquery) in every review
  • I default to UNION ALL and use UNION only for real set semantics
  • I know PG12+ CTE inlining, when to write MATERIALIZED, and how data-modifying CTEs share a snapshot
  • I can write a recursive CTE for a tree or graph with a depth guard and CYCLE protection
  • I use window functions for top-N per group, dedup, running totals, LAG deltas and gaps-and-islands, always with a unique tiebreaker, and I know the last_value frame trap
  • I can pivot with conditional aggregation and know when CASE in WHERE disables indexes
  • I can spot a correlated SubPlan with a large loop count and rewrite it as a derived table, window or LATERAL
  • I return nested documents with jsonb_agg/jsonb_build_object for bounded child sets, and I report percentiles instead of means for time-like data
  • I query jsonb with @> on a GIN index and expression B-trees for ranges, and I know the text-comparison and null-vs-missing traps
  • I write zero-filled time reports with generate_series, sargable ranges and explicit AT TIME ZONE
  • I use RETURNING, multi-row inserts with unnest, and guarded ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE that never regresses terminal state
  • I can write UPDATE ... FROM and DELETE ... USING, batch large modifications, and I know what happens on multi-match
  • I can implement a FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED job queue with a partial index, a reaper and backoff, and I never hold a row lock across I/O
  • I know FOR NO KEY UPDATE and why FOR UPDATE on a parent blocks child inserts
  • I use COPY for bulk loads via a staging table, and I know TRUNCATE's lock and CASCADE behavior
  • I read the six essential lines of EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before shipping any query that runs more than once per second
  • I follow the process: write for correctness, check the plan on realistic data, add the index or reshape, verify under volume and concurrency
  • I know what TypeORM take() with joins and Sequelize limit with hasMany includes generate, and when to drop to raw SQL in a typed repository method
  • I never build SQL from user strings; parameters always, allowlists for dynamic identifiers

Part 17 — Key Takeaways

  • The column stays bare. Every function, cast or arithmetic on the column side of a predicate turns an index seek into a table scan.
  • LEFT JOIN filters go in ON. A right-side condition in WHERE silently makes the join inner.
  • Read the join node: nested loop with small loops and index probes is a healthy OLTP plan; hash join with one batch is a healthy report plan; anything with loops in the millions or Batches above one is a bug.
  • Aggregate children to the parent's grain before joining anything else. Row multiplication is the most common wrong number in production reports.
  • OFFSET reads and discards. Keyset pagination on (sort_col, id) with a row-value comparison is constant-cost at any depth.
  • NOT IN with a nullable subquery returns nothing and looks like success. NOT EXISTS is the anti-join.
  • UNION ALL unless you need set semantics; UNION hashes every row.
  • CTEs are inlined in PG12+; write MATERIALIZED only when the fence is the point. Recursive CTEs need a depth guard and CYCLE.
  • Window functions solve top-N per group, dedup, running totals and deltas in one sorted pass; always add a unique tiebreaker, and give last_value a frame.
  • A correlated subquery is a loop. Fine for 20 outer rows; a report over millions needs a derived table, a window, or LATERAL with a small outer set.
  • Return nested JSON from one query with jsonb_agg for bounded children; report p50/p90, not averages.
  • RETURNING saves a round trip; unnest beats parameter limits; upserts need a WHERE guard so a late event cannot overwrite a terminal state.
  • FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED plus a partial index is a transactional job queue with no extra infrastructure, up to a few thousand jobs per second. Never hold a row lock across a network call; prefer FOR NO KEY UPDATE.
  • The ORM is for the boring 80 percent. Window functions, recursive CTEs, LATERAL, guarded upserts and queue claims live as raw SQL in typed repository methods, tuned with EXPLAIN before they ship.
  • Write for correctness, check the plan on real volume, add the index, verify under concurrency. Ten minutes per query, and most of the incidents in this book never happen.

Part 18 — PostgreSQL Internals

PostgreSQL is the component in your stack that you can least afford to treat as a black box. Redis can be restarted. A NestJS pod can be killed and replaced. The database holds the only copy of the truth, and every performance incident, every lock pile-up, and every "why is disk full at 3 a.m." page eventually leads back to how PostgreSQL works underneath.

This part teaches those mechanics: processes and memory, how a query travels through the server, how rows are stored, how MVCC keeps readers and writers from blocking each other, why VACUUM is not optional, how locks queue, and how the planner decides what to do. Every example uses the same e-commerce schema, so you can run everything on a local PostgreSQL 15 or 16.

-- Running schema used across Part 18 and Part 19
CREATE TABLE users (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  email        text NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  sku          text NOT NULL,
  name         text NOT NULL,
  attributes   jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  price_cents  integer NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  status       text NOT NULL,              -- PENDING, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED
  total_cents  integer NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id     bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity     integer NOT NULL,
  price_cents  integer NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id               bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id         bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  provider_ref     text NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL,          -- INITIATED, CAPTURED, FAILED
  amount_cents     integer NOT NULL,
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE inventory (
  product_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity     integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0),
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

18.1 PostgreSQL process architecture

18.1.1 Processes and shared memory

Concept

PostgreSQL is not one program. It is a family of operating-system processes that share one region of memory. There is one parent process called the postmaster. When your NestJS app opens a connection, the postmaster forks a brand-new child process, called a backend, that serves only that connection for its whole life. Around them run a handful of background processes that do housekeeping: writing dirty pages, flushing the write-ahead log, vacuuming, archiving, collecting statistics.

All of these processes talk through shared memory: a big block of RAM that holds the page cache (shared_buffers), the WAL buffers, the lock table, and the list of running transactions.

Why does it exist?

A process-per-connection model was chosen in the 1990s for isolation: if one backend crashes on a bug, the postmaster notices, and because memory could be corrupted, it restarts all backends but the data files are protected by the WAL. The background processes exist because certain jobs (flushing dirty pages, vacuuming) must happen continuously regardless of whether any client is connected. Without a checkpointer, crash recovery would have to replay the entire WAL since the server started. Without autovacuum, tables would grow forever.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant. The postmaster is the host at the door. Every guest (connection) gets a dedicated waiter (backend process) who does nothing else until the guest leaves. The kitchen (shared memory) is shared by all waiters. In the back, cleaners (autovacuum), a dishwasher (background writer), a bookkeeper writing every order into a ledger before food is served (WAL writer), and a manager who periodically makes sure everything is filed (checkpointer) keep the restaurant running. If you invite 500 guests at once, you need 500 waiters, and they all crowd the same kitchen.

How it works

flowchart TB
  app1["NestJS pod 1"] -->|"TCP 5432"| pm["postmaster"]
  app2["NestJS pod 2"] -->|"TCP 5432"| pm
  pm -->|"fork per connection"| be1["backend 1"]
  pm --> be2["backend 2"]
  pm --> be3["backend N"]
  subgraph SharedMemory
    sb["shared_buffers 8 KB pages"]
    wb["WAL buffers"]
    lt["lock table and proc array"]
  end
  be1 --> sb
  be2 --> sb
  be3 --> wb
  be1 --> lt
  subgraph BackgroundProcesses
    bw["background writer"]
    cp["checkpointer"]
    ww["WAL writer"]
    av["autovacuum launcher and workers"]
    ar["archiver"]
    sc["stats and logger"]
  end
  sb --> bw
  sb --> cp
  wb --> ww
  av --> sb
  cp -->|"flush dirty pages"| data["data files"]
  bw --> data
  ww -->|"fsync"| wal["pg_wal segments"]
  ar -->|"copy full segments"| arch["WAL archive S3"]

Step by step:

  1. postmaster starts, allocates shared memory, opens the listening socket, and launches the background processes. It never touches data itself. If a backend dies abnormally, the postmaster kills all other backends and restarts, because shared memory might be corrupt.
  2. backend process (one per connection) authenticates the client, then loops: read query, parse, plan, execute, send results. It reads and writes pages only through shared_buffers. Each backend also keeps private memory: the relation cache and catalog cache (metadata for tables it has touched), work_mem for sorts, and a prepared statement cache. This private memory is why an idle connection still costs 5 to 10 MB, and more after it has touched many tables.
  3. background writer wakes every bgwriter_delay (200 ms) and writes some dirty pages to disk so backends rarely have to evict a dirty page themselves.
  4. checkpointer periodically writes all dirty pages and records a checkpoint in the WAL. Recovery only needs WAL after the last checkpoint. Covered in 18.6.
  5. WAL writer flushes WAL buffers to the pg_wal directory every wal_writer_delay (200 ms) and on commit.
  6. autovacuum launcher starts up to autovacuum_max_workers (default 3) autovacuum workers, each of which vacuums or analyzes one table at a time.
  7. archiver copies completed 16 MB WAL segments to an archive location when archive_mode = on. This is how point-in-time recovery works.
  8. stats collector existed through PostgreSQL 14 as a separate process receiving UDP packets from backends. Since PostgreSQL 15, cumulative statistics live in shared memory and there is no collector process, but the views (pg_stat_user_tables, pg_stat_activity) are the same.
  9. logger writes server logs when logging_collector = on. On managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL) this is always on.
  10. Replication adds WAL sender processes on the primary (one per replica) and WAL receiver plus startup processes on each replica.

You can see every process type:

SELECT backend_type, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY backend_type
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
 backend_type                 | count
------------------------------+-------
 client backend               |    42
 autovacuum worker            |     2
 walsender                    |     2
 checkpointer                 |     1
 background writer            |     1
 walwriter                    |     1
 autovacuum launcher          |     1
 logical replication launcher |     1

Practical example

Your NestJS order service runs 6 pods, each with a pool of 10 connections. That is 60 backend processes sitting inside PostgreSQL, whether they are busy or not. Each holds a private relation cache. When you deploy and all 6 pods restart at once, 60 connections close and 60 new ones open within a second, so the postmaster forks 60 processes in a burst. On a small instance (2 vCPU) that fork storm alone can take 300 to 800 ms and spike CPU to 100 percent, which is why the first requests after a deploy are slow even though nothing in your code changed.

PostgreSQL example

Look at what one backend is doing and what it costs:

-- One row per process; pid maps to an OS process you can see with `ps`
SELECT pid, backend_type, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       now() - backend_start AS connected_for,
       now() - xact_start    AS in_txn_for,
       left(query, 60)       AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
ORDER BY backend_start;

On Linux, ps -o pid,rss,cmd -C postgres shows the resident memory per backend. Fresh backends sit at 4 to 6 MB; backends that have touched hundreds of tables and run many distinct queries grow to 20 to 50 MB because of the catalog cache. On a 2 GB RDS instance with 300 connections that is the difference between "fine" and OOM.

Production scenario

A typical medium e-commerce deployment: PostgreSQL 16 on an 8 vCPU, 32 GB instance. shared_buffers = 8GB, max_connections = 200. Twenty NestJS pods across four services, each pooling 8 connections, gives 160 backends. Peak traffic 1,200 requests per second, 3,000 queries per second, median query 1.2 ms. Autovacuum runs 3 workers almost continuously on orders, order_items, and inventory because they are update-heavy. The checkpointer writes 400 to 900 MB every 5 minutes.

Monitoring you must have: pg_stat_activity counts by state, backend memory (RSS) totals, pg_stat_bgwriter (or pg_stat_checkpointer on PG 17) for checkpoint frequency, and autovacuum worker occupancy.

Failure scenario

At 14:07 a product-catalog import ran a single UPDATE products SET attributes = attributes || '{"imported": true}' on 4 million rows inside a transaction, then the importer crashed with an unhandled promise rejection but the Node process stayed alive. The backend stayed in idle in transaction. Nothing looked wrong for two hours. Then autovacuum could not clean any dead rows newer than that transaction on any table, the inventory table (updated 500 times per second) bloated from 60 MB to 2.1 GB, sequential scans that used to take 4 ms took 300 ms, and the API p99 went from 80 ms to 2.5 s. The fix was one SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid), and a permanent idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s'. Every one of those mechanisms is explained in the sections that follow.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A crash of a single backend (segfault, out of memory kill) restarts all backends: every pooled connection in every pod drops at once.
  • OOM killer on Linux picks the process with the largest RSS, often the postmaster or a backend running a large sort; on Kubernetes-hosted PostgreSQL set memory limits with a wide margin.
  • Fork storms after a deploy: 100+ new connections in one second on a small instance can push connect latency above the pool's connectionTimeoutMillis.
  • Background processes compete with backends for I/O; a checkpoint and an autovacuum on the same disk at the same time cause a visible latency bump.
  • max_connections is also a shared memory sizing input: raising it requires a restart, and each slot reserves memory even when unused.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They think of connections as a scarce, expensive resource that must be budgeted like CPU. They ask "how many backends will exist in total across all services and pods, and does the instance have RAM and CPU for that many processes?" before increasing any pool size. They refuse to solve "too many connections" by raising max_connections; they put a pooler in front. They explain to a product manager: "The database is a kitchen with a fixed number of cooks. Adding more waiters does not make food come faster; it makes the kitchen slower."

Common mistakes

  • Treating connections as free and opening one per request. Every one is a process fork plus authentication (5 to 20 ms) plus 5 MB.
  • Setting max_connections = 1000 "to be safe". The server now allows 1000 processes to fight over 8 cores.
  • Ignoring backend_type when counting connections and panicking about autovacuum workers.
  • Assuming a killed query frees everything: the backend is still there; only pg_terminate_backend ends it.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a PostgreSQL connection expensive compared to a Redis connection? Expected: each PostgreSQL connection is a forked OS process with private caches (5 to 10 MB, growing), while Redis is single-threaded with cheap client structures. Follow-up: how do you keep connection count under control across 50 pods?
  2. What happens when one backend process crashes? Expected: the postmaster restarts all backends because shared memory may be corrupt; data is safe because of WAL; all client connections drop. Follow-up: how should the app react?
  3. Name five background processes and one thing each does.
  4. Why does PostgreSQL restart all connections after a single backend segfault instead of only that one? Expected: shared memory is shared; a bug that crashed one process may have corrupted structures others rely on.
  5. What changed about the stats collector in PostgreSQL 15?

Practical exercise

Run PostgreSQL 16 in Docker with -c max_connections=20. Write a small script that opens 25 connections with pg. Observe the FATAL: sorry, too many clients already error, then inspect pg_stat_activity and ps to correlate pids with RSS. Acceptance criteria: you can explain which processes are backends, which are background, and how much memory the 20 backends use in total.

18.2 Connections and connection pooling

18.2.1 Why each connection costs so much, and what max_connections really limits

Concept

max_connections (default 100) is the maximum number of simultaneous backends. Every app pool slot, every psql session, every migration runner and every replication sender counts. A handful of slots (superuser_reserved_connections, default 3) are held back for superusers so an admin can still log in when the app has exhausted everything.

Why does it exist?

There must be a cap, because each backend consumes memory (private caches, work_mem per sort operation), CPU (context switches among hundreds of runnable processes), and shared-memory structures (proc array, lock table slots). Beyond roughly 2 to 4 backends per CPU core that are actively running queries, throughput goes down, not up, because of contention on shared buffers and lock manager latches.

Mental model

Imagine a bank with 8 tellers (CPU cores). Letting 500 people into the hall (connections) does not serve anyone faster. It creates a crowd where tellers spend time managing the line instead of serving. A queue outside the door (a pooler) with 16 people inside at any time is strictly faster for everyone.

How it works

  1. A client connects; the postmaster forks a backend and runs authentication (password, SCRAM, or IAM token). Cost: 5 to 20 ms and a few MB.
  2. The backend registers itself in the proc array in shared memory; there are exactly max_connections slots.
  3. Every query that sorts or hashes may allocate up to work_mem per operation. 300 connections × 3 sorts × 64 MB work_mem is 57 GB of theoretical demand; this is why work_mem must be sized against connection count.
  4. Idle backends still hold their relation cache and stay registered, and idle-in-transaction backends additionally pin the oldest visible transaction id, which holds back vacuum (18.4).
  5. Benchmarks on an 8-core box: throughput peaks at roughly 20 to 40 active connections and drops 30 to 50 percent at 300 connections because of latch contention and context switching. Latency, meanwhile, becomes bimodal: most queries are fast, but some wait behind a runnable-queue of hundreds of processes.

Why 500 application connections is bad even if the server "accepts" them:

Number of backends Memory (idle, 8 MB each) Active on 8 cores Effect
40 320 MB up to 40 Healthy; cores are busy, little contention
200 1.6 GB 200 Context switching, work_mem risk, p99 climbs
500 4 GB 500 Lock manager and buffer contention; throughput falls; OOM risk during sorts

Practical example

Four NestJS services (orders, catalog, payments, notifications) each run 8 pods with a pool of 15. That is 4 × 8 × 15 = 480 connections plus 3 workers with 10 each = 510. On a max_connections = 500 server the last pods to start get too many clients already, their readiness probes fail, Kubernetes restarts them, they reconnect and steal slots from another service, and you get a rolling connection storm across the fleet. The fix is not max_connections = 1000; it is a pool budget per service and a pooler.

NestJS example

Pool settings live in the TypeOrmModule options and should come from environment config, sized by a budget, not by guess:

// app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true }),
    TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (cfg: ConfigService) => ({
        type: 'postgres',
        url: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL'),
        autoLoadEntities: true,
        synchronize: false,                   // never in production
        // `extra` is passed straight to pg-pool
        extra: {
          max: cfg.get<number>('DB_POOL_MAX', 8),          // per pod
          min: 0,
          idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,        // release idle clients
          connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,   // fail fast when the pool is starved
          maxLifetimeSeconds: 1_800,        // recycle, spreads reconnects
          statement_timeout: 10_000,        // server-side safety belt, ms
          idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30_000,
          application_name: 'orders-api',   // shows up in pg_stat_activity
        },
      }),
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

application_name is not decoration: when 400 backends are fighting, it tells you which service they belong to.

PostgreSQL example

Count connections by application and state so you can see who is spending the budget:

SELECT application_name, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 3 DESC;
 application_name | state               | count
------------------+---------------------+-------
 orders-api       | idle                |   112
 catalog-api      | idle                |    96
 orders-api       | active              |    14
 payments-worker  | idle in transaction |     6   <-- investigate

Then check remaining headroom:

SELECT current_setting('max_connections')::int
       - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity) AS free_slots;

TypeORM example

extra maps directly to pg-pool's constructor: max, min, idleTimeoutMillis, connectionTimeoutMillis, maxUses, maxLifetimeSeconds, allowExitOnIdle. Everything else in extra (like statement_timeout) is passed through to the pg client, which sends recognised ones as startup parameters.

// data-source.ts (used by CLI and by tests)
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  extra: { max: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_MAX ?? 8), connectionTimeoutMillis: 5000 },
  entities: [__dirname + '/**/*.entity.{ts,js}'],
