  migrations: [__dirname + '/migrations/*.{ts,js}'],
});

Sequelize example

Sequelize has its own pool (built on sequelize-pool), configured with pool:

import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export const sequelize = new Sequelize(process.env.DATABASE_URL!, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  logging: false,
  pool: {
    max: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_MAX ?? 8), // per pod
    min: 0,
    acquire: 5_000,   // ms to wait for a free connection before throwing
    idle: 30_000,     // ms before an idle connection is destroyed
    evict: 10_000,    // how often the evictor runs
  },
  dialectOptions: {
    statement_timeout: 10_000,
    idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30_000,
    application_name: 'orders-api',
  },
});

acquire is the equivalent of pg-pool's connectionTimeoutMillis: how long a request waits for a slot before failing with ResourceRequest timed out.

Production scenario

The correct order of operations for a connection budget:

  1. Decide the server's healthy active-connection count. Rule of thumb from the PostgreSQL wiki: connections = (cores * 2) + effective_spindle_count. On 8 cores with SSD that is roughly 16 to 24 active connections. Allow idle headroom: budget 100 to 150 backends total.
  2. Divide by services and pods: 4 services × 8 pods gives 32 pools; 120 / 32 gives a pool of 3 to 4 per pod. That feels tiny. It is fine when queries take 2 ms: one connection can serve 500 queries per second.
  3. If the math does not fit (many pods, spiky traffic, serverless), put PgBouncer or RDS Proxy in front so pods can hold 20 client connections each while the database sees 50.

Latency check: with a 4-connection pool and 2 ms queries, a pod handling 400 requests per second that each run 2 queries needs 400 × 2 × 2 ms = 1.6 connection-seconds per second: 40 percent utilisation. Comfortable.

Failure scenario

"Connection storm after deploy": at 10:00 a deploy rolled 30 pods with a pool max: 20 and min: 20 (someone set min to "pre-warm"). 600 connect attempts hit a max_connections = 400 server within 3 seconds. The postmaster forked 400 backends, CPU hit 100 percent, authentication took 2 s each, and pools timed out at connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000, retried, and produced a second wave. The API was down for 9 minutes without any code bug. Fixes: min: 0, a pooler, and a pool max sized by budget.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Pool max per pod × replicas × services × environments (staging shares the instance) exceeds max_connections.
  • Horizontal pod autoscaler scales from 8 to 40 pods during a sale; every new pod brings its full pool.
  • Health checks that open a new connection each time instead of using the pool.
  • Connection leak: a QueryRunner created and never released; the pool empties one slot per leaked call until every request waits connectionTimeoutMillis and fails.
  • maxUses or maxLifetimeSeconds forcing all connections to recycle at the same instant (they were created together at pod start); add jitter or rely on idleTimeoutMillis.
  • A long DNS TTL after a failover: pools keep connecting to the old primary IP.
  • TLS handshake cost (2 to 5 ms) multiplies during storms.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They keep a written connection budget and treat it as capacity planning. They know that a smaller pool with a queue in the app is better than a bigger pool that makes the database thrash. They put connectionTimeoutMillis low (2 to 5 s) so overload fails fast and visibly instead of piling up. They ask: "Can it timeout? Can it become slow? Can it partially succeed?" and answer with timeouts at every layer: pool acquire timeout, statement_timeout, HTTP timeout.

Common mistakes

  • Sizing the pool by "more is safer".
  • min equal to max for warm-up, which turns every deploy into a storm.
  • Sharing one database instance among ten microservices with independent pools that nobody totals.
  • No connectionTimeoutMillis: requests hang forever when the pool is empty, which looks like a database outage.

Interview questions

  1. Ten services, 8 pods each, max_connections = 300. How big is the pool per pod? Expected: about 3 to 4, or use a pooler; explain the budget arithmetic and why active-connection count should stay near 2× cores.
  2. Why is a pool of 4 enough for a pod doing 400 RPS? Expected: Little's law; 2 ms queries mean each connection can serve hundreds of queries per second.
  3. What does connectionTimeoutMillis protect against?
  4. What is superuser_reserved_connections for?

Practical exercise

Instrument a NestJS service with a Prometheus gauge for pool.totalCount, pool.idleCount, and pool.waitingCount (available on the pg Pool object, reachable through dataSource.driver). Load test with autocannon at increasing concurrency. Acceptance criteria: you can show the point where waitingCount starts to rise and relate it to p99 latency, and you can justify a pool size with the numbers.

18.2.2 PgBouncer, pooling modes, and RDS Proxy

Concept

PgBouncer is a small, single-threaded proxy that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol. Applications connect to PgBouncer (cheap, thousands of client connections cost a few KB each). PgBouncer keeps a much smaller set of real server connections and lends them out. Pooling mode decides how long a client keeps a server connection: for a whole session, for one transaction, or for one statement.

RDS Proxy is Amazon's managed equivalent with IAM auth integration and automatic failover handling; it uses transaction-style multiplexing and "pins" a client to a server connection when the client does something session-specific.

Why does it exist?

Because 50 pods × 20 client connections = 1,000 client connections cannot become 1,000 backends. A pooler turns 1,000 client connections into 40 backends. It also absorbs connection storms (the pooler queues clients instead of forking backends) and makes failover smoother (clients stay connected to the pooler while it reconnects to the new primary).

Mental model

Imagine a hotel with 40 real phone lines but 1,000 rooms. In session mode a room keeps a line as long as the phone is off the hook, even when nobody is talking. In transaction mode you get a line when you dial and lose it when you hang up after one call. In statement mode you lose the line after every sentence, which makes it impossible to have a conversation (a transaction).

How it works

Mode Server connection assigned Released What works What breaks
session On client connect On client disconnect Everything No multiplexing benefit beyond storm absorption
transaction At BEGIN or first statement At COMMIT/ROLLBACK Normal queries, transactions, SET LOCAL, pg_advisory_xact_lock Session state: SET, session prepared statements, pg_advisory_lock, LISTEN, temp tables, WITH HOLD cursors, search_path
statement Per statement After each statement Autocommit single statements only Multi-statement transactions

Transaction mode is the one everyone wants, and what breaks in it needs care:

  1. Prepared statements. A named prepared statement lives in one backend. In transaction mode your next transaction may land on a different backend that has never seen it: prepared statement "s1" does not exist. PgBouncer 1.21+ can track protocol-level prepared statements (max_prepared_statements = 200), but only with the extended protocol, not SQL PREPARE. pg (node-postgres) uses named prepared statements only when you pass name in the query config; TypeORM and Sequelize do not by default, so most NestJS apps are fine.
  2. SET. SET search_path = tenant_42 sticks to a backend; the next transaction from your client may land elsewhere, and worse, another tenant's transaction may inherit it. Use SET LOCAL inside a transaction.
  3. Advisory locks. pg_advisory_lock(key) is session-level; after your transaction ends the server connection goes back to the pool still holding the lock, and your code can never unlock it. Use pg_advisory_xact_lock, which releases at transaction end.
  4. LISTEN/NOTIFY. Notifications arrive on the backend that ran LISTEN; that backend is shared. Use a dedicated direct connection for listeners.
  5. Temp tables, session cursors, pg_temp schemas all belong to the backend.

Practical example

A checkout worker does this in Sequelize: await sequelize.query("SET statement_timeout = 60000") at startup, then processes jobs. Through PgBouncer in transaction mode, that SET landed on one server connection. The orders API later borrowed that connection and inherited a 60 s timeout for a user-facing request, while the worker sometimes got a connection with the default 10 s and failed. Nobody could reproduce it locally because local ran without PgBouncer. Replacing SET with SET LOCAL inside the job transaction fixed it.

NestJS example

Advisory locks that survive transaction pooling: use the transaction-scoped form inside a transaction.

// inventory-reservation.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class InventoryReservationService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  // Serialise reservations per product without touching the row lock
  async reserve(productId: number, qty: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
      // xact-scoped: released automatically at COMMIT/ROLLBACK,
      // safe behind PgBouncer transaction mode
      await em.query('SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock($1)', [productId]);

      const [{ quantity }] = await em.query(
        'SELECT quantity FROM inventory WHERE product_id = $1',
        [productId],
      );
      if (quantity < qty) throw new Error('INSUFFICIENT_STOCK');

      await em.query(
        'UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - $2, updated_at = now() WHERE product_id = $1',
        [productId, qty],
      );
    });
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Minimal PgBouncer config for a NestJS fleet:

[databases]
shop = host=10.0.1.5 port=5432 dbname=shop

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 40        ; server connections per user+database pair
max_client_conn = 2000        ; cheap client side
reserve_pool_size = 5
server_idle_timeout = 600
max_prepared_statements = 200 ; PgBouncer 1.21+

Observe it: connect to the admin database and run SHOW POOLS; to see cl_active, cl_waiting, sv_active, sv_idle. A rising cl_waiting with sv_idle = 0 means the server-side pool is the bottleneck.

TypeORM example

When behind transaction pooling, keep session state out of your connection setup. Do not use extra.options with -c search_path=...; instead set per-transaction:

await dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
  await em.query(`SET LOCAL search_path TO tenant_${tenantId}, public`);
  return em.getRepository(Order).find({ where: { status: 'PENDING' }, take: 100 });
});

Sequelize example

Sequelize's sequelize.transaction() acquires one connection for the whole callback, which is exactly what transaction pooling needs. Sequelize's dialectOptions.statement_timeout is sent as a startup parameter, which PgBouncer applies when it opens the server connection, so it behaves consistently across all clients of that pool.

Production scenario

RDS Proxy notes for the same fleet: pods connect to the proxy endpoint; the proxy holds up to MaxConnectionsPercent of the instance's max_connections. Any of SET, PREPARE, LISTEN, advisory locks, or large result sets over 16 KB left unread cause session pinning: the client keeps one backend until it disconnects, and you silently lose multiplexing. CloudWatch metric DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlySessionPinned tells you how many. A NestJS app using TypeORM without named prepared statements and without SET pins almost never.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged for "prepared statement does not exist" errors at 3 percent of requests. A developer had enabled pg's query name option to "speed up" a hot query. Locally it worked. In production, PgBouncer 1.18 in transaction mode routed the second execution to a backend that had never prepared it. Rolling back the change fixed it; the long-term fix was upgrading PgBouncer to 1.21 and enabling max_prepared_statements.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • PgBouncer is single-threaded: one instance handles about 10,000 to 20,000 queries per second on one core; run several behind a load balancer for more.
  • server_idle_timeout too low causes reconnect churn; too high keeps backends around.
  • default_pool_size × number of PgBouncer instances × databases × users must fit max_connections.
  • Failover: the pooler hides it from clients, but in-flight transactions still fail; clients must retry.
  • SET from a migration tool run through the pooler leaks into app connections.
  • Long-running reporting queries through the pooler hold a server slot; give analytics its own pool.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They default to transaction mode and design the app for it: no session state, SET LOCAL only, transaction-level advisory locks, a dedicated direct connection for LISTEN. They put the pooler in from day one on any system with more than a handful of pods, because retrofitting it means auditing every SET and every prepared statement. They ask "what state does this connection carry?" before every feature that touches the session.

Common mistakes

  • Running SET search_path per tenant through a transaction pooler.
  • Using session-level advisory locks behind PgBouncer and wondering why "someone else" holds the lock forever.
  • Putting the pooler in and then keeping pool max: 50 per pod because "PgBouncer handles it": cl_waiting still grows and max_client_conn is finite.

Interview questions

  1. Explain PgBouncer's three modes and what breaks in transaction mode. Expected: prepared statements, SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables; the fix for each. Why it matters: multi-tenant search_path bugs are a classic cross-tenant data leak.
  2. How do you implement per-tenant schemas safely behind a transaction pooler? Expected: SET LOCAL inside a transaction, or schema-qualified names.
  3. What is RDS Proxy session pinning and what causes it?
  4. Why does a pooler make failover smoother but not transparent?

Practical exercise

Run PgBouncer in Docker in transaction mode. From a Node script, run SET application_name = 'a' on one client then read current_setting('application_name') on another; show the leak. Then repeat with SET LOCAL inside a transaction. Acceptance criteria: you can demonstrate session state leakage and its fix, and explain SHOW POOLS output.

18.3 The lifecycle of a query

18.3.1 Parse, rewrite, plan, execute

Concept

Every statement your backend receives passes through four stages: the parser turns text into a tree and checks that tables and columns exist; the rewriter expands views and applies rules; the planner (also called optimizer) chooses how to execute (which index, which join order, which join algorithm) by estimating costs; the executor runs the chosen plan, pulling rows through a tree of nodes and sending them to the client.

Why does it exist?

SQL says what you want, not how to get it. SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 has dozens of possible executions (sequential scan and sort, index scan on user_id and sort, index scan on (user_id, created_at) with no sort). The planner exists to pick a good one using statistics. Separating stages also allows plan caching: parse and plan once, execute many times.

Mental model

Imagine ordering at a restaurant. The waiter checks the menu (parse: does this dish exist?), the head chef rewrites "the special" into concrete dishes (rewrite: expand views), the kitchen manager decides which station cooks what in which order to be fastest (plan), then cooks execute (execute).

How it works

flowchart LR
  q["SQL text"] --> p["Parser and analyzer"]
  p -->|"query tree"| r["Rewriter"]
  r -->|"expanded tree"| pl["Planner"]
  pl -->|"plan tree"| ex["Executor"]
  ex -->|"rows"| c["Client"]
  st["pg_statistic and catalogs"] --> pl
  sb["shared_buffers"] --> ex
  1. Parse. Lexing and grammar produce a raw parse tree. The analyzer resolves names against the catalog (pg_class, pg_attribute), checks types, and produces a query tree. Errors like column "user_ids" does not exist come from here. Cost: tens of microseconds for simple statements, milliseconds for 2,000-line reporting queries.
  2. Rewrite. Views are replaced by their definitions; INSTEAD OF rules and row-level security policies are applied.
  3. Plan. The planner enumerates access paths (seq scan, index scans, bitmap scans), join orders and join methods, estimates each path's cost from statistics, and keeps the cheapest. For joins of up to 8 tables it searches exhaustively; beyond geqo_threshold (12) it uses a genetic search. Detailed in 18.9.
  4. Execute. The executor is a pull-based tree: the top node asks its child for the next row, which asks its child, down to scans that read pages from shared_buffers. LIMIT 20 stops pulling after 20 rows, which is why an index that returns rows in the right order is such a big win.
  5. Results stream back to the client in the wire protocol; the backend marks the transaction complete (or waits for the next statement if inside BEGIN).

EXPLAIN shows stages 1 to 3; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs stage 4 and reports actual numbers. Reading plans line by line is Part 19's core skill.

Practical example

Orders API endpoint GET /orders?userId=42. Query text is identical each time except the parameter. Without caching, the backend parses and plans every call: 0.2 ms out of a 1.5 ms request. Small, until you run 5,000 queries per second on a 4-core instance, where planning is 15 percent of CPU. That is where prepared statements come in.

PostgreSQL example

Watch the stages: EXPLAIN alone stops before execution; add ANALYZE to execute.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, total_cents
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=0.57..45.12 rows=20 width=21) (actual time=0.031..0.079 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=24
  ->  Index Scan Backward using idx_orders_user_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..1783.40 rows=800 width=21) (actual time=0.029..0.074 rows=20 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (user_id = 42)
        Buffers: shared hit=24
Planning Time: 0.142 ms
Execution Time: 0.098 ms

Planning took 0.142 ms; execution 0.098 ms. For this cheap query, planning costs more than running it.

Production scenario

A 6,000 query-per-second workload, mostly 3 or 4 statement shapes. pg_stat_statements shows total_plan_time (PG 13+, needs pg_stat_statements.track_planning = on) as 12 percent of total time. Switching the hottest shapes to prepared statements (see next section) removed that cost, saving roughly half a vCPU.

Failure scenario

A reporting query joined 14 tables. Above geqo_threshold, the genetic optimizer produced a different plan on different runs, so the query took 3 s sometimes and 90 s other times. Fixing it meant rewriting with CTEs materialised (WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED) to force a structure and raising join_collapse_limit only for that session.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Planning cost explodes with partitioned tables (hundreds of partitions) unless partition pruning can happen at plan time.
  • Row-level security policies added in rewrite can silently add a subquery to every statement.
  • Views on views on views: each layer expands, and the planner sometimes cannot push predicates through aggregate views.
  • search_path changes make the same text resolve to different tables; plan caches are keyed on the resolved objects, so plans are invalidated.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that the same SQL text can produce different plans on different days (stats change) and design for that with auto_explain in production so a plan flip is visible instead of mysterious. They measure planning time on hot paths before adopting prepared statements.

Common mistakes

  • Reading EXPLAIN (estimates) as if it were EXPLAIN ANALYZE (actuals).
  • Assuming the ORM's generated SQL is the query; always log the exact text and parameters the driver sends.

Interview questions

  1. Describe the four stages a query passes through and what each can fail on.
  2. Why can EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE disagree? Expected: estimates from statistics vs actual rows; stale or missing stats.
  3. When does the planner stop searching join orders exhaustively?

Practical exercise

Take three queries from your service. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and record planning time vs execution time. Acceptance criteria: identify one query where planning is more than 20 percent of the total and explain what you would do about it.

18.3.2 Prepared statements and plan caching: generic vs custom plans

Concept

A prepared statement parses (and possibly plans) a statement once with placeholders ($1, $2), then executes it many times with different values. PostgreSQL caches the plan per backend. It first builds custom plans that use the actual parameter values, and after five executions it considers switching to a generic plan that does not look at values at all.

Why does it exist?

Parsing and planning cost CPU on every execution. For a hot query executed thousands of times per second, caching the plan is a real saving. The generic/custom split exists because a plan that ignores parameter values can be badly wrong for skewed data (a user_id with 2 million orders vs one with 3), while always replanning wastes the cache.

Mental model

Imagine a delivery driver who learns a route. For the first five trips they check the map each time (custom plan). Then they decide whether the "usual route" is good enough on average (generic plan). If one customer lives across the river, the usual route is a disaster for that customer, but the driver has stopped checking the map.

How it works

  1. PREPARE (SQL) or a protocol-level Parse message stores the parsed query in the backend's cache.
  2. Executions 1 to 5 build a custom plan using actual values, and PostgreSQL records their average estimated cost.
  3. At execution 6 it builds a generic plan (parameters treated as unknown, selectivity from column averages). If the generic plan's estimated cost is not higher than the average custom cost (plus a small planning-cost allowance), it switches to generic for all future executions.
  4. plan_cache_mode (PG 12+) overrides this: auto (default), force_custom_plan, force_generic_plan.
  5. Cache invalidation: any DDL on referenced tables or an ANALYZE that changes statistics invalidates the cached plan, and the next execution replans.
  6. In node-postgres, passing { name: 'orders_by_user', text, values } creates a named prepared statement per connection; without name, the extended protocol still uses an unnamed statement that is parsed per execution (parameterised, safe from injection, but not plan-cached). TypeORM and Sequelize do not set name, so plans are not cached across executions unless you use the driver directly.

Practical example

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. For a normal user (average 12 orders) the custom plan is an index scan on (user_id, created_at). The generic plan uses the average too, so it is the same. Safe. Now SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = $1. Status distribution: PAID 92 percent, PENDING 0.4 percent. Custom plans for PENDING use a partial index; the generic plan assumes 33 percent selectivity (1/3 distinct values) and chooses a sequential scan for every value, including PENDING. After five calls the query flips from 1 ms to 4 s.

NestJS example

Use the driver's named statement only where it pays, and keep an escape hatch:

// orders.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository {
  private readonly pool: Pool;

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {
    // TypeORM's postgres driver exposes the underlying pg Pool as `master`
    this.pool = (this.dataSource.driver as unknown as { master: Pool }).master;
  }

  async recentForUser(userId: number, limit = 20) {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query({
      name: 'orders_recent_for_user',        // named: plan cached per backend
      text: `SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
               FROM orders
              WHERE user_id = $1
              ORDER BY created_at DESC
              LIMIT $2`,
      values: [userId, limit],
    });
    return rows;
  }
}

Only do this when (a) you are not behind an old PgBouncer in transaction mode, and (b) the parameter distribution is not badly skewed. Otherwise leave TypeORM's default unnamed statements alone.

PostgreSQL example

See the flip happen:

PREPARE cnt(text) AS SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = $1;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) EXECUTE cnt('PENDING');   -- run this 6 times

Runs 1 to 5:

Aggregate  (actual time=0.412..0.413 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Index Only Scan using idx_orders_pending on orders
        (actual time=0.020..0.300 rows=812 loops=1)

Run 6 onward (generic plan chosen):

Aggregate  (actual time=3910.221..3910.222 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders  (actual time=0.018..3700.114 rows=812 loops=1)
        Filter: (status = $1)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 199999188

Fix per session or per role:

SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan;
-- or: ALTER ROLE orders_api SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan;

TypeORM example

TypeORM does not name statements, so the generic-plan problem does not occur through the repository API. If you need plan caching for a hot query, use the raw pool as above, or accept the planning cost.

Sequelize example

Same story: sequelize.query(sql, { bind: [...] }) uses the extended protocol without a statement name. Sequelize is safe from the generic-plan flip by default.

Production scenario

A payments service using a Go client with automatic statement caching (some drivers prepare everything) flipped a WHERE merchant_id = $1 query to a generic plan; the largest merchant (40 percent of rows) got a nested loop plan designed for the average merchant (0.01 percent) and caused 20 s timeouts every evening. The fix was plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan on that role, at the cost of 0.3 ms planning per call.

Failure scenario

"The query is fast in psql but slow in the app." Almost always one of: different parameter types (a text parameter compared with a bigint column prevents index use), a generic plan in the app but custom in psql, or a different search_path. Reproduce with PREPARE and EXECUTE six times, not with literals.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Parameter type mismatch: sending '42' as text for a bigint column forces a cast and may skip the index.
  • Plan cache invalidation storms after ALTER TABLE on a hot table: every backend replans at once.
  • Backends caching thousands of distinct prepared statements (dynamic SQL with names) grow memory without bound.
  • PgBouncer transaction mode before 1.21 and named statements.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They only use named statements for hot, evenly distributed queries, and they document the decision. They add a regression test that runs the hot query seven times through the same connection and asserts on EXPLAIN output, or they set plan_cache_mode explicitly for the role.

Common mistakes

  • Enabling driver-level statement caching globally and getting a generic-plan flip on one skewed query.
  • Debugging with literals in psql when the app uses parameters.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a custom plan and a generic plan, and when does PostgreSQL switch? Expected: five custom executions, then a cost comparison; plan_cache_mode to force. Why it matters: it is a common cause of "fast in psql, slow in prod".
  2. Does TypeORM cache plans server-side? Expected: no named statements by default; unnamed extended-protocol statements are parameterised but re-planned.
  3. How would you reproduce a generic-plan problem in psql?

Practical exercise

Create an orders table with 5 million rows and a skewed status column. Reproduce the generic-plan flip with PREPARE/EXECUTE, then fix it two ways (partial index plus force_custom_plan; rewriting to avoid the parameter). Acceptance criteria: you show both plans and the timing difference, and explain why EXPLAIN on run 6 differs from run 1.

18.4 Shared buffers and on-disk storage

18.4.1 Shared buffers: PostgreSQL's own page cache

Concept

PostgreSQL never reads or writes a row directly from disk. Everything happens in units of 8 KB pages (also called blocks). A page is loaded from the data file into shared buffers, a fixed-size array of 8 KB slots in shared memory, and every backend reads and modifies rows inside those slots. Modified pages are called dirty and are written back later by the background writer or the checkpointer, never by your COMMIT.

The setting shared_buffers decides how many slots exist. The default (128 MB) is tiny; production servers use roughly 25 percent of RAM.

Why does it exist?

Disk is slow and page-oriented. An NVMe random read costs about 100 microseconds, an EBS gp3 read 0.5 to 1 ms, while a page already in shared buffers costs well under a microsecond to pin. A cache that holds the hot working set (recent orders, the inventory table, the top of every B-tree) turns most queries into pure memory operations. Having PostgreSQL's own cache (rather than relying only on the OS page cache) lets it track which pages are dirty, pin pages that are in use, and control write ordering relative to the WAL, which the operating system cannot do for it.

Mental model

Imagine a librarian with a desk (shared buffers) and an archive room (disk). Every book requested is brought to the desk. The desk has a fixed number of slots; when it is full, the least-recently-used book goes back to the archive. If someone wrote notes in a book (dirty page), it must be copied back to the archive before the slot can be reused. The librarian also keeps a stack of the most-touched books close at hand: that is why the top pages of a B-tree index practically never leave memory.

How it works

  1. A backend needs page 12,345 of orders. It hashes (relation, fork, block number) into the buffer mapping table in shared memory.
  2. Hit: the page is present. The backend pins it (increments a pin count so nobody evicts it), bumps its usage count (0 to 5), reads the tuples, unpins. Cost: roughly 0.1 to 1 microsecond plus lock overhead.
  3. Miss: the backend runs the clock-sweep algorithm: it walks a circular pointer over the buffer array, decrementing usage counts, until it finds a buffer with count 0 that is not pinned. If that buffer is dirty, the backend must write it out first (this shows up as buffers_backend in pg_stat_bgwriter, or in pg_stat_io on PG 16+). Then it issues a read() syscall for the 8 KB page. The OS may serve it from its page cache (5 to 20 microseconds) or from disk (100 microseconds to 1 ms).
  4. The background writer runs ahead of the clock hand and writes dirty, low-usage buffers so that step 3 rarely has to write. bgwriter_lru_maxpages (100) and bgwriter_delay (200 ms) limit how much it does per round.
  5. Large sequential scans (tables bigger than a quarter of shared buffers), bulk writes, and VACUUM use a small ring buffer (256 KB for scans, 16 MB for COPY) so that one reporting query does not evict your whole hot set.
  6. Double caching: the OS page cache also holds file data. A page can sit in both. This is why shared_buffers above roughly 8 to 16 GB gives diminishing returns on most workloads: the OS cache already holds the rest, and huge shared buffers make checkpoints write more at once. The planner is told about the combined cache size through effective_cache_size (typically 50 to 75 percent of RAM); this only influences cost estimates, it allocates nothing.
Backend wants a page
   |
   v
 buffer mapping table (hash) --hit--> pin, read, unpin   (~0.5 us)
   |
  miss
   |
   v
 clock sweep: find victim slot (evict, write if dirty)
   |
   v
 read() 8 KB from OS
   |--- OS page cache hit  (~10 us)
   '--- disk read         (NVMe ~100 us, EBS ~500-1000 us)

Buffer hit ratio. pg_stat_database.blks_hit counts shared-buffer hits, blks_read counts reads from the OS (which may still be OS-cache hits, not disk). A ratio below 99 percent on an OLTP database usually means the working set does not fit or a scan is churning the cache. Turning on track_io_timing makes blk_read_time show real time spent waiting for reads, which separates OS-cache reads from disk reads.

Realistic numbers: a 32 GB instance with shared_buffers = 8GB and a 40 GB database. The hot set (last 30 days of orders, all of inventory, all index upper levels) is about 6 GB; the hit ratio sits at 99.7 percent. A monthly report that scans all of order_items (25 GB) pushes hit ratio to 97 percent for ten minutes and p99 latency doubles, because even with the ring buffer it evicts OS-cache pages and causes real disk reads for everyone else.

Practical example

GET /products/:id reads one product row through the primary key index. Index root and internal pages: always in shared buffers. Leaf page: usually cached. Heap page: cached if that product was read recently. Cold product on a cold instance: 3 or 4 disk reads at 0.7 ms each on EBS gives a 3 ms request instead of 0.3 ms. After a restart or a failover, the whole cache is cold, and for the first minutes every request pays this. That is the "slow after failover" effect, and pg_prewarm exists to fix it.

NestJS example

A health endpoint that exposes buffer hit ratio and disk read time, which you can scrape with Prometheus. It uses the @nestjs/terminus health check style with a custom indicator.

// db-cache.health.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthIndicatorService } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class DbCacheHealthIndicator {
  constructor(
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    private readonly health: HealthIndicatorService,
  ) {}

  async isHealthy(key = 'pg_cache') {
    const indicator = this.health.check(key);
    const [row] = await this.dataSource.query(`
      SELECT round(100.0 * blks_hit / greatest(blks_hit + blks_read, 1), 2) AS hit_ratio,
             blk_read_time                                                  AS read_ms
      FROM pg_stat_database
      WHERE datname = current_database()`);
    const hitRatio = Number(row.hit_ratio);
    // 99% is a reasonable floor for OLTP; below that, investigate scans or RAM
    return hitRatio >= 99
      ? indicator.up({ hitRatio, readMs: Number(row.read_ms) })
      : indicator.down({ hitRatio, readMs: Number(row.read_ms) });
  }
}

Health checks like this are for dashboards and alerts, not for Kubernetes readiness; a cold cache after failover should not take pods out of rotation.

PostgreSQL example

Inspect what is actually in the cache with pg_buffercache:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_buffercache;

SELECT c.relname,
       count(*)                                   AS buffers,
       pg_size_pretty(count(*) * 8192)            AS cached,
       round(100.0 * count(*) /
             (SELECT setting::int FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'shared_buffers'), 1)
                                                  AS pct_of_cache,
       sum(CASE WHEN b.isdirty THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS dirty
FROM pg_buffercache b
JOIN pg_class c ON b.relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(c.oid)
WHERE b.reldatabase = (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database())
GROUP BY c.relname
ORDER BY buffers DESC
LIMIT 8;
 relname                  | buffers | cached  | pct_of_cache | dirty
--------------------------+---------+---------+--------------+-------
 orders                   |  412880 | 3226 MB |         39.4 | 18211
 idx_orders_user_created  |  201330 | 1573 MB |         19.2 |  4410
 order_items              |  188002 | 1469 MB |         17.9 |  9002
 inventory                |    7680 |   60 MB |          0.7 |  7620   <-- almost every page dirty
 idx_orders_pkey          |   98110 |  766 MB |          9.4 |  1201

inventory being almost entirely dirty tells you it is rewritten constantly (500 updates per second) and that every checkpoint rewrites all 60 MB of it.

Warm the cache after a restart or failover instead of letting users do it:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_prewarm;
SELECT pg_prewarm('inventory');                        -- whole table
SELECT pg_prewarm('idx_orders_user_created', 'buffer'); -- into shared buffers

With shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_prewarm' and pg_prewarm.autoprewarm = on, PostgreSQL records the buffer contents periodically and reloads them automatically on start.

TypeORM example

The cache is invisible to TypeORM, but your entity design decides how many pages a query touches. Selecting only needed columns keeps wide or TOASTed columns out of the read path:

// Avoid pulling the jsonb attributes column (possibly TOASTed) into a listing
const products = await productRepo.find({
  select: { id: true, sku: true, name: true, priceCents: true },
  where: { sku: In(skus) },
});

Sequelize example

const products = await Product.findAll({
  attributes: ['id', 'sku', 'name', 'priceCents'],
  where: { sku: { [Op.in]: skus } },
});

Production scenario

Sizing on a 64 GB RDS instance running a 300 GB database: shared_buffers = 16GB, effective_cache_size = 48GB. The daily working set is 30 GB, so it does not fit in shared buffers but does fit in shared buffers plus OS cache. Hit ratio is 98.5 percent, which is acceptable because blk_read_time shows that most "reads" are OS cache hits at 15 microseconds. The team's alert is not on hit ratio; it is on blk_read_time per second and on EBS read IOPS, which is what actually hurts latency.

Monitoring checklist: hit ratio per database, pg_stat_io (PG 16+) per backend type, buffers_backend (backends forced to write), EBS/NVMe read IOPS and latency, and pg_buffercache snapshots of the top relations.

Failure scenario

At 06:00 a nightly analytics job ran SELECT ... FROM order_items JOIN orders ... across two years of data on the primary. The ring buffer protected shared buffers, but the 30 GB scan flushed the OS page cache. For the next 20 minutes, every cold read of an orders page went to EBS at 0.8 ms, the API p99 rose from 90 ms to 700 ms, and the pool's connectionTimeoutMillis started firing because each request held its connection 8 times longer. The fix was to run analytics on a replica (see Part 22 — Replication and Scaling Reads) and to warm the cache after the job.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cold cache after restart, failover, or instance resize: minutes of elevated latency; use pg_prewarm and warm-up traffic before switching load balancers.
  • A single SELECT * on a table wider than the cache thrashes the OS cache even though shared buffers are protected by the ring.
  • Very large shared_buffers (over 50 percent of RAM) starves the OS cache and work_mem, and makes checkpoints heavier.
  • Huge pages: on Linux, huge_pages = try reduces TLB pressure for big shared buffers; on containers it may silently fail to allocate.
  • pg_buffercache scanning itself takes a lock on every buffer briefly; do not run it every second on a 64 GB cache.
  • Checksums (data_checksums, enabled at initdb) detect corruption when a page is read into shared buffers; a checksum failure on a hot page turns into repeated errors until the page is repaired from a replica or backup.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They care less about the hit ratio number and more about what is in the cache and why it left. They keep analytics off the primary. They budget RAM as shared_buffers + (max_connections × work_mem × expected sorts) + OS cache. They warm caches before traffic shifts. They explain to a product manager: "After a database failover the first few minutes are slow because the new server has an empty memory cache; we pre-load it so customers do not notice."

Common mistakes

  • Setting shared_buffers to 80 percent of RAM because "more cache is better".
  • Alerting on hit ratio alone and missing that blks_read are OS cache hits.
  • Running reports on the primary and blaming the API code for latency.
  • Forgetting that effective_cache_size is a planner hint, not an allocation.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between shared_buffers and the OS page cache, and why does PostgreSQL keep both? Expected: PostgreSQL needs dirty tracking, pinning and WAL ordering; the OS cache is a second layer it cannot control. Follow-up: what does effective_cache_size do?
  2. Why can a 97 percent buffer hit ratio be fine on one system and a disaster on another? Expected: the misses may be OS-cache hits (cheap) or EBS reads (expensive); track_io_timing separates them.
  3. How does a large sequential scan avoid evicting the hot working set? Expected: ring buffers.
  4. What happens to latency right after a failover and how do you mitigate it?

Practical exercise

On a local instance, create orders with 20 million rows. Restart PostgreSQL, run a point lookup and record EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output (shared read). Run it again (shared hit). Then pg_prewarm the table and index and repeat after another restart. Acceptance criteria: you can show read turning into hit, explain the timing difference, and describe when pg_prewarm belongs in a failover runbook.

18.4.2 Heap pages, tuple layout, and TOAST

Concept

A table's rows live in a heap: a plain sequence of 8 KB pages with no ordering. Each row is stored as a tuple, which is a header (23 bytes) plus the column data. Inside a page, tuples are found through a small array of line pointers at the start of the page. A row's physical address, called the ctid, is (page number, line pointer number); every index entry stores a ctid, which is how an index scan finds the heap row.

Values that do not fit comfortably in a page (a 50 KB jsonb document, a long text description) are compressed and, if still too big, sliced into chunks and stored in a side table. That mechanism is called TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique).

Why does it exist?

Fixed 8 KB pages make caching, WAL and I/O simple, but rows have variable sizes and can exceed a page. Line pointers let tuples move within a page (during defragmentation by VACUUM or HOT pruning) without changing their ctid, so indexes stay valid. TOAST exists so that a table with one occasionally-huge column does not force every row read to drag megabytes through the cache.

Mental model

Imagine a filing cabinet drawer (page). At the front is an index card listing where each document sits in the drawer (line pointers). Documents (tuples) are stacked from the back. If a document is too thick, you keep a sticky note in its place saying "see box 17 in the basement" (TOAST pointer), and the basement (toast table) holds the thick document cut into numbered chunks.

How it works

Page layout:

+-----------------------------+ 0
| page header (24 bytes)      |  pd_lsn, pd_checksum, pd_lower, pd_upper, pd_special ...
+-----------------------------+
| line pointers (4 bytes each)|  lp1 -> offset 8100, lp2 -> offset 8040, lp3 (dead) ...
|  ...grows downward          |
+-----------------------------+ pd_lower
|                             |
|        free space           |
|                             |
+-----------------------------+ pd_upper
| tuple 3 | tuple 2 | tuple 1 |  tuples grow upward from the end
+-----------------------------+ 8192  (special space is empty for heap pages)

Tuple layout:

  1. Header, 23 bytes: t_xmin (transaction that inserted it), t_xmax (transaction that deleted or updated it, 0 if none), t_cid (command id within the transaction), t_ctid (points to itself, or to the newer version after an update), t_infomask and t_infomask2 (flag bits: has nulls, committed hints, HOT flags), t_hoff (offset to data).
  2. Null bitmap (only if any column is null): one bit per column, rounded up to bytes.
  3. Padding to an 8-byte boundary (MAXALIGN), so the header effectively costs 24 bytes.
  4. Column data in declared column order, each aligned to its type's requirement: int4 to 4 bytes, int8/timestamptz/float8 to 8 bytes, text/jsonb are variable-length with a 1 or 4 byte length prefix.

So a row (id bigint, quantity int, updated_at timestamptz) costs 24 header + 8 + 4 + 4 padding + 8 = 48 bytes, plus a 4-byte line pointer: 52 bytes. Reordering columns so 8-byte types come first (id, updated_at, quantity) saves the 4 padding bytes. On a 500 million row table, that is 2 GB of heap and cache. The maximum number of tuples per 8 KB page is 291; a typical orders row of about 100 bytes gives roughly 70 rows per page.

TOAST, step by step:

  1. When a tuple is about to exceed TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD (about 2 KB), PostgreSQL looks at its variable-length columns, largest first.
  2. Depending on the column's storage strategy (EXTENDED is the default for text, jsonb, bytea), it first tries to compress the value (pglz by default, lz4 if default_toast_compression = lz4 on PG 14+, which is 3 to 5 times faster to compress and decompress).
  3. If the tuple still exceeds toast_tuple_target (2 KB by default, settable per table), the value is moved out of line into the table's toast relation pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>, split into chunks of about 2,000 bytes, indexed by (chunk_id, chunk_seq). The main tuple keeps an 18-byte pointer.
  4. Reading the column later means an index lookup plus one heap fetch per chunk in the toast table, then decompression. A 200 KB jsonb value is about 100 chunks: 100 extra page reads.
  5. Updating any other column copies the toast pointer, not the value; TOAST data is only rewritten when the toasted column itself changes.

Storage strategies you can set with ALTER TABLE products ALTER COLUMN attributes SET STORAGE ...:

Strategy Compress? Out-of-line? Use when
PLAIN no no fixed-size types only
MAIN yes last resort you want the value kept in the main tuple
EXTENDED yes yes default; general purpose
EXTERNAL no yes already-compressed data (images, gzip), or substring access on text/bytea

Practical example

products.attributes holds a jsonb document per product: usually 1 to 3 KB, but for 5 percent of products (with rich specification sheets) 40 to 120 KB. Those 5 percent live in the toast table. GET /products?category=... listing 50 products with SELECT * fetches all toast chunks even though the listing renders only name and price_cents: 50 products × (about 2 to 60 chunk reads) instead of 50 heap reads. The fix is to select only the columns the endpoint needs, or move rarely-read attributes to a separate product_details table.

PostgreSQL example

Look inside a page with pageinspect, and measure toast:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;

-- Tuples on the first page of orders: xmin/xmax are the MVCC columns (see 11.7)
SELECT lp, lp_flags, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid, t_hoff
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('orders', 0))
LIMIT 5;
 lp | lp_flags |  t_xmin  |  t_xmax  | t_ctid | t_hoff
----+----------+----------+----------+--------+--------
  1 |        1 | 48812201 |        0 | (0,1)  |     24
  2 |        1 | 48812201 | 48819903 | (0,7)  |     24   <-- updated; new version at (0,7)
  3 |        3 |          |          |        |          <-- redirect (HOT chain)
  4 |        1 | 48812210 |        0 | (0,4)  |     24
-- How much of products actually lives in TOAST?
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('products'))               AS heap,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(reltoastrelid))             AS toast,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('products'))                 AS indexes
FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'products';
 heap    | toast   | indexes
---------+---------+---------
 610 MB  | 4.2 GB  | 280 MB

Switch to LZ4 for new values and reduce CPU spent decompressing:

ALTER TABLE products ALTER COLUMN attributes SET COMPRESSION lz4;   -- PG 14+
-- existing values keep pglz until rewritten; VACUUM FULL or pg_repack rewrites them

TypeORM example

Declare the column with the right PostgreSQL type; simple-json stores a string in text, which loses jsonb operators and indexing.

@Entity('products')
export class Product {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' })
  id!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  sku!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  name!: string;

  // jsonb: binary, indexable with GIN, TOASTed when large
  @Column({ type: 'jsonb', default: () => "'{}'" })
  attributes!: Record<string, unknown>;

  @Column({ name: 'price_cents', type: 'integer' })
  priceCents!: number;
}

Sequelize example

Product.init(
  {
    id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, autoIncrement: true, primaryKey: true },
    sku: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false },
    name: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false },
    attributes: { type: DataTypes.JSONB, allowNull: false, defaultValue: {} },
    priceCents: { type: DataTypes.INTEGER, allowNull: false, field: 'price_cents' },
  },
  { sequelize, tableName: 'products', underscored: true },
);

Production scenario

A catalogue of 2 million products: heap 610 MB, toast 4.2 GB, because a sync job rewrites attributes for every product every night even when nothing changed. Each rewrite creates a new toast tuple set (100 chunks for a big product) and leaves the old ones dead until autovacuum on the toast table cleans them. Toast tables have their own autovacuum statistics and are often forgotten. The sync job was changed to UPDATE ... WHERE attributes IS DISTINCT FROM $2, which reduced nightly toast churn by 96 percent and shrank the table by 3 GB after pg_repack.

Failure scenario

"Index row size 3168 exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704 for index". A developer added a B-tree index on products.attributes (the whole jsonb) to "speed up searches". B-tree entries must fit in a third of a page; large TOASTed values cannot be indexed that way. The migration failed in production after succeeding on a dev database with small documents. The right tool is a GIN index on the jsonb or an expression index on the specific key (Part 19).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • TOAST bloat when large values are rewritten frequently; monitor pg_stat_all_tables for pg_toast.* relations.
  • SELECT * on wide tables through an ORM silently detoasts every row.
  • Column order padding waste on very large tables.
  • Values over roughly 2.7 KB cannot go in a B-tree index entry.
  • pglz decompression CPU on hot paths; switch to lz4.
  • bytea images in the database: the database becomes a slow, expensive blob store; use object storage and keep a key.
  • Toast chunks are read with their own index; a bloated toast index makes reads of large values slower still.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design tables so that hot, small columns stay in the main tuple and large, rarely-read blobs live elsewhere (a side table, or S3 with a key). They order columns to avoid padding on tables that will reach hundreds of millions of rows. They know a jsonb column of 100 KB is a toast table with its own vacuum needs and its own I/O cost, and they ask "how often is it read, how often is it rewritten?" before agreeing to it.

Common mistakes

  • Storing large blobs or entire API responses in jsonb columns on hot tables.
  • Rewriting unchanged jsonb values in sync jobs.
  • Expecting a B-tree index on a jsonb column to work.
  • Not vacuuming or monitoring toast tables.

Interview questions

  1. What is a ctid and why do indexes store it? Expected: physical row address (page, line pointer); indexes point to heap tuples; VACUUM and HOT rely on line pointers so ctids stay stable within a page.
  2. When does a value get TOASTed and what does reading it cost? Expected: tuple above about 2 KB triggers compression then out-of-line storage in 2 KB chunks; reading is an index lookup plus a heap read per chunk.
  3. Why does column order matter for storage? Expected: alignment padding.
  4. Why did a B-tree index on a jsonb column fail in production but not in dev?

Practical exercise

Create products with a jsonb column and insert 100,000 rows with 5 percent having 60 KB documents. Measure heap, toast and index sizes. Compare EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for SELECT * vs SELECT id, name for 50 rows. Then change the column to lz4 compression, rewrite the values, and measure again. Acceptance criteria: you show buffer counts differing by an order of magnitude and explain where the extra reads come from.

18.5 The write-ahead log (WAL)

18.5.1 Why every write goes to the WAL first

Concept

The write-ahead log is an append-only file stream in the pg_wal directory. Before PostgreSQL changes any data page in shared buffers in a way that must survive a crash, it first writes a record describing that change to the WAL. At COMMIT, PostgreSQL forces the WAL up to that transaction's commit record onto disk (fsync) and only then tells your application "committed". The dirty data pages themselves are written to the data files later, at leisure, by the checkpointer and background writer.

The WAL is the single most important structure in PostgreSQL: crash recovery, streaming replication, logical replication, point-in-time recovery, and backups all read it.

Why does it exist?

Writing data pages directly on commit would mean random 8 KB writes all over the disk for every transaction, and a crash halfway through a multi-page update would leave the database inconsistent. Appending a small sequential record to one file is far cheaper (one fsync of a few hundred bytes at the end of a file), and replaying the log after a crash brings the pages back to the committed state. The write-ahead rule is exactly this: a data page may not be written to disk before the WAL records describing its changes are on disk.

Mental model

Imagine an accountant who writes every transaction into a bound journal (WAL) immediately, in ink, and only later updates the many ledger books (data files) at a convenient time. If the office floods, the ledgers may be out of date, but the journal is complete and the ledgers can be rebuilt from it. The journal is fast to write because you only ever add a line at the end.

How it works

flowchart LR
  app["NestJS COMMIT"] --> be["backend"]
  be -->|"1 WAL record"| wb["WAL buffers"]
  be -->|"2 modify page"| sb["shared_buffers dirty page"]
  wb -->|"3 flush and fsync at commit"| wal["pg_wal segment files"]
  wal -->|"stream"| rep["replica walreceiver"]
  wal -->|"archive_command"| arch["S3 WAL archive"]
  sb -->|"4 later: checkpointer or bgwriter"| data["data files"]
  wal -->|"5 crash recovery replays from last checkpoint"| data
  1. Your UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE product_id = 7 runs. The backend pins the heap page, and before modifying it, builds a WAL record: "in relation X, page Y, replace tuple Z with this new version". It copies that record into WAL buffers in shared memory (size wal_buffers, default 1/32 of shared_buffers up to 16 MB) and gets back an LSN (log sequence number: a 64-bit byte offset into the log, displayed like 1A/3F2B8C40).
  2. The page is modified in shared buffers and stamped with that LSN in its header (pd_lsn). The page is now dirty.
  3. On COMMIT, the backend writes a commit record and calls XLogFlush up to it: the WAL buffers are written to the current 16 MB segment file and fsync'd. The commit returns only after the fsync succeeds. Cost: 0.1 to 0.3 ms on local NVMe, 1 to 3 ms on EBS. Concurrent committers share one fsync (group commit), which is why throughput scales with concurrency even though each commit waits.
  4. The WAL writer process also flushes WAL buffers every wal_writer_delay (200 ms) so that asynchronous commits and long transactions do not keep everything in memory.
  5. Dirty pages reach the data files later. The write-ahead rule is enforced when a page is about to be written: the writer first checks the page's pd_lsn and flushes the WAL up to it.
  6. Crash recovery: on startup PostgreSQL reads pg_control for the last checkpoint's redo point, then replays every WAL record from there to the end of the log. Replay is idempotent because it compares each record's LSN with the target page's pd_lsn: if the page already has that change, the record is skipped.
  7. Replication is "ship the WAL somewhere else and replay it there". PITR is "keep a base backup plus every WAL segment since, and replay up to a chosen time" (recovery_target_time).

synchronous_commit controls step 3 and is one of the few knobs you can set per transaction:

Value Commit returns after You can lose on primary crash Use
on (default) local WAL fsync nothing money, orders, inventory
off WAL record in memory up to about 3 × wal_writer_delay (600 ms) of commits; never corruption audit logs, analytics events, click tracking
local local fsync, ignores sync replicas nothing locally same as on when sync replication is configured
remote_write replica has received and written (not fsync'd) nothing unless both crash near-sync HA
remote_apply replica has applied nothing; reads on replica see it read-your-writes across replicas at a latency cost

fsync = off is a different, dangerous thing: it stops PostgreSQL from ever forcing data to disk and allows real corruption on a crash. Never in production.

Full-page writes. The OS and disk typically write in 4 KB units, but a PostgreSQL page is 8 KB. A crash mid-write can leave a torn page: half new, half old. To survive this, the first modification of any page after a checkpoint writes the entire 8 KB page into the WAL (full_page_writes = on), not just the change. Replay then restores the full image before applying later diffs. Consequence: right after each checkpoint, WAL volume spikes because every hot page gets a full-page image again. wal_compression = lz4 (PG 15+) shrinks those images by 50 to 80 percent for a little CPU.

WAL volume. Every insert, update, delete, index change, TOAST chunk, and commit writes WAL. Typical sizes: a small orders insert with 4 indexes is roughly 500 to 900 bytes of WAL; an update of a wide row that touches an indexed column is 1 to 2 KB plus index records; a full-page image is 8 KB (before compression). A workload of 3,000 writes per second easily produces 5 to 20 MB of WAL per second, which is 0.5 to 1.7 TB per day. That volume drives disk write IOPS, replication bandwidth, replica lag, archive storage cost, and backup size.

Practical example

Order placement in the checkout service: one transaction inserts an orders row, three order_items, a payments row, and updates three inventory rows. That is roughly 15 WAL records including index updates, about 6 KB of WAL, and one fsync at commit. At 200 checkouts per second, that is 1.2 MB/s of WAL and 200 fsyncs per second, which group commit collapses into maybe 60 real disk flushes. On EBS gp3 at 2 ms per flush that is fine; on a network disk at 10 ms per flush, 200 sequential commits per second on one connection would be impossible, and only concurrency (group commit) keeps throughput up.

NestJS example

Relax durability only where the business allows it, and only for that transaction. SET LOCAL keeps it scoped to the transaction, which is also safe behind PgBouncer transaction mode.

// product-view-events.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class ProductViewEventsService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  // Losing the last ~600 ms of view events on a primary crash is acceptable;
  // waiting 2 ms for fsync on every page view is not.
  async record(userId: number | null, productId: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
      await em.query(`SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = 'off'`);
      await em.query(
        `INSERT INTO product_view_events (user_id, product_id, viewed_at)
         VALUES ($1, $2, now())`,
        [userId, productId],
      );
    });
  }
}

Never do this for orders, payments or inventory. The question to ask is: "If the database crashes one second after we told the customer 'success', is that acceptable?"

PostgreSQL example

Measure WAL generation and see what a single statement costs:

-- Where is the log right now?
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();                        -- e.g. 1A/3F2B8C40

-- WAL bytes generated in the last minute (run twice, 60 s apart)
SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), '1A/3F2B8C40') AS bytes_since;

-- PG 14+: cumulative WAL statistics
SELECT wal_records, wal_fpi, pg_size_pretty(wal_bytes) AS wal_bytes,
       wal_buffers_full, wal_write, wal_sync, wal_sync_time
FROM pg_stat_wal;
 wal_records | wal_fpi  | wal_bytes | wal_buffers_full | wal_write | wal_sync | wal_sync_time
-------------+----------+-----------+------------------+-----------+----------+---------------
  9184423110 | 41022019 | 6812 GB   |           120433 |  55129811 | 30188211 |   61302241.5

wal_fpi (full-page images) being 0.4 percent of records but a large share of bytes tells you checkpoints are the source of most WAL volume. wal_buffers_full above zero at high rate means wal_buffers is too small. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL) (PG 13+) shows WAL per statement:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL)
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1, updated_at = now() WHERE product_id = 7;
Update on inventory  (actual time=0.081..0.082 rows=0 loops=1)
  WAL: records=2 bytes=213
  ->  Index Scan using inventory_pkey on inventory ...

Replication slot retention, the classic disk-full cause:

SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, wal_status,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained_wal
FROM pg_replication_slots;
 slot_name        | slot_type | active | wal_status | retained_wal
------------------+-----------+--------+------------+--------------
 replica_1        | physical  | t      | reserved   | 48 MB
 debezium_orders  | logical   | f      | extended   | 212 GB      <-- consumer dead since Friday

max_slot_wal_keep_size = '50GB' (PG 13+) caps this: the slot is invalidated (wal_status = lost) rather than the primary running out of disk.

TypeORM example

The same per-transaction durability choice with a QueryRunner, useful when you need explicit control:

const qr = dataSource.createQueryRunner();
await qr.connect();
await qr.startTransaction();
try {
  await qr.query(`SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = 'off'`);
  await qr.manager.insert(ProductViewEvent, { userId, productId, viewedAt: new Date() });
  await qr.commitTransaction();
} catch (e) {
  await qr.rollbackTransaction();
  throw e;
} finally {
  await qr.release();   // forgetting this leaks a pooled connection
}

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await sequelize.query(`SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = 'off'`, { transaction: t });
  await ProductViewEvent.create({ userId, productId, viewedAt: new Date() }, { transaction: t });
});

Production scenario

Streaming replication for a 300 GB database with two replicas: the primary generates 8 MB/s of WAL at peak. Replicas apply it with roughly 50 to 300 ms lag over a same-region network; cross-region replicas see 1 to 3 s. Backups use a base backup every night plus continuous WAL archiving to S3 (archive_mode = on, archive_command or a tool such as pgBackRest or WAL-G), giving recovery to any second in the last 14 days. The team monitors: WAL generation rate, pg_stat_replication.replay_lag, archive failures (pg_stat_archiver.failed_count), and pg_wal directory size.

Production-first answers: What can go wrong? Slow fsync storage makes every commit slow; a dead slot fills the disk; archive failure silently breaks PITR. How do I monitor it? The four metrics above. How do I scale it? Faster disks for WAL (separate volume on self-managed), wal_compression, fewer indexes, batching small transactions. When should I not touch it? Never disable fsync or full_page_writes unless the storage guarantees atomic 8 KB writes (ZFS) and you have verified it.

Failure scenario

Saturday 03:40: PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.12345": No space left on device. The primary crashed and refused to restart because it could not write WAL. A Debezium connector that fed the search index had been failing since Friday 18:00; its logical replication slot kept 212 GB of WAL on a 250 GB volume. Recovery meant resizing the volume (RDS: storage increase takes minutes to hours), starting the server, and dropping the slot with pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_orders'). Permanent fixes: max_slot_wal_keep_size, an alert on pg_replication_slots where active = false for more than 10 minutes, and a disk-usage alert at 70 percent.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Disk full from WAL retention (slot, failed archive, wal_keep_size too large) crashes the primary.
  • Archive command failing silently: pg_stat_archiver.failed_count climbs, pg_wal grows, PITR is broken from the last successful segment.
  • synchronous_commit = remote_apply with a slow replica: every commit waits for the replica; a replica outage stalls all writes unless synchronous_standby_names allows a quorum.
  • WAL burst after checkpoint from full-page images causing replica lag spikes every checkpoint_timeout.
  • Bulk loads (COPY of 100 million rows) generating WAL faster than replicas can apply or archive can upload.
  • Transaction with 1 GB of changes: WAL is written incrementally, but the commit record is tiny; rollbacks are cheap (no undo log), which is a deliberate MVCC design choice (see 18.7).
  • Storage that lies about fsync (some consumer SSDs, misconfigured virtual disks) corrupts on power loss; pg_test_fsync measures real flush latency.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see WAL as the cost model for writes: every index, every wide update, every tiny separate transaction is WAL bytes and fsyncs. They batch where the business allows (one transaction for 500 inventory updates instead of 500 transactions). They relax synchronous_commit per transaction for genuinely non-critical writes, and document why. They never let a replication slot exist without an alert on it. They ask before every "stream the database changes to X" proposal: "who watches the slot, and what happens to the primary when X is down for a weekend?"

Common mistakes

  • Creating logical replication slots for experiments and forgetting them.
  • Setting synchronous_commit = off globally "for performance" and losing paid orders in a crash.
  • Assuming a commit is durable on the replica because it is durable on the primary.
  • Thousands of single-row transactions per second when a batch would cost one fsync.

Interview questions

  1. What does "write-ahead" guarantee, and why does it make commits fast? Expected: WAL record is durable before any data page write; sequential append plus one fsync per commit group instead of random page writes.
  2. What is the difference between synchronous_commit = off and fsync = off? Expected: the first risks losing recent commits, never consistency; the second risks corruption. Why it matters: candidates who confuse them can destroy a database.
  3. Why does WAL volume spike after a checkpoint? Expected: full-page writes for the first modification of each page.
  4. A replication slot's consumer dies. What happens over the next 48 hours? Expected: WAL retention grows, disk fills, primary PANICs; max_slot_wal_keep_size and alerting prevent it.
  5. How does crash recovery know where to start and when it can skip a record? Expected: checkpoint redo pointer in pg_control; page LSN comparison.

Practical exercise

On a local instance, run 10,000 single-row inserts as separate transactions and time them; then 10,000 inserts in one transaction; then 10,000 separate transactions with synchronous_commit = off. Record pg_stat_wal before and after each run. Acceptance criteria: you present a table with total time, WAL bytes and wal_sync count per run, and explain each difference in terms of fsync and group commit.

18.6 Checkpoints

18.6.1 What a checkpoint does and why it causes I/O spikes

Concept

A checkpoint is the moment PostgreSQL guarantees that every data page dirtied before a certain WAL position has been written to the data files. After a checkpoint completes, crash recovery only needs to replay WAL written after it, and older WAL segments can be recycled. The checkpointer process does this on a timer (checkpoint_timeout, default 5 minutes) or when enough WAL has accumulated (max_wal_size, default 1 GB), whichever comes first.

Why does it exist?

Without checkpoints, dirty pages could sit in shared buffers forever, WAL could never be deleted, and a crash would require replaying days of WAL. Checkpoints bound recovery time and WAL disk usage. The price is a burst of writes: every dirty page in the cache must reach disk.

Mental model

Imagine the accountant from the WAL story. Once an hour they stop taking new journal entries for a moment, note "all journal lines up to number 84,120 are now reflected in the ledgers", and carry every pending change into the ledger books. After that, old journal pages can be archived. The more they let pile up, the bigger and more disruptive the hourly catch-up.

How it works

flowchart TB
  t["trigger: checkpoint_timeout or max_wal_size"] --> s["checkpointer starts, records redo point LSN"]
  s --> w["write dirty pages spread over checkpoint_completion_target"]
  w --> f["fsync every touched data file"]
  f --> r["write checkpoint record to WAL, update pg_control"]
  r --> rc["recycle or remove WAL segments before redo point"]
  r --> fpw["next write to each page logs a full-page image"]
  1. The checkpointer records the current WAL position as the redo point.
  2. It scans shared buffers for dirty pages and writes them, sleeping between writes so that the whole set finishes at checkpoint_completion_target (0.9) of the interval. With checkpoint_timeout = 15min, writes are spread across 13.5 minutes.
  3. It fsyncs every data file it touched. This sync phase is where the I/O spike happens: the OS has been buffering the writes, and now it must push them all. On EBS or slow disks, the sync phase can take seconds and every other I/O waits behind it.
  4. It writes a checkpoint record to the WAL and stores the redo point in pg_control.
  5. WAL segments older than the redo point are recycled (renamed for reuse, up to min_wal_size) or removed, unless a replication slot or wal_keep_size holds them.
  6. Because a checkpoint just finished, the next modification of every page writes a full-page image (see 18.5). This is the WAL burst.

Timed vs requested: pg_stat_bgwriter.checkpoints_timed and checkpoints_req (on PG 17 these moved to pg_stat_checkpointer as num_timed and num_requested). Requested checkpoints happen because max_wal_size was reached before the timer fired. If most checkpoints are requested, max_wal_size is too small for your write rate and you are checkpointing too often, which multiplies full-page images.

Tradeoff table:

Setting Smaller / shorter Larger / longer
checkpoint_timeout Faster crash recovery; more WAL from FPIs; more I/O spikes Slower recovery (more WAL to replay); less WAL; smoother I/O
max_wal_size Requested checkpoints during bursts Bigger pg_wal directory; checkpoints stay timed
checkpoint_completion_target Writes concentrated (bad) 0.9 spreads them (good)

Typical production values: checkpoint_timeout = 15min, max_wal_size = 8GB (larger on heavy-write systems), checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9, log_checkpoints = on (default since PG 15).

Practical example

The inventory table (60 MB, every page dirty at all times from 500 updates per second) is rewritten in full at every checkpoint. With a 5 minute timeout, that is 60 MB every 5 minutes plus 60 MB of full-page images in WAL right after. Moving to 15 minutes cuts both by two thirds. The hot orders index pages behave the same way.

PostgreSQL example

Read the checkpoint log lines; they tell the whole story:

LOG:  checkpoint starting: time
LOG:  checkpoint complete: wrote 48213 buffers (5.9%); 0 WAL file(s) added, 12 removed,
      31 recycled; write=809.913 s, sync=2.412 s, total=812.610 s;
      sync files=214, longest=0.930 s, average=0.011 s;
      distance=712345 kB, estimate=980112 kB

sync=2.412 s with longest=0.930 s for one file is your latency spike. distance is how much WAL was generated since the last checkpoint; if it approaches max_wal_size, checkpoints are about to become requested. A different line is a warning that must not be ignored:

LOG:  checkpoints are occurring too frequently (18 seconds apart)
HINT: Consider increasing the configuration parameter "max_wal_size".

Statistics:

-- PG 16 and earlier
SELECT checkpoints_timed, checkpoints_req, checkpoint_write_time, checkpoint_sync_time,
       buffers_checkpoint, buffers_clean, buffers_backend, maxwritten_clean
FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;
 checkpoints_timed | checkpoints_req | checkpoint_write_time | checkpoint_sync_time | buffers_checkpoint | buffers_clean | buffers_backend | maxwritten_clean
-------------------+-----------------+-----------------------+----------------------+--------------------+---------------+-----------------+------------------
              2011 |             388 |             812094311 |              9021177 |          120993412 |      33012881 |        14022107 |            88123

buffers_backend at more than 10 percent of buffers_checkpoint means backends are writing pages themselves because the background writer cannot keep up; raise bgwriter_lru_maxpages and lower bgwriter_delay. maxwritten_clean counts rounds where the background writer hit its cap.

Force a checkpoint before a planned failover or a base backup so that the switchover replays less WAL:

CHECKPOINT;   -- superuser or pg_checkpoint role (PG 15+)

Production scenario

Write-heavy e-commerce system on EBS gp3 (3,000 IOPS baseline): checkpoints every 5 minutes wrote 400 to 900 MB, and the sync phase caused 200 to 400 ms p99 spikes every 5 minutes that were visible on the API latency graph as a comb pattern. Changes: checkpoint_timeout = 20min, max_wal_size = 16GB, wal_compression = lz4, IOPS provisioned to 6,000. Result: WAL volume dropped 35 percent (fewer full-page images), spikes became 40 ms and every 20 minutes, and crash recovery time went from about 30 s to about 2 min, which the team accepted because failover to a replica (not crash recovery) is their HA mechanism.

How do I monitor it? Checkpoint frequency and type, write and sync times, buffers_backend ratio, and disk write latency during the sync phase. How do I scale it? Better disks, longer intervals, fewer dirty pages (HOT updates, fewer indexes), wal_compression. When should I not lengthen it? When you rely on crash recovery of a single instance for availability and need it to be fast, or when pg_wal disk is small.

Failure scenario

At 11:30, a bulk UPDATE products SET ... of 4 million rows dirtied 3 GB of pages and generated 6 GB of WAL in two minutes. max_wal_size was 1 GB, so the checkpointer was triggered repeatedly (checkpoints are occurring too frequently (14 seconds apart)), each one writing gigabytes and fsync'ing, while the replicas fell 40 s behind because of full-page-image storms. API latency tripled for 10 minutes. The bulk job had not changed; the database configuration simply had never been tuned for bursts. max_wal_size = 8GB and running the update in 50,000-row batches with pauses removed the problem.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • max_wal_size is a soft limit; a burst can exceed it, and the directory grows until the checkpoint catches up.
  • Checkpoint during a base backup: forced at backup start (pg_backup_start performs one), so backups on a loaded system cause a spike.
  • Very long intervals with a huge shared_buffers: the checkpoint may write tens of GB; recovery after a crash can take many minutes; replicas replay slowly.
  • Full-page-image storms hitting replication bandwidth quotas.
  • Shutdown checkpoint: a clean shutdown performs a checkpoint, which is why pg_ctl stop on a dirty cache can take a long time; -m immediate skips it and forces crash recovery on next start.
  • On replicas, restart points play the role of checkpoints; a replica with slow disks lags at every restart point.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read log_checkpoints output during incident reviews. They know the comb-shaped latency graph on sight. They size max_wal_size from measured WAL rate × desired interval, not from defaults. They treat recovery-time objectives as an explicit decision: "we accept 2 minutes of crash recovery because failover handles availability".

Common mistakes

  • Leaving max_wal_size = 1GB on a write-heavy system.
  • Not enabling log_checkpoints and guessing.
  • Running bulk updates without batching and blaming the database for lag.
  • Tuning shared_buffers up without reconsidering checkpoint impact.

Interview questions

  1. What happens during a checkpoint and why does it spike I/O? Expected: write all dirty pages, fsync files, record redo point; the sync phase is the spike. Follow-up: how do you smooth it?
  2. What does "checkpoints are occurring too frequently" mean and what do you change?
  3. Explain the relationship between checkpoint interval and WAL volume. Expected: full-page writes after each checkpoint.
  4. How does a longer checkpoint interval affect crash recovery time and why might that be acceptable?

Practical exercise

Set checkpoint_timeout = 30s, max_wal_size = 256MB, log_checkpoints = on locally. Run a pgbench-style write load for five minutes and collect the checkpoint log lines and pg_stat_wal. Then set checkpoint_timeout = 10min, max_wal_size = 4GB and repeat. Acceptance criteria: a comparison table of checkpoint count, WAL bytes, wal_fpi and p99 latency, with an explanation of the full-page-write effect.

18.7 MVCC: multi-version concurrency control

18.7.1 Row versions, transaction ids, snapshots and visibility

Concept

PostgreSQL never modifies a row in place. When you UPDATE a row, it writes a new version of the row and marks the old version as expired. When you DELETE, it only marks the version as expired. Both versions stay in the table until VACUUM removes the expired one. Each version carries two transaction ids in its header: xmin, the transaction that created it, and xmax, the transaction that expired it (0 if it is still current).

Every query runs against a snapshot: a record of which transactions had committed when the query started. A row version is visible to the query if its creating transaction had committed at snapshot time and its expiring transaction had not. This is MVCC: readers see a consistent past, writers create the future, and neither waits for the other.

Why does it exist?

The alternative is locking: a reader takes a shared lock on rows, a writer takes an exclusive lock, and they block each other. With hundreds of concurrent connections, a reporting query would freeze checkout, and checkout would freeze reporting. MVCC lets SELECT never wait for UPDATE and UPDATE never wait for SELECT, at the cost of storing multiple versions and cleaning them up later. It also makes ROLLBACK almost free: PostgreSQL just marks the transaction as aborted, and every version it created becomes invisible.

Mental model

Imagine a shared document where nobody is allowed to erase. Every edit is written as a new line stamped with the editor's ticket number and the ticket number of whoever replaces it later.
