When you open the document, you are given a list of tickets that were "done" at that moment, and you read only the lines whose creator is on your list and whose replacer is not. Two people can edit and read at once without waiting; the paper simply gets longer until someone (VACUUM) tears out the lines nobody can see any more.

How it works

flowchart LR
  v1["version 1  xmin=100 xmax=0  qty=10"] -->|"UPDATE by txn 105"| v1b["version 1  xmin=100 xmax=105  qty=10  dead once nobody needs it"]
  v1b -->|"t_ctid points to"| v2["version 2  xmin=105 xmax=0  qty=9"]
  v2 -->|"UPDATE by txn 131"| v2b["version 2  xmin=105 xmax=131"]
  v2b -->|"t_ctid points to"| v3["version 3  xmin=131 xmax=0  qty=8"]
  s1["snapshot taken at txn 104 sees version 1"] -.-> v1
  s2["snapshot taken at txn 120 sees version 2"] -.-> v2
  s3["snapshot taken at txn 140 sees version 3"] -.-> v3
  1. Transaction ids (xids) are 32-bit counters assigned when a transaction first writes. Read-only transactions get only a virtual id and cost nothing. SELECT pg_current_xact_id() forces assignment and shows the value.
  2. Insert writes a tuple with xmin = my xid, xmax = 0.
  3. Delete sets xmax = my xid on the current version. Nothing is removed.
  4. Update does both: inserts a new version (xmin = my xid) and sets xmax = my xid on the old one, pointing the old tuple's t_ctid at the new version.
  5. Commit or abort is recorded in the commit log (pg_xact, two bits per xid). The tuples are not touched at commit time; that is why commit is fast regardless of how many rows changed.
  6. Hint bits. The first backend that reads a tuple after its transaction has finished looks up pg_xact, then caches the result in the tuple's t_infomask (XMIN_COMMITTED, XMAX_ABORTED and so on) so later readers skip the lookup. This dirties the page: a plain SELECT after a bulk load can generate writes (and WAL, if wal_log_hints or checksums are enabled). That is the "why is my read-only query writing to disk" surprise.
  7. Snapshot. At statement start (READ COMMITTED) or transaction start (REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE), the backend records xmin (the oldest transaction still running), xmax (the next xid to be assigned), and the list of xids in progress between them. SELECT pg_current_snapshot() shows it as xmin:xmax:xip_list.
  8. Visibility rule (simplified): a version is visible if its xmin is committed, is below the snapshot's xmax, and is not in the in-progress list; and its xmax is either 0, aborted, still in progress, or at or above the snapshot's xmax. Everything else is invisible to this snapshot.
  9. Row locks live in the header too. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE sets xmax to the locker's xid with a flag bit saying "this is a lock, not a deletion". That is why row locks cost no lock-table memory and why a million-row FOR UPDATE is possible.

A version is dead when its xmax is committed and no snapshot in the system is old enough to still need it. The oldest snapshot in the system is called the xmin horizon. Anything a long-running transaction can still see cannot be cleaned. This is the link between "an idle transaction" and "table bloat", and it is the reason for the incidents in 18.8 and 18.10.

Practical example

Checkout reads inventory.quantity for product 7 (snapshot sees 10). At the same moment a warehouse job updates it to 9 and commits. The checkout's SELECT did not block, and returned 10, which was true when its statement began. If checkout then runs UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE product_id = 7, in READ COMMITTED the update re-reads the latest committed version (9) and produces 8. This re-check on write is how PostgreSQL avoids lost updates for simple arithmetic updates; for read-then-write logic in application code you need FOR UPDATE or optimistic versioning, which Part 20 — Database Transactions covers in depth.

NestJS example

Reading in a consistent snapshot across several statements (for example, a report of an order and its items and payments that must agree with each other) is a REPEATABLE READ transaction. TypeORM's DataSource.transaction takes the isolation level as its first argument.

// order-report.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class OrderReportService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  // All three reads see the same snapshot even if the order is being updated
  async snapshotOf(orderId: number) {
    return this.dataSource.transaction('REPEATABLE READ', async (em) => {
      const [order] = await em.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [orderId]);
      const items = await em.query('SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1', [orderId]);
      const payments = await em.query('SELECT * FROM payments WHERE order_id = $1', [orderId]);
      return { order, items, payments };
    });
  }
}

Keep such transactions short. Every second they stay open, they hold the xmin horizon back for the whole database.

PostgreSQL example

Watch versions appear and die:

BEGIN;
SELECT pg_current_xact_id();                     -- e.g. 48819903
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE product_id = 7;
SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, quantity FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 7;
   xmin   | xmax | ctid  | quantity
----------+------+-------+----------
 48819903 |    0 | (3,9) |        9      <-- the new version, inserted by our txn

From a second session while the first is still open:

SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, quantity FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 7;
   xmin   |   xmax   | ctid  | quantity
----------+----------+-------+----------
 48812201 | 48819903 | (3,2) |       10     <-- the old version, marked with our xmax, still visible here

Two sessions, two answers, no waiting. After COMMIT in session one, session two sees (3,9) with 9. The old version at (3,2) is now dead and awaits VACUUM. SELECT pg_current_snapshot() in session two during the overlap returns something like 48819903:48819904:48819903, meaning "48819903 is in progress; do not show me its work".

TypeORM example

The per-transaction snapshot also matters for optimistic locking. @VersionColumn implements compare-and-set on top of MVCC: the UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 finds zero rows if another version has been committed since your read.

@Entity('inventory')
export class Inventory {
  @PrimaryColumn({ name: 'product_id', type: 'bigint' })
  productId!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'integer' })
  quantity!: number;

  @VersionColumn()
  version!: number;   // TypeORM adds "AND version = :v" to UPDATEs and throws OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError
}

Sequelize example

Sequelize offers the same through version: true on the model definition; a stale save throws OptimisticLockError.

Inventory.init(
  {
    productId: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, primaryKey: true, field: 'product_id' },
    quantity: { type: DataTypes.INTEGER, allowNull: false },
  },
  { sequelize, tableName: 'inventory', version: true, underscored: true },
);

Production scenario

A 200 million row orders table receives 300 inserts and 900 updates per second (status transitions, updated_at bumps). Every update creates a new version: 900 dead versions per second, 3.2 million per hour, 78 million per day. Readers never block, which is why the API can serve 5,000 reads per second alongside. But that is 78 million tuples per day that VACUUM must remove, and if each update also creates index entries (non-HOT), each of the table's 6 indexes grows by 78 million entries per day too. MVCC's cost is paid later, by VACUUM, in I/O.

Failure scenario

At 09:30 a data analyst opened a REPEATABLE READ transaction in a notebook to explore orders and went to a meeting. For three hours, every update on every table produced dead versions that VACUUM could not remove ("dead but not yet removable" in the vacuum logs), because that snapshot could theoretically still need them. inventory grew from 60 MB to 1.4 GB, index-only scans stopped working (pages were no longer all-visible), and p99 latency doubled. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout was set to 15 minutes for the analysts' role the same afternoon.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Long-lived snapshots (idle in transaction, long analytics, pg_dump, hot_standby_feedback from replicas) hold the xmin horizon and cause bloat everywhere, not just on the tables they read.
  • Hint-bit writes after bulk loads: the first full scan after loading 100 million rows dirties every page; run VACUUM (or VACUUM FREEZE) right after the load to set hints and freeze in one pass.
  • Aborted transactions leave dead tuples exactly like deletes; a job that inserts 1 million rows and rolls back leaves 1 million dead tuples.
  • READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement; a two-statement read can see different states. Use REPEATABLE READ when consistency across statements matters.
  • Row-lock information stored in xmax interacts with multixacts (FOR KEY SHARE, foreign keys); multixact ids have their own wraparound (age(relminmxid)).
  • Cursors and WITH HOLD cursors keep snapshots alive beyond what you might expect.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see every UPDATE as an insert plus a delete and price it accordingly. They know that "readers don't block writers" is paid for by VACUUM I/O, and they design write patterns so the debt stays payable: fewer updates of wide rows, no indexes on columns that churn, short transactions. They watch the xmin horizon like a resource: SELECT max(age(backend_xmin)) FROM pg_stat_activity is on their dashboard. To a product manager: "The database keeps old copies of rows so that reports never block checkouts; we have to clean those copies constantly, and anything that stops the cleaning slowly makes everything slower."

Common mistakes

  • Believing UPDATE modifies in place and being surprised that a table with 10 million live rows occupies 40 GB.
  • Leaving transactions open across HTTP calls or user interactions.
  • Treating a SELECT as free of side effects (hint bits).
  • Confusing MVCC snapshot isolation with serializability; Part 20 covers the anomalies.

Interview questions

  1. Explain xmin, xmax and how PostgreSQL decides whether a row version is visible. Expected: creator and expirer xids; snapshot with xmin, xmax and in-progress list; committed-before-snapshot and not-expired-before-snapshot. Follow-up: where is commit status stored and what are hint bits?
  2. Why don't readers block writers in PostgreSQL, and what is the cost? Expected: multiple versions; the cost is dead tuples, bloat and VACUUM.
  3. What does an UPDATE physically do? Expected: new tuple version plus xmax on the old, plus index entries unless HOT.
  4. Why does a long idle transaction bloat tables it never touched? Expected: xmin horizon is global.
  5. Why is ROLLBACK cheap in PostgreSQL but expensive in some other databases? Expected: no undo log; abort is a bit in pg_xact.

Practical exercise

With two psql sessions, reproduce the visibility example above, including pg_current_snapshot(). Then leave session one idle in transaction, run 100,000 updates on inventory from session two, and query pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup and VACUUM (VERBOSE) inventory. Acceptance criteria: you show the "dead but not yet removable" line, commit session one, vacuum again, and show the tuples being removed.

18.7.2 What UPDATE really costs: bloat and HOT updates

Concept

Every non-HOT update inserts one new heap tuple and one new entry in every index on the table, even indexes on columns that did not change, because index entries point at a specific tuple version (ctid). A HOT update (heap-only tuple) is the optimisation that avoids the index work: when the update changes no indexed column and the new version fits on the same page as the old one, PostgreSQL chains the new version to the old one inside the page and leaves every index untouched.

Bloat is the space occupied by dead versions (in the heap and in indexes) that VACUUM has not yet reclaimed, or that has been reclaimed but sits as scattered free space no longer used efficiently.

Why does it exist?

Index maintenance is the largest hidden cost of updates. On orders with 6 indexes, one non-HOT update is 7 writes and 7 sets of WAL records. HOT exists because most updates in real applications touch a few non-indexed columns (a status, a counter, a timestamp), and for those the index churn is pure waste.

Mental model

Imagine a library catalogue (index) that lists the shelf position of each book. If you rewrite a book and put the new edition on the same shelf next to the old one, and leave a note in the old slot saying "see next slot", the catalogue does not need to change. If the new edition must go to another shelf, or if the catalogue lists an attribute you changed (the title), every catalogue card must be updated.

How it works

  1. The backend evaluates the UPDATE. It checks whether any column that appears in any index (including partial index predicates and expression indexes) changed value.
  2. If none changed and the page has room (this is what fillfactor below 100 reserves), the new version is placed on the same page. The old tuple's t_ctid points to the new one, and the old one is flagged HEAP_HOT_UPDATED; the new one is HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE. Index entries still point at the root line pointer; an index scan follows the chain inside the page to the visible version.
  3. HOT pruning: any backend that later reads the page and sees the chain can, without VACUUM, remove dead intermediate versions and turn the root line pointer into a redirect. This is opportunistic, cheap and happens constantly on hot pages, which is why a fillfactor = 90 inventory table can sustain 500 updates per second without growing.
  4. If an indexed column changed, or the page is full, the new version goes wherever there is space (often a different page), and every index gets a new entry. Old index entries become dead and are removed later by VACUUM (index vacuum) or, on PG 14+, by bottom-up index deletion when a B-tree page is about to split.
  5. pg_stat_user_tables tells you the ratio: n_tup_hot_upd / n_tup_upd. Above 80 percent is healthy for a status-churn table; below 30 percent means something indexed is changing on every update (very often updated_at).

Cost comparison for one update on orders (6 indexes), measured on an NVMe instance:

Update type Heap writes Index writes WAL bytes (approx) Latency
HOT (status only, status not indexed) 1 page 0 150 to 300 0.05 ms
Non-HOT (updated_at indexed) 1 page 6 entries 1,200 to 2,500 0.3 ms
Non-HOT, page split in two indexes 1 page 6 entries plus 2 splits 20,000 plus 1 to 5 ms

Practical example

orders.updated_at is bumped by every status change. A developer adds CREATE INDEX ON orders (updated_at) to support a "recently changed orders" admin screen. HOT ratio drops from 92 percent to 3 percent overnight: every status change now writes to all 7 indexes. WAL volume doubles, replicas lag, autovacuum on the indexes never catches up. The admin screen could have used (status, updated_at) on a partial set, or a separate small order_events table.

PostgreSQL example

-- Leave 30% free space on each page so new versions fit in place
ALTER TABLE inventory SET (fillfactor = 70);
VACUUM FULL inventory;   -- or pg_repack; fillfactor applies to new pages only

-- Watch the HOT ratio
SELECT relname, n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd,
       round(100.0 * n_tup_hot_upd / greatest(n_tup_upd, 1), 1) AS hot_pct,
       n_dead_tup, n_live_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname IN ('orders', 'inventory');
 relname   | n_tup_upd  | n_tup_hot_upd | hot_pct | n_dead_tup | n_live_tup
-----------+------------+---------------+---------+------------+------------
 orders    | 3120041022 |      91021103 |     2.9 |   18922011 |  201233104   <-- indexed column churn
 inventory |  844120033 |     811203112 |    96.1 |      30122 |     420011

Find which index is responsible: list indexes whose columns are touched by your hottest UPDATE statement in pg_stat_statements, or check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_tup_read growth against writes.

TypeORM example

Keep churning columns out of indexes and set fillfactor in a migration. TypeORM's @Index has no storage-parameter option, so raw SQL in a migration is the right tool.

import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class InventoryFillfactor1725600000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  async up(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`ALTER TABLE inventory SET (fillfactor = 70)`);
    // Do NOT index updated_at on hot tables: it defeats HOT updates
    await qr.query(`DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_updated_at`);
  }
  async down(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`ALTER TABLE inventory RESET (fillfactor)`);
  }
}

Sequelize example

export async function up({ context: queryInterface }: { context: QueryInterface }) {
  await queryInterface.sequelize.query(`ALTER TABLE inventory SET (fillfactor = 70)`);
  await queryInterface.removeIndex('orders', 'idx_orders_updated_at');
}

Production scenario

An inventory table of 400,000 rows updated 500 times per second stays at 60 MB for months with fillfactor = 70, HOT ratio 96 percent, and autovacuum running every 2 minutes for a few hundred milliseconds. The same table with an index on updated_at grew to 2.1 GB in a week and needed pg_repack. Monitoring: HOT ratio per table, n_dead_tup, table size trend, and WAL bytes per second.

Failure scenario

"The table is 40 GB but has 10 GB of data." A products table received nightly full rewrites (every row updated whether changed or not) for a year; autovacuum reclaimed space but the free space was scattered across pages, so new rows went into old gaps, sequential scans read four times more pages than needed, and index-only scans were rare because pages kept losing their all-visible bit. pg_repack shrank it to 10.5 GB in 40 minutes with no downtime.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Indexing updated_at, version, counters, or last_seen_at on hot tables destroys HOT.
  • Expression and partial indexes count: an index WHERE status = 'PENDING' makes any change to status non-HOT.
  • fillfactor applies only to new pages; existing pages need a rewrite.
  • Very wide rows: fewer versions fit per page, HOT fails more often.
  • Bulk updates that touch every row create a full copy of the table's live data as dead tuples.
  • Bloat in indexes is separate from heap bloat and often worse; see Part 19 for REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "which columns change most, and are any of them indexed?" before every index review. They budget fillfactor on hot tables. They prefer narrow, append-mostly event tables over wide rows that churn. They measure the HOT ratio after every schema change.

Common mistakes

  • Adding indexes to hot tables without checking write patterns.
  • Rewriting unchanged rows in sync jobs.
  • Using VACUUM FULL on a production table to "fix bloat" and locking the API for an hour.

Interview questions

  1. What is a HOT update and what prevents it? Expected: same-page new version with no index changes; prevented by changing an indexed column or a full page. Follow-up: how do you measure the HOT ratio?
  2. Why does an index on updated_at hurt more than an index on user_id?
  3. What does fillfactor do and when do you lower it?
  4. A table has 10 GB of live data and is 40 GB on disk. What happened and what are the options?

Practical exercise

Create inventory with 1 million rows and fillfactor = 100. Run 500,000 random single-row updates on quantity; record size and HOT ratio. Repeat with fillfactor = 70. Repeat again with an index on updated_at while bumping updated_at in every update. Acceptance criteria: a table of size, HOT percent, WAL bytes and dead tuples for each run, with a one-paragraph recommendation.

18.7.3 Transaction id wraparound

Concept

Transaction ids are 32-bit numbers: about 4 billion values, used in a circle. PostgreSQL compares them modulo 2 to the 32: xid A is "older" than xid B if it is within 2 billion behind it. A tuple whose xmin is more than 2 billion transactions in the past would suddenly compare as being in the future, and become invisible to everyone. That is data loss without any disk failure. To prevent it, VACUUM freezes old tuples by setting a flag bit that means "created so long ago that it is visible to all transactions forever"; frozen tuples are never compared by xid again.

Why does it exist?

Using 32 bits was a storage decision (8 bytes of xids per tuple header instead of 16). The circular comparison and freezing are the price. Busy systems burn through 2 billion xids in weeks: at 2,000 write transactions per second, that is 11.5 days.

Mental model

Imagine an odometer that rolls over. If you record when each item entered the warehouse by odometer reading, and the odometer rolls over, everything old suddenly looks like it arrived in the future. Freezing means replacing the reading on very old items with a stamp that says "ancient, always valid".

How it works

  1. Each table records the oldest unfrozen xid it may contain in pg_class.relfrozenxid; the database's minimum is pg_database.datfrozenxid. age(relfrozenxid) says how many transactions ago that was.
  2. Regular VACUUM freezes tuples older than vacuum_freeze_min_age (50 million) on the pages it visits. When a table's age exceeds vacuum_freeze_table_age (150 million), VACUUM scans all pages not marked all-frozen in the visibility map (an "aggressive" vacuum) so that relfrozenxid can advance.
  3. When a table's age exceeds autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200 million), autovacuum launches an anti-wraparound vacuum on it, even if autovacuum is disabled for that table, and even if it has no dead tuples. In pg_stat_activity it appears as autovacuum: VACUUM public.orders (to prevent wraparound).
  4. On PG 14+, when a table's age passes vacuum_failsafe_age (1.6 billion), VACUUM enters failsafe mode: it skips index cleanup and cost-based delays and freezes as fast as possible.
  5. When the database age passes about 2 billion minus 40 million, every transaction logs a warning: database "shop" must be vacuumed within N transactions. At about 3 million remaining, the server stops accepting commands to protect data. On PG 14 and later you can still run VACUUM in normal mode at that point; older versions require single-user mode. Either way, your application is down until the vacuum finishes, which on a multi-terabyte database can be hours.

What makes freezing fall behind (the same list as VACUUM starvation, because it is VACUUM):

  • Long-open transactions and idle-in-transaction sessions (the horizon).
  • Orphaned prepared transactions (SELECT * FROM pg_prepared_xacts); these survive restarts.
  • Replication slots with hot_standby_feedback and a lagging replica.
  • Temporary tables in long-lived sessions: autovacuum cannot vacuum another session's temp tables, and their age counts.
  • A table so large that a throttled vacuum takes longer than the time it takes the system to burn 200 million xids.
  • Autovacuum workers all busy on other tables; anti-wraparound vacuums are prioritised, but three workers are three workers.

Practical example

An event-ingest database burns 3,000 xids per second (each event its own transaction) on a 4 TB events table with 12 indexes. Autovacuum, throttled to a few MB/s, needs about 30 hours to freeze the table; the system burns 200 million xids in 18.5 hours. The table's age keeps rising, anti-wraparound vacuum runs continuously, and one day the warnings begin. The permanent fix was batching events (100 per transaction cut xid consumption 100 times), partitioning events by month so old partitions freeze once and stay frozen, and raising autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit.

PostgreSQL example

The queries every team should have in a dashboard:

-- Per database: how close to the wall?
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
       round(100.0 * age(datfrozenxid) / 2147483647, 1) AS pct_to_wraparound
FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;

-- Per table: who is oldest, and is autovacuum handling it?
SELECT c.relname, age(c.relfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)) AS size,
       s.last_autovacuum, s.autovacuum_count
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
LEFT JOIN pg_stat_user_tables s ON s.relid = c.oid
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r', 'm', 't') AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Anything holding the horizon back?
SELECT pid, state, age(backend_xmin) AS xmin_age, now() - xact_start AS open_for, left(query, 50)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL ORDER BY 3 DESC LIMIT 5;
SELECT * FROM pg_prepared_xacts;
SELECT slot_name, active, xmin, catalog_xmin FROM pg_replication_slots;

Alert at 50 percent of autovacuum_freeze_max_age (100 million) so you find the cause while there is still a week of runway, not at 1.9 billion.

Freezing on your own terms, during a quiet window:

VACUUM (FREEZE, VERBOSE) orders;   -- aggressive freeze; on PG 16+ use VACUUM (VERBOSE) after
                                   --   the table's age passes vacuum_freeze_table_age

NestJS example

Transactions per second is a wraparound input, so batching writes is also a wraparound defence. A queue consumer that commits one event per message burns one xid per message; grouping 200 messages per transaction cuts xid consumption 200 times and the fsync count with it.

// events-ingest.consumer.ts (BullMQ worker style, batch of jobs)
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class EventsIngestConsumer {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async ingestBatch(events: Array<{ orderId: number; type: string; payload: unknown }>) {
    // One transaction, one xid, one fsync for the whole batch
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
      await em
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .insert()
        .into('order_events')
        .values(events.map((e) => ({ orderId: e.orderId, type: e.type, payload: e.payload })))
        .execute();
    });
  }
}

Production scenario

A well-run 2 TB database at 1,500 write transactions per second: database age hovers between 60 and 180 million as anti-wraparound and regular vacuums advance relfrozenxid; autovacuum_freeze_max_age left at default; vacuum_failsafe_age at default as the last line of defence; alerts at 500 million (page) and 1 billion (wake the DBA). Large append-only tables are partitioned monthly so that closed partitions are frozen once (their visibility map is all-frozen) and never scanned again.

Failure scenario

Monday 08:15: ERROR: database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss in database "shop". Root cause found in 20 minutes: a pg_prepared_xacts row from a two-phase-commit experiment nine months earlier had been holding the horizon since the experiment's coordinator was decommissioned. Every anti-wraparound vacuum since then had run, logged "oldest xmin" warnings, and freed nothing. ROLLBACK PREPARED 'test-2pc-1' and a database-wide VACUUM took four hours on the 3 TB database. Total downtime: four and a half hours. Two alerts would have prevented it: database age above 500 million, and any prepared transaction older than 10 minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Multixact wraparound (age(relminmxid)) from heavy FOR KEY SHARE and foreign-key locking; same emergency, different counter.
  • autovacuum = off on a table "temporarily" to stop I/O; anti-wraparound still runs, but regular freezing does not.
  • Very large tables where a single vacuum takes longer than the xid burn interval; partition them.
  • Replicas cannot vacuum; wraparound is a primary problem, but hot_standby_feedback from replicas extends the primary's horizon.
  • Restoring from a logical dump resets ages; restoring from a physical backup does not.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat wraparound as a scheduled certainty, not a rare accident, and they have two dashboards: database age and horizon holders. They reduce xid consumption by batching. They partition huge append-only tables so freezing is a one-time cost per partition. They ban prepared transactions unless a specific coordinator owns their cleanup.

Common mistakes

  • Not knowing the current database age.
  • Disabling autovacuum during a busy period and forgetting to re-enable it.
  • Letting an experiment leave prepared transactions or replication slots behind.
  • Committing per row at thousands of rows per second.

Interview questions

  1. What is transaction id wraparound and how does PostgreSQL prevent it? Expected: 32-bit circular xids; freezing by VACUUM; anti-wraparound autovacuum at 200 million; failsafe at 1.6 billion; shutdown near 2 billion. Why it matters: it is one of the few ways to lose data on healthy hardware.
  2. Name four things that stop freezing from advancing.
  3. How does partitioning help with wraparound? Expected: frozen partitions are all-frozen in the visibility map and are skipped.
  4. Your database is at age 1.9 billion. What do you do in the next 30 minutes? Expected: find and kill horizon holders (idle transactions, prepared transactions, dead slots), then run VACUUM on the oldest tables with vacuum_cost_delay = 0.

Practical exercise

On a test instance, set autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 200000 on a table (the minimum is 100,000) and generate 300,000 small write transactions. Observe the anti-wraparound autovacuum appear in pg_stat_activity and age(relfrozenxid) drop. Then open an idle transaction and repeat; observe age not dropping. Acceptance criteria: you can show both outcomes and name the horizon holder using pg_stat_activity.backend_xmin.

18.8 VACUUM and autovacuum

18.8.1 What VACUUM does and why autovacuum falls behind

Concept

VACUUM is the garbage collector for MVCC. It walks a table, finds row versions that no transaction can see any more (dead tuples), removes their index entries, removes the tuples themselves, records the freed space so new rows can reuse it, marks pages that contain only visible rows in the visibility map, and freezes old tuples to prevent wraparound. It does not shrink the file (except trailing empty pages at the end) and it does not block reads or writes.

Autovacuum is the set of background workers that run VACUUM and ANALYZE automatically when a table has accumulated enough changes. It is on by default and must never be turned off; it only needs tuning.

Why does it exist?

Without VACUUM, every update and delete makes the table permanently bigger, the visibility map never says "all visible" (so index-only scans never happen), and transaction ids never freeze (so the database eventually shuts down). MVCC defers cleanup so that writes are fast; VACUUM is where the deferred cost is paid.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel where guests never check out formally; they just leave and the room stays marked "occupied" with their things inside. Housekeeping (VACUUM) walks the floors, checks which rooms are truly empty (nobody could still come back), removes the belongings, and marks the room free so a new guest can take it. If housekeeping is too slow, or a single guest keeps insisting "I might still need to see the old rooms", the hotel fills with ghost rooms and you must build a new wing (the table grows).

How it works

  1. Trigger. The autovacuum launcher wakes every autovacuum_naptime (1 minute) and compares each table's dead-tuple count against autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor × reltuples (50 + 0.2 × rows). For analyze: 50 + 0.1 × rows. PG 13+ also triggers on inserts: 1000 + 0.2 × rows inserted since the last vacuum, so append-only tables get their visibility map and freezing maintained.
  2. Heap scan, phase 1. A worker scans the table's pages, skipping pages the visibility map marks all-visible (or all-frozen, for aggressive vacuums). It collects the TIDs of dead tuples into memory (autovacuum_work_mem, falling back to maintenance_work_mem). It also prunes HOT chains and freezes tuples older than vacuum_freeze_min_age.
  3. Index vacuum. For each index on the table, it scans the entire index and deletes entries whose TIDs are in the dead list. This is why many indexes make VACUUM slow: 10 indexes means 10 full index scans per batch. If the dead-TID array fills up (about 1 GB before PG 17), it must do this phase multiple times.
  4. Heap scan, phase 2. It revisits pages with dead tuples, removes them, compacts the page, updates the free space map (FSM) with the free bytes, and sets the visibility-map bits for pages that are now all visible.
  5. Truncate. If the tail of the file is empty pages, it takes a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and truncates the file. This is the one moment VACUUM can conflict with queries; vacuum_truncate = off per table disables it.
  6. Catalog update. pg_class.reltuples, relpages, relfrozenxid are updated; statistics for the planner are refreshed if ANALYZE runs too.
  7. Throttling. Each page touched adds cost (vacuum_cost_page_hit 1, vacuum_cost_page_miss 2, vacuum_cost_page_dirty 20). When the accumulated cost reaches autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit (200 by default, inherited from vacuum_cost_limit), the worker sleeps autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay (2 ms). With defaults that is roughly 8 MB/s of reads and 4 MB/s of dirtying, which is far too slow for a modern SSD. RDS and other managed services raise the limit substantially; on self-managed systems set autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 1000 to 2000.

Why autovacuum falls behind, with numbers:

Cause What you see Fix
scale_factor 0.2 on a 200 M row table Vacuum starts only after 40 M dead tuples; table already 20 percent bloated Per-table autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, threshold = 20000
Throttling at 8 MB/s A 100 GB table takes 3.5 hours per vacuum; dead tuples accumulate faster Raise autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit, lower cost_delay
3 workers for 400 tables Hot small tables wait behind one giant table's vacuum for hours autovacuum_max_workers = 6 (restart), partition giant tables
Long transaction or idle in transaction Log says N are dead but not yet removable, oldest xmin: X; vacuum runs and frees nothing idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout, kill the session
Replication slot with hot_standby_feedback Same "not yet removable", horizon held by pg_replication_slots.xmin Bound replica lag; accept query cancellation on the replica instead
Many indexes Index vacuum phase dominates; each vacuum scans 10 indexes fully Drop unused indexes (Part 19); PG 13+ PARALLEL index vacuum for manual runs
autovacuum = off "temporarily" Bloat and wraparound risk accumulate silently Never; tune instead

Practical example

orders has 200 million rows and receives 900 updates per second, 60 percent of them non-HOT. That is 540 dead tuples per second, about 47 million per day. With default settings, autovacuum starts after 40 million dead tuples, roughly every 20 hours, and then must read the whole table (skipping all-visible pages, which by then are few) and scan 6 indexes. At the default throttle that takes 6 to 8 hours, during which another 15 million dead tuples appear. The table is never clean. With scale_factor = 0.005 (1 million dead tuples) and cost_limit = 2000, vacuum runs every 30 minutes for about 4 minutes and the table stays within 2 percent bloat.

NestJS example

Autovacuum is a server-side concern, but the application decides whether it can succeed. Two application rules that matter more than any server knob: never hold a transaction across I/O you do not control, and always release query runners. A NestJS interceptor that refuses to let a request hold a transaction longer than a budget:

// transaction-budget.interceptor.ts
import {
  CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor, RequestTimeoutException,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, throwError, TimeoutError } from 'rxjs';
import { catchError, timeout } from 'rxjs/operators';

@Injectable()
export class TransactionBudgetInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  // Requests that own a DB transaction must finish inside this budget,
  // so they can never hold the xmin horizon for minutes.
  constructor(private readonly budgetMs = 5_000) {}

  intercept(_ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    return next.handle().pipe(
      timeout(this.budgetMs),
      catchError((err) =>
        err instanceof TimeoutError
          ? throwError(() => new RequestTimeoutException('transaction budget exceeded'))
          : throwError(() => err),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Pair it with the server-side belts (idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout) from 18.2; the interceptor gives up on the request, the server settings guarantee the backend does too.

PostgreSQL example

Per-table tuning for the hot tables, which is where most of the value is:

ALTER TABLE orders SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor  = 0.005,   -- 1 M dead tuples on 200 M rows
  autovacuum_vacuum_threshold     = 50000,
  autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.002,
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit    = 2000     -- let it use the SSD
);

ALTER TABLE inventory SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.0,      -- pure threshold on a small hot table
  autovacuum_vacuum_threshold    = 5000,
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay   = 0         -- no throttling; the table is 60 MB
);

Watch it work:

-- What are the workers doing right now?
SELECT p.pid, a.query_start, c.relname, p.phase,
       p.heap_blks_total, p.heap_blks_scanned, p.heap_blks_vacuumed,
       p.index_vacuum_count, p.num_dead_tuples
FROM pg_stat_progress_vacuum p
JOIN pg_stat_activity a USING (pid)
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = p.relid;
 pid  | query_start | relname | phase             | heap_blks_total | heap_blks_scanned | heap_blks_vacuumed | index_vacuum_count | num_dead_tuples
------+-------------+---------+-------------------+-----------------+-------------------+--------------------+--------------------+-----------------
 4411 | 10:02:11    | orders  | vacuuming indexes |         3921033 |           3921033 |                  0 |                  1 |         1044201
-- Which tables are behind?
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / greatest(n_live_tup, 1), 1) AS dead_pct,
       last_autovacuum, autovacuum_count
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10;

Set log_autovacuum_min_duration = 1000 (ms) and read the log lines; they contain the single most useful diagnostic sentence in PostgreSQL:

LOG:  automatic vacuum of table "shop.public.orders": index scans: 1
      pages: 0 removed, 3921033 remain, 402011 scanned (10.25% of total)
      tuples: 1044201 removed, 200912311 remain, 8812001 are dead but not yet removable
      removable cutoff: 48812201, which was 3120041 XIDs old when operation ended
      index scan needed: 380211 pages from table (9.70% of total) had 1044201 dead item identifiers removed
      avg read rate: 41.2 MB/s, avg write rate: 12.3 MB/s
      system usage: CPU: user: 12.11 s, system: 4.02 s, elapsed: 241.31 s

8812001 are dead but not yet removable with a cutoff 3 million xids old means something has held a snapshot for 3 million transactions; go find it in pg_stat_activity (18.7.3 shows the query).

TypeORM example

Bulk deletes are a classic way to produce a mountain of dead tuples at once. Batch them and give autovacuum a chance between batches:

// Purge abandoned carts older than 30 days without creating 50 M dead tuples in one go
async purgeAbandonedCarts(dataSource: DataSource): Promise<number> {
  let total = 0;
  for (;;) {
    const result = await dataSource.query(
      `DELETE FROM carts
        WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM carts
                      WHERE status = 'ABANDONED' AND updated_at < now() - interval '30 days'
                      LIMIT 5000)`,
    );
    const deleted = Number(result[1] ?? 0);   // pg returns [rows, rowCount] for DELETE via TypeORM query()
    total += deleted;
    if (deleted < 5000) return total;
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200));   // let autovacuum and replicas breathe
  }
}

For "delete everything older than X" on very large tables, partition by time and DROP the partition: no dead tuples at all.

Sequelize example

let deleted: number;
do {
  [, deleted] = await sequelize.query(
    `DELETE FROM carts WHERE id IN (
       SELECT id FROM carts WHERE status = 'ABANDONED' AND updated_at < now() - interval '30 days' LIMIT 5000)`,
    { type: QueryTypes.DELETE } as any,
  ) as unknown as [unknown, number];
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200));
} while (deleted === 5000);

Production scenario

A 1 TB database with 300 tables: autovacuum_max_workers = 6, autovacuum_naptime = 30s, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 2000, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 2ms, maintenance_work_mem = 1GB, and per-table overrides on the 8 hottest tables. Vacuum I/O runs at 30 to 60 MB/s continuously and is budgeted as part of the disk IOPS plan. Alerts: n_dead_tup above 5 percent of n_live_tup on any table over 1 GB, any table not vacuumed in 24 hours that has writes, backend_xmin age above 50 million, and vacuum log lines with "not yet removable" above 1 million.

What can go wrong? Starvation, horizon holders, truncation lock conflicts on replicas. How do I monitor it? The four alerts above plus pg_stat_progress_vacuum. How do I scale it? More workers, higher cost limit, fewer indexes, partitioning. When should I not touch it? Do not disable it, and do not run manual VACUUM in cron on tables autovacuum already handles unless you have measured a gap.

Failure scenario

"Idle in transaction from a forgotten await blocked vacuum for 3 days." A payments reconciliation worker did this:

const qr = dataSource.createQueryRunner();
await qr.connect();
await qr.startTransaction();
qr.query('INSERT INTO reconciliation_runs ...');   // missing await: promise abandoned
await qr.commitTransaction();                      // throws on some paths; finally { release } was missing

On one code path an exception fired between startTransaction and commitTransaction, the QueryRunner was never released, and the connection sat in the pool idle in transaction with an open snapshot. The worker ran once a day and leaked one connection per run. By day three, orders had 130 million "dead but not yet removable" tuples, the checkout p99 was 3 times its baseline, and the pool had lost three connections. Detection took ten minutes once someone looked at pg_stat_activity sorted by xact_start. Prevention: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s' for application roles, a finally { await qr.release() } rule enforced in code review, and an alert on any backend idle in transaction for more than 2 minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Vacuum's tail truncation takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE briefly; on replicas with hot_standby_feedback off this can cancel long queries.
  • maintenance_work_mem too small forces multiple index-vacuum passes on huge tables.
  • Toast tables have their own autovacuum settings and are easy to forget.
  • Per-table autovacuum_enabled = false left over from a migration.
  • A table that receives only inserts never triggered vacuum before PG 13, so its visibility map was empty and index-only scans did nothing.
  • Manual VACUUM in a cron job that overlaps with autovacuum on the same table: they serialise, no harm, but wasted time.
  • Autovacuum workers are killed by DDL that needs a conflicting lock (regular autovacuum yields; anti-wraparound does not).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat autovacuum as a first-class workload with an I/O budget, not as background noise. They tune per table rather than globally. They know the "dead but not yet removable" line by heart. They design write paths that generate fewer dead tuples in the first place. And they ask, for every long-running thing that touches the database: "what snapshot does it hold, and for how long?"

Common mistakes

  • Disabling autovacuum because "it was using I/O during the incident".
  • Leaving defaults on tables with hundreds of millions of rows.
  • Running VACUUM FULL in production as a routine.
  • Blaming "the database is slow" when the cause is a client holding a transaction open.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through what VACUUM does, phase by phase. Expected: heap scan collecting dead TIDs, index vacuum per index, heap cleanup and FSM/VM updates, truncation, catalog update.
  2. Why does autovacuum fall behind on very large tables with default settings? Expected: scale_factor 0.2 and throttling; per-table tuning.
  3. What does "dead but not yet removable" mean and what do you do? Expected: horizon held by a snapshot; find and end it.
  4. Does VACUUM shrink the table file? Expected: only trailing empty pages; pg_repack or VACUUM FULL for a rewrite.
  5. Why do many indexes make VACUUM expensive?

Practical exercise

Create orders with 20 million rows and 5 indexes. Run 2 million random updates on an indexed column. Watch pg_stat_progress_vacuum during the autovacuum, and capture the log_autovacuum_min_duration line. Then tune the table with per-table settings and repeat. Acceptance criteria: you report the vacuum duration, the index scan count and the read/write rates for both runs, and you explain the difference.

18.8.2 Bloat measurement, VACUUM FULL and pg_repack

Concept

Bloat is the gap between the space a table (or index) uses on disk and the space its live data needs. VACUUM keeps bloat from growing but does not remove it once it exists. Removing it requires a rewrite: VACUUM FULL (locks the table for the whole duration) or pg_repack (online, with a short lock at the end).

Why does it exist?

Because free space inside a heap is reusable but not returnable to the OS without rewriting the file, and because rewriting a 200 GB table cannot be done for free. The tools exist for the cases where bloat has already happened: after a bulk delete, after a period of vacuum starvation, or after a schema change that rewrote every row.

Mental model

Imagine a bookshelf where removed books leave gaps. New books go into the gaps (VACUUM makes this possible), but the shelf never gets shorter. To reclaim the length you have to take all the books off and put them back tightly (VACUUM FULL, shop closed) or build a second shelf next to it, move books across while the shop stays open, and swap the shelves at closing time (pg_repack).

How it works

  1. Measuring. pgstattuple gives exact numbers by scanning the whole table (pgstattuple('orders') returns dead_tuple_percent, free_percent); pgstattuple_approx samples the visibility map and is fast enough for cron. Estimation queries based on pg_stats.avg_width (widely shared as the "bloat query") are roughly right without scanning. pg_relation_size vs n_live_tup × average row width is the quick sanity check.
  2. VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, copies live tuples into a new file, rebuilds every index, swaps files, and drops the old ones. It needs up to twice the table's size in free disk. Nobody can read or write the table until it finishes: on a 100 GB table, 20 to 60 minutes of total outage for that table.
  3. pg_repack (an extension plus a CLI) creates a log table with a trigger to capture changes, copies the table into a new one, builds indexes, replays the log, then takes a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to swap. Needs twice the space, runs for as long as VACUUM FULL would, but the table stays online. It also repacks indexes individually (pg_repack -i).
  4. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (PG 12+) handles index-only bloat online; Part 19 covers it.
  5. CLUSTER is VACUUM FULL that also orders rows by an index; same lock.
Tool Lock Extra disk Table online? Use
VACUUM none that matters none yes continuously
VACUUM FULL ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole run 2× no small tables, maintenance windows
pg_repack brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE at swap 2× yes large hot tables
REINDEX CONCURRENTLY SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE 2× index yes index bloat

PostgreSQL example

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;

SELECT * FROM pgstattuple_approx('orders');
 table_len    | scanned_percent | approx_tuple_count | approx_tuple_len | approx_tuple_percent | dead_tuple_count | dead_tuple_len | dead_tuple_percent | approx_free_space | approx_free_percent
--------------+-----------------+--------------------+------------------+----------------------+------------------+----------------+--------------------+-------------------+---------------------
 42011230208  |           12.4  |          200912311 |      22100354210 |                52.6  |          1044201 |      114862110 |               0.27 |       18240011000 |               43.4

43 percent free space with almost no dead tuples means VACUUM did its job, but the file is twice the size of the data. Rewrite it online:

pg_repack --dbname shop --table public.orders --jobs 4 --no-superuser-check

For a small table in a maintenance window, VACUUM FULL orders; is fine; for a 40 GB table serving checkout, it is an outage.

Production scenario

Quarterly, a job runs pgstattuple_approx on every table over 1 GB and files a ticket for anything above 30 percent free space. pg_repack runs at 03:00 on the worst two, with disk headroom verified first (pg_repack on a 40 GB table needs 40 GB free plus index space). The job is skipped automatically if replication lag is above 30 s, because the copy produces a burst of WAL.

Failure scenario

VACUUM FULL products was run on a Friday afternoon to "fix a slow query". It took an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and because the products table is joined by nearly every endpoint, every API request queued behind it for 35 minutes (the lock queue mechanism in 18.11). The slow query was later fixed by an index; the bloat was irrelevant to it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • pg_repack needs the extension installed on the server and free disk; it aborts (safely) if it cannot get the final lock within its timeout, and must be rerun.
  • pg_repack on a table with a long-running transaction waits for it, or with --no-kill-backend off, kills it.
  • VACUUM FULL on a table with foreign keys referencing it still requires the exclusive lock, and queries on referencing tables that check the FK wait too.
  • Rewrites invalidate cached plans and change ctids; nothing in the application should depend on ctids.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask whether bloat is actually causing a symptom before rewriting anything: 40 percent free space on a table read only by primary key costs disk, not latency. They schedule rewrites like deploys, with disk checks, replica lag checks, and a rollback story.

Common mistakes

  • VACUUM FULL on a hot table during business hours.
  • Rewriting without enough free disk and running the server out of space.
  • Confusing "bloat" with "dead tuples"; a fully vacuumed table can still be bloated.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL? Expected: in-place cleanup vs full rewrite under an exclusive lock.
  2. How does pg_repack avoid the long lock? Expected: copy plus change log replay, brief swap.
  3. How would you decide whether a bloated table needs a rewrite?

Practical exercise

Bloat a 5 million row table by deleting 70 percent of rows. Measure with pgstattuple. Reclaim with VACUUM FULL while a second session tries to SELECT; observe the wait. Restore the bloat and reclaim with pg_repack; observe that the second session continues. Acceptance criteria: sizes before and after, lock wait evidence from pg_stat_activity, and a written rule for when you would use each.

18.9 ANALYZE and planner statistics

18.9.1 Statistics, pg_stats, and stale stats after bulk loads

Concept

ANALYZE samples a table and stores summary statistics about each column: how many distinct values, which values are most common and how often, a histogram of the value distribution, how many nulls, the average width, and how well the physical row order matches the column's order. The planner uses these to estimate how many rows each step of a query will return, which decides whether it uses an index, which join method it picks, and in which order it joins tables. Autovacuum runs ANALYZE automatically after roughly 10 percent of a table changes.

Why does it exist?

The planner cannot look at the data while planning; that would be as slow as running the query. It needs a cheap, approximate picture. When the picture is wrong (stale after a bulk load, too coarse for a skewed column, blind to correlations between columns), the planner makes confident, wrong decisions: a nested loop over 10 million rows because it expected 10.

Mental model

Imagine planning a road trip using a map that shows the usual traffic. If the map is from before a new stadium was built, you will route past it on game day. ANALYZE redraws the map; default_statistics_target decides how detailed it is.

How it works

  1. ANALYZE reads a random sample of 300 × default_statistics_target rows (30,000 rows by default), chosen by random block sampling, so it costs seconds even on a terabyte table.
  2. From the sample it computes, per column, and stores in pg_statistic (viewable through pg_stats):
    • null_frac: fraction of nulls.
    • avg_width: average bytes per value.
    • n_distinct: number of distinct values; positive is an absolute count, negative is a fraction of rows (-1 means unique).
    • most_common_vals and most_common_freqs (MCV): the top values and their frequencies, up to statistics_target entries.
    • histogram_bounds: equal-frequency buckets over the remaining values, used for range estimates.
    • correlation: from -1 to 1, how well the physical order follows the column order; near 1 means an index scan reads the heap almost sequentially, which makes the planner prefer index scans over bitmap scans.
  3. Expression indexes get their own statistics rows (under the index name in pg_stats), collected only when ANALYZE runs after the index exists.
  4. Selectivity estimation: status = 'PENDING' looks up the MCV list; created_at > now() - interval '1 day' interpolates in the histogram; user_id = $1 with an unknown value uses 1 / n_distinct; two conditions are multiplied as if independent (the correlation problem, solved by extended statistics in 18.12).
  5. Autoanalyze triggers at 50 + 0.1 × rows changed rows. For a table that goes from 0 to 50 million rows in one bulk load, autoanalyze fires after the load, some time in the next minute, and until then the planner believes the table is empty.

Practical example

A new order_items table is created by a migration and back-filled with 80 million rows in a 20-minute INSERT ... SELECT. Traffic switches to the new table immediately. For the next 90 seconds, pg_class.reltuples is 0, the planner estimates every filter returns 1 row, chooses nested-loop joins everywhere, and a query that should take 5 ms takes 40 s. Then autoanalyze finishes and everything is fine, which makes the incident look like a mystery. The rule: ANALYZE order_items is the last statement of every bulk load, before traffic.

PostgreSQL example

-- Look at what the planner believes about orders.status
SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs, correlation
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname IN ('status', 'user_id', 'created_at');
 attname    | null_frac | n_distinct | most_common_vals                   | most_common_freqs                    | correlation
------------+-----------+------------+------------------------------------+--------------------------------------+-------------
 status     |         0 |          4 | {PAID,SHIPPED,CANCELLED,PENDING}   | {0.612,0.371,0.0129,0.0041}          |     0.11
 user_id    |         0 |    2803991 |                                    |                                      |     0.03
 created_at |         0 |         -1 |                                    |                                      |     0.99

status = 'PENDING' is estimated at 0.41 percent: the planner will happily use a partial index. created_at has correlation 0.99: range scans on it are cheap index scans. user_id shows 2.8 million distinct values in the sample; the real number is 5 million (sampling underestimates distinct counts for high-cardinality columns), which makes the planner overestimate rows per user by nearly two times. Fix it explicitly:

ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN user_id SET (n_distinct = 5000000);
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status  SET STATISTICS 500;   -- more MCV detail for the skewed column
ANALYZE orders;

Watch for stale statistics:

SELECT relname, n_mod_since_analyze, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze, n_live_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_mod_since_analyze > 0.05 * greatest(n_live_tup, 1)
ORDER BY n_mod_since_analyze DESC;

TypeORM example

Make ANALYZE part of the migration that back-fills, so nobody has to remember:

export class BackfillOrderItems1725600001000 implements MigrationInterface {
  async up(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, price_cents)
                    SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity, price_cents FROM legacy_order_lines`);
    await qr.query(`ANALYZE order_items`);   // refresh planner stats before traffic arrives
  }
  async down(): Promise<void> {}
}

Sequelize example

await queryInterface.bulkInsert('order_items', rows);      // or a COPY-based loader
await queryInterface.sequelize.query('ANALYZE order_items');

Production scenario

Nightly ETL replaces a 30 million row product_prices table with TRUNCATE and reload. The job ends with ANALYZE product_prices, and the on-call runbook lists "stats stale?" as the first check for any sudden plan change. default_statistics_target is 200 globally (cost: ANALYZE samples 60,000 rows, negligible) and 1,000 on three skewed columns. auto_explain (18.14) logs any query over 500 ms with its plan so that a plan flip after ANALYZE is visible within minutes.

Failure scenario

"Plan flips after ANALYZE." A query on orders WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at > $1 ran in 3 ms for months. One autoanalyze sampled a period where a payment provider outage had left 8 percent of recent orders PENDING; the MCV frequency for PENDING jumped from 0.4 percent to 2 percent, the estimated row count crossed the threshold where a bitmap heap scan looked cheaper than the partial index scan, and the query went to 400 ms across 200 requests per second. It flipped back at the next analyze. The fix was a composite partial index that is cheap under both estimates, and SET STATISTICS 1000 on status; the deeper lesson was that plan stability matters as much as plan speed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stats after bulk load, TRUNCATE, or partition attach are empty or stale until ANALYZE runs.
  • n_distinct underestimation on high-cardinality columns in huge tables.
  • Expression indexes without a following ANALYZE have no statistics.
  • Statistics on parent partitioned tables are not collected by autovacuum (through PG 15); run ANALYZE parent manually for queries that scan many partitions.
  • Very wide MCV lists on text columns bloat pg_statistic and slow planning slightly.
  • Temporary tables have no stats until you ANALYZE them, which matters for large ETL temp tables.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat "ANALYZE after bulk change" as a rule with no exceptions. They raise statistics targets per column with evidence (skewed MCV, bad estimates in EXPLAIN ANALYZE). They know that an estimate off by 100 times is the smoking gun in most slow-plan investigations, and they look at rows= estimated vs actual before anything else.

Common mistakes

  • Backfilling and switching traffic without ANALYZE.
  • Raising default_statistics_target to 10,000 globally "to be safe" and making ANALYZE and planning slower everywhere.
  • Ignoring n_mod_since_analyze.

Interview questions

  1. What does ANALYZE collect and how does the planner use it? Expected: null fraction, n_distinct, MCV, histogram, correlation; selectivity estimation and cost.
  2. A query is 1,000 times slower right after a big data load. First suspect? Expected: stale statistics; run ANALYZE.
  3. Why can the same query plan differently on two days? Expected: sampled statistics changed.
  4. When would you set n_distinct manually?

Practical exercise

Create an empty orders table, insert 10 million rows in one statement, and immediately run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on a join with order_items before autoanalyze fires. Capture the estimated vs actual rows and the plan. Run ANALYZE and repeat. Acceptance criteria: you present both plans, identify the misestimate, and add the ANALYZE to a migration.

18.10 Transactions in practice

18.10.1 BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, savepoints, and the "idle in transaction" trap

Concept

A transaction is a group of statements that PostgreSQL treats as one unit: all of it becomes visible to others at COMMIT, or none of it does after ROLLBACK. Without an explicit BEGIN, every statement is its own transaction (autocommit). Between BEGIN and COMMIT, the connection is in a transaction, and if it is not currently running a statement it is idle in transaction: holding locks, holding a snapshot, holding a pooled connection, doing nothing.

A savepoint is a marker inside a transaction that you can roll back to without losing the whole transaction. Isolation levels (what a transaction can see of others) are the subject of Part 20 — Database Transactions; here we cover the mechanics that matter for the server.

Why does it exist?

Checkout writes an order, three items, a payment and three inventory updates. If the process dies after the third statement, you must not have an order with no items. Transactions give atomicity. Savepoints exist because some errors inside a transaction are expected (a unique violation you want to handle) and PostgreSQL otherwise aborts the entire transaction on any error.

Mental model

Imagine a shopping session at a market where you fill a basket (statements) and pay at the end (COMMIT). Until you pay, nothing is yours and the stall keepers hold the items for you (locks). If you wander off to make a phone call with a full basket (idle in transaction), the stall keepers cannot sell those items to anyone else and cannot restock the shelf (vacuum). A savepoint is a note saying "if the next item turns out to be bad, put back everything after this note, but keep the rest".

How it works

  1. BEGIN marks the connection as in a transaction; no transaction id is assigned yet (only a virtual one) so read-only transactions are free.
  2. The first statement that writes assigns a real xid (18.7). Every row it writes carries that xid in xmin or xmax.
  3. Each statement acquires locks (18.11) that are held until the transaction ends, never released earlier, even if the statement finished long ago.
  4. On error, the transaction enters an aborted state: every further statement fails with current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block until you ROLLBACK. Node code that catches an error and keeps using the same transaction produces exactly this message.
  5. SAVEPOINT s starts a subtransaction with its own sub-xid once it writes. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s aborts only the subtransaction; the outer one continues. RELEASE SAVEPOINT s merges it. Each backend caches only 64 sub-xids in shared memory; a transaction with more than 64 savepoints (ORMs that wrap every statement in a savepoint, or loops creating one per row) overflows that cache, and every snapshot in the system must then consult the pg_subtrans on-disk structure. That is a well-known performance cliff, worst on replicas.
  6. COMMIT writes the commit record to WAL, flushes it (18.5), marks the xid committed in pg_xact, releases all locks, and drops the snapshot. ROLLBACK marks the xid aborted and releases locks; the rows it wrote are dead tuples for VACUUM.
  7. While the connection is idle in transaction, pg_stat_activity.state shows idle in transaction, xact_start shows when it began, and backend_xmin shows the snapshot it holds. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout kills such sessions after the given duration; transaction_timeout (PG 17+) bounds the whole transaction regardless of activity.

The damage of idle in transaction, in order of how quickly it hurts:

Held resource Effect Visible as
Row locks Other writers of those rows wait forever wait_event_type = Lock on other backends
Table locks (ACCESS SHARE from a SELECT) Any ALTER TABLE, and then every query behind it, waits (18.11) Lock queue pile-up
Snapshot (backend_xmin) VACUUM cannot remove anything newer; bloat everywhere "dead but not yet removable" in vacuum logs
Pool connection One fewer connection for the app; eventually pool exhaustion waitingCount rising, connectionTimeoutMillis errors

Practical example

The Node patterns that cause idle in transaction, all from real code reviews:

  • An await fetch(paymentProvider) inside dataSource.transaction(...): a 30 s provider timeout is 30 s of idle in transaction holding a lock on the order row and the inventory rows.
  • A missing await on a query inside a QueryRunner transaction; the code continues, the promise resolves later or rejects unobserved, and commitTransaction is skipped on an error path without finally { release() }.
  • A WebSocket handler that starts a transaction, sends a prompt to the user, and waits for the reply.
  • for await (const row of stream) reading a cursor inside a transaction while processing each row with slow I/O.

NestJS example

Do the external call first, then a short transaction with only database work. If you must reserve first, use a short transaction to reserve with a status, call the provider outside any transaction, then a second short transaction to finalise.

// checkout.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { PaymentGateway } from './payment.gateway';

@Injectable()
export class CheckoutService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource, private readonly gateway: PaymentGateway) {}

  async pay(orderId: number, amountCents: number, idempotencyKey: string) {
    // 1. Short transaction: claim the order, no external I/O inside
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
      const updated = await em.query(
        `UPDATE orders SET status = 'PAYING', updated_at = now()
          WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'PENDING'`,
        [orderId],
      );
      if (updated[1] !== 1) throw new Error('ORDER_NOT_PAYABLE');
    });

    // 2. External call OUTSIDE any transaction (may take seconds, may time out)
    const result = await this.gateway.charge({ amountCents, idempotencyKey });

    // 3. Second short transaction to record the outcome
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
      await em.query(
        `INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider_ref, status, amount_cents)
         VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)`,
        [orderId, result.providerRef, result.ok ? 'CAPTURED' : 'FAILED', amountCents],
      );
      await em.query(`UPDATE orders SET status = $2, updated_at = now() WHERE id = $1`, [
        orderId,
        result.ok ? 'PAID' : 'PENDING',
      ]);
    });
  }
}

The state machine (PENDING to PAYING to PAID) replaces the long lock. A crash between steps leaves a PAYING order that a reconciliation job can resolve using the idempotency key.

PostgreSQL example

Savepoints for an expected error, and the aborted-transaction message:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, status, total_cents) VALUES (42, 'PENDING', 1999);
SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
INSERT INTO coupon_redemptions (coupon_code, user_id) VALUES ('WELCOME10', 42);
-- ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "coupon_redemptions_pkey"
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_coupon;   -- the order insert survives
COMMIT;

Without the savepoint, the second INSERT error would have aborted the whole transaction and COMMIT would silently behave as ROLLBACK (it returns ROLLBACK, which drivers surface as a successful command). Find the idle offenders:

SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state,
       now() - xact_start  AS txn_open_for,
       now() - state_change AS idle_for,
       age(backend_xmin)   AS horizon_age,
       left(query, 80)     AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start;
 pid  | usename    | application_name | state               | txn_open_for | idle_for  | horizon_age | last_query
------+------------+------------------+---------------------+--------------+-----------+-------------+------------------------------------------
 8812 | orders_api | payments-worker  | idle in transaction | 2 days 03:12 | 2 days .. |     3120044 | INSERT INTO reconciliation_runs ...

Set the belts for application roles, not globally (migrations and admins need different limits):

ALTER ROLE orders_api SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
ALTER ROLE orders_api SET statement_timeout = '10s';
ALTER ROLE orders_api SET lock_timeout = '5s';

TypeORM example

TypeORM nests transactions with savepoints automatically: calling manager.transaction inside a running transaction, or queryRunner.startTransaction() when one is already active, issues SAVEPOINT typeorm_N. Use that for the expected-error pattern, and never call startTransaction in a loop of thousands of rows (the 64 sub-xid cliff).

await dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
  await em.insert(Order, { userId: 42, status: 'PENDING', totalCents: 1999 });
  try {
    // Nested transaction => SAVEPOINT; a unique violation here does not poison the outer txn
    await em.transaction(async (inner) => {
      await inner.insert(CouponRedemption, { couponCode: 'WELCOME10', userId: 42 });
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (!(e instanceof QueryFailedError) || (e as any).code !== '23505') throw e;
    // already redeemed: continue without the discount
  }
});

Sequelize example

Sequelize creates a savepoint when you pass the parent transaction to a nested sequelize.transaction:

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await Order.create({ userId: 42, status: 'PENDING', totalCents: 1999 }, { transaction: t });
  try {
    await sequelize.transaction({ transaction: t }, async (sp) => {   // SAVEPOINT
      await CouponRedemption.create({ couponCode: 'WELCOME10', userId: 42 }, { transaction: sp });
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (!(e instanceof UniqueConstraintError)) throw e;
  }
});

Production scenario

An orders API handles 1,200 transactions per second with a median transaction time of 3 ms and a p99 of 25 ms. With the role-level timeouts above, the maximum damage one bad code path can do is 30 s of a held lock, then the server ends the session and the pool reconnects. The team graphs max(now() - xact_start) for the app role and alerts at 20 s. pg_stat_database.xact_rollback / xact_commit is also on the dashboard: a rollback ratio jumping from 0.5 percent to 10 percent means a code path is throwing inside transactions.

Failure scenario

"Aborted transaction, silent data loss." A NestJS service caught a QueryFailedError inside dataSource.transaction, logged it, and continued to run two more statements and let the callback return normally. TypeORM issued COMMIT, PostgreSQL answered ROLLBACK (because the transaction was aborted), the driver did not throw, and the API returned 201 Created for an order that did not exist. Detection took two weeks. Rule: an error inside a transaction either propagates (so TypeORM rolls back and the request fails) or is handled with a savepoint; there is no third option.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • COMMIT on an aborted transaction returns ROLLBACK without an error in most drivers.
  • Savepoint storms (one per row) hit the 64 sub-xid cache limit and slow the whole server.
  • Prepared transactions (PREPARE TRANSACTION) survive restarts and hold locks and horizon until resolved; do not use without a coordinator.
  • SET LOCAL values revert at transaction end; SET values persist for the session (and leak through poolers).
  • A transaction that only reads still holds ACCESS SHARE locks and a snapshot; "read-only" does not mean harmless.
  • Retrying a whole transaction after a serialization failure or deadlock must be done by the application, with a bound on attempts.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They keep transactions short and free of external I/O, no exceptions. They model long business processes as state machines with short transactions per step. They set server-side timeouts per role so that a bug is bounded in blast radius. They review every try/catch inside a transaction with one question: "does this swallow an error that has already aborted the transaction?"

Common mistakes

  • Awaiting HTTP calls, queue publishes or Redis calls inside a database transaction.
  • Catching and ignoring errors inside a transaction.
  • Forgetting queryRunner.release() in a finally.
  • Using SET where SET LOCAL was meant.

Interview questions

  1. What does "idle in transaction" hold, and what are the consequences over minutes and over days? Expected: locks, snapshot, connection; lock queue pile-ups within minutes, bloat and wraparound risk over days.
  2. What happens if you keep running statements after an error inside a transaction? Expected: aborted state; COMMIT becomes ROLLBACK.
  3. When do you use savepoints and what is their hidden cost? Expected: expected errors; sub-xid cache overflow above 64.
  4. Design the payment flow so no transaction spans the provider call. Expected: state machine with two short transactions and an idempotency key.

Practical exercise

Write a NestJS service method with a transaction that calls a fake payment gateway with a 20 s delay inside the transaction. Observe pg_stat_activity and a second request blocking on the same inventory row. Refactor to the two-transaction state machine and show the lock is held for milliseconds. Acceptance criteria: before/after pg_stat_activity output and a test that simulates a crash between steps and a reconciliation that resolves it.

18.11 Locks

18.11.1 Lock modes, DDL, row locks and the lock queue

Concept

Every statement takes table-level locks on the tables it touches, in one of eight modes from ACCESS SHARE (a plain SELECT) to ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (DROP TABLE, most ALTER TABLE). Modes conflict or not according to a fixed matrix. Locks are held until the transaction ends. Waiting requests form a queue, and a request waits behind any earlier request it conflicts with, even if the current holder alone would not have blocked it. Separately, writes take row-level locks on the rows they modify, stored in the tuple header rather than in the lock table.

Why does it exist?

MVCC handles readers versus writers, but two writers on the same row need ordering, and structural changes (dropping a column) cannot happen while a query is reading that column. The lock modes exist so that compatible operations (two INSERTs, a SELECT and an UPDATE) proceed in parallel while incompatible ones (ALTER TABLE and anything) serialise. The queue exists to prevent starvation: without it, a stream of SELECTs could keep an ALTER TABLE waiting forever.

Mental model

Imagine a single-lane bridge with a signal. Cars in the same direction (compatible locks) flow together. A maintenance truck (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) needs the bridge empty. The rule "no one may enter behind a waiting truck" prevents the truck from waiting forever, but it also means that one slow car already on the bridge plus one waiting truck stops every car behind the truck. That is the whole ALTER TABLE incident in one picture.

How it works

Lock modes and what takes them:

Mode Taken by Conflicts with
ACCESS SHARE SELECT ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
ROW SHARE SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE EXCLUSIVE, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
ROW EXCLUSIVE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE SHARE, SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE, EXCLUSIVE, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE VACUUM, ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, ALTER TABLE ... SET (storage params), CREATE STATISTICS, COMMENT ON itself and everything stronger
SHARE CREATE INDEX (blocks writes, allows reads) ROW EXCLUSIVE and stronger, except itself
SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE CREATE TRIGGER, ALTER TABLE ... ADD FOREIGN KEY (both tables), ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE/DISABLE TRIGGER ROW EXCLUSIVE and stronger, including itself
EXCLUSIVE REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY everything except ACCESS SHARE
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER, REINDEX, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, ALTER TABLE (ADD/DROP COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN TYPE, SET/DROP NOT NULL, ADD PRIMARY KEY, ADD CHECK, RENAME), LOCK TABLE everything

Some DDL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE but holds it for milliseconds (ADD COLUMN without a volatile default on PG 11+, SET DEFAULT, DROP COLUMN, RENAME); some holds it for the entire rewrite (ALTER COLUMN TYPE that changes storage, ADD COLUMN with a volatile default, VACUUM FULL). Both are dangerous because of the queue, not because of the duration.

Row-level locks:

Row lock Taken by Blocks
FOR KEY SHARE Foreign-key checks on the referenced row (inserting an order_items row locks the orders row this way) FOR UPDATE
FOR SHARE SELECT ... FOR SHARE FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR UPDATE
FOR NO KEY UPDATE UPDATE that does not change key columns FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR UPDATE
FOR UPDATE DELETE, UPDATE that changes a unique key, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE all row locks

This distinction is why inserting order_items does not block a concurrent UPDATE orders SET status = ... on the parent row (KEY SHARE and NO KEY UPDATE are compatible), but does block DELETE FROM orders and does block SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the order. If your code locks the order with FOR UPDATE while inserting items in another transaction, you get waits you did not expect. FOR NO KEY UPDATE in the application is usually what you mean.

The lock queue, step by step:

flowchart LR
  h["holder: reporting SELECT on orders, ACCESS SHARE, running 4 min"] --> w1["waiter 1: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN, wants ACCESS EXCLUSIVE"]
  w1 --> w2["waiter 2: GET /orders SELECT, wants ACCESS SHARE, compatible with holder but queued behind waiter 1"]
  w2 --> w3["waiter 3: POST /orders INSERT, wants ROW EXCLUSIVE"]
  w3 --> w4["waiters 4 to 160: every pooled connection in every pod"]
  1. A request checks the lock table in shared memory for conflicting holders and conflicting waiters ahead of it.
  2. If neither exists, it is granted immediately.
  3. If a conflicting holder or waiter exists, it joins the queue and its backend sleeps with wait_event_type = Lock.
  4. When a lock is released, the queue is re-examined from the front; waiters are granted in order as long as they do not conflict with holders or with earlier waiters.
  5. lock_timeout makes the waiting request give up after the given time with canceling statement due to lock timeout, and leave the queue, unblocking everyone behind it.
  6. Every second (deadlock_timeout), a waiter checks for a cycle among waiters; a deadlock aborts one participant (Part 20 covers deadlock patterns).

Practical example

"ALTER TABLE at 10:00 froze the whole API." A migration ran ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN gift_message text during business hours. A finance report had started a 4-minute SELECT over orders at 09:58. The ALTER queued behind it. Every GET /orders, every checkout INSERT, every UPDATE queued behind the ALTER.
