Within 8 seconds all 160 pooled connections across the fleet were waiting, health checks failed, pods restarted and reconnected into the same queue. At 10:02 the report finished, the ALTER ran in 4 ms, the queue drained in a second, and a 4-minute outage was over. The ADD COLUMN itself was instant; the report plus the queue rule did the damage. Fix: lock_timeout in the migration with retries, and no reports on the primary.

NestJS example

A migration helper that never lets DDL wait long enough to cause a pile-up, and retries with backoff:

// migrations/ddl.helper.ts
import { QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export async function ddlWithLockTimeout(
  qr: QueryRunner,
  sql: string,
  { lockTimeout = '3s', attempts = 10, backoffMs = 2_000 } = {},
): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      // lock_timeout applies to the wait for the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock;
      // a waiting ALTER that gives up after 3 s unblocks the queue behind it
      await qr.query(`SET lock_timeout = '${lockTimeout}'`);
      await qr.query(sql);
      await qr.query(`RESET lock_timeout`);
      return;
    } catch (err: any) {
      const lockTimedOut = err?.code === '55P03';   // lock_not_available
      if (!lockTimedOut || attempt >= attempts) throw err;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, backoffMs * attempt));
    }
  }
}

// usage inside a migration
// await ddlWithLockTimeout(qr, `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN gift_message text`);

PostgreSQL example

Who is blocking whom, and what they are waiting on:

SELECT a.pid,
       a.state,
       a.wait_event_type,
       a.wait_event,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)            AS blocked_by,
       now() - a.query_start              AS waiting_for,
       left(a.query, 60)                  AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity a
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) > 0
ORDER BY a.query_start;
 pid  | state  | wait_event_type | wait_event | blocked_by | waiting_for | query
------+--------+-----------------+------------+------------+-------------+------------------------------------------------
 5120 | active | Lock            | relation   | {4410}     | 00:02:10    | ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN gift_message text
 5133 | active | Lock            | relation   | {5120}     | 00:02:09    | SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1
 5134 | active | Lock            | relation   | {5120}     | 00:02:09    | INSERT INTO orders (user_id, status, total_cent

The root is pid 4410 (the report). Then decide: cancel the report (pg_cancel_backend(4410)), or cancel the ALTER (pg_cancel_backend(5120)), which drains the queue immediately. Cancel the ALTER first; it is the one that can be retried. Full lock detail is in pg_locks:

SELECT l.pid, l.locktype, l.relation::regclass AS rel, l.mode, l.granted
FROM pg_locks l
WHERE l.relation = 'orders'::regclass
ORDER BY l.granted DESC, l.pid;

Turn on log_lock_waits = on so that any wait longer than deadlock_timeout (1 s) is logged with both pids; this is the evidence you need after the fact.

TypeORM example

Row locks with the right strength, and non-blocking variants for queues:

// Lock the order row without blocking child inserts (FOR NO KEY UPDATE)
const order = await em
  .createQueryBuilder(Order, 'o')
  .setLock('for_no_key_update')
  .where('o.id = :id', { id: orderId })
  .getOneOrFail();

// Queue claim: take one PENDING job, skip rows other workers hold
const job = await em
  .createQueryBuilder(OutboxMessage, 'm')
  .setLock('pessimistic_write')        // FOR UPDATE
  .setOnLocked('skip_locked')          // SKIP LOCKED
  .where('m.status = :s', { s: 'PENDING' })
  .orderBy('m.created_at', 'ASC')
  .limit(1)
  .getOne();

Both must run inside a transaction (dataSource.transaction or a QueryRunner), or the lock is released immediately.

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const order = await Order.findByPk(orderId, { transaction: t, lock: t.LOCK.NO_KEY_UPDATE });
  const job = await OutboxMessage.findOne({
    where: { status: 'PENDING' },
    order: [['createdAt', 'ASC']],
    lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE,
    skipLocked: true,
    transaction: t,
  });
});

Production scenario

Rules that a mature team enforces for DDL on a database serving 1,000 requests per second: every migration sets lock_timeout = '3s' and retries; DDL that rewrites the table (ALTER COLUMN TYPE, ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT volatile()) is done as add-new-column, backfill in batches, swap; constraints are added NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (which takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE); indexes are always CONCURRENTLY (Part 19); statement_timeout for the app role is 10 s so that no request can be the 4-minute holder. Monitoring: count of backends with wait_event_type = Lock (alert above 10 for more than 10 s), log_lock_waits entries, and deadlocks in pg_stat_database.

Failure scenario

A deploy added a foreign key: ALTER TABLE order_items ADD CONSTRAINT fk_order FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id). This takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both tables and scans order_items (300 million rows, 6 minutes) to validate. Writes to both orders and order_items blocked for 6 minutes. The safe version: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID (instant, still enforces for new rows), then ALTER TABLE order_items VALIDATE CONSTRAINT fk_order, which holds only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE and lets writes through during the scan.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a parent row blocks all child inserts because of KEY SHARE; use FOR NO KEY UPDATE.
  • Locks are held to transaction end: a statement that finished 5 minutes ago still holds its locks if the transaction is open.
  • TRUNCATE in tests against a shared database takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and can deadlock with app transactions.
  • Lock table exhaustion (out of shared memory ... max_locks_per_transaction) when a transaction touches thousands of partitions or tables.
  • lock_timeout also applies to row-lock waits, which may not be what you want in application code; set it per role deliberately.
  • Autovacuum (non-wraparound) gives up its lock when DDL wants it; anti-wraparound vacuum does not, and a migration can wait behind it for hours.
  • Replicas: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks replay on standbys and conflict with running queries there (max_standby_streaming_delay).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They picture the queue before typing any ALTER. They know that "this DDL is instant" is not a safety argument, only "this DDL cannot wait long" is. They keep a migration checklist: lock_timeout, retry, CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID then VALIDATE, no rewrites, off-peak. They ask the question "who holds ACCESS SHARE on this table for minutes?" and the answer is usually a report that belongs on a replica.

Common mistakes

  • Running migrations through the same pool and role as the app without lock_timeout.
  • Adding foreign keys or check constraints without NOT VALID.
  • Using FOR UPDATE where FOR NO KEY UPDATE was meant.
  • Reading pg_locks without pg_blocking_pids and chasing the wrong pid.

Interview questions

  1. Why can an ALTER TABLE that takes 4 ms cause a 4-minute outage? Expected: it queues behind a long ACCESS SHARE holder and everything else queues behind it. Follow-up: name three mitigations.
  2. Which lock does CREATE INDEX take versus CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY? Expected: SHARE (blocks writes) versus SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (allows writes).
  3. Explain FOR KEY SHARE and why it exists. Expected: FK checks; allows non-key updates on parent concurrently.
  4. How do you add a foreign key to a 300 million row table without blocking writes? Expected: NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT.
  5. How do you find the root blocker in a lock pile-up? Expected: pg_blocking_pids, follow the chain.

Practical exercise

Reproduce the lock queue with three psql sessions: a long SELECT pg_sleep(120) FROM orders LIMIT 1 inside a transaction, an ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN x int, and a plain SELECT count(*) FROM orders. Show the third one blocking. Cancel the ALTER and show the third proceed. Then rerun the ALTER with lock_timeout = '2s'. Acceptance criteria: pg_blocking_pids output for each step and a migration helper with retry.

18.11.2 Advisory locks: application-level mutual exclusion

Concept

An advisory lock is a lock on a number you choose, with no table or row behind it. PostgreSQL only manages it; your application decides what the number means (hash('cron:reconcile-payments'), or a user id). They come in session scope (held until you unlock or disconnect) and transaction scope (released at commit or rollback), and in blocking (pg_advisory_lock) and non-blocking (pg_try_advisory_lock) forms.

Why does it exist?

Some mutual exclusion has no natural row: "only one pod may run the nightly reconciliation", "serialise all checkout attempts for user 42 even across different orders", "one migration runner at a time". Without advisory locks, teams build lock tables with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT and expiry columns, or lean on Redis locks that are not transactional with the data. Advisory locks are cheap (lock-table entries, no I/O), transactional if you want them to be, and released automatically on disconnect.

Mental model

Imagine a wall of numbered hooks by the office door. Anyone who wants exclusive use of the meeting room takes the key from hook 17. The building does not know what hook 17 means; the team agreed that it means "the meeting room". If someone leaves the building with the key in their pocket (session lock behind a pooler), the room is locked forever.

How it works

  1. pg_advisory_lock(key bigint) or pg_advisory_lock(key1 int, key2 int) blocks until the lock is available. pg_try_advisory_lock returns false immediately instead of waiting.
  2. pg_advisory_xact_lock and pg_try_advisory_xact_lock are the transaction-scoped forms; they cannot be unlocked early and disappear at transaction end. Prefer these; they work behind PgBouncer transaction mode (18.2.2).
  3. Session locks are released with pg_advisory_unlock(key) (once per acquisition; they are re-entrant and counted) or pg_advisory_unlock_all() or on disconnect.
  4. The key space is one 64-bit space per database, shared by every feature. Derive keys from names with hashtext('feature:name') (32-bit, use the two-int form with a feature id) or from a bigint id, and document the namespace.
  5. They appear in pg_locks with locktype = 'advisory'; classid and objid hold the key parts.
  6. Advisory locks participate in deadlock detection like any other lock.

Practical example

Three pods run a @Cron('0 * * * *') job that reconciles payments. Without coordination, all three run it, and the provider API rate-limits you. With pg_try_advisory_lock, the first pod gets the lock and runs; the other two see false and skip. If the winning pod crashes mid-way, the connection drops, the lock is released, and the next hour's run takes over.

NestJS example

Session-scoped lock on a dedicated connection (a QueryRunner pins one connection for lock and unlock). Use this only when the app connects to PostgreSQL directly or through PgBouncer in session mode; behind transaction pooling, wrap the whole job in one transaction and use the xact form instead.

// payments-reconcile.job.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

const LOCK_NS = 1001;                 // feature namespace, documented in one place
const LOCK_ID = 1;                    // job id within the namespace

@Injectable()
export class PaymentsReconcileJob {
  private readonly log = new Logger(PaymentsReconcileJob.name);
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  @Cron('0 * * * *')
  async run(): Promise<void> {
    const qr = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();   // one pinned connection
    await qr.connect();
    try {
      const [{ got }] = await qr.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1, $2) AS got', [LOCK_NS, LOCK_ID]);
      if (!got) {
        this.log.log('another pod holds the reconcile lock, skipping');
        return;
      }
      try {
        await this.reconcile(qr);                        // may take minutes; lock held on this connection
      } finally {
        await qr.query('SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1, $2)', [LOCK_NS, LOCK_ID]);
      }
    } finally {
      await qr.release();                               // returns the connection; a crash also releases the lock
    }
  }

  private async reconcile(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    // batches of short transactions; never one multi-minute transaction
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Per-entity serialisation inside a transaction: all checkout attempts for a user are processed one at a time, without locking any row that other flows need.

BEGIN;
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(42);          -- user 42; released automatically at COMMIT
-- read cart, validate stock, create order, decrement inventory
COMMIT;

Inspect advisory locks:

SELECT pid, classid AS key1, objid AS key2, granted, mode
FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype = 'advisory';

TypeORM example

await dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
  await em.query('SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock($1)', [userId]);   // released at transaction end
  // ... checkout logic for this user
});

Sequelize example

await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await sequelize.query('SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(:key)', { replacements: { key: userId }, transaction: t });
  // ... checkout logic
});

Production scenario

Advisory locks in an orders platform: migration runner lock (session-scoped, held for the whole migration run so two CI jobs cannot race), per-user checkout serialisation (xact-scoped), and singleton cron jobs (session-scoped with try). Throughput cost is negligible: acquiring an uncontended advisory lock is a few microseconds. The team keeps a registry of namespaces in the repository.

Failure scenario

"Someone else holds the lock, forever." A job took a session-level advisory lock through PgBouncer in transaction mode. The lock was taken on server connection A; the job's next statement ran on connection B; the unlock ran on connection C and returned false (nothing to unlock there). Connection A went back to the pool holding the lock, and every subsequent run of the job saw pg_try_advisory_lock return false until PgBouncer recycled that server connection hours later. The fix was the xact-scoped form inside a single transaction.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Session locks behind transaction pooling leak.
  • Key collisions between features using the same 64-bit space.
  • A lock holder that blocks on something else (an HTTP call) holds the lock and a connection for as long as that takes.
  • Advisory locks are per database, not per cluster; two databases cannot coordinate through them.
  • Session locks are re-entrant and counted; unlocking once after locking twice leaves it held.
  • They are not visible in pg_stat_user_tables or any table-level view; only pg_locks.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They prefer transaction-scoped advisory locks and treat session-scoped ones as a special tool with a pooling caveat written next to every use. They use them for coordination that belongs with the data and use Redis locks only for coordination that does not involve the database at all. They document the key namespace like an API.

Common mistakes

  • Session locks through PgBouncer transaction mode.
  • Using pg_advisory_lock (blocking) in a request path with no timeout.
  • Reusing an id-based key across features (user_id for both checkout and notifications) and serialising unrelated work.

Interview questions

  1. Session versus transaction advisory locks: when do you use which? Expected: xact for anything inside a transaction and behind poolers; session for long jobs on a pinned connection.
  2. How do you make sure a cron job runs on exactly one of N pods? Expected: pg_try_advisory_lock on a pinned connection, or a xact lock for single-transaction jobs.
  3. What goes wrong with advisory locks and PgBouncer?

Practical exercise

Implement the singleton cron job in NestJS with pg_try_advisory_lock, run three instances locally, and verify only one executes each tick. Kill the running instance mid-job and verify another takes over on the next tick. Acceptance criteria: logs from three processes, pg_locks output while the job runs, and a note on what changes behind PgBouncer.

18.12 The query planner and optimizer

18.12.1 Cost model, cardinality estimation and join order

Concept

The planner takes a query tree and produces the cheapest plan it can find. "Cheapest" means the lowest estimated cost, a unit-less number computed from a handful of cost constants (how expensive a sequential page read is, a random page read, processing one row, evaluating one operator) and from cardinality estimates (how many rows each step will produce), which come from the statistics of 18.9. The planner never measures anything; it predicts.

Why does it exist?

There are dozens of ways to run even a simple two-table join and millions for a ten-table one. Trying them all for real would take longer than running the query. A cost model lets the planner compare alternatives in microseconds. It is remarkably good when its inputs are accurate, and confidently wrong when they are not: the inputs (statistics, cost constants, memory settings) are what a backend engineer controls.

Mental model

Imagine a delivery dispatcher who has never driven the routes but has a map with estimated speeds per road type and estimated numbers of parcels per neighbourhood. The dispatcher picks the route with the lowest estimated time. If the map says "highway, 100 km/h" but the highway has been a parking lot for a year (a stale random_page_cost on SSD, or stale row counts), every route decision is wrong in the same direction.

How it works

The cost constants, with defaults and what they mean:

Setting Default Meaning Typical change
seq_page_cost 1.0 One page read during a sequential scan leave
random_page_cost 4.0 One page read in random order (index scans) 1.1 on SSD or NVMe; RDS gp3 too
cpu_tuple_cost 0.01 Processing one row leave
cpu_index_tuple_cost 0.005 Processing one index entry leave
cpu_operator_cost 0.0025 Evaluating one operator or function leave
effective_cache_size 4 GB How much of the data the planner may assume is cached (OS plus shared buffers) 50 to 75 percent of RAM
parallel_setup_cost, parallel_tuple_cost 1000, 0.1 Cost of starting workers and passing rows leave

  1. Access paths. For each table in the query the planner lists ways to get rows: sequential scan, index scan per usable index, index-only scan, bitmap scan, TID scan. It costs each. A sequential scan of orders (3.9 million pages, 200 million rows) with one filter costs about 3,921,033 × 1.0 + 200,000,000 × 0.01 + 200,000,000 × 0.0025 = 6,421,033. An index scan costs the index pages read plus heap pages read (random cost, scaled down toward sequential cost when the column's correlation is high) plus per-row CPU. random_page_cost = 4 says heap fetches via an index are four times more expensive than a sequential page, which was true for spinning disks and is false for SSDs; on SSD the planner will wrongly prefer sequential scans and bitmap scans until you set it to about 1.1.

  2. Selectivity. Each WHERE condition is turned into a fraction of rows using pg_stats: MCV lookups for equality on common values, 1/n_distinct for equality on unknown values, histogram interpolation for ranges, and defaults when it has nothing (0.5 for an unknown boolean expression, 0.005 for equality with a function it cannot analyse). Conditions combined with AND are multiplied as if independent; OR uses inclusion-exclusion. Multiplying is the independence assumption, and it is the single most common cause of bad plans on real data: country = 'DE' AND currency = 'EUR' is estimated as 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04 of rows when the truth is about 0.2.

  3. Join methods. For every pair of inputs it considers:

    Method Cost shape Wins when
    Nested Loop outer rows × cost of inner lookup outer side is small and inner side has an index (user_id = ? then items by order_id)
    Hash Join build hash of smaller side (needs work_mem) plus one pass over the larger both sides large, no useful ordering; the default for analytics joins
    Merge Join sort both (or use indexes) then one pass both sides already sorted on the join key, or very large inputs

    A misestimate that says "10 rows" when the truth is 10 million turns a nested loop into 10 million index probes, and that is the 40-second query.

  4. Join order. Up to join_collapse_limit and from_collapse_limit (8) tables, the planner uses dynamic programming to consider every join order. Above geqo_threshold (12) it switches to a genetic algorithm that is fast but non-deterministic. Writing joins in explicit JOIN syntax and setting join_collapse_limit = 1 forces your written order, which is a blunt but sometimes necessary tool.

  5. Parallelism. For large scans and joins the planner may add Gather nodes and up to max_parallel_workers_per_gather (2) workers; tables smaller than min_parallel_table_scan_size (8 MB) are never parallelised.

  6. JIT. On PG 12+, jit = on compiles expressions for queries with estimated cost above jit_above_cost (100,000). For OLTP it can add 5 to 50 ms of compile time to an occasional query and is often disabled (jit = off) on transactional systems.

The enable_* settings (enable_seqscan, enable_nestloop, enable_hashjoin, enable_mergejoin, enable_indexscan, enable_bitmapscan, enable_sort) do not disable anything; they add a huge penalty (10 billion) to that node type. They are for diagnosis in a session: "would the index plan be faster if the planner chose it?" Never set them in postgresql.conf or for a role.

Extended statistics teach the planner about correlated columns:

CREATE STATISTICS orders_country_currency (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv)
  ON shipping_country, currency FROM orders;
ANALYZE orders;

dependencies captures functional dependencies (currency depends on country), ndistinct captures distinct counts of the combination (for GROUP BY country, currency), and mcv (PG 12+) stores the most common combinations. They cost one more ANALYZE pass and a few KB.

Practical example

SELECT ... FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id WHERE o.shipping_country = 'DE' AND o.currency = 'EUR' AND o.created_at > now() - interval '7 days'. Truth: 1.2 million orders in DE, all in EUR, 180,000 in the last week. Independence assumption: 200 million × 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.005 = 40,000 orders estimated. The planner picks a nested loop into order_items expecting 40,000 index probes; it does 180,000, each reading 3 or 4 random pages: 12 s. With extended statistics the estimate becomes 200,000, the planner picks a hash join with a bitmap scan, and the query takes 1.1 s.

PostgreSQL example

Before and after extended statistics, on the filter alone:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT count(*) FROM orders
WHERE shipping_country = 'DE' AND currency = 'EUR' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days';

Before:

Aggregate  (cost=48211.10..48211.11 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=2210.442..2210.443 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created_at on orders
        (cost=0.57..48111.02 rows=40032 width=0) (actual time=0.034..2181.201 rows=180114 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (created_at > (now() - '7 days'::interval))
        Filter: ((shipping_country = 'DE') AND (currency = 'EUR'))
        Rows Removed by Filter: 719886
        Buffers: shared hit=812203 read=98211

After CREATE STATISTICS and ANALYZE:

Aggregate  (cost=61233.10..61233.11 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=310.114..310.115 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=9021.11..60731.20 rows=200811 width=0) (actual time=42.010..291.120 rows=180114 loops=1)
        Recheck Cond: ((shipping_country = 'DE') AND (created_at > (now() - '7 days'::interval)))
        Filter: (currency = 'EUR')
        Heap Blocks: exact=41022
        Buffers: shared hit=44120 read=2201
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_country_created  (cost=0.00..8971.02 rows=200811 width=0) ...

rows=40032 versus actual 180114 was the tell: an estimate off by more than three or four times is worth investigating; off by 100 times is the bug. Diagnose "would an index be better?" without changing anything permanent:

SET enable_seqscan = off;      -- session only, for diagnosis
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...;
RESET enable_seqscan;

And check what the planner thinks about your storage:

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('random_page_cost', 'seq_page_cost', 'effective_cache_size', 'work_mem', 'jit');

TypeORM example

A plan regression test that runs in CI against a seeded database, so an index removal or a query rewrite that changes the plan fails a test instead of a production night:

// orders.repository.plan.spec.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

describe('recentForUser plan', () => {
  let ds: DataSource;
  beforeAll(async () => { ds = await createTestDataSource(); });   // seeded with skewed data

  it('uses the composite index and no sort', async () => {
    const [{ 'QUERY PLAN': plan }] = await ds.query(
      `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)
       SELECT id, status, total_cents FROM orders
       WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`,
      [42],
    );
    const root = plan[0].Plan;
    const nodes: any[] = [];
    (function walk(n: any) { nodes.push(n); (n.Plans ?? []).forEach(walk); })(root);

    expect(nodes.some((n) => n['Index Name'] === 'idx_orders_user_created')).toBe(true);
    expect(nodes.some((n) => n['Node Type'] === 'Sort')).toBe(false);   // ordered by the index
  });
});

Sequelize example

Same idea with sequelize.query(..., { type: QueryTypes.SELECT }) and the JSON plan; Sequelize adds nothing planner-specific. What matters is that the SQL the ORM generates is the SQL you test.

Production scenario

A well-tuned OLTP instance: random_page_cost = 1.1, effective_cache_size = 24GB (on 32 GB), work_mem = 32MB, jit = off, default_statistics_target = 200, extended statistics on the four column pairs that appear together in the top 20 queries, and auto_explain logging any plan over 500 ms. Plan flips are caught within minutes because auto_explain output is parsed into a dashboard of "plans seen per query id".

What can go wrong? Misestimates from stale or missing statistics, correlation, generic plans, or wrong cost constants. How do I monitor it? auto_explain plus pg_stat_statements mean time per query id. How do I fix it? In order: ANALYZE, statistics target, extended statistics, the right index, query rewrite, cost constants, and only then hints (pg_hint_plan) or enable_* in a single transaction as a last resort.

Failure scenario

ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 with a rare filter. SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 with an index on created_at but not on user_id: the planner assumes user 7's rows are spread evenly through the table, so it expects to find 20 matches after scanning a few thousand index entries backward. User 7 placed 3 orders in 2019. The scan walks 200 million index entries and heap pages: 90 s. The estimate was fine on average; the assumption of uniform distribution was the problem, and only the right composite index (user_id, created_at DESC) fixes it for every user (Part 19 has the full case study).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Independence assumption on correlated columns; fix with extended statistics.
  • LIMIT with the uniform-distribution assumption; fix with a composite index that satisfies both filter and order.
  • Functions and expressions without statistics (lower(email), data->>'sku', date_trunc); fix with an expression index plus ANALYZE, which creates statistics for the expression.
  • work_mem too small: hash joins spill into batches, sorts go to disk, and the planner may avoid a hash join it should have used; too large: memory blow-up under concurrency.
  • Join order search cut off by geqo_threshold: non-deterministic plans on 12-plus table queries.
  • Generic plans in prepared statements (18.3.2).
  • Partition pruning failing because the partition key is compared with a function or a parameter of the wrong type.
  • Row-level security or views with security_barrier preventing predicate pushdown.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read the estimated-versus-actual rows before anything else in a plan. They fix inputs (statistics, cost constants) before forcing outcomes (hints). They know which queries in their system are sensitive to a plan flip and test those plans in CI. They are suspicious of any query that "usually" runs fast.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving random_page_cost = 4 on SSD and wondering why indexes are ignored.
  • Setting enable_seqscan = off globally.
  • Adding an index for every slow query instead of asking why the estimate was wrong.
  • Trusting EXPLAIN without ANALYZE.

Interview questions

  1. How does the planner estimate the cost of an index scan versus a sequential scan, and what inputs can you change? Expected: page costs, CPU costs, correlation, effective_cache_size, statistics; random_page_cost on SSD.
  2. What is the independence assumption and how do you fix a bad estimate caused by it? Expected: multiplied selectivities; CREATE STATISTICS.
  3. When does a nested loop beat a hash join? Expected: small outer input with an indexed inner side.
  4. What are enable_* settings for, and what must you never do with them?
  5. Why can ORDER BY ... LIMIT queries be catastrophically slow for rare filter values?

Practical exercise

Build orders with correlated shipping_country and currency (each country has one currency). Run the DE/EUR query, capture the misestimate, add extended statistics, and capture the new plan. Then set random_page_cost = 4 and 1.1 in turn and record which plan the planner chooses for a 0.5 percent selective range query. Acceptance criteria: four plans with row estimates, actuals, buffers and timing, and a paragraph on which input fixed which problem.

18.13 Configuration knobs a backend engineer must know

18.13.1 The settings that decide behaviour under load

Concept

PostgreSQL has about 350 settings. A backend engineer needs to understand roughly twenty, because those twenty decide whether the database survives your traffic pattern: memory per sort, memory for maintenance, what the planner believes about the hardware, and the safety belts that limit how much damage one bad query, one bad transaction, or one bad deploy can do.

Why does it exist?

Defaults are chosen so that PostgreSQL starts on a laptop with 1 GB of RAM. Production hardware is 30 to 500 times bigger, workloads vary from 50 connections doing 1 ms lookups to 5 connections doing hour-long reports, and the same knob (work_mem) that makes reports fast makes an OLTP server run out of memory. There is no safe universal value, so the knobs exist and you must set them.

Mental model

Imagine a kitchen where each cook (backend) may use a certain number of pans at once (work_mem per operation). Give each cook 20 pans and 200 cooks will burn the kitchen down. Give them 2 and the head chef preparing a banquet (a report) cannot work. The senior answer is "2 by default, and the banquet chef gets 20 for that dish only" (SET LOCAL work_mem).

How it works

Where a setting can be set, in increasing precedence: postgresql.conf or the RDS parameter group; ALTER SYSTEM SET (writes postgresql.auto.conf); ALTER DATABASE shop SET; ALTER ROLE orders_api SET; SET in a session; SET LOCAL in a transaction. pg_settings.context tells you whether a change needs a restart (postmaster), a reload (sighup), or nothing (user, superuser).

Setting Default What it controls Sensible production value Why
shared_buffers 128 MB PostgreSQL page cache (18.4) 25 percent of RAM, rarely above 16 GB Working set in memory; restart required
effective_cache_size 4 GB Planner's belief about total cache 50 to 75 percent of RAM Makes index scans look as cheap as they are
work_mem 4 MB Memory per sort or hash operation (a query can have several; every connection can run one) 16 to 64 MB globally; raise per transaction for reports Sorts and hashes spill to disk when exceeded; too high risks OOM
hash_mem_multiplier 2.0 (PG 15+) Hash operations may use work_mem × multiplier leave Hash joins are memory-hungry
maintenance_work_mem 64 MB CREATE INDEX, VACUUM, ALTER TABLE ADD FOREIGN KEY 1 to 2 GB Index builds are several times faster with enough memory
autovacuum_work_mem -1 (uses maintenance) Per autovacuum worker 256 MB to 1 GB Fewer index passes on big tables
random_page_cost 4.0 Planner cost of random reads 1.1 on SSD Otherwise the planner avoids indexes
effective_io_concurrency 1 Prefetching during bitmap heap scans 200 on SSD Bitmap scans get much faster
max_connections 100 Backend slots (18.2) 100 to 300 with a pooler Each is a process; restart required
statement_timeout 0 (off) Max statement duration 10 to 30 s for app roles; 0 for migrations One runaway query cannot hold a connection for an hour
lock_timeout 0 (off) Max wait for any lock 3 to 5 s for migrations; per role for apps Prevents lock-queue pile-ups (18.11)
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 0 (off) Kill sessions idle in a transaction 30 to 60 s for app roles Stops horizon holders and lock holders (18.10)
log_min_duration_statement -1 (off) Log statements slower than this 500 ms (200 ms on tight systems) The slow query log
log_lock_waits off Log waits longer than deadlock_timeout on Evidence for lock incidents
log_temp_files -1 Log temp files above this size 0 (all) Shows which queries spill work_mem
log_checkpoints on (PG 15+) Checkpoint details (18.6) on Comb-shaped latency diagnosis
log_autovacuum_min_duration 10 min (PG 15+) Log autovacuum runs longer than this 1 s The "not yet removable" line (18.8)
track_io_timing off Measure read/write time in stats and EXPLAIN on (cheap on modern clocks) Separates cache misses from disk time
shared_preload_libraries empty Extensions loaded at start pg_stat_statements,auto_explain Observability (18.14); restart required
max_wal_size, checkpoint_timeout 1 GB, 5 min Checkpoint frequency (18.6) 8 GB plus, 15 min Fewer full-page writes, smoother I/O
jit on JIT compilation of expressions off for OLTP Avoids compile latency on short queries
max_parallel_workers_per_gather 2 Parallel workers per query 2 to 4 on OLTP; more on analytics Parallel scans use CPU that OLTP needs
temp_file_limit -1 Max temp disk per session 10 to 50 GB A bad report cannot fill the disk

A starter configuration for an 8 vCPU, 32 GB OLTP instance on SSD:

shared_buffers = 8GB
effective_cache_size = 24GB
work_mem = 32MB
maintenance_work_mem = 1GB
random_page_cost = 1.1
effective_io_concurrency = 200
max_connections = 200
max_wal_size = 8GB
checkpoint_timeout = 15min
checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9
wal_compression = lz4
jit = off
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements,auto_explain'
log_min_duration_statement = 500
log_lock_waits = on
log_temp_files = 0
log_autovacuum_min_duration = 1000
track_io_timing = on
autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 2000
autovacuum_max_workers = 5
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 60000

Per-role belts go on top, because migrations, analysts and the API need different limits.

work_mem deserves its own arithmetic. It is per operation, not per connection or per query: a query with two sorts and a hash join can use three times work_mem. With 200 connections and work_mem = 256MB, the theoretical peak is 200 × 3 × 256 MB = 150 GB. Real usage is far lower because most queries never sort, but a traffic spike that makes 100 connections run the same report at once has taken down real servers. The pattern is work_mem = 32MB globally and SET LOCAL work_mem = '512MB' inside the specific transaction that runs the monthly report.

Practical example

The GET /orders/export endpoint sorts up to 2 million rows for large B2B customers. With work_mem = 4MB the sort spills to disk (Sort Method: external merge Disk: 312400kB) and takes 9 s. With SET LOCAL work_mem = '512MB' in the export transaction it sorts in memory in 1.4 s. Raising the global work_mem to 512 MB instead would have exposed the whole server to memory exhaustion the first time 50 customers exported at the same time.

NestJS example

Belts and per-transaction memory from configuration, not from code literals:

// reports.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class ReportsService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource, private readonly cfg: ConfigService) {}

  async exportOrders(userId: number) {
    const workMem = this.cfg.get<string>('REPORT_WORK_MEM', '256MB');
    const timeoutMs = this.cfg.get<number>('REPORT_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS', 60_000);

    return this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
      // Scoped to this transaction only; safe behind PgBouncer transaction mode
      await em.query(`SET LOCAL work_mem = '${workMem}'`);
      await em.query(`SET LOCAL statement_timeout = ${timeoutMs}`);   // longer than the API default
      return em.query(
        `SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total_cents, o.created_at
           FROM orders o
          WHERE o.user_id = $1
          ORDER BY o.created_at DESC`,
        [userId],
      );
    });
  }
}

Validate REPORT_WORK_MEM against a whitelist pattern at startup; it is interpolated into SQL.

PostgreSQL example

Find out what applies where, and which settings need a restart:

SELECT name, setting, unit, source, context, pending_restart
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('shared_buffers', 'work_mem', 'random_page_cost', 'statement_timeout',
               'idle_in_transaction_session_timeout', 'max_connections')
ORDER BY name;
 name                                | setting | unit | source             | context    | pending_restart
-------------------------------------+---------+------+--------------------+------------+-----------------
 idle_in_transaction_session_timeout | 60000   | ms   | configuration file | user       | f
 max_connections                     | 200     |      | configuration file | postmaster | f
 random_page_cost                    | 1.1     |      | configuration file | user       | f
 shared_buffers                      | 1048576 | 8kB  | configuration file | postmaster | f
 statement_timeout                   | 10000   | ms   | database           | user       | f
 work_mem                            | 32768   | kB   | configuration file | user       | f

Role-level overrides and reload without restart:

ALTER ROLE analyst SET work_mem = '256MB';
ALTER ROLE analyst SET statement_timeout = '10min';
ALTER ROLE analyst SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '2min';
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = '250ms';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Spot spilling sorts in the log with log_temp_files = 0:

LOG:  temporary file: path "base/pgsql_tmp/pgsql_tmp8812.3", size 327155712
STATEMENT:  SELECT o.id, ... FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = $1 ORDER BY o.created_at DESC

TypeORM example

Startup parameters through extra apply to every pooled connection of that service; use them for the belts the service should always have, and keep the per-transaction ones in code:

extra: {
  max: 8,
  statement_timeout: 10_000,                   // ms; sent as a startup parameter
  idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30_000,
  lock_timeout: 5_000,
  application_name: 'orders-api',
}

Sequelize example

dialectOptions: {
  statement_timeout: 10_000,
  idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30_000,
  lock_timeout: 5_000,
  application_name: 'orders-api',
}

Production scenario

A managed RDS instance: shared_buffers and max_connections come from the parameter group with RDS defaults derived from instance memory; the team overrides random_page_cost, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, log_min_duration_statement, log_lock_waits, track_io_timing, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit, max_wal_size, checkpoint_timeout, jit, and shared_preload_libraries (which RDS calls out as needing a reboot). Application roles carry their timeouts. The parameter group is version-controlled and reviewed like code.

Failure scenario

"OOM at 09:05 every Monday." A weekly job ran 40 concurrent report queries each with two large hash joins. work_mem had been raised to 1 GB globally to make a single report fast. 40 × 2 × up to 2 GB (hash multiplier) of demand on a 64 GB server: the OOM killer took a backend, the postmaster restarted all connections, and the API fleet reconnected in a storm (18.2). work_mem went back to 32 MB globally, the report role got 512 MB, and the job's concurrency was capped at 5.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • work_mem multiplied by operations, connections and hash_mem_multiplier.
  • statement_timeout set globally kills long migrations and pg_dump; set it per role.
  • lock_timeout on application roles also cancels legitimate row-lock waits in hot-row scenarios; choose the value with that in mind.
  • shared_preload_libraries changes need a restart; plan them with a failover.
  • ALTER SYSTEM on a replica is overwritten if you rebuild it from the primary; keep configuration in the parameter group or infrastructure code.
  • jit = on with jit_above_cost at default causing occasional 50 ms stalls on queries that normally take 2 ms.
  • temp_file_limit unset: one report fills the disk and takes the primary down.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know the twenty settings and why each has its value. They never change a knob globally to fix one query. They keep belts (timeouts) per role and verify them with pg_settings after every deploy. They version the parameter group. They ask, for every setting change: "what is the worst case if 200 connections exercise this at once?"

Common mistakes

  • Global work_mem in the hundreds of MB.
  • Never enabling track_io_timing, log_lock_waits, log_temp_files.
  • Changing random_page_cost on a replica only.
  • Setting timeouts in application code strings instead of role or pool configuration, so that psql sessions and scripts have none.

Interview questions

  1. Why is work_mem dangerous to raise globally, and what is the alternative? Expected: per operation × connections; SET LOCAL per transaction or per role.
  2. Which three timeouts do you set for an application role and why? Expected: statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  3. What does effective_cache_size allocate? Expected: nothing; it is a planner hint.
  4. Which settings require a restart and how do you find out? Expected: pg_settings.context = 'postmaster'.

Practical exercise

Take a 5 million row sort query. Run it with work_mem at 4 MB, 64 MB and 512 MB (via SET LOCAL), capturing Sort Method and timing from EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Then compute the worst-case memory for your service's pool size at each value. Acceptance criteria: a table of the three runs and a written recommendation for global versus per-transaction values with the arithmetic.

18.14 Observing PostgreSQL

18.14.1 The views and extensions a backend engineer must know

Concept

PostgreSQL tells you almost everything about itself through ordinary SQL. There is no agent to install and no proprietary console you need: the statistics collector maintains a set of views (pg_stat_*), the lock manager exposes pg_locks, and two extensions (pg_stat_statements, auto_explain) turn "the database is slow" into "this query, this many times, this much time". Learning eight views is the difference between guessing during an incident and knowing.

Why does it exist?

Because the application's view of the database is a single number: latency. When that number moves, the application cannot tell you whether it is a bad plan, a lock queue, a saturated connection pool, a checkpoint, a vacuum that has stopped working, or a replica falling behind. Each of those has a different fix and some of them have opposite fixes. The statistics views are how you distinguish them, and they cost almost nothing to read.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital. pg_stat_activity is the live ward: who is in a bed right now, what they are doing, and who is waiting for the operating theatre. pg_stat_statements is the year's case history: which procedures consumed the most surgeon-hours in total, not which one was longest once. pg_stat_user_tables is the maintenance log for each room. pg_locks is the theatre booking sheet, showing who holds it and who is queued behind them. During an incident you look at the ward; during planning you look at the case history.

How it works

pg_stat_activity — what is happening right now. One row per backend process. The columns that matter: state (active, idle, idle in transaction, idle in transaction (aborted)), wait_event_type and wait_event (why an active backend is not running), xact_start (when its transaction began, which is what holds the xmin horizon), query_start, backend_xmin, application_name and query.

-- Everything that is not idle, longest-running first
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, now() - query_start AS query_age,
       state, wait_event_type, wait_event, application_name, left(query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' AND state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST;
  pid  | xact_age  | query_age | state               | wait_event_type | wait_event   | application_name | query
-------+-----------+-----------+---------------------+-----------------+--------------+------------------+---------------------------
 21440 | 00:14:02  | 00:14:02  | active              | IO              | DataFileRead | reporting        | SELECT o.id, ... FROM orders
 22107 | 00:11:19  | 00:11:19  | active              | Lock            | relation     | migrations       | ALTER TABLE orders ADD COL
 22300 | 00:11:14  | 00:11:14  | active              | Lock            | relation     | orders-api       | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE
 22488 | 00:04:51  | 00:00:00  | idle in transaction | Client          | ClientRead   | orders-api       | UPDATE inventory SET ...

Read it in four moves. wait_event_type = 'Lock' means blocked by another session, and that is a lock incident. wait_event_type = 'IO' means reading from disk, which is a memory or plan problem. wait_event_type = 'LWLock' with BufferContent or WALWrite means internal contention. state = 'idle in transaction' with a large xact_age is the single most dangerous row in this view: it holds locks and freezes the xmin horizon, which stops vacuum everywhere (18.8).

Finding the blocker is one function call:

SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocked.wait_event, left(blocked.query, 60) AS blocked_query,
       blocker.pid AS blocking_pid, blocker.state, now() - blocker.xact_start AS blocker_xact_age,
       left(blocker.query, 60) AS blocking_query
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN LATERAL unnest(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) AS b(pid) ON true
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocker ON blocker.pid = b.pid
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) > 0;

pg_blocking_pids(pid) returns the pids this backend is waiting for, transitively through the lock queue. Follow the chain to the root and you have the one session to cancel (pg_cancel_backend) or terminate (pg_terminate_backend).

pg_stat_statements — where the time actually goes. Requires shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements' and a restart, then CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements. It normalises queries (constants become $1) and accumulates counters per queryid since the last reset.

SELECT calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms,
       round((100 * total_exec_time / sum(total_exec_time) OVER ())::numeric, 1) AS pct,
       rows / greatest(calls, 1) AS rows_per_call,
       shared_blks_hit, shared_blks_read,
       left(query, 70) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
 calls   | total_ms  | mean_ms | pct  | rows_per_call | shared_blks_hit | shared_blks_read | query
---------+-----------+---------+------+---------------+-----------------+------------------+--------------------------
 4821003 |  1204811  |    0.25 | 31.2 |             1 |      19204118   |            8112  | SELECT * FROM users WHERE i
    1902 |   901255  |  473.85 | 23.4 |         41022 |       4881200   |         1902144  | SELECT o.id, ... GROUP BY
  882014 |   402118  |    0.46 | 10.4 |            12 |       9902441   |             912  | SELECT * FROM order_items W

The lesson of that output is why you sort by total_exec_time and not by mean_exec_time: the top row is a 0.25 ms query, and it is the biggest consumer in the database because it runs 4.8 million times. Sorting by mean finds the slow report; sorting by total finds the thing that is actually eating the server. Do both, and also sort by shared_blks_read to find what is not fitting in shared_buffers.

Reset before a load test or after a fix so the numbers describe the period you care about: SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();. Record the reset time somewhere, because the view has no memory of it and "total time" is meaningless without a window. pg_stat_statements.max (default 5,000) caps the number of tracked statements; when it is exceeded, the least-used entries are evicted and your numbers get holes.

pg_stat_user_tables — per-table health. Sequential scans, dead tuples and vacuum history.

SELECT relname,
       seq_scan, idx_scan,
       n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / greatest(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 1), 1) AS dead_pct,
       n_mod_since_analyze,
       last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_live_tup > 10000
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
LIMIT 15;

A large seq_scan count on a large table is a missing index (or a planner that thinks a scan is cheaper: check statistics). dead_pct above 20 percent on a busy table, or a last_autovacuum that is hours old on a table with millions of dead tuples, means autovacuum is not keeping up or is being blocked (18.8). n_mod_since_analyze climbing into the millions means the planner is working from stale statistics and will start choosing wrong plans.

pg_stat_user_indexes — indexes nobody uses. Every index costs write amplification, WAL and disk.

SELECT s.relname AS table_name, s.indexrelname AS index_name, s.idx_scan,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0 AND NOT i.indisunique AND NOT i.indisprimary
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

Two cautions before you drop anything: the counters are since the last pg_stat_reset() or since the server was rebuilt, so check the age of the statistics; and the counters are per node, so an index unused on the primary may be essential on a read replica.

pg_locks joined to activity — the lock queue. pg_locks shows one row per held or awaited lock, with granted telling you which it is.

SELECT l.locktype, l.relation::regclass AS relation, l.mode, l.granted,
       a.pid, a.state, now() - a.xact_start AS xact_age, left(a.query, 60) AS query
FROM pg_locks l
JOIN pg_stat_activity a ON a.pid = l.pid
WHERE l.relation = 'public.orders'::regclass
ORDER BY l.granted DESC, a.xact_start;

Everything with granted = false is queued. The lock queue is ordered: a pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request blocks every later request, even a plain SELECT that would otherwise be compatible with the current holder. That single fact explains incident (a) in the next section.

pg_stat_replication — how far behind the replicas are. Run on the primary.

SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, sync_state,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), sent_lsn))   AS pending_send,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn))             AS pending_replay,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

Two different lags matter. Bytes (pg_wal_lsn_diff) tells you how much WAL the replica has not applied, which predicts recovery time and disk pressure. Seconds (replay_lag, or on the replica now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()) tells you how stale a read on that replica is, which is what your application cares about when it reads its own writes (Part 28 — Distributed Systems). A replica with 0 bytes pending and 40 seconds of replay_lag is idle, not late; a replica with 8 GB pending is a problem.

pg_stat_database — the whole-database counters.

SELECT datname, numbackends, xact_commit, xact_rollback, deadlocks,
       temp_files, pg_size_pretty(temp_bytes) AS temp_bytes, conflicts,
       round(100.0 * blks_hit / greatest(blks_hit + blks_read, 1), 2) AS cache_hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();

deadlocks should be near zero and any increase is a code problem (20.3). temp_files and temp_bytes growing means queries are spilling work_mem to disk; pair with log_temp_files = 0 to see which ones. conflicts is non-zero only on replicas and counts queries cancelled by recovery conflicts. cache_hit_pct below about 98 percent on an OLTP database usually means the working set does not fit in shared_buffers, though it is a blunt instrument: a single big report can drag it down while every OLTP query is served from memory.

Bloat. Dead tuples that vacuum has reclaimed as free space but not returned to the operating system make tables and indexes bigger than their data, which makes every scan read more pages.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
-- Sampling estimate: cheap enough to run on a large table
SELECT * FROM pgstattuple_approx('orders');
-- table_len | scanned_percent | approx_free_percent | dead_tuple_percent
-- 48 GB     |            4.10 |               61.20 |               3.90
SELECT * FROM pgstatindex('orders_pkey');
-- avg_leaf_density 42.1  -> healthy is 85-90; this index is roughly half air

approx_free_percent above 40 and avg_leaf_density under 60 mean it is time for REINDEX CONCURRENTLY or pg_repack. Never VACUUM FULL a busy table: it takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole rewrite.

auto_explain and log_min_duration_statement. The slow-query log tells you what was slow; auto_explain tells you why, by logging the plan of the actual execution, including the parameters the planner really saw.

shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements,auto_explain'
auto_explain.log_min_duration = '500ms'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on        # real row counts, not estimates
auto_explain.log_buffers = on        # shared hit/read per node
auto_explain.log_timing = off        # cheaper; turn on when you need per-node times
auto_explain.log_nested_statements = on   # plans inside functions and triggers
auto_explain.sample_rate = 0.25      # log a quarter of qualifying statements on a busy server
log_min_duration_statement = 500
log_lock_waits = on
log_temp_files = 0
log_autovacuum_min_duration = 1000
track_io_timing = on

log_analyze = on means the statement is instrumented, which costs a few percent; log_timing = off removes most of that cost while keeping row counts. sample_rate keeps a busy server from writing more log than query results.

First five queries to run when the database is unhealthy

In order, with what each rules out. This is the runbook; put it in a snippet file every engineer has.

flowchart TB
    S["Alert: API p99 up, database suspected"] --> Q1["1. pg_stat_activity: what is not idle?"]
    Q1 -->|"many wait_event_type Lock"| L["Lock incident: find the root blocker"]
    Q1 -->|"many active, wait IO"| IO["Plan or memory problem: check pg_stat_statements"]
    Q1 -->|"hundreds idle"| C["Connection problem: pool or pooler"]
    Q1 -->|"idle in transaction, old xact"| X["Horizon holder: vacuum is stopped"]
    L --> Q2["2. pg_blocking_pids chain to the root"]
    IO --> Q3["3. pg_stat_statements top 10 by total time"]
    C --> Q4["4. count by state and application_name vs max_connections"]
    X --> Q5["5. pg_stat_user_tables dead tuples and last_autovacuum"]
  1. Who is not idle, and why? The pg_stat_activity query above. This single result usually names the category of incident in ten seconds.
  2. Who is blocking whom? The pg_blocking_pids query. Follow to the root; the root is usually one session and often one migration or one report.
  3. What is consuming the server? pg_stat_statements ordered by total_exec_time, and again by mean_exec_time. Compare against yesterday's snapshot if you keep one.
  4. How many connections, in what state? SELECT state, application_name, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC; next to SHOW max_connections. Hundreds of idle connections with low CPU is a pooling problem, not a database problem.
  5. Is maintenance keeping up? pg_stat_user_tables for dead tuples and last_autovacuum, plus SELECT max(age(backend_xmin)) FROM pg_stat_activity; and SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots;.

NestJS example

Expose the five as an internal, authenticated diagnostics endpoint so the on-call does not need a psql session and a bastion host at 02:14:

// src/ops/db-diagnostics.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { InternalOnlyGuard } from './internal-only.guard';

@Controller('internal/db')
@UseGuards(InternalOnlyGuard)              // network policy plus a token; never public
export class DbDiagnosticsController {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly db: DataSource) {}

  @Get('activity')
  activity() {
    return this.db.query(
      `SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
              application_name, left(query, 120) AS query
         FROM pg_stat_activity
        WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' AND state <> 'idle'
        ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST LIMIT 50`);
  }

  @Get('blockers')
  blockers() {
    return this.db.query(
      `SELECT b.pid AS blocked, unnest(pg_blocking_pids(b.pid)) AS blocker,
              left(b.query, 120) AS blocked_query
         FROM pg_stat_activity b
        WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(b.pid)) > 0`);
  }

  @Get('top-queries')
  topQueries() {
    return this.db.query(
      `SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric) AS total_ms,
              round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms, left(query, 120) AS query
         FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 20`);
  }
}

Run it on a small, separate pool (extra: { max: 2 }) with its own role and a short statement_timeout, so diagnostics still work when the main pool is exhausted. A diagnostics endpoint that cannot get a connection during a connection incident is worthless.

Production scenario

A team scrapes six of these queries every 30 seconds into Prometheus with postgres_exporter, and alerts on four things only: pg_stat_activity count in state idle in transaction older than 60 seconds, any backend waiting on a lock for more than 30 seconds, replication lag bytes above 1 GB, and dead-tuple percentage above 25 on the five largest tables. Everything else is a dashboard. Four alerts, each with a runbook link, is a pager that people still answer after six months.

Failure scenario

At 03:20 the on-call is paged for API latency. They open Grafana: database CPU is 18 percent, disk is quiet, and every panel looks fine. The instinct is "not the database". pg_stat_activity shows 340 connections, 331 of them idle, and nine active all waiting on Lock. The database was almost idle because it was blocked: one idle in transaction session from a crashed worker held a row lock on a hot inventory row, and every checkout queued behind it. Dashboards showing resource usage would never have shown this; the view that shows waiting shows it in one query.

18.15 Three incidents from the database

18.15.1 Incident A: the eleven-minute ALTER TABLE

Symptoms. 10:00:12, every read endpoint starts returning 500s. Error rate 100 percent on the orders API within 40 seconds. Database CPU falls to 6 percent. No deploy of application code; a migration job ran as part of the release.

Timeline.

Time Event
09:47:31 A finance report starts: SELECT ... FROM orders JOIN order_items ... GROUP BY .... It takes an ACCESS SHARE lock on orders and will run for 24 minutes. The reporting role has no statement_timeout.
10:00:04 The release's migration runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN fulfilment_channel text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web';. It requests ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on orders, which conflicts with the report's ACCESS SHARE, so it waits.
10:00:05 The next SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 from the API requests ACCESS SHARE. It is compatible with the report, but the queue already contains a pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and PostgreSQL's lock queue is ordered. The SELECT waits behind the ALTER.
10:00:05 – 10:00:35 Every subsequent query touching orders joins the queue. The application's 20 connections per pod are all consumed by waiting queries within 30 seconds.
10:00:45 The pool's connectionTimeoutMillis starts firing. The API returns 500s. Health checks that query orders fail; Kubernetes starts restarting pods, which makes it worse.
10:11:22 The report finishes. The ALTER acquires the lock and completes in 6 ms (PostgreSQL 11+ stores the default in the catalog and does not rewrite the table). The queue drains.
10:11:40 Error rate back to zero.

Investigation queries actually run. The on-call ran the activity query and saw twenty rows with wait_event_type = 'Lock' and one row with application_name = 'migrations' also waiting. Then:

SELECT blocked.pid, blocked.application_name, blocked.wait_event,
       blocker.pid AS blocker_pid, blocker.application_name AS blocker_app,
       now() - blocker.xact_start AS blocker_age, left(blocker.query, 60)
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN LATERAL unnest(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) AS b(pid) ON true
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocker ON blocker.pid = b.pid;

The chain was: 43 API sessions blocked by pid 22107 (migrations), which was blocked by pid 21440 (reporting, age 13 minutes). One SELECT pg_cancel_backend(21440); would have ended the incident in one second. The on-call did exactly that at 10:11 (thirty seconds before the report finished on its own).

sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Report
    participant M as Migration
    participant A as ApiSelect
    participant L as LockManager
    R->>L: ACCESS SHARE on orders (granted 09:47)
    M->>L: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on orders
    L-->>M: queued, conflicts with ACCESS SHARE
    A->>L: ACCESS SHARE on orders
    L-->>A: queued behind ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
    Note over L: Queue is ordered. Compatible does not mean allowed.
    R->>L: commit, release
    L-->>M: granted, ALTER runs in 6 ms
    M->>L: commit, release
    L-->>A: granted, queue drains

Root cause. The lock queue is FIFO, and a queued ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request blocks readers that would otherwise be compatible with the current holder. The DDL itself was cheap; the wait for it was the outage. Nobody had set lock_timeout on the migration role.

Prevention, all of which shipped that week.

-- In every migration, before any DDL:
SET lock_timeout = '3s';        -- fail fast rather than build a queue
SET statement_timeout = '0';    -- the DDL itself may legitimately take time once it starts

Plus: a retry wrapper that catches 55P03 lock_not_available and retries with backoff up to ten times; statement_timeout = '10min' on the reporting role; log_lock_waits = on so the log names the blocker; an alert on any backend waiting on a lock for more than 30 seconds; and a rule that migrations run in a low-traffic window with a pre-check that no transaction older than 60 seconds exists.

18.15.2 Incident B: the forgotten await that bloated a table to 4x

Symptoms. Nothing, for three days. Then on Friday, GET /orders p99 drifts from 40 ms to 900 ms, disk usage on the primary is up 180 GB, and the storage alarm fires at 85 percent.

Timeline.

Time Event
Tue 14:10 A deploy ships a refactor of the inventory sync worker. One code path calls queryRunner.startTransaction() and then calls an async method without await; the function returns, the promise is never resolved into a commit, and the QueryRunner is never released. The connection sits in idle in transaction forever.
Tue 14:10 onward That session's backend_xmin freezes the xmin horizon. Autovacuum runs on orders and order_items every few minutes and removes nothing, because every dead tuple is still potentially visible to that ancient transaction.
Wed – Thu orders grows from 41 million live tuples and 2 percent dead to 41 million live and 39 million dead. The heap goes from 46 GB to 178 GB. The primary key index leaf density falls from 88 to 39. Every index scan reads more pages; the cache hit ratio falls from 99.4 to 96.1 percent.
Fri 09:30 p99 crosses the alert threshold. Disk alarm at 11:05.

Investigation queries actually run.

-- 1. Who is holding the horizon?
SELECT pid, application_name, state, now() - xact_start AS xact_age,
       backend_xmin, age(backend_xmin) AS xmin_age
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' OR backend_xmin IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC NULLS LAST;
-- pid 9184 | inventory-worker | idle in transaction | 2 days 19:24:11 | 894231004 | 41,882,617
-- 2. Confirm vacuum is running but reclaiming nothing
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, autovacuum_count
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname IN ('orders', 'order_items');
-- orders | 41,203,551 | 39,882,110 | 2024-xx-xx 11:02 | 918

The autovacuum log line (visible because log_autovacuum_min_duration = 1000) was the smoking gun:

LOG:  automatic vacuum of table "shop.public.orders": index scans: 0
      pages: 0 removed, 22318112 remain
      tuples: 0 removed, 41203551 remain, 39882110 are dead but not yet removable,
      oldest xmin: 894231004

"Dead but not yet removable" is the phrase to memorise. It means vacuum is working perfectly and is being prevented from doing anything by an old snapshot.

Root cause. A floating promise left a transaction open. The database has no idea the application forgot; from its side, a client has an open transaction and may still read.

Fix. SELECT pg_terminate_backend(9184); then a manual VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) orders; which took 22 minutes and reclaimed the space as free space inside the files (disk usage did not drop). pg_repack in the Sunday window returned 130 GB to the filesystem without an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration.

Prevention.

ALTER ROLE orders_api SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
ALTER ROLE inventory_worker SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';

Plus @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises as an error in CI, a rule that transactions go through dataSource.transaction(async (em) => ...) rather than manual QueryRunner lifecycles, and an alert on max(age(backend_xmin)) > 50_000_000 and on any session idle in transaction for more than two minutes. That last alert would have paged on Tuesday at 14:12 instead of Friday at 09:30.

18.15.3 Incident C: the connection storm after a deploy

Symptoms. 16:42, immediately after a routine deploy. The API returns 500s on roughly a third of requests. The error in the logs is FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections and, in the pool, Connection terminated due to connection timeout. Database CPU is 14 percent and disk is idle. The database is not busy; it is full.

Timeline.

Time Event
16:41:50 Rolling deploy starts. The Deployment has 40 replicas and maxSurge: 50%, so up to 60 pods exist at once.
16:41:55 Each pod's TypeORM pool is configured max: 20. New pods open connections eagerly on startup because the readiness probe runs a query and the entity metadata load opens several connections. Demand goes from 800 to 1,200 connections.
16:42:03 max_connections is 500 (a db.r6g.2xlarge default with superuser_reserved_connections = 3). Connection attempt 498 fails.
16:42:03 – 16:47 New pods cannot reach readiness (their probe query cannot get a connection), so Kubernetes never terminates old pods, so the surge never drains. The deploy is stuck at 60 pods, all fighting for 500 slots. Meanwhile old pods that lost connections retry immediately, adding load.
16:47:30 On-call scales the Deployment to 20 replicas manually. Connections drop to 400, the pool recovers, the deploy is rolled back.

Investigation queries actually run.

SELECT count(*) AS total,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle') AS idle,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle in transaction') AS idle_in_txn
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';
-- total 497 | active 11 | idle 486 | idle_in_txn 0

SELECT application_name, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
-- orders-api 441 | worker 44 | reporting 8 | psql 1
SHOW max_connections;   -- 500

Eleven active connections out of 497. The database was doing 2 percent of its capacity while the application could not talk to it at all. That contrast (active tiny, total at the ceiling, CPU low) is the signature of a connection incident and nothing else looks like it.

Root cause. Nobody had multiplied. pods × pool.max was 40 × 20 = 800 against a max_connections of 500, and the deploy's surge made it 1,200. It had worked for months because pods never all opened their full pool at once; the deploy made them do exactly that. Each PostgreSQL connection is a process with about 5–10 MB of private memory, so raising max_connections to 1,200 was not the answer either (18.2).

Fix and prevention. PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode between the application and the database (18.3): 1,200 client connections map onto a server pool of 60. Application pool.max dropped from 20 to 5, because with a pooler the pod's pool only needs to cover its own concurrency. maxSurge reduced to 25 percent. An alert at 70 percent of max_connections. And a documented arithmetic check in the deployment template: replicas × maxSurge × pool.max must be under the pooler's client limit, and the pooler's server pool must be under max_connections minus reserved slots.

18.16 Edge cases and failure modes

  • Transaction id wraparound approaching. PostgreSQL's transaction ids are 32-bit and wrap. If age(datfrozenxid) approaches 2 billion the server starts screaming in the log and eventually refuses to accept new write transactions until you vacuum in single-user mode. It is caused by autovacuum being unable to freeze: a long-lived prepared transaction, an abandoned replication slot, or a table whose autovacuum keeps being cancelled. Watch it: SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC; and alert above 500 million. Fix before it is urgent, because the emergency fix is downtime.

  • A replication slot filling the disk. A physical or logical slot guarantees the primary keeps WAL until the consumer has it. If the consumer is gone (a decommissioned replica, a stopped Debezium connector), WAL accumulates forever and fills pg_wal until the primary shuts down. Watch SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots; and set max_slot_wal_keep_size (PG13+) so PostgreSQL invalidates a slot rather than dying with it.

  • Checkpoint I/O storms. A checkpoint that is not spread out writes gigabytes of dirty buffers in a burst, and latency shows a comb pattern every checkpoint_timeout. log_checkpoints = on plus pg_stat_bgwriter.checkpoints_req (requested, not timed) tells you max_wal_size is too small and checkpoints are being forced by WAL volume rather than by time.

  • TOAST bloat. Large text, jsonb and bytea values live in a side table. Updating a row's JSONB column rewrites the TOAST chunks, and the TOAST table bloats independently of the main table. pg_stat_user_tables does not show it; check pg_total_relation_size against pg_relation_size, and vacuum the TOAST relation.

  • Plan flips after ANALYZE. New statistics can change a good nested loop into a bad hash join or vice versa, instantly, with no deploy. If p99 jumps at the exact moment last_autoanalyze changed, that is your cause. Fix with better statistics (ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS 500, extended statistics for correlated columns) rather than by disabling plan types.

  • Autovacuum starvation on a huge table. Default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.2 means a 500-million-row table waits for 100 million dead tuples before vacuum starts, and then a single worker crawls it under the cost limit while three other workers are busy. Set per-table: ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 4000);.

  • Lock queue pile-ups behind one DDL statement. Incident A. Any ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request (most ALTER TABLE forms, REINDEX without CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM FULL, TRUNCATE) that has to wait blocks everything behind it. lock_timeout on every migration, always.

  • Temp file explosions from an under-sized work_mem. A report that spills 300 GB of temp files fills the disk and takes the primary down for everyone. temp_file_limit per role is the seatbelt; log_temp_files = 0 is the warning light.

  • A long analytics query on a replica cancelled by conflict. ERROR: canceling statement due to conflict with recovery. The primary vacuumed rows the replica's query still needed. Options: hot_standby_feedback = on (which moves the problem to the primary as bloat), max_standby_streaming_delay (which moves it to replication lag), or accept the cancellation and retry. There is no free choice; pick which cost you prefer and write it down.

  • Prepared-statement generic plans going bad. After five executions, PostgreSQL may switch a prepared statement to a generic plan built without the actual parameters. For a skewed column (status = 'pending' matching 0.1 percent, status = 'shipped' matching 80 percent) the generic plan is wrong for one of them and latency doubles for a subset of traffic with no code change. Diagnose by comparing EXPLAIN with and without parameters; control with plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan on that role or session.

  • Statistics views resetting silently. A server restart or a pg_stat_reset() zeroes the counters. "This index has zero scans" means nothing if the statistics are two hours old. Always check stats_reset in pg_stat_database.

  • pg_stat_statements eviction. With pg_stat_statements.max too low on a system that generates many distinct query shapes (dynamic SQL, unparameterised queries from a reporting tool), entries are evicted and the top-N list is incomplete. Unparameterised queries also explode the table because each constant creates a new entry.

  • Observability that needs a connection during a connection incident. The exporter, the diagnostics endpoint and the on-call's psql session all need a slot. Reserve them: superuser_reserved_connections, a dedicated monitoring role with its own small pool, and a bastion path that does not go through the application's pooler.

Senior Checklist — Part 18

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can draw PostgreSQL's process architecture and name what the postmaster, the backends, the WAL writer, the background writer, the checkpointer and the autovacuum launcher each do
  • I can compute pods × pool.max against max_connections and say when a connection pooler becomes mandatory
  • I know the difference between session, transaction and statement pooling in PgBouncer, and which application features break in each
  • I can explain the lifecycle of a query from parse to plan to execute, and where the plan cache and prepared statements fit
  • I can size shared_buffers and effective_cache_size and explain why they are not the same kind of setting
  • I can explain WAL, full-page writes and why max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout control latency spikes
  • I can read log_checkpoints output and tell a timed checkpoint from a requested one
  • I can explain MVCC, xmin/xmax, tuple visibility and why an old snapshot stops vacuum everywhere
  • I recognise "dead but not yet removable" in an autovacuum log line and know the three things that cause it
  • I can tune autovacuum per table and explain scale factor, threshold, cost limit and cost delay
  • I know when ANALYZE matters, what extended statistics fix, and how a plan can flip with no deploy
  • I can name PostgreSQL's table-level lock modes and say which pairs conflict
  • I know that a queued ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocks compatible readers behind it, and I set lock_timeout in every migration
  • I can read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and identify a bad plan, a bad estimate and a spill to disk
  • I know the twenty configuration settings that matter and why each has its value in my environment
  • I can run the five diagnostic queries from memory when the database is unhealthy
  • I use pg_stat_statements sorted by total time, not just mean time, and I record when I last reset it
  • I can find the root blocker with pg_blocking_pids and decide between cancel and terminate
  • I monitor replication lag in both bytes and seconds and know which one my application cares about
  • I watch age(datfrozenxid), replication slot retention and dead tuple percentage before they become incidents

Part 18 — Key Takeaways

  • PostgreSQL is a process per connection. Connections are memory and context switches, not free handles; pods × pool.max is arithmetic you must do before the deploy, not after.
  • A busy database and a blocked database look completely different in pg_stat_activity and identical in a CPU graph. Always look at what backends are waiting for.
  • The lock queue is ordered. One ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request waiting behind a long report blocks every reader behind it, which is how a 6 ms ALTER TABLE becomes an eleven-minute outage.
  • SET lock_timeout in every migration. Failing fast and retrying is strictly better than building a queue you cannot see.
  • idle in transaction is the most expensive state in the database: it holds locks and freezes the xmin horizon, which stops vacuum on every table.
  • "Dead but not yet removable" means vacuum is working and something older is preventing it. Find the old snapshot, the abandoned slot or the prepared transaction.
  • MVCC makes readers and writers not block each other, and the price is dead tuples, vacuum, bloat and wraparound. That price is paid by operations, not by the query.
  • Sort pg_stat_statements by total time to find what is eating the server, and by mean time to find what is annoying a user. They are usually different queries.
  • Replication lag has two units: bytes predict recovery and disk, seconds predict staleness. Alert on both.
  • Plans change without deploys. ANALYZE, parameter skew and generic plans move latency, so latency alerts need plan evidence (auto_explain) attached.
  • Statistics views reset on restart. Never drop an index or draw a conclusion without checking how old the counters are.
