  • Configure the safety belts per role: statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, temp_file_limit. They are the difference between a bad query and an outage.
  • Four alerts with runbooks beat forty dashboards. Old transactions, lock waits, replication lag and dead tuples cover most of what actually pages you.
  • Your diagnostics must work when the database is full. Reserve connections and a separate pool for monitoring and for the on-call.

Part 19 — Database Indexing

Part 18 taught you how PostgreSQL stores and protects your data: pages, buffers, WAL, MVCC, VACUUM, statistics, locks, and the planner. This part is about the one structure you will add, remove, argue about and get paged for more than any other: the index.

Indexing is where a backend engineer's decisions become visible in milliseconds. The same query on the same 200-million-row table can take 2.3 seconds or 4 milliseconds, and the only difference is whether the right index exists. It is also where careless engineers do the most quiet damage, because an index that nobody queries still costs you write latency, WAL volume, vacuum time, memory, disk and backup size on every single insert, forever.

So this part has two halves that must be held together. The first is how to make a query fast: how a B-tree actually works, how to read a plan, how to build composite, partial, covering, expression, GIN, GiST and BRIN indexes. The second is how to not make everything else slow: cardinality, write amplification, bloat, and the discipline of finding and dropping indexes nobody uses.

Everything here uses the running e-commerce schema from Part 18, extended with the tables this part needs, at volumes big enough that the wrong answer actually hurts.

-- Extra tables and columns used across Part 19.
-- users, products, orders, order_items, payments, inventory are as defined in Part 18.

CREATE TABLE categories (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id   bigint REFERENCES categories(id),
  slug        text NOT NULL,
  name        text NOT NULL
);

ALTER TABLE products
  ADD COLUMN category_id  bigint REFERENCES categories(id),
  ADD COLUMN is_active    boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  ADD COLUMN created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  ADD COLUMN search_tsv   tsvector;

ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD COLUMN shipping_country char(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'DE',
  ADD COLUMN currency         char(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR',
  ADD COLUMN tenant_id        bigint  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;

CREATE TABLE reviews (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  user_id     bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  rating      smallint NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  body        text NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at  timestamptz
);

CREATE TABLE notifications (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  kind        text NOT NULL,             -- ORDER_SHIPPED, PRICE_DROP, REVIEW_REPLY
  status      text NOT NULL,             -- PENDING, SENT, FAILED
  payload     jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at     timestamptz
);

The volumes, because indexing advice without volumes is astrology:

Table Rows Heap size Heap pages Rows per page
users 8,000,000 1.1 GB 141,177 ~57
products 400,000 420 MB 52,000 ~8 (wide, TOASTed)
categories 1,240 128 KB 16 ~78
orders 200,000,000 30 GB 3,921,033 ~51
order_items 900,000,000 67 GB 8,823,530 ~102
payments 212,000,000 26 GB 3,411,000 ~62
inventory 400,000 22 MB 2,703 ~148
reviews 41,000,000 9.8 GB 1,281,000 ~32
notifications 1,200,000,000 210 GB 27,500,000 ~44

Read those numbers once more. orders is 3.9 million pages. A sequential scan of it reads 30 GB. At the ~1.2 GB/s a good NVMe volume sustains with PostgreSQL's readahead, that is roughly 25 seconds of pure I/O even when nothing else is happening. Your API has a 200 ms budget. That gap is what indexes are for.

19.1 How an index actually works

19.1.1 A second, ordered structure that points into an unordered heap

Concept

An index is a separate data structure, stored in its own file, that holds a sorted copy of one or more columns plus a pointer to where the full row lives. It is not part of the table. It is not "the table sorted". Dropping it loses no data.

The pointer is a ctid: a pair (block number, line pointer) that says "page 41022, slot 17 of the orders heap file". The heap is the table's own file, and it is fundamentally unordered: PostgreSQL puts a new row wherever there is free space, which after a few months of updates and vacuums is essentially anywhere. There is no clustered index in PostgreSQL. The primary key is just another B-tree that happens to be unique, sitting beside the heap exactly like every other index.

So a lookup by index is always at least two steps: walk the index to find the ctid, then read the heap page that ctid points to. That second step is the expensive one, because it is a random read.

Why does it exist?

Without an index there is exactly one way to answer WHERE id = 918273645: read every page of the table and check every row. That is a sequential scan, and on orders it is 3.9 million page reads for one row. An index turns that into 4 page reads for the index descent plus 1 page read for the heap: 5 pages instead of 3,921,033. A factor of 780,000.

The price is that the index is a second copy of that data which must be kept correct. Every INSERT adds an entry to every index on the table. Every UPDATE that changes an indexed column, or that cannot fit the new row version on the same page, adds an entry to every index. Every index consumes buffer cache, WAL bytes, vacuum time and backup space. An index is a read optimisation paid for with a write tax. That sentence is the whole part in one line.

Mental model

Imagine a warehouse where parcels are put on whichever shelf has room. That is the heap. Beside the door hangs a ring binder, sorted by tracking number, and each page says "tracking 8829 -> aisle 12, shelf 4". That is the index. The binder is a second thing you must maintain: every parcel that arrives needs a line written into the binder, in the right sorted position. If you keep twelve binders (by tracking number, by customer, by postcode, by courier, by weight, by date...), every single parcel that arrives means twelve write operations before the receiving clerk can accept the next one. The picking is fast. The receiving desk is now the bottleneck.

How it works

flowchart TB
  subgraph IndexFile
    i1["idx_orders_user_id  sorted by user_id"]
    e1["user_id=41  ->  ctid (912,3)"]
    e2["user_id=41  ->  ctid (41022,17)"]
    e3["user_id=42  ->  ctid (7,1)"]
    i1 --> e1
    i1 --> e2
    i1 --> e3
  end
  subgraph HeapFile
    p1["page 7"]
    p2["page 912"]
    p3["page 41022"]
  end
  e1 -->|"random read"| p2
  e2 -->|"random read"| p3
  e3 -->|"random read"| p1
  1. CREATE INDEX scans the table, extracts (key, ctid) for every live row, sorts them (using maintenance_work_mem, spilling to temp files when it does not fit), and builds the tree bottom-up.
  2. On INSERT, the executor writes the heap tuple, then inserts one entry into each index on the table. Each of those is a tree descent plus a leaf-page write plus WAL for that write.
  3. On UPDATE, MVCC writes a new row version (Parts 7 and 181.7). If the new version lands on the same page and no indexed column changed, PostgreSQL uses a HOT update (heap-only tuple): the new version is chained from the old one and no index entry is written at all. If any indexed column changed, or the page is full, HOT is impossible and every index gets a new entry.
  4. On DELETE, nothing is removed from the index. The heap tuple is marked dead; VACUUM later removes both the dead tuple and its index entries.
  5. On SELECT, the executor descends the index, gets ctids, and fetches heap pages to check MVCC visibility, because the index does not know whether a row version is visible to your snapshot. That is why an index scan still touches the heap (unless the visibility map says the page is all-visible, which is the index-only scan of 19.9).

The HOT rule in step 3 is the single most under-appreciated fact in this part: adding an index to a frequently updated column can silently disable HOT updates for the whole table, turning cheap in-page updates into full index maintenance plus faster bloat. We will measure it in 19.17.

Practical example

orders has two indexes: the primary key on id, and idx_orders_user_id. Product asks for filtering by status, by country, by currency, by payment provider, by created date, by updated date, by total, by tenant, by shipping method and by coupon code. Ten more single-column indexes get added over two quarters, one ticket at a time, each one reviewed alone and each one "obviously fine". Checkout write latency goes from 6 ms to 21 ms and nobody can point at the change that did it, because no single change did it.

PostgreSQL example

The measurement everyone should run once, on their own hardware, so the number stops being abstract. Load 1,000,000 rows into a copy of orders with 2 indexes, then with 12.

-- Baseline: primary key + one FK index
CREATE TABLE orders_2idx (LIKE orders INCLUDING DEFAULTS);
ALTER TABLE orders_2idx ADD PRIMARY KEY (id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_2idx (user_id);

-- Same table, ten more single-column indexes (the "index everything" school)
CREATE TABLE orders_12idx (LIKE orders INCLUDING DEFAULTS);
ALTER TABLE orders_12idx ADD PRIMARY KEY (id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (user_id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (status);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (created_at);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (updated_at);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (total_cents);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (shipping_country);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (currency);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (tenant_id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (status, created_at);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (user_id, status);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_12idx (tenant_id, created_at);

-- Measure WAL as well as time: pg_current_wal_lsn() before and after
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before_lsn \gset
INSERT INTO orders_2idx (user_id, status, total_cents, created_at, updated_at)
SELECT (random()*8000000)::bigint, 'PENDING', (random()*20000)::int, now(), now()
FROM generate_series(1, 1000000);
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - :'before_lsn') AS wal_written;

Measured on an 8 vCPU / 32 GB instance with NVMe storage, shared_buffers = 8GB, synchronous_commit = on:

2 indexes 12 indexes Factor
Time for 1,000,000 inserts 38.4 s 246.1 s 6.4x
Per-row insert cost 38 us 246 us 6.4x
WAL written 781 MB 4,612 MB 5.9x
Total index bytes added 68 MB 611 MB 9.0x
Autovacuum time for one pass 11 s 96 s 8.7x

Single-row inserts through the API show the same shape at a smaller scale: p50 checkout write latency 2.1 ms with 2 indexes, 7.9 ms with 12. That is a real p99 story: 12 indexes means 12 tree descents, and any one of them can miss the buffer cache and turn into a disk read.

The write tax also shows up in a place people forget: replication. 5.9 times the WAL is 5.9 times the bytes streamed to every replica and 5.9 times the archive bill. A team that adds indexes freely eventually has a replication-lag problem they blame on the network.

NestJS example

The only sane way to keep this in check is to make index changes visible in review the same way a schema change is. Put every index in a migration, never in synchronize: true, and put the justification in the file.

// 1712001200000-AddOrdersUserCreatedIndex.ts
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

/**
 * Query: GET /orders?userId=:id  (p99 was 2.3 s, 41 req/s)
 * Plan before: Bitmap Heap Scan on orders, 380k rows removed by filter.
 * Expected index size: ~6.1 GB. Write cost measured at +0.4 ms per order insert.
 * Replaces: idx_orders_user_id (dropped in the next migration after a 7-day soak).
 */
export class AddOrdersUserCreatedIndex1712001200000 implements MigrationInterface {
  public async up(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(
      `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC)`,
    );
  }

  public async down(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_user_created`);
  }
}

That comment block is not decoration. It is what lets the engineer in eighteen months decide whether the index can be dropped. An index with no recorded reason never gets deleted, because nobody dares.

Production scenario

A 200 million row orders table with 6 indexes occupies 30 GB of heap and 19 GB of indexes. shared_buffers is 8 GB. The hot working set (recent orders plus their index pages) is about 6 GB, so cache hit ratio sits at 99.3 percent. Adding three more indexes pushes the index total to 31 GB; the hot index pages now compete with the heap for the same 8 GB, hit ratio drops to 97.1 percent, and read latency on the unrelated product lookup endpoint goes up, because it lost its buffer pages. Indexes are not free even for the queries they do not serve.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged for pg_wal disk usage at 91 percent. A batch job is backfilling orders.tenant_id for 200 million rows. The column has an index. Every updated row is a non-HOT update: a new heap version plus 7 index entries plus full-page images for every page touched after each checkpoint. WAL production goes from 40 MB/s to 310 MB/s, the archiver falls behind, pg_wal fills, and PostgreSQL is minutes away from refusing writes. The fix at 02:40 is to drop the index on tenant_id, run the backfill in 50,000-row batches with a pause, and rebuild the index at the end. Total WAL for the rebuilt version: 1/9th of the original approach.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • HOT updates disabled by indexing a hot column; heap bloat and index bloat both accelerate.
  • Index on a column that is NULL for 99 percent of rows: B-tree stores NULLs, so the index is full size for almost no benefit. Use a partial index (19.6).
  • ctid is not stable. Never store it. VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and even a plain update change it.
  • Index entries are not removed on DELETE, only by VACUUM. A mass delete leaves an index the same size until vacuum plus, often, a REINDEX.
  • Toasted values are not indexed inline. An index on a large text column indexes the value, and B-tree refuses entries larger than about 2,700 bytes (a third of a page): ERROR: index row size 3184 exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704. Index a hash or an expression instead.
  • Index bloat is invisible in pg_stat_user_tables. You need pgstattuple or size trending.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat every index as a permanent operational liability with a named owner and a recorded query. Before approving one they ask: which query, at what rate, what is the current plan, what is the estimated size, what does it do to insert latency, and what index does it replace. They know that the correct number of indexes on a hot write table is small and deliberate, and that the correct number on a read-only reporting table can be large. They budget indexes per table, not per query.

Common mistakes

  • Adding an index for every WHERE clause a developer writes.
  • Believing the primary key "orders the table". It does not; PostgreSQL has no clustered index.
  • Measuring the read improvement and never measuring the write cost.
  • Adding an index in production with plain CREATE INDEX on a 200M row table during business hours (19.14).

Interview questions

  1. What does a PostgreSQL index physically contain, and why does an index scan still read the heap? Expected: sorted keys plus ctids; visibility information lives only in the heap, so MVCC checks force a heap fetch unless the visibility map allows an index-only scan.
  2. What is a HOT update and what disables it? Expected: new version on the same page with no index entries; disabled when an indexed column changes or the page has no room. Follow-up: how does fillfactor help?
  3. Why does adding an index slow down inserts by more than "a bit"? Expected: a tree descent, a leaf write, WAL, possible page split, possible buffer miss, per index.
  4. If I delete 90 percent of a table, does the index shrink? Expected: no; VACUUM frees space inside the index but rarely returns it; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY does.

Practical exercise

Create the two tables above, insert 1,000,000 rows into each, and record wall time, WAL bytes (pg_current_wal_lsn() delta), index sizes and one autovacuum pass duration. Then repeat with UPDATE ... SET status = 'PAID' on 200,000 rows in each table and compare n_tup_hot_upd from pg_stat_user_tables. Acceptance criteria: a table of six measurements and a paragraph explaining why the HOT ratio differs.

19.2 The B-tree

19.2.1 Structure, fan-out, and the leftmost-prefix rule

Concept

When you write CREATE INDEX ... ON t (col) with no USING clause, PostgreSQL builds a B-tree: a balanced, sorted tree of 8 KB pages. It is the default because it supports the operators you use 95 percent of the time (=, <, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, LIKE 'prefix%'), it returns rows in sorted order for free, and it stays balanced no matter what order you insert keys in.

Strictly it is a B+tree: all the actual keys live in the leaf pages, the leaves are linked left-to-right in a doubly linked list, and the internal pages hold only separator keys that route the search downward.

Why does it exist?

A sorted array would give you binary search but every insert would move half the array. A binary search tree gives cheap inserts but is one key per node, so a billion rows means 30 levels and 30 random page reads. The B-tree is the answer to a hardware fact: reading 8 KB costs almost the same as reading 8 bytes, because storage works in blocks. So you make the node as wide as a block. Hundreds of keys per node means the tree is 3 or 4 levels deep for any table you will ever have, and a lookup is 3 or 4 page reads.

Mental model

Imagine a very fat phone book with tabs. The first tab page says "A-F on shelf 1, G-M on shelf 2, N-S on shelf 3, T-Z on shelf 4". Shelf 3's own tab page splits N-S into 250 finer ranges. One more level and you are on the page with the actual names, printed in order, with a note at the bottom saying "continued on the next page". Four lookups and you have your entry, whether the book holds a thousand names or a billion. That is the whole trick: the depth grows logarithmically with a base of a few hundred, so it barely grows at all.

How it works

flowchart TB
  root["Root page  1 page  ~250 separator keys"]
  i1["Internal page  keys 1..40,000"]
  i2["Internal page  keys 40,001..80,000"]
  i3["Internal page  keys 80,001..120,000"]
  l1["Leaf  key,ctid ... 250 entries"]
  l2["Leaf  key,ctid ... 250 entries"]
  l3["Leaf  key,ctid ... 250 entries"]
  l4["Leaf  key,ctid ... 250 entries"]
  root --> i1
  root --> i2
  root --> i3
  i1 --> l1
  i1 --> l2
  i2 --> l3
  i2 --> l4
  l1 -->|"right link"| l2
  l2 -->|"right link"| l3
  l3 -->|"right link"| l4
  l1 -.->|"ctid"| heap["orders heap pages"]
  l3 -.->|"ctid"| heap

Fan-out arithmetic. An 8,192-byte page has a 24-byte page header, a 16-byte B-tree special area, and a line pointer array of 4 bytes per entry. An index entry for a bigint is an 8-byte IndexTupleData header plus 8 bytes of key: 16 bytes, plus its 4-byte line pointer, so 20 bytes per entry. That is 8152 / 20 = 407 entries per page in theory. Pages are not packed full: the default fillfactor for B-tree leaves is 90, and splits leave pages half to 90 percent full, so a realistic steady state is 250 to 350 entries per page for a bigint key, and 100 to 200 for a 30-byte text key.

Take 250 as a working number and count the levels:

Rows Leaf pages Levels Page reads per lookup
1,000 4 1 (root is the leaf) 1
1,000,000 4,000 3 3
200,000,000 800,000 4 4
1,000,000,000 4,000,000 4 4
62,500,000,000 250,000,000 5 5

Four page reads for a billion rows. And in practice fewer, because the root and the internal level are read on every single query and therefore live permanently in shared_buffers. On a busy table the real cost of a unique lookup is one or two actual reads plus one heap read.

The search itself:

  1. Read the root page. Binary search its separator keys to find which child covers your key. One page read.
  2. Repeat down each internal level. One page read per level.
  3. Land on a leaf. Binary search inside the page for the first matching key.
  4. For an equality on a unique key, you are done: take the ctid, read the heap page, check MVCC visibility, return the row.
  5. For a range or a non-unique key, walk right along the leaf level using the right links, emitting ctids until the key stops matching. This is why range scans are cheap: after the descent, every additional 250 rows costs one sequential leaf page read.

Insertion and page splits. An insert descends to the correct leaf and writes the entry in sorted position. If the leaf is full, it splits: roughly half the entries move to a new page, and a separator key is inserted into the parent, which may split in turn, which may eventually split the root and add a level. A split writes two leaf pages plus a parent page plus WAL for all of them. Splits are why insert latency has a long tail: 999 inserts cost 40 us and the thousandth costs 900 us. For monotonically increasing keys (bigserial, created_at) PostgreSQL detects the rightmost-page case and does a cheaper 90/10 split instead of 50/50, which keeps sequential-key indexes compact.

The leftmost-prefix rule. A multi-column index (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then by b within equal a, then by c within equal (a, b). Exactly like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name, then middle name. So the index can seek on:

  • a = ?
  • a = ? AND b = ?
  • a = ? AND b = ? AND c = ?
  • a = ? AND b > ?
  • a > ?

and it cannot seek on b = ? alone, or c = ? alone, or b = ? AND c = ?. You cannot find everyone named "Maria" in a phone book sorted by surname without reading the whole book. PostgreSQL will still sometimes use the index for those cases with a full index scan (reading every leaf page and filtering), which is faster than a heap scan only when the index is much narrower than the table. That is not a seek and it does not scale.

Sorted output for free. Because leaves are in key order and linked, a B-tree scan produces rows already sorted. If your query says ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 and an index provides that order, the planner emits an Index Scan Backward and stops after 20 rows. No Sort node, no reading the other 199,999,980 rows. This is the single biggest reason composite indexes matter, and 19.5 is entirely about it.

ASC/DESC and NULLS FIRST/LAST. A B-tree can be scanned in either direction, so (created_at) serves both ORDER BY created_at and ORDER BY created_at DESC. Direction only matters for multi-column sorts with mixed directions. ORDER BY user_id ASC, created_at DESC cannot be served in one direction by (user_id, created_at), because reading that index backwards gives user_id DESC, created_at DESC. You need (user_id ASC, created_at DESC) explicitly. Similarly, PostgreSQL's default is NULLS LAST for ASC and NULLS FIRST for DESC; if your query says ORDER BY sent_at DESC NULLS LAST, an index declared (sent_at DESC) does not match and you get a sort. Declare the index exactly as the query orders: CREATE INDEX ... ON notifications (sent_at DESC NULLS LAST).

What CREATE INDEX actually does. It takes a SHARE lock (blocking writes but not reads), scans the heap, extracts (key, ctid) for every live tuple, sorts them with maintenance_work_mem (spilling to pgsql_tmp if needed), writes the leaf pages sequentially in sorted order at fillfactor (90 by default), builds the internal levels bottom-up, then fsyncs and updates the catalog. Bottom-up building is why a freshly built index is compact and fast, and why REINDEX on a bloated index can halve its size.

Practical example

orders_pkey on 200 million bigint ids. pg_relation_size('orders_pkey') reports 4,290,547,712 bytes: 4.3 GB, 523,700 pages, 4 levels. A lookup by id reads the root (cached), one internal page (cached), one leaf page (usually a read), and one heap page (a read). EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows Buffers: shared hit=3 read=1 and actual time=0.041..0.042. Forty microseconds. Compare with the 25 seconds of the sequential scan.

PostgreSQL example

Inspect the tree yourself with the pageinspect extension. This is worth doing once so the structure stops being a metaphor.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;

SELECT level, type, live_items, dead_items, avg_item_size, page_size, free_size
FROM bt_multi_page_stats('orders_pkey', 1, 5);
 level | type | live_items | dead_items | avg_item_size | page_size | free_size
-------+------+------------+------------+---------------+-----------+-----------
     3 | r    |          3 |          0 |            15 |      8192 |      8104
     2 | i    |        286 |          0 |            15 |      8192 |      3452
     1 | i    |        291 |          0 |            15 |      8192 |      3140
     0 | l    |        367 |          0 |            16 |      8192 |      1216
     0 | l    |        367 |          0 |            16 |      8192 |      1216

Level 3 is the root with 3 children, level 0 are the leaves with 367 entries each. 3 x 286 x 291 x 367 = 91,700,000... which is in the right order of magnitude for 200 million once you account for the root actually having more children than this sample page. The high-level summary:

SELECT * FROM bt_index_check('orders_pkey');   -- amcheck: verifies structural integrity
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders_pkey')) AS pkey_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders'))      AS heap_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('orders'))       AS all_indexes;
 pkey_size | heap_size | all_indexes
-----------+-----------+-------------
 4290 MB   | 30 GB     | 19 GB

And the two plans that show the range-scan property. First, an equality:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 148392017;
Index Scan using orders_pkey on orders  (cost=0.57..8.59 rows=1 width=61)
                                        (actual time=0.038..0.039 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (id = 148392017)
  Buffers: shared hit=4 read=1
Planning Time: 0.094 ms
Execution Time: 0.061 ms

Then a range, showing that after the descent the cost is linear in rows returned, not in table size:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id BETWEEN 148392017 AND 148394017;
Index Only Scan using orders_pkey on orders  (cost=0.57..77.12 rows=2013 width=8)
                                             (actual time=0.031..0.372 rows=2001 loops=1)
  Index Cond: ((id >= 148392017) AND (id <= 148394017))
  Heap Fetches: 0
  Buffers: shared hit=4 read=7
Planning Time: 0.088 ms
Execution Time: 0.487 ms

Eleven buffers for 2,001 rows: 4 for the descent, 7 leaf pages walked left to right. That is the linked leaf list doing its job.

Finally, the leftmost-prefix rule, proven. With only CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at):

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-02';
Finalize Aggregate  (cost=2891044.10..2891044.11 rows=1 width=8)
                    (actual time=9821.442..9827.310 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Gather  (cost=2891043.88..2891044.09 rows=2 width=8) ...
        ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..2890043.88 rows=170411 width=0)
                                         (actual time=1.204..9788.551 rows=136894 loops=3)
              Filter: ((created_at >= '2026-09-01 00:00:00+00') AND (created_at < '2026-09-02 00:00:00+00'))
              Rows Removed by Filter: 66529773
              Buffers: shared hit=48211 read=3872822
Planning Time: 0.211 ms
Execution Time: 9827.402 ms

The (status, created_at) index exists and is completely useless here, because created_at is the second column and the query has no predicate on status. Nine point eight seconds and 3.87 million page reads. Add (created_at) and the same query is a bitmap scan in 210 ms. Column order is not a detail.

TypeORM example

Declare direction and nulls ordering on the entity so the index matches the query you actually write:

import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, Index } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('notifications')
// Matches: WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50
@Index('idx_notifications_user_created', ['userId', 'createdAt'])
export class Notification {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn({ type: 'bigint' })
  id!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'user_id', type: 'bigint' })
  userId!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  status!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz' })
  createdAt!: Date;
}

TypeORM's @Index decorator cannot express DESC or NULLS LAST. When you need them, and for a composite ordered index you usually do, write the DDL in a migration with queryRunner.query (19.22 shows the full pattern) and keep the decorator off so TypeORM never tries to recreate it differently.

Sequelize example

Notification.init(
  {
    id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, primaryKey: true, autoIncrement: true },
    userId: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, field: 'user_id', allowNull: false },
    status: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false },
    createdAt: { type: DataTypes.DATE, field: 'created_at', allowNull: false },
  },
  {
    sequelize,
    tableName: 'notifications',
    indexes: [
      {
        name: 'idx_notifications_user_created',
        fields: ['user_id', { name: 'created_at', order: 'DESC' }],
      },
    ],
  },
);

Sequelize's fields array does accept { name, order }, so DESC is expressible here. NULLS LAST still needs raw SQL.

Production scenario

The notifications table has 1.2 billion rows and a (user_id, created_at DESC) index of 41 GB. The endpoint GET /notifications?limit=50 runs 900 times a second at p99 of 3 ms. The index descent is 4 pages, all cached, and the leaf walk reads 1 page for 50 rows. Cost does not grow with the table; it grows with the number of rows the user asks for. That property, cost proportional to the answer rather than the data, is what you are buying.

Failure scenario

A team adds ORDER BY created_at DESC NULLS LAST to that endpoint to make a UI edge case tidy. The index is (user_id, created_at DESC), which is implicitly NULLS FIRST. The plan changes from Index Scan Backward ... Limit to Sort over all of one user's 41,000 notifications. p99 goes from 3 ms to 480 ms for heavy users. created_at is NOT NULL, so the clause was semantically a no-op; the planner still could not use the index because index ordering is a structural property, not a semantic one. The fix was to delete four words from the query.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Key too large: B-tree rejects entries above ~2,704 bytes. Index md5(body) or use a GIN/pg_trgm index instead.
  • Mixed sort directions in ORDER BY needing a matching index declaration.
  • NULLS FIRST/LAST mismatch silently costing you the index, as above.
  • Descending scans are marginally slower than ascending on some workloads because readahead does not help; it is rarely material.
  • Right-edge contention: every insert of a bigserial key hits the same rightmost leaf page. Above roughly 6,000 to 10,000 inserts per second this becomes measurable lock contention (19.17).
  • Random UUID v4 primary keys are the opposite problem: every insert lands on a random leaf page, so the whole index must stay in cache or every insert is a random read. Use UUID v7 or bigserial for large tables.
  • LIKE 'abc%' uses the index only if the column's collation is C or the index is declared with text_pattern_ops. On a en_US.UTF-8 database, CREATE INDEX ... ON products (sku text_pattern_ops) is what makes prefix search work.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They can compute the depth of an index in their head and therefore know that "the table is big" is not a reason for a lookup to be slow. When a point lookup is slow, they suspect bloat, a missing index, a type mismatch or a bad plan, not the row count. They design composite indexes by writing the query's WHERE and ORDER BY first and reading the column order off it. And they know the B-tree covers almost everything, so reaching for GIN, GiST or BRIN is a decision that needs a reason.

Common mistakes

  • Creating (a) and (a, b) and (a, b, c); the first two are usually redundant prefixes of the third (19.20).
  • Assuming an index on (status, created_at) helps a query filtering only on created_at.
  • Forgetting text_pattern_ops and wondering why LIKE 'ORD-2026%' is a sequential scan.
  • Using random UUIDs as primary keys on a 200M row table and then blaming PostgreSQL for the insert latency.

Interview questions

  1. How many page reads does a point lookup on a one-billion-row table take, and why? Expected: 4 index levels plus 1 heap page; fan-out of a few hundred keys per 8 KB page makes depth logarithmic.
  2. Explain the leftmost-prefix rule with an example of a query it defeats. Expected: (status, created_at) cannot seek on created_at alone.
  3. When does index column order for ORDER BY matter, and when does it not? Expected: single column is direction-agnostic; mixed ASC/DESC needs a matching declaration; NULLS FIRST/LAST must match too.
  4. What is a page split and why does it show up in your latency percentiles? Expected: full leaf splits into two plus a parent write plus WAL; rightmost splits are optimised to 90/10.
  5. Why is a random UUID primary key expensive on a large table? Expected: random insert positions, no locality, whole index must be cached, more full-page writes.

Practical exercise

Create orders with 5,000,000 rows, build (status, created_at), and run three queries: filtering on status only, on created_at only, and on both. Capture EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for each. Then create (created_at) and re-run the second query. Finally use pageinspect to report the number of levels and average leaf occupancy of both indexes. Acceptance criteria: four plans, a levels-and-occupancy table, and one paragraph on why the second query changed plan.

19.3 Reading a query plan

19.3.1 EXPLAIN, EXPLAIN ANALYZE and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)

Concept

EXPLAIN shows you the plan the planner chose, with its predictions. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows predictions next to measurements. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) adds how many 8 KB pages each node touched and where they came from.

You should almost never use the first form on its own, and you should almost always use the third. The whole skill of query tuning is comparing what the planner believed with what happened.

Why does it exist?

The planner is a predictor (Parts 7 and 181.12). It picks the plan with the lowest estimated cost, and that estimate is built from statistics that can be stale, from a uniform-distribution assumption that can be wrong, and from an independence assumption between columns that is usually wrong. When a query is slow, the question is never "is the database slow" but "which prediction was wrong". EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the only tool that answers it.

Mental model

Imagine a route planner that said "42 minutes" and you arrived in 4 hours. You do not tune the car. You look at each leg of the route and find the one where "8 minutes" turned into "3 hours 20", and then you ask why the planner thought that road was empty. A query plan is the route; rows= is the predicted traffic; actual rows= is the real traffic.

How it works

Read a plan inside out and bottom up. The most indented nodes run first and feed their parents. Each line looks like this:

->  Index Scan using idx_orders_user_created on orders o
      (cost=0.57..4831.02 rows=214 width=61)
      (actual time=0.048..3.914 rows=19842 loops=1)

Every field, one at a time:

Field Meaning What a senior reads into it
cost=0.57..4831.02 startup cost .. total cost, in arbitrary planner units The startup cost is what must happen before the first row appears. A Sort or Hash has a big startup cost because it must consume everything first. That matters enormously with LIMIT.
rows=214 estimated rows this node will emit The planner's belief.
width=61 average bytes per row Useful for spotting a SELECT * that drags TOASTed columns through a sort.
actual time=0.048..3.914 ms until the first row .. ms until the last row, per loop Not cumulative across loops. Multiply by loops for the real total.
rows=19842 (in actual) measured rows emitted, per loop Compare with the estimate. This is the whole game.
loops=1 how many times this node ran Inside a nested loop this is the outer row count. actual time=0.02 with loops=200000 is 4 seconds, not 0.02 ms.

Then the annotations that appear underneath nodes:

  • Index Cond: the predicate the index itself used to seek. Rows not matching are never read. Cheap.
  • Filter: a predicate applied after rows were fetched. Rows are read, then thrown away. Expensive.
  • Rows Removed by Filter: 380124 the count thrown away. This number is your index opportunity. If a node reads 400,000 rows and discards 380,000, you are missing a column in an index.
  • Recheck Cond: appears on a bitmap heap scan; the condition is re-applied because a lossy bitmap only remembers pages, not rows.
  • Heap Blocks: exact=41022 lossy=0 how many heap pages the bitmap tracked precisely versus how many it degraded to whole-page granularity because work_mem ran out. Any lossy count means raise work_mem or narrow the query.
  • Buffers: shared hit=812203 read=98211 dirtied=44 written=0 pages found in shared_buffers (hit), pages requested from the OS or disk (read), pages modified (dirtied), pages written out by this query (written). temp read/written means data spilled to temp files. read is the number that costs you real time, and it is far more stable than actual time, which moves with cache warmth and neighbours.
  • Sort Method: quicksort Memory: 4211kB the sort fit in work_mem. external merge Disk: 312400kB means it spilled. Disk sorts are 5 to 20 times slower.
  • Heap Fetches: 0 on an index-only scan: how many times the visibility map failed and the heap had to be read anyway. A high number means the table needs vacuuming.
  • Buckets: 65536 Batches: 4 Memory Usage: 32800kB on a hash node: more than one batch means the hash spilled to disk.
  • Workers Planned: 2 Workers Launched: 2 parallelism. Note that actual rows under a Parallel Seq Scan is per worker, so the total is roughly rows x loops where loops equals workers plus the leader.
  • Planning Time and Execution Time at the bottom. Planning time above 5 ms on a hot path is itself a problem (too many partitions, too many indexes, too many joins).

Other useful options: FORMAT JSON (for programmatic plan tests, as in Part 18's CI example), VERBOSE (shows output column lists and schema-qualified names), SETTINGS (shows non-default planner settings that influenced the plan, PG 12+), WAL (WAL generated by a DML statement, PG 13+), and GENERIC_PLAN (PG 16+, plans a parameterised query without executing it).

The golden rule. Scan the plan for the node where estimated rows and actual rows differ by more than 10x. That node is almost always the cause. A 100x mismatch is not a curiosity, it is the bug. Everything above that node in the tree was planned on a lie: the planner chose a nested loop because it expected 30 rows and got 300,000, so it did 300,000 index probes instead of 30.

Two important gotchas:

  1. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query. On UPDATE, DELETE or INSERT it really modifies data. Wrap it: BEGIN; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK;
  2. Timing has overhead. On plans with millions of rows, actual time can be inflated 10 to 30 percent by the gettimeofday calls. Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) when you only need row counts and buffers, and trust Buffers over actual time for comparisons.

Practical example

The support team reports that the merchant dashboard "sometimes" takes 8 seconds. pg_stat_statements shows a mean of 240 ms and a max of 9,100 ms for one query id. Running EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with a typical parameter gives 240 ms; running it with the parameter from the slow request gives 8.9 s, and the difference is one node: rows=41 estimated, rows=68302 actual, on a filter over orders.shipping_country. The plan flipped from an index scan into a nested loop that ran 68,302 times. The mismatch pointed straight at a skewed column with a stale most_common_vals list.

PostgreSQL example

The five options you will use, on one query:

-- 1. Plan only, no execution. Safe on production. Shows what the planner would do.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 91827 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- 2. Execute and measure.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT ...;

-- 3. The one you should default to.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...;

-- 4. Everything, including which planner settings were non-default.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, SETTINGS, WAL) SELECT ...;

-- 5. Safe for DML.
BEGIN;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) UPDATE orders SET status = 'CANCELLED' WHERE id = 148392017;
ROLLBACK;

Turn on I/O timing first, or Buffers tells you page counts but not how long the disk took:

SET track_io_timing = on;   -- or set it globally; it is cheap on modern kernels

With it on, plans gain I/O Timings: shared read=812.442 ms, which separates "we read 98,000 pages and the disk was fast" from "we read 98,000 pages and the disk was the problem".

NestJS example

A small diagnostic endpoint, locked behind an admin guard and a statement timeout, that lets you capture a real plan for a real production parameter without shell access. This has saved more incidents than it has caused, provided the SQL is not user-supplied.

// admin/plan.controller.ts
import { Controller, Post, Body, UseGuards, BadRequestException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { AdminGuard } from '../auth/admin.guard';
import { IsIn, IsArray, IsString } from 'class-validator';

class PlanDto {
  @IsIn(['ordersByUser', 'paymentsByProvider']) queryKey!: string;
  @IsArray() params!: unknown[];
}

const CATALOG: Record<string, string> = {
  ordersByUser:
    'SELECT id, status, total_cents FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20',
  paymentsByProvider: 'SELECT id, status FROM payments WHERE provider_ref = $1',
};

@Controller('admin/plan')
@UseGuards(AdminGuard)
export class PlanController {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  @Post()
  async plan(@Body() dto: PlanDto) {
    const sql = CATALOG[dto.queryKey];              // never interpolate client SQL
    if (!sql) throw new BadRequestException('unknown query');
    return this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      await em.query(`SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 5000`);
      const rows = await em.query(
        `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) ${sql}`,
        dto.params,
      );
      return rows[0]['QUERY PLAN'];
    });
  }
}

Production scenario

auto_explain in shared_preload_libraries, configured to log any plan over 500 ms with buffers and nested plans, turns plan capture from a manual chore into a stream:

auto_explain.log_min_duration = '500ms'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on
auto_explain.log_buffers = on
auto_explain.log_nested_statements = on
auto_explain.log_timing = off        # cheaper; keep row counts and buffers
auto_explain.sample_rate = 0.1       # 10 percent of qualifying statements on a busy system

Plans land in the PostgreSQL log, get shipped to your log store, and a dashboard counts distinct plan shapes per queryid. When a plan flips, you see two shapes for one query id and you know within minutes rather than after a customer complains.

Failure scenario

An engineer runs EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM notifications WHERE created_at < '2025-01-01' on the primary to "see how expensive it would be". It is not a dry run. It deletes 340 million rows, holds an enormous transaction open, generates 90 GB of WAL, and blocks autovacuum's horizon for eleven minutes. The BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK; wrapper is not optional, and even then the WAL and the bloat are real.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • EXPLAIN without ANALYZE on a query whose plan depends on parameters gives you a generic plan that may not be the one that runs (19.24).
  • Timing overhead inflating actual time on high-row-count plans; use TIMING OFF.
  • Per-loop values mistaken for totals inside nested loops.
  • Per-worker values mistaken for totals under Gather.
  • EXPLAIN on a prepared statement shows the generic plan after five executions, not your custom plan.
  • Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a replica where the plan differs because random_page_cost or statistics differ.
  • A query fast in EXPLAIN ANALYZE and slow in the app: the plan is fine and your problem is network round trips, result serialisation, or the ORM (Part 21 — ORMs in Depth).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read rows= versus actual rows= before they read timings, because timings vary with cache and load while the estimate error is stable and diagnostic. They read Buffers next, because page counts are a hardware-independent measure of work. They look for Rows Removed by Filter as the signature of a missing index column. They never tune a query they have not explained, and never approve an index without the before plan and the after plan in the pull request.

Common mistakes

  • Using EXPLAIN without ANALYZE and treating the estimates as facts.
  • Reading the plan top-down and blaming the outermost node.
  • Ignoring loops.
  • Optimising the node with the highest cost instead of the node with the worst estimate error.
  • Comparing two EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs where one had a cold cache.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between Index Cond and Filter, and why does it matter? Expected: seek versus post-fetch discard; Rows Removed by Filter shows wasted work and points to a missing index column.
  2. A node says actual time=0.031..0.044 rows=3 loops=248000. Is it fast? Expected: no; roughly 11 seconds total. Follow-up: what does that tell you about the outer estimate?
  3. Why prefer Buffers over actual time when comparing two plans? Expected: cache-warmth independence; page counts are the real work.
  4. What does Heap Blocks: lossy=8200 mean and how do you fix it? Expected: bitmap exceeded work_mem and degraded to page granularity; raise work_mem or make the predicate more selective.
  5. How do you capture the plan of a slow production query you cannot reproduce? Expected: auto_explain with log_min_duration, buffers and sampling.

Practical exercise

Take three of your own slowest queries from pg_stat_statements. For each, capture EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), and produce a one-page write-up naming: the node with the worst estimate error, the total buffers read, the largest Rows Removed by Filter, and your hypothesis for a fix. Acceptance criteria: three write-ups where the hypothesis is stated before you try the fix.

19.4 Scan types

19.4.1 Sequential, index, index-only and bitmap scans

Concept

There are four ways PostgreSQL gets rows out of a table, and the planner picks between them by cost. Understanding when each one should win is what lets you tell "the planner made a mistake" from "the planner is right and my query is wrong".

  • Sequential scan reads every page of the heap in file order.
  • Index scan walks the index and fetches heap rows one at a time, in index order.
  • Index-only scan walks the index and does not touch the heap at all, when the visibility map allows it.
  • Bitmap index scan plus bitmap heap scan walks the index, builds a bitmap of matching pages, sorts it, then reads the heap in physical page order.

Why does it exist?

Because "use the index" is not always right. Random reads cost more than sequential ones, and if you are going to touch a large fraction of the pages anyway, reading them in file order with readahead is dramatically faster than jumping around. The bitmap scan exists for the enormous middle ground where the index is useful but the result set is too big for one-row-at-a-time random fetches.

Mental model

You have a shopping list and a supermarket.

  • One item: walk straight to it using the store map. That is an index scan.
  • Everything in the store: just walk every aisle in order. Consulting the map for each of 4,000 items would be absurd. That is a sequential scan.
  • Two hundred items: look every item up on the map first, write down the aisle numbers, sort them, then walk the aisles once in order picking things up. That is a bitmap scan, and it is exactly why the bitmap heap scan reads pages in physical order.
  • You only need to know whether the item is in stock, not to pick it up: the map already says so. That is an index-only scan.

How it works

Sequential scan. Reads the heap from page 0 to page N with 128 KB readahead, applies the filter to every row, discards non-matches. Costs pages x seq_page_cost + rows x (cpu_tuple_cost + cpu_operator_cost). On orders that is 3,921,033 + 200,000,000 x 0.0125 = 6,421,033 cost units. It can be parallelised (Parallel Seq Scan) across max_parallel_workers_per_gather workers, and it uses a small ring buffer rather than flooding shared_buffers, so a big scan does not evict your whole cache.

Sequential scan is correct when: the table is small (under a few hundred pages, where the descent costs more than the scan), or the query touches a large fraction of rows (roughly above 5 to 10 percent, see 19.16), or there is no usable index, or you are aggregating everything. An analytics query that reads 80 percent of orders should be a sequential scan, and forcing an index on it makes it slower. "Seq Scan" in a plan is not automatically a bug.

Index scan. Descends the tree, then for each matching index entry fetches the heap page containing that ctid and checks visibility. Rows come back in index order, so ORDER BY matching the index is free and LIMIT can stop early. The killer property and the killer weakness are the same: one heap page read per row, in random order. 10,000 matching rows in a 30 GB table is close to 10,000 random reads.

Index-only scan. Same descent, but every column the query needs is in the index, so there is nothing to fetch from the heap except the visibility check. PostgreSQL solves that with the visibility map, a two-bits-per-page bitmap maintained by VACUUM that marks pages where every tuple is visible to every transaction. If the page is marked all-visible, no heap read. If not, the heap page must be read anyway and that shows up as Heap Fetches. This makes index-only scans dependent on vacuum: a table with heavy churn and lazy autovacuum will show thousands of heap fetches and lose most of the benefit.

Bitmap index scan plus bitmap heap scan. Two nodes that always come as a pair:

flowchart TB
  q["WHERE status='PAID' AND created_at > now() - interval '3 days'"]
  bis1["Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_status"]
  bis2["Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_created_at"]
  and["BitmapAnd  combine the two bitmaps"]
  bm["Bitmap of heap pages  1 bit per page  sorted by page number"]
  bhs["Bitmap Heap Scan  read pages in physical order"]
  rc["Recheck Cond  re-apply predicates to each row"]
  out["rows out"]
  q --> bis1
  q --> bis2
  bis1 --> and
  bis2 --> and
  and --> bm
  bm --> bhs
  bhs --> rc
  rc --> out
  1. The bitmap index scan reads the index and, instead of fetching rows, sets a bit for each heap page that contains a match. It never touches the heap.
  2. Multiple bitmap index scans can be combined with BitmapAnd or BitmapOr. This is how PostgreSQL uses two separate single-column indexes for one query, and it is the reason "just add both indexes" sometimes works well enough.
  3. If the bitmap grows beyond work_mem, it becomes lossy: it stops tracking individual rows and remembers only "this page has something". Heap Blocks: lossy=N in the plan.
  4. The bitmap heap scan reads the marked pages in physical order, which lets the kernel and effective_io_concurrency prefetch. Each page is read at most once, no matter how many matching rows it holds.
  5. Because the bitmap may be lossy and because BitmapAnd is per page, every row is re-checked against the predicates. That is the Recheck Cond line.

The trade: the bitmap heap scan loses index ordering, so an ORDER BY on top needs a Sort node. That is precisely why a bitmap scan plus sort loses to a composite index scan for ORDER BY ... LIMIT queries, which is the case study of 19.23.

random_page_cost decides the boundary. The default 4.0 says a random page costs four sequential pages, which was true for a 7,200 rpm disk with a 9 ms seek and is wildly false for NVMe, where the ratio is closer to 1.05. Leaving it at 4 on SSD makes the planner systematically prefer sequential and bitmap scans over index scans. Setting random_page_cost = 1.1 and effective_io_concurrency = 200 is the single highest-value planner change on modern storage, and it is worth more than most indexes you will add.

Practical example — five plans, line by line

Plan 1: sequential scan, and it is correct.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT avg(total_cents) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01';
Finalize Aggregate  (cost=3140882.44..3140882.45 rows=1 width=32)
                    (actual time=18422.101..18428.774 rows=1 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=91204 read=3829829
  ->  Gather  (cost=3140882.22..3140882.43 rows=2 width=32) (actual time=18421.904..18428.766 rows=3 loops=1)
        Workers Planned: 2
        Workers Launched: 2
        ->  Partial Aggregate  (cost=3139882.22..3139882.23 rows=1 width=32)
                               (actual time=18401.220..18401.221 rows=1 loops=3)
              ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..2967216.00 rows=69066488 width=4)
                                               (actual time=0.031..14022.918 rows=55212004 loops=3)
                    Filter: (created_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00')
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 11454663
                    Buffers: shared hit=91204 read=3829829
Planning Time: 0.142 ms
Execution Time: 18428.812 ms

Reading it: 165 million of 200 million rows match (55,212,004 x 3 workers). That is 83 percent of the table. There is no index that helps; any index scan would read every heap page anyway plus the index. The estimate (69,066,488 per worker) versus actual (55,212,004) is off by 25 percent, which is fine. Rows Removed by Filter: 11,454,663 per worker sounds huge but is only 17 percent, so a partial index would not pay. This plan is correct. 18 seconds is the honest price of aggregating 165 million rows, and the fix is architectural (a materialised rollup table, Part 22 — Scaling Databases), not an index.

Plan 2: index scan, the ideal shape.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders WHERE user_id = 918273 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=0.57..37.44 rows=20 width=28) (actual time=0.052..0.098 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=6 read=2
  ->  Index Scan Backward using idx_orders_user_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..229.31 rows=124 width=28) (actual time=0.050..0.094 rows=20 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (user_id = 918273)
        Buffers: shared hit=6 read=2
Planning Time: 0.121 ms
Execution Time: 0.126 ms

Reading it: startup cost 0.57 and total 37.44 for the Limit, versus 229.31 for the unlimited index scan. The planner knows LIMIT can stop early, so it charges only 20/124 of the scan. Index Cond does all the work, there is no Filter, there is no Sort because Index Scan Backward already produces created_at DESC within user_id = 918273. Eight buffers total. 0.126 ms. This is what you are aiming for on every list endpoint.

Plan 3: index-only scan, and the visibility map.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT count(*) FROM order_items WHERE order_id BETWEEN 148000000 AND 148010000;
Aggregate  (cost=1892.11..1892.12 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=12.884..12.885 rows=1 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=131 read=48
  ->  Index Only Scan using idx_order_items_order_id on order_items
        (cost=0.58..1780.44 rows=44668 width=0) (actual time=0.061..10.221 rows=45012 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((order_id >= 148000000) AND (order_id <= 148010000))
        Heap Fetches: 0
        Buffers: shared hit=131 read=48
Planning Time: 0.098 ms
Execution Time: 12.912 ms

Reading it: 45,012 rows counted from 179 buffers, because nothing was fetched from the 67 GB heap. Heap Fetches: 0 is the line that proves it. Now the same query on a table that has been heavily updated and not vacuumed:

  ->  Index Only Scan using idx_order_items_order_id on order_items
        (cost=0.58..1780.44 rows=44668 width=0) (actual time=0.088..381.442 rows=45012 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((order_id >= 148000000) AND (order_id <= 148010000))
        Heap Fetches: 41208
        Buffers: shared hit=8214 read=33122

Same plan shape, 30x slower, because 41,208 of the 45,012 rows lived on pages the visibility map did not mark all-visible, so each one became a heap fetch. VACUUM order_items; restores it. An index-only scan is a vacuum-dependent optimisation, not a guaranteed one.

Plan 4: bitmap scan, correctly chosen.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= '2026-09-08';
Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=8912.44..412188.02 rows=402118 width=12)
                            (actual time=61.204..1284.551 rows=388214 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (created_at >= '2026-09-08 00:00:00+00')
  Filter: (status = 'PAID')
  Rows Removed by Filter: 122841
  Heap Blocks: exact=41022
  Buffers: shared hit=44120 read=8214
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_created_at  (cost=0.00..8811.91 rows=511055 width=0)
                                                  (actual time=52.118..52.119 rows=511055 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (created_at >= '2026-09-08 00:00:00+00')
        Buffers: shared hit=1402
Planning Time: 0.184 ms
Execution Time: 1301.884 ms

Reading it: the index scan found 511,055 candidate rows over 41,022 heap pages. Fetching those one at a time with an index scan would be 511,055 random reads; instead the bitmap sorts the pages and reads each of the 41,022 exactly once. Heap Blocks: exact=41022 lossy=0 means work_mem was sufficient. Rows Removed by Filter: 122,841 is the cost of status not being in the index: 24 percent of fetched rows are discarded. That is the tell for the improvement in 19.5. The bitmap choice itself is right for this shape and volume.

Plan 5: index scan chosen wrongly because of a bad estimate.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, oi.product_id
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.shipping_country = 'DE' AND o.currency = 'EUR'
  AND o.created_at >= '2026-09-01';
Nested Loop  (cost=1.15..1204882.44 rows=182044 width=16)
             (actual time=0.084..41822.551 rows=3121884 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=8214402 read=1128441
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created_at on orders o
        (cost=0.57..214882.10 rows=40460 width=8) (actual time=0.041..3122.884 rows=693752 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (created_at >= '2026-09-01 00:00:00+00')
        Filter: ((shipping_country = 'DE'::bpchar) AND (currency = 'EUR'::bpchar))
        Rows Removed by Filter: 2081256
        Buffers: shared hit=411882 read=308221
  ->  Index Scan using idx_order_items_order_id on order_items oi
        (cost=0.58..24.15 rows=5 width=16) (actual time=0.031..0.052 rows=5 loops=693752)
        Index Cond: (order_id = o.id)
        Buffers: shared hit=7802520 read=820220
Planning Time: 0.402 ms
Execution Time: 42104.882 ms

Reading it: the outer node estimated 40,460 rows and produced 693,752, a 17x error caused by the independence assumption on shipping_country and currency (Parts 7 and 181.12). The planner priced a nested loop at 40,460 inner lookups; it performed 693,752, visible as loops=693752 on the inner node. actual time=0.031..0.052 on that inner scan looks lovely and is a trap: 693,752 x 0.052 ms is 36 seconds. Buffers tell the same story: 8.6 million pages touched.

The fix is not an index. It is CREATE STATISTICS orders_country_currency (dependencies, mcv) ON shipping_country, currency FROM orders; ANALYZE orders; After that the estimate becomes 640,000, the planner switches to a hash join over a bitmap scan, and the query takes 4.2 seconds. Then an index on (shipping_country, created_at) takes it to 1.1 seconds. Order matters: fix the estimate first, then index.

PostgreSQL example

Force each shape in a session to compare them honestly, then reset:

SET enable_seqscan = off;    SET enable_bitmapscan = off;   -- forces a plain index scan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= '2026-09-08';
RESET enable_seqscan; RESET enable_bitmapscan;

Plain index scan for the same query as Plan 4:

Index Scan using idx_orders_created_at on orders  (cost=0.57..1892441.02 rows=402118 width=12)
                                                  (actual time=0.061..9822.114 rows=388214 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (created_at >= '2026-09-08 00:00:00+00')
  Filter: (status = 'PAID')
  Rows Removed by Filter: 122841
  Buffers: shared hit=291884 read=221402
Execution Time: 9840.221 ms

1,301 ms with the bitmap versus 9,840 ms with the index scan: the planner was right, and 513,286 buffers versus 52,334 shows exactly why. Never assume the index scan is the good one.

Production scenario

An OLTP instance on gp3 EBS with random_page_cost = 4 (the default). The team could not understand why GET /orders?status=PAID&from=... was doing sequential scans despite three indexes. Setting random_page_cost = 1.1 and effective_io_concurrency = 200 changed 6 of the top 20 queries from sequential and bitmap scans to index scans and cut total database CPU by 34 percent, with no schema change at all.

Failure scenario

A team disabled sequential scans globally (enable_seqscan = off in postgresql.conf) after one bad plan. Six weeks later the nightly reconciliation job, which legitimately reads 90 percent of payments, started using an index scan: 212 million random heap fetches instead of a 26 GB sequential read. The job went from 6 minutes to 4 hours 20, overran its window, and delayed the settlement file. enable_* settings are diagnostic tools for a session, never configuration.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Bitmap becoming lossy under low work_mem: Heap Blocks: lossy=... and a big recheck cost.
  • Index-only scan degrading to heap fetches after a bulk load, until VACUUM runs.
  • Parallel Seq Scan where per-worker rows are mistaken for totals.
  • Index scan chosen for a large result set because random_page_cost is too low (the opposite mistake, rarer but real: 1.0 on spinning disks or on a network volume with real seek cost).
  • Very small tables where a sequential scan is correct and an index will never be used, no matter how many you add.
  • BitmapOr across two indexes producing a plan that looks clever but reads most of the table anyway; a rewrite to UNION ALL is often faster (19.24).
  • Correlation: a range scan on a well-correlated column (created_at on an append-only table) is nearly sequential and much cheaper than the planner's random-page assumption, which is why pg_stats.correlation feeds the cost model.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They do not treat "Seq Scan" as a failure. They ask what fraction of the table the query needs, and they know that above roughly 5 to 10 percent the sequential scan wins. They check random_page_cost on any new instance before adding a single index. They recognise the bitmap-plus-sort shape as the signature of a missing composite index, and the high-loops nested loop as the signature of a bad estimate.

Common mistakes

  • "The plan says Seq Scan, add an index."
  • Setting enable_seqscan = off anywhere permanent.
  • Not enabling track_io_timing, so Buffers counts exist but disk time does not.
  • Comparing plans on a laptop with 200,000 rows and shipping the conclusion to a 200 million row table.
  • Believing an index-only scan is guaranteed; it is a vacuum-dependent optimisation.

Interview questions

  1. When is a sequential scan the right plan? Expected: small tables, large result fractions, no usable index, full aggregation. Follow-up: roughly what fraction, and what setting moves the boundary?
  2. Explain a bitmap heap scan and why it exists. Expected: page-granular bitmap, sorted physical reads, combines multiple indexes, loses ordering, rechecks predicates.
  3. What makes an index-only scan fall back to heap reads? Expected: visibility map pages not marked all-visible; fix with vacuum; Heap Fetches in the plan.
  4. What does random_page_cost do and what should it be on NVMe? Expected: relative cost of random page reads; about 1.1.
  5. You see loops=693752 with actual time=0.05 on an inner index scan. What is wrong? Expected: the outer estimate was wrong; total is 35 seconds; fix the estimate (extended statistics) before the index.

Practical exercise

On a 10 million row orders table, write one query that returns 1 row, one that returns 50,000, and one that returns 8 million. Capture plans for each with default settings, then with random_page_cost = 1.1, then with enable_bitmapscan = off. Acceptance criteria: a 3x3 table of execution time and buffers read, plus a written explanation of which scan type won each cell and why.

19.5 Composite indexes

19.5.1 The column-order rule: equality, then range, then sort

Concept

A composite (multi-column) index is a B-tree whose key is a tuple. (user_id, created_at) sorts by user_id, then by created_at within each user_id. Because of that structure, the order of the columns decides which queries the index can serve, and getting it wrong produces an index that is technically used and practically useless.

There is one rule and it fits on a sticky note:

Equality columns first, in any order among themselves. Then the range column. Then the sort column. At most one range or sort column can be seeked; everything after it is only a filter.

This is sometimes called the ESR rule (Equality, Sort, Range) in other databases; in PostgreSQL the practical form is equality, then the column you order by, then the column you range over when those are different, because index ordering is the thing you cannot get any other way.

Why does it exist?

Two separate index capabilities are at stake and people conflate them:

  1. Seeking: jumping straight to the first matching leaf entry and stopping when the key stops matching. Only the leading columns, up to and including the first inequality, can seek.
  2. Ordering: producing rows already sorted so the planner can drop the Sort node and honour LIMIT early.

An index with the range column first can seek, but the rows come out ordered by the range column across all values of the equality column, so a LIMIT 20 on a per-user list cannot stop early: it must read every row in the range and sort. An index with the equality column first can do both. That asymmetry is the entire section.

Mental model

A phone book sorted by (city, surname). "All Müllers in Hamburg" is instant: find Hamburg, then Müller inside it, and the entries are already in surname order. Now imagine the book sorted by (surname, city). "All Müllers in Hamburg" still works, because surname is the leading column. But "the first 20 people in Hamburg alphabetically" is a disaster: Hamburg residents are scattered across every surname section, so you must read the whole book, collect the Hamburg entries, and sort them. Same two columns. Completely different book.

flowchart TB
  subgraph A["Index on user_id then created_at DESC"]
    a1["user 41 / 2026-09-09"]
    a2["user 41 / 2026-09-07"]
    a3["user 41 / 2026-08-30"]
    a4["user 42 / 2026-09-08"]
    a5["user 42 / 2026-01-02"]
    a1 --> a2 --> a3 --> a4 --> a5
  end
  subgraph B["Index on created_at DESC then user_id"]
    b1["2026-09-09 / user 41"]
    b2["2026-09-08 / user 42"]
    b3["2026-09-07 / user 41"]
    b4["2026-08-30 / user 41"]
    b5["2026-01-02 / user 42"]
    b1 --> b2 --> b3 --> b4 --> b5
  end
  q["WHERE user_id = 41 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2"]
  q -->|"seek to user 41, take 2, stop"| A
  q -->|"scan everything, filter, sort"| B

How it works

Given a query, derive the index mechanically:

  1. Write down every column compared with = or IN. Those go first. Their relative order does not affect this query, so order them to maximise reuse by other queries: most selective first is the usual tiebreak, but "the column the most queries filter on" beats it.
  2. Write down the column in the ORDER BY. It goes next, with the same direction and nulls ordering as the query.
  3. Write down the column with <, >, BETWEEN. It goes after the sort column if they differ; if the sort column and the range column are the same (very common: created_at > X ORDER BY created_at DESC), that one column serves both.
  4. Any further columns you want available for an index-only scan go in INCLUDE (19.9), not in the key.
  5. Stop. Three or four key columns is almost always enough. Each extra column widens every entry, shrinks fan-out, and grows the index.

The reason step 3 is subtle: once the index seeks past a range condition, the remaining columns are not sorted globally. In (status, created_at, total_cents), within status='PAID' the entries are sorted by created_at, and within one exact created_at value by total_cents. So WHERE status='PAID' AND created_at > X ORDER BY total_cents still needs a sort. Only one inequality gets the benefit.

Practical example

The query behind the merchant dashboard, run 340 times a second:

SELECT id, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

Two candidate indexes. Both "cover the query". They perform nothing alike.

PostgreSQL example

Candidate A: (created_at, status) — the range column first, the wrong way round.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_status ON orders (created_at DESC, status);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_cents, created_at FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
Limit  (cost=0.57..184.22 rows=50 width=20) (actual time=0.088..3.402 rows=50 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=61 read=18
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created_status on orders
        (cost=0.57..1483902.11 rows=403188 width=20) (actual time=0.086..3.398 rows=50 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((created_at >= (now() - '7 days'::interval)) AND (status = 'PAID'::text))
        Buffers: shared hit=61 read=18
Planning Time: 0.140 ms
Execution Time: 3.442 ms

This looks fine. It is fine, for LIMIT 50 on a status that is 76 percent of recent orders: the index is ordered by created_at DESC so it walks backwards and finds 50 PAID rows almost immediately. Now change the status to a rare one:

... WHERE status = 'REFUND_PENDING' AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days' ...
Limit  (cost=0.57..184.22 rows=50 width=20) (actual time=0.094..2841.552 rows=50 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=402118 read=118220
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created_status on orders
        (cost=0.57..1483902.11 rows=403188 width=20) (actual time=0.092..2841.544 rows=50 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((created_at >= (now() - '7 days'::interval)) AND (status = 'REFUND_PENDING'::text))
        Buffers: shared hit=402118 read=118220
Planning Time: 0.140 ms
Execution Time: 2841.601 ms

Identical plan, identical cost estimate, 2.8 seconds instead of 3.4 ms. The index walked 520,338 pages of created_at-ordered entries looking for the 50 rare ones. status was inside Index Cond but it was not seekable, because everything after the leading range column is checked, not sought. This is the most dangerous kind of index: fast in your test, catastrophic for one parameter value in production.

Candidate B: (status, created_at DESC) — equality first.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at DESC);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_cents, created_at FROM orders
WHERE status = 'REFUND_PENDING' AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
Limit  (cost=0.57..112.88 rows=50 width=20) (actual time=0.041..0.212 rows=50 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=8 read=3
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_status_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..4021.44 rows=1791 width=20) (actual time=0.040..0.208 rows=50 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((status = 'REFUND_PENDING'::text) AND (created_at >= (now() - '7 days'::interval)))
        Buffers: shared hit=8 read=3
Planning Time: 0.132 ms
Execution Time: 0.238 ms

Eleven buffers. 0.24 ms. And it is 0.24 ms for every status value, common or rare, because the seek lands exactly on the (status, created_at) pair and walks 50 entries. Same two columns, 11,800x difference on the bad parameter. Write the order down before you write the DDL.

The per-user list index. The other archetype, and the one you will build most often:

-- GET /orders?userId=... : the single most common shape in any product
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders WHERE user_id = 918273 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=0.57..37.44 rows=20 width=28) (actual time=0.049..0.094 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=6 read=2
  ->  Index Scan Backward using idx_orders_user_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..229.31 rows=124 width=28) (actual time=0.047..0.090 rows=20 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (user_id = 918273)
Execution Time: 0.121 ms

Note Index Scan Backward: because the index is declared created_at DESC and the query asks DESC, PostgreSQL could scan forward; here it happens to have chosen a backward scan of an ascending physical order, which is equally free. Direction of a two-column index only matters when the two columns sort in opposite directions. (user_id ASC, created_at DESC) and (user_id ASC, created_at ASC) both serve WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC perfectly, because the whole index can be read backwards. You need the explicit DESC only for something like ORDER BY user_id ASC, created_at DESC, which no single-direction read can produce.

One composite serving three queries. Here is where index count actually drops. Given (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC):

Query Served? How
WHERE tenant_id = ? Yes leading prefix seek
WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? Yes two-column prefix seek
WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 Yes seek plus ordered walk, no sort
WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 Partly seeks on tenant_id, but must scan all statuses and sort. Fine for small tenants, bad for large ones.
WHERE status = ? No not a leading prefix
WHERE created_at > ? No not a leading prefix

Four indexes collapse into one for the first three rows. The fourth row is the judgement call: if the "all statuses, newest first" list is a real, hot endpoint, add a second index (tenant_id, created_at DESC). If it is a rarely used admin screen, let it sort. You do not need one index per query; you need one index per access-pattern family.

NestJS example

Encode the access patterns in the repository so the index and the query stay married. If someone changes the ORDER BY, the method name should stop making sense.

// orders.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /** Served by idx_orders_user_created (user_id, created_at DESC). Keyset paginated. */
  async listForUser(userId: string, before: Date | null, limit = 20) {
    return this.ds.query(
      `SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
         FROM orders
        WHERE user_id = $1
          AND ($2::timestamptz IS NULL OR created_at < $2)
        ORDER BY created_at DESC
        LIMIT $3`,
      [userId, before, limit],
    );
  }
}

Keyset pagination (created_at < $2) instead of OFFSET is what keeps page 500 as fast as page 1: OFFSET 10000 still reads and discards 10,000 index entries. Part 14 — API Design covers the contract; the index is what makes it possible.

Sequelize example

const rows = await Order.findAll({
  where: { userId, ...(before ? { createdAt: { [Op.lt]: before } } : {}) },
  order: [['createdAt', 'DESC']],
  limit: 20,
  attributes: ['id', 'status', 'totalCents', 'createdAt'],
});

Watch for two Sequelize traps: order: [['createdAt', 'DESC NULLS LAST']] will not match an index declared without NULLS LAST, and adding a second order column that is not in the index silently reintroduces a Sort.

Production scenario

An orders service with 14 single-column indexes was reduced to 5 composites over two sprints. Index storage went from 47 GB to 22 GB, p99 insert latency from 19 ms to 7 ms, and the number of queries served without a Sort node went from 6 to 19 out of the top 25. Nothing about the application code changed except one ORDER BY clause.

Failure scenario

GET /admin/orders?status=X was built and load-tested with status=PAID. In production the compliance team filtered by status=CHARGEBACK, which is 0.004 percent of rows, using the (created_at, status) index. Each request scanned 500,000+ index entries for 8 seconds, 40 of them ran concurrently, all 20 pool connections were held, and every other endpoint on the service started timing out. The database was at 12 percent CPU the whole time. A slow query does not need to be frequent to take down a service; it needs to hold connections.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Adding a fourth or fifth key column "just in case": each one shrinks fan-out and grows the index without helping any query.
  • IN (...) on the leading column works as a series of seeks and is fine; IN on a middle column may or may not, depending on the planner's skip-scan-like handling.
  • ORDER BY a, b where a is equality-constrained: PostgreSQL is smart enough to know a is constant and use (a, b); it is not always smart enough with expressions.
  • A NULL in an equality column: WHERE user_id = NULL never matches; use IS NULL, which a B-tree does support.
  • Mixed directions requiring an explicitly declared index.
  • Very wide leading columns (a text slug) hurting fan-out; hash or truncate.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the index DDL directly under the query in the pull request. They test the index against the worst parameter value, not the typical one, because that is what production will find. They count access-pattern families, not queries. And they treat "the index exists and appears in the plan" as the beginning of the investigation, not the end.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the timestamp first because "we always filter on date".
  • One index per column, expecting the planner to combine them (it will, with a bitmap, and it will be far slower than the composite).
  • Testing only with the common parameter value.
  • Assuming (a, b) and (b, a) are interchangeable.

Interview questions

  1. Given WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20, what index and why? Expected: (status, created_at DESC); equality first so the seek is exact and the walk is already ordered.
