  2. Why can (created_at, status) be fast for one parameter and 1000x slower for another? Expected: status is a check, not a seek, after the leading range; scan length depends on value frequency.
  3. When does the declared direction of a composite index matter? Expected: only for mixed-direction ORDER BY, and for NULLS FIRST/LAST matching.
  4. How many indexes do you need for five queries on one table? Expected: as many as there are access-pattern families; show the prefix analysis.

Practical exercise

Build orders with 20 million rows and a skewed status (76 percent PAID, 0.004 percent CHARGEBACK). Create both (created_at DESC, status) and (status, created_at DESC). Run the dashboard query with both statuses against each index (use DROP INDEX or enable_indexscan tricks to isolate). Acceptance criteria: a 2x2 table of execution time and buffers, and a written rule you would put in your team's review checklist.

19.6 Partial indexes

19.6.1 Indexing 0.01 percent of a table

Concept

A partial index has a WHERE clause of its own. It indexes only the rows matching that predicate. Everything else is not in the index at all: not the keys, not the ctids, nothing.

CREATE INDEX idx_notifications_pending
  ON notifications (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'PENDING';

This is the highest leverage index feature in PostgreSQL and the one most teams have never used.

Why does it exist?

Queue tables. Soft deletes. Feature flags. Any table where a query only ever looks at a tiny, well-defined slice, but the table is enormous. notifications has 1.2 billion rows; at any moment about 120,000 are PENDING. A full index on (status, created_at) covers 1.2 billion entries, costs about 41 GB, and must be updated on every one of the 14,000 inserts per second. A partial index covers 120,000 entries, costs 3 MB, and only gets an entry when a row enters the pending state.

Mental model

A restaurant kitchen has a ticket rail. It holds only the orders that are not yet served. Nobody keeps a rail of every order from the last three years; the finished tickets go in a box and the rail stays short enough to read at a glance. A partial index is the rail. A full index is a rail with three years of tickets on it, where the cook has to find today's among them.

How it works

  1. CREATE INDEX ... WHERE pred builds entries only for rows satisfying pred.
  2. On INSERT, PostgreSQL evaluates pred. If false, no index entry is written at all. This is the write-cost saving, and it is why a partial index on a rare state is almost free.
  3. On UPDATE, a row that leaves the predicate gets its entry removed (marked dead) and a row that enters it gets one added. The queue "drain" is exactly this: status goes PENDING -> SENT and the entry leaves the index.
  4. The planner uses the index only if it can prove your query's predicate implies the index's predicate. Proof is syntactic and conservative. WHERE status = 'PENDING' matches WHERE status = 'PENDING'. WHERE status IN ('PENDING') matches. WHERE status <> 'SENT' does not match, even if PENDING and SENT are the only two values, because the planner cannot know that.
  5. The predicate's columns do not have to be in the key. (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING' has a 8-byte key and still fully answers WHERE status='PENDING' ORDER BY created_at.

The size arithmetic on notifications:

Index Entries Size Insert cost per row
(status, created_at) full 1,200,000,000 41 GB ~28 us always
(created_at) WHERE status='PENDING' ~120,000 3.1 MB ~28 us for 0.01 percent of rows, 0.4 us (predicate eval only) for the rest

Three megabytes. It lives permanently in shared_buffers and every queue poll is a cache hit.

Practical example — the queue claim

-- The worker's claim query, run 40 times a second by 12 workers
SELECT id, user_id, payload
FROM notifications
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
ORDER BY created_at
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 100;

Before the partial index, with only (status):

Limit  (cost=0.00..8291884.22 rows=100 width=118) (actual time=4211.884..4212.001 rows=100 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=1928441 read=8821004
  ->  LockRows  (cost=0.00..9948221.44 rows=119983 width=118) (actual time=4211.882..4211.994 rows=100 loops=1)
        ->  Sort  (cost=9821004.11..9821304.07 rows=119983 width=118)
                  (actual time=4198.221..4198.884 rows=100 loops=1)
              Sort Key: created_at
              Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 44kB
              ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on notifications  (cost=2911.02..9812884.44 rows=119983 width=118)
                                                     (actual time=612.114..4102.884 rows=119412 loops=1)
                    Recheck Cond: (status = 'PENDING'::text)
                    Heap Blocks: exact=118820
                    ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_notifications_status  (cost=0.00..2881.07 rows=119983 width=0)
                          Index Cond: (status = 'PENDING'::text)
Execution Time: 4212.204 ms

4.2 seconds, 10.7 million buffers, and it reads all 119,412 pending rows into a sort just to take the oldest 100. Twelve workers doing this every 25 ms is a database on fire.

After:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_notifications_pending
  ON notifications (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';
Limit  (cost=0.42..14.88 rows=100 width=118) (actual time=0.084..1.204 rows=100 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=112 read=4
  ->  LockRows  (cost=0.42..17342.11 rows=119983 width=118) (actual time=0.083..1.198 rows=100 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using idx_notifications_pending on notifications
              (cost=0.42..16142.28 rows=119983 width=118) (actual time=0.041..0.402 rows=100 loops=1)
Execution Time: 1.281 ms

4,212 ms to 1.3 ms, 10.7 million buffers to 116, and no Sort node because the index is already in created_at order within the pending set. The index is 3.1 MB.

PostgreSQL example — partial unique indexes

The other killer use: uniqueness that only applies to some rows. A plain UNIQUE constraint cannot express "one active address per user" or "one open cart per user", because the historical rows must be allowed to duplicate.

-- One primary address per user, but any number of non-primary ones
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_addresses_one_primary
  ON addresses (user_id) WHERE is_primary;

-- One open cart per user; closed carts accumulate forever
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_carts_one_open
  ON carts (user_id) WHERE status = 'OPEN';

-- One non-deleted review per (user, product); soft-deleted rows may repeat
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_reviews_active
  ON reviews (user_id, product_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

The last one is worth dwelling on. With a plain UNIQUE (user_id, product_id), a user who deletes a review can never write another one for that product, because the soft-deleted row still occupies the key. With the partial unique index, soft-deleted rows fall out of the index entirely and the user can review again. This is the correct pattern for soft delete plus uniqueness, and it is a five-line migration that replaces a page of application-level checking.

Test it:

INSERT INTO carts (user_id, status) VALUES (41, 'OPEN');
INSERT INTO carts (user_id, status) VALUES (41, 'OPEN');
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "uq_carts_one_open"
DETAIL:  Key (user_id)=(41) already exists.
UPDATE carts SET status = 'CHECKED_OUT' WHERE user_id = 41;
INSERT INTO carts (user_id, status) VALUES (41, 'OPEN');   -- succeeds

TypeORM example

TypeORM's @Index supports a where option, and it does emit a partial index:

@Entity('reviews')
@Index('uq_reviews_active', ['userId', 'productId'], {
  unique: true,
  where: '"deleted_at" IS NULL',   // raw SQL fragment, quoted column names
})
export class Review { /* ... */ }

Two warnings. First, the where string is raw SQL and must match the database column names, not the entity property names. Second, TypeORM's schema differ compares the predicate as text, so a whitespace difference between your entity and the database makes it want to drop and recreate the index on every synchronize run. On any table above a few million rows, define partial indexes in migrations only.

Sequelize example

await queryInterface.addIndex('reviews', ['user_id', 'product_id'], {
  name: 'uq_reviews_active',
  unique: true,
  where: { deleted_at: null },   // Sequelize translates this to WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
});

Sequelize accepts a where object and converts it. For anything more complex than equality and IS NULL, drop to queryInterface.sequelize.query with the DDL.

Production scenario

A payments reconciliation table with 212 million rows and 900 rows in the NEEDS_REVIEW state. The full (status) index was 4.6 GB and the review queue query took 900 ms. The partial index is 44 KB, the query takes 0.3 ms, and the index has never left the buffer cache since it was created.

Failure scenario

An engineer created CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status = 'PENDING' and then, three months later, someone "improved" the worker query to WHERE status != 'SENT' AND status != 'FAILED'. Semantically identical for the two-value enum in use. The planner could not prove the implication, the partial index became invisible, and the query fell back to the 4.2 second bitmap plan. The queue backed up to 3 million messages over a weekend. The predicate in the query must textually imply the predicate in the index. Add a plan assertion test so this fails in CI, not in production.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Predicate mismatch, as above. The number one cause of "my partial index is not used".
  • A parameterised predicate: WHERE status = $1 cannot match WHERE status = 'PENDING' even when $1 is 'PENDING', because the proof happens at plan time. If the planner has the value (custom plan), it can; with a generic plan it cannot. This is a real trap with prepared statements (19.24).
  • The predicate must be immutable-ish: WHERE created_at > now() - interval '30 days' is rejected, because now() is not immutable. A rolling window cannot be a partial index predicate. Use a boolean column maintained by the application, or partitioning.
  • Partial unique indexes are not constraints: they cannot be the target of a foreign key, and ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT does not work (you must use ON CONFLICT (cols) WHERE pred).
  • ANALYZE collects statistics for the table, not the partial index's subset, so estimates for the partial predicate can still be poor.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Whenever they see a query with a constant, low-cardinality filter that selects a small slice, they reach for a partial index before a composite one. They check the pg_stat_statements query text against the index predicate character by character. And they use partial unique indexes as the default answer to "we need uniqueness but only sometimes", instead of application-level checks that lose every race.

Common mistakes

  • Indexing (status, created_at) fully when only one status is ever queried.
  • Writing the query predicate differently from the index predicate.
  • Trying to use now() in the predicate.
  • Forgetting that ON CONFLICT needs the matching WHERE clause for a partial unique index.

Interview questions

  1. When would you choose a partial index over a composite one? Expected: a small, constant-defined slice of a large table; queue tables, soft delete, rare states.
  2. How do you enforce "one open cart per user" with historical carts? Expected: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... (user_id) WHERE status = 'OPEN'.
  3. Why can't the predicate use now()? Expected: immutability; index contents would depend on evaluation time.
  4. Your partial index is not being used. Name three causes. Expected: predicate does not imply, generic plan with a parameter, stale statistics making a seq scan look cheaper.

Practical exercise

Build notifications with 20 million rows of which 5,000 are PENDING. Create the full (status, created_at) index and the partial one. Record both sizes with pg_relation_size, both plans, and the insert throughput of 100,000 rows with each index present. Then change the worker query to status <> 'SENT' and capture the plan again. Acceptance criteria: sizes, three plans, and a one-line rule about predicate matching.

19.7 Unique indexes and constraints

19.7.1 The same mechanism, two names, and a race-condition guard

Concept

A UNIQUE constraint in PostgreSQL is implemented by a unique index. When you write ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_users_email UNIQUE (email), PostgreSQL creates a unique B-tree named uq_users_email and records a constraint entry pointing at it. There is no separate enforcement mechanism.

The differences are administrative, not behavioural:

UNIQUE constraint CREATE UNIQUE INDEX
Appears in information_schema.table_constraints Yes No
Can be referenced by a foreign key Yes No
Supports partial (WHERE) No Yes
Supports expressions (lower(email)) No Yes
Can be created with CONCURRENTLY Not directly Yes
ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT name Yes No (use ON CONFLICT (cols))

Why does it exist?

Because application-level uniqueness checks are always wrong under concurrency. "Select to see if the email exists, then insert" has a window between the two statements, and at 200 requests per second that window is hit several times a day. The database is the only place where uniqueness can be enforced atomically, because the unique index insert and the heap insert happen in one atomic operation with the index page locked.

How it works

On insert, the executor descends the unique index to the insertion point. If a matching key exists and the owning transaction has committed, it raises 23505 unique_violation. If the owning transaction is still in flight, the inserter waits on that transaction (this is one of the few places a plain INSERT blocks), then either fails or proceeds depending on whether the other transaction commits or rolls back.

That wait is why ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING under high concurrency still serialises briefly on the same key: it is a correct, cheap serialisation point, and it is exactly the guarantee you want.

PostgreSQL example — the idempotency guard

The single most valuable use of a unique index in a backend system is not data hygiene, it is race-condition and duplicate-request protection:

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  provider_ref  text NOT NULL,
  status        text NOT NULL,
  amount_cents  integer NOT NULL,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- The provider's reference is globally unique. Two webhook deliveries cannot both insert.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_payments_provider_ref ON payments (provider_ref);

-- One captured payment per order, but failed attempts may repeat
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_payments_one_capture
  ON payments (order_id) WHERE status = 'CAPTURED';

And the insert that turns a duplicate into a no-op instead of a 500:

INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider_ref, status, amount_cents)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'CAPTURED', $3)
ON CONFLICT (provider_ref) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;

Zero rows returned means "already processed". For the partial unique index the syntax must include the predicate so PostgreSQL can identify the arbiter index:

INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider_ref, status, amount_cents)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'CAPTURED', $3)
ON CONFLICT (order_id) WHERE status = 'CAPTURED' DO NOTHING;

Omit the WHERE and you get ERROR: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification.

NestJS example

Catch the constraint violation by code, never by parsing the message string:

// payments.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, QueryFailedError } from 'typeorm';

const UNIQUE_VIOLATION = '23505';

@Injectable()
export class PaymentsService {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async capture(orderId: string, providerRef: string, amountCents: number) {
    try {
      const [row] = await this.ds.query(
        `INSERT INTO payments (order_id, provider_ref, status, amount_cents)
         VALUES ($1, $2, 'CAPTURED', $3)
         ON CONFLICT (provider_ref) DO NOTHING
         RETURNING id`,
        [orderId, providerRef, amountCents],
      );
      if (!row) return { duplicate: true };            // webhook redelivery, already handled
      return { duplicate: false, paymentId: row.id };
    } catch (e) {
      // Hits uq_payments_one_capture: a different provider_ref already captured this order
      if (e instanceof QueryFailedError && (e.driverError as { code?: string }).code === UNIQUE_VIOLATION) {
        throw new ConflictException('Order already captured');
      }
      throw e;
    }
  }
}

Edge cases & failure modes

  • NULL is not equal to NULL in a unique index, so UNIQUE (user_id, deleted_at) allows unlimited rows with deleted_at IS NULL. That trick is a classic and a trap: it works, but PG 15+ UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes the behaviour, and a partial unique index expresses the intent far more clearly.
  • A unique index on a soft-deleted table blocks re-creation; use the partial form.
  • ON CONFLICT requires the exact arbiter columns and predicate.
  • Adding a unique index to an existing table with duplicates fails; deduplicate first, and use CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY then ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX name to attach it as a constraint without a long lock.
  • Unique index inserts on the same key serialise; a hot key (a shared idempotency value) becomes a contention point.

Interview questions

  1. What is the relationship between a unique constraint and a unique index? Expected: the constraint is implemented by the index; differences are catalogue and capability, not enforcement.
  2. How do you add a unique constraint to a 200 million row table without blocking writes? Expected: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX.
  3. How do you make a webhook handler idempotent at the database level? Expected: unique index on the provider reference plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING.
  4. How do you keep uniqueness with soft deletes? Expected: partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

19.8 Expression indexes

19.8.1 Indexing what you query, not what you store

Concept

An expression index (also called a functional index) stores the result of an expression as the key: lower(email), (attributes->>'sku'), date_trunc('day', created_at). It exists because any function applied to a column in a WHERE clause defeats a normal index. WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com' cannot use an index on email, because the index holds 'A@B.com' and the planner has no way to invert lower.

Mental model

The phone book is sorted by surname as written: "MacDonald", "Macdonald", "macdonald" all in different places. If you always search case-insensitively, you need a second book sorted by the lowercased surname. You cannot make the first book answer the question.

How it works

  1. CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)) evaluates lower(email) for every row at build time and stores the results as keys.
  2. On insert and update, the expression is evaluated again. A costly expression makes your inserts costly.
  3. The expression must be IMMUTABLE: same input, same output, forever. lower() is immutable. now(), random() and timestamptz-to-date casts (which depend on TimeZone) are not. PostgreSQL refuses non-immutable expressions: ERROR: functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE.
  4. The planner matches the query's expression against the index's expression structurally. lower(email) matches lower(email). It does not match lower(email || '') or upper(email), and email ILIKE 'a@b.com' does not match either (that needs pg_trgm, 19.11).
  5. Bonus: ANALYZE collects statistics for the expression, which often fixes estimate errors that were the real problem all along.

PostgreSQL example

Three expression indexes you will actually build:

-- 1. Case-insensitive unique login. Both the lookup and the uniqueness.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email));

-- 2. A jsonb attribute promoted to a first-class lookup key.
CREATE INDEX idx_products_sku_attr ON products ((attributes->>'sku'));

-- 3. Daily rollup grouping. date_trunc on timestamptz needs an explicit zone to be immutable.
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_day
  ON orders ((date_trunc('day', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')));

Note the double parentheses in 2 and 3: PostgreSQL requires them around any expression that is not a bare function call.

Before, on 8 million users:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'anna.schmidt@example.com';
Gather  (cost=1000.00..164882.44 rows=40000 width=8) (actual time=141.884..1284.221 rows=1 loops=1)
  Workers Planned: 2  Workers Launched: 2
  ->  Parallel Seq Scan on users  (cost=0.00..159882.44 rows=16667 width=8)
                                  (actual time=821.114..1272.884 rows=0 loops=3)
        Filter: (lower(email) = 'anna.schmidt@example.com'::text)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 2666666
        Buffers: shared hit=8214 read=132963
Execution Time: 1284.402 ms

Two things to notice beyond the 1.28 seconds. First, rows=40000 estimated for a query that returns 1: with no statistics on the expression, the planner used its 0.5 percent default for an unknown function. Second, Rows Removed by Filter: 2,666,666 per worker.

After CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email)); ANALYZE users;:

Index Scan using uq_users_email_lower on users  (cost=0.56..8.58 rows=1 width=8)
                                                (actual time=0.038..0.039 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (lower(email) = 'anna.schmidt@example.com'::text)
  Buffers: shared hit=4 read=1
Execution Time: 0.058 ms

rows=1 estimated and 1 actual: the ANALYZE after creating the index built statistics for the expression, so the planner now knows the expression is unique. 1,284 ms to 0.058 ms, and a correctness bonus (the unique index makes duplicate-case signups impossible).

For the jsonb one, the same shape:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE attributes->>'sku' = 'DK-9928-XL';
Index Scan using idx_products_sku_attr on products  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=48)
                                                    (actual time=0.041..0.042 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: ((attributes ->> 'sku'::text) = 'DK-9928-XL'::text)
  Buffers: shared hit=4
Execution Time: 0.061 ms

Down from a 210 ms sequential scan of 52,000 pages. This is usually a better answer than a GIN index when you always query one known key; GIN is for when the queried key varies (19.11).

TypeORM and Sequelize

Neither ORM can declare an expression index on an entity. TypeORM's @Index takes column names or a raw synchronize: false escape hatch, and Sequelize's fields accepts { name, ... } for columns only. Write them in migrations:

// TypeORM migration
await queryRunner.query(
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email))`,
);
// Sequelize migration
await queryInterface.sequelize.query(
  `CREATE INDEX idx_products_sku_attr ON products ((attributes->>'sku'))`,
);

And make sure the ORM query actually emits the expression. TypeORM's where: { email: value } emits email = $1, not lower(email) = $1. You need a query builder:

await this.ds.getRepository(User)
  .createQueryBuilder('u')
  .where('lower(u.email) = lower(:email)', { email })   // matches the index
  .getOne();

Careful: lower(:email) on the right side is fine (it is a constant folded at plan time), but lower(u.email) = :email with an un-lowercased parameter is a silent correctness bug. Normalise in the application and index the expression.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Non-immutable expressions rejected: date_trunc('day', created_at) on a timestamptz is stable, not immutable, unless you pin the zone with AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'.
  • A custom function must be declared IMMUTABLE and must actually be immutable. Marking a mutable function immutable to get past the error produces an index that silently returns wrong answers, and the corruption survives REINDEX only if you fix the function.
  • The expression must match textually-equivalent structure; lower(trim(email)) and lower(email) are different indexes.
  • Expression evaluation cost is paid on every insert and every non-HOT update.
  • citext is an alternative to lower(email): a case-insensitive text type that works with a normal index. It is convenient and slightly slower, and it changes comparison semantics everywhere the column is used.

Interview questions

  1. Why does WHERE lower(email) = $1 not use an index on email? Expected: the index stores the raw value; functions are not invertible for the planner.
  2. What does IMMUTABLE mean and why does an index need it? Expected: deterministic for the same input; otherwise stored keys stop matching recomputed ones and lookups silently miss rows.
  3. When would you use an expression index on jsonb instead of GIN? Expected: when one known key is always queried; smaller, cheaper, supports ordering and uniqueness.
  4. What extra benefit do you get from ANALYZE after creating an expression index? Expected: statistics for the expression, fixing the planner's default-selectivity guess.

Practical exercise

On an 8 million row users table, measure WHERE lower(email) = $1 before and after an expression index, capturing the estimated rows in both plans. Then create a deliberately wrong index on upper(email) and confirm the query does not use it. Finally, try to create an index on date_trunc('day', created_at) without AT TIME ZONE and record the exact error. Acceptance criteria: three plans, one error message, and a paragraph on immutability.

19.9 Covering indexes and INCLUDE

19.9.1 Index-only scans and the visibility map

Concept

An index covers a query when every column the query needs is available from the index, so the heap never has to be read. The plan node is called an Index Only Scan. Since PostgreSQL 11 you can add non-key columns with INCLUDE:

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created_inc
  ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (status, total_cents);

user_id and created_at are key columns: sorted, seekable, usable in Index Cond. status and total_cents are payload: stored only in the leaf pages, not sorted, not seekable, but available to satisfy the SELECT list.

Why does it exist?

The heap fetch is the expensive half of an index scan. Reading 200 rows through an index means up to 200 random page reads across a 30 GB file. If the index already holds everything the query returns, those 200 reads disappear and the query costs only the index pages, which are dense and usually cached.

INCLUDE exists because adding a column to the key has costs you may not want: it widens every internal page (shrinking fan-out and deepening the tree), it participates in uniqueness (so UNIQUE (a, b) is not the same constraint as UNIQUE (a) INCLUDE (b)), and it forces sort-order maintenance on a column you never sort by.

Mental model

The warehouse binder again. Normally the binder says "tracking 8829 -> aisle 12, shelf 4" and you walk to the shelf to read the parcel's weight. A covering binder also prints the weight next to the tracking number. If the only thing the caller ever asks is "how heavy is 8829?", you never leave the desk. INCLUDE is printing extra facts in the binder without re-sorting the binder by them.

How it works

The index does not know whether a row version is visible to your transaction; that information lives in the heap tuple header (Parts 7 and 181.7). So an index-only scan needs a shortcut, and the shortcut is the visibility map (VM): a tiny bitmap file, two bits per heap page, maintained by VACUUM. One bit means "every tuple on this page is visible to every current transaction".

flowchart TB
  q["SELECT status, total_cents WHERE user_id = 41"]
  idx["Index Only Scan on (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (status, total_cents)"]
  leaf["Leaf entry: user 41 | 2026-09-09 | PAID | 4200 | ctid (41022,17)"]
  vm{"Visibility map: is page 41022 all-visible?"}
  ok["Yes: return values from the index. Heap Fetches stays 0"]
  heap["No: read heap page 41022, check xmin/xmax, then return. Heap Fetches + 1"]
  vac["VACUUM sets the all-visible bit"]
  q --> idx --> leaf --> vm
  vm -->|"bit set"| ok
  vm -->|"bit clear"| heap
  vac --> vm
  1. The scan descends and reads a leaf entry.
  2. It checks the VM bit for the page the ctid points at. The VM for a 30 GB table is about 1 MB, so it is always in cache.
  3. Bit set: return the values straight from the index entry. No heap I/O.
  4. Bit clear: read the heap page, do the normal MVCC check, and increment Heap Fetches.

The consequence is blunt: index-only scans are only as good as your vacuum. On an append-only table that is vacuumed nightly, Heap Fetches is near zero. On a table where 5 percent of rows are updated every hour, most pages are not all-visible and the "index-only" scan reads almost as much heap as a normal index scan.

Practical example

The order list endpoint returns id, status, total_cents, created_at for a user. With (user_id, created_at DESC) the plan fetches 20 heap pages. With INCLUDE (id, status, total_cents) it fetches none. At 20 rows the difference is 0.12 ms versus 0.09 ms and not worth it. At LIMIT 500 for the "export my orders" screen it is 4.1 ms versus 0.6 ms. At the analytics query that sums 400,000 rows for one merchant it is 3.9 seconds versus 180 ms. Covering pays in proportion to rows returned.

PostgreSQL example

-- Before: key-only index
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT sum(total_cents) FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 918273 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01';
Aggregate  (cost=4218.44..4218.45 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=41.884..41.885 rows=1 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=1204 read=811
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_user_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..4201.02 rows=6968 width=4) (actual time=0.061..40.114 rows=7021 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((user_id = 918273) AND (created_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00'))
        Buffers: shared hit=1204 read=811
Execution Time: 41.921 ms

7,021 rows, 2,015 buffers: 30 index pages plus roughly 1,985 heap pages, because this user's orders are spread across the 30 GB heap by creation time.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created_inc
  ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_cents);
VACUUM ANALYZE orders;
Aggregate  (cost=284.11..284.12 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=2.114..2.115 rows=1 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=41 read=3
  ->  Index Only Scan using idx_orders_user_created_inc on orders
        (cost=0.57..266.61 rows=6968 width=4) (actual time=0.048..1.402 rows=7021 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((user_id = 918273) AND (created_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00'))
        Heap Fetches: 0
        Buffers: shared hit=41 read=3
Execution Time: 2.148 ms

41.9 ms to 2.1 ms, 2,015 buffers to 44, Heap Fetches: 0. Now skip the vacuum and update 2 percent of the table:

  ->  Index Only Scan using idx_orders_user_created_inc on orders
        (cost=0.57..266.61 rows=6968 width=4) (actual time=0.052..28.884 rows=7021 loops=1)
        Heap Fetches: 5912
        Buffers: shared hit=1102 read=684
Execution Time: 28.912 ms

Same node type, most of the benefit gone. Check the health of the mechanism directly:

SELECT relname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid, 'vm')) AS vm_size,
       n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_stat_user_tables s ON s.relid = c.oid
WHERE relname IN ('orders', 'order_items');

INCLUDE versus a key column

Add to key (a, b, c) Add with INCLUDE (c)
Usable in Index Cond Yes No (appears as Filter)
Usable for ORDER BY c Yes No
Participates in UNIQUE Yes No
Stored in internal pages Yes (shrinks fan-out) No (leaf only)
Index size impact Larger, deeper Larger leaves only
Right tool for columns you filter or sort on columns you only SELECT

The UNIQUE row is the killer feature: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_orders_ref ON orders (order_ref) INCLUDE (user_id, status) enforces uniqueness on order_ref alone while letting the lookup return the other two columns without a heap fetch. You cannot do that by widening the key.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • SELECT * destroys covering. Any column not in the index forces the heap read. Covering indexes and SELECT * are mutually exclusive, and this is one of the strongest practical arguments for explicit column lists.
  • Wide INCLUDE payloads bloat the index; a 200-byte payload on 200M rows is 40 GB.
  • INCLUDE columns cannot be used in Index Cond, only as an after-the-fact Filter. That still avoids the heap fetch but does not reduce rows scanned.
  • On a hot-update table the visibility map is rarely set and the whole optimisation quietly evaporates. Tune autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor down for such tables (Parts 7 and 181.8).
  • Toasted INCLUDE values are stored inline in the index up to the limit and then rejected; do not INCLUDE a text body column.

Interview questions

  1. What is an index-only scan and what can prevent it? Expected: all columns in the index; visibility map bits not set; SELECT *.
  2. When is INCLUDE better than adding the column to the key? Expected: when the column is only selected, not filtered or sorted; keeps fan-out and keeps a UNIQUE key narrow.
  3. Heap Fetches: 5912 on an index-only scan. What do you do? Expected: vacuum the table; tune autovacuum for it.

19.10 Hash indexes

19.10.1 Equality only, and why B-tree usually still wins

Concept

A hash index stores hash(key) -> ctid in buckets. It supports exactly one operator: =. No ranges, no ordering, no LIKE, no multi-column keys, no unique constraints, no INCLUDE.

Before PostgreSQL 10 hash indexes were not WAL-logged, which meant they did not survive a crash and could not be used on replicas. That is fixed: since PG 10 they are crash-safe and replicated, and the implementation was substantially improved.

Why does it exist?

For a very wide key, a hash index is much smaller than a B-tree, because it stores a 4-byte hash instead of the full key. Indexing a 400-byte URL: the B-tree stores 400 bytes per entry and may refuse entries above 2,704 bytes; the hash index stores 4.

How it works

The key is hashed into a bucket number; the bucket is a page (with overflow pages when it fills). A lookup hashes, reads the bucket page, and scans its entries comparing hashes, then re-checks the actual value from the heap because hashes collide. Growth is handled by incremental bucket splitting.

When to use it, honestly

Situation Use hash? Why
Equality on a bigint or short text No B-tree is the same speed, plus ranges, plus ordering, plus uniqueness
Equality on a very long string (URLs, tokens over 100 bytes) Maybe Smaller index; but an expression index on md5(url) or hashtext(url) in a B-tree gives you the same size win plus everything else
Need UNIQUE No Hash indexes cannot enforce uniqueness
Need ORDER BY or ranges No Hash cannot
Need index-only scans No Hash does not support them

Real measurement on 8 million users with a 320-byte session_url column: B-tree 3.1 GB, hash 268 MB, lookup 0.041 ms versus 0.038 ms. The size win is real; the speed difference is noise. And a B-tree on md5(session_url) is 512 MB with all the B-tree features intact.

PostgreSQL example

CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_token_hash ON sessions USING hash (token);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT user_id FROM sessions WHERE token = 'a3f9...';
Index Scan using idx_sessions_token_hash on sessions  (cost=0.00..8.02 rows=1 width=8)
                                                      (actual time=0.036..0.037 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (token = 'a3f9...'::text)
  Buffers: shared hit=3 read=1
Execution Time: 0.054 ms
-- This returns nothing useful: hash indexes cannot answer ranges or ordering
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE token > 'a' ORDER BY token;   -- Seq Scan + Sort

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know hash indexes exist, know they are safe since PG 10, and use them roughly once every few years, for a very wide equality-only key where the size difference is measured and material. Otherwise B-tree, every time, because optionality is worth more than 8 percent.

Interview questions

  1. When would you pick a hash index over a B-tree? Expected: very wide equality-only key where index size matters; note the md5() B-tree alternative.
  2. What changed for hash indexes in PostgreSQL 10? Expected: WAL logging, so crash-safe and replicated.
  3. Can a hash index enforce uniqueness or support index-only scans? Expected: no to both.

19.11 GIN indexes

19.11.1 Inverted indexes for jsonb, arrays, full text and trigrams

Concept

GIN stands for Generalized Inverted Index. A B-tree maps one key to one row. GIN maps one element inside a value to many rows. It is the structure behind every search engine: a dictionary of terms, and under each term a sorted list of the rows containing it (the posting list).

Use GIN when one column holds many searchable things: a jsonb document with many keys, a text[] of tags, a tsvector of words, or a string you want to search with LIKE '%substring%' via trigrams.

Why does it exist?

WHERE attributes @> '{"colour":"red"}' cannot use a B-tree, because the B-tree key would be the whole jsonb document and you are asking about one fragment of it. WHERE 'organic' = ANY(tags) has the same problem. WHERE name ILIKE '%toothbrush%' has it too: there is no prefix to seek on. Without GIN, all three are sequential scans over the whole table forever.

Mental model

The index at the back of a textbook. Not sorted by page; sorted by term, and under each term a list of page numbers: "mitochondria: 41, 88, 204, 391". Looking up two terms and intersecting their page lists is exactly how a GIN AND works.

flowchart TB
  subgraph Entries["GIN entry tree (B-tree of extracted keys)"]
    k1["colour:red"]
    k2["colour:blue"]
    k3["size:XL"]
    k4["brand:oral-b"]
  end
  p1["posting list: ctids 41, 88, 204, 391, 4022 ..."]
  p2["posting list: ctids 7, 19, 350 ..."]
  p3["posting tree (large): B-tree of ctids"]
  p4["posting list: ctids 88, 204 ..."]
  k1 --> p1
  k2 --> p2
  k3 --> p3
  k4 --> p4
  q["query: attributes contains colour red AND brand oral-b"] --> k1
  q --> k4
  p1 --> inter["intersect posting lists -> 88, 204"]
  p4 --> inter

How it works

  1. An extract function per data type turns one value into a set of keys. For jsonb with the default jsonb_ops, every key and every value becomes a key. For tsvector, every lexeme. For pg_trgm, every 3-character sequence.
  2. Those keys are stored in a B-tree (the entry tree). Under each key sits a posting list of ctids, compressed. When a key appears in very many rows, the posting list becomes a posting tree, a B-tree of its own.
  3. A query extracts keys the same way and walks the posting lists, intersecting or unioning them, producing a bitmap. GIN always produces a bitmap, so the plan is always Bitmap Index Scan plus Bitmap Heap Scan with a recheck. GIN cannot produce sorted output and cannot do index-only scans.
  4. Inserts are expensive. A single 30-key jsonb document means up to 30 entry-tree updates. To soften this, GIN has a pending list: with fastupdate = on (the default), new entries go into an unsorted pending list appended at the end of the index, and are merged into the main structure later by autovacuum or when the list exceeds gin_pending_list_limit (4 MB default).
  5. The pending list is a trade: inserts get fast, but queries must scan the entire pending list linearly in addition to the tree. A 4 MB pending list adds real latency to every search. And the merge, when it happens, is a latency spike on whichever unlucky insert triggers it.

The operator class matters

Type Operator class Supports Size
jsonb jsonb_ops (default) @>, ?, ?&, `? , @?, @@`
jsonb jsonb_path_ops @> and @? only 30 to 50 percent smaller, faster for @>
text[] array_ops (default) @>, <@, &&, = Moderate
tsvector tsvector_ops (default) @@ Moderate
text gin_trgm_ops (extension pg_trgm) LIKE, ILIKE, ~, % similarity Large: 3 trigrams per character

If your only jsonb query is containment (@>), use jsonb_path_ops. It is smaller and faster because it hashes whole paths instead of indexing keys and values independently.

PostgreSQL example — jsonb

400,000 products with a jsonb attributes column averaging 14 keys.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"brand":"Oral-B","type":"electric"}';

Before:

Seq Scan on products  (cost=0.00..64882.00 rows=400 width=48)
                      (actual time=0.412..884.221 rows=1182 loops=1)
  Filter: (attributes @> '{"type": "electric", "brand": "Oral-B"}'::jsonb)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 398818
  Buffers: shared hit=8214 read=43786
Execution Time: 884.311 ms
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs ON products USING gin (attributes jsonb_path_ops);
ANALYZE products;

After:

Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (cost=44.12..1682.44 rows=412 width=48)
                              (actual time=1.884..6.221 rows=1182 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (attributes @> '{"type": "electric", "brand": "Oral-B"}'::jsonb)
  Heap Blocks: exact=1121
  Buffers: shared hit=1140 read=12
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_products_attrs  (cost=0.00..44.02 rows=412 width=0)
                                               (actual time=1.681..1.681 rows=1182 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (attributes @> '{"type": "electric", "brand": "Oral-B"}'::jsonb)
        Buffers: shared hit=31
Execution Time: 6.284 ms

884 ms to 6.3 ms. Index sizes: jsonb_ops 218 MB, jsonb_path_ops 122 MB, for the same query performance on @>.

PostgreSQL example — full text and trigrams

-- Full text: maintain a tsvector column (generated, so it cannot drift)
ALTER TABLE products
  ADD COLUMN search_tsv tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name,'') || ' ' || coalesce(description,''))) STORED;

CREATE INDEX idx_products_tsv ON products USING gin (search_tsv);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, name, ts_rank(search_tsv, q) AS rank
FROM products, plainto_tsquery('english', 'electric toothbrush') q
WHERE search_tsv @@ q ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=1884.44..1884.49 rows=20 width=52) (actual time=8.114..8.121 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (cost=1884.44..1889.44 rows=2000 width=52) (actual time=8.112..8.116 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: (ts_rank(products.search_tsv, q.q)) DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 28kB
        ->  Nested Loop  (cost=28.11..1831.22 rows=2000 width=52) (actual time=0.884..7.402 rows=3104 loops=1)
              ->  Function Scan on plainto_tsquery q  (cost=0.25..0.26 rows=1 width=32) ...
              ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (cost=27.86..1811.96 rows=2000 width=52) ...
                    Recheck Cond: (search_tsv @@ q.q)
                    ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_products_tsv (actual time=0.641..0.641 rows=3104 loops=1)
Execution Time: 8.184 ms
-- Substring search: pg_trgm makes LIKE '%...%' indexable
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX idx_products_name_trgm ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%toothbrush%';
Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (cost=112.44..2104.88 rows=1840 width=48)
                              (actual time=3.114..11.884 rows=2211 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (name ~~* '%toothbrush%'::text)
  Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 41
  Heap Blocks: exact=1904
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_products_name_trgm  (cost=0.00..111.98 rows=1840 width=0)
                                                   (actual time=2.884..2.884 rows=2252 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (name ~~* '%toothbrush%'::text)
Execution Time: 11.921 ms

From a 210 ms sequential scan to 12 ms, and Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 41 shows the trigram index is approximate: it finds candidates, and the recheck applies the real ILIKE. That is expected and correct.

The insert-throughput cost, measured

products with 400,000 rows, inserting 100,000 more:

Indexes present Time WAL Per-row
B-tree on id only 3.1 s 62 MB 31 us
plus GIN jsonb_path_ops on attributes, fastupdate=on 11.4 s 214 MB 114 us
plus the same GIN with fastupdate=off 38.8 s 388 MB 388 us
plus GIN gin_trgm_ops on name as well 71.2 s 690 MB 712 us

A GIN index can make inserts 10 to 20 times more expensive. On notifications at 14,000 inserts per second, a GIN index on payload is simply not affordable. Tune it explicitly when you do use one:

ALTER INDEX idx_products_attrs SET (fastupdate = on, gin_pending_list_limit = 2048);  -- kB

Small gin_pending_list_limit means more frequent, smaller merges: lower query latency, more consistent insert latency. fastupdate = off means no pending list at all: queries never scan it, inserts pay full price. For a search table with heavy reads and batched writes, fastupdate = off plus batched loads is often the right shape.

NestJS example

// product-search.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class ProductSearchService {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /** Uses idx_products_tsv (GIN on the generated tsvector column). */
  async search(term: string, limit = 20) {
    return this.ds.query(
      `SELECT p.id, p.name, ts_rank(p.search_tsv, q) AS rank
         FROM products p, plainto_tsquery('english', $1) q
        WHERE p.search_tsv @@ q
          AND p.is_active
        ORDER BY rank DESC
        LIMIT $2`,
      [term, limit],
    );
  }

  /** Uses idx_products_attrs (GIN jsonb_path_ops). Containment only. */
  async byAttributes(filter: Record<string, unknown>, limit = 50) {
    return this.ds.query(
      `SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE attributes @> $1::jsonb LIMIT $2`,
      [JSON.stringify(filter), limit],
    );
  }
}

Note attributes @> $1::jsonb. If you build the filter with attributes->>'brand' = $1 instead, the GIN index is not used at all (that needs the expression index of 19.8). The operator you write decides which index can serve you.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GIN never returns sorted rows and never does index-only scans; an ORDER BY always adds a Sort.
  • The pending list making a "fast" index slow to query; watch gin_pending_list_limit and pg_stat_user_indexes.
  • jsonb_ops on documents with high-cardinality values (UUIDs inside jsonb) exploding the entry tree.
  • gin_trgm_ops on short search terms: a 2-character search produces no full trigram and degrades to a scan. Enforce a minimum term length of 3 in the API.
  • GIN builds are slow and memory-hungry; raise maintenance_work_mem to 2 GB before building one on a large table.
  • A GIN index on a column nobody queries is the most expensive useless index you can have (19.17).

Interview questions

  1. What is an inverted index and why is GIN the right structure for jsonb and full text? Expected: term to posting list; one value contains many searchable elements.
  2. What is the GIN pending list and what does it trade? Expected: fast unsorted inserts against slower queries that must scan it; merged by autovacuum or at the limit.
  3. jsonb_ops versus jsonb_path_ops? Expected: full operator support and bigger, versus containment only and 30 to 50 percent smaller and faster.
  4. How do you make LIKE '%term%' fast? Expected: pg_trgm with gin_trgm_ops; the index is approximate and rechecked.
  5. Why might you refuse a GIN index on a hot write table? Expected: 10 to 20x insert cost and WAL amplification.

19.12 GiST indexes

19.12.1 Ranges, geometry, exclusion constraints and nearest neighbour

Concept

GiST is the Generalized Search Tree: a balanced tree where each internal node stores a predicate that is true for everything below it, rather than a sorted key. "Everything under this node is inside this bounding box." "Everything under this node falls within this time range."

That generality is why GiST is the index behind geometric types, range types (tstzrange, int4range), ltree, exclusion constraints, and nearest-neighbour ordering.

Why does it exist?

Some questions have no total order. "Which delivery zones contain this point?" and "which bookings overlap 14:00 to 16:00?" cannot be answered by sorting, because containment and overlap are not orderings. GiST answers them by descending only into subtrees whose predicate could still match, pruning the rest.

Mental model

A set of nested boxes. The outer box says "everything in here is somewhere in Germany". Inside are boxes for Hamburg, Berlin, Munich. Looking for a point in Berlin, you open the Germany box, skip Hamburg and Munich immediately because their boxes do not contain your point, and descend into Berlin. Boxes can overlap, which is why GiST sometimes descends into more than one subtree, and why GiST lookups are usually a little slower than B-tree lookups but answer questions B-trees cannot.

How it works

  1. Each data type provides seven support functions: consistent (could this subtree match?), union (bounding predicate for a set), penalty (cost of adding an entry here), picksplit (how to divide a full page), and others.
  2. Insert descends by minimum penalty, which keeps bounding predicates tight.
  3. Search descends into every child whose consistent returns true. Overlapping bounding boxes mean multiple descents, so GiST is not a strict logarithmic guarantee.
  4. Nearest neighbour: GiST supports ORDER BY column <-> value LIMIT k natively, walking the tree in distance order. This is the KNN feature and it is genuinely special: no other index type gives you "20 nearest stores" without scanning.

PostgreSQL example — the non-overlapping booking constraint

The most valuable GiST feature for a backend engineer is the exclusion constraint: a database-enforced guarantee that no two rows overlap. This is how you make double-booking structurally impossible instead of hoping your application locking is right.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;   -- lets scalar equality join a GiST constraint

CREATE TABLE delivery_slots (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  courier_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  during      tstzrange NOT NULL,
  order_id    bigint REFERENCES orders(id),
  -- No two slots for the SAME courier may overlap in time.
  EXCLUDE USING gist (courier_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
);

courier_id WITH = needs btree_gist, because plain GiST has no equality operator class for bigint. The constraint creates a GiST index automatically.

INSERT INTO delivery_slots (courier_id, during)
VALUES (41, tstzrange('2026-09-09 14:00+00', '2026-09-09 16:00+00'));

INSERT INTO delivery_slots (courier_id, during)
VALUES (41, tstzrange('2026-09-09 15:00+00', '2026-09-09 17:00+00'));
ERROR:  conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "delivery_slots_courier_id_during_excl"
DETAIL:  Key (courier_id, during)=(41, ["2026-09-09 15:00:00+00","2026-09-09 17:00:00+00")) 
         conflicts with existing key (courier_id, during)=(41, ["2026-09-09 14:00:00+00","2026-09-09 16:00:00+00")).

Two concurrent transactions attempting overlapping inserts: the second waits on the first and then fails. No application lock, no race, no lost booking. Compare that to the read-check-insert pattern, which loses under concurrency every time (Part 20 — Database Transactions covers why).

The overlap query itself:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, order_id FROM delivery_slots
WHERE courier_id = 41 AND during && tstzrange(now(), now() + interval '2 hours');
Index Scan using delivery_slots_courier_id_during_excl on delivery_slots
    (cost=0.28..8.44 rows=3 width=16) (actual time=0.041..0.044 rows=2 loops=1)
  Index Cond: ((courier_id = 41) AND (during && tstzrange(now(), (now() + '02:00:00'::interval))))
  Buffers: shared hit=4
Execution Time: 0.061 ms

PostgreSQL example — nearest neighbour

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS cube;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS earthdistance;

CREATE INDEX idx_stores_location ON stores USING gist (ll_to_earth(lat, lon));

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, name FROM stores
ORDER BY ll_to_earth(lat, lon) <-> ll_to_earth(53.5511, 9.9937)
LIMIT 10;
Limit  (cost=0.28..12.44 rows=10 width=40) (actual time=0.102..0.288 rows=10 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using idx_stores_location on stores  (cost=0.28..3821.44 rows=3140 width=40)
                                                      (actual time=0.101..0.284 rows=10 loops=1)
        Order By: (ll_to_earth(lat, lon) <-> '(3785.4, 663.1, 5107.2)'::earth)
        Buffers: shared hit=12
Execution Time: 0.311 ms

Order By: inside an index scan node, not a separate Sort. That is KNN.

When GiST versus GIN for text search

Both index tsvector. GIN is 2 to 3 times faster for search and 3 times slower to build and update. GiST is lossy (it stores a signature, so every hit needs a heap recheck) and therefore slower to query but cheaper to maintain. Default to GIN for text search; consider GiST only when the table has very heavy write volume and modest search volume. For range types and geometry there is no choice: GiST (or SP-GiST for non-overlapping partitioned spaces like IP prefixes and quadtrees).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GiST index quality depends on the picksplit implementation; badly overlapping bounding boxes make searches degenerate toward scanning.
  • btree_gist is required for scalar equality inside an exclusion constraint, and it is an extension you must install in every environment including CI.
  • Exclusion constraints cannot be created with CONCURRENTLY directly; build the index concurrently and then attach with ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX (which works for unique, and for exclusion requires a plain ADD CONSTRAINT, so plan a maintenance window).
  • KNN ordering with a WHERE that is not indexable can still scan.
  • GiST on tstzrange with unbounded ranges ([x,)) makes bounding predicates useless.

Interview questions

  1. How does GiST differ structurally from a B-tree? Expected: internal nodes hold predicates, not sorted keys; search descends every possibly-matching child.
  2. How do you prevent double-booking at the database level? Expected: EXCLUDE USING gist (resource WITH =, during WITH &&) plus btree_gist.
  3. GIN or GiST for full-text search, and why? Expected: GIN for query speed, GiST for cheaper maintenance and lossy signatures.
  4. What is a KNN index scan? Expected: ORDER BY col <-> point LIMIT k served by walking the GiST tree in distance order.

19.13 BRIN indexes

19.13.1 Three megabytes for nine hundred million rows

Concept

BRIN is Block Range INdex. Instead of one entry per row, it stores one small summary per range of heap pages (128 pages by default, so 1 MB of heap). For each range it records the minimum and maximum value of the indexed column.

A query for created_at BETWEEN X AND Y reads the tiny BRIN index, collects the ranges whose min/max overlap [X, Y], and scans only those heap pages. Everything else is skipped without being read.

Why does it exist?

Because for append-only time-series data, a B-tree is absurd overkill. notifications has 1.2 billion rows; a B-tree on created_at is 36 GB and must be maintained on every insert. A BRIN index on the same column is 4 MB and costs almost nothing to maintain, because an insert into the last page range usually just widens that range's max value.

Mental model

A library where books were shelved strictly in the order they arrived. You do not need a card catalogue with one card per book. You need a sign at the end of each shelf saying "this shelf: January 3rd to January 9th". To find everything from January 5th you read the signs, ignore 4,000 shelves, and walk the two that could contain it. The signs fit on one page.

flowchart TB
  subgraph BRIN["BRIN index: one summary per 128 heap pages"]
    r1["range 0 (pages 0-127): min 2024-01-01  max 2024-01-02"]
    r2["range 1 (pages 128-255): min 2024-01-02  max 2024-01-03"]
    r3["range 2871 (pages 367488-367615): min 2026-09-08  max 2026-09-09"]
  end
  q["WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-08'"]
  q -->|"min/max does not overlap: skip"| r1
  q -->|"min/max does not overlap: skip"| r2
  q -->|"overlaps: scan these 128 pages"| r3
  r3 --> heap["Bitmap Heap Scan of 128 pages, recheck each row"]

How it works

  1. CREATE INDEX ... USING brin (col) walks the heap and records min/max per block range (pages_per_range, default 128).
  2. Inserts into the last range update its summary in place. Inserts into an already-summarised earlier range desummarise nothing; the range just widens, which is why out-of-order data destroys BRIN effectiveness.
  3. New pages beyond the summarised area are not indexed until brin_summarize_new_values() runs or autovacuum summarises them (autosummarize = on, off by default, and you almost always want it on).
  4. A query builds a bitmap of candidate page ranges and hands it to a bitmap heap scan, which rechecks every row. BRIN is always lossy: it tells you which pages might match, never which rows.

Correlation is everything. pg_stats.correlation for the column is the number that decides whether BRIN works:

correlation Meaning BRIN verdict
0.99 to 1.0 Physical order matches value order (append-only created_at) Excellent
0.7 to 0.95 Mostly ordered, some churn Usable, more pages scanned
under 0.5 Values scattered across the heap Useless: every range's min/max spans everything
user_id on any real table Random Never 
SELECT attname, correlation, n_distinct
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'notifications' AND attname IN ('created_at', 'user_id');
  attname   | correlation | n_distinct
------------+-------------+------------
 created_at |    0.999812 |         -1
 user_id    |    0.000411 |    7982114

created_at at 0.9998 is a perfect BRIN candidate. user_id at 0.0004 would produce an index where every single range says "min 1, max 7,982,114", matching everything, scanning the whole table plus the index.

PostgreSQL example

900 million rows in a partition-free notifications table, indexed three ways:

CREATE INDEX idx_notif_created_btree ON notifications (created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_notif_created_brin  ON notifications USING brin (created_at) WITH (pages_per_range = 128, autosummarize = on);

SELECT indexrelname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE relname = 'notifications';
      indexrelname       |  size
-------------------------+---------
 idx_notif_created_btree | 27 GB
 idx_notif_created_brin  | 3520 kB

27 GB versus 3.4 MB. A factor of 7,800. Now the query, a one-day analytics window over that 210 GB table:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT count(*), kind FROM notifications
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-08' AND created_at < '2026-09-09'
GROUP BY kind;

With BRIN:

HashAggregate  (cost=1284402.11..1284402.14 rows=3 width=40)
               (actual time=2884.114..2884.221 rows=3 loops=1)
  Group Key: kind
  Buffers: shared hit=8214 read=118820
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on notifications  (cost=412.02..1264882.44 rows=3903934 width=32)
                                         (actual time=18.884..2214.882 rows=3884102 loops=1)
        Recheck Cond: ((created_at >= '2026-09-08 00:00:00+00') AND (created_at < '2026-09-09 00:00:00+00'))
        Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 412008
        Heap Blocks: lossy=127034
        Buffers: shared hit=8214 read=118820
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_notif_created_brin  (cost=0.00..411.02 rows=3903934 width=0)
                                                         (actual time=17.114..17.114 rows=1270340 loops=1)
              Index Cond: ((created_at >= '2026-09-08 00:00:00+00') AND (created_at < '2026-09-09 00:00:00+00'))
              Buffers: shared hit=440
Execution Time: 2884.402 ms

Read the key lines. The BRIN index scan itself cost 440 buffers and 17 ms on a 210 GB table. Heap Blocks: lossy=127034 means it identified 127,034 candidate pages out of 27.5 million: it skipped 99.5 percent of the table. Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 412,008 is the price of page granularity: it read some rows outside the window and threw them away, about 10 percent overhead.

With the B-tree the same query runs in 2,102 ms: about 27 percent faster, using 27 GB of storage and paying full B-tree insert cost on 14,000 inserts per second. For this workload BRIN is the right answer and it is not close.

Where BRIN dies:

CREATE INDEX idx_notif_user_brin ON notifications USING brin (user_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM notifications WHERE user_id = 918273;
Aggregate  (cost=27884102.44..27884102.45 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=98221.884..98221.885 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on notifications  (cost=8214.02..27883902.44 rows=80000 width=0)
                                         (actual time=214.114..98218.884 rows=41 loops=1)
        Recheck Cond: (user_id = 918273)
        Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1199999959
        Heap Blocks: lossy=27500000
Execution Time: 98221.902 ms

Every block range matched. It read the entire 210 GB table plus the index and threw away 1.2 billion rows. 98 seconds, slower than a plain sequential scan. That is what an uncorrelated BRIN index does.

Practical guidance

  • Use BRIN on append-only or time-partitioned tables where the indexed column tracks insertion order: created_at, event_time, a monotonically increasing id, or a partition key.
  • Always set autosummarize = on, or new data is not indexed until vacuum happens to run.
  • Tune pages_per_range: smaller (32) means a bigger, more precise index; larger (512) means smaller and coarser. 128 is a good default; drop to 32 if your ranges are wide because of moderate churn.
  • Check correlation before creating it and after any bulk reorganisation. CLUSTER or a partitioned rewrite can restore correlation.
  • BRIN plus CLUSTER is a real combination for cold archival tables: cluster on the column once, then BRIN is near-perfect.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Out-of-order inserts (backfills, late-arriving events) widening ranges and destroying selectivity, permanently, until REINDEX.
  • Updates moving rows to new pages, which does the same.
  • autosummarize off, so the newest data (the data everyone queries) is unindexed.
  • Using BRIN for a point lookup: never right.
  • Deleting old rows and reusing their pages for new rows, which scrambles correlation.

Interview questions

  1. How does BRIN differ from a B-tree in what it stores? Expected: min/max per block range versus one entry per row; lossy versus exact.
  2. What single statistic decides whether BRIN will work? Expected: pg_stats.correlation for the column.
  3. Give a case where BRIN is slower than a sequential scan. Expected: uncorrelated column; every range matches, so full scan plus index plus recheck.
  4. Why must autosummarize be on? Expected: otherwise new block ranges are unsummarised and excluded from the index until vacuum.

Practical exercise

Build a 50 million row notifications table with created_at strictly increasing. Create both a B-tree and a BRIN index on it, record both sizes, and run a one-day range query against each (isolate with DROP INDEX or enable_*). Then insert 5 million rows with created_at values scattered randomly across the whole history, re-run, and record how the BRIN plan degrades. Acceptance criteria: two size numbers, four plans, and the correlation value before and after the scattered insert.

19.14 Creating indexes in production

19.14.1 CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and what it costs you

Concept

CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock on the table. SHARE is compatible with reads and with other SHARE holders, and it conflicts with ROW EXCLUSIVE, which is what every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE takes. So a plain CREATE INDEX on orders blocks every write to that table for as long as the build takes. On 200 million rows that is 14 to 40 minutes.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (often written CIC) takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, which does not conflict with writes. Writes continue throughout. In exchange it does more work, takes roughly two to three times longer, and can fail in a way that leaves a broken index behind.

Why does it exist?

Because the alternative is a maintenance window, and modern products do not get maintenance windows for adding an index. Every index you add to a live table after launch must be added concurrently. There is no debate about this; the only question is whether you have the operational discipline the mechanism requires.

Mental model

Imagine re-cataloguing a library that stays open. The plain way: lock the doors, catalogue everything, unlock. Fast, correct, and nobody can borrow a book for forty minutes. The concurrent way: walk the shelves and write cards while people are borrowing and returning, then walk the shelves a second time to catch everything that moved while you were on the first pass, then wait until every borrower who started before you finished has left, and only then declare the catalogue trustworthy. Slower, more work, and if you trip over halfway you leave a half-written catalogue on the floor that someone must throw away.

How it works

flowchart TB
  s1["Phase 1: take SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, insert catalog row as INVALID and NOT READY, commit"]
  w1["Wait for all transactions that could still be using the old snapshot to finish"]
  s2["Phase 2: first heap scan, build the index from a snapshot, mark READY, commit"]
  w2["Wait again for all transactions started before phase 2 ended"]
  s3["Phase 3: second heap scan, add every tuple written during phase 2"]
  w3["Wait a third time for transactions that could still see the index as invalid"]
  s4["Mark the index VALID. Planner starts using it"]
  fail["Any failure or cancellation leaves an INVALID index that must be dropped"]
  s1 --> w1 --> s2 --> w2 --> s3 --> w3 --> s4
  s2 -.-> fail
  s3 -.-> fail
  w2 -.-> fail

The three critical properties:

  1. Two full table scans. That is why it is slower and why it generates roughly twice the I/O of a plain build.

  2. It waits for concurrent transactions, three times. Any long-running transaction anywhere in the database, including an idle-in-transaction session or a long analytics query on an unrelated table, blocks the wait. A CIC on a busy database can sit at 99 percent for twenty minutes waiting for one forgotten psql session. Kill it first:

    SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS age, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle' AND xact_start < now() - interval '2 minutes'
ORDER BY xact_start;

  3. It cannot run inside a transaction block. ERROR: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block. This is the single most common way it fails, because almost every migration framework wraps migrations in a transaction by default.

The INVALID index. If CIC fails or is cancelled, PostgreSQL leaves the index in the catalogue marked indisvalid = false. That index:

  • is not used by the planner for queries,
  • is still maintained on every insert and update, so you pay the entire write cost for zero benefit,
  • occupies disk,
  • and for a unique index, still enforces uniqueness, which can reject writes for a constraint nobody knows exists.

Find and clean them up:

SELECT c.relname AS index_name, t.relname AS table_name,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(c.oid)) AS size
FROM pg_index i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
JOIN pg_class t ON t.oid = i.indrelid
WHERE NOT i.indisvalid;
        index_name         | table_name |  size
---------------------------+------------+---------
 idx_orders_status_created | orders     | 4218 MB

The fix is always the same: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status_created; then retry. Never try to "repair" it; a REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on an invalid index is not guaranteed to help and PostgreSQL documents dropping and rebuilding as the correct action.

Practical example — the safe production recipe

-- 1. Belts first. Never let DDL queue behind, or ahead of, application traffic.
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
SET statement_timeout = 0;             -- the build itself must not be killed by a timeout
SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB';      -- big builds are 2 to 4 times faster with memory

-- 2. Check for long transactions that would stall the waits.
SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start < now() - interval '1 minute' AND state <> 'idle';

-- 3. Build.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_created
  ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

-- 4. Verify. This is not optional.
SELECT indisvalid, indisready FROM pg_index WHERE indexrelid = 'idx_orders_user_created'::regclass;

-- 5. Give the planner fresh statistics for the new index's expression, if any.
ANALYZE orders;

lock_timeout deserves a word. CIC needs a brief SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE at the start. If a long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE holder (another migration) is in front of it, CIC queues, and everything behind it queues too, including ordinary SELECTs, because the PostgreSQL lock queue is FIFO and does not let later-arriving compatible requests jump ahead. That is how a single index build takes an entire API down for four minutes without ever holding a conflicting lock itself. lock_timeout = '5s' makes the DDL give up instead of starting a pile-up. Part 23 — Database Migrations covers the general pattern; for indexes it is non-negotiable.

Timing on real hardware, orders at 200 million rows, maintenance_work_mem = 2GB, NVMe:

Operation Lock Duration Writes blocked
CREATE INDEX on (user_id, created_at) SHARE 11 min Yes, 11 min
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, same SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE 26 min No
Same, with maintenance_work_mem = 64MB SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE 71 min No
DROP INDEX ACCESS EXCLUSIVE under 1 s Yes, briefly, and blocks reads too
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE ~5 s No

Note the last two rows. DROP INDEX takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which blocks reads as well as writes. It is fast, but if it queues behind a 30-second query, every request to that table stacks up behind it for 30 seconds. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY with lock_timeout for anything on a hot table.

TypeORM example

TypeORM wraps each migration in a transaction by default, so CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside one fails. The fix is the static transaction = false property on the migration class:

// 1712004500000-AddOrdersUserCreatedIndexConcurrently.ts
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class AddOrdersUserCreatedIndexConcurrently1712004500000 implements MigrationInterface {
  // Tells TypeORM not to wrap this migration in BEGIN/COMMIT.
  // Without it: "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block"
  public transaction = false as const;

  public async up(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`SET lock_timeout = '5s'`);
    await queryRunner.query(`SET statement_timeout = 0`);
    await queryRunner.query(`SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB'`);
    await queryRunner.query(
      `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_orders_user_created
         ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC)`,
    );
    // Fail the migration loudly if the build ended up INVALID.
    const [{ ok }] = await queryRunner.query(
      `SELECT indisvalid AS ok FROM pg_index WHERE indexrelid = 'idx_orders_user_created'::regclass`,
    );
    if (!ok) throw new Error('idx_orders_user_created is INVALID; drop it and retry');
  }

  public async down(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS idx_orders_user_created`);
  }
}

Three details that matter. IF NOT EXISTS makes a retry after a partial failure idempotent only if you dropped the invalid index first, so keep the validity check. transaction = false means this migration is not atomic: if it does three things and the second fails, the first is not rolled back. Therefore a transaction = false migration must do exactly one thing. And statement_timeout = 0 is essential if your migration role inherits a timeout, because a 26-minute build will otherwise be cancelled at 30 seconds and leave you an invalid index every single time.

Sequelize example

Sequelize's addIndex supports concurrently: true. The transaction problem is the same, and Sequelize's umzug-based runners typically do not wrap migrations in a transaction unless you ask, but check yours:

// migrations/20260909120000-add-orders-user-created-index.js
module.exports = {
  async up(queryInterface) {
    await queryInterface.sequelize.query(`SET lock_timeout = '5s'`);
    await queryInterface.sequelize.query(`SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB'`);
    await queryInterface.addIndex('orders', {
      name: 'idx_orders_user_created',
      fields: ['user_id', { name: 'created_at', order: 'DESC' }],
      concurrently: true,          // emits CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
    });
  },
  async down(queryInterface) {
    await queryInterface.removeIndex('orders', 'idx_orders_user_created', { concurrently: true });
  },
};

If your runner does wrap in a transaction, disable it for this migration ({ transaction: undefined } in your own runner config, or run the DDL through a separate connection). Verify by looking at the actual error, not by hoping.

NestJS example

A startup guard that refuses to boot when an invalid or missing critical index is detected turns a silent performance cliff into a deploy failure:

// db-health.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationBootstrap } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

const REQUIRED_INDEXES = ['idx_orders_user_created', 'idx_notifications_pending'];

@Injectable()
export class DbHealthService implements OnApplicationBootstrap {
  private readonly log = new Logger(DbHealthService.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async onApplicationBootstrap() {
    const rows: { indexname: string; valid: boolean }[] = await this.ds.query(
      `SELECT c.relname AS indexname, i.indisvalid AS valid
         FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
        WHERE c.relname = ANY($1)`,
      [REQUIRED_INDEXES],
    );
    const found = new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.indexname, r.valid]));
    for (const name of REQUIRED_INDEXES) {
      if (!found.has(name)) throw new Error(`Missing required index ${name}`);
      if (!found.get(name)) throw new Error(`Index ${name} is INVALID; drop and rebuild`);
    }
    this.log.log(`Verified ${REQUIRED_INDEXES.length} required indexes`);
  }
}

Production scenario

A team ships index migrations in a dedicated pipeline stage that runs before the application deploy, on a role with statement_timeout = 0, lock_timeout = 5s, maintenance_work_mem = 2GB, and a pre-flight check that fails the pipeline if any transaction older than 60 seconds is running. Each migration adds exactly one index. Rollback is DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Nothing about the application deploy depends on the index existing, so a failed build does not block a release; it just gets retried.

Failure scenario

At 03:12 a nightly deploy runs CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on order_items (900 million rows). At 03:38 the pipeline's 30-minute job timeout fires and kills the connection. PostgreSQL leaves idx_order_items_product_created as INVALID, 18 GB on disk. Nobody notices, because no query got slower: the planner ignores invalid indexes. Two weeks later the team investigates why order_items insert throughput dropped 22 percent and why pg_wal grew. The invalid index has been maintained on every one of 4 million daily inserts, for zero benefit, for fourteen days. SELECT ... WHERE NOT indisvalid belongs in your monitoring, not in your incident retrospective.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CIC inside a transaction block: the framework default that bites everyone.
  • Long-running transactions stalling the three waits indefinitely; also, on a hot standby, a long query on the replica with hot_standby_feedback = on holds the primary's horizon and stalls CIC.
  • Invalid index left behind after failure, cancellation, deploy timeout, or a pg_terminate_backend.
  • CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY failing at the very end because of a duplicate that appeared during the build: you get an invalid index and no useful error location. Deduplicate first and add a partial unique guard if writes continue.
  • Disk: a CIC needs room for the full new index plus temp sort files. A 20 GB index build on a volume with 25 GB free will fill the disk and take down the primary.
  • Replication lag: the index build streams a lot of WAL. On a synchronous replica this directly slows every commit on the primary.
  • REINDEX and CIC on the same table conflict.
  • Partitioned tables: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY is not supported on a partitioned parent. Build on each partition concurrently, then CREATE INDEX ... ON ONLY parent and ALTER INDEX parent_idx ATTACH PARTITION child_idx for each.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat an index build as an operation with a blast radius, not as a schema edit. They know the exact lock each DDL takes and they set lock_timeout before every one. They run one index per migration. They check indisvalid afterwards and monitor for it continuously. And they build indexes on a replica-promoted staging copy first, so the duration is known before it happens in production.

Common mistakes

  • Plain CREATE INDEX on a live table.
  • Forgetting transaction = false and shipping a migration that cannot run.
  • A pipeline timeout shorter than the build.
  • Not checking indisvalid.
  • DROP INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a hot table during peak.
  • Leaving maintenance_work_mem at 64 MB, making every build three times longer than necessary.

Interview questions

  1. What lock does CREATE INDEX take and what does it block? Expected: SHARE; blocks all writes, allows reads.
  2. Walk me through what CONCURRENTLY does differently. Expected: two scans, three waits for concurrent transactions, weaker lock, can leave an invalid index.
  3. Why can't it run inside a transaction, and what does that mean for your migration tool? Expected: it commits between phases; TypeORM transaction = false, one statement per migration, no atomic rollback.
  4. You find an INVALID index. What is the impact and the fix? Expected: maintained on writes, unused by the planner, still enforces uniqueness if unique; DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and retry.
  5. How can an index build with a non-blocking lock still take your API down? Expected: FIFO lock queue behind an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE holder; lock_timeout prevents the pile-up.

Practical exercise

On a 20 million row table, run CREATE INDEX in one session while a script inserts rows in another; record how long the inserts block. Repeat with CONCURRENTLY. Then start a BEGIN; SELECT 1; in a third session, run CIC, and observe it stalling; record how long, and where in the process it waits. Finally kill a CIC halfway and produce the invalid-index detection query output. Acceptance criteria: three timings, one stall observation, and the invalid-index query result.

19.15 Index maintenance

19.15.1 Bloat, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, fillfactor and measuring size

Concept

Indexes decay. Deleted and updated rows leave dead entries that VACUUM marks reusable but rarely returns to the operating system. Page splits leave leaves half full. Over months a B-tree that should be 4 GB becomes 9 GB, and every scan reads twice the pages it needs to.

Bloat is the gap between the size an index has and the size it would have if rebuilt.

Why does it exist?

Because PostgreSQL's MVCC design (Parts 7 and 181.7) never removes anything in place, and because returning space to the OS would require rewriting the whole file under an exclusive lock. VACUUM's job is to make space reusable, not to shrink files. For a table that keeps growing this is fine, because the free space gets refilled.
