For an index whose key distribution has changed (a queue table that was once huge, a table after a mass delete), the free space is in the wrong places and never gets reused.

Mental model

A filing cabinet where removed files leave empty hanging folders. The cabinet is still four drawers wide even though it holds one drawer of paper. New files can go in the empty folders, but only if they sort into those exact positions. If all your new files are for surnames starting with Z and all your empty folders are under A to F, the cabinet keeps growing.

How it works — measuring

Start with plain sizes:

SELECT
  t.relname AS table_name,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(t.oid))          AS heap,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(t.oid))           AS indexes,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(t.oid))    AS total,
  round(100.0 * pg_indexes_size(t.oid) / nullif(pg_relation_size(t.oid), 0), 1) AS index_pct
FROM pg_class t
WHERE t.relkind = 'r' AND t.relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(t.oid) DESC
LIMIT 10;
 table_name    | heap   | indexes | total  | index_pct
---------------+--------+---------+--------+-----------
 notifications | 210 GB | 63 GB   | 273 GB |      30.0
 order_items   | 67 GB  | 41 GB   | 108 GB |      61.2
 orders        | 30 GB  | 19 GB   | 49 GB  |      63.3
 payments      | 26 GB  | 9 GB    | 35 GB  |      34.6
 reviews       | 9.8 GB | 4.1 GB  | 14 GB  |      41.8

index_pct above roughly 60 percent is a flag, not a verdict: on a lookup-heavy table it can be legitimate. Above 100 percent, you have more index than data and you should be reading 19.20.

Then per index, with the scan counts that tell you whether the size is earning anything:

SELECT
  s.indexrelname AS index_name,
  s.relname AS table_name,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size,
  s.idx_scan, s.idx_tup_read, s.idx_tup_fetch
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
WHERE s.relname = 'orders'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;
        index_name         | table_name |  size   | idx_scan  | idx_tup_read | idx_tup_fetch
---------------------------+------------+---------+-----------+--------------+---------------
 idx_orders_user_created   | orders     | 6142 MB | 411882014 |   8214402118 |    4102214882
 orders_pkey               | orders     | 4290 MB | 188204112 |    188204112 |     188204112
 idx_orders_status_created | orders     | 5104 MB |  41882014 |   2114882014 |    1024882014
 idx_orders_created_at     | orders     | 4212 MB |    118204 |   8214402118 |     820221488
 idx_orders_tenant_id      | orders     |  921 MB |         0 |            0 |             0

For real bloat estimation, pgstattuple measures it directly (it reads the whole index, so run it off-hours or on a replica):

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
SELECT * FROM pgstatindex('idx_orders_status_created');
 version | tree_level | index_size | root_block_no | internal_pages | leaf_pages | empty_pages |
 deleted_pages | avg_leaf_density | leaf_fragmentation
---------+------------+------------+---------------+----------------+------------+-------------+
       4 |          3 | 5352079360 |          412 |           2418 |     650800 |           0 |
         28114 |            42.11 |              31.44

avg_leaf_density: 42.11 is the number. A freshly built index at the default fillfactor = 90 has a density around 88 to 90. At 42 this index is holding less than half the entries it could, so it is roughly 2.1 times bigger than necessary: 5.1 GB where 2.4 GB would do. leaf_fragmentation: 31.44 means leaf pages are out of physical order, so range scans do more random I/O than they should.

Rules of thumb: rebuild when avg_leaf_density is under 50 to 60, or when the index is more than about 1.5 times the size of a freshly built copy, and the index is actually used.

How it works — rebuilding

-- The safe one. PG 12+. Builds a new index alongside, swaps it, drops the old.
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status_created;

-- All indexes on one table, concurrently
REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY orders;

-- The unsafe one: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole rebuild. Never on a live hot table.
REINDEX INDEX idx_orders_status_created;

REINDEX ... CONCURRENTLY behaves like CIC: weak lock, two passes, cannot run in a transaction, waits for concurrent transactions, and can leave an invalid index behind with a _ccnew suffix if it fails:

SELECT c.relname FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid WHERE NOT i.indisvalid;
      relname
---------------------------------
 idx_orders_status_created_ccnew

Drop those with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and retry. Also note the disk requirement: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY needs space for both copies at once, so rebuilding a 20 GB index needs 20 GB free plus sort space.

Before and after on that index:

before: 5104 MB, avg_leaf_density 42.11, range scan 88 ms, buffers read 11204
after:  2402 MB, avg_leaf_density 89.44, range scan 41 ms, buffers read 4881

Halving the pages roughly halves the buffers, which roughly halves the time on a cache-miss-bound scan. It also gives you 2.7 GB of shared_buffers competition back.

Fillfactor

fillfactor is how full a page is packed at build time.

Setting Default Effect
B-tree index fillfactor 90 Leaves 10 percent free in leaves for in-place growth. Lower it (70 to 80) for indexes on columns with heavy random inserts, to reduce page splits. Raise it (100) for read-only or append-only indexes to make them smaller and denser.
Table fillfactor 100 Leaves no free space, so an update must go to a new page and cannot be HOT. Lower it (85 to 90) on tables with frequent updates to non-indexed columns, so HOT updates stay possible. 
-- Append-only archive index: pack it tight
CREATE INDEX idx_events_created ON events_archive (created_at) WITH (fillfactor = 100);

-- Hot update table: leave room so HOT updates stay in page
ALTER TABLE inventory SET (fillfactor = 85);
VACUUM FULL inventory;   -- small table; rewrites with the new fillfactor

The inventory change is a real, measurable win: 400,000 rows updated constantly by stock movements. At fillfactor = 100, 71 percent of updates were non-HOT; at 85, 96 percent are HOT, index maintenance on updates dropped accordingly, and the table's bloat growth rate fell by two thirds.

Fillfactor only applies to new pages, so changing it requires a rewrite (VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER, REINDEX, or pg_repack) to take effect on existing data.

Production scenario

A monthly maintenance job, run from a scheduled worker on a Sunday morning, that reindexes only what needs it:

-- Candidates: used, large, and low density. Run pgstatindex only on the top 20 by size.
WITH big AS (
  SELECT s.indexrelid, s.indexrelname, s.idx_scan, pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) AS bytes
  FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
  WHERE pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) > 1024*1024*1024   -- over 1 GB
  ORDER BY bytes DESC LIMIT 20
)
SELECT b.indexrelname, pg_size_pretty(b.bytes) AS size, b.idx_scan,
       (pgstatindex(b.indexrelid::regclass)).avg_leaf_density
FROM big b
WHERE b.idx_scan > 0
ORDER BY 4 ASC;

Anything under 55 percent density gets a REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY, one at a time, with lock_timeout = '5s' and a check for invalid _ccnew leftovers afterwards. pg_repack is the alternative when you also need to compact the heap and cannot take VACUUM FULL's ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

Failure scenario

A notifications cleanup job deleted 800 million processed rows over a weekend. The heap did not shrink (expected: the space is reusable) and neither did the 27 GB created_at B-tree. But the queue index and the (user_id, created_at) index were now 85 percent dead entries in the old key ranges, while all new inserts landed at the right edge. avg_leaf_density was 14. Queries that read the newest data were fine; the nightly analytics range scans were reading five times the pages they needed and had gone from 40 minutes to 3 hours 20. REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY notifications over two nights returned 41 GB of disk and put the job back to 44 minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on a primary key or a constraint-backing index works in PG 12+, but the constraint's index name changes internally; verify the constraint afterwards.
  • Invalid _ccnew indexes after a failed reindex, doubling storage silently.
  • VACUUM FULL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and rewrites the whole table plus all indexes; on orders that is 49 GB of rewriting with the table completely unavailable. It is not a maintenance strategy, it is a last resort.
  • Reindexing an unused index: wasted I/O. Check idx_scan first.
  • Disk exhaustion mid-reindex, which on a primary means the database stops accepting writes.
  • Bloat estimation queries based on catalogue statistics (the popular pgsql-bloat-estimation queries) are approximations and can be off by 30 percent; pgstattuple is exact but expensive.
  • On a replica, pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan counts only the replica's own scans; primary and replica statistics are separate.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They trend index sizes over time in Grafana rather than measuring them once. They know that bloat is a symptom and the cause is usually an update pattern or a vacuum that cannot keep up (Parts 7 and 181.8), so they fix autovacuum settings before scheduling monthly reindexes. They never run VACUUM FULL on a production table without an agreed window. And they reindex the small number of indexes that are both bloated and used, not everything.

Common mistakes

  • Scheduling REINDEX (non-concurrent) as a cron job.
  • Believing DELETE shrinks anything.
  • Using VACUUM FULL for routine maintenance.
  • Reindexing an index with idx_scan = 0 instead of dropping it.
  • Not checking free disk before a reindex.
  • Ignoring fillfactor on a heavily updated table and then fighting the bloat forever.

Interview questions

  1. What is index bloat and how do you measure it? Expected: dead entries plus half-empty pages; pgstatindex.avg_leaf_density, size trending, pgstattuple.
  2. Difference between REINDEX, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY and VACUUM FULL? Expected: lock strength, online versus offline, table plus indexes versus index only, disk requirements.
  3. When do you lower table fillfactor and why? Expected: frequently updated tables, to preserve HOT updates and reduce index maintenance.
  4. A 6 GB index has idx_scan = 0 for 60 days. What do you do? Expected: verify across all replicas and after a stats reset, then DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY with a rollback plan.
  5. Why did a mass delete not free any disk? Expected: VACUUM makes space reusable, not returned; only a rewrite shrinks files.

Practical exercise

Create a 10 million row table with an index, delete 80 percent of the rows in a scattered pattern, run VACUUM, and record pg_relation_size and pgstatindex before and after. Then run REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY and record them again, along with the timing of a range scan at each stage. Finally, set the table fillfactor to 85, rewrite it, run 500,000 updates on a non-indexed column, and compare n_tup_hot_upd against the same test at fillfactor = 100. Acceptance criteria: a six-row measurement table and a written recommendation for your own busiest table.

19.16 Cardinality, selectivity and statistics

19.16.1 Why an index on a three-value column is usually useless

Concept

Two words decide whether an index will ever be used:

  • Cardinality: how many distinct values a column has. orders.id has 200,000,000 distinct values. orders.status has 6.
  • Selectivity: what fraction of the table a specific predicate returns. WHERE id = 42 selects 0.0000005 percent. WHERE status = 'PAID' selects 76 percent.

An index pays off when the predicate is selective. Not when the column has many distinct values, and not when the query "filters on something". Selectivity is about the specific value, which is why a single index can be perfect for one parameter and useless for another.

Why does it exist?

Because reading a row through an index costs more than reading a row in a sequential scan. Roughly: an index scan pays a tree descent plus one random heap page per row; a sequential scan pays one sequential page per ~51 rows and no descent. So there is a break-even fraction, and above it the sequential scan wins no matter how good your index is. The planner's job is to find that break-even, and your job is to know it exists.

Mental model

You want to find everyone in a 500-page phone book. Would you use the index at the back? Of course not, you would read the book. Now find one person: the index, obviously. Somewhere between "one person" and "everyone" the index stops being worth the page-flipping. For a real database on real storage that crossover is around 5 to 10 percent of rows, and it moves with random_page_cost, with the column's physical correlation, and with how wide the rows are.

How it works

The planner computes selectivity from pg_stats (Parts 7 and 181.9):

Statistic What it is How selectivity is derived
n_distinct Distinct values; negative means a ratio of rows = value on an unknown value: 1 / n_distinct
most_common_vals / most_common_freqs The top default_statistics_target values and their frequencies = value on a listed value: its exact frequency
histogram_bounds Equal-frequency buckets of the remaining values Range predicates: interpolate across buckets
null_frac Fraction of NULLs IS NULL selectivity
correlation -1 to 1, how well physical order matches value order Scales the cost of an index scan's heap fetches toward sequential

Look at them for the columns that matter:

SELECT attname, n_distinct, null_frac, correlation,
       most_common_vals::text[] AS mcv,
       most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname IN ('status','user_id','created_at','shipping_country');
    attname      | n_distinct | null_frac | correlation |                  mcv                    |        most_common_freqs
-----------------+------------+-----------+-------------+-----------------------------------------+----------------------------------
 status          |          6 |         0 |    0.612044 | {PAID,SHIPPED,PENDING,CANCELLED,REFUND_PENDING,CHARGEBACK} | {0.761,0.182,0.041,0.0116,0.0040,0.00004}
 user_id         |   -0.03991 |         0 |    0.001204 | {918273,41,102994}                      | {0.00021,0.00019,0.00018}
 created_at      |         -1 |         0 |    0.999841 |                                         |
 shipping_country|         14 |         0 |    0.041882 | {DE,AT,CH,NL,FR}                        | {0.612,0.144,0.101,0.061,0.040}

Read it carefully, because everything about indexing this table follows from these four rows.

  • status: 6 distinct values, and PAID is 76.1 percent of the table. An index on status alone can never help a status = 'PAID' query, because 152 million rows is not a needle. It can help status = 'CHARGEBACK' (0.004 percent, 8,000 rows). One column, one index, two completely different answers. This is why "low cardinality means no index" is a rule of thumb and not a law: what matters is the frequency of the value you query.
  • user_id: n_distinct = -0.03991 means 3.991 percent of the row count, so about 7,982,000 distinct users. Average 25 orders each. WHERE user_id = ? selects 0.0000125 percent. Perfect index candidate.
  • created_at: n_distinct = -1 (every value distinct) and correlation = 0.9998 (rows are physically in creation order). A range scan on it is nearly sequential, which is why the planner prices it cheaply and why BRIN works on it (19.13).
  • shipping_country: correlation = 0.04, so a DE index scan means truly random heap access across the whole 30 GB.

The rule of thumb. With random_page_cost = 1.1 on NVMe, an index scan tends to lose to a sequential scan somewhere around 8 to 12 percent of rows for a well-correlated column and around 3 to 5 percent for an uncorrelated one. With the default random_page_cost = 4 those numbers drop to about 2 percent and 0.5 percent, which is why unusable-index complaints are so often really random_page_cost complaints. The planner will typically prefer a bitmap scan across most of the middle range, because it converts random reads into sorted ones.

Correlated columns and CREATE STATISTICS. The planner multiplies selectivities of ANDed predicates as if the columns were independent. When they are not, the estimate collapses:

shipping_country = 'DE' AND currency = 'EUR' -> estimated 0.612 x 0.68 = 0.416 ... except every German order is in EUR, so the truth is 0.612. A 47 percent underestimate here is mild. The classic disaster is (city, postcode):

-- 8,400 cities, 41,000 postcodes; each postcode belongs to exactly one city
SELECT count(*) FROM addresses WHERE city = 'Hamburg' AND postcode = '20095';

Independence says (1/8400) x (1/41000) = 2.9e-9, so on 12 million addresses the planner estimates 1 row. The truth is 340. A factor of 340, and if this is the outer side of a join, the plan is a nested loop that runs 340 times instead of once, or worse, it feeds a join that expected 1 row and gets 340.

CREATE STATISTICS addresses_city_postcode (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv)
  ON city, postcode FROM addresses;
ANALYZE addresses;

dependencies teaches it "postcode implies city", ndistinct gives the true count of distinct combinations (41,000, not 8400 x 41,000), and mcv stores common pairs. The estimate becomes 338. Same for (shipping_country, currency) on orders, (product_id, category_id) on order_items, and any pair where one column functionally determines the other.

Check the effect:

SELECT stxname, stxkeys, stxddependencies, stxdndistinct
FROM pg_statistic_ext JOIN pg_statistic_ext_data d ON d.stxoid = pg_statistic_ext.oid;

Practical example

The support tool lets an agent filter orders by status. Product wants it fast. A developer adds CREATE INDEX ON orders (status). The index is 3.8 GB. Here is what it does for each status:

Status Rows Selectivity Plan chosen Time Index helped?
PAID 152,200,000 76.1% Parallel Seq Scan 21.4 s No, and it never will
SHIPPED 36,400,000 18.2% Parallel Seq Scan 20.9 s No
PENDING 8,200,000 4.1% Bitmap Heap Scan 6.2 s Marginally
CANCELLED 2,320,000 1.16% Bitmap Heap Scan 1.9 s Yes
REFUND_PENDING 800,000 0.40% Bitmap Heap Scan 0.7 s Yes
CHARGEBACK 8,000 0.004% Index Scan 12 ms Enormously

Three of the six values get nothing from a 3.8 GB index that costs write latency on every insert. The correct answer is not an index on status; it is partial indexes on the rare statuses plus composite indexes for the common ones:

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_chargeback ON orders (created_at DESC) WHERE status = 'CHARGEBACK';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_refund_pending ON orders (created_at DESC) WHERE status = 'REFUND_PENDING';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at DESC);

Total size: 3 MB + 280 MB + 5.1 GB, and every one of those bytes serves a query that could not be served otherwise. The status-only index is gone.

PostgreSQL example — proving the crossover

-- 0.004 percent: index scan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'CHARGEBACK';
Aggregate  (cost=8214.02..8214.03 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=11.884..11.885 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Index Only Scan using idx_orders_status_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..8194.02 rows=8004 width=0) (actual time=0.061..11.204 rows=8021 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (status = 'CHARGEBACK'::text)
        Heap Fetches: 0
        Buffers: shared hit=41 read=8
Execution Time: 11.921 ms
-- 18.2 percent: the planner refuses the index, correctly
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'SHIPPED';
Finalize Aggregate  (cost=3184402.11..3184402.12 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=20918.114..20924.882 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Gather ... Workers Launched: 2
        ->  Partial Aggregate  (cost=3183402.11..3183402.12 rows=1 width=8) ...
              ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..3145402.11 rows=15200000 width=0)
                                               (actual time=0.041..19882.114 rows=12133333 loops=3)
                    Filter: (status = 'SHIPPED'::text)
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 54533334
                    Buffers: shared hit=91204 read=3829829
Execution Time: 20924.921 ms

Force the index to see whether the planner was right:

SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'SHIPPED';
RESET enable_seqscan;
Aggregate  (cost=8912440.22..8912440.23 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=61884.114..61884.115 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Index Only Scan using idx_orders_status_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..8821440.11 rows=36400000 width=0) (actual time=0.084..58221.884 rows=36400000 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (status = 'SHIPPED'::text)
        Heap Fetches: 0
        Buffers: shared hit=112044 read=1918204
Execution Time: 61884.184 ms

61.9 seconds with the index, 20.9 seconds without. The planner was right by a factor of three, and this is even an index-only scan; a plain index scan would have been minutes. When someone says "the planner is ignoring my index", check this before assuming a bug.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Skewed columns where the average is meaningless. user_id averages 25 orders; one B2B account has 4.1 million. The plan chosen for the average user is a disaster for that one. Watch for pg_stat_statements max/mean ratios above 50.
  • default_statistics_target = 100 keeps only 100 MCVs. On a column with 400 meaningfully frequent values, values 101 to 400 all get the "average of the rest" estimate. Raise it per column: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN shipping_country SET STATISTICS 500; then ANALYZE.
  • Statistics stale after a bulk load. A 40 million row import with no ANALYZE leaves the planner thinking the table is empty. Always ANALYZE after a bulk load; autovacuum will get there eventually, and "eventually" is after your batch job has already run 200 bad plans.
  • n_distinct badly estimated on large tables, because it is sampled. If you know the truth, tell it: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN user_id SET (n_distinct = -0.04);
  • Partitioned tables need statistics on the parent for cross-partition plans; ANALYZE parent does that in PG 14+.
  • Correlation destroyed by an update-heavy pattern, quietly making previously cheap range scans expensive.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Before proposing an index they run SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE <predicate> for the typical and the worst parameter values and divide by the table size. If the worst case is above 10 percent, the index is not the answer; a different query, a rollup table, or a partial index is. They check pg_stats before believing any plan. And when a plan is bad they fix the estimate first, because a correct estimate often produces the right plan with no new index at all.

Common mistakes

  • Indexing booleans and enums with two or three values (the fix is almost always a partial index).
  • Assuming high cardinality means the index will be used, ignoring the specific value's frequency.
  • Never running ANALYZE after a bulk load.
  • Fighting the planner with hints instead of giving it extended statistics.

Interview questions

  1. Why is an index on a boolean column usually useless, and when is it not? Expected: selectivity near 50 percent; useful when one value is rare, and then a partial index is better.
  2. What fraction of a table makes a sequential scan win, and what changes it? Expected: roughly 5 to 10 percent; random_page_cost, correlation, row width, effective_cache_size.
  3. What is CREATE STATISTICS for? Expected: correlated columns; dependencies, ndistinct, mcv; fixes the independence assumption.
  4. pg_stats says n_distinct = -0.04. What does that mean? Expected: 4 percent of the row count are distinct.
  5. A query is fast for most users and 40 seconds for one. Where do you look? Expected: data skew; MCV list; per-parameter plan differences; pg_stat_statements max versus mean.

19.17 When an index makes things SLOWER

19.17.1 Five cases, with numbers

Concept

Every index has a cost that is paid on writes and a benefit that is paid on reads. When the benefit is zero or negative, the index is a pure tax. Here are the five ways that actually happens in production, each with the measurement that proves it.

Case 1: a low-selectivity index the planner picks wrongly

Statistics were collected when notifications.status = 'PENDING' covered 0.01 percent of rows. A provider outage pushed 40 million notifications into PENDING overnight, but ANALYZE had not run because autovacuum's threshold (autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.1) needs 10 percent of 1.2 billion rows to change.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id FROM notifications WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1000;
Limit  (cost=0.57..3821.44 rows=1000 width=8) (actual time=0.084..184221.882 rows=1000 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=8214402 read=4118204
  ->  Index Scan using idx_notifications_created_at on notifications
        (cost=0.57..458821440.11 rows=120000 width=8) (actual time=0.083..184221.204 rows=1000 loops=1)
        Filter: (status = 'PENDING'::text)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 118204882
Execution Time: 184221.944 ms

Three minutes. The planner believed 120,000 rows matched and that walking created_at order would find 1,000 of them quickly. In reality the oldest 118 million notifications are all SENT, so it walked 118 million index entries and heap rows before finding 1,000 pending ones. The estimate rows=120000 versus the reality (40 million, but concentrated at the end of created_at order) is the bug.

ANALYZE notifications; alone fixes the plan. The durable fix is the partial index of 19.6, which cannot be fooled by this. A stale statistic turned a good index into a three-minute query.

Case 2: write amplification on a 14-index orders table

flowchart TB
  ins["INSERT INTO orders (one row)"]
  heap["1 heap page write"]
  i1["orders_pkey"]
  i2["idx_user_id"]
  i3["idx_status"]
  i4["idx_created_at"]
  i5["idx_updated_at"]
  i6["idx_total_cents"]
  i7["... 8 more indexes"]
  wal["WAL record per index write, plus full page images after a checkpoint"]
  ins --> heap
  ins --> i1
  ins --> i2
  ins --> i3
  ins --> i4
  ins --> i5
  ins --> i6
  ins --> i7
  heap --> wal
  i1 --> wal
  i2 --> wal
  i7 --> wal

Measured on orders, single-row inserts through the connection pool at 400 inserts per second:

Indexes p50 insert p99 insert WAL per insert Index bytes per row
2 1.8 ms 4.1 ms 780 B 68 B
6 3.4 ms 9.2 ms 1,940 B 214 B
10 5.9 ms 16.8 ms 3,410 B 402 B
14 8.7 ms 28.4 ms 4,880 B 611 B

The p99 is the story: 4.1 ms to 28.4 ms. Each additional index is another tree descent that can miss the buffer cache, another page that can split, and another WAL record. At 400 inserts per second, 14 indexes produce 1.95 MB/s of WAL from the writes alone, against 312 KB/s at 2 indexes.

And the checkout endpoint that does one insert into orders plus three into order_items inside one transaction goes from 9 ms to 41 ms at p99, which shows up directly in your API SLO.

Case 3: index bloat after a mass delete

The GDPR job deletes 12 million users' order history: 310 million rows across orders and order_items, scattered across the whole key range.

before delete: idx_orders_user_created  6142 MB, avg_leaf_density 88.4, list query 0.12 ms
after delete:  idx_orders_user_created  6142 MB, avg_leaf_density 21.7, list query 0.14 ms
after VACUUM:  idx_orders_user_created  6142 MB, avg_leaf_density 21.9, list query 0.14 ms
after REINDEX: idx_orders_user_created  1584 MB, avg_leaf_density 89.1, list query 0.11 ms

Point lookups barely changed, which is why nobody noticed. The damage was elsewhere: 4.5 GB of shared_buffers competition, 4.5 GB in every backup, 4.5 GB more for every replica to keep, and range scans over that index reading four times the pages. The lesson is that bloat is usually not visible in the query that uses the index; it is visible in everything else.

Case 4: hot-page contention on a monotonically increasing key

Every insert of a bigserial primary key writes to the same rightmost leaf page. At low rates this is a cache-friendly gift. At 8,000 inserts per second across 60 connections, all 60 backends want an exclusive buffer lock on one 8 KB page.

SELECT wait_event_type, wait_event, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
 wait_event_type |   wait_event    | count
-----------------+-----------------+-------
 LWLock          | BufferContent   |    38
 Lock            | transactionid   |     4
 IO              | WALWrite        |     3

38 backends waiting on LWLock:BufferContent is the signature. Measured throughput on notifications with a bigserial primary key:

Insert rate attempted Achieved p99 Dominant wait
2,000/s 2,000/s 3 ms WALWrite
6,000/s 5,950/s 9 ms WALWrite
10,000/s 8,100/s 44 ms LWLock BufferContent
14,000/s 8,400/s 190 ms LWLock BufferContent

The ceiling is around 8,400 per second and adding connections makes it worse. Three fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Batch the inserts. 100 rows in one INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...) writes one WAL record and takes the page lock once. This alone took the same workload to 34,000 rows per second.
  2. Partition by time (Part 22 — Scaling Databases). Each partition has its own index and its own right edge, and if you route by hash instead of time you spread the edge across N pages.
  3. Change the key distribution. UUID v7 keeps rough time ordering with enough entropy to spread across several leaf pages. Random UUID v4 solves contention and creates a far worse problem (random I/O across the whole index).

Note that this is a primary key problem, so "drop the index" is not on the table. It is the clearest example of an index cost you cannot remove, only architect around.

Case 5: a GIN index on a jsonb column nobody queries

An engineer added CREATE INDEX ON notifications USING gin (payload) "because we might want to search notifications later". Nobody ever did.

Index size:                       84 GB
idx_scan since creation (9 months): 0
Insert throughput before:         8,400/s
Insert throughput after:          1,180/s
WAL per insert before:            980 B
WAL per insert after:             4,210 B
Autovacuum pass on notifications: 41 min -> 3 h 20
Backup size increase:             +84 GB, +18 min
Monthly storage cost (gp3):       +$7 per replica per month, x4 environments

An 86 percent reduction in insert throughput for zero queries. This is the purest form of the problem: an index's cost is unconditional and its benefit is conditional. Dropping it restored everything within an hour.

Practical example — the audit

Run this against your own database right now. It takes ten seconds and it is usually uncomfortable:

SELECT
  s.relname AS table_name,
  s.indexrelname AS index_name,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size,
  s.idx_scan,
  CASE WHEN s.idx_scan = 0 THEN 'NEVER USED'
       WHEN s.idx_scan < 50 THEN 'BARELY USED'
       ELSE 'ok' END AS verdict,
  (SELECT stats_reset FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database()) AS stats_since
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE NOT i.indisprimary AND NOT i.indisunique
ORDER BY s.idx_scan ASC, pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

Edge cases & failure modes

  • An index that is used, on the wrong query: it serves an admin screen 4 times a day and costs 8 ms on 40 million inserts.
  • An index used only by a nightly job, where a temporary index (create, run, drop) would be cheaper.
  • Indexes that prevent HOT updates on a hot column, multiplying both heap and index bloat.
  • A unique index that serialises writes on a hot key.
  • An index that makes the planner's search space larger, adding planning time to every query on that table.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "what does this cost when nobody queries it?" as the first question about any proposed index, not the last. They know that read benefit is easy to demonstrate and write cost is easy to ignore, so they demand both numbers. And they treat index count on hot write tables as a budget: orders gets five, and adding a sixth means removing one or making a case.

Interview questions

  1. Give three ways an index can make a system slower. Expected: write amplification, planner misuse under stale statistics, buffer cache and vacuum competition, bloat, HOT prevention.
  2. You are at 8,000 inserts per second and see LWLock:BufferContent. Diagnose and fix. Expected: right-edge contention on a monotonic key; batch, partition, or change key distribution.
  3. What does a GIN index cost on a write-heavy table? Expected: 10 to 20x insert cost, big WAL, long vacuum, huge size.
  4. A mass delete left the index the same size. What is the impact and the fix? Expected: bloat costs cache, backups, replicas and range scans; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

19.18 Why "add indexes everywhere" is bad advice

19.18.1 The full cost model

Concept

"Just add an index" is the most repeated and least examined advice in backend engineering. It is repeated because the read benefit is dramatic and easy to measure in isolation, and because the costs are diffuse, delayed and spread across systems nobody is looking at during the ticket.

Here is the complete bill for one index, on one hot table.

The worked table

One additional B-tree index on orders (updated_at), 200 million rows, 400 inserts and 900 updates per second.

Cost dimension Measurement Where it hurts
Write latency +0.9 ms p50, +3.2 ms p99 per insert; +1.1 ms per non-HOT update Checkout endpoint SLO; connection hold time; pool saturation
HOT prevention updated_at changes on every update, so every update becomes non-HOT: HOT ratio 94% -> 0% 7 index entries written per update instead of 0; heap bloat rate up 4x
WAL volume +610 B per insert, +1,240 B per update; total +1.36 MB/s Replication bandwidth, archive storage (+3.4 TB/year), replica apply lag
Vacuum work One more index to scan per vacuum pass: +9 min per pass, 6 passes/day Autovacuum worker occupancy; longer to reclaim; higher bloat
shared_buffers competition 4.2 GB index, ~800 MB hot 10% of an 8 GB cache taken from other tables; measured hit ratio 99.3% -> 98.6%, which doubles physical reads
Storage 4.2 GB primary + 4.2 GB x 3 replicas + 4.2 GB in each of 2 staging copies ~25 GB provisioned; on gp3 about $2/month, trivial; the IOPS it consumes is not
Backup and restore +4.2 GB per base backup, +6 min restore time RTO. A 40-minute restore becoming 52 minutes is a real availability number
Planner search space One more access path to cost for every query on orders; planning time 0.14 ms -> 0.19 ms At 3,000 queries/s that is 150 ms of CPU per second, 15% of a core, for nothing
Schema change cost Every future ALTER TABLE that rewrites the table rebuilds this index too Migration windows get longer forever
Cognitive cost One more thing nobody dares drop Compounding: the index that exists because nobody knows why

If that index serves a query that runs 4 times a day on an admin page, you have made a bad trade. If it serves a query that runs 3,000 times a second, you have made an excellent one. The bill is the same either way; only the benefit changes.

The decision flow

flowchart TB
  start["A query is slow"]
  q1{"Have you read EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS?"}
  q2{"Is estimated vs actual rows off by more than 10x?"}
  fix1["Fix statistics first: ANALYZE, statistics target, CREATE STATISTICS"]
  q3{"What fraction of the table does the worst-case parameter return?"}
  seq["Over 10 percent: no index will help. Rewrite the query, add a rollup, or partition"]
  q4{"Can an existing index serve it by adding a column or reordering?"}
  extend["Extend or replace the existing index. Net index count unchanged"]
  q5{"Is the predicate a small constant slice?"}
  partial["Partial index"]
  q6{"How many times per second does this query run?"}
  rare["Under 1 per minute: accept the latency, or build a temporary index for the job"]
  q7{"What is the write rate on this table?"}
  measure["Measure insert p99 before and after on a staging copy with production volume"]
  add["Add it CONCURRENTLY, record the reason in the migration, set a review date"]
  start --> q1
  q1 -->|"no"| q1
  q1 -->|"yes"| q2
  q2 -->|"yes"| fix1
  fix1 --> q1
  q2 -->|"no"| q3
  q3 -->|"over 10 percent"| seq
  q3 -->|"under 10 percent"| q4
  q4 -->|"yes"| extend
  q4 -->|"no"| q5
  q5 -->|"yes"| partial
  q5 -->|"no"| q6
  q6 -->|"rarely"| rare
  q6 -->|"often"| q7
  q7 --> measure --> add

The counter-argument, honestly

There is a real category where "add indexes freely" is correct: read replicas and analytics copies that take no application writes. An index there costs storage, replication of the index's own WAL from the primary (so it is not free), and vacuum, but no user-facing write latency. If your reporting workload lives on a dedicated replica, index it generously. The advice is bad as a universal rule, not as a rule for every situation.

Similarly, small tables (categories at 1,240 rows, inventory at 400,000) can carry more indexes without anyone noticing, because the write rates are low and everything fits in cache.

The rule that survives contact with production is:

Index budgets are per table and proportional to the write rate. A table taking 5,000 writes per second gets 3 to 5 carefully chosen indexes. A table taking 5 writes per second can have 15.

Practical example — the index budget in review

A pull request adding an index must answer six questions, and a template in the repository makes it automatic:

### Index proposal
- **Query**: `SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`
- **Rate**: 340 req/s (p99 SLO 150 ms)
- **Current plan**: Bitmap Heap Scan, 388k rows, 122k removed by filter, 1,301 ms
- **Proposed**: `(tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)`
- **Replaces**: `idx_orders_tenant_id`, `idx_orders_status` (both become redundant prefixes)
- **Estimated size**: 7.4 GB (measured on staging restore)
- **Write cost**: insert p99 8.1 ms -> 8.9 ms measured on staging at production insert rate
- **Net index count on orders**: 6 -> 5

The last line is the one that keeps a codebase healthy for five years.

Failure scenario

A "performance sprint" added 31 indexes across 9 tables in two weeks, each justified by a slow query. Read latencies improved by 40 percent. Six weeks later: checkout p99 up 3.4x, WAL up 4.1x, the replica 90 seconds behind at peak, autovacuum never finishing on orders, pg_wal filling twice, and the base backup window overrunning into business hours. The remediation took two months and dropped 22 of the 31 indexes, because by then nobody could tell which queries the other 9 served. Adding indexes is fast; removing them requires evidence you did not collect at the time. Record the reason at creation or accept that you can never remove it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They think in budgets and in totals, not per ticket. They ask what the index does to the slowest thing in the system, not the thing in front of them. They insist that every index has a recorded query, a recorded rate, and a review date. They know the read win is provable in 5 minutes and the write cost takes a load test, and they do the load test anyway. And when a product manager asks why a "simple index" needs a staging measurement, they answer: "because the last one cost us four hours of checkout latency and we could not prove which one it was."

Common mistakes

  • Treating each index decision in isolation.
  • Measuring the read gain and not the write cost.
  • Adding indexes during an incident and never revisiting them.
  • Never dropping anything, so index storage exceeds table storage.
  • Copying an index set from another service with a completely different read/write ratio.

Interview questions

  1. Name six costs of an index beyond disk space. Expected: write latency, WAL and replication, vacuum time, buffer cache competition, planning time, backup and restore, HOT prevention, migration cost.
  2. When is "index everything" reasonable advice? Expected: read-only replicas, analytics copies, small low-write tables.
  3. How do you decide whether to add an index? Expected: the decision flow; statistics first, selectivity check, extend an existing index, partial index, rate justification, measured write cost.
  4. Your index storage exceeds your table storage. Is that wrong? Expected: not automatically; it depends on the access pattern, but it demands an audit of idx_scan and duplicates.
  5. How would you explain the cost of an index to a product manager? Expected: every order placed now writes 14 things instead of 2, so checkout gets slower for everyone to make one report faster for a few.

Practical exercise

Take your busiest write table. Produce a table with one row per index: size, idx_scan, the query you believe it serves, and whether it is a prefix of another index. Then, on a staging copy restored from production, measure insert p50 and p99 with all indexes, and again with the three least-used indexes dropped. Acceptance criteria: the per-index table, two latency measurements, and a written recommendation with a rollback plan.

19.19 Finding missing indexes

19.19.1 pg_stat_statements, seq_scan, auto_explain and hypopg

Concept

PostgreSQL has no "missing index" view. SQL Server invents one and it is famously wrong. What PostgreSQL gives you is better: four sources of evidence that, combined, tell you exactly which query is costing you the most and what an index would do about it before you build it.

  1. pg_stat_statements ranks queries by total time. This is where you start, always.
  2. pg_stat_user_tables shows which tables are being sequentially scanned and how many rows those scans read.
  3. auto_explain captures the actual plan of slow statements as they happen.
  4. hypopg lets you create a hypothetical index and ask the planner what it would do, without building anything.

Why does it exist?

Because the query you think is slow is usually not the query that is costing you. A query that takes 900 ms and runs twice a day costs 1.8 seconds a day. A query that takes 14 ms and runs 3,000 times a second costs 42 seconds per second. Total time, not mean time, is what you optimise.

Mental model

A restaurant losing money. You do not start with the dish the chef finds most annoying to cook. You start with the ledger: which line item, multiplied by how often it is sold, accounts for the biggest share of cost? That is total_exec_time. Only then do you look at how the dish is made.

How it works

Step 1: rank by total time.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;   -- needs shared_preload_libraries

SELECT
  round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0)              AS total_ms,
  calls,
  round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)               AS mean_ms,
  round(max_exec_time::numeric, 2)                AS max_ms,
  round(stddev_exec_time::numeric, 2)             AS stddev_ms,
  rows,
  round(100.0 * shared_blks_hit /
        nullif(shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read, 0), 1) AS hit_pct,
  left(regexp_replace(query, '\s+', ' ', 'g'), 90) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE query NOT LIKE '%pg_stat_statements%'
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
 total_ms   | calls    | mean_ms | max_ms  | stddev_ms | rows      | hit_pct | query
------------+----------+---------+---------+-----------+-----------+---------+--------------------------------
 41882014   | 18204112 |    2.30 | 9104.22 |    118.44 | 364082240 |    91.2 | SELECT id, status, total_cents FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 AND status
  9814402   |    41882 |  234.34 | 1204.88 |     88.12 |   4188200 |    62.1 | SELECT count(*), kind FROM notifications WHERE created_at >= $1 GROUP BY
  4211884   |  8214402 |    0.51 |   84.22 |      1.94 |   8214402 |    99.8 | SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1
  2884102   |    18204 |  158.43 | 2104.11 |    204.88 |    918204 |    41.2 | SELECT p.id, p.name FROM products p WHERE p.attributes @> $1
  1204882   |   918204 |    1.31 |  412.88 |     18.22 |  18364080 |    97.4 | SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1

Read the columns together, not one at a time:

  • Row 1 is 41,882 seconds of total database time, 42 percent of everything. Its mean is a comfortable 2.3 ms but max_ms is 9,104 and stddev is 118. A stddev 50 times the mean means parameter-dependent plans: some users are cheap and some are catastrophic. This is the query to fix, and 19.23 fixes it.
  • Row 2 has a 62 percent buffer hit rate: it is reading from disk. A candidate for BRIN or a rollup.
  • Row 3 is 8.2 million calls at 0.51 ms with 99.8 percent hits. This is healthy. Do not touch it. If you want it faster, the answer is caching (Part 26 — Caching), not indexing.
  • Row 4 has a 41 percent hit rate and 158 ms mean: the GIN index probably does not exist yet.

Reset the counters when you start an optimisation cycle so the numbers describe the current system:

SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();

Step 2: find the tables being scanned.

SELECT
  relname,
  seq_scan, seq_tup_read,
  CASE WHEN seq_scan > 0 THEN seq_tup_read / seq_scan ELSE 0 END AS avg_rows_per_seq_scan,
  idx_scan,
  n_live_tup,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(relid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE seq_scan > 0
ORDER BY seq_tup_read DESC
LIMIT 10;
   relname     | seq_scan | seq_tup_read  | avg_rows_per_seq_scan | idx_scan  | n_live_tup  | size
---------------+----------+---------------+-----------------------+-----------+-------------+--------
 orders        |    41882 | 8376400000000 |             200000000 | 641882014 | 200000000   | 30 GB
 products      |  1820441 |  728176400000 |                400000 |   8214402 |    400000   | 420 MB
 categories    | 18204112 |   22573101880 |                  1240 |         0 |      1240   | 128 KB
 notifications |      882 |  1058400000000 |            1200000000 | 918204112 | 1200000000  | 210 GB

Interpretation, row by row:

  • orders: 41,882 full scans of a 200 million row table. Each one reads 30 GB. That is 1.25 petabytes of reads. Something is scanning this table and it should not be.
  • products: 1.8 million full scans of 400,000 rows each. The table is small enough that each scan is only 420 MB and takes 210 ms, so nobody complained, but 1.8 million x 210 ms is 106 hours of database time. This is the classic hidden cost: a table small enough to scan and big enough to matter.
  • categories: 18 million sequential scans and idx_scan = 0. This is correct. At 1,240 rows in 16 pages, a sequential scan is faster than any index and the whole table is permanently in cache. Do not add an index here.
  • notifications: only 882 scans, but each reads 1.2 billion rows. Those are the analytics queries from row 2 of pg_stat_statements.

The key ratio is seq_tup_read / seq_scan. Small means small tables (fine). Large means a big table is being fully scanned (investigate).

Step 3: capture the actual plans.

shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements,auto_explain'
auto_explain.log_min_duration = '500ms'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on
auto_explain.log_buffers = on
auto_explain.log_verbose = off
auto_explain.log_nested_statements = on   # catches statements inside functions and triggers
auto_explain.log_timing = off             # cheaper on high-row plans
auto_explain.sample_rate = 0.2            # 20 percent, to bound the logging cost

log_nested_statements matters more than people expect: ORM-generated queries inside a stored procedure, or a slow query inside a trigger, are invisible without it.

Step 4: ask the planner what an index would do, without building it.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS hypopg;

-- Create a hypothetical index. Nothing is written to disk; it exists only in this session.
SELECT * FROM hypopg_create_index(
  'CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, status, created_at DESC)'
);
 indexrelid |                 indexname
------------+--------------------------------------------
      13452 | <13452>btree_orders_user_id_status_created_at
EXPLAIN SELECT id, status, total_cents FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 918273 AND status = 'PAID' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=0.57..41.22 rows=20 width=20)
  ->  Index Scan using "<13452>btree_orders_user_id_status_created_at" on orders
        (cost=0.57..214.44 rows=104 width=20)
        Index Cond: ((user_id = 918273) AND (status = 'PAID'::text))

The planner chose the hypothetical index and the estimated cost dropped from 412,188 to 41. That is a strong signal, obtained in one second, with zero disk written and zero locks taken.

SELECT hypopg_get_indexdef(13452);          -- what it would be
SELECT pg_size_pretty(hypopg_relation_size(13452));   -- estimated size: 7412 MB
SELECT hypopg_reset();                      -- clean up (also happens at session end)

hypopg cannot give you EXPLAIN ANALYZE, because the index does not exist and cannot be executed against. It gives you the planner's choice and its estimated cost and size, which is exactly enough to decide whether the real build is worth 26 minutes.

Practical example

An afternoon of index work, in order:

  1. pg_stat_statements ordered by total_exec_time gives 5 candidates covering 71 percent of database time.
  2. For each, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with both a typical and a worst-case parameter.
  3. For the two with estimate errors above 10x, ANALYZE and CREATE STATISTICS first, then re-explain. Two of the five are now fixed with no index at all.
  4. For the remaining three, hypopg the candidate index and confirm the planner picks it and the estimated cost collapses.
  5. Check whether an existing index can be extended instead (19.20's redundancy query).
  6. Measure the size estimate and the write cost on a staging restore.
  7. Build with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, one per migration.

NestJS example

A scheduled job that ships the top queries to your metrics system, so index work is driven by data instead of by whoever complains loudest:

// db-insights.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class DbInsightsService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(DbInsightsService.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_HOUR)
  async reportTopQueries() {
    const rows = await this.ds.query(`
      SELECT queryid, calls,
             round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0) AS total_ms,
             round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)  AS mean_ms,
             round(stddev_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS stddev_ms,
             left(regexp_replace(query, '\\s+', ' ', 'g'), 200) AS query
      FROM pg_stat_statements
      WHERE calls > 100
      ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
      LIMIT 20`);

    for (const r of rows) {
      // Emit as metrics; a stddev far above the mean means parameter-dependent plans.
      this.log.log({
        msg: 'pg_top_query',
        queryid: r.queryid,
        totalMs: Number(r.total_ms),
        meanMs: Number(r.mean_ms),
        skew: Number(r.stddev_ms) / Math.max(Number(r.mean_ms), 0.01),
        query: r.query,
      });
    }
  }
}

Alert on skew > 20 for any query in the top 10. That single alert catches the "fast for most users, 40 seconds for one" class of bug before the customer does.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • pg_stat_statements.max defaults to 5,000 distinct queries; on a system with unnormalised SQL (string-concatenated values) it overflows and the numbers become meaningless. Always use parameterised queries.
  • pg_stat_statements normalises constants but not IN list lengths before PG 14, so IN (1,2) and IN (1,2,3) are separate entries.
  • Statistics are cumulative since the last reset or restart; a number without a stats_reset timestamp is uninterpretable.
  • seq_scan counts scans, not their cost; a 16-page table with 18 million scans is fine, a 3.9 million page table with 40,000 is not.
  • auto_explain with log_analyze = on and log_timing = on adds real overhead on high-row plans; use sampling and turn timing off.
  • hypopg only supports B-tree, BRIN and hash hypothetical indexes; it cannot simulate GIN or GiST.
  • On replicas, statistics are per-node; an index unused on the primary may be the busiest one on a replica.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They optimise total time, not the loudest complaint. They look at stddev/mean to find parameter-dependent plans, which are the bugs that page you at 3 a.m. They use hypopg to make index decisions cheap and reversible. And they always ask whether the answer is an index, a query rewrite, a rollup table, or a cache, in that order of increasing architectural commitment.

Interview questions

  1. How do you find which query to optimise first? Expected: pg_stat_statements by total_exec_time, not mean_exec_time.
  2. What does a high stddev_exec_time relative to the mean tell you? Expected: parameter-dependent plans or data skew; find the bad parameter.
  3. A table has 18 million sequential scans. Is that a problem? Expected: depends on size; 1,240 rows in 16 pages is correct behaviour.
  4. How do you evaluate an index before building it on a 200 million row table? Expected: hypopg plus the planner's choice and estimated cost and size, then a staging build for the real timing.
  5. What does auto_explain.log_nested_statements catch? Expected: slow statements inside functions and triggers.

19.20 Finding unused and duplicate indexes

19.20.1 idx_scan = 0, redundant prefixes, and dropping safely

Concept

Every database that has been alive for three years has indexes nobody uses. Finding them is a ten-line query. Dropping them safely is the part that requires discipline, because idx_scan = 0 on the primary does not mean unused, and dropping a unique index changes semantics, not just performance.

The unused-index query

SELECT
  s.schemaname, s.relname AS table_name, s.indexrelname AS index_name,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size,
  s.idx_scan,
  i.indisunique, i.indisprimary,
  pg_get_indexdef(s.indexrelid) AS definition
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0
  AND NOT i.indisprimary
  AND pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) > 8 * 1024 * 1024   -- ignore anything under 8 MB
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;
 table_name    |        index_name         |  size   | idx_scan | indisunique | indisprimary
---------------+---------------------------+---------+----------+-------------+--------------
 notifications | idx_notifications_payload | 84 GB   |        0 | f           | f
 orders        | idx_orders_updated_at     | 4218 MB |        0 | f           | f
 orders        | idx_orders_tenant_id      |  921 MB |        0 | f           | f
 order_items   | idx_order_items_price     | 3104 MB |        0 | f           | f
 reviews       | uq_reviews_legacy_key     |  412 MB |        0 | t           | f

92 GB of indexes that have never been scanned. But look at the last row: indisunique = true. That index is enforcing a constraint. idx_scan = 0 for a unique index means nobody queries it, not that nobody needs it, because it is doing its job on every insert. Never drop a unique index on the basis of idx_scan.

The duplicate and redundant-prefix query

An index (a) is redundant if (a, b) exists, because any query the first can serve, the second can serve too, using its leading prefix. It is not always exactly as fast (the wider index has fewer entries per page, so scans read more pages), but the difference is usually 10 to 20 percent, and dropping a whole index is worth 10 percent on one query.

-- Exact duplicates: same columns, same order, same predicate, same opclass
SELECT
  indrelid::regclass AS table_name,
  array_agg(indexrelid::regclass) AS duplicates,
  pg_size_pretty(sum(pg_relation_size(indexrelid))) AS total_size
FROM pg_index
GROUP BY indrelid, indkey, indclass, indexprs, indpred
HAVING count(*) > 1;
 table_name |                     duplicates                     | total_size
------------+----------------------------------------------------+------------
 orders     | {idx_orders_user_id, orders_user_id_idx}           | 8420 MB

Two identically defined indexes, 8.4 GB, created by a developer and by a TypeORM synchronize run. Drop one and reclaim 4.2 GB immediately.

-- Redundant prefixes: index A's columns are a leading prefix of index B's
SELECT
  a.indrelid::regclass          AS table_name,
  ai.relname                    AS redundant_index,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(a.indexrelid)) AS redundant_size,
  bi.relname                    AS covered_by,
  pg_get_indexdef(a.indexrelid) AS redundant_def,
  pg_get_indexdef(b.indexrelid) AS covering_def
FROM pg_index a
JOIN pg_index b
  ON a.indrelid = b.indrelid
 AND a.indexrelid <> b.indexrelid
 AND a.indnatts < b.indnatts
 AND a.indkey::int2[] = (b.indkey::int2[])[1:a.indnatts]     -- A's columns are B's leading prefix
 AND a.indpred IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.indpred                -- same partial predicate (or both none)
 AND NOT a.indisunique                                        -- never propose dropping a unique index
 AND NOT a.indisprimary
JOIN pg_class ai ON ai.oid = a.indexrelid
JOIN pg_class bi ON bi.oid = b.indexrelid
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(a.indexrelid) DESC;
 table_name |     redundant_index     | redundant_size |         covered_by         
------------+-------------------------+----------------+----------------------------
 orders     | idx_orders_user_id      | 4210 MB        | idx_orders_user_created    
 orders     | idx_orders_status       | 3821 MB        | idx_orders_status_created  
 order_items| idx_order_items_order   | 12 GB          | idx_order_items_order_prod

20 GB recoverable from three indexes that are each a leading prefix of a larger one. This is by far the most common form of index waste, and it accumulates because each composite was added later without anyone checking what it superseded.

Two cautions on redundancy:

  1. A narrow index is smaller and denser. If it serves a very hot equality lookup millions of times a second, keeping it can be worth it. Measure before dropping.
  2. indisunique matters. UNIQUE (a) is not covered by (a, b), because the constraint is different.

Dropping safely: the monitoring window

Never drop an index the same day you find it. The procedure:

  1. Reset statistics and wait a full business cycle. SELECT pg_stat_reset(); then wait at least 7 days, and 35 days if you have monthly jobs (month-end reconciliation is exactly the kind of thing that uses one index once a month).

  2. Check every replica. Statistics are per node. A reporting replica may be the only user.

    -- run on each node
SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE indexrelname = 'idx_orders_tenant_id';

  3. Check it is not backing a constraint.

    SELECT conname, contype FROM pg_constraint WHERE conindid = 'idx_orders_tenant_id'::regclass;

  4. Make it invisible before making it gone. PostgreSQL has no ALTER INDEX ... INVISIBLE like MySQL, but you can get the same effect reversibly in a transaction:

    BEGIN;
UPDATE pg_index SET indisvalid = false WHERE indexrelid = 'idx_orders_tenant_id'::regclass;
-- planner now ignores it; writes still maintain it
COMMIT;

    This is a catalogue hack. It works, it is reversible, and it is not supported. Use it only on a system where you can roll back quickly, and always in a change window. The safer equivalent is to run the candidate queries with SET enable_indexscan tricks or hypopg's hypopg_hide_index() (PG 13+ versions of the extension), which does the same thing per session with no catalogue writes:

    SELECT hypopg_hide_index('idx_orders_tenant_id'::regclass);
EXPLAIN SELECT ... ;    -- plan without that index, session-local, safe
SELECT hypopg_unhide_all_indexes();

  5. Drop it concurrently and record the exact DDL for the rollback:

    DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_id;
-- rollback: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_id ON orders (tenant_id);

  6. Watch for 48 hours. pg_stat_statements mean times on the affected table, and seq_scan on the table.

Production scenario

A quarterly "index review" ritual: reset statistics on the first of the quarter, run the three queries above at the end, and produce a single migration that drops everything with zero scans across all nodes, excluding unique indexes and anything created in the last 90 days. In one such review a team removed 41 indexes totalling 190 GB, cut insert p99 on their busiest table by 44 percent, and shortened their base backup by 26 minutes. Nothing got slower.

Failure scenario

An engineer dropped idx_payments_provider_ref because idx_scan was 0 after a 3-day window. It was a unique index, and it was the entire idempotency guarantee for the payment provider's webhooks (19.7). It had zero scans because ON CONFLICT inserts do not increment idx_scan in a way that showed up in their query, and because the duplicate path was rare. Two weeks later a provider retry storm during an outage inserted 14,000 duplicate payment records, and the reconciliation took nine days. Check indisunique and pg_constraint before every drop, without exception.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Statistics reset by a server restart, crash, or a major-version upgrade; pg_stat_database.stats_reset tells you when.
  • Replica-only usage.
  • Indexes used only by monthly, quarterly or year-end jobs.
  • Unique and exclusion indexes that enforce correctness with zero scans.
  • Indexes backing foreign keys: a child index on order_items(order_id) may have low idx_scan but is required to keep DELETE FROM orders from scanning the child table (and to avoid lock escalation on cascade deletes).
  • idx_scan does not count index maintenance or constraint checks, only planner-chosen scans.
  • Dropping an index a query planner was relying on for a good estimate: rare, but expression indexes also provide statistics (19.8).

Interview questions

  1. How do you find unused indexes and what must you check before dropping one? Expected: pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan with a long window; unique/constraint check, FK support, replicas, periodic jobs.
  2. What is a redundant index and how do you detect it? Expected: leading-prefix containment with the same predicate; the indkey prefix query.
  3. Why can an index with idx_scan = 0 still be essential? Expected: uniqueness and exclusion constraints, foreign key support.
  4. How do you test the impact of dropping an index without dropping it? Expected: hypopg_hide_index, or the indisvalid catalogue trick in a controlled window.

19.21 An indexing catalogue for common access patterns

19.21.1 The lookup table you will actually use

Concept

Most indexing decisions in a backend system are one of about fifteen shapes. Here they are, each with the query, the index, and the reason. Sizes are for the volumes at the top of this part.

# Access pattern Query Index Why
1 Lookup by primary key WHERE id = $1 PRIMARY KEY (id) (automatic) 4 index pages plus 1 heap page for any table size
2 Lookup by foreign key WHERE order_id = $1 on order_items CREATE INDEX ON order_items (order_id) PostgreSQL does not auto-index FKs. Without it, every DELETE FROM orders scans 900M rows to check the child, and ON DELETE CASCADE is catastrophic
3 List by owner, newest first WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 (user_id, created_at DESC) Equality then sort; no Sort node, LIMIT stops early. The single most common shape in any product
4 List by owner filtered by state WHERE user_id = $1 AND status = $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 (user_id, status, created_at DESC) Two equalities then the sort column. Supersedes #3 as a prefix, so drop #3
5 Queue claim WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100 (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING' 3 MB instead of 41 GB; no index entry written for the 99.99 percent of rows that are not pending
6 Uniqueness with soft delete insert a review UNIQUE (user_id, product_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL Soft-deleted rows leave the index so the user can re-review
7 One active child per parent insert a cart UNIQUE (user_id) WHERE status = 'OPEN' Race-proof at the database level; no application locking
8 Idempotency guard webhook insert UNIQUE (provider_ref) plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING Duplicate delivery becomes a no-op instead of a duplicate payment
9 Case-insensitive login WHERE lower(email) = $1 UNIQUE INDEX ON users (lower(email)) Expression must match the query exactly; also prevents duplicate-case signups
10 Prefix search WHERE sku LIKE 'DK-9928%' (sku text_pattern_ops) Needed on non-C collations; a plain B-tree will not serve LIKE there
11 Substring / fuzzy search WHERE name ILIKE '%toothbrush%' USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops) Trigrams make leading wildcards indexable; results are rechecked
12 Full-text search WHERE search_tsv @@ plainto_tsquery($1) USING gin (search_tsv) on a generated tsvector column Generated column cannot drift from the source text
13 jsonb attribute, fixed key WHERE attributes->>'sku' = $1 ((attributes->>'sku')) B-tree Smaller and faster than GIN when the key is always the same; supports ordering and uniqueness
14 jsonb containment, varying keys WHERE attributes @> $1::jsonb USING gin (attributes jsonb_path_ops) 30 to 50 percent smaller than jsonb_ops and faster for @>
15 Time-range analytics on append-only data WHERE created_at >= $1 AND created_at < $2 on 1.2B rows USING brin (created_at) WITH (autosummarize = on) 3.5 MB versus 27 GB; requires correlation above ~0.9
16 Non-overlapping bookings insert a delivery slot EXCLUDE USING gist (courier_id WITH =, during WITH &&) Structural impossibility of double-booking; needs btree_gist
17 Nearest stores ORDER BY location <-> $1 LIMIT 10 USING gist (ll_to_earth(lat, lon)) KNN ordering inside the index scan, no Sort node
18 Multi-tenant everything every query has WHERE tenant_id = $1 tenant_id first in every composite: (tenant_id, user_id, created_at DESC) Restricts every scan to one tenant's slice; also the natural partition key later
19 Covering a hot read SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC (user_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (status, total_cents) Index-only scan removes the heap fetch; requires healthy vacuum
20 Keyset pagination WHERE user_id = $1 AND created_at < $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 same as #3 Page 500 costs the same as page 1; OFFSET 10000 does not

The multi-tenant rule, expanded

Row 18 deserves emphasis because getting it wrong is expensive and getting it right is free. In a multi-tenant system every query is scoped to a tenant. Therefore:

  • Every composite index starts with tenant_id.
  • Every unique constraint includes tenant_id: UNIQUE (tenant_id, order_ref), not UNIQUE (order_ref). Two tenants can legitimately use the same reference.
  • Any index that does not start with tenant_id is either a mistake or a deliberate cross-tenant admin query, and it should be justified in the migration comment.
  • When you eventually partition by tenant_id or by hash of it (Part 22 — Scaling Databases), the indexes are already in the right shape.

The counter-case: a table where one tenant holds 80 percent of the rows. Then tenant_id first is still correct for correctness and pruning, but the selectivity for that tenant is poor, and the second column has to do the real work. Check most_common_vals on tenant_id before assuming.

The foreign-key rule, expanded

Row 2 is the one most teams get wrong, and it is worth a plan. order_items has 900 million rows and a foreign key to orders. Without an index on order_items(order_id):

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 148392017;
Delete on orders  (cost=0.57..8.59 rows=0 width=0) (actual time=31882.114..31882.115 rows=0 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using orders_pkey on orders  (cost=0.57..8.59 rows=1 width=6)
                                              (actual time=0.041..0.043 rows=1 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (id = 148392017)
Trigger for constraint order_items_order_id_fkey: time=31881.884 calls=1
Execution Time: 31882.204 ms

The DELETE itself took 0.04 ms. The foreign key trigger took 31.9 seconds, because it had to scan all 900 million order_items rows to check that none referenced the deleted order. Trigger for constraint ... in the plan output is the line to look for, and it is invisible if you only read the plan tree.

With CREATE INDEX ON order_items (order_id):

Delete on orders  (actual time=0.088..0.089 rows=0 loops=1)
Trigger for constraint order_items_order_id_fkey: time=0.211 calls=1
Execution Time: 0.318 ms

Every foreign key column should have an index unless you can prove the parent is never deleted or updated. This is one of the few "always" rules in this part.

Practical exercise

Take your own schema. For each table, list its access patterns from the code (grep for the repository methods), map each one to a row in the catalogue above, and write down the index each requires. Then compare with the indexes that actually exist: list the ones that serve no pattern and the patterns that have no index. Acceptance criteria: a two-column gap analysis and a prioritised migration plan with one index per migration.

19.22 Indexes in TypeORM and Sequelize

19.22.1 What the decorators can express, and what needs raw SQL

Concept

Both ORMs can declare simple indexes on entities. Neither can express the whole of PostgreSQL's index syntax, and both have a "sync the schema" mode that will happily drop and rebuild a 6 GB index on a live table. So the working rule is:

Declare indexes in migrations. Use entity decorators only as documentation, and only when the ORM can express the index exactly.

Why does it exist?

Because ORM schema synchronisation is a development convenience that becomes a production hazard the moment a table is bigger than a few million rows. synchronize: true issues plain CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX, inside a transaction, with no CONCURRENTLY, no lock_timeout, and no ordering guarantees. On orders that is an 11-minute write outage triggered by a deploy.

TypeORM example

What the decorators can do:

import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, Index, Unique, ManyToOne, JoinColumn } from 'typeorm';
import { User } from './user.entity';

@Entity('orders')
// Composite index. Column order is the array order.
@Index('idx_orders_user_created', ['userId', 'createdAt'])
// Composite with a partial predicate (raw SQL fragment, DATABASE column names).
@Index('idx_orders_open', ['userId'], { where: `"status" IN ('PENDING','PAID')` })
// Unique across two columns; creates a real constraint.
@Unique('uq_orders_tenant_ref', ['tenantId', 'orderRef'])
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn({ type: 'bigint' })
  id!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'tenant_id', type: 'bigint' })
  tenantId!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'order_ref', type: 'text' })
  orderRef!: string;

  // Single-column index on a property.
  @Index('idx_orders_status')
  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  status!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'user_id', type: 'bigint' })
  userId!: string;

  @Column({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz' })
  createdAt!: Date;

  // @ManyToOne does NOT create an index on the FK column. You must add it.
  @ManyToOne(() => User, { onDelete: 'RESTRICT' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'user_id' })
  user!: User;
}

That last comment is the one that bites teams: TypeORM creates the foreign key constraint but not an index on the FK column. Every @ManyToOne needs a matching @Index or a migration, or you get the 31-second delete of 19.21.

What the decorators cannot do, and therefore what belongs in a migration:

Feature Decorator? Migration SQL
DESC / NULLS LAST No CREATE INDEX ... (created_at DESC NULLS LAST)
INCLUDE No CREATE INDEX ... (user_id) INCLUDE (status, total_cents)
Expression index No CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON users (lower(email))
USING gin/gist/brin/hash No CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (attributes jsonb_path_ops)
Operator class (text_pattern_ops) No CREATE INDEX ... (sku text_pattern_ops)
CONCURRENTLY No see below
fillfactor, pages_per_range No WITH (fillfactor = 90)
Exclusion constraint No EXCLUDE USING gist (...)
Partial predicate Yes (where) but text-compared, so migrations are safer

The concurrent-index migration pattern, complete:

// 1712009000000-AddOrdersHotIndexes.ts
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class AddOrdersHotIndexes1712009000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  // Required: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction block.
  // Consequence: this migration is NOT atomic, so it does exactly one thing.
  public transaction = false as const;

  public async up(q: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await q.query(`SET lock_timeout = '5s'`);
    await q.query(`SET statement_timeout = 0`);
    await q.query(`SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB'`);
    await q.query(`
      CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_orders_user_status_created
        ON orders (user_id, status, created_at DESC)
    `);
    const [row] = await q.query(`
      SELECT indisvalid FROM pg_index
      WHERE indexrelid = to_regclass('idx_orders_user_status_created')
    `);
    if (!row?.indisvalid) {
      throw new Error('idx_orders_user_status_created is INVALID; DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and retry');
    }
  }

  public async down(q: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await q.query(`SET lock_timeout = '5s'`);
    await q.query(`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS idx_orders_user_status_created`);
  }
}

And the configuration that keeps synchronize from ever running against production:

// data-source.ts
export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  entities: [Order, User /* ... */],
  migrations: ['dist/migrations/*.js'],
  synchronize: false,          // never true outside a throwaway local database
  migrationsRun: false,        // migrations run in a pipeline stage, not at app boot
  extra: { max: 10, statement_timeout: 10_000, lock_timeout: 5_000, application_name: 'orders-api' },
});

migrationsRun: false matters for indexes specifically: if 12 pods boot simultaneously and each tries to run a 26-minute CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, eleven of them fail and leave invalid indexes.

Sequelize example

Order.init(
  {
    id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, primaryKey: true, autoIncrement: true },
    tenantId: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, field: 'tenant_id', allowNull: false },
    userId: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, field: 'user_id', allowNull: false },
    status: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false },
    createdAt: { type: DataTypes.DATE, field: 'created_at', allowNull: false },
  },
  {
    sequelize,
    tableName: 'orders',
    indexes: [
      { name: 'idx_orders_user_created', fields: ['user_id', { name: 'created_at', order: 'DESC' }] },
      { name: 'uq_orders_tenant_ref', unique: true, fields: ['tenant_id', 'order_ref'] },
      { name: 'idx_orders_open', fields: ['user_id'], where: { status: ['PENDING', 'PAID'] } },
      { name: 'idx_products_attrs', fields: ['attributes'], using: 'gin' },   // `using` IS supported
    ],
  },
);

Sequelize is slightly more expressive than TypeORM: fields accepts { name, order, collate, operator }, and using accepts the access method. operator is how you get an operator class:

{ name: 'idx_products_attrs', fields: [{ name: 'attributes', operator: 'jsonb_path_ops' }], using: 'gin' }
{ name: 'idx_products_sku_prefix', fields: [{ name: 'sku', operator: 'text_pattern_ops' }] }

The concurrent migration:

// migrations/20260909130000-add-orders-user-status-created.js
module.exports = {
  async up(queryInterface) {
    await queryInterface.sequelize.query(`SET lock_timeout = '5s'`);
    await queryInterface.sequelize.query(`SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB'`);
    await queryInterface.addIndex('orders', {
      name: 'idx_orders_user_status_created',
      fields: ['user_id', 'status', { name: 'created_at', order: 'DESC' }],
      concurrently: true,
    });
  },
  async down(queryInterface) {
    await queryInterface.removeIndex('orders', 'idx_orders_user_status_created', { concurrently: true });
  },
};

And sequelize.sync() gets the same treatment as synchronize: development only, never against a database anyone cares about.

Making sure the ORM emits the query your index serves

An index is useless if the ORM writes different SQL from what you designed for. Two checks worth automating.

Log the SQL in tests and assert on it:

// orders.repository.spec.ts
it('emits the exact predicate the partial index expects', async () => {
  const sql = repo
    .createQueryBuilder('o')
    .where('o.status = :s', { s: 'PENDING' })       // must match: WHERE status = 'PENDING'
    .orderBy('o.created_at', 'ASC')
    .limit(100)
    .getSql();
  expect(sql).toContain(`"status" = $1`);
  expect(sql).not.toContain('!=');                   // a rewrite to <> would lose the partial index
});

Assert the plan in CI against a seeded database, which is the version that actually catches regressions:

it('uses idx_orders_user_status_created with no Sort node', async () => {
  const [{ 'QUERY PLAN': plan }] = await ds.query(
    `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)
     SELECT id, status, total_cents FROM orders
     WHERE user_id = $1 AND status = $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`,
    [42, 'PAID'],
  );
  const nodes: any[] = [];
  (function walk(n: any) { nodes.push(n); (n.Plans ?? []).forEach(walk); })(plan[0].Plan);
  expect(nodes.some((n) => n['Index Name'] === 'idx_orders_user_status_created')).toBe(true);
  expect(nodes.some((n) => n['Node Type'] === 'Sort')).toBe(false);
  expect(nodes.some((n) => n['Node Type'] === 'Seq Scan')).toBe(false);
});

This test fails when someone adds a column to the ORDER BY, changes = to IN, or drops the index. It is fifteen lines and it is the difference between finding a regression in a pull request and finding it in a pager alert.

Common mistakes

  • synchronize: true or sequelize.sync() against a real database.
  • Assuming @ManyToOne or references creates an index on the FK column.
  • Declaring a partial index in a decorator and a slightly different one in a migration, so the schema differ recreates it forever.
  • Running migrations at application boot with many replicas.
  • Writing the index for a query the ORM does not actually emit.

19.23 Case study: 2.3 seconds to 4 milliseconds

19.23.1 GET /orders over 200 million rows

The symptom

GET /orders?userId=...&status=PAID is the busiest authenticated endpoint in the shop: 340 requests per second at peak. The SLO is p99 under 150 ms. Grafana shows p50 at 41 ms, p99 at 2,310 ms, and a long tail reaching 9 seconds. Errors are 502s from the gateway timing out at 10 s. Database CPU is 38 percent; nothing looks broken.

pg_stat_statements:

 total_ms  | calls    | mean_ms | max_ms  | stddev_ms | query
-----------+----------+---------+---------+-----------+-------------------------------------------
 41882014  | 18204112 |    2.30 | 9104.22 |    118.44 | SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 AND status = $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20

Mean 2.30 ms, max 9,104 ms, stddev 118. A stddev 51 times the mean is the signature of a plan that depends on the parameter. Some users are fast; some are catastrophic.

The existing indexes on orders:

 orders_pkey                (id)                    4290 MB
 idx_orders_user_id         (user_id)               4210 MB
