 idx_orders_created_at      (created_at)            4212 MB
 idx_orders_status          (status)                3821 MB
 idx_orders_updated_at      (updated_at)            4218 MB
 idx_orders_tenant_id       (tenant_id)              921 MB

Six indexes, 21.7 GB, and not one of them serves this query well.

The before plan

Captured from auto_explain for a heavy user (a B2B account with 412,000 orders):

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 4471002 AND status = 'PAID'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=418822.44..418822.49 rows=20 width=28)
       (actual time=2298.114..2298.121 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=182044 read=204118
  ->  Sort  (cost=418822.44..418901.02 rows=31432 width=28)
            (actual time=2298.112..2298.117 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: created_at DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 28kB
        Buffers: shared hit=182044 read=204118
        ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=8214.02..417984.11 rows=31432 width=28)
                                        (actual time=118.884..2211.402 rows=312884 loops=1)
              Recheck Cond: (user_id = 4471002)
              Filter: (status = 'PAID'::text)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 380118
              Heap Blocks: exact=204118
              Buffers: shared hit=182044 read=204118
              ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_user_id
                    (cost=0.00..8206.16 rows=412884 width=0)
                    (actual time=88.114..88.114 rows=412884 loops=1)
                    Index Cond: (user_id = 4471002)
                    Buffers: shared hit=1204
Planning Time: 0.184 ms
Execution Time: 2298.204 ms

The reasoning, line by line

Six observations, each pointing at the same conclusion.

  1. Rows Removed by Filter: 380118. The scan fetched 693,002 rows from the heap and threw away 380,118 of them because status was not PAID. Every one of those was a heap tuple read for nothing. status is in a Filter, not an Index Cond, which means it is not in the index the query used.
  2. Heap Blocks: exact=204118. Two hundred thousand 8 KB heap pages, 1.6 GB, read to answer a request for twenty rows.
  3. Sort with Sort Key: created_at DESC. The query needs the newest twenty. The plan produced all 312,884 matching rows and then sorted them. top-N heapsort is the cheap kind of sort, but it still had to see every row. The ordering was not available from any index.
  4. LIMIT 20 bought nothing. The Limit node's startup cost (418,822) equals the Sort's total cost, because a sort cannot emit its first row until it has consumed its last input row. This is the classic trap: LIMIT only helps when the rows arrive already ordered.
  5. rows=31432 estimated versus 312884 actual on the bitmap heap scan: a 10x error. The planner multiplied user_id selectivity by status selectivity assuming independence. This user's orders are almost all PAID, so the truth is far higher. The error is not the main problem here, but it explains why the planner thought this plan was acceptable.
  6. buffers read=204118 versus hit=182044: 53 percent of pages came from outside the cache. At 340 requests per second this query alone was demanding gigabytes per second of I/O, which is why other endpoints were also slow.

The two facts that determine the fix: status must be a seekable index column, and created_at DESC must be the index's ordering so the twenty rows come out sorted.

flowchart TB
  subgraph Before
    b1["Bitmap Index Scan on (user_id): 412,884 ctids"]
    b2["Bitmap Heap Scan: read 204,118 heap pages"]
    b3["Filter status='PAID': discard 380,118 rows"]
    b4["Sort 312,884 rows by created_at DESC"]
    b5["Limit 20"]
    b1 --> b2 --> b3 --> b4 --> b5
  end
  subgraph After
    a1["Index Scan on (user_id, status, created_at DESC): seek to (4471002, PAID)"]
    a2["Walk 20 entries in created_at DESC order"]
    a3["Fetch 20 heap rows"]
    a4["Limit 20 satisfied, stop"]
    a1 --> a2 --> a3 --> a4
  end

The index chosen

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_status_created
  ON orders (user_id, status, created_at DESC);

Why this and not the alternatives:

Candidate Verdict
(user_id, created_at DESC) Removes the sort but still filters status in the heap. Better (about 180 ms), not good.
(status, user_id, created_at DESC) Works identically for this query, but status first is useless as a prefix for the many queries that filter only on user_id. Worse reuse.
(user_id, status, created_at DESC) Chosen. Two equality seeks then ordered walk. Also a prefix-superset of idx_orders_user_id, so that index can be dropped.
(user_id, status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_cents) Would make it index-only. orders has heavy updates so the visibility map is patchy; measured Heap Fetches was 60 percent, giving little benefit for 1.4 GB more index. Rejected.
Partial WHERE status = 'PAID' PAID is 76 percent of rows, so the partial index saves almost nothing, and the endpoint also serves other statuses. Rejected.

The after plan

Limit  (cost=0.57..44.12 rows=20 width=28) (actual time=0.038..0.061 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=7 read=2
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_user_status_created on orders
        (cost=0.57..680842.11 rows=312884 width=28)
        (actual time=0.036..0.057 rows=20 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((user_id = 4471002) AND (status = 'PAID'::text))
        Buffers: shared hit=7 read=2
Planning Time: 0.142 ms
Execution Time: 0.084 ms

Everything that was wrong is gone. No Sort. No Filter. No Rows Removed. Index Cond carries both predicates. Nine buffers instead of 386,162. The scan node's total cost is still 680,842 (reading all 312,884 rows would be expensive) but the startup cost is 0.57, so LIMIT 20 genuinely costs 20/312,884 of it. That is the difference between an ordered index scan and a sort.

The latency change

Deployed at 14:20 on a Tuesday. The index took 24 minutes to build concurrently and 7.4 GB.

Metric Before After
p50 41 ms 3 ms
p90 180 ms 4 ms
p99 2,310 ms 4 ms
p99.9 8,900 ms 11 ms
max 9,104 ms 62 ms
502s from gateway timeout 41 per hour 0
Database CPU at peak 38% 21%
Shared buffer reads/s from this query 1.9 GB/s 6 MB/s

The p99 dropping from 2,310 ms to 4 ms is not the interesting number. The interesting number is that p50, p90 and p99 converged. A query whose cost is proportional to the answer size rather than the data size has almost no tail. That is what an index-ordered LIMIT buys you, and it is why "make the p99 better" is usually really "stop sorting".

The unrelated improvement matters too: freeing 1.9 GB/s of I/O made the product search endpoint's p99 drop from 240 ms to 90 ms without touching it.

The write-cost check afterwards

The work was not finished at deploy. The next day:

-- 1. Is the new index actually being used?
SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE relname = 'orders' ORDER BY idx_scan DESC;
        indexrelname             |  idx_scan
---------------------------------+------------
 idx_orders_user_status_created  | 29102884
 orders_pkey                     |  8214402
 idx_orders_created_at           |   118204
 idx_orders_user_id              |        0     <- superseded
 idx_orders_status               |        0     <- superseded
 idx_orders_updated_at           |        0     <- was never used
 idx_orders_tenant_id            |        0     <- was never used
-- 2. What did it cost the write path?
-- Measured on staging at production insert rate, before and after:
--   insert p50 5.9 ms -> 6.4 ms ; p99 16.8 ms -> 18.1 ms ; WAL/insert 3,410 B -> 3,980 B

An extra 0.5 ms at p50 on inserts, in exchange for 2,306 ms at p99 on the read path that runs 53 times more often. Clearly worth it. But the cost was then removed entirely, because four indexes were now provably unused:

-- After a 14-day monitoring window across primary and both replicas
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_id;      -- 4210 MB, prefix of the new index
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status;       -- 3821 MB, never selective enough
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_updated_at;   -- 4218 MB, zero scans in 14 days
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_id;    --  921 MB, zero scans in 14 days

Final state:

Before After
Indexes on orders 6 3
Index storage 21.7 GB 15.9 GB
Insert p50 / p99 5.9 / 16.8 ms 3.6 / 9.1 ms
WAL per insert 3,410 B 2,140 B
Endpoint p99 2,310 ms 4 ms

Reads 575 times faster and writes 1.8 times faster, with less storage. That is the shape a good indexing project takes: not "add an index", but "add the right one and remove the four it makes redundant".

19.24 Edge cases and failure modes

19.24.1 Every way an index quietly fails to be used

1. Type mismatch

-- user_id is bigint, the parameter arrives as text
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = '918273';           -- fine: literal is coerced to bigint
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id::text = $1;           -- BROKEN: expression on the column
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1;                 -- with $1 bound as text: may not use the index
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..4921033.00 rows=1000000 width=61)
  Filter: ((user_id)::text = '918273'::text)

The cast is on the column side, so the index on user_id cannot be used. This happens constantly with ORMs and drivers that bind numeric ids as strings, and with uuid columns compared against text. The fix is to cast the parameter, not the column: WHERE user_id = $1::bigint. In TypeORM, bigint columns are returned and often bound as strings; verify the generated SQL.

Related: comparing varchar to text is free (same type family), comparing int to bigint is free (implicit widening on the constant side), but numeric to bigint and text to uuid are not.

2. A function on the column

WHERE lower(email) = $1              -- needs an index on lower(email)
WHERE date(created_at) = $1          -- needs an index on the expression, or a range rewrite
WHERE created_at::date = CURRENT_DATE

Rewrite as a range whenever you can, because a range works with the plain index:

WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE AND created_at < CURRENT_DATE + 1

This is strictly better than an expression index: no extra index to maintain, works with the existing (created_at) or composite, and it is sargable across time zones if you are careful.

3. Leading-wildcard LIKE

WHERE name LIKE '%brush%'      -- no B-tree can help: no prefix to seek
WHERE name LIKE 'brush%'       -- B-tree works, IF the collation is C or the index uses text_pattern_ops
WHERE name ILIKE 'brush%'      -- case-insensitive: needs lower(name) index or citext or pg_trgm

On a en_US.UTF-8 database:

CREATE INDEX idx_products_name_prefix ON products (name text_pattern_ops);  -- for LIKE 'x%'
CREATE INDEX idx_products_name_trgm ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops); -- for LIKE '%x%'

4. OR conditions

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 OR order_ref = $2;

OR across different columns cannot use a single composite index. PostgreSQL will use a BitmapOr if an index exists on each side, which is often fine. When it is not, rewrite to UNION ALL:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_ref = $2 AND user_id <> $1;   -- the guard prevents duplicates

Measured on orders: BitmapOr 412 ms, UNION ALL 1.8 ms, because the UNION ALL lets each branch use its own index scan with its own LIMIT-friendly ordering. OR inside a WHERE with a LIMIT and an ORDER BY is the worst case; that combination almost always needs the rewrite.

5. IS NULL on a non-partial index

B-trees do index NULLs, so WHERE sent_at IS NULL can use a plain index on sent_at. But if 99 percent of rows are NULL, the index is huge and the predicate is not selective, so the planner correctly ignores it. And if 0.01 percent are NULL, a partial index is 10,000 times smaller:

CREATE INDEX idx_notifications_unsent ON notifications (created_at) WHERE sent_at IS NULL;

Note that NOT NULL columns are cheaper in every index because there is no null bitmap to store.

6. Generic plans from prepared statements

PostgreSQL builds a custom plan (using the actual parameter values) for the first five executions of a prepared statement, then compares the average custom cost with the generic plan cost. If the generic plan is not worse, it switches to it permanently for that session, saving planning time.

For a skewed column that is a disaster: the generic plan is built for the average parameter, and the average user has 25 orders while one has 412,000.

-- See it happen
PREPARE p(bigint, text) AS SELECT id FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 AND status = $2 LIMIT 20;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) EXECUTE p(4471002, 'PAID');   -- runs 1..5: custom plan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) EXECUTE p(4471002, 'PAID');   -- run 6+: possibly generic

-- Force one or the other for the session
SET plan_cache_mode = 'force_custom_plan';      -- always re-plan with real values
SET plan_cache_mode = 'auto';                   -- default
SET plan_cache_mode = 'force_generic_plan';

The practical impact for Node.js: pg does not use server-side prepared statements unless you name a query, and TypeORM does not by default, so most applications are on custom plans. But PgBouncer in transaction mode plus named prepared statements is a known trap (Parts 7 and 181.3), and any service using prepare: true on skewed columns should set plan_cache_mode = 'force_custom_plan' for that role.

Also note: a partial index whose predicate depends on a parameter cannot be proven under a generic plan, so partial indexes silently stop being used.

7. Stale statistics after a bulk load

COPY orders FROM '/tmp/orders.csv' CSV;    -- 40 million rows
SELECT ... ;                               -- planner still thinks the table has 0 rows

reltuples is only updated by ANALYZE and VACUUM. Immediately after a load, the planner may pick a nested loop over what it thinks is an empty table and run it 40 million times. Always ANALYZE at the end of a bulk load, before any query runs:

COPY ...;
ANALYZE orders;                            -- or VACUUM ANALYZE orders;

The same applies after a large DELETE, after a partition attach, and after restoring a dump (pg_restore does not analyze).

8. An INVALID index after a failed CONCURRENTLY

Covered fully in 19.14. The signature: a query that should be fast is not, the index appears in \d table, and EXPLAIN never mentions it.

SELECT c.relname FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid WHERE NOT i.indisvalid;

Put that query in your monitoring with an alert. It costs nothing and it catches a class of silent 20 percent throughput loss.

9. Bitmap scan chosen for a large result set

Sometimes correct (19.4, Plan 4), sometimes the sign that your composite index is missing. The distinguishing question: does the plan also contain a Sort, or a large Rows Removed by Filter? If yes, a better index exists. If the bitmap scan reads the pages it needs and returns them unordered to an aggregate, it is doing the right thing.

10. Indexes on replicas

  • Indexes are physically replicated: you cannot have an index on a streaming replica that does not exist on the primary. (Logical replication subscribers can have their own.)
  • pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan is per node. An index unused on the primary may be the busiest one on the reporting replica.
  • A long-running query on a replica with hot_standby_feedback = on holds back the primary's xmin horizon, which stalls CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and vacuum.
  • Building an index on the primary streams the whole index through WAL to every replica; on a synchronous replica this slows every commit for the duration of the build.

11. LIMIT making the planner over-optimistic

The failure mode Part 18 introduced and this part fixes:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

With only (created_at), the planner reasons: "user 7 has 25 orders out of 200 million, uniformly distributed, so scanning backwards through created_at I should find 20 of them within about 160 million... no wait, within 20 / (25/200000000) = 160 million rows." Actually the planner's estimate is often far more optimistic than that, because it assumes the matching rows are spread evenly and it will hit them early. When user 7's orders are all from 2019, the scan walks nearly the whole index.

Limit  (cost=0.57..184.44 rows=20 width=61) (actual time=88214.114..88214.882 rows=3 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan Backward using idx_orders_created_at on orders
        (cost=0.57..1841022.44 rows=200 width=61) (actual time=88214.112..88214.878 rows=3 loops=1)
        Filter: (user_id = 7)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 199842118

Estimated cost 184, actual 88 seconds. The tell is rows=20 estimated against rows=3 actual on a LIMIT 20: the plan could not even fill the limit, which means it read everything. The only fix is the composite index (user_id, created_at DESC).

12. Other quiet failures worth knowing

  • NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL makes the whole predicate unusable and often forces a scan; use NOT EXISTS.
  • ORDER BY with a collation different from the index's (ORDER BY name COLLATE "de_DE" against an index built with the database default) forces a sort.
  • A glibc or ICU collation change during an OS upgrade silently corrupts every text index's ordering. Symptoms: unique violations that make no sense, missing rows in range queries. The fix is REINDEX every text index after the upgrade, and it is a genuine data-integrity issue, not a performance one.
  • SELECT * preventing index-only scans, forever.
  • Very large IN lists (thousands of values) where the planner gives up and scans; batch them or use = ANY($1::bigint[]) with a join against unnest.
  • ORDER BY random() LIMIT 1 which no index can ever serve; use TABLESAMPLE or a random-id probe.
  • Foreign key with no index on the child, giving the 31-second delete of 19.21.
  • Index on a column that is always the same value in practice (tenant_id in a single-tenant deployment): zero selectivity, full cost.

Interview questions

  1. Name five reasons an index that exists is not used. Expected: type mismatch/cast on the column, function on the column, leading wildcard, low selectivity, stale statistics, generic plan, invalid index, predicate mismatch on a partial index.
  2. What is plan_cache_mode and when do you change it? Expected: custom versus generic plans after five executions; force custom for skewed columns behind prepared statements.
  3. Why does an OR sometimes need a UNION ALL rewrite? Expected: no single index serves both sides; BitmapOr loses ordering and LIMIT early-exit.
  4. What happens to text indexes after an OS collation change? Expected: ordering silently changes; REINDEX all text indexes; correctness issue.
  5. A LIMIT 20 query estimated at cost 184 takes 88 seconds. Explain. Expected: uniform distribution assumption with a rare filter value; the scan never fills the limit; fix with a composite index.

Practical exercise

Reproduce eight of the twelve failure modes above on a seeded database and capture the plan for each: type mismatch, function on column, leading wildcard, OR, IS NULL on a mostly-null column, generic plan on a skewed column, missing ANALYZE after a bulk load, and the LIMIT over-optimism case. For each, write down the plan signature that identifies it and the one-line fix. Acceptance criteria: an eight-row diagnostic table you could hand to a teammate during an incident.

Senior Checklist — Part 19

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain what an index physically stores and why an index scan still reads the heap
  • I can compute B-tree depth from row count and fan-out, and explain why a billion-row lookup is 4 page reads
  • I read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) estimated-versus-actual rows before I read timings, and I account for loops
  • I can identify all four scan types in a plan and say when each one is correct
  • I know that a sequential scan is often the right plan and I do not "fix" it
  • I derive composite index column order from the query: equality, then sort, then range
  • I test every proposed index against the worst parameter value, not the typical one
  • I reach for a partial index whenever a query targets a small, constant-defined slice
  • I use partial unique indexes for soft delete and "one active X per Y", not application checks
  • I know that expression indexes require immutability and must match the query textually
  • I know INCLUDE versus a key column, and that index-only scans depend on vacuum
  • I can choose between B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN and hash and justify it with numbers
  • I know GIN costs 10 to 20 times more on inserts and I refuse it on hot write tables without a reason
  • I check pg_stats.correlation before proposing BRIN
  • I never run plain CREATE INDEX on a live table, and I set lock_timeout before every DDL
  • I know CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction and I set transaction = false in the migration
  • I monitor for NOT indisvalid indexes continuously
  • I can measure index bloat with pgstatindex and decide between REINDEX CONCURRENTLY and doing nothing
  • I can compute selectivity and know the ~5 to 10 percent crossover where a sequential scan wins
  • I use CREATE STATISTICS for correlated column pairs before adding an index
  • I can name the full cost of an index: write latency, WAL, vacuum, cache, storage, backup, planning, HOT
  • I find work with pg_stat_statements ordered by total_exec_time, not mean_exec_time
  • I use hypopg to evaluate an index before spending 26 minutes building it
  • I run the unused and redundant-prefix queries quarterly and drop with a monitoring window
  • I never drop a unique or constraint-backing index on the basis of idx_scan = 0
  • Every foreign key column in my schema has an index
  • Every composite index in my multi-tenant schema starts with tenant_id
  • I declare indexes in migrations, never with synchronize or sync
  • I have a CI test that asserts the plan of my most important query

Part 19 — Key Takeaways

  • An index is a separate sorted structure of (key -> ctid); the heap stays unordered, so an index scan is always a seek plus a random heap fetch unless the visibility map allows an index-only scan.
  • Every index is a read optimisation paid for on every write, forever: 2 indexes to 12 measured 6.4x insert time and 5.9x WAL on the same 1,000,000 rows.
  • A B-tree's fan-out of 250 to 400 keys per 8 KB page means 4 page reads for a billion rows; slow point lookups are never caused by table size.
  • Column order is the whole game: (status, created_at) and (created_at, status) differed by 11,800x on the same query with an unlucky parameter.
  • Read plans inside-out, compare estimated with actual rows first, multiply by loops, and trust Buffers over actual time.
  • Rows Removed by Filter and a Sort node above an index scan are the two signatures of a missing composite index.
  • A sequential scan is correct above roughly 5 to 10 percent of rows; forcing an index there made a query three times slower.
  • Partial indexes are the highest-leverage feature most teams never use: 41 GB to 3 MB, 4,212 ms to 1.3 ms on a queue table, and the predicate must textually imply the query's.
  • Use unique indexes as race-condition guards with ON CONFLICT, and partial unique indexes for soft delete and "one active X per Y".
  • Choose the access method by the question: B-tree for order and ranges, GIN for containment and text, GiST for overlap and nearest-neighbour, BRIN for correlated append-only time-series (3.5 MB versus 27 GB), hash almost never.
  • Always CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, always with lock_timeout, always one per migration, always verify indisvalid afterwards.
  • Fix the estimate before you add the index: ANALYZE, statistics target, CREATE STATISTICS. Two out of five slow queries need no index at all.
  • Find work with pg_stat_statements by total time, evaluate candidates with hypopg, and drop unused and redundant-prefix indexes on a schedule.
  • The best indexing change usually removes more indexes than it adds: one composite replaced four, made reads 575x faster and writes 1.8x faster, and used less storage.

Part 20 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control

Every backend bug that costs real money has the same shape: two things happened at the same time and the code assumed they would not. Two customers bought the last unit. Two workers picked up the same job. A payment was recorded but the order was not. A commit was acknowledged and then vanished when the disk lost power.

Transactions are the database's answer to "at the same time". They are also the most misunderstood tool in the backend developer's kit, because they look simple (BEGIN ... COMMIT) while hiding a lot of machinery: snapshots, row versions, locks, wait queues, deadlock detection, write-ahead logs and fsync calls. This part opens that machinery up. Every example is PostgreSQL, and wherever it matters we show two sessions side by side so you can see exactly what each one observes at each step. Then we map all of it onto TypeORM and Sequelize inside NestJS, including the mistakes that appear in almost every codebase we have reviewed.

Keep the senior mantra next to you while reading: Can it timeout? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed? Transactions exist to answer the last two.

20.1 ACID — the four promises

Concept

A transaction is a group of reads and writes that the database treats as one unit. ACID is the list of promises the database makes about that unit:

  • Atomicity — all of the writes happen, or none of them do. There is no "half".
  • Consistency — the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another valid state. "Valid" is defined by your constraints: primary keys, foreign keys, CHECK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, exclusion constraints, and triggers.
  • Isolation — concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work. How strictly this is enforced is configurable (the isolation level, section 20.2).
  • Durability — once the database says "committed", the data survives a crash, a power cut or a kernel panic.

Why does it exist?

Without atomicity, a crash in the middle of "create order, decrement stock, record payment" leaves a paid order with no stock reserved, or reserved stock with no order. Without consistency, application code becomes the only guard against negative stock, and application code has bugs. Without isolation, a report that sums balances while a transfer is in flight prints money that does not exist. Without durability, "your order is confirmed" is a lie the database tells before the bytes are on disk.

Each of these has a real incident behind it. Let us tell four.

Mental model

Imagine a bank teller processing a transfer on paper. She writes "minus 500 from account A" and "plus 500 to account B" on the same slip, and the slip goes into the ledger only when both lines are written and she has stamped it. If the pen runs dry after the first line, the slip is torn up and nothing happened (atomicity). The ledger has a rule printed on the cover: "no account may go below zero", and she checks it before stamping (consistency). While she is writing, other tellers cannot peek at her slip; they only see the ledger, which still shows the old balances (isolation). Once stamped, the slip is copied to the vault log before she tells the customer "done", so even if the office burns down tonight the transfer is in the vault (durability).

How it works

  1. BEGIN opens a transaction. PostgreSQL assigns a transaction id (xid) lazily, at the first write.
  2. Every row version written carries the xid that created it (xmin) and, when deleted or replaced, the xid that ended it (xmax). This is MVCC: multi-version concurrency control. Old versions are not overwritten in place; new versions are appended and old ones are cleaned up later by VACUUM.
  3. Reads use a snapshot: a record of which transaction ids were committed at the moment the snapshot was taken. A row version is visible if its xmin is committed in the snapshot and its xmax is not.
  4. Writes take a row-level lock on the row version they modify. A second writer of the same row waits.
  5. Constraints are checked as each statement runs (immediate constraints) or at commit (deferred constraints).
  6. COMMIT writes a commit record to the write-ahead log (WAL), flushes the WAL to disk (fsync), then marks the xid as committed in the commit log (pg_xact). Only after the flush does the client receive "COMMIT".
  7. ROLLBACK marks the xid as aborted. Row versions it created become invisible to everyone; nothing needs to be "undone" on disk.

Notice step 7: PostgreSQL rollback is cheap because MVCC never overwrote anything. The cost is paid later by VACUUM, which removes the dead versions.

Practical example — four incidents

Atomicity: the partial order. A checkout handler did three awaited calls without a transaction: INSERT INTO orders, then INSERT INTO order_items in a loop, then UPDATE products SET stock = stock - qty. A pod was killed by the Kubernetes scheduler (OOMKilled) between the second and third step. Result: an order with items but no stock decrement, sold again ten minutes later to another customer. With BEGIN ... COMMIT around all three, the kill would have left an aborted transaction and no order at all. The customer would have retried, which is exactly the outcome you want.

Consistency: the constraint that saved you. The same shop had CHECK (stock >= 0) on products. A later bug in a discount flow computed qty as NaN, which became NULL, which passed the JavaScript if (qty > stock) guard. The statement UPDATE products SET stock = stock - NULL would have set stock to NULL; the NOT NULL constraint rejected it. The transaction rolled back, the error was logged, and nobody sold ghost inventory. Constraints are the last line of defence and the only one that cannot be bypassed by a code path you forgot.

Isolation: the last item. Two customers clicked "Buy" on the last unit at 21:00:00.120 and 21:00:00.135. Both handlers read stock = 1, both compared 1 >= 1, both wrote stock = 0. Two orders, one unit. This is the lost update anomaly; section 20.3 shows the timeline and every fix.

Durability: the commit that vanished. A team set synchronous_commit = off on the primary to speed up a bulk import and forgot to turn it back on. Six weeks later the instance lost power. PostgreSQL recovered cleanly from WAL, but the last ~600 ms of commits (about 40 orders during a busy minute) were gone. The clients had received COMMIT for all of them. The confirmation emails had been sent. Section 20.9 explains exactly which synchronous_commit level means what.

NestJS example

The checkout use case with the three writes inside one transaction. The important line is the manager argument: every query inside must go through it.

// src/orders/checkout.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { OrderItem } from './order-item.entity';
import { Product } from '../products/product.entity';

@Injectable()
export class CheckoutService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async checkout(userId: string, lines: { productId: string; qty: number }[]): Promise<Order> {
    return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const order = await manager.save(Order, { userId, status: 'CREATED' });

      for (const line of lines) {
        // Atomic conditional decrement: no read-then-write race (see 13.3 and 13.10).
        const result = await manager
          .createQueryBuilder()
          .update(Product)
          .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
          .where('id = :id AND stock >= :qty', { id: line.productId, qty: line.qty })
          .execute();

        if (result.affected !== 1) {
          // Throwing inside the callback rolls the whole transaction back.
          throw new ConflictException(`Insufficient stock for ${line.productId}`);
        }
        await manager.save(OrderItem, { orderId: order.id, productId: line.productId, qty: line.qty });
      }
      return order;
    });
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The schema the whole part uses, with the constraints that make "consistency" mean something.

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  sku         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        text NOT NULL,
  price_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0),
  stock       integer NOT NULL CHECK (stock >= 0),
  version     integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('CREATED','PAID','CANCELLED')),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  qty         integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

-- Atomic unit: either all rows exist or none.
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, status) VALUES ('0c1...', 'a9f...', 'CREATED');
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 2 WHERE id = 'p1...' AND stock >= 2;
-- application checks that the UPDATE returned "UPDATE 1", otherwise issues ROLLBACK
INSERT INTO order_items VALUES ('0c1...', 'p1...', 2);
COMMIT;

TypeORM example

The same unit of work using a QueryRunner, which is what dataSource.transaction does for you underneath. You need this form when the transaction must outlive a single callback (for example, a multi-step saga with explicit commit).

const queryRunner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
await queryRunner.connect();            // takes one connection from the pool
await queryRunner.startTransaction();   // BEGIN
try {
  await queryRunner.manager.insert(Order, { id: orderId, userId, status: 'CREATED' });
  await queryRunner.manager.query(
    'UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND stock >= $1',
    [qty, productId],
  );
  await queryRunner.commitTransaction(); // COMMIT
} catch (err) {
  await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction(); // ROLLBACK
  throw err;
} finally {
  await queryRunner.release();           // ALWAYS: returns the connection to the pool
}

Sequelize example

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const order = await Order.create({ userId, status: 'CREATED' }, { transaction: t });
  const [affected] = await Product.update(
    { stock: this.sequelize.literal('stock - 2') },
    { where: { id: productId, stock: { [Op.gte]: 2 } }, transaction: t },
  );
  if (affected !== 1) throw new ConflictException('Insufficient stock');
  await OrderItem.create({ orderId: order.id, productId, qty: 2 }, { transaction: t });
});

Forgetting { transaction: t } on any one of those three calls silently runs that query on a different pooled connection, outside the transaction. It is the single most common Sequelize bug; section 20.12 returns to it.

Production scenario

An e-commerce API at 400 requests per second, of which 30 per second are checkouts. Each checkout transaction touches 1 orders row, 1–5 order_items rows and 1–5 products rows and holds its locks for about 4 ms on a local PostgreSQL. Lock contention is negligible unless one product is "hot" (a flash sale, where 500 checkouts per second hit the same products row). Then the row lock becomes a queue: each transaction waits for the previous one, throughput is bounded by 1 / lock_hold_time, and 4 ms per transaction means at most ~250 checkouts per second on that row, regardless of how many API pods you add. Section 20.10 covers the hot-row patterns.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call got paged: "orders with zero items". A deploy had introduced a try/catch around the items loop that logged the error and continued, so the outer transaction committed an order with no lines. Atomicity was intact at the database level; the application had decided to commit a broken unit. The fix was to rethrow inside the transaction callback. The lesson: the database can only roll back what you let it see as an error.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A client timeout (HTTP 504) does not roll back a server-side transaction that is still running. The transaction commits later, and the client retries, producing a duplicate. Idempotency keys (see Part 14 — API Design) are the fix, not shorter transactions alone.
  • COMMIT can itself fail (serialization failure at commit under SERIALIZABLE, deferred constraint violation, or the connection dropping during the fsync). Treat "commit threw" as "unknown outcome" and reconcile, never as "definitely rolled back".
  • A connection that dies mid-transaction is rolled back by PostgreSQL when it notices the socket close, which may take until the next write or tcp_keepalives_idle seconds.
  • Deferred constraints (DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED) move the consistency check to COMMIT, so a violation surfaces as a failed commit far from the offending statement.
  • Durability is only as good as the storage underneath. A cloud disk that acknowledges writes from a volatile cache violates the promise for you.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior question is not "is this ACID?" but "what is the unit of work, and which of its steps are inside the database?". Anything outside the database (an HTTP call to Stripe, a Kafka publish, an email) cannot be rolled back, so it must be either idempotent and retried, or moved after the commit via an outbox (section 20.8 and Part 29 — Distributed Transactions and Sagas). Explaining to a product manager: "The database guarantees we never sell what we do not have. It cannot guarantee the email goes out; for that we have a retry queue."

Common mistakes

  • Wrapping a single UPDATE in an explicit transaction "for safety". A single statement is already atomic; the extra round trips (BEGIN, COMMIT) double latency for nothing.
  • Believing that the ORM's save() is atomic across multiple entities. It is only atomic per statement unless you are inside a transaction.
  • Catching errors inside the transaction callback and not rethrowing, which commits partial work.
  • Treating CHECK constraints as "validation the ORM already does". The ORM validates one code path; the constraint validates every path, including the migration script someone runs by hand.

Interview questions

  1. What does "atomic" mean if PostgreSQL never undoes writes on rollback? Expected: MVCC appends new row versions; rollback marks the transaction aborted so its versions are invisible; VACUUM reclaims them. Follow-up: why is rollback cheap and vacuum expensive?
  2. When does a client receive COMMIT relative to the disk write? Expected: after the WAL commit record is fsynced, unless synchronous_commit is lowered. Follow-up: what does synchronous_commit = off risk, and for how long?
  3. Give an example where a database constraint caught a bug the application missed. Why it matters: shows the candidate treats the schema as a safety net, not decoration.
  4. Is a single UPDATE statement atomic without BEGIN? Expected: yes, autocommit wraps every statement in its own transaction.
  5. What happens to an open transaction when the Node process crashes? Expected: the socket closes, PostgreSQL aborts the transaction; but a Kubernetes SIGKILL and a NAT that keeps the socket half-open can delay that.

Practical exercise

Build a POST /checkout endpoint that creates an order, its items and decrements stock inside one transaction. Then write an integration test that injects a failure after the second item insert and asserts that no order, no items and no stock change survive. Acceptance criteria: the test passes; the products table has CHECK (stock >= 0); the endpoint returns 409 when stock is insufficient and the response contains no partial order id.

20.2 Isolation levels in PostgreSQL

Concept

The isolation level tells PostgreSQL how much of other people's concurrent work your transaction is allowed to notice. Stricter levels give you a more stable view of the data at the cost of more aborted transactions (which you must retry) and, in SERIALIZABLE, extra bookkeeping.

PostgreSQL implements three real levels: READ COMMITTED (the default), REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE. The SQL standard's READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted syntactically but behaves exactly like READ COMMITTED; PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data to anyone.

Why does it exist?

If every transaction saw a perfectly frozen world, PostgreSQL would have to abort a lot of work whenever two transactions touched the same data. If every transaction saw everything as it happens, your code would need to handle values changing between two lines. Isolation levels let you choose, per transaction, where on that spectrum you want to be. Most OLTP code lives happily at READ COMMITTED plus explicit locks; reports and multi-row invariants need REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE.

Mental model

Imagine reading a busy news website.

  • READ COMMITTED is refreshing the page before every glance. Each glance is consistent (you never see a half-written article), but two glances may show different headlines.
  • REPEATABLE READ is printing the site the moment you sit down and reading only the printout. Nothing changes under you. If you try to edit an article that someone else edited after your printout, the editor rejects your change: your printout is stale.
  • SERIALIZABLE is the printout plus an editor who also checks whether what you read influenced what you wrote in a way that could contradict someone else's edit, even on different articles. If so, one of you is rejected.

How it works

The mechanism is the snapshot.

  1. A snapshot records: the lowest xid still running (xmin), the next xid to be assigned (xmax), and the list of xids in between that are still in progress.
  2. A row version is visible to the snapshot if its creating transaction committed before the snapshot and its deleting transaction (if any) did not.
  3. READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot at the start of every statement.
  4. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE take one snapshot at the first statement of the transaction (not at BEGIN; the snapshot is taken when the first query runs) and use it for every statement until commit.
  5. Writes never use the snapshot to decide what row to lock. They always lock the newest committed version. This difference between "what I read" and "what I write" is where the interesting behaviour lives.
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as SessionA
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    participant B as SessionB
    A->>PG: BEGIN READ COMMITTED
    A->>PG: SELECT stock WHERE id = p1
    PG-->>A: stock is 5 (snapshot 1)
    B->>PG: UPDATE products SET stock = 2 WHERE id = p1 and COMMIT
    PG-->>B: UPDATE 1
    A->>PG: SELECT stock WHERE id = p1
    PG-->>A: stock is 2 (snapshot 2, new statement)
    A->>PG: COMMIT

The same script under REPEATABLE READ returns 5 both times for session A.

20.2.1 Read Uncommitted

Syntax is accepted (BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED) and silently upgraded to READ COMMITTED. Dirty reads are impossible in PostgreSQL. If you are migrating from MySQL or SQL Server, where READ UNCOMMITTED is a real (and dangerous) level used for "fast counts", know that the trick does nothing here and the count is still consistent.

20.2.2 Read Committed — the default

Each statement sees a fresh snapshot. Two consequences you will meet in production:

The re-read sees new data. Setup: products row p1 with stock = 5.

Step Session A Session B What A sees
1 BEGIN;
2 SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; 5
3 UPDATE products SET stock = 2 WHERE id = 'p1'; (autocommit)
4 SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; 2
5 COMMIT;

Within one transaction, A saw two different values. That is a non-repeatable read, allowed at this level. Code that reads a value, does some logic, and re-reads it "to be sure" is not made safer by being inside a transaction at READ COMMITTED.

UPDATE re-checks the WHERE on the latest version. This is the behaviour that makes the atomic conditional update safe. Setup: stock = 1.

Step Session A Session B Result
1 BEGIN; BEGIN;
2 UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 'p1' AND stock >= 1; UPDATE 1; A holds the row lock; stock (uncommitted) is 0
3 UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 'p1' AND stock >= 1; B blocks: row is locked by A
4 COMMIT; A's version (stock 0) is now committed
5 (wakes up) PostgreSQL re-fetches the newest version, re-evaluates stock >= 1 on it: false. UPDATE 0
6 application sees 0 rows affected, issues ROLLBACK;

Step 5 is the important one. PostgreSQL does not apply B's update to the version B's snapshot saw (stock 1). It waits, then re-evaluates the WHERE clause against the latest committed version. If the condition still holds, the update proceeds on the new version; if not, the row is skipped. This is documented as the "EvalPlanQual" re-check. It means UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= qty cannot oversell, at any isolation level, without any explicit lock.

The same re-check applies to DELETE and to SELECT ... FOR UPDATE: after waiting for a lock, the returned row is the latest version and rows that no longer match the WHERE are dropped from the result.

20.2.3 Repeatable Read — one snapshot per transaction

Every statement uses the snapshot taken at the first statement. Reads are stable. The price is paid on writes: if your transaction tries to UPDATE or DELETE (or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) a row that another transaction has modified and committed since your snapshot, PostgreSQL cannot both honour your snapshot and apply your write, so it aborts you:

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
SQLSTATE 40001
Step Session A Session B Result
1 BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
2 SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; 5 (snapshot taken now)
3 UPDATE products SET stock = 2 WHERE id = 'p1'; (autocommit) commits
4 SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; still 5
5 UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 'p1'; ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
6 ROLLBACK; then retry the whole transaction second attempt sees 2

If at step 3 B had not yet committed, A would block at step 5 until B finished; if B then committed, A gets the error; if B rolled back, A proceeds. Note that in the SQL standard REPEATABLE READ still allows phantom reads; PostgreSQL's implementation prevents them too, because the snapshot covers the whole transaction, not individual rows.

REPEATABLE READ does not prevent write skew (section 20.3.5), because write skew involves no two transactions writing the same row.

20.2.4 Serializable — SSI and predicate locks

SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL is Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI). It starts as REPEATABLE READ and adds a detector: PostgreSQL tracks what each transaction read (as predicate locks, SIReadLock entries in pg_locks, on rows, pages or whole relations) and what it wrote, and looks for the dangerous pattern of read/write dependencies that could make the outcome different from some serial ordering. When it finds the pattern, it aborts one of the transactions:

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during commit attempt.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.
SQLSTATE 40001

Three things to know before switching a workload to SERIALIZABLE:

  1. You must retry. Every transaction at this level can fail with 40001 through no fault of its own, even at commit time. Code without a retry loop will surface random 500s under load.
  2. Predicate locks are not real locks. They do not block anyone; they only feed the detector. Memory for them is bounded by max_pred_locks_per_transaction (default 64) and the related max_pred_locks_per_relation / max_pred_locks_per_page settings; when exhausted, PostgreSQL escalates to page or relation granularity, which increases false-positive aborts.
  3. Every transaction touching the data must be serializable for the guarantee to hold. A READ COMMITTED writer mixed in is invisible to the detector. Read-only serializable transactions can declare READ ONLY DEFERRABLE to wait for a safe snapshot and then never abort, which is ideal for long reports.

Practical example

An inventory service used READ COMMITTED with read-then-write logic in Node and oversold during a flash sale. The team's first instinct was "switch everything to SERIALIZABLE". It worked functionally, but the abort rate hit 18% at peak and their code had no retry, so users saw errors. The eventual fix was the atomic conditional UPDATE at READ COMMITTED (no aborts, no retries) for the stock path, and SERIALIZABLE with a retry loop only for the one multi-row invariant they could not express as a single statement (a per-customer credit limit across several pending orders).

NestJS example

A generic retry wrapper for serialization failures (40001) and deadlocks (40P01). Note that only the whole transaction is retried, and only if the work inside is safe to repeat.

// src/database/retry-transaction.ts
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';

const RETRYABLE = new Set(['40001', '40P01']); // serialization_failure, deadlock_detected

export async function withSerializableRetry<T>(
  dataSource: DataSource,
  work: (manager: EntityManager) => Promise<T>,
  maxAttempts = 5,
): Promise<T> {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await dataSource.transaction('SERIALIZABLE', work);
    } catch (err: any) {
      const code = err?.code ?? err?.driverError?.code;
      if (!RETRYABLE.has(code) || attempt >= maxAttempts) throw err;
      // Exponential backoff with jitter: 10-20ms, 20-40ms, 40-80ms, ...
      const base = 10 * 2 ** (attempt - 1);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, base + Math.random() * base));
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

-- Per transaction
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- or, after BEGIN and before the first query:
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

-- Per session / per role / per database (rarely a good idea globally)
SET default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read';
ALTER ROLE reporting SET default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read';

-- Inspect what a session is running at
SHOW transaction_isolation;

-- A long report that must never abort and never block writers:
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE;
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at), sum(total_cents) FROM orders GROUP BY 1;
COMMIT;

TypeORM example

// Isolation level as the first argument
await this.dataSource.transaction('REPEATABLE READ', async (manager) => {
  const product = await manager.findOneByOrFail(Product, { id });
  // ... a serialization failure here surfaces as a QueryFailedError with driverError.code === '40001'
});

// Same with a QueryRunner
await queryRunner.startTransaction('SERIALIZABLE');

Valid values are 'READ UNCOMMITTED' | 'READ COMMITTED' | 'REPEATABLE READ' | 'SERIALIZABLE'.

Sequelize example

import { Transaction } from 'sequelize';

await this.sequelize.transaction(
  { isolationLevel: Transaction.ISOLATION_LEVELS.SERIALIZABLE },
  async (t) => {
    const product = await Product.findByPk(id, { transaction: t });
    // ... error.original.code === '40001' on serialization failure
  },
);

Production scenario

A payments ledger at 200 transactions per second moved its "post journal entry and check that debits equal credits across the batch" transaction to SERIALIZABLE. Contention was low (each batch touched its own rows), so the abort rate was under 0.3%, and a 3-attempt retry made user-visible failures effectively zero. The extra cost of predicate lock tracking was about 5–8% CPU on the primary. That is a good trade. The same level on the "hot product row" checkout path was not: 18% aborts, retries amplifying load, p99 latency tripled.

Failure scenario

A reporting job ran a 40-minute REPEATABLE READ transaction against the primary every night. Nobody noticed for months. Then a table with a high update rate started bloating: VACUUM could not remove any row version newer than the report's snapshot, because the report might still need it. Dead tuples piled up for 40 minutes every night; index bloat followed; p99 latency on that table doubled. The fix was to run the report on a replica with hot_standby_feedback considered carefully, and to set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so a forgotten transaction could not do the same by accident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The snapshot for REPEATABLE READ is taken at the first statement, not at BEGIN. Code that opens a transaction, awaits something slow, then queries, sees data as of the query, not the BEGIN.
  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE under REPEATABLE READ can also raise 40001 if the row changed since the snapshot. Pessimistic locks are not a way to avoid retries at this level.
  • Under SERIALIZABLE, a transaction can be aborted after it did everything right, because another transaction created the dependency. The retry loop must reload all data; reusing values from the failed attempt defeats the purpose.
  • Sequence values (nextval) and advisory locks are not transactional and are not rolled back; retries burn ids, which is fine, and re-acquire locks, which you must account for.
  • SERIALIZABLE and hot standby: serializable transactions on a streaming replica are downgraded to REPEATABLE READ behaviour (predicate tracking does not run on standbys).
  • Mixing levels: if writers are READ COMMITTED and one reader is SERIALIZABLE, the reader gets a consistent snapshot but no serializability guarantee about the writers' logic.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior default is: stay at READ COMMITTED, make each write self-defending (conditional UPDATE, unique constraints, FOR UPDATE where a read must be followed by a dependent write), and reach for SERIALIZABLE only for invariants that span multiple rows and cannot be expressed as constraints. They never turn on SERIALIZABLE globally without a retry wrapper and a dashboard of the 40001 rate. They ask: "What is the invariant? Can the schema enforce it? If not, can one statement enforce it? If not, which rows do I lock? If locking is impractical, SERIALIZABLE with retry."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a transaction at the default level gives repeatable reads. It does not; every statement is a new snapshot.
  • Switching to REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE without a retry loop, then treating the resulting 40001 errors as "database flakiness".
  • Retrying only the failing statement instead of the whole transaction. After 40001 the transaction is aborted; every statement until ROLLBACK returns current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block.
  • Believing SERIALIZABLE prevents lost updates between a serializable transaction and a read-committed one. It does not.

Interview questions

  1. Why does READ UNCOMMITTED exist in PostgreSQL if it behaves like READ COMMITTED? Expected: SQL standard compliance; MVCC never exposes uncommitted versions, so there is nothing to opt into.
  2. A READ COMMITTED UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= 1 waits on a locked row. What does it evaluate when it wakes up? Expected: the newest committed version, re-checking the WHERE; if false, zero rows. Why it matters: this is the basis of every safe atomic decrement.
  3. What error does a REPEATABLE READ transaction get when it updates a row someone else changed after its snapshot, and what should the application do? Expected: 40001 could not serialize access due to concurrent update; roll back and retry the whole transaction with fresh reads.
  4. How does PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE differ from taking locks? Expected: SSI tracks read/write dependencies with non-blocking predicate locks and aborts on dangerous cycles; nothing waits, some things fail. Follow-up: what happens when predicate lock memory runs out?
  5. When would you use READ ONLY DEFERRABLE? Expected: long serializable reports that must not abort or cause others to abort.

Practical exercise

Open two psql sessions. Reproduce all three tables from this section step by step and record what each session prints. Then write a Jest integration test that runs two concurrent REPEATABLE READ TypeORM transactions on the same row, asserts that exactly one fails with driverError.code === '40001', and that wrapping both in withSerializableRetry makes both eventually succeed with the correct final stock. Acceptance criteria: the test is deterministic (use a barrier or explicit ordering, not setTimeout guesses) and passes ten times in a row.

20.3 Concurrency anomalies, one timeline at a time

Concept

An anomaly is a result that could not have happened if the transactions had run one after another. There are five you must be able to draw on a whiteboard: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update, and write skew. Each has a precise definition, a precise two-session reproduction, and a precise set of fixes. Senior engineers do not memorise the SQL-standard table; they memorise what PostgreSQL actually does, which differs from the standard in two places.

Why does it exist?

Anomalies exist because the database lets transactions overlap in time for throughput. If PostgreSQL ran one transaction at a time, none of these could happen, and a 32-core server would run at the speed of one connection. Every anomaly is the price of a particular kind of overlap, and every isolation level is a decision about which prices you are willing to pay.

Mental model

Imagine several people editing the same spreadsheet. A dirty read is reading a cell someone is still typing in. A non-repeatable read is reading a cell, looking away, and finding a different value when you look back. A phantom is counting the rows, looking away, and finding a new row. A lost update is two people reading "5", each typing "5 minus 1", and the cell ending at 4 instead of 3. Write skew is two people each checking "is there at least one other person marked on-call?", both seeing yes, and both removing themselves.

How it works

Each anomaly below is shown with the setup, the two-session timeline, the PostgreSQL behaviour at each level, and the fixes. Run them yourself with two psql windows; the tables are the ones from section 20.1.

20.3.1 Dirty read

Reading data written by a transaction that has not committed (and may roll back).

Step Session A Session B What B sees
1 BEGIN;
2 UPDATE products SET price_cents = 100 WHERE id = 'p1';
3 SELECT price_cents FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; old value (say 2500), never 100
4 ROLLBACK;

PostgreSQL: impossible at every level. MVCC only ever shows committed versions to other sessions. If you come from MySQL InnoDB with READ UNCOMMITTED, or from SQL Server with NOLOCK hints, this is the anomaly those settings allow. There is nothing to fix here in PostgreSQL; we list it so the table at the end is complete.

20.3.2 Non-repeatable read

Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because someone committed in between.

Step Session A Session B What A sees
1 BEGIN;
2 SELECT price_cents FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; 2500
3 UPDATE products SET price_cents = 2000 WHERE id = 'p1'; (autocommit)
4 SELECT price_cents FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; 2000 at READ COMMITTED; 2500 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE

Where this hurts: a checkout that reads the price to show the user, then re-reads to compute the total on the same request, and charges a different amount than it displayed. Fixes: read once and carry the value; or REPEATABLE READ; or lock the row with FOR SHARE if a concurrent price change must be blocked for the duration.

20.3.3 Phantom read

Re-running a query with a WHERE clause and seeing rows that were not there before (or missing rows that were).

Step Session A Session B What A sees
1 BEGIN;
2 SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = 'u1' AND status = 'CREATED'; 2
3 INSERT INTO orders (user_id, status) VALUES ('u1', 'CREATED'); (autocommit)
4 SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = 'u1' AND status = 'CREATED'; 3 at READ COMMITTED; 2 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE

The SQL standard allows phantoms at REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL does not, because its snapshot covers every row, not just the ones you touched. The place phantoms bite is rule enforcement by counting: "a user may have at most 3 open orders". Two concurrent inserts each count 2, each proceed, and the user has 4. Row locks cannot fix this, because the row that breaks the rule does not exist yet when you would lock it. The fixes are a constraint (unique/exclusion where expressible), a lock on a parent row (SELECT ... FROM users WHERE id = 'u1' FOR UPDATE to serialise all order creation for that user), an advisory lock keyed on the user id, or SERIALIZABLE.

20.3.4 Lost update

Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value from what it read, and each writes; the second write silently overwrites the first.

This is the anomaly that oversells inventory, double-spends wallets and loses counter increments. The classic buggy code:

// The bug. Looks reasonable, loses updates under any concurrency at all.
const product = await repo.findOneByOrFail({ id });      // read: stock = 1
if (product.stock < qty) throw new ConflictException();
product.stock -= qty;                                    // compute in JavaScript
await repo.save(product);                                // write: stock = 0
Step Session A Session B Stock (committed)
0 1
1 BEGIN; SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; returns 1 1
2 BEGIN; SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 'p1'; returns 1 1
3 UPDATE products SET stock = 0 WHERE id = 'p1'; 1 (A holds row lock)
4 UPDATE products SET stock = 0 WHERE id = 'p1'; blocks 1
5 COMMIT; 0
6 unblocks; at READ COMMITTED the WHERE id = 'p1' still matches, so UPDATE 1; COMMIT; 0

Two orders, one unit, no error anywhere. The CHECK (stock >= 0) did not fire because each session wrote the literal 0, not stock - 1.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as CheckoutA
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    participant B as CheckoutB
    A->>PG: SELECT stock WHERE id = p1
    PG-->>A: 1
    B->>PG: SELECT stock WHERE id = p1
    PG-->>B: 1
    A->>PG: UPDATE SET stock = 0 WHERE id = p1
    PG-->>A: UPDATE 1 then COMMIT
    B->>PG: UPDATE SET stock = 0 WHERE id = p1
    PG-->>B: UPDATE 1 then COMMIT
    Note over A,B: Both orders accepted for one unit. Second write silently overwrote the first.

Fix 1 — atomic UPDATE (best when the new value is a function of the old value).

UPDATE products
SET    stock = stock - 1
WHERE  id = 'p1' AND stock >= 1
RETURNING stock;

Session B blocks on A's row lock, then re-evaluates stock >= 1 against the committed version (0), matches nothing, returns UPDATE 0. The application treats zero affected rows as "sold out". No explicit lock, no retry, works at READ COMMITTED. The CHECK constraint is a second net: even without the WHERE, stock - 1 would go to -1 and fail.

Fix 2 — pessimistic lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) when the logic between read and write is too complex for one statement.

BEGIN;
SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 'p1' FOR UPDATE;   -- B blocks here until A commits
-- application logic: check reservations, apply bundle rules, compute new stock
UPDATE products SET stock = 0 WHERE id = 'p1';
COMMIT;

B's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE waits, then returns the new committed value (0), so B's logic sees the truth. Section 20.6 covers the lock modes and their costs.

Fix 3 — optimistic version column.

-- read
SELECT stock, version FROM products WHERE id = 'p1';     -- stock 1, version 7
-- write, only if nobody else wrote since our read
UPDATE products
SET    stock = 0, version = version + 1
WHERE  id = 'p1' AND version = 7;
-- UPDATE 1 => we won; UPDATE 0 => someone else wrote first, reload and retry or fail

No lock is held between read and write, so this works even when the "think time" is a human filling a form for two minutes. Section 20.5 covers TypeORM @VersionColumn and Sequelize version: true.

Fix 4 — REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE. At either level, session B's UPDATE at step 6 fails with 40001 could not serialize access due to concurrent update, because the row changed after B's snapshot. B must retry. This fixes lost updates without changing the SQL, which makes it attractive for legacy code, at the cost of retries.

Not a fix: SELECT ... FOR SHARE on both sides. Both hold a share lock, both try to upgrade to a write lock, and PostgreSQL detects a deadlock and kills one. It "works" by accident and pollutes your logs.

20.3.5 Write skew

Two transactions read overlapping data, each makes a decision based on what it read, and each writes to a different row. Neither write conflicts with the other, so no row lock and no REPEATABLE READ check ever fires, yet the combined result violates an invariant.

On-call doctors. Invariant: at least one doctor must be on call. Two doctors are on call; both ask to go off at the same time.

CREATE TABLE shifts (doctor_id text PRIMARY KEY, on_call boolean NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO shifts VALUES ('alice', true), ('bob', true);
Step Session A (Alice) Session B (Bob) Result
1 BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
2 SELECT count(*) FROM shifts WHERE on_call; returns 2
3 SELECT count(*) FROM shifts WHERE on_call; returns 2
4 UPDATE shifts SET on_call = false WHERE doctor_id = 'alice'; UPDATE 1
5 UPDATE shifts SET on_call = false WHERE doctor_id = 'bob'; UPDATE 1 (different row, no conflict)
6 COMMIT; COMMIT; both succeed; nobody is on call

REPEATABLE READ did nothing, because neither transaction updated a row the other had updated. At SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL's SSI sees that A read rows that B wrote and B read rows that A wrote (a read/write dependency cycle) and aborts one at commit with could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions.

Overselling across two rows. The same shape appears in e-commerce when stock is split across warehouses and the rule is "total stock across warehouses >= qty": each checkout reads both rows, sees enough in total, and decrements a different warehouse row.

Fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Make it a single-row invariant so a constraint or conditional UPDATE can enforce it (keep an on_call_count in a single row and UPDATE ... WHERE on_call_count > 1).
  2. Materialise the conflict: lock a common parent row (SELECT ... FROM rota WHERE id = 'night' FOR UPDATE) at the start of both transactions, so they serialise.
  3. Advisory lock keyed on the invariant (pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('rota:night'))).
  4. SERIALIZABLE with a retry loop, when the rows involved are not known in advance.

Nothing weaker than these works, because there is no shared row for REPEATABLE READ or FOR UPDATE to notice.

20.3.6 Which anomaly at which level — PostgreSQL, not the standard

Anomaly READ UNCOMMITTED (= RC in PG) READ COMMITTED REPEATABLE READ SERIALIZABLE
Dirty read impossible impossible impossible impossible
Non-repeatable read possible possible impossible impossible
Phantom read possible possible impossible (standard says possible) impossible
Lost update (read, compute, write) possible possible impossible: writer gets 40001 impossible: 40001
Write skew possible possible possible impossible: 40001
Serialization failures you must retry none none on concurrent row update on any dangerous dependency, even at commit

Two rows of that table differ from the textbook: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ blocks phantoms, and PostgreSQL's READ UNCOMMITTED is not a distinct level.

Practical example

A wallet service had balance_cents per user and a "withdraw" endpoint written as read-check-write. Under a load test of 50 concurrent withdrawals on one wallet, the final balance was wrong by a random amount every run. The team fixed it with a single statement: UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance_cents >= $1 RETURNING balance_cents, plus CHECK (balance_cents >= 0). Zero lost updates at any concurrency, no lock code, and the endpoint got faster because it went from two round trips to one.

NestJS example

The wallet withdrawal with all three defences: atomic statement, constraint, and affected-row check.

// src/wallets/wallets.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Wallet } from './wallet.entity';

@Injectable()
export class WalletsService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Wallet) private readonly wallets: Repository<Wallet>) {}

  async withdraw(walletId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<number> {
    const result = await this.wallets
      .createQueryBuilder()
      .update(Wallet)
      .set({ balanceCents: () => 'balance_cents - :amount' })
      .where('id = :id AND balance_cents >= :amount', { id: walletId, amount: amountCents })
      .returning(['balance_cents'])
      .execute();

    if (result.affected === 0) {
      // Either the wallet does not exist or funds are insufficient; distinguish with one cheap read.
      const exists = await this.wallets.exist({ where: { id: walletId } });
      if (!exists) throw new NotFoundException('Wallet not found');
      throw new ConflictException('Insufficient funds');
    }
    return Number(result.raw[0].balance_cents);
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

A phantom-safe "max 3 open orders per user" rule using a parent-row lock, which is cheaper and more predictable than SERIALIZABLE for this shape.

BEGIN;
-- Serialise all order creation for this user. Other users are unaffected.
SELECT id FROM users WHERE id = 'u1' FOR NO KEY UPDATE;

-- Now this count cannot be raced by another creation for u1.
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = 'u1' AND status = 'CREATED';
-- application checks count < 3, else ROLLBACK

INSERT INTO orders (user_id, status) VALUES ('u1', 'CREATED');
COMMIT;

FOR NO KEY UPDATE rather than FOR UPDATE because we do not intend to change the user's primary key, and it does not block concurrent INSERTs into tables that reference users (see 20.4 for why that matters).

TypeORM example

await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  await manager
    .createQueryBuilder(User, 'u')
    .setLock('pessimistic_write')            // for_no_key_update is also available as a lock mode
    .where('u.id = :id', { id: userId })
    .getOne();

  const open = await manager.count(Order, { where: { userId, status: 'CREATED' } });
  if (open >= 3) throw new ConflictException('Too many open orders');
  await manager.insert(Order, { userId, status: 'CREATED' });
});

Sequelize example

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await User.findByPk(userId, { transaction: t, lock: t.LOCK.NO_KEY_UPDATE });
  const open = await Order.count({ where: { userId, status: 'CREATED' }, transaction: t });
  if (open >= 3) throw new ConflictException('Too many open orders');
  await Order.create({ userId, status: 'CREATED' }, { transaction: t });
});

Production scenario

A ride-booking platform assigns drivers to rides. The invariant "a driver has at most one active ride" was enforced by counting active rides before insert. At 1,200 ride requests per minute in a dense city, two dispatchers assigned the same driver about 30 times a day. The fix was a partial unique index, CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_ride_per_driver ON rides (driver_id) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE', which turns the phantom into a constraint violation (23505) the second inserter can catch. No locks, no isolation level change, and the index is tiny because it only contains active rides.

Failure scenario

At 11:03 on Black Friday the inventory dashboard showed -37 for a headphone SKU. The CHECK (stock >= 0) had been dropped in a migration two months earlier "because it made the bulk importer fail". The checkout code was read-compute-write. Every one of the 37 oversold units became a cancellation email and a support ticket. Three fixes shipped that day: the constraint came back (the importer was fixed to insert valid data), the decrement became an atomic conditional UPDATE, and a nightly job started comparing sum(order_items.qty) against stock movements.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lost updates also happen on JSON columns: read the jsonb, modify one key in JavaScript, write the whole document back. Use jsonb_set in the UPDATE or lock the row.
  • Counters incremented via ORM save() are lost-update machines: entity.viewCount++ then save() is read-compute-write. Use increment() (TypeORM repository.increment(criteria, 'viewCount', 1), Sequelize Model.increment).
  • A conditional UPDATE that matches zero rows is indistinguishable from "row does not exist". Check existence separately when the error message matters.
  • Write skew hides inside "check then insert" flows: uniqueness across two columns enforced by a SELECT before INSERT is write skew; the unique index is the fix.
  • Under SERIALIZABLE, sequences and now() are not part of the serial order; do not build invariants on them.
  • Batch jobs that read a whole table at READ COMMITTED over many statements see a mix of old and new rows; use REPEATABLE READ for a consistent batch view.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They classify every write path by shape. "New value depends on old value of the same row" gets an atomic UPDATE. "Decision depends on several rows, writes one row" gets a parent-row lock or advisory lock. "Rule about the set of rows" gets a constraint if it can be expressed (unique, partial unique, exclusion), otherwise a lock or SERIALIZABLE. They refuse the phrase "it is unlikely two requests hit at the same time"; at 100 requests per second with 5 ms transactions, "unlikely" is several times per minute.

Common mistakes

  • Reading, then writing, with the read and write in the same transaction, and calling that "transactional". It is still a lost update at READ COMMITTED.
  • Fixing lost updates with REPEATABLE READ and then not handling 40001.
  • Thinking FOR UPDATE fixes write skew. It only serialises transactions that lock the same rows.
  • Enforcing "at most N" by counting, without a lock or constraint.
  • Dropping a constraint to make an import pass.

Interview questions

  1. Show a lost update with two sessions and list four fixes. Expected: the table above; atomic update, FOR UPDATE, version column, REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE with retry. Follow-up: which one has no retries and no locks beyond the statement itself?
  2. What is write skew and why does REPEATABLE READ not prevent it? Expected: different rows written after overlapping reads; no row conflict for the first-updater-wins check to catch. Follow-up: name three fixes that are not SERIALIZABLE.
  3. How does PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ differ from the SQL standard on phantoms? Expected: prevents them via whole-transaction snapshot.
  4. "At most three open orders per user" — how do you enforce it under concurrency? Expected: lock the user row, or advisory lock, or SERIALIZABLE; note a partial unique index works for "at most one".
  5. Why is SELECT ... FOR SHARE on both sides of a read-modify-write a bad fix? Expected: lock upgrade deadlock.

Practical exercise

Write a script that runs 100 concurrent withdrawals of 10 cents against a wallet with 500 cents, using (a) read-compute-write, (b) atomic conditional UPDATE, (c) SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, (d) a version column with retry, and (e) SERIALIZABLE with retry. For each, record the final balance, the number of successful withdrawals, the number of retries, and the p99 latency. Acceptance criteria: (a) ends with a wrong balance and you can explain why; (b) through (e) end with exactly 50 successes and a balance of 0; you can rank (b) through (e) by latency and explain the ranking.

20.4 Locks in PostgreSQL

Concept

A lock is a promise the database keeps for you: "nobody else will do X to this thing until you are done". PostgreSQL has locks on rows, on tables, on transaction ids, on pages, and a general-purpose kind called advisory locks that mean whatever your application says they mean. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers for plain reads (that is MVCC's job); locks exist to order writers against writers and to protect schema changes.

Why does it exist?

Snapshots solve reading. They do not solve "two transactions want to change the same row" or "someone wants to drop a column while a query is reading it". For those, someone must wait. Locks decide who waits for whom, and for how long.

Mental model

Imagine a library with a rule: anyone may read a book at the table, but only one person may write in the margins at a time, and to do so they check the book out with a marker slip. FOR UPDATE is the slip. Someone who only wants to make sure the book is not removed from the shelf while they cite it uses a lighter slip (FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE). Rebuilding the shelf (ALTER TABLE) needs the whole aisle empty. And an advisory lock is a note on the whiteboard, "Praveen is reorganising the poetry section", that everyone agrees to respect even though the library itself does not enforce it.

How it works

20.4.1 Row-level locks

There are four row lock modes, from strongest to weakest:

Mode Taken by Conflicts with
FOR UPDATE DELETE; UPDATE that changes a key column (PK or unique); SELECT ... FOR UPDATE all four modes
FOR NO KEY UPDATE UPDATE that does not change key columns (the common case); SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE
FOR SHARE SELECT ... FOR SHARE FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE
FOR KEY SHARE foreign-key checks on the referenced row (an INSERT into order_items takes this on the products row); SELECT ... FOR KEY SHARE FOR UPDATE only

Two lines of that table drive real production behaviour:

  • A normal UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 takes FOR NO KEY UPDATE, which is compatible with FOR KEY SHARE. So inserting order lines that reference a product does not wait for a concurrent stock update. Good.
  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes the strongest mode, which conflicts with FOR KEY SHARE. So if your checkout locks the product with FOR UPDATE, every other transaction inserting an order_items row for that product waits for your whole transaction. TypeORM's pessimistic_write and Sequelize's t.LOCK.UPDATE both emit FOR UPDATE. If you do not intend to delete the row or change its key, prefer FOR NO KEY UPDATE (TypeORM lock mode for_no_key_update, Sequelize t.LOCK.NO_KEY_UPDATE).

Row locks live in the row header (xmax plus info bits), not in shared memory, so you can lock a million rows without running out of lock memory. Waiting is implemented by waiting on the transaction id of the holder, which is why deadlock messages talk about "ShareLock on transaction 12345".

Two modifiers change what happens when the row is already locked:

-- Wait forever (default). Bounded by lock_timeout if set.
SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE;

-- Fail immediately with 55P03 lock_not_available.
SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;

-- Skip rows that are locked, return the rest. The queue pattern (13.10).
