SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

20.4.2 Table-level locks

Every statement takes a table-level lock on each table it touches, mostly to keep DDL out of the way:

Mode Taken by Blocks
ACCESS SHARE SELECT only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
ROW SHARE SELECT ... FOR UPDATE/SHARE EXCLUSIVE, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
ROW EXCLUSIVE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE SHARE and above
SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE VACUUM, ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, some ALTER TABLE forms itself and above
SHARE CREATE INDEX (non-concurrent) writes
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, most ALTER TABLE everything, including SELECT

The dangerous mechanic is the lock queue. Table locks are granted in order. If a two-hour report holds ACCESS SHARE on orders, an ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN queues behind it for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and every new SELECT on orders queues behind the ALTER. One idle migration can take the whole API down while blocking nothing itself. Always run DDL with SET lock_timeout = '3s' and retry; Part 23 — Safe Schema Migrations covers this in depth.

20.4.3 The lock escalation myth

SQL Server and older MySQL versions escalate many row locks into a table lock when a transaction locks too many rows. PostgreSQL never does this. A transaction that updates 10 million rows holds 10 million row locks (in row headers) and one ROW EXCLUSIVE table lock, and other transactions can still update the rows it did not touch. What PostgreSQL does have is the shared lock table for table-level and advisory locks, bounded by max_locks_per_transaction (default 64) times max_connections; exhausting it fails with out of shared memory when a transaction touches thousands of tables or partitions, which is a different problem.

20.4.4 Foreign-key locks

When you insert or update a child row, PostgreSQL must make sure the parent row exists and stays existing until you commit. It does that with SELECT 1 FROM products WHERE id = $1 FOR KEY SHARE behind the scenes. Consequences:

  • Deleting a parent, or updating its primary key, takes FOR UPDATE and waits for every open transaction that inserted a child referencing it.
  • Before PostgreSQL 9.3, FK checks took FOR SHARE, which conflicted with every parent UPDATE; a busy products row would block all order-line inserts. Modern versions do not have this problem, but explicit FOR UPDATE on the parent recreates it.
  • A hot parent row (a tenants row that thousands of child inserts reference per second) can still see contention if anyone updates its key or deletes it, or if code locks it with FOR UPDATE "to be safe".

20.4.5 Advisory locks

Advisory locks are locks on an integer key that PostgreSQL does not interpret. Your code decides what the key means.

-- Transaction-scoped: released automatically at COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Prefer this form.
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('rota:night-shift'));

-- Two-key form keeps namespaces apart: (namespace, id)
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(1, 42);

-- Non-blocking: returns false instead of waiting
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('report:daily-2026-09-06'));

-- Session-scoped: survives COMMIT, must be released explicitly. Dangerous with connection pooling.
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(7);
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(7);

Use them for: serialising a critical section that has no natural row to lock (write skew fixes), leader election for a cron job across pods, and "one importer at a time" guards. Do not use session-level advisory locks through PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode; the next transaction on that server connection belongs to someone else and inherits your lock.

Practical example

The "one active ride per driver" rule in section 20.3 was ultimately a partial unique index. Before that, the team's interim fix was pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('driver:' || driver_id)) at the top of the assignment transaction. It worked, it was five lines, and it bought them the week they needed to write the migration. That is the right way to use advisory locks: as a targeted, temporary or structural serialisation tool, not as a general mutex library.

NestJS example

A cron job that must run on exactly one of the eight API pods.

// src/reports/daily-report.job.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class DailyReportJob {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(DailyReportJob.name);
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  @Cron('0 2 * * *')
  async run(): Promise<void> {
    const queryRunner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
    await queryRunner.connect();
    await queryRunner.startTransaction();
    try {
      // Non-blocking attempt; the other seven pods get false and exit.
      const [{ locked }] = await queryRunner.query(
        'SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1)) AS locked',
        ['job:daily-report'],
      );
      if (!locked) {
        this.logger.log('Another instance holds the lock, skipping');
        await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction();
        return;
      }
      await this.buildReport(queryRunner.manager);
      await queryRunner.commitTransaction(); // releases the advisory lock
    } catch (err) {
      await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction();
      throw err;
    } finally {
      await queryRunner.release();
    }
  }

  private async buildReport(manager: import('typeorm').EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await manager.query('INSERT INTO daily_reports (day, total_cents) SELECT current_date - 1, coalesce(sum(total_cents), 0) FROM orders WHERE created_at::date = current_date - 1');
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Finding out who is blocking whom, which you will do at 02:00 one day.

-- Sessions that are waiting on a lock, and the pid holding it
SELECT a.pid,
       a.state,
       a.wait_event_type,
       now() - a.xact_start        AS xact_age,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)     AS blocked_by,
       left(a.query, 80)           AS query
FROM   pg_stat_activity a
WHERE  a.wait_event_type = 'Lock'
ORDER  BY xact_age DESC;

-- Every lock held by one pid, granted or not
SELECT locktype, relation::regclass, mode, granted, transactionid
FROM   pg_locks
WHERE  pid = 48213;

-- The usual culprit: a transaction that did work and then went idle
SELECT pid, now() - state_change AS idle_for, left(query, 80)
FROM   pg_stat_activity
WHERE  state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER  BY idle_for DESC;

-- Kill it if you must
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(48213);

Production scenario

A B2B ordering system with 300 tenants ran UPDATE tenants SET last_seen_at = now() WHERE id = $1 on every request, and locked the tenant row with FOR UPDATE in the order-creation transaction "to avoid concurrent quota issues". Order creation took 40 ms because it called the pricing service while holding the lock. Every other request from that tenant, including plain product listings that updated last_seen_at, queued behind order creation. The pricing service had a p99 of 900 ms. During its slow moments, tenants saw everything hang. Three changes fixed it: last_seen_at moved to a Redis key flushed every minute, the quota lock became FOR NO KEY UPDATE, and the pricing call moved before the transaction with its result passed in.

Failure scenario

At 09:31 on a Monday a developer ran ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN channel text from a laptop. It needed ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. A BI tool had an ACCESS SHARE lock from a 25-minute query. The ALTER queued. Every SELECT on orders queued behind the ALTER. Within 40 seconds all 200 connections in the pool were waiting, the API returned 503, and the on-call restarted the API pods (which did nothing, because the queue was in PostgreSQL). Resolution: pg_terminate_backend on the ALTER session. Prevention: lock_timeout on every migration and a rule that DDL only runs through the deploy pipeline.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • FOR UPDATE with LIMIT locks rows as they are scanned; with an ORDER BY that requires a sort, PostgreSQL may lock more rows than the limit returns. Use an index that provides the order.
  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a view or a join locks the rows of every underlying table unless you say FOR UPDATE OF alias.
  • SKIP LOCKED skips rows locked in any conflicting mode, including rows an UPDATE in another transaction is touching, so a job can be "skipped" for reasons unrelated to job claiming.
  • lock_timeout applies to table and row locks but not to waiting on a transaction id inside SERIALIZABLE conflict resolution; statement_timeout catches that.
  • Sub-transactions (savepoints) multiply the transaction ids a row lock can point at; heavy savepoint use plus heavy locking can cause MultiXact contention. Rare, but it exists.
  • Advisory lock keys from hashtext() can collide; two different strings serialising against each other is a performance bug, not a correctness bug.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "what is the weakest lock that still protects the invariant?" and "how long will I hold it?" before writing FOR UPDATE. They know that TypeORM's pessimistic_write emits FOR UPDATE and that it blocks FK inserts, and they use for_no_key_update unless they are going to delete. They treat every table lock queue as a potential outage and put lock_timeout on DDL by policy. And they can read pg_stat_activity and pg_locks faster than they can open a dashboard.

Common mistakes

  • Using FOR UPDATE where FOR NO KEY UPDATE was enough, silently serialising unrelated child inserts.
  • Session-level advisory locks with a connection pool or PgBouncer.
  • Assuming PostgreSQL escalates locks, and designing around a problem that does not exist while ignoring the lock queue problem that does.
  • Running DDL without lock_timeout.
  • Locking rows in a transaction that then makes a network call.

Interview questions

  1. What lock does a plain UPDATE take on the row, and why does it matter for foreign keys? Expected: FOR NO KEY UPDATE, compatible with the FOR KEY SHARE taken by FK checks, so child inserts do not block on parent updates; but explicit FOR UPDATE does block them.
  2. Does PostgreSQL escalate row locks to table locks? Expected: no; row locks live in tuple headers; the shared lock table is for table/advisory locks.
  3. Explain how one ALTER TABLE can block reads it does not touch. Expected: lock queue; ACCESS EXCLUSIVE waits behind ACCESS SHARE, and new ACCESS SHARE requests wait behind it. Follow-up: how do you make DDL safe?
  4. When would you use an advisory lock rather than a row lock? Expected: no natural row; cross-row invariants; leader election; must be transaction-scoped when pooled.
  5. What does SKIP LOCKED change about SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and what is it for? Expected: skips rows already locked; job queues.

Practical exercise

In two psql sessions: (1) lock a product row with FOR UPDATE in session A, then try to insert an order_items row for it in session B and observe the wait; (2) repeat with FOR NO KEY UPDATE and observe no wait; (3) with session A holding a long SELECT on orders, run ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN x int in B with lock_timeout = '2s' and observe the failure; (4) use pg_blocking_pids to identify the blocker in case (1). Acceptance criteria: a written log of each observation with the lock modes seen in pg_locks.

20.5 Optimistic locking

Concept

Optimistic locking holds no database lock while the user or the application "thinks". Instead, every row carries a version number (or an updated-at timestamp). You read the row with its version, do your work, and write back with WHERE version = <the one I read>. If zero rows are affected, someone else wrote first; you reload and decide whether to retry, merge, or tell the user.

Why does it exist?

Pessimistic locks must be held for the whole read-think-write window. When that window contains a human editing a form for three minutes, or a call to a slow external API, holding a row lock (and a pooled connection) that long is unacceptable. Optimistic locking moves conflict detection to the write and makes it cost nothing until a conflict actually occurs.

Mental model

Imagine editing a shared document with a revision number in the corner. You take a copy at revision 41, make changes, and hand it back. The editor checks: is the master still at 41? If yes, your changes become revision 42. If someone already made 42, your copy is rejected and you are shown the new master to redo your edits.

How it works

flowchart TB
    R["Read row with version v"] --> W["UPDATE ... SET ..., version = v + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = v"]
    W --> C{"rows affected?"}
    C -->|"1"| OK["Commit: we won"]
    C -->|"0"| X["Conflict: someone wrote first"]
    X --> D{"Retry policy"}
    D -->|"reload and retry"| R
    D -->|"give up"| E["Return 409 Conflict with current version"]
  1. Add an integer version column, default 0, NOT NULL.
  2. Every read that will lead to a write carries the version to the caller (an API client, or just the service method).
  3. The write is a single conditional UPDATE that increments the version and matches on the old one.
  4. affected === 0 means conflict. The row was not changed. There is nothing to roll back if this is your only write; if it is part of a transaction, throw so the transaction rolls back.
  5. Retry policy depends on who is thinking. Machine think time: reload and retry a few times with backoff. Human think time: return 409 Conflict with the current state and let the person decide.

Practical example

An admin panel where staff edit product descriptions and prices. Two staff members open the same product; one changes the price, the other fixes a typo and saves 30 seconds later. Without versioning, the typo fix silently reverts the price change (a lost update over a 30-second window). With version, the second save gets 409, the UI shows "This product was changed by Asha at 14:02; reload to see her changes", and nothing is lost.

NestJS example

TypeORM has @VersionColumn, but read the caveat carefully: repository.save() increments the version but does not check it. It emits UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1, unconditionally. The OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError is thrown only by find with lock: { mode: 'optimistic', version }, which compares the loaded row's version with the one you pass, and that still leaves a window between the check and the save. To get real optimistic locking with TypeORM, write the conditional UPDATE yourself.

// src/products/product.entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('products')
export class Product {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column('text') name: string;
  @Column('bigint') priceCents: string; // bigint comes back as string from pg
  @VersionColumn() version: number;      // TypeORM increments this on save(); it does not check it
}

// src/products/products.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Product } from './product.entity';
import { UpdateProductDto } from './dto/update-product.dto'; // contains expectedVersion: number

@Injectable()
export class ProductsService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Product) private readonly products: Repository<Product>) {}

  async update(id: string, dto: UpdateProductDto): Promise<Product> {
    const result = await this.products
      .createQueryBuilder()
      .update(Product)
      .set({ name: dto.name, priceCents: dto.priceCents, version: () => 'version + 1' })
      .where('id = :id AND version = :version', { id, version: dto.expectedVersion })
      .execute();

    if (result.affected === 0) {
      const current = await this.products.findOneBy({ id });
      if (!current) throw new NotFoundException();
      // 409 with the current state lets the client merge or overwrite deliberately.
      throw new ConflictException({ message: 'Stale version', current });
    }
    return this.products.findOneByOrFail({ id });
  }
}

The find variant, useful when you want TypeORM to do the compare on load (for example as a cheap pre-check before a longer operation):

// Throws OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError if the row's version differs from 7
const product = await this.products.findOne({ where: { id }, lock: { mode: 'optimistic', version: 7 } });

PostgreSQL example

ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

-- Read
SELECT id, name, price_cents, version FROM products WHERE id = 'p1';   -- version 7

-- Write
UPDATE products
SET    name = 'Wireless Headphones', price_cents = 19900, version = version + 1
WHERE  id = 'p1' AND version = 7;
-- UPDATE 1: success. UPDATE 0: conflict (or row gone).

A timestamptz updated_at can serve as the version, but it has microsecond resolution and clock-based edge cases; an integer is simpler and never ambiguous.

TypeORM example

Covered above; the important API facts are: @VersionColumn() (increment only), lock: { mode: 'optimistic', version } in find* (compare on load, throws OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError), and update().where('version = :v') plus result.affected for the real check.

Sequelize example

Sequelize implements optimistic locking properly at the instance level. With version: true, instance.save() adds WHERE version = <loaded version> and throws OptimisticLockError when nothing matched.

import { Model, DataTypes, OptimisticLockError } from 'sequelize';

class Product extends Model {}
Product.init(
  {
    id: { type: DataTypes.UUID, defaultValue: DataTypes.UUIDV4, primaryKey: true },
    name: DataTypes.TEXT,
    priceCents: DataTypes.BIGINT,
  },
  { sequelize, tableName: 'products', version: true }, // adds an integer "version" column
);

async function updateProduct(id: string, dto: { name: string; expectedVersion: number }) {
  const product = await Product.findByPk(id, { rejectOnEmpty: true });
  if (product.get('version') !== dto.expectedVersion) throw new ConflictException('Stale version');
  product.set('name', dto.name);
  try {
    await product.save(); // UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?; version = version + 1
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof OptimisticLockError) throw new ConflictException('Stale version');
    throw err;
  }
}

Model.update() (the static, bulk form) does not check the version; only instance save() does.

Production scenario

A CMS with 40 editors and 200,000 articles. Conflicts happen perhaps 20 times a day. Optimistic locking costs nothing on the 99.99% of saves without a conflict, holds no connection while editors type, and turns the conflicts into a clear UI message. Pessimistic locking here would mean holding a row lock and a pooled connection for the length of an editing session, which is impossible.

Failure scenario

A team added @VersionColumn to Product, saw the version go up on every save, and declared inventory "safe from race conditions". Six months later the flash-sale oversell happened anyway, because save() never checked the version. The post-mortem line was: "the column was decorative". The fix was the conditional UPDATE above, plus a test that runs two concurrent saves with the same expected version and asserts exactly one succeeds.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Retry storms: at high contention on one row, optimistic retries amplify load (each conflict is a wasted read and write). Above roughly 10–20% conflict rate, switch that path to pessimistic locking or an atomic statement.
  • Clients that never send the version (or send a stale cached one) always conflict; make expectedVersion required in the DTO.
  • Optimistic locking protects one row. Multi-row invariants still need locks, constraints or SERIALIZABLE.
  • Version overflow is not a realistic concern for integer (2 billion updates per row), but use bigint if it costs you nothing.
  • A 409 on a non-idempotent client that retries blindly can loop forever; the client must reload before retrying.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Optimistic when contention is low and think time is long (humans, external calls, multi-step wizards). Pessimistic when contention is high and think time is short (inventory decrement, wallet debit, job claim). Atomic single statements whenever the logic fits in one UPDATE, because they are both. They verify, with a concurrent test, that the ORM feature actually checks the version, rather than trusting the decorator's name.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting TypeORM's @VersionColumn to reject stale writes.
  • Checking the version with a SELECT and then writing without the WHERE version = clause (the check and the write are not atomic).
  • Using updated_at as the version and comparing with second precision.
  • Retrying optimistic conflicts on a human-facing endpoint instead of returning 409.

Interview questions

  1. How does optimistic locking detect a conflict without holding a lock? Expected: conditional UPDATE on version; zero rows affected means conflict.
  2. Does TypeORM's @VersionColumn implement optimistic locking? Expected: it increments on save but does not check; real checking requires a conditional update or the find optimistic mode plus care. Why it matters: separates people who read decorators from people who read SQL logs.
  3. When is optimistic worse than pessimistic? Expected: high contention, short think time, retries amplify load.
  4. A client sends expectedVersion and gets 409. What should it do? Expected: reload, show diff or merge, resubmit with the new version.

Practical exercise

Add real optimistic locking to a PATCH /products/:id endpoint. Write a test that loads version 3, fires two concurrent PATCH requests with expectedVersion: 3, and asserts one 200 and one 409 whose body includes the current version. Acceptance criteria: the test passes with TypeORM (conditional update) and, in a second implementation, with Sequelize version: true; the SQL log shows WHERE ... version = $n in both.

20.6 Pessimistic locking

Concept

Pessimistic locking takes the row lock before reading, with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (or FOR NO KEY UPDATE), so that nobody else can change the row between your read and your write. Other transactions wanting the same row wait. It is the right tool when contention is high and the critical section is short.

Why does it exist?

Some logic between read and write cannot be squeezed into one UPDATE: apply bundle discounts across five products, check three tables of reservation rules, compute a fee from a lookup table. For those, you need the read to be stable until the write. A lock guarantees it without retries.

Mental model

Imagine a single-occupancy fitting room. You take the key, go in, try things on, come out, return the key. Everyone else waits outside. It is fair and simple; it is a disaster if you take the key and then go for lunch.

How it works

  1. BEGIN.
  2. SELECT ... FOR [NO KEY] UPDATE on every row you will modify, in a consistent order (by primary key, ascending) to prevent deadlocks.
  3. Do the logic. No network calls. No waiting on anything that is not the database.
  4. UPDATE the rows. COMMIT. Locks release.
  5. Waiters wake in FIFO order for that lock, re-check their WHERE, and proceed with fresh data.

Practical example

A checkout with bundle pricing: if the cart contains a phone and a case, the case is 50% off, and stock for both must be decremented atomically. Lock both product rows (ordered by id), read stock and prices, compute, write both, commit. Total lock hold time about 3 ms.

NestJS example

// src/checkout/bundle-checkout.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, In } from 'typeorm';
import { Product } from '../products/product.entity';

@Injectable()
export class BundleCheckoutService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async reserve(lines: { productId: string; qty: number }[]): Promise<void> {
    // Sort first: consistent lock order across all concurrent transactions prevents deadlocks.
    const ids = [...new Set(lines.map((l) => l.productId))].sort();

    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      // Lock in find options; requires an active transaction, otherwise TypeORM throws.
      const products = await manager.find(Product, {
        where: { id: In(ids) },
        order: { id: 'ASC' },
        lock: { mode: 'for_no_key_update' }, // does not block child inserts referencing these products
      });
      if (products.length !== ids.length) throw new ConflictException('Unknown product');

      for (const line of lines) {
        const p = products.find((x) => x.id === line.productId)!;
        if (p.stock < line.qty) throw new ConflictException(`Out of stock: ${p.name}`);
        p.stock -= line.qty; // safe: we hold the lock, nobody else can change stock
      }
      await manager.save(products);
    });
  }
}

The QueryBuilder form gives you NOWAIT/SKIP LOCKED:

const job = await manager
  .createQueryBuilder(Job, 'j')
  .setLock('pessimistic_write')
  .setOnLocked('skip_locked')   // or 'nowait'
  .where('j.status = :s', { s: 'PENDING' })
  .orderBy('j.created_at', 'ASC')
  .getOne();

Lock modes available to TypeORM find and setLock: pessimistic_read (FOR SHARE), pessimistic_write (FOR UPDATE), for_no_key_update, for_key_share, pessimistic_partial_write (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), pessimistic_write_or_fail (FOR UPDATE NOWAIT), dirty_read (no-op on PostgreSQL), optimistic.

PostgreSQL example

BEGIN;
SELECT id, stock, price_cents
FROM   products
WHERE  id IN ('p-case', 'p-phone')
ORDER  BY id
FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
-- logic
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 'p-case';
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 'p-phone';
COMMIT;

Note the ORDER BY id: with FOR UPDATE, PostgreSQL locks rows in the order it scans them, and the scan order follows the plan, not your IN list. An index scan on the primary key gives you ascending order; a sequential scan gives you physical order. Adding ORDER BY id makes the order explicit.

TypeORM example

Covered above. Two more facts: (1) lock in find throws PessimisticLockTransactionRequiredError if you are not inside a transaction, because a lock outside a transaction is released immediately and protects nothing; (2) save() on a locked entity still does its own SELECT first (see Part 21), which is harmless but costs a round trip; update() is cheaper.

Sequelize example

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const products = await Product.findAll({
    where: { id: ids },
    order: [['id', 'ASC']],
    lock: t.LOCK.NO_KEY_UPDATE,   // t.LOCK.UPDATE emits FOR UPDATE; SHARE and KEY_SHARE also exist
    transaction: t,
  });
  // ...
  await Promise.all(products.map((p) => p.save({ transaction: t })));
});

// Queue claim with SKIP LOCKED
const job = await Job.findOne({
  where: { status: 'PENDING' },
  order: [['createdAt', 'ASC']],
  lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE,
  skipLocked: true,
  transaction: t,
});

Sequelize v6 has no NOWAIT option; use sequelize.query('... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT', { transaction: t }) for that.

Production scenario

A wallet service at 800 debits per second across 2 million wallets. Contention per wallet is tiny, but a handful of "merchant" wallets receive 50 credits per second each. Pessimistic locking on the wallet row with a 2 ms critical section gives a per-wallet ceiling of ~500 transactions per second, which is well above 50. If a single wallet ever needed 5,000 per second, this design would cap out, and the answer would be a sharded balance (section 20.10), not a faster lock.

Failure scenario

An order-confirmation flow locked the order row with FOR UPDATE, then called the payment provider (p99 of 4 seconds, occasionally 30 seconds on their side), then updated the row. A degraded afternoon at the provider caused every lock to be held for 30 seconds. Connections piled up: 40 in the pool, each waiting on a locked row or on the provider. The API stopped serving all endpoints, because the pool was exhausted, including endpoints that never touched orders. The rule that came out of it is now a lint check in that codebase: no await of anything except the EntityManager inside a transaction callback.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lock wait pile-up: waiters hold pool connections. Set lock_timeout (for example SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2s') inside hot transactions so a stuck holder fails waiters fast instead of exhausting the pool.
  • FOR UPDATE in REPEATABLE READ can still raise 40001 if the row changed since the snapshot.
  • Locking rows through a join or a subquery locks more than you think; use FOR UPDATE OF alias.
  • SKIP LOCKED with LIMIT 1 and no index on the ordering column scans and locks unpredictably under load.
  • Locks are released only at transaction end. A savepoint rollback does not release row locks taken before the savepoint.
  • Lock held across an await that never resolves (a forgotten promise) is a leaked connection and a leaked lock, until idle_in_transaction_session_timeout fires.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Three rules they do not negotiate: lock in a consistent order, keep the critical section to database calls only, and bound the wait with lock_timeout. They use FOR NO KEY UPDATE by default. And they measure: pg_stat_activity wait events and a histogram of transaction duration tell them whether the lock is the bottleneck long before users do.

Common mistakes

  • Locking outside a transaction (TypeORM throws; raw SQL silently does nothing useful).
  • Locking in the order the client sent the items.
  • HTTP call, Kafka publish, Redis BLPOP, or setTimeout inside the locked section.
  • Locking a parent row with FOR UPDATE and wondering why unrelated child inserts stall.
  • Forgetting that find with lock and relations locks the joined tables too unless you scope it.

Interview questions

  1. Why must pessimistic locks be taken in a consistent order? Expected: to prevent deadlocks; A locks 1 then 2, B locks 2 then 1 is a cycle.
  2. What happens if you SELECT ... FOR UPDATE outside a transaction? Expected: lock released at statement end; protects nothing; TypeORM refuses.
  3. Why should you not call an external API while holding a row lock? Expected: lock hold time becomes the API's latency; waiters exhaust the pool; unrelated endpoints fail.
  4. FOR UPDATE versus FOR NO KEY UPDATE: when does the difference show? Expected: FK inserts of children block only on FOR UPDATE.

Practical exercise

Implement the bundle checkout above and load test it with 200 concurrent requests on the same two products. Acceptance criteria: no oversell, no deadlocks in the PostgreSQL log, p99 under 50 ms on a local database, and a deliberate variant with reversed lock order that does produce deadlock detected so you have seen it.

20.7 Deadlocks

Concept

A deadlock is two (or more) transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds. Neither can proceed. PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one of the transactions with ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01); the other continues. Deadlocks are not a database bug; they are a symptom of inconsistent lock ordering in application code.

Why does it exist?

Detection exists because prevention cannot be enforced by the database: it does not know in what order your application will touch rows. Rather than hang forever, PostgreSQL periodically checks the wait-for graph and breaks cycles.

Mental model

Imagine two people passing in a narrow corridor, each holding a door for the other and refusing to step back. A supervisor walks by every second; when she sees the standoff she sends one of them back to the start.

How it works

  1. Transaction A locks row 1. Transaction B locks row 2.
  2. A requests row 2 and waits on B's transaction id. B requests row 1 and waits on A's.
  3. After a waiter has waited for deadlock_timeout (default 1 second), it runs the deadlock detector: a depth-first search over the wait-for graph in shared memory.
  4. If a cycle is found, the detecting transaction (the one whose timer fired) is aborted with 40P01. Its locks release; the other proceeds.
  5. If no cycle is found, the waiter keeps waiting; the check is not repeated unless log_lock_waits is on (which logs the long wait) and does not cost anything further.
flowchart LR
    A["Transaction A holds order_items row 1"] -->|"waits for row 2"| B["Transaction B holds order_items row 2"]
    B -->|"waits for row 1"| A
    D["Deadlock detector after deadlock_timeout"] -->|"aborts one with 40P01"| A

Practical example

An order-editing endpoint updates the quantity of each line in the order the client sent them. Two staff members edit the same two-line order at once; one's UI sent lines [1, 2], the other's sent [2, 1].

Step Session A Session B Result
1 BEGIN; BEGIN;
2 UPDATE order_items SET qty = 3 WHERE order_id = 'o1' AND product_id = 'p1'; A holds row (o1,p1)
3 UPDATE order_items SET qty = 5 WHERE order_id = 'o1' AND product_id = 'p2'; B holds row (o1,p2)
4 UPDATE order_items SET qty = 4 WHERE order_id = 'o1' AND product_id = 'p2'; A waits for B
5 UPDATE order_items SET qty = 6 WHERE order_id = 'o1' AND product_id = 'p1'; B waits for A: cycle
6 (after ~1 s) one session gets the error below; the other's UPDATE succeeds 
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 48213 waits for ShareLock on transaction 771204; blocked by process 48377.
         Process 48377 waits for ShareLock on transaction 771203; blocked by process 48213.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (3,17) in relation "order_items"

Prevention: sort the lines by (order_id, product_id) before updating, or lock the parent orders row first with FOR NO KEY UPDATE, which serialises all edits of that order and makes the line order irrelevant.

NestJS example

Retry on 40P01, but only around the whole transaction, and only for idempotent work.

// src/orders/order-lines.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { OrderItem } from './order-item.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrderLinesService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async setQuantities(orderId: string, lines: { productId: string; qty: number }[]): Promise<void> {
    // Consistent order removes the cycle; the retry is belt-and-braces for other paths.
    const sorted = [...lines].sort((a, b) => a.productId.localeCompare(b.productId));

    for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
      try {
        await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
          for (const line of sorted) {
            await manager.update(OrderItem, { orderId, productId: line.productId }, { qty: line.qty });
          }
        });
        return;
      } catch (err: any) {
        const code = err?.driverError?.code ?? err?.code;
        if (code !== '40P01' || attempt >= 3) throw err;
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20 * attempt + Math.random() * 20));
      }
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

-- Defaults and diagnostics
SHOW deadlock_timeout;              -- 1s
SET log_lock_waits = on;            -- log waits longer than deadlock_timeout (needs superuser or ALTER SYSTEM)

-- Lowering deadlock_timeout makes detection faster but runs the detector more often under contention.
-- 200ms to 500ms is reasonable for OLTP with short transactions; do not go below ~50ms.
ALTER SYSTEM SET deadlock_timeout = '500ms';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

-- Prevent the order-lines deadlock structurally: serialise per order.
BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = 'o1' FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
UPDATE order_items SET qty = 3 WHERE order_id = 'o1' AND product_id = 'p1';
UPDATE order_items SET qty = 4 WHERE order_id = 'o1' AND product_id = 'p2';
COMMIT;

TypeORM example

Deadlocks surface as QueryFailedError with driverError.code === '40P01'. The retry pattern above applies. A subtle TypeORM source of deadlocks is save() on an array of entities: it may issue updates in an order you did not choose; sorting the array by primary key before save() restores determinism.

Sequelize example

Errors surface as DatabaseError with original.code === '40P01'. Model.bulkCreate with updateOnDuplicate issues one multi-row INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, which locks rows in the order given; sort the input by the conflict key.

Production scenario

A marketplace saw 30–50 deadlocks per hour, all between "update inventory for order" and "update inventory for cancellation", which iterated products in different orders. Each deadlock cost one transaction a 1-second wait plus a retry. Users rarely noticed; the database log was unreadable. Sorting by product id in both paths took the count to zero. Deadlocks are almost always this boring: two code paths, two orders.

Failure scenario

A retry-on-deadlock wrapper without backoff, around a transaction that was not the cause of the deadlock (it was the victim of a poorly ordered batch job). When the batch job ran, 200 API transactions per second each deadlocked, retried immediately, deadlocked again. Every retry restarted the 1-second detection timer. Throughput fell to almost zero for the batch job's 8-minute duration, and the retry storm doubled CPU on the primary. Fixes: backoff with jitter, a retry cap of 3, and the batch job locking its rows in primary-key order with lock_timeout = '1s' so it fails fast instead of the API.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Deadlocks across different tables (A: products then orders; B: orders then products) are the most common in ORM code, because each service locks "its" table first.
  • Foreign keys create implicit locks; inserting children while another transaction deletes the parent can deadlock with no explicit lock in your code.
  • Under SERIALIZABLE, the same cycle can surface as 40001 instead of 40P01; retry both.
  • A deadlock between a transaction and VACUUM/CREATE INDEX is a table-lock deadlock; the fix is lock_timeout on DDL.
  • deadlock_timeout is also the threshold for log_lock_waits; lowering it makes your logs noisier.
  • The victim is the transaction that detected the cycle, not the "cheapest" one; PostgreSQL does not pick by cost.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

"Which two code paths lock the same rows, and in what order?" is their first question. They never accept "we retry deadlocks" as a fix; retry is a safety net, ordering is the fix. They read the DETAIL lines of the error (which processes, which tuples, which relation) and the server log (log_lock_waits) to find both queries, not just the victim.

Common mistakes

  • Retrying without backoff.
  • Retrying non-idempotent work (a retry that resends an email or re-publishes an event).
  • Lowering deadlock_timeout to 10 ms "to fail faster", which makes the detector run constantly under normal lock waits.
  • Locking child rows without a stable order and calling it "fine because it is only two rows".

Interview questions

  1. How does PostgreSQL detect a deadlock and which transaction does it abort? Expected: wait-for graph checked after deadlock_timeout; the detecting waiter is aborted with 40P01.
  2. Two services deadlock on products and orders. How do you fix it structurally? Expected: agree on a global lock order (for example parent before child, then by primary key), or lock a single parent row first.
  3. What is wrong with immediate retry on deadlock? Expected: retry storm; each retry restarts the timer; backoff with jitter and a cap.
  4. Can a deadlock happen with no explicit FOR UPDATE anywhere? Expected: yes, from UPDATE/DELETE row locks and FK locks.

Practical exercise

Reproduce the order-lines deadlock with two psql sessions and capture the full error including DETAIL. Then fix it three ways (sort by key; parent-row lock; SERIALIZABLE with retry) and, for each, run 500 concurrent random-order edits and report the deadlock count from the PostgreSQL log. Acceptance criteria: zero deadlocks for the first two fixes; a measured retry rate for the third.

20.8 Transaction scope design

Concept

Transaction scope is the answer to two questions: where does the transaction start and end, and what is allowed inside it. A well-scoped transaction contains exactly the database writes that must succeed or fail together, and nothing else. Everything slow, remote, or non-rollbackable lives before it or after it.

Why does it exist?

A transaction holds resources for its whole lifetime: a pooled connection, row locks, a snapshot that blocks VACUUM, and, at SERIALIZABLE, predicate locks. Every millisecond you extend it, you extend all of those. And some side effects cannot be undone: an email is sent, a Kafka message is published, Stripe has charged the card. If those happen inside a transaction that later rolls back, you have lied to the outside world.

Mental model

Imagine a surgeon. Everything that must be done while the patient is open happens quickly, with everything prepared in advance and nobody leaving the room to make a phone call. Deciding on the procedure, ordering supplies, calling the family: before or after. Never during.

How it works

The three-phase shape every write endpoint should have:

flowchart LR
    P["Phase 1: prepare outside the transaction"] --> T["Phase 2: short transaction, DB writes only"]
    T --> A["Phase 3: side effects after COMMIT"]
    P -->|"validate DTO, load reference data, call pricing API, check idempotency key"| P
    T -->|"INSERT order, UPDATE stock, INSERT outbox row"| T
    A -->|"outbox relay publishes to Kafka, sends email, invalidates cache"| A
  1. Prepare. Validate input. Read reference data that does not need to be locked. Call external services whose result you need (pricing, fraud score, address validation). Check the idempotency key. None of this holds a connection in a transaction.
  2. Transact. BEGIN. Lock what must be locked, in order. Write. Insert an outbox row describing the event to publish. COMMIT. Target: single-digit milliseconds.
  3. Side effects. A relay process reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka or sends the email, marking each row done. If the process dies, the row is still there. This is the transactional outbox pattern; Part 29 — Distributed Transactions and Sagas covers the relay in depth, and Part 27 — Messaging covers consumer idempotency.

What must never be inside the transaction: HTTP calls, message publishes (except to the outbox table), email/SMS, Redis calls you wait on, file uploads, setTimeout, waiting for user input, or logging that blocks.

Transaction length versus lock hold time. They are not the same. A transaction that reads for 500 ms and then writes one row holds that row lock for only the tail of its life, but it holds its snapshot and connection for all of it. A transaction that locks first and then reads for 500 ms holds the lock for all of it. Lock as late as possible, commit as early as possible.

Idle in transaction. The worst state a connection can be in: BEGIN was issued, some work was done, and now the client is doing something else (awaiting an HTTP call, or just forgot to commit). It holds locks and blocks vacuum while doing nothing. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout kills such sessions after a threshold; set it to a few seconds for API workloads.

Savepoints give partial rollback inside a transaction:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders ...;
SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
UPDATE coupons SET uses = uses + 1 WHERE code = 'SAVE10' AND uses < max_uses;
-- suppose that returned UPDATE 0: coupon exhausted, but we still want the order
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
-- transaction is still alive; the order insert is intact
COMMIT;

Savepoints are also how you survive an error mid-transaction: after any error, PostgreSQL puts the transaction in an aborted state and refuses further statements until ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT. Without a savepoint, a caught exception inside a transaction leaves it unusable.

Timeouts inside transactions. SET LOCAL scopes a setting to the current transaction:

BEGIN;
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '2s';   -- any single statement longer than 2 s fails
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '500ms';     -- any lock wait longer than 500 ms fails with 55P03
...
COMMIT;

Read-only transactions on replicas. BEGIN READ ONLY (or default_transaction_read_only = on on a standby) rejects writes with a clear error, catches accidental writes in "read" code paths, and lets you route the whole transaction to a replica. Remember replication lag: a read-only transaction on a replica may not see the write you just committed on the primary (section 20.14).

Practical example

A food-delivery order placement: validate the cart, call the restaurant availability service (80 ms), compute delivery fee from a geo service (30 ms), then in a 4 ms transaction insert the order, decrement any limited-stock items, insert an outbox row order.placed. After commit, the outbox relay publishes to Kafka within ~50 ms; the restaurant tablet, the courier dispatcher and the notification service consume it independently.

NestJS example

// src/orders/place-order.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { OutboxMessage } from '../outbox/outbox-message.entity';
import { RestaurantClient } from '../restaurants/restaurant.client';
import { PricingService } from '../pricing/pricing.service';
import { PlaceOrderDto } from './dto/place-order.dto';

@Injectable()
export class PlaceOrderService {
  constructor(
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    private readonly restaurants: RestaurantClient,
    private readonly pricing: PricingService,
  ) {}

  async place(dto: PlaceOrderDto, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<Order> {
    // Phase 1: everything slow, before BEGIN.
    const available = await this.restaurants.isOpen(dto.restaurantId);   // HTTP, ~80 ms
    if (!available) throw new ConflictException('Restaurant closed');
    const quote = await this.pricing.quote(dto);                          // HTTP, ~30 ms

    // Phase 2: short transaction, DB only.
    const order = await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      await manager.query(`SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '2s'`);
      await manager.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '500ms'`);

      const inserted = await manager
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .insert()
        .into(Order)
        .values({ idempotencyKey, userId: dto.userId, totalCents: quote.totalCents, status: 'PLACED' })
        .orIgnore()                      // ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on the unique idempotency_key
        .returning('*')
        .execute();
      if (inserted.raw.length === 0) {
        // Duplicate request: return the existing order, do not create side effects again.
        return manager.findOneByOrFail(Order, { idempotencyKey });
      }
      const order = inserted.raw[0] as Order;

      await manager.insert(OutboxMessage, {
        aggregateId: order.id,
        type: 'order.placed',
        payload: { orderId: order.id, userId: dto.userId, totalCents: quote.totalCents },
      });
      return order;
    });

    // Phase 3 happens in the outbox relay, not here.
    return order;
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

-- Server-side guard rails for an API role
ALTER ROLE api SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE api SET statement_timeout = '10s';
ALTER ROLE api SET lock_timeout = '3s';

-- Outbox table the relay polls (index makes the poll cheap)
CREATE TABLE outbox_messages (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_id uuid NOT NULL,
  type         text NOT NULL,
  payload      jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox_messages (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- Relay claim (see 13.10.4): several relay pods can run safely
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM outbox_messages
  WHERE  published_at IS NULL
  ORDER  BY id
  LIMIT  100
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
SELECT m.* FROM outbox_messages m JOIN next USING (id);

TypeORM example

Savepoints: in TypeORM 0.3, calling startTransaction() on a QueryRunner that is already in a transaction issues SAVEPOINT typeorm_N, and rollbackTransaction() at that depth issues ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT. Through the callback API this looks like nesting:

await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  await manager.insert(Order, order);
  try {
    // Nested call on the transactional manager becomes a savepoint, not a new transaction.
    await manager.transaction(async (inner) => {
      const r = await inner.update(Coupon, { code, uses: LessThan(maxUses) }, { uses: () => 'uses + 1' });
      if (r.affected === 0) throw new Error('coupon exhausted');
    });
  } catch {
    // Savepoint rolled back; outer transaction is still healthy and the order insert survives.
  }
});

Sequelize example

Nested transactions are savepoints when you pass the parent:

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await Order.create(order, { transaction: t });
  try {
    await this.sequelize.transaction({ transaction: t }, async (sp) => {
      const [n] = await Coupon.update({ uses: literal('uses + 1') }, { where: { code, uses: { [Op.lt]: maxUses } }, transaction: sp });
      if (n === 0) throw new Error('coupon exhausted');
    });
  } catch {
    // savepoint rolled back, t still alive
  }
});

Production scenario

An API at 600 requests per second with a 30-connection pool. If the average transaction is 5 ms, the pool is ~10% utilised. If one code path holds a transaction for 400 ms (an HTTP call inside), 600 × 0.4 = 240 connection-seconds per second are demanded from a pool that can supply 30. Within a second, every request is waiting for a connection, and the "one slow endpoint" has taken down everything. The arithmetic is the argument: transaction duration multiplied by rate must stay well below pool size.

Failure scenario

At 16:40 a payment webhook handler began timing out. The handler opened a transaction, updated the payment row, then inside the transaction called the fraud-scoring vendor, whose p99 had climbed from 200 ms to 9 seconds. Every webhook held a connection and a lock on its payment row for 9 seconds. The pool (20 connections) was gone in two seconds. Checkout, which needed the same pool, returned 503. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout was not set. The fix took ten minutes (move the vendor call before BEGIN); the outage lasted 35.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • SET LOCAL inside a transaction started by an ORM works only if you run it through the same manager/query runner.
  • Savepoint rollback does not release row locks taken before the savepoint, and it does not undo sequence increments or advisory locks.
  • A caught exception without a savepoint leaves the transaction aborted; the next query fails with 25P02 current transaction is aborted.
  • Outbox rows must be inserted in the same transaction as the business write; a separate transaction reintroduces the partial-failure window.
  • statement_timeout cancels the statement, not the transaction; the client still has to ROLLBACK.
  • Read-only transactions on a replica can still be cancelled by replication conflicts (40001 canceling statement due to conflict with recovery) unless hot_standby_feedback or max_standby_streaming_delay is tuned.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They draw the three phases before writing code and can say for every line whether it is before, inside or after the transaction. They assume every external call will one day take 30 seconds and ask what that does to the pool. They set the three timeouts (statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout) at the role level so no code path can forget them. And they treat "publish after commit" as a correctness requirement with a table behind it, not a finally block.

Common mistakes

  • await axios.post(...) inside dataSource.transaction.
  • Publishing to Kafka inside the transaction, then rolling back; or after commit without an outbox, then crashing before publish.
  • Request-scoped "transaction per request" middleware that opens BEGIN at request start and commits at response time, holding a connection for the whole request including all external calls.
  • Catching errors inside the transaction and continuing without a savepoint.
  • Relying on the client-side timeout to end a stuck transaction (it does not).

Interview questions

  1. What should never be inside a database transaction and why? Expected: anything that cannot roll back or may be slow; lock and pool hold time; outbox for events.
  2. Explain the outbox pattern and what problem it solves. Expected: atomic write of business data and event; relay publishes after commit; at-least-once with consumer idempotency.
  3. A transaction hit an error; you caught it and issued another query. What happens? Expected: 25P02; need savepoint or rollback.
  4. What is idle in transaction and how do you prevent it from hurting you? Expected: open transaction doing nothing; holds locks and blocks vacuum; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  5. Transaction duration is 400 ms at 600 rps with a 30-connection pool. What happens? Expected: demand of 240 connection-seconds per second against 30; pool exhaustion within a second.

Practical exercise

Refactor an existing order-placement endpoint that calls an external pricing API inside its transaction into the three-phase shape with an outbox table and a relay worker using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Acceptance criteria: the transaction duration histogram (log it) shows p99 under 10 ms; killing the relay mid-run and restarting it publishes every event exactly once to a test consumer that deduplicates on outbox.id; a SET LOCAL lock_timeout is visible in the query log.

20.9 Durability: WAL, fsync and what "committed" means

Concept

Durability is the promise that once PostgreSQL says COMMIT, the transaction survives a crash. The mechanism is the write-ahead log (WAL): a sequential file to which every change is written before the data pages are modified, and which is flushed to stable storage before the commit is acknowledged.

Why does it exist?

Writing data pages in place for every commit would be slow (random I/O) and unsafe (a crash mid-write leaves a torn page). Writing a sequential log is fast (one append, one fsync) and safe (recovery replays the log). Durability, in other words, is a performance design as much as a safety one.

Mental model

Imagine a ship's captain who writes every order in the logbook before it is carried out. If the crew falls asleep mid-manoeuvre, the next watch reads the logbook and finishes what was started. The captain does not tell the admiral "done" until the ink is dry.

How it works

  1. A statement modifies a data page in shared memory (the buffer pool) and appends a WAL record describing the change to the WAL buffers.
  2. At COMMIT, PostgreSQL writes a commit record to WAL and calls fsync on the WAL file (subject to synchronous_commit, below). Only then does the client see COMMIT.
  3. Dirty data pages are written to the data files later, by the background writer and at checkpoints (checkpoint_timeout, default 5 minutes, or when max_wal_size is reached).
  4. On crash recovery, PostgreSQL finds the last checkpoint and replays every WAL record after it. Transactions with a commit record are redone; those without are effectively rolled back.
  5. With streaming replication, WAL records are also shipped to standbys, which replay them continuously.

synchronous_commit controls how far the commit must get before the client is told "done":

Level Client gets COMMIT after... Survives primary crash? Survives primary loss (failover)? Visible on standby at ack?
off WAL written to buffers, not flushed no: up to ~3 × wal_writer_delay (about 600 ms) of commits can be lost no no
local WAL fsynced on primary yes no no
remote_write plus standby has received and written WAL to its OS cache yes mostly: lost only if primary and standby OS both crash no
on (default) plus standby has fsynced WAL (only when synchronous_standby_names is set; otherwise same as local) yes yes not necessarily
remote_apply plus standby has applied the WAL yes yes yes

off never risks corruption; recovery is always consistent. It risks losing the last few hundred milliseconds of acknowledged commits. That is acceptable for some tables (analytics events, audit trails you can rebuild) and unacceptable for orders and payments. Because it can be set per transaction, you can choose per write.

What "committed" means when the primary dies. With asynchronous replication (the common cloud default, synchronous_standby_names empty), a commit acknowledged by the primary may not have reached the standby. If the primary is lost and the standby is promoted, those commits are gone, and the application already told the customer they succeeded. Synchronous replication (synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_a, standby_b)') closes that gap at the cost of one network round trip per commit (about 1–2 ms across availability zones, 80 ms or more across regions, which is why cross-region synchronous replication is rarely used).

Practical example

An orders database on AWS RDS Multi-AZ. Multi-AZ uses synchronous block-level replication to the standby, so an acknowledged commit is on two disks in two data centres; failover loses nothing but takes 60–120 seconds. Read replicas, by contrast, are asynchronous; promoting one after a primary loss can lose committed rows.

NestJS example

Turning durability down for a high-volume, low-value write path, per transaction.

// src/analytics/click-events.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { ClickEvent } from './click-event.entity';

@Injectable()
export class ClickEventsService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async recordBatch(events: Partial<ClickEvent>[]): Promise<void> {
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      // Losing the last ~600 ms of click events on a crash is acceptable; skipping the fsync
      // lets this path sustain far higher commit rates on the same disk.
      await manager.query(`SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off`);
      await manager.insert(ClickEvent, events);
    });
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

SHOW synchronous_commit;            -- on
SHOW synchronous_standby_names;     -- '' means replication is asynchronous, so "on" behaves like "local"
SHOW fsync;                         -- on; never turn this off on a production primary
SHOW wal_writer_delay;              -- 200ms; with synchronous_commit=off, max loss is roughly 3x this

-- Per-transaction opt-out
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off;
INSERT INTO audit_log (actor, action) VALUES ('u1', 'viewed_report');
COMMIT;

-- How far behind is each standby?
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS replay_lag_bytes,
       replay_lag
FROM   pg_stat_replication;

Production scenario

On NVMe local disks an fsync costs 0.05–0.5 ms; on network block storage (EBS gp3) 1–3 ms. A single-row insert transaction is therefore bounded by fsync latency: roughly 300–1,000 commits per second per connection on EBS if each commits separately. PostgreSQL groups concurrent commits into one fsync (group commit; commit_delay can widen the window), so aggregate throughput across many connections is much higher: tens of thousands of commits per second is normal. The lesson for the application: batch small writes into one transaction where the semantics allow, and the fsync cost is paid once.

Failure scenario

The incident from section 20.1: synchronous_commit = off set globally for a bulk import and never reverted. Power loss took the last ~600 ms of acknowledged commits: 40 orders, all with confirmation emails already sent by the outbox relay. Recovery of the database was clean; recovery of customer trust was not. Two follow-ups: settings changed for imports are now SET LOCAL inside the import transaction, and an alert fires if synchronous_commit is not on at the cluster level.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • fsync = off is not the same as synchronous_commit = off. fsync = off risks corruption on crash; it belongs only on throwaway test databases.
  • Storage that lies about flushes (consumer SSDs with volatile write caches, some virtual disks) breaks durability underneath PostgreSQL. Cloud providers' persistent disks are honest; verify anything else.
  • A synchronous standby that goes down stalls every commit on the primary until it returns or is removed from synchronous_standby_names. Use ANY 1 (a, b) with two standbys to survive one loss.
  • remote_apply makes reads on the standby see the write, but each commit now waits for standby apply, which can lag under heavy replay.
  • Checkpoints cause I/O spikes; checkpoint_completion_target (default 0.9) spreads them. A misconfigured max_wal_size causes frequent checkpoints and latency spikes on write-heavy systems.
  • WAL archiving failures (archive_command failing) fill the disk with unarchived WAL; the primary stops accepting writes when the disk is full.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know which tables are money and which are telemetry, and they let telemetry use synchronous_commit = off per transaction while money stays at on with a synchronous standby. They know that "committed" on an async-replicated primary is "committed unless we fail over in the next few hundred milliseconds" and design payment reconciliation to tolerate that. They check pg_stat_replication lag on the dashboard next to API latency.

Common mistakes

  • Setting synchronous_commit = off globally for a one-off job.
  • Assuming a read replica can be promoted with no data loss.
  • Confusing fsync and synchronous_commit.
  • Committing every row of a 100,000-row import in its own transaction and blaming PostgreSQL for the fsync cost.

Interview questions

  1. Describe what happens between COMMIT and the client receiving the acknowledgement. Expected: commit record to WAL, fsync (per synchronous_commit), optional wait for standby, then ack; data pages written later.
  2. What does synchronous_commit = off risk, and what does it not risk? Expected: loss of the last few hundred ms of acknowledged commits; never corruption.
  3. Your primary dies with async replication. What is the state of the last commits? Expected: potentially lost on promotion; synchronous replication or reconciliation needed.
  4. Why is WAL faster than writing data pages directly? Expected: sequential append, one fsync, group commit, torn-page safety via full-page writes.

Practical exercise

On a local PostgreSQL, benchmark 10,000 single-row inserts with synchronous_commit = on versus off, and then the same 10,000 rows in batches of 500 with on. Acceptance criteria: a table of commits per second for the three variants and a one-paragraph explanation of why batching closes most of the gap without sacrificing durability.

20.10 Concurrency patterns for common backend problems

This section is a catalog. Each pattern gives the invariant, the full SQL, and the reason it is safe. All of them work at the default READ COMMITTED level unless stated.

20.10.1 Inventory decrement

Invariant: stock never goes below zero; exactly qty units are reserved per successful call.

UPDATE products
SET    stock = stock - $2
WHERE  id = $1 AND stock >= $2
RETURNING stock;
-- 1 row: reserved, new stock returned. 0 rows: insufficient (or unknown id).

Safe because the WHERE is re-evaluated on the latest row version after any lock wait (section 20.2.2), and CHECK (stock >= 0) backs it up. Under a hot SKU, throughput is bounded by row-lock hold time; keep this the only statement in the transaction, or the first one.

20.10.2 Unique reservation

Invariant: a username, coupon code, seat label, or idempotency key is claimed by at most one owner.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX usernames_unique ON users (lower(username));

INSERT INTO users (id, username, email)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (lower(username)) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;
-- 1 row: claimed. 0 rows: taken. No SELECT-then-INSERT race exists.

For "claim and return the existing owner in one statement":

INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, response_status, response_body)
VALUES ($1, NULL, NULL)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET key = EXCLUDED.key   -- no-op update to lock and return the row
RETURNING key, response_status, response_body, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;

xmax = 0 is true for a freshly inserted row and false for an updated existing one; it is a well-known PostgreSQL trick to distinguish the two branches of an upsert.

20.10.3 Wallet transfer with lock ordering

Invariant: money is neither created nor destroyed; no wallet goes negative; no deadlock when A pays B while B pays A.

BEGIN;
-- Lock both rows in a deterministic order regardless of direction.
SELECT id, balance_cents
FROM   wallets
WHERE  id IN ($1, $2)
ORDER  BY id
FOR NO KEY UPDATE;

-- Application verifies the source has enough; the UPDATE re-checks anyway.
UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - $3 WHERE id = $1 AND balance_cents >= $3;
-- application: if 0 rows, ROLLBACK with "insufficient funds"
UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents + $3 WHERE id = $2;

INSERT INTO ledger_entries (from_wallet, to_wallet, amount_cents, idempotency_key)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4);   -- unique on idempotency_key makes the transfer replay-safe
COMMIT;

A pure single-statement form with no explicit lock is also possible for two rows, using a CTE, but it is harder to read and to extend with ledger writes; the locked form is the one we recommend.

20.10.4 Job claim with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

Invariant: each pending job is processed by exactly one worker at a time; workers never wait for each other.

-- Claim up to 10 jobs in one statement; safe with any number of workers.
UPDATE jobs
SET    status = 'RUNNING', locked_by = $1, locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE  id IN (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE  status = 'PENDING' AND run_at <= now()
  ORDER  BY priority DESC, run_at
  LIMIT  10
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
RETURNING *;

-- Supporting index: the subquery is an index range scan, not a table scan.
CREATE INDEX jobs_pending ON jobs (priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- Recover jobs whose worker died: a sweeper runs every minute.
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'PENDING', locked_by = NULL
WHERE  status = 'RUNNING' AND locked_at < now() - interval '5 minutes';

The claim transaction commits immediately; the work happens outside any transaction, and completion is a separate UPDATE jobs SET status = 'DONE' WHERE id = $1 AND locked_by = $2. Holding the claim transaction open for the duration of the work is the classic mistake: it works with two workers and collapses with fifty.

20.10.5 Counter updates under contention

Invariant: the count is exact. Problem: a single hot row (posts.like_count for a viral post at 3,000 likes per second) serialises every writer, and each UPDATE also creates a dead tuple, so the row's page churns and VACUUM struggles.

Options, in order of complexity:

-- 1. Atomic increment: correct, but bounded by lock hold time (~2-5k/s per row).
UPDATE posts SET like_count = like_count + 1 WHERE id = $1;

-- 2. Sharded counter: N rows per post, writers pick a random shard, readers sum.
CREATE TABLE post_like_shards (post_id uuid, shard smallint, count bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
                               PRIMARY KEY (post_id, shard));
INSERT INTO post_like_shards (post_id, shard, count)
VALUES ($1, floor(random() * 16), 1)
ON CONFLICT (post_id, shard) DO UPDATE SET count = post_like_shards.count + 1;
SELECT sum(count) FROM post_like_shards WHERE post_id = $1;   -- 16 rows, cheap

-- 3. Buffer in Redis (INCR is ~100k/s), flush to PostgreSQL every second per key.

Option 3 trades a second of staleness and a small loss window for near-unlimited write rate; for "likes" that is fine, for "money" it is not.

20.10.6 Booking a seat or a time slot

Invariant: one booking per seat per event; or no overlapping bookings per room.

-- Discrete seats: a unique index turns the race into a constraint violation.
CREATE TABLE seat_bookings (
  event_id uuid NOT NULL, seat_no text NOT NULL, user_id uuid NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_no)
);
INSERT INTO seat_bookings VALUES ($1, $2, $3) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING seat_no;

-- Time ranges: an exclusion constraint forbids overlapping intervals per room.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE TABLE room_bookings (
  id      uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  room_id uuid NOT NULL,
  during  tstzrange NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during) VALUES ($1, tstzrange($2, $3, '[)'));
-- Second overlapping insert fails with 23P01 exclusion_violation; catch it and return 409.

Exclusion constraints are checked with the same locking as unique indexes, so two concurrent overlapping inserts cannot both succeed, at any isolation level.

20.10.7 Choosing a pattern

Problem shape Pattern Locks held Retries Works at READ COMMITTED
New value depends on old value of one row atomic conditional UPDATE row, for the statement none yes
Claim a unique thing INSERT ... ON CONFLICT with unique index index entry, for the statement none yes
Multi-row update with logic between SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE in key order rows, for the transaction none yes
Work queue FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claimed rows, for the claim transaction none yes
Hot counter sharded rows or Redis buffer tiny none yes
Overlap or set-level rule unique/partial/exclusion constraint index, for the statement none yes
Rule across rows not expressible as constraint parent-row lock, advisory lock, or SERIALIZABLE parent row or predicate only for SERIALIZABLE yes, except SERIALIZABLE needs retry
Human think time between read and write optimistic version column none reload on 409 yes

Interview questions

  1. Implement a job queue in PostgreSQL that scales to 50 workers. Expected: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claim, partial index, short claim transaction, sweeper for dead workers.
  2. How would you prevent double-booking a meeting room? Expected: exclusion constraint on (room_id, tstzrange).
  3. A single row receives 5,000 increments per second. What breaks and what do you do? Expected: lock serialisation and dead tuples; sharded counters or Redis buffering.
  4. Transfer between two wallets in both directions concurrently: how do you avoid deadlock? Expected: lock in id order.

Practical exercise

Build the job queue from 20.10.4 as a NestJS worker using @nestjs/schedule polling every 500 ms, run 20 replicas against one table with 100,000 jobs, and verify that every job is processed exactly once (a unique processed_jobs(job_id) table will tell you). Then kill five workers mid-run and confirm the sweeper returns their jobs. Acceptance criteria: zero duplicates, zero lost jobs, and the claim query's EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows an index scan on jobs_pending.

20.11 TypeORM transactions

Everything above was SQL. Now we map it onto TypeORM as used inside NestJS, where most of the transaction bugs we see in code review come from one source: not understanding that a TypeORM transaction is a specific pooled connection, and that any query not routed through that connection is not in the transaction.

20.11.1 dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => ...)

The callback API. TypeORM creates a QueryRunner, takes a connection from the pool, issues START TRANSACTION, runs your callback with an EntityManager bound to that connection, then COMMIT if the callback resolves or ROLLBACK if it throws, and releases the connection in all cases.

const order = await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const order = await manager.save(Order, { userId, status: 'CREATED' });   // this connection
  await manager.insert(OrderItem, items.map((i) => ({ ...i, orderId: order.id }))); // same connection
  return order;                                                              // resolve => COMMIT
});

Rules: return or throw, never swallow; every query goes through manager; the callback's promise must settle before you consider the work done (do not fire-and-forget inside it).

20.11.2 The QueryRunner manual flow

Use it when the transaction must be controlled across method boundaries or when you need SET LOCAL before your first statement and want full visibility.

const queryRunner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
await queryRunner.connect();                       // acquire pooled connection
await queryRunner.startTransaction('REPEATABLE READ');
try {
  await queryRunner.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '1s'`);
  await queryRunner.manager.update(Product, { id }, { stock: () => 'stock - 1' });
  await queryRunner.commitTransaction();
} catch (err) {
  await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction();         // safe to call even if commit threw
  throw err;
} finally {
  await queryRunner.release();                     // never skip; a leaked runner is a leaked connection
}

release() in finally is not optional. A QueryRunner that is never released holds its connection forever; after pool.max such leaks the application hangs on every query. Releasing twice throws QueryRunnerAlreadyReleasedError, so structure the code so release() runs exactly once.

20.11.3 Isolation level parameter

dataSource.transaction('SERIALIZABLE', cb), manager.transaction('REPEATABLE READ', cb) and queryRunner.startTransaction('SERIALIZABLE') all emit START TRANSACTION followed by SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL .... Combine with the retry wrapper from section 20.2 for anything above READ COMMITTED.

20.11.4 Repository versus manager: the number one bug

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as OrdersService
    participant TM as TransactionalManager
    participant R as InjectedRepository
    participant P as Pool
    S->>TM: dataSource.transaction begins on connection 7
    TM->>P: BEGIN on connection 7
    S->>TM: manager.save(order)
    TM->>P: INSERT on connection 7 (inside transaction)
    S->>R: this.itemsRepository.insert(items)
    R->>P: INSERT on connection 12 (autocommit, outside transaction)
    S->>TM: throw error
    TM->>P: ROLLBACK on connection 7
    Note over P: Order rolled back. Items committed. Orphan rows.

The injected Repository<T> from @InjectRepository() is bound to dataSource.manager, which uses any free pooled connection in autocommit mode. Calling it inside a transaction callback runs the query on a different connection, outside the transaction. Worse, if the transaction holds a lock that the repository's query needs, the request deadlocks against itself: connection 7 holds the lock and waits for the callback to finish; connection 12 waits for the lock. The request hangs until lock_timeout or forever.

The fix is mechanical: inside a transaction, obtain everything from the transactional manager.

await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const orders = manager.getRepository(Order);          // bound to the transaction
  const items = manager.withRepository(this.itemsRepository); // custom repository, rebound to the transaction
  const order = await orders.save({ userId, status: 'CREATED' });
  await items.insert(lines.map((l) => ({ ...l, orderId: order.id })));
});

manager.withRepository(repo) (TypeORM 0.3) returns a copy of a custom repository whose manager is the transactional one, so custom methods keep working.

20.11.5 Propagating a transaction across services

Once OrdersService.place() needs InventoryService.reserve() and PaymentsService.record() inside the same transaction, you need a way to hand the transactional manager around. Three options, from explicit to magical.

Option A: pass the EntityManager as a parameter. Simple, visible, testable. Every service method that can participate takes an optional manager and defaults to the injected one.

// src/inventory/inventory.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class InventoryService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Product) private readonly products: Repository<Product>) {}

  async reserve(productId: string, qty: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    const repo = manager ? manager.getRepository(Product) : this.products;
    const r = await repo
      .createQueryBuilder()
      .update(Product)
      .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
      .where('id = :id AND stock >= :qty', { id: productId, qty })
      .execute();
    if (r.affected !== 1) throw new ConflictException('Insufficient stock');
  }
}

// src/orders/orders.service.ts
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const order = await manager.save(Order, { userId, status: 'CREATED' });
  for (const line of lines) await this.inventory.reserve(line.productId, line.qty, manager);
  await this.payments.record(order.id, total, manager);
});

Option B: AsyncLocalStorage (CLS) with a small context service. The transactional manager is stored in async-local storage for the duration of the callback; repositories look it up.

// src/database/transaction-context.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';
import { IsolationLevel } from 'typeorm/driver/types/IsolationLevel';

@Injectable()
export class TransactionContext {
  private readonly als = new AsyncLocalStorage<EntityManager>();
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  /** The manager to use right now: transactional if inside run(), otherwise the default one. */
  get manager(): EntityManager {
    return this.als.getStore() ?? this.dataSource.manager;
  }

  /** Join an existing transaction or start a new one. */
  run<T>(work: () => Promise<T>, isolation: IsolationLevel = 'READ COMMITTED'): Promise<T> {
    if (this.als.getStore()) return work();
    return this.dataSource.transaction(isolation, (manager) => this.als.run(manager, work));
  }
}

// Any service: no manager parameter, no injected repository.
@Injectable()
export class InventoryService {
  constructor(private readonly tx: TransactionContext) {}
  async reserve(productId: string, qty: number): Promise<void> {
    const r = await this.tx.manager.getRepository(Product).decrement({ id: productId }, 'stock', qty);
    // decrement() has no conditional WHERE; use the query builder form above for stock checks
  }
}

Option C: typeorm-transactional. A maintained package that does option B for you with a @Transactional() decorator, propagation modes and post-commit hooks.

// main.ts, before NestFactory.create
import { initializeTransactionalContext, StorageDriver } from 'typeorm-transactional';
initializeTransactionalContext({ storageDriver: StorageDriver.AUTO });

// app.module.ts
TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({ type: 'postgres', url: config.get('DATABASE_URL'), autoLoadEntities: true }),
  inject: [ConfigService],
  async dataSourceFactory(options) {
    return addTransactionalDataSource(new DataSource(options));
  },
});

// orders.service.ts
import { Transactional, Propagation, IsolationLevel, runOnTransactionCommit } from 'typeorm-transactional';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  @Transactional({ isolationLevel: IsolationLevel.READ_COMMITTED })
  async place(dto: PlaceOrderDto): Promise<Order> {
    const order = await this.orders.save({ ... });          // injected repositories are patched to use the context
    await this.inventory.reserve(...);                        // joins the same transaction (Propagation.REQUIRED)
