    runOnTransactionCommit(() => this.events.emit('order.placed', order.id)); // after COMMIT only
    return order;
  }
}

Tradeoffs: option A is boring and never surprises anyone; option B is 20 lines you own; option C is convenient but every injected repository now silently depends on the context being initialised, and a missed initializeTransactionalContext() in a worker entrypoint or a test means queries quietly run outside transactions. Whichever you choose, use one; mixing them is how the "number one bug" comes back.

20.11.6 Nested transactions and savepoints

In TypeORM 0.3, starting a transaction on a query runner that is already in one creates a savepoint (SAVEPOINT typeorm_1), and rolling back at that depth rolls back to it. manager.transaction(cb) on a transactional manager reuses its query runner, so it nests as a savepoint. dataSource.transaction(cb) always creates a new query runner and therefore a separate transaction on a separate connection, even when called from inside another transaction. That difference is a frequent source of self-deadlock.

20.11.7 Locks in find options

await manager.find(Product, { where: { id: In(ids) }, order: { id: 'ASC' }, lock: { mode: 'for_no_key_update' } });
await manager.findOne(Job, { where: { status: 'PENDING' }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write', onLocked: 'skip_locked' } });

Pessimistic modes require an active transaction (PessimisticLockTransactionRequiredError otherwise). With relations, the lock applies to joined tables too unless you pass lock.tables. Section 20.6 lists the modes.

20.11.8 The @Transaction() decorator is gone

TypeORM 0.2 shipped @Transaction(), @TransactionManager() and @TransactionRepository() decorators. They were deprecated and removed in 0.3 because they tied transaction handling to method signatures and broke under dependency injection. If you see them in a codebase, it is on 0.2 and overdue for an upgrade; replace with dataSource.transaction or one of the propagation options above.

20.11.9 Testing transactions

Three layers of tests are worth writing.

  1. Rollback test. Call the service with a failure injected after the first write (a spy that throws on the second insert), then assert the first write is absent. This catches the injected-repository bug directly.
  2. Concurrency test. Run two calls in parallel with Promise.allSettled against a real PostgreSQL (Docker or Testcontainers; not SQLite, which has different locking) and assert the invariant: exactly one success, correct final stock.
  3. Leak test. After the suite, assert dataSource.driver pool has no checked-out connections ((dataSource.driver as PostgresDriver).master.totalCount versus idleCount with the pg pool), or simply run the suite with pool.max = 2 so a leak surfaces as a hang.
// test/checkout.concurrency.spec.ts (excerpt)
it('sells the last unit exactly once', async () => {
  await dataSource.query(`UPDATE products SET stock = 1 WHERE id = $1`, [productId]);
  const results = await Promise.allSettled([
    service.checkout(userA, [{ productId, qty: 1 }]),
    service.checkout(userB, [{ productId, qty: 1 }]),
  ]);
  expect(results.filter((r) => r.status === 'fulfilled')).toHaveLength(1);
  const [{ stock }] = await dataSource.query(`SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1`, [productId]);
  expect(stock).toBe(0);
});

Avoid "wrap each test in a transaction and roll back" for code that opens its own transactions: dataSource.transaction takes a new connection, so it does not nest inside the test's transaction and the rollback does not cover it. Truncate tables between tests instead, or use one schema per Jest worker.

20.12 Sequelize transactions

20.12.1 Managed transactions

await this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  const order = await Order.create({ userId, status: 'CREATED' }, { transaction: t });
  await OrderItem.bulkCreate(lines.map((l) => ({ ...l, orderId: order.id })), { transaction: t });
});
// resolves => COMMIT; throws => ROLLBACK; the connection is returned in both cases

20.12.2 Unmanaged transactions

const t = await this.sequelize.transaction();
try {
  await Order.create({ userId, status: 'CREATED' }, { transaction: t });
  await t.commit();
} catch (err) {
  await t.rollback();   // rollback after a failed commit is safe; Sequelize tracks the state
  throw err;
}

Needed when the transaction spans callbacks you do not control, for example a stream consumer that commits per batch.

20.12.3 Passing { transaction: t } to every query, and the bug when you forget

Sequelize has no ambient transaction unless you enable CLS. Every create, update, findAll, increment, destroy, bulkCreate, count and raw sequelize.query inside the callback must receive { transaction: t }. One that does not runs on a different pooled connection in autocommit mode: it is not rolled back with the others, it does not see the transaction's uncommitted writes, and it can block on the transaction's own locks (a self-deadlock that ends only at lock_timeout or pool timeout). The same bug hides inside associations: order.createItem(...), product.getTags(...) and instance save() also take { transaction: t }.

20.12.4 CLS: cls-hooked and AsyncLocalStorage

Sequelize v6 can pick up the current transaction from a continuation-local-storage namespace, so you stop passing t everywhere:

// src/database/sequelize-cls.ts, imported before SequelizeModule.forRootAsync runs
import { createNamespace } from 'cls-hooked';
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export const sequelizeNamespace = createNamespace('sequelize-transactions');
Sequelize.useCLS(sequelizeNamespace);

// Later, anywhere:
await this.sequelize.transaction(async () => {
  await Order.create({ ... });             // automatically uses the transaction
  await this.inventory.reserve(productId); // any query inside this async chain joins it
});

useCLS is a static, process-wide setting; call it once before any Sequelize instance is created. Explicit { transaction: t } still overrides CLS, and { transaction: null } opts a query out (useful for writing an audit row that must survive rollback). Sequelize v7 (in alpha at the time of writing) uses Node's AsyncLocalStorage natively and enables this behaviour by default. With @nestjs/sequelize, call Sequelize.useCLS() in a module file that is imported before the root module.

20.12.5 Isolation levels

import { Transaction } from 'sequelize';
await this.sequelize.transaction({ isolationLevel: Transaction.ISOLATION_LEVELS.REPEATABLE_READ }, async (t) => { ... });
// Or a default for all transactions:
new Sequelize(url, { isolationLevel: Transaction.ISOLATION_LEVELS.READ_COMMITTED });

Serialization failures surface as DatabaseError with original.code === '40001'; wrap with the same retry loop as TypeORM.

20.12.6 Locks

await Product.findAll({ where: { id: ids }, order: [['id', 'ASC']], lock: t.LOCK.NO_KEY_UPDATE, transaction: t });
await Job.findOne({ where: { status: 'PENDING' }, lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE, skipLocked: true, transaction: t });
await Order.findByPk(id, { lock: { level: t.LOCK.UPDATE, of: Order }, include: [OrderItem], transaction: t }); // FOR UPDATE OF orders only

lock: true is shorthand for t.LOCK.UPDATE. NOWAIT is not exposed; use a raw query.

20.12.7 Hooks inside transactions and afterCommit

Model hooks receive the query options, including transaction. Any query a hook makes must forward it, or the hook's write escapes the transaction:

Order.addHook('afterCreate', async (order, options) => {
  await AuditLog.create({ entity: 'order', entityId: order.id, action: 'created' }, { transaction: options.transaction });
});

Side effects that must only happen if the transaction commits go through afterCommit, which is a method on the transaction object, not a model hook:

Order.addHook('afterCreate', (order, options) => {
  const publish = () => this.kafka.emit('order.created', { id: order.id });
  if (options.transaction) options.transaction.afterCommit(publish);
  else publish();
});

afterCommit callbacks run after COMMIT returns; if the process dies between commit and the callback, the event is lost, which is why the outbox (section 20.8) remains the reliable option for anything that matters. afterCommit is fine for cache invalidation and metrics.

20.13 Common ORM transaction mistakes

Mistake What you see Why it happens Fix
Not passing the manager/transaction orphan rows after rollback; request hangs on its own lock query runs on another pooled connection manager.getRepository, withRepository, { transaction: t }, or CLS; add a rollback test
Awaiting an HTTP call inside the transaction pool exhaustion, idle in transaction, 503s on unrelated endpoints lock and connection held for the call's latency move the call before BEGIN; outbox for after
Transaction per request via request-scoped providers connections held for the full request; high pool usage at low DB load BEGIN at middleware, COMMIT at response, everything in between inside transaction per use case, opened in the service, as short as possible
Catching errors and not rolling back 25P02 current transaction is aborted; partial commits error swallowed inside callback rethrow; or savepoint for expected failures
Releasing the query runner twice or never QueryRunnerAlreadyReleasedError; or pool hangs after N requests release() outside finally, or in both catch and finally one release() in finally
Long transactions on hot rows rising lock waits; throughput plateaus at 1/hold-time logic or waits inside the locked section lock late, commit early; atomic statements
save() for upsert duplicate key errors under concurrency; or duplicate rows without a unique index save() is SELECT then INSERT/UPDATE, two statements with a race window upsert(), insert().orUpdate(), ON CONFLICT
Running migrations with synchronize: true columns silently dropped or types changed in production schema diffed and applied at boot synchronize: false, migrations in CI/CD (Part 21)
Retrying non-idempotent work after 40001/40P01 duplicate emails, double events, double charges retry loop wraps side effects retry only the DB transaction; side effects after commit via outbox
Using dataSource.transaction inside another transaction self-deadlock, or inner commits while outer rolls back new query runner, new connection manager.transaction for savepoints; pass the manager

On request-scoped transactions. A NestJS interceptor that starts a transaction before the handler and commits after looks elegant and appears in many tutorials. It means every request, including those that make three external calls, holds a connection in a transaction for its whole lifetime. With a 20-connection pool and a p99 request time of 800 ms, you cap at about 25 requests per second before queuing. Transactions belong in the service layer around the specific unit of work.

On save() as upsert. repository.save() issues a SELECT by primary key, then INSERT or UPDATE. Two concurrent saves of a new row with the same unique key both SELECT nothing and both INSERT; the second fails with 23505. Without a unique index you get two rows. Neither is what "upsert" means. Use repository.upsert() (TypeORM), Model.upsert() (Sequelize), or SQL ON CONFLICT.

20.14 Edge cases and failure modes

  • Deadlock under a retry storm. A batch job with bad lock ordering makes hundreds of API transactions deadlock; each retries immediately, restarting the 1-second detection timer and doubling load. Backoff with jitter, cap at 3, and fix the ordering; give batch jobs lock_timeout so they are the victims.
  • Lock wait pile-up. One long holder, many waiters, each holding a pooled connection. lock_timeout on the waiters (SET LOCAL or role-level) turns a pool-wide outage into fast 55P03 failures on one endpoint.
  • Serialization failures at load. SERIALIZABLE abort rates grow superlinearly with contention. Monitor the 40001 rate; above a few percent, move that path to atomic statements or explicit locks.
  • Transaction ID wraparound from long transactions. Transaction ids are 32-bit; VACUUM must "freeze" old rows before ~2 billion ids pass. A long-open transaction (or a forgotten idle in transaction session, or a stuck replication slot) prevents freezing; when age(datfrozenxid) approaches the limit PostgreSQL first warns, then refuses writes. Alert on age(datfrozenxid) > 1e9 and on transactions older than a few minutes.
  • Replica lag when reading your own writes. The API commits on the primary, redirects the client to a GET served by a replica, and the row is not there yet (typical lag 10–200 ms, seconds under load). Options: read-your-writes routing (serve reads for a user from the primary for a few seconds after a write), remote_apply synchronous commit for that path, or return the created resource in the write response so no read is needed.
  • Partial commit illusions with autocommit. Three statements without BEGIN are three transactions. If the second fails, the first is committed. Code reads as a unit; the database did not treat it as one. Any multi-statement write needs an explicit transaction.
  • Transactions spanning multiple databases. A NestJS app writing to PostgreSQL and MongoDB, or to two PostgreSQL clusters, cannot make both commits atomic with local transactions. PostgreSQL supports two-phase commit (PREPARE TRANSACTION), but it needs a coordinator and careful recovery; in practice the answer is sagas with compensations and the outbox pattern. See Part 29 — Distributed Transactions and Sagas.
  • Client disconnect mid-transaction. PostgreSQL rolls back when it notices; if the NestJS process keeps the connection open and idle, nothing rolls back until idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  • Commit acknowledged, response lost. The client times out after the server committed, retries, and creates a duplicate. Only idempotency keys fix this; shorter transactions reduce the window but never close it.

Senior Checklist — Part 20

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can draw dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update and write skew as two-session timelines
  • I know which anomalies PostgreSQL allows at each isolation level and where it differs from the SQL standard
  • I can explain why UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= qty is safe at READ COMMITTED
  • I choose between atomic statement, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, version column and SERIALIZABLE by contention and think time
  • I know that TypeORM's @VersionColumn increments but does not check, and I write the conditional UPDATE
  • I lock rows in a consistent order and can read a deadlock detected message to find both queries
  • I never await a network call inside a transaction, and I use an outbox for events
  • I set statement_timeout, lock_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout for API roles
  • I can explain what synchronous_commit levels mean and what "committed" means during failover
  • I use the transactional EntityManager (or { transaction: t } / CLS) for every query inside a transaction and have a rollback test proving it
  • I can build a job queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and a seat booking with a unique or exclusion constraint

Part 20 — Key Takeaways

  • A transaction is a specific connection in a specific state; any query not routed through it is not in it.
  • READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement and re-checks WHERE after lock waits; that is why one conditional UPDATE beats read-then-write every time.
  • REPEATABLE READ prevents lost updates and phantoms in PostgreSQL by aborting with 40001; SERIALIZABLE also prevents write skew; both require a retry loop.
  • Write skew has no shared row to lock; fix it with a constraint, a parent-row or advisory lock, or SERIALIZABLE.
  • Plain UPDATE takes FOR NO KEY UPDATE; explicit FOR UPDATE (TypeORM pessimistic_write, Sequelize LOCK.UPDATE) also blocks child-row inserts. Prefer for_no_key_update.
  • PostgreSQL does not escalate row locks, but a queued ACCESS EXCLUSIVE from DDL can block every reader; always run DDL with lock_timeout.
  • Deadlocks are an application ordering bug; retry with backoff is the net, consistent ordering is the fix.
  • Optimistic locking is for long think time and low contention; pessimistic for short critical sections and high contention; atomic statements whenever the logic fits in one.
  • Prepare before BEGIN, write inside, publish after COMMIT through an outbox; never hold a lock across a network call.
  • COMMIT means "WAL fsynced" at synchronous_commit = on; with asynchronous replication it does not mean "on the standby", and a failover can lose it.
  • Transaction duration times request rate must stay far below pool size, or one slow path takes down every endpoint.
  • Test transactions with injected failures and real concurrency on real PostgreSQL; decorators and configuration are not proof.

Part 21 — ORM Engineering: TypeORM, Sequelize and Raw SQL

An ORM (object-relational mapper) is a translation layer between the objects your TypeScript code works with and the rows PostgreSQL stores. Most NestJS teams use TypeORM or Sequelize, most of them use about 20% of the feature set, and most production incidents involving the database trace back to the other 80%: what save() really does, how relations are loaded, which decorator emits which SQL, why a LIMIT returned fewer parents than expected, and where the connection went when the pool ran dry.

This part treats the ORM as an engineering component with a cost model, not as magic. For each feature we show the SQL it generates, the round trips it costs, and the failure it hides. We use one schema throughout (products, orders, order items, tags, addresses) so you can compare TypeORM and Sequelize on the same problem, and we finish with a comparison against raw SQL and a decision procedure for when to use which. Transactions were covered in depth in Part 20 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control; here we only recap and point back.

One principle runs through every section: the ORM is not the database. It cannot enforce uniqueness, it cannot make save() atomic across two processes, and it cannot see the query plan. The schema, the constraints and the SQL log are the source of truth; the ORM is a convenience on top of them.

21.1 What an ORM actually does

Concept

An ORM keeps a description of your tables as classes (entities or models), generates SQL from method calls and options objects, sends that SQL through a driver, and turns the returned rows back into class instances (hydration). Around that core it adds conveniences: relation loading, migrations, transactions, soft delete, lifecycle hooks, and a query builder for when the option objects are not enough.

Why does it exist?

Without an ORM, every table needs hand-written INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE statements, hand-written row-to-object mapping, and hand-written relation assembly. That is tedious and error-prone for the 80% of queries that are plain CRUD on a single aggregate. An ORM makes those 80% cheap to write, consistent across a team, and type-checked. It does not make the other 20% (reports, bulk operations, window functions, queues) better; it often makes them worse, and knowing where that line is what this part is about.

Mental model

Imagine a professional interpreter between you and a very literal, very fast clerk who only speaks SQL. For everyday requests ("file this order", "fetch that customer") the interpreter is perfect. For a complicated request ("give me the top three products per category by revenue in the last 30 days, excluding returns") the interpreter starts improvising, and you are better off writing the request in the clerk's language yourself and having the interpreter only carry the paper.

How it works

flowchart TB
    S["NestJS service"] --> R["Repository or Model API: find, save, include"]
    R --> QB["Query builder: options to SQL string plus parameters"]
    QB --> D["Driver: pg"]
    D -->|"wire protocol, parameters bound separately"| PG["PostgreSQL"]
    PG -->|"rows as arrays of text or binary"| D
    D --> H["Hydration: rows to entity instances, relation trees, transformers"]
    H --> S
    QB -. "Raw SQL bypass: manager.query, sequelize.query" .-> D
  1. Your service calls repository.find({ where: { userId }, relations: { items: true } }) or Order.findAll({ where: { userId }, include: [Items] }).
  2. The ORM consults the entity metadata (built once at startup from decorators or init() calls): table names, column names and types, relations and their join columns.
  3. It builds a SQL string with placeholders ($1, $2) and a separate parameter array. Values are never concatenated into the string; this is what makes ORM queries SQL-injection safe by default.
  4. The driver (pg) sends the query using the extended protocol: parse, bind, execute. PostgreSQL plans and runs it and streams rows back. A simple primary-key lookup takes about 0.3–1 ms of database time on a local instance; the network and driver add roughly the same again.
  5. Rows arrive as flat records. For a join, one row per combination of parent and child. The ORM de-duplicates parents by primary key and nests children under them. This hydration step is CPU work in your Node process: for 1,000 orders with 5 items each, TypeORM must process 5,000 rows and allocate 6,000 objects; expect 5–20 ms.
  6. Column values are converted by type: pg returns numeric and bigint as strings (JavaScript numbers cannot represent them safely), timestamptz as Date, jsonb as parsed objects. The ORM applies any transformers you configured.
  7. On writes, the ORM computes what changed, generates INSERT/UPDATE, runs lifecycle hooks, and may cascade to related entities, each as its own statement.

Overhead relative to raw SQL is small for single-row queries (tens of microseconds) and grows with result size and relation depth. It is rarely the bottleneck; the queries the ORM chose to run usually are.

Practical example

The schema used for the rest of this part. An e-commerce catalog with orders.

erDiagram
    CUSTOMERS ||--o| ADDRESSES : "has default"
    CUSTOMERS ||--o{ ORDERS : places
    ORDERS ||--o{ ORDER_ITEMS : contains
    PRODUCTS ||--o{ ORDER_ITEMS : "appears in"
    PRODUCTS ||--o{ PRODUCT_TAGS : tagged
    TAGS ||--o{ PRODUCT_TAGS : labels
    PRODUCTS {
        uuid id PK
        text sku
        text name
        numeric price
        integer stock
        jsonb attributes
        text status
        integer version
    }
    ORDERS {
        uuid id PK
        uuid customer_id FK
        text status
        bigint total_cents
        timestamptz created_at
    }
    ORDER_ITEMS {
        uuid id PK
        uuid order_id FK
        uuid product_id FK
        integer qty
        bigint unit_price_cents
    }

NestJS example

Both ORMs are registered at the root module and expose per-feature registration. Everything else in this part builds on these two registrations.

// src/app.module.ts (TypeORM variant)
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true }),
    TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
        type: 'postgres',
        url: config.getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL'),
        autoLoadEntities: true,   // entities registered with forFeature() are picked up
        synchronize: false,       // never true outside a throwaway local database
        logging: ['error', 'warn'],
      }),
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

// src/orders/orders.module.ts
@Module({
  imports: [TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Order, OrderItem, Product])],
  providers: [OrdersService],
  controllers: [OrdersController],
})
export class OrdersModule {}
// Sequelize variant of the root registration
import { SequelizeModule } from '@nestjs/sequelize';

SequelizeModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    dialect: 'postgres',
    uri: config.getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL'),
    autoLoadModels: true,
    synchronize: false,
    define: { underscored: true, timestamps: true },
  }),
});
// and per feature: SequelizeModule.forFeature([Order, OrderItem, Product])

PostgreSQL example

The DDL the entities in the next sections map to. Write it (or generate it via migrations) before writing entities; the schema is the contract.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE addresses (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  line1       text NOT NULL,
  city        text NOT NULL,
  country     char(2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  sku        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name       text NOT NULL,
  price      numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  stock      integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (stock >= 0),
  attributes jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  status     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE' CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE', 'ARCHIVED')),
  version    integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at timestamptz
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'CREATED' CHECK (status IN ('CREATED','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED')),
  total_cents bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  order_id         uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  qty              integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price_cents bigint NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (order_id, product_id)
);
CREATE INDEX order_items_product ON order_items (product_id);

CREATE TABLE tags (
  id   uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name text NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE product_tags (
  product_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (product_id, tag_id)
);

Production scenario

A catalog API serving 1,200 requests per second, 90% reads. With TypeORM, a GET /products/:id that loads the product plus its tags takes about 2 ms of database time and 0.4 ms of ORM overhead; that overhead is invisible next to the 15 ms of network to the client. The same service's nightly "revenue by category" report, written with the ORM's query builder, generated a 14-way join with hydration of 2 million rows and took 11 minutes; rewritten as one SQL statement with a CTE and GROUP BY, it took 9 seconds. Both facts are typical. Use the ORM where it is cheap and go around it where it is expensive.

Failure scenario

At 07:50 a deploy went out with a new Product.description column added to the entity and synchronize: true still on from local development. TypeORM diffed the entity against production, found that an old column legacy_notes (present in the database, absent from the entity) should not exist, and dropped it. Two years of merchandising notes were gone before the first coffee. Restore from the previous night's backup took four hours and lost the morning's edits. The fix is one line (synchronize: false) and one process (migrations reviewed in pull requests; section 21.7).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The ORM's picture of the schema and the real schema drift silently when migrations are hand-edited or applied out of order; a column the entity thinks is NOT NULL may be nullable in production and vice versa.
  • Hydration of large joined results is CPU-bound in Node and blocks the event loop; a single 50,000-row leftJoinAndSelect can stall every other request on that pod for hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Drivers return numeric/bigint as strings; code that does price * qty gets string concatenation or NaN (section 21.2 and 21.25).
  • Entity metadata is built at startup; a circular import between entity files can leave a relation undefined and produce Entity metadata for X#y was not found only at runtime.
  • Two ORMs on one database (a migration from Sequelize to TypeORM in progress) each maintain their own migration table and their own idea of the schema; only one should own DDL.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read the SQL log before they trust an ORM method. They ask: how many statements does this produce, how many rows come back, how many objects get allocated, and does any of it run inside a transaction? They keep the schema as the source of truth, with constraints, and treat entity decorators as documentation of it. They pick one way to do each thing (loading relations, transactions, upserts) and make it the team convention, because ORM bugs come from mixing styles.

Common mistakes

  • Learning the ORM instead of learning SQL, and then being unable to read the queries it generates.
  • Using synchronize: true or sync({ alter: true }) anywhere near production data.
  • Treating hydration as free and returning entity trees with thousands of nodes.
  • Choosing the ORM by popularity rather than by whether its model (Active Record versus Data Mapper, eager versus explicit loading) matches the team's habits.

Interview questions

  1. What does an ORM do between repository.find() and the rows coming back? Expected: metadata lookup, SQL generation with bound parameters, driver round trip, hydration and de-duplication of joined rows, type conversion. Why it matters: separates users of the tool from engineers of it.
  2. Where does ORM overhead actually show up? Expected: hydration of large joined results and the number of statements chosen, not per-query CPU.
  3. Why should the database schema, not the entity class, be the source of truth? Expected: constraints are enforced for every code path; entities only describe.
  4. Name a query shape where you would bypass the ORM entirely. Expected: reports with CTEs/window functions, bulk upserts, queue claims with SKIP LOCKED.

Practical exercise

Enable query logging and run one request that loads an order with items and products through your ORM. Count the statements, the rows returned by each, and the total time. Then write the same load as one raw SQL statement and compare. Acceptance criteria: a short write-up with both SQL texts, row counts, timings, and one sentence on which you would ship and why.

21.2 TypeORM entities

Concept

An entity is a class whose decorators describe a table: @Entity() names the table, @Column() describes each column's type, nullability and default, @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() the primary key, and the date/version/delete decorators cover the bookkeeping columns. TypeORM reads the decorators at startup into metadata used for every query and for schema generation.

Why does it exist?

Without entities you would repeat column names and types in every query and every mapping. The entity centralises them, gives the compiler something to check against, and lets find() know how to hydrate a row. The cost is that the decorators are a second description of the schema and can disagree with the first.

How it works

  1. Decorators register metadata in a global store when the file is imported.
  2. DataSource.initialize() builds EntityMetadata for every entity: columns, relations, indices, listeners.
  3. Every repository method consults that metadata to build SQL; migrations compare it with the live schema.
  4. The type option is passed to PostgreSQL almost verbatim ('timestamptz', 'jsonb', 'numeric'); if you omit it, TypeORM infers from the TypeScript type via emitDecoratorMetadata (string becomes character varying, number becomes integer, Date becomes timestamp without time zone, boolean becomes boolean), which is usually not what you want.

TypeORM example

The three core entities with every decorator that matters in production.

// src/products/product.entity.ts
import {
  Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column, CreateDateColumn, UpdateDateColumn,
  DeleteDateColumn, VersionColumn, Index, OneToMany, ManyToMany, JoinTable,
} from 'typeorm';
import { OrderItem } from '../orders/order-item.entity';
import { Tag } from '../tags/tag.entity';

export enum ProductStatus { ACTIVE = 'ACTIVE', ARCHIVED = 'ARCHIVED' }

/** numeric(12,2) comes back from pg as a string; convert deliberately, never implicitly. */
const numericToString = { to: (v: string) => v, from: (v: string | null) => v };

@Entity({ name: 'products' })
export class Product {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')
  id: string;

  @Index({ unique: true })
  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  sku: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  name: string;

  // Money. Keep it a string (or a Decimal from decimal.js); a JS number loses cents at scale.
  @Column({ type: 'numeric', precision: 12, scale: 2, transformer: numericToString })
  price: string;

  @Column({ type: 'integer', default: 0 })
  stock: number;

  @Column({ type: 'jsonb', default: () => `'{}'::jsonb` })
  attributes: Record<string, unknown>;

  // PostgreSQL enum type products_status_enum is created; see the enum discussion below.
  @Column({ type: 'enum', enum: ProductStatus, default: ProductStatus.ACTIVE })
  status: ProductStatus;

  @VersionColumn()
  version: number;

  // Without { type: 'timestamptz' } these become timestamp WITHOUT time zone.
  @CreateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'created_at' })
  createdAt: Date;

  @UpdateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'updated_at' })
  updatedAt: Date;

  // Soft delete: softRemove()/softDelete() set this; find*() exclude rows where it is not null.
  @DeleteDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'deleted_at' })
  deletedAt: Date | null;

  @OneToMany(() => OrderItem, (item) => item.product)
  orderItems: OrderItem[];

  @ManyToMany(() => Tag, (tag) => tag.products)
  @JoinTable({
    name: 'product_tags',
    joinColumn: { name: 'product_id', referencedColumnName: 'id' },
    inverseJoinColumn: { name: 'tag_id', referencedColumnName: 'id' },
  })
  tags: Tag[];
}
// src/orders/order.entity.ts
@Entity({ name: 'orders' })
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id: string;

  // Keep the FK column as a plain column too: readable without loading the relation.
  @Column({ type: 'uuid', name: 'customer_id' }) customerId: string;

  @ManyToOne(() => Customer, (c) => c.orders, { nullable: false, onDelete: 'RESTRICT' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'customer_id' })
  customer: Customer;

  @Column({ type: 'text', default: 'CREATED' }) status: 'CREATED' | 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED' | 'CANCELLED';

  // bigint is also returned as a string by pg. Convert to number only if you know it fits.
  @Column({ type: 'bigint', name: 'total_cents', transformer: { to: (v: number) => v, from: (v: string) => Number(v) } })
  totalCents: number;

  @OneToMany(() => OrderItem, (item) => item.order, { cascade: ['insert'] })
  items: OrderItem[];

  @CreateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'created_at' }) createdAt: Date;
  @UpdateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'updated_at' }) updatedAt: Date;
}

// src/orders/order-item.entity.ts
@Entity({ name: 'order_items' })
@Unique(['orderId', 'productId'])
export class OrderItem {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column({ type: 'uuid', name: 'order_id' }) orderId: string;
  @Column({ type: 'uuid', name: 'product_id' }) productId: string;

  @ManyToOne(() => Order, (o) => o.items, { nullable: false, onDelete: 'CASCADE' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'order_id' })
  order: Order;

  @ManyToOne(() => Product, (p) => p.orderItems, { nullable: false, onDelete: 'RESTRICT' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'product_id' })
  product: Product;

  @Column({ type: 'integer' }) qty: number;
  @Column({ type: 'bigint', name: 'unit_price_cents', transformer: { to: (v: number) => v, from: (v: string) => Number(v) } })
  unitPriceCents: number;
}

Type mapping you must know.

TypeScript Decorator PostgreSQL type Returned as Notes
string id @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') uuid DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4() string needs uuid-ossp; set uuidExtension: 'pgcrypto' in options to use gen_random_uuid()
number id @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() serial/integer with sequence number 'increment' strategy; fine for internal tables
string @Column('text') text string prefer text over varchar(n); a length limit is a CHECK, not a performance feature
number @Column('integer') integer number up to 2.1 billion
number @Column('bigint') bigint string pg refuses to lose precision; add a transformer
string @Column('numeric', { precision, scale }) numeric(p,s) string money; never float/double precision
boolean @Column('boolean') boolean boolean
Date @Column('timestamptz') timestamp with time zone Date always timestamptz; plain timestamp is parsed in the Node process's local zone by pg
Date @Column('date') date string 'YYYY-MM-DD' by default pg returns date as a string unless a type parser is registered
object @Column('jsonb') jsonb parsed object json preserves key order and whitespace but cannot be indexed usefully
enum @Column({ type: 'enum', enum }) CREATE TYPE ..._enum string migrations for new values are awkward; text + CHECK is often simpler
string[] @Column('text', { array: true }) text[] array index with GIN
Buffer @Column('bytea') bytea Buffer do not store files here
anything @Column('simple-json') / 'simple-array' text parsed avoid; not queryable; use jsonb

Decimal as string. pg returns numeric and bigint as strings because a JavaScript number has 53 bits of integer precision and binary floating point; 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, and 9007199254740993 cannot be represented. TypeORM does not convert. If you write product.price * qty you get either a string-coerced float or NaN. Options, best first: store money as integer cents in an integer column (safe up to 21 million currency units) or bigint with a Number transformer when you know the magnitude; keep numeric as a string and do arithmetic with decimal.js; or pg.types.setTypeParser(1700, parseFloat) globally, which is convenient and wrong for money.

Timestamps. @CreateDateColumn() without a type creates timestamp without time zone. pg parses those as local time of the Node process. A pod in UTC and a developer laptop in Asia/Kolkata disagree by 5.5 hours on the same row. Always timestamptz, and run Node with TZ=UTC anyway.

Enums. type: 'enum' creates a PostgreSQL enum type named <table>_<column>_enum. Adding a value later requires ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE, which cannot run inside a transaction block before PostgreSQL 12 and, in TypeORM-generated migrations, is usually expressed as rename-type, create-new-type, alter-column, drop-old-type, which locks the table. text with a CHECK (status IN (...)) constraint changes with a plain ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT / ADD CONSTRAINT, and the TypeScript union type gives you the same compile-time safety.

Soft delete. @DeleteDateColumn makes find* and count add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL automatically, repository.softDelete(criteria) and softRemove(entity) set the timestamp, restore()/recover() clear it, and withDeleted: true (or .withDeleted() on the query builder) shows the rows. Two traps: unique indexes still see soft-deleted rows (re-creating a deleted SKU fails unless the unique index is partial, WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), and foreign keys still reference them (a soft-deleted product still appears on old orders, which is usually what you want).

PostgreSQL example

What migration:generate emits for the Product entity, so you can compare it with the hand-written DDL above and see what the decorators bought you and what they did not (no CHECK constraints, no ON DELETE unless specified, an enum type instead of text).

CREATE TYPE "public"."products_status_enum" AS ENUM('ACTIVE', 'ARCHIVED');
CREATE TABLE "products" (
  "id" uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
  "sku" text NOT NULL,
  "name" text NOT NULL,
  "price" numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,
  "stock" integer NOT NULL DEFAULT '0',
  "attributes" jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  "status" "public"."products_status_enum" NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
  "version" integer NOT NULL,
  "created_at" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  "updated_at" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  "deleted_at" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE,
  CONSTRAINT "PK_0806c755e0aca124e67c0cf6d7d" PRIMARY KEY ("id")
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "IDX_c44ac33a05b144dd0d9ddcf932" ON "products" ("sku");

Note the generated index names. Name them yourself (@Index('products_sku_unique', ['sku'], { unique: true })) so that EXPLAIN output and lock messages are readable.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A property without an explicit type and with a TypeScript union type ('A' | 'B') has no runtime type information; TypeORM throws at startup with a "data type is not defined" error.
  • default: () => 'now()' is a SQL expression; default: new Date() is evaluated once at process start and baked into the DDL.
  • @Column({ select: false }) (for password hashes) hides the column from find* and from save()'s change detection; loading it requires addSelect in a query builder.
  • Changing a column's name in the entity generates a DROP COLUMN and ADD COLUMN, not a rename; data is lost unless you edit the migration.
  • @VersionColumn increments on save() but is not checked (Part 20, section 20.5).
  • Entities with bigint primary keys return string ids; where: { id: 42 } still works, but === comparisons in application code fail.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the DDL first, with constraints, and then write the entity to match it, with explicit type on every column. They ban float for money and timestamp without zone, and they name every index and constraint. They know that decorators cannot express CHECK constraints or partial indexes and add those in migrations by hand. They treat simple-json and eager: true as smells in code review.

Common mistakes

  • Omitting type and getting character varying, integer and timestamp by inference.
  • Using number for a bigint or numeric property and being surprised by strings.
  • Using PostgreSQL enums for anything that will gain values.
  • Forgetting that soft-deleted rows still hit unique indexes.
  • Two entities mapping the same table with different column sets, so save() from one nulls columns the other depends on.

Interview questions

  1. Why does pg return bigint and numeric as strings, and what do you do about it? Expected: precision; integer cents, transformers, or a decimal library.
  2. What is wrong with @CreateDateColumn() without options in PostgreSQL? Expected: timestamp without time zone, parsed as process-local time.
  3. PostgreSQL enum versus text plus CHECK: when do you pick which? Expected: enums are compact and typed but painful to evolve; text plus CHECK for anything that changes.
  4. How does soft delete interact with unique constraints? Expected: deleted rows still occupy the index; partial unique index on deleted_at IS NULL.

Practical exercise

Write the Customer and Address entities for the schema above with explicit types, named indexes and a partial unique index on products.sku WHERE deleted_at IS NULL added via a migration. Acceptance criteria: migration:generate after your migration produces an empty diff; a test soft-deletes a product and re-creates the same SKU successfully; SELECT pg_typeof(created_at) returns timestamp with time zone.

21.3 TypeORM relations

Concept

A relation is a foreign key described from the object's point of view: an Order has many OrderItems, an OrderItem belongs to one Product. TypeORM has four relation decorators: @ManyToOne, @OneToMany, @OneToOne and @ManyToMany. Only some of them create columns; the rest are views over the other side.

Why does it exist?

So that order.items[0].product.name is a property access rather than three hand-written joins and a nesting loop. The price is that each relation is a potential query, and how and when it runs is the source of most ORM performance problems.

Mental model

Imagine a paper order form with a customer number written at the top. The customer number is the owning side: it lives on the form. The customer's folder that lists all their orders is the inverse side: it is derived by looking through every form. Only the form carries data; the folder is a view.

How it works

  1. @ManyToOne is always the owning side. It creates the foreign key column (order_id) on this entity's table. @JoinColumn({ name }) names that column; without it TypeORM uses <property>Id (orderId).
  2. @OneToMany is always the inverse side. It creates no column. It exists so that loading can go from parent to children and so that cascades can flow from parent to children. It requires the @ManyToOne on the other entity.
  3. @OneToOne creates a foreign key on whichever side has @JoinColumn, plus a unique index on it. The other side is inverse.
  4. @ManyToMany needs a join table. The side with @JoinTable owns it. TypeORM manages the join table for you: product.tags = [...]; save(product) inserts and deletes join rows to match.
  5. nullable: false makes the FK column NOT NULL. onDelete sets the database-level referential action ('CASCADE' | 'SET NULL' | 'RESTRICT' | 'NO ACTION'); onUpdate similarly. orphanedRowAction on the inverse side decides what happens to children removed from a parent's array on save() ('nullify' by default, 'delete', 'soft-delete' or 'disable').
  6. Loading is explicit: find({ relations: { items: { product: true } } }) produces LEFT JOINs (or separate queries with relationLoadStrategy: 'query'). Unloaded relations are simply undefined on the instance; there is no lazy proxy unless you declare the property as a Promise (section 21.8).

TypeORM example

When to model the join table explicitly. @ManyToMany is right for a pure association with no attributes (product to tag). The moment the association carries data (quantity, price at time of order, created-at, position), model it as its own entity with two @ManyToOnes, which is exactly what OrderItem is. You will also want an explicit entity when you need to query the join table directly, soft-delete associations, or paginate them. A common evolution is starting with @ManyToMany and, when the first extra column appears, migrating to an explicit entity; do it early, the migration is painful once the join table has millions of rows.

// One-to-one, owning side on Address (holds customer_id with a unique index)
@Entity({ name: 'addresses' })
export class Address {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column({ type: 'uuid', name: 'customer_id' }) customerId: string;
  @OneToOne(() => Customer, (c) => c.defaultAddress, { nullable: false, onDelete: 'CASCADE' })
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'customer_id' })
  customer: Customer;
  @Column('text') line1: string;
  @Column('text') city: string;
  @Column({ type: 'char', length: 2 }) country: string;
}

@Entity({ name: 'customers' })
export class Customer {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column('text') email: string;
  @OneToOne(() => Address, (a) => a.customer, { cascade: ['insert', 'update'] })
  defaultAddress?: Address;                       // inverse side: no column here
  @OneToMany(() => Order, (o) => o.customer) orders: Order[];
}

// Loading relations explicitly (object syntax, TypeORM 0.3)
const orders = await this.orders.find({
  where: { customerId },
  relations: { items: { product: true } },        // LEFT JOIN order_items, LEFT JOIN products
  order: { createdAt: 'DESC' },
  take: 20,
});

// Same, with separate queries instead of joins (avoids row multiplication for wide parents)
const ordersQ = await this.orders.find({
  where: { customerId },
  relations: { items: true },
  relationLoadStrategy: 'query',                   // SELECT orders; SELECT order_items WHERE order_id IN (...)
});

// Only the ids of related rows, no join of the related table's columns
const withTagIds = await this.products.find({ where: { status: ProductStatus.ACTIVE }, loadRelationIds: { relations: ['tags'] } });

Two habits worth adopting. First, declare the plain FK column (orderId) next to the relation (order) and map both to the same database column; you can then filter and insert by id without loading the relation, and @RelationId becomes unnecessary. Second, never set eager: true on a relation that can be large (section 21.8).

PostgreSQL example

What the relation options become. The differences matter at 02:00.

-- @ManyToOne(..., { nullable: false, onDelete: 'CASCADE' }) on OrderItem.order
ALTER TABLE "order_items" ADD CONSTRAINT "FK_order_items_order"
  FOREIGN KEY ("order_id") REFERENCES "orders"("id") ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE NO ACTION;

-- @ManyToOne(..., { onDelete: 'RESTRICT' }) on OrderItem.product
ALTER TABLE "order_items" ADD CONSTRAINT "FK_order_items_product"
  FOREIGN KEY ("product_id") REFERENCES "products"("id") ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE NO ACTION;

-- The FK column is NOT indexed automatically. Add it, or every parent delete scans the child table.
CREATE INDEX "order_items_order_id_idx" ON "order_items" ("order_id");

-- @OneToOne with @JoinColumn creates a unique constraint on the FK
ALTER TABLE "addresses" ADD CONSTRAINT "UQ_addresses_customer" UNIQUE ("customer_id");

PostgreSQL does not create indexes on foreign-key columns. TypeORM does not either. Every @ManyToOne needs an @Index() on its FK column (or a composite index that starts with it), or deletes of the parent and joins from parent to child become sequential scans.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A @OneToMany without the matching @ManyToOne fails at startup with a metadata error; a @ManyToOne without the @OneToMany is fine (one-directional relation).
  • relations with take on a find uses TypeORM's two-query pagination (distinct ids first); the same join in a query builder with .limit() instead of .take() returns fewer parents (section 21.5).
  • @ManyToMany save() diffing loads the current join rows first; on a product with 10,000 tags every save reads 10,000 rows.
  • onDelete: 'CASCADE' at the database and cascade: ['remove'] in TypeORM are different mechanisms (section 21.10); using both is harmless, using only the ORM one is unreliable.
  • Circular imports between entity files are resolved by the arrow-function () => Product form; a direct class reference in a decorator can be undefined at decoration time.
  • Self-referencing relations (Category.parent) work with @ManyToOne(() => Category, (c) => c.children); recursive loading needs a recursive CTE or @Tree entities.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They decide, per relation, whether it is ever loaded together with its parent in a hot path, and if so, how large it can get. They index every FK column on day one. They model anything with attributes as an explicit entity. They prefer relationLoadStrategy: 'query' or explicit joins over eager loading and check the SQL log for the number of statements after every change to relations.

Common mistakes

  • Putting @JoinColumn on both sides of a one-to-one (two FK columns, two unique indexes, confusion).
  • Forgetting the index on the FK column.
  • Loading relations: ['items', 'items.product', 'items.product.tags'] for a list endpoint that shows order numbers and totals.
  • Using @ManyToMany for order lines and then trying to add a qty column.
  • Setting eager: true on both sides of a relation (TypeORM refuses) or on any large collection.

Interview questions

  1. Which relation decorators create columns and which do not? Expected: @ManyToOne and the @JoinColumn side of @OneToOne create FK columns; @OneToMany and inverse @OneToOne create none; @ManyToMany with @JoinTable creates a join table.
  2. When do you replace @ManyToMany with an explicit entity? Expected: as soon as the association has attributes, needs direct querying, soft delete, or pagination.
  3. Does PostgreSQL index foreign-key columns? Does TypeORM? Expected: neither; you must.
  4. What is the difference between relations in find and leftJoinAndSelect with limit in a query builder? Expected: find with take paginates by distinct parent ids; limit cuts joined rows.

Practical exercise

Model Category with a self-referencing parent relation and Product.category. Write a find that loads products with their category and the category's parent, then the same with relationLoadStrategy: 'query', and compare the SQL. Then add a position column to the product-tag association and migrate it from @ManyToMany to an explicit ProductTag entity without losing data. Acceptance criteria: both loading strategies return identical JSON; the migration is reversible; every FK column has an index (verify with \di in psql).

21.4 Repository and EntityManager

Concept

Repository<T> is the object you inject to work with one entity: find, save, insert, update, delete, upsert, count, increment, softDelete, restore, createQueryBuilder. EntityManager has the same methods but takes the entity class as the first argument, so one manager can touch any table. A repository is literally an entity manager with the target pre-filled; transactions hand you a manager because a transaction spans tables.

Why does it exist?

Repositories give each module a narrow, typed surface over its own tables, which is what dependency injection wants. The manager exists for the cases that cut across modules: transactions, generic tooling, and raw SQL.

How it works

  1. TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Order]) registers a provider whose token is the repository for Order; @InjectRepository(Order) resolves it. Underneath it is dataSource.getRepository(Order), bound to dataSource.manager, which uses any free pooled connection in autocommit mode.
  2. Each method builds a query through the query builder (section 21.5) or, for save(), through the persist executor, which decides between INSERT and UPDATE per entity.
  3. Inside dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => ...), manager.getRepository(Order) returns a repository bound to that connection. The injected repository is not (Part 20, section 20.11.4).

21.4.1 The find family

import { In, Not, LessThan, MoreThanOrEqual, Between, ILike, IsNull, Raw } from 'typeorm';

// Full options object
const orders = await this.orders.find({
  select: { id: true, status: true, totalCents: true, createdAt: true },   // SELECT only these columns
  where: [                                                                  // array => OR between elements
    { customerId, status: In(['CREATED', 'PAID']) },
    { customerId, totalCents: MoreThanOrEqual(100_000) },
  ],
  relations: { items: true },
  order: { createdAt: 'DESC' },
  skip: 40,
  take: 20,
  withDeleted: false,
});

// Shorthands
await this.orders.findBy({ customerId });                                   // where only
await this.orders.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { items: { product: true } } }); // where is required in 0.3
await this.orders.findOneBy({ id });                                        // null if missing
await this.orders.findOneByOrFail({ id });                                  // throws EntityNotFoundError
const [rows, total] = await this.orders.findAndCount({ where: { customerId }, take: 20 });
await this.orders.count({ where: { status: 'CREATED' } });
await this.orders.exists({ where: { id } });                                // SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1

// Operators that map to SQL
await this.products.findBy({ stock: LessThan(10), deletedAt: IsNull() });
await this.products.findBy({ name: ILike('%headphone%') });
await this.products.findBy({ price: Between('10.00', '50.00') });
await this.orders.findBy({ createdAt: Raw((alias) => `${alias} > now() - interval '7 days'`) });

where: { items: { productId } } filters through a relation (TypeORM adds the join). findOne without where throws in 0.3; findOne(id) from 0.2 is gone, use findOneBy({ id }). findOne with order and no where is a full-table sort; watch for it.

21.4.2 save versus insert versus update versus upsert

These four look interchangeable and are not. Here is what each sends to PostgreSQL for a Product with an existing id, taken from the query log.

save(entity)

START TRANSACTION
SELECT "Product"."id", "Product"."sku", "Product"."name", "Product"."price", ... FROM "products" "Product" WHERE "Product"."id" IN ($1)
UPDATE "products" SET "name" = $1, "version" = "version" + 1, "updated_at" = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE "id" IN ($2)
COMMIT

save() first SELECTs the current row (to decide insert versus update and to compute which columns changed), then writes only the changed columns, bumps @VersionColumn and @UpdateDateColumn, runs listeners and subscribers, cascades to relations marked cascade, and returns the entity with generated values filled in. If no transaction is active it opens one around all of that. For an array it batches the SELECT with IN (...) and the inserts in chunks, but issues one UPDATE per changed entity. Properties that are undefined are skipped; null is written. Passing a partial object (save({ id, name })) works and updates only name, which is convenient for PATCH handlers and dangerous when the partial accidentally contains a stale value for another column.

insert(values)

INSERT INTO "products"("id", "sku", "name", "price", "stock", ...) VALUES (DEFAULT, $1, $2, $3, $4, ...) RETURNING "id", "version", "created_at", "updated_at"

One statement, no SELECT, no cascade, no change detection. Duplicate key fails with 23505. Entity listener methods (@BeforeInsert) run only if you pass an entity instance (repo.create({...})), not a plain object. Use it for bulk loads and for "I know this is new".

update(criteria, partial)

UPDATE "products" SET "stock" = $1, "version" = "version" + 1, "updated_at" = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE "id" = $2

One statement, returns UpdateResult with affected. No SELECT, no cascade, no entity listeners, no save()-style change detection; but it does bump the version and update-date columns. set({ stock: () => 'stock - 1' }) gives you SQL expressions, which is how atomic updates are written (Part 20, section 20.10).

upsert(values, conflictPaths)

INSERT INTO "products"("sku", "name", "price") VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT ("sku") DO UPDATE SET "name" = EXCLUDED."name", "price" = EXCLUDED."price"
await this.products.upsert(
  rows.map((r) => ({ sku: r.sku, name: r.name, price: r.price })),
  { conflictPaths: ['sku'], skipUpdateIfNoValuesChanged: true },
);
// For a partial unique index: { conflictPaths: ['sku'], indexPredicate: 'deleted_at IS NULL' }

This is the only one of the four that is race-safe for "insert or update by natural key"; save() is SELECT then INSERT, and two concurrent saves of a new SKU both insert (Part 20, section 20.13).

Method Statements Cascades Listeners Race-safe upsert Use for
save SELECT + INSERT/UPDATE (+ cascades), in a transaction yes yes no aggregates with relations, entity-centric code
insert 1 INSERT no instances only no (fails on duplicate) bulk loads, known-new rows
update 1 UPDATE no no n/a partial updates, atomic expressions, criteria-based
upsert 1 INSERT ... ON CONFLICT no no yes idempotent writes by natural key
preload + save SELECT + SELECT + UPDATE yes yes no PATCH with DTO merge

21.4.3 Custom repositories in NestJS

TypeORM 0.2's @EntityRepository() is gone. The 0.3 pattern is a class that extends Repository<T> and is a normal NestJS provider.

// src/orders/orders.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository extends Repository<Order> {
  constructor(dataSource: DataSource) {
    super(Order, dataSource.createEntityManager());   // NOT transactional; see withRepository below
  }

  findOpenForCustomer(customerId: string, limit = 20): Promise<Order[]> {
    return this.createQueryBuilder('o')
      .where('o.customer_id = :customerId', { customerId })
      .andWhere('o.status IN (:...statuses)', { statuses: ['CREATED', 'PAID'] })
      .orderBy('o.created_at', 'DESC')
      .take(limit)
      .getMany();
  }
}

// orders.module.ts: providers: [OrdersRepository, OrdersService]
// Inside a transaction: const repo = manager.withRepository(this.ordersRepository);

manager.withRepository(repo) returns a copy of the custom repository bound to the transactional manager, keeping your custom methods. Without it, the custom repository's queries run on a separate connection.

21.4.4 When to use EntityManager directly

Transactions (dataSource.transaction, queryRunner.manager), generic code that works over many entities (audit, tenant scoping), manager.query(sql, params) for raw SQL, and one-off scripts. Inject with @InjectEntityManager() or take DataSource and use dataSource.manager. Business services should mostly see repositories; if every service injects the manager, module boundaries have dissolved.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • save() on an entity whose primary key is set but whose row was deleted inserts a new row with that id.
  • save() with @Column({ select: false }) columns cannot see their current value, so change detection treats them as unchanged; to update a password hash use update().
  • findOne with relations and where on a relation column, combined with order on the parent, can generate a query whose ORDER BY refers to a joined alias not in SELECT DISTINCT; TypeORM usually handles it, but check the SQL.
  • count() with relations joins them; countBy does not.
  • exists() is exist() in TypeORM versions before 0.3.17; both work in later versions with a deprecation warning on the old one.
  • remove(entity) needs the primary key on the instance; delete(criteria) is one statement and skips listeners and cascades.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They choose the method by the SQL it produces: save for aggregates, update for targeted changes, insert for bulk, upsert for idempotent writes. They know save() costs a SELECT and a transaction. They keep repositories per module and pass managers only for transactions.

Common mistakes

  • save() in a loop of 10,000 items (30,000 statements).
  • save() as upsert.
  • Reading a column with select: false through find and being surprised by undefined.
  • Using the injected repository inside a transaction.
  • findOne({ where: {} }) when the id is undefined (matches everything, returns the first row). Validate ids before querying.

Interview questions

  1. What SQL does repository.save() execute for an existing entity, and why? Expected: SELECT by PK then UPDATE of changed columns, in a transaction; change detection and cascades need the current state.
  2. When is update() better than save()? Expected: targeted partial updates, atomic expressions, no need for the entity, one statement.
  3. Why is save() not an upsert? Expected: two statements with a race window; upsert() uses ON CONFLICT.
  4. How do you write a custom repository in TypeORM 0.3 with NestJS? Expected: extend Repository<T>, super(Entity, dataSource.createEntityManager()), register as provider; use withRepository in transactions.

Practical exercise

Implement PATCH /products/:id three ways: preload + save, update() with a partial, and upsert() keyed on sku. Capture the SQL log for each and count statements. Then run 50 concurrent PATCHes on one product with each approach and record which produce lost updates. Acceptance criteria: a table of statement counts; an explanation of why update() with stock: () => 'stock - 1' is the only one that does not lose updates without extra locking.

21.5 QueryBuilder

Concept

The query builder is a fluent API that assembles a SQL statement piece by piece (select, from, join, where, orderBy, limit) with a parameters map, then either returns raw rows (getRawMany) or hydrates entities (getMany). It exists for the queries the options object cannot express: joins with conditions, aggregates, subqueries, locks, bulk writes with expressions.

Why does it exist?

find options cover filters, relations and ordering. They cannot express SUM(item.qty), HAVING, a join on a condition other than the foreign key, a subquery in WHERE, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or an UPDATE ... SET x = x - 1. The query builder can, while still binding parameters safely and hydrating entities when you want it to.

How it works

  1. repository.createQueryBuilder('o') creates a SelectQueryBuilder with o as the alias for the entity's table.
  2. Each method appends to an expression map; nothing is sent until a get* or execute() call.
  3. :name placeholders in strings are collected into a parameters object and emitted as $1, $2 in order. :...ids expands an array into $1, $2, $3.
  4. getQuery() and getParameters() show the SQL and values; getQueryAndParameters() gives both. Use them in tests.
  5. getMany/getOne run the query and hydrate entities (de-duplicating joined rows); getRawMany/getRawOne return rows with aliased column names (o_id, item_qty); getRawAndEntities returns both.

21.5.1 Selecting, joining and filtering

const orders = await this.orders
  .createQueryBuilder('o')
  .leftJoinAndSelect('o.items', 'item')                    // join and hydrate items
  .leftJoinAndSelect('item.product', 'product')
  .leftJoin('o.customer', 'customer')                      // join for filtering only; not selected
  .where('customer.email ILIKE :email', { email: `%${domain}` })
  .andWhere('o.created_at >= :since', { since })
  .andWhere('o.status IN (:...statuses)', { statuses: ['PAID', 'SHIPPED'] })
  .andWhere(new Brackets((qb) => qb.where('o.total_cents > :big', { big: 50_000 }).orWhere('product.sku = :sku', { sku })))
  .orderBy('o.created_at', 'DESC')
  .addOrderBy('item.id', 'ASC')
  .getMany();

Never interpolate values into the string. .where(\o.status = '${status}'`)is SQL injection waiting for a status of' OR '1'='1. The only things that may be interpolated are identifiers you control (column names chosen from an allow-list for dynamic sorting). Everything else goes through :param`.

Joins can take a condition: .leftJoin('o.items', 'item', 'item.qty > :minQty', { minQty: 2 }). Joining an unrelated table: .leftJoin(Refund, 'r', 'r.order_id = o.id').

21.5.2 getMany versus getRawMany

getMany hydrates entities and only includes columns that map to entity properties. addSelect('SUM(item.qty)', 'itemCount') is not visible on the entity after getMany; it is in the raw row only. For aggregates, use getRawMany and type the result yourself, or getRawAndEntities to zip them.

// Revenue per product, last 30 days: a report query. Raw rows, no hydration.
interface ProductRevenueRow { productId: string; name: string; revenueCents: string; units: string }

const rows = await this.dataSource
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .select('p.id', 'productId')
  .addSelect('p.name', 'name')
  .addSelect('SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price_cents)', 'revenueCents')   // bigint sum => string
  .addSelect('SUM(i.qty)', 'units')
  .from(OrderItem, 'i')
  .innerJoin('i.product', 'p')
  .innerJoin('i.order', 'o', 'o.status IN (:...paid)', { paid: ['PAID', 'SHIPPED'] })
  .where('o.created_at >= now() - interval \'30 days\'')
  .groupBy('p.id')
  .addGroupBy('p.name')
  .orderBy('"revenueCents"', 'DESC')
  .limit(50)
  .getRawMany<ProductRevenueRow>();

Note the quoting in orderBy('"revenueCents"'): aliases with capitals must be double-quoted to survive PostgreSQL's case folding.

21.5.3 Pagination: skip/take versus offset/limit and the join-multiplication bug

limit/offset are raw SQL LIMIT/OFFSET. With a leftJoinAndSelect on a one-to-many relation, the database returns one row per child, so LIMIT 20 returns 20 order-item rows, which hydrate into perhaps 6 orders. The page is wrong and the count varies with the data.

take/skip know about joins. When joins are present TypeORM runs two queries: first the distinct parent ids for the page, then the full joined rows for those ids.

-- Query 1: which parents are on this page
SELECT DISTINCT "distinctAlias"."o_id" AS "ids_o_id", "distinctAlias"."o_created_at"
FROM (SELECT "o"."id" AS "o_id", "o"."created_at" AS "o_created_at", ...
      FROM "orders" "o" LEFT JOIN "order_items" "item" ON "item"."order_id" = "o"."id"
      WHERE "o"."customer_id" = $1) "distinctAlias"
ORDER BY "distinctAlias"."o_created_at" DESC, "o_id" ASC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

-- Query 2: everything for those parents
SELECT "o".*, "item".* FROM "orders" "o" LEFT JOIN "order_items" "item" ON ...
WHERE "o"."id" IN ($1, $2, ..., $20)
ORDER BY "o"."created_at" DESC;

Cost: two round trips, and the first query sorts joined rows before de-duplicating, which on a customer with 50,000 items is slow. The cleaner alternative for wide relations is to paginate the parents alone (take without joins, or a plain LIMIT on the parent table) and load children with a second IN (...) query, which is what relationLoadStrategy: 'query' does.

Rule: take/skip whenever there is a *AndSelect join; limit/offset only when there is no join or you are using getRawMany.

21.5.4 getManyAndCount cost

getManyAndCount() runs the page query plus SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT("o"."id")) FROM "orders" "o" LEFT JOIN ... with all your joins and filters. On a million-row table with a join that is a full scan per request: 200–800 ms every page load. Options: a separate count() without joins when the joins do not affect the count; a cached or approximate count (reltuples from pg_class, or a counter table) for large tables; or keyset pagination, which needs no count at all and is the right answer for infinite-scroll APIs (see Part 19 on indexes and EXPLAIN ANALYZE for why OFFSET degrades).

21.5.5 Locks

.setLock('pessimistic_write'), .setLock('for_no_key_update'), .setOnLocked('skip_locked' | 'nowait'); requires an active transaction (.setQueryRunner(queryRunner) or a transactional manager's createQueryBuilder). Part 20, sections 20.6 and 20.10, covers the patterns.

21.5.6 Subqueries

// Products that sold more than 100 units in the last week
const hot = this.dataSource
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .subQuery()
  .select('i.product_id')
  .from(OrderItem, 'i')
  .innerJoin('i.order', 'o')
  .where("o.created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'")
  .groupBy('i.product_id')
  .having('SUM(i.qty) > :units')
  .getQuery();                                              // returns "(SELECT ...)" string

const products = await this.products
  .createQueryBuilder('p')
  .where(`p.id IN ${hot}`)
  .setParameter('units', 100)                                // parameters of the subquery are set on the outer builder
  .getMany();

Also possible: .from((qb) => qb.select(...).from(...), 'sub') for a derived table, and .addSelect((qb) => qb.select('COUNT(*)').from(OrderItem, 'i').where('i.order_id = o.id'), 'itemCount') for a correlated scalar subquery.

21.5.7 Insert, update and delete builders

// Bulk insert with conflict handling (one statement, up to ~1,000 rows per call to stay under the parameter limit)
await this.dataSource.createQueryBuilder().insert().into(Product)
  .values(rows)
  .orUpdate(['name', 'price'], ['sku'], { skipUpdateIfNoValuesChanged: true })   // ON CONFLICT ("sku") DO UPDATE
  .execute();
await this.dataSource.createQueryBuilder().insert().into(Tag).values(tags).orIgnore().execute(); // DO NOTHING

// Atomic update with expression and RETURNING
const r = await this.products.createQueryBuilder().update(Product)
  .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
  .where('id = :id AND stock >= :qty', { id, qty })
  .returning(['id', 'stock'])
  .execute();
// r.affected, r.raw[0].stock

// Delete and soft delete by criteria
await this.orders.createQueryBuilder().delete().from(OrderItem).where('order_id = :id', { id }).execute();
await this.products.createQueryBuilder().softDelete().where('status = :s', { s: 'ARCHIVED' }).execute();

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Column names in strings are database names when prefixed by a table alias (o.created_at) and property names when prefixed by an entity alias in where on find; mixing o.createdAt and o.created_at works only because TypeORM maps property paths on known aliases. Be consistent.
  • getOne() with joins and no take can hydrate one parent from thousands of rows; getOne() uses LIMIT only when there are no joins.
  • orderBy on a computed alias needs quotes; orderBy on a joined column with take must be included in the distinct subquery (TypeORM does this, but orderBy(RANDOM()) breaks it).
  • :...ids with an empty array generates IN (), a syntax error; guard with an early return.
  • Parameter names are global to the builder; two :id with different values overwrite each other silently.
  • .stream() requires pg-query-stream installed and returns raw rows only.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the SQL they want first, then express it in the builder, then check getQuery() matches. They use getRawMany for reports and reserve hydration for aggregates the code will mutate. They use take/skip with joins and know why. They have a query-count and query-time log per request and look at it after every builder change.

Common mistakes

  • String interpolation of user input.
  • limit() with leftJoinAndSelect.
  • getManyAndCount() on a large joined table for every page.
  • Expecting addSelect aggregates to appear on entities after getMany.
  • Building dynamic filters by concatenating where strings instead of andWhere with parameters.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the difference between take and limit in TypeORM. Expected: take paginates parents by distinct ids with two queries when joins exist; limit cuts joined rows.
  2. How would you write a "top 50 products by revenue" query with TypeORM? Expected: query builder with aggregates and getRawMany, or raw SQL; not hydration.
  3. How do you prevent SQL injection in a dynamic filter? Expected: parameters for values, allow-list for identifiers.
  4. Why is getManyAndCount expensive and what are the alternatives? Expected: count query repeats joins; separate cheap count, estimate, keyset.

Practical exercise

Build GET /orders?customerId=&status=&sort=&page= with dynamic filters and sorting via an allow-list, loading items with take/skip. Log the SQL. Then implement keyset pagination (createdAt, id cursor) for the same endpoint and compare p99 at page 1 and page 500 on a table with 2 million orders. Acceptance criteria: no string interpolation of user values (grep the code); page results are stable; keyset p99 is flat across pages.

21.6 Transactions (recap)

dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => ...) for the callback form; createQueryRunner() with connect/startTransaction/commitTransaction/rollbackTransaction/release in finally for manual control; isolation level as the first argument; every query inside through the transactional manager (manager.getRepository, manager.withRepository, or a CLS context); nested manager.transaction becomes a savepoint; locks through find({ lock }) or setLock(). The full treatment, including propagation across services and the injected-repository bug, is Part 20 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control, sections 20.11 and 20.13.

21.7 Migrations

Concept

A migration is a versioned, ordered script that changes the database schema (and sometimes data). TypeORM keeps a migrations table recording which scripts have run, generates candidate scripts by diffing your entities against the live schema, and runs pending ones in order.

Why does it exist?

Schema changes must be reviewable, repeatable across environments, reversible, and coordinated with code deploys. synchronize: true gives you none of that; it applies whatever diff it computes, at boot, with no review and no rollback. Migrations turn schema change into code you can read in a pull request.

Mental model

Imagine renovation plans for a building that people live in. You do not "make the building match the drawing" overnight; you file dated work orders, each one small, each one checked, each one with a way to undo it, and you keep a logbook of which have been done. The migrations table is the logbook.

How it works

  1. A DataSource configuration for the CLI (src/data-source.ts) points at entities and the migrations directory.
  2. migration:generate connects, loads entity metadata, reads the live schema, computes the diff, and writes a class with up() and down() containing raw SQL.
  3. You review and edit that SQL. Generated migrations are drafts; they are correct about what differs and often wrong about how to get there safely (they drop and re-add a renamed column, they add NOT NULL without a default to a populated table, they create indexes without CONCURRENTLY).
  4. migration:run reads the migrations table, finds classes whose timestamp is not recorded, runs their up() in timestamp order and inserts a row per migration. migration:revert runs the last one's down() and deletes its row.
  5. Transaction mode controls whether all pending migrations run in one transaction (all, the default), one per migration (each), or none. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE (on older PostgreSQL) cannot run inside a transaction block; those migrations need none or a per-migration opt-out.
// src/data-source.ts (used by the CLI; the NestJS module has its own config that shares the same values)
import 'reflect-metadata';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export default new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  entities: ['src/**/*.entity.ts'],
  migrations: ['src/migrations/*.ts'],
  migrationsTableName: 'migrations',
  migrationsTransactionMode: 'each',
  synchronize: false,
});
# Generate from the entity diff (review the output!)
npx typeorm-ts-node-commonjs migration:generate ./src/migrations/AddChannelToOrders -d ./src/data-source.ts
# Create an empty migration for hand-written SQL or data backfills
npx typeorm-ts-node-commonjs migration:create ./src/migrations/BackfillOrderChannel
# Apply, inspect, undo
npx typeorm-ts-node-commonjs migration:run -d ./src/data-source.ts
npx typeorm-ts-node-commonjs migration:show -d ./src/data-source.ts
npx typeorm-ts-node-commonjs migration:revert -d ./src/data-source.ts
# Override the transaction mode for one run
npx typeorm-ts-node-commonjs migration:run -d ./src/data-source.ts --transaction none

A generated migration for renaming Order.channel to Order.salesChannel, exactly as TypeORM writes it, and the version you should commit:

// GENERATED: loses every value in the column
export class RenameChannel1757200000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  name = 'RenameChannel1757200000000';
  public async up(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" DROP COLUMN "channel"`);
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD "sales_channel" text`);
  }
  public async down(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" DROP COLUMN "sales_channel"`);
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD "channel" text`);
  }
}

// EDITED: a rename is metadata-only in PostgreSQL and keeps the data
