export class RenameChannel1757200000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  name = 'RenameChannel1757200000000';
  public async up(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`SET lock_timeout = '3s'`);
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" RENAME COLUMN "channel" TO "sales_channel"`);
  }
  public async down(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" RENAME COLUMN "sales_channel" TO "channel"`);
  }
}

And an index migration that must run outside a transaction:

export class IndexOrdersStatus1757200100000 implements MigrationInterface {
  name = 'IndexOrdersStatus1757200100000';
  transaction = false;   // supported in recent 0.3 releases; otherwise run with --transaction none
  public async up(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS "orders_status_created_idx" ON "orders" ("status", "created_at" DESC)`);
  }
  public async down(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS "orders_status_created_idx"`);
  }
}

Where to run migrations.

Approach How Pros Cons
CI/CD step before rollout pipeline job runs migration:run against production, then deploys pods one runner, clear logs, fails the deploy on error, no race between pods needs DB credentials in the pipeline; migrations must be backward compatible with the old code still running
At application startup (migrationsRun: true) each pod runs pending migrations on boot zero extra infrastructure N pods race (TypeORM takes no lock; you get duplicate key on the migrations table or worse), slow boots fail readiness probes, a bad migration crash-loops the whole deployment
Kubernetes Job or init container a one-off Job runs migrations; deployment waits on it isolates DB access, one runner more YAML; must handle "job already ran" idempotently

Startup migrations are acceptable for a single-instance internal tool. For anything with more than one replica, run migrations from the pipeline or a Job, before the new code rolls out, and write them so the old code keeps working while both versions overlap (expand/contract). Part 23 — Safe Schema Migrations covers the full playbook: adding columns with defaults, backfilling in batches, NOT NULL via CHECK ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE, and dropping columns two deploys later.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two branches generate migrations with interleaved timestamps; the merged order runs them in timestamp order, which may not be the order they were tested in. Rebase and regenerate.
  • A migration that half-succeeded under --transaction none leaves the schema in between; the next run fails at the first statement. Make each statement idempotent (IF NOT EXISTS, IF EXISTS).
  • migration:generate sees differences it cannot express (a CHECK constraint added by hand) and generates a DROP CONSTRAINT. Add hand-written constraints to the entity via @Check() so the diff stays empty.
  • Enum changes generate type-recreation SQL that rewrites the column and locks the table.
  • The migrations table is per database, not per schema; multi-schema setups need migrationsTableName per data source.
  • migration:revert runs down() of the last migration only; reverting three needs three runs, and down() of a data-loss migration cannot restore data.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat generated migrations as a starting point and review every line for locks (lock_timeout), data loss, table rewrites and index creation without CONCURRENTLY. They run migrations from the pipeline, never from pods. They keep synchronize: false in every environment, including local, so that local matches production and the migration is exercised before review. They write backward-compatible migrations and ship the code that needs the new schema in a later deploy.

Common mistakes

  • synchronize: true in a shared environment.
  • Committing generated migrations unread.
  • migrationsRun: true on a multi-replica deployment.
  • Adding a NOT NULL column without a default to a large table (full rewrite, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for minutes).
  • Creating an index without CONCURRENTLY on a hot table.
  • Renaming via drop-and-add.

Interview questions

  1. Why is synchronize: true dangerous, and what replaces it? Expected: unreviewed, potentially destructive diffs at boot; migrations.
  2. Where should migrations run in a Kubernetes deployment and why? Expected: pipeline step or Job before rollout; pods racing and readiness failures otherwise.
  3. Why can CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY not run in a TypeORM migration by default, and how do you handle it? Expected: cannot run in a transaction block; migrationsTransactionMode: 'each' plus per-migration opt-out or --transaction none.
  4. A generated migration drops and re-adds a column. What happened and what do you do? Expected: property rename; edit to RENAME COLUMN.

Practical exercise

Rename Product.attributes to Product.metadata, add a NOT NULL currency char(3) column with a default to a table with 1 million rows, and add a concurrent index on orders (status, created_at), as three migrations. Acceptance criteria: none of them take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock longer than 100 ms (measure with log_lock_waits and lock_timeout = '100ms'); migration:generate afterwards produces an empty diff; migration:revert three times restores the schema.

21.8 Eager and lazy loading

Concept

A relation can be loaded three ways: explicitly (relations: {...} or a join in the query builder), eagerly (eager: true on the decorator: TypeORM always loads it with find*), or lazily (the property is typed Promise<T> and TypeORM queries when you await it). Only the first one keeps the query count under your control.

Why does it exist?

Eager loading exists so that a relation you always need (a product's currency, a user's role) comes along without every caller remembering to ask. Lazy loading exists so that code can walk an object graph naturally. Both trade explicitness for convenience, and the bill arrives as query counts.

Mental model

Imagine ordering a coffee. Explicit loading is saying "a latte with oat milk". Eager loading is a café that puts oat milk in every drink because someone once asked. Lazy loading is a café that hands you an empty cup and makes the coffee when you lift it to your mouth, and does that again for every sip.

How it works

Eager. @ManyToOne(() => Currency, { eager: true }). Every find, findOne, findBy on the owning entity adds a LEFT JOIN for it, recursively through eager relations of the joined entity. It does not apply to createQueryBuilder (you must join yourself) and cannot be set on both sides of a relation. The danger is transitive: Order eagerly loads Customer, Customer eagerly loads Addresses, Address eagerly loads Country; now find(Order) is a four-way join for a list endpoint that shows order numbers. find({ loadEagerRelations: false }) turns it off per call.

Lazy. Declare items: Promise<OrderItem[]> and TypeORM installs a getter that runs SELECT ... WHERE order_id = $1 the first time you await order.items, caching the result on the instance. Each instance queries separately: a loop over 100 orders awaiting items is 101 queries (section 21.9). Lazy relations also make entity types awkward (await everywhere, serialisation produces {} for pending promises), and they need emitDecoratorMetadata to detect the Promise type.

Explicit. relations: { items: { product: true } }, relationLoadStrategy: 'join' | 'query', or query-builder joins. The relation is loaded exactly when the code says so, and the SQL log shows it.

TypeORM example

// What to avoid
@Entity() export class Order {
  @OneToMany(() => OrderItem, (i) => i.order, { eager: true }) items: OrderItem[];   // every find joins items
  @ManyToOne(() => Customer) customer: Promise<Customer>;                          // lazy: one query per access
}

// What to do: no eager, no lazy, explicit per use case
const list = await this.orders.find({ where: { customerId }, select: { id: true, status: true, totalCents: true }, take: 20 });
const detail = await this.orders.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { items: { product: true }, customer: true } });

Edge cases & failure modes

  • eager: true relations are also loaded by save()'s internal SELECT, adding join cost to every write.
  • Lazy relation promises hold a reference to the entity manager; entities serialised to JSON after their transaction ended can trigger queries on a released query runner and throw.
  • relations and eager compose: an explicit relation on an eager entity loads the eager ones too.
  • relationLoadStrategy: 'query' issues one extra query per relation level (not per parent), which is usually right for wide parents and wrong for tiny ones.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Explicit by default. eager: true only on small, always-needed lookups with no further eager relations. Lazy relations not at all in new code. Every list endpoint selects columns and loads no collections; every detail endpoint loads exactly the relations the response needs.

Common mistakes

  • Chained eager relations that turn every query into a multi-way join.
  • Lazy relations accessed in a loop.
  • Returning entities with lazy properties from controllers and getting {} in the JSON.

Interview questions

  1. What does eager: true change about find and about createQueryBuilder? Expected: find* auto-joins; query builder does not.
  2. Why are lazy relations a performance trap? Expected: one query per instance per relation; N+1 hidden in property access.
  3. How do you load a relation for one endpoint without affecting others? Expected: relations or joins per call.

Practical exercise

Take an entity with two eager relations and one lazy one, enable query logging, and record the statements for a list endpoint and a detail endpoint. Convert to explicit loading. Acceptance criteria: the list endpoint runs one query with no joins; the detail endpoint runs the minimum number of statements for its response; no Promise-typed relation properties remain.

21.9 The N+1 problem

Concept

N+1 is the pattern of one query to fetch N parent rows followed by N more queries, one per parent, to fetch their children. It is the single most common ORM performance bug, it scales linearly with data, and it is invisible in development because N is small there.

Why does it exist?

Because ORMs make "get the children of this parent" a property access or a one-line call, and loops are how developers process lists. Nothing in the code looks expensive.

Mental model

Imagine a librarian asked for the authors of 200 books. The N+1 librarian walks to the catalogue 200 times, once per book. The batched librarian writes down all 200 titles and walks once.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Service
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    S->>PG: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 (returns 100 rows)
    loop for each of the 100 orders
        S->>PG: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1
        PG-->>S: items for one order
    end
    Note over S,PG: 101 round trips, ~1 ms each on a local DB, 100 ms total, 10 s at 100 ms cross-region
    S->>PG: Batched alternative: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ANY($1)
    PG-->>S: all items in one round trip

The query log makes it obvious once you look. With logging: ['query']:

query: SELECT "o"."id", "o"."status" FROM "orders" "o" WHERE "o"."customer_id" = $1 -- PARAMETERS: ["c1"]
query: SELECT "i"."id", "i"."qty" FROM "order_items" "i" WHERE "i"."order_id" = $1 -- PARAMETERS: ["o1"]
query: SELECT "i"."id", "i"."qty" FROM "order_items" "i" WHERE "i"."order_id" = $1 -- PARAMETERS: ["o2"]
query: SELECT "i"."id", "i"."qty" FROM "order_items" "i" WHERE "i"."order_id" = $1 -- PARAMETERS: ["o3"]
... 97 more

Each query is fast (0.5 ms of database time), so nothing shows up in slow-query logs. What shows up is total request latency, connection churn, and CPU on the primary from parse/plan overhead. At 100 requests per second this endpoint issues 10,100 queries per second.

Practical example

The buggy code and the three fixes.

// BUG: 1 + N queries
const orders = await this.orders.findBy({ customerId });
for (const order of orders) {
  order.items = await this.items.findBy({ orderId: order.id });   // one query per order
}

// FIX 1: join through relations (one query; rows multiply by items per order)
const orders1 = await this.orders.find({ where: { customerId }, relations: { items: true } });

// FIX 2: two queries, no row multiplication (best for wide parents or many children)
const orders2 = await this.orders.find({ where: { customerId }, relations: { items: true }, relationLoadStrategy: 'query' });

// FIX 3: manual batch, when the children come from somewhere the ORM cannot join (another service, a cache, raw SQL)
const orders3 = await this.orders.findBy({ customerId });
const items = await this.items.findBy({ orderId: In(orders3.map((o) => o.id)) });   // WHERE order_id IN ($1..$N)
const byOrder = new Map<string, OrderItem[]>();
for (const item of items) (byOrder.get(item.orderId) ?? byOrder.set(item.orderId, []).get(item.orderId)!).push(item);
for (const o of orders3) o.items = byOrder.get(o.id) ?? [];

The DataLoader pattern. When the code that needs children is spread across resolvers or nested service calls (GraphQL is the usual case), you cannot restructure into one batch by hand. A DataLoader collects every load(id) call made during one tick of the event loop, issues a single batched query, and hands each caller its result. The dataloader package implements it; in NestJS it must be request-scoped so the cache does not leak between users.

// src/orders/order-items.loader.ts
import { Injectable, Scope } from '@nestjs/common';
import DataLoader from 'dataloader';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { In, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { OrderItem } from './order-item.entity';

@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })          // one loader (and cache) per request
export class OrderItemsLoader {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(OrderItem) private readonly items: Repository<OrderItem>) {}

  readonly byOrderId = new DataLoader<string, OrderItem[]>(async (orderIds) => {
    const rows = await this.items.findBy({ orderId: In([...orderIds]) });   // ONE query for all ids in this tick
    const grouped = new Map<string, OrderItem[]>();
    for (const r of rows) (grouped.get(r.orderId) ?? grouped.set(r.orderId, []).get(r.orderId)!).push(r);
    return orderIds.map((id) => grouped.get(id) ?? []);                      // must return results in input order
  });
}

// In a resolver or service: await this.loader.byOrderId.load(order.id) from 100 places => one query

Measuring. A custom TypeORM logger that counts queries per request (store a counter in AsyncLocalStorage keyed by request, log it in an interceptor when the response finishes, warn above a threshold such as 20) catches N+1 in staging before users do. On the database side, pg_stat_statements shows the offending statement with calls in the millions and a tiny mean_exec_time; that signature is N+1.

PostgreSQL example

The batched form uses an array parameter, which sidesteps the parameter-count limit of IN ($1, ..., $N) and produces a stable plan:

SELECT i.* FROM order_items i WHERE i.order_id = ANY($1::uuid[]) ORDER BY i.order_id, i.id;
Index Scan using order_items_order_id_idx on order_items i  (cost=0.43..412.10 rows=520 width=64) (actual time=0.031..0.611 rows=498 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (order_id = ANY ('{...}'::uuid[]))
  Buffers: shared hit=112
Planning Time: 0.140 ms
Execution Time: 0.702 ms

One round trip, 0.7 ms, against 100 round trips of 0.5 ms each plus network.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • N+1 on writes: save() in a loop, or cascades that insert children one statement each.
  • N+1 across services: a loop calling GET /products/:id over HTTP is the same disease with 50 ms per iteration.
  • DataLoader caches per request; using a singleton leaks data between users and serves stale rows.
  • Batching too aggressively: IN lists over a few thousand ids should be chunked; = ANY($1) handles large arrays but the plan can flip to a sequential scan.
  • Join-based fixes multiply rows; for 1,000 parents with 200 children each, the join returns 200,000 rows and hydration becomes the bottleneck. Use the two-query strategy.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume every loop that touches a repository is N+1 until the log proves otherwise. They put a per-request query counter in staging. They pick join versus two-query versus DataLoader by the shape: narrow parents with few children, join; wide parents or many children, two queries; scattered access, DataLoader.

Common mistakes

  • Fixing N+1 with eager: true, which turns it into an always-on join.
  • Batching with IN (...) and 50,000 ids in one statement.
  • Not noticing N+1 because each query is fast.
  • A DataLoader registered as a singleton.

Interview questions

  1. How do you detect N+1 in a running system? Expected: per-request query count; pg_stat_statements with high calls and low mean time.
  2. Explain the DataLoader pattern and why it must be request-scoped. Expected: batches loads per tick; per-request cache to avoid cross-user leaks.
  3. When is a join the wrong fix for N+1? Expected: wide parents or many children; row multiplication; use two queries.
  4. What is the write-side version of N+1? Expected: save() per item; cascades; fix with bulk insert.

Practical exercise

Introduce a query-count interceptor that logs queries=N per request. Find every endpoint in a sample app with N greater than 10, fix each with the appropriate strategy, and re-measure. Acceptance criteria: no endpoint exceeds 5 queries for a page of 50 parents; the fix for at least one endpoint uses a request-scoped DataLoader.

21.10 Cascades

Concept

Cascade means "when I do X to the parent, do X to the children too". There are two unrelated mechanisms with the same name: ORM-level cascade (cascade option on the relation: TypeORM saves or removes related entities that are present on the object when you save()/remove() the parent) and database-level referential actions (onDelete: 'CASCADE' on the foreign key: PostgreSQL deletes child rows when the parent row is deleted, no matter who issued the delete).

Why does it exist?

Aggregates are saved as a unit: create an order with its items in one save(order). Deleting a parent must not leave orphans. ORM cascade handles the first; database cascade handles the second reliably.

How it works

@OneToMany(() => OrderItem, (i) => i.order, { cascade: ['insert', 'update'], orphanedRowAction: 'delete' })
items: OrderItem[];

@ManyToOne(() => Order, (o) => o.items, { onDelete: 'CASCADE' })   // FOREIGN KEY ... ON DELETE CASCADE
order: Order;
  1. save(order) with cascade: ['insert', 'update']: TypeORM inserts the order, then inserts each new item (one statement each, or a batched insert), and updates each changed existing item. Items missing from order.items that exist in the database are handled per orphanedRowAction: nullify (default, sets order_id = NULL, which fails if the column is NOT NULL), delete, soft-delete, or disable.
  2. remove(order) with cascade: ['remove'] (or cascade: true): TypeORM deletes the items that are loaded on the object, then the order. Items not loaded are not deleted; with onDelete: 'CASCADE' PostgreSQL deletes them anyway; without it the delete fails on the foreign key.
  3. delete(criteria) and query-builder deletes never cascade at the ORM level; only the database action applies.

Why database-level is more reliable. It runs for every path: ORM remove, ORM delete, raw SQL, a DBA in psql, a bulk job, another service. It is atomic with the parent delete. It needs no loading of children into memory (a parent with 100,000 children is one statement, not 100,001). ORM cascade only sees what is loaded, is only invoked by save/remove, and issues one statement per child. Use ORM cascade for creating aggregates, database cascade for deleting them, and RESTRICT where deleting must be impossible (an order item referencing a product).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • cascade: ['remove'] on a @ManyToMany removes the related entities, not just the join rows: deleting a product with cascade remove on tags deletes tags that other products use. To remove associations, set product.tags = [] and save.
  • cascade: true on both sides of a relation creates infinite recursion risk in save() when object graphs are circular; TypeORM guards against it, but the persisted result can surprise.
  • Database cascade on a deep hierarchy (customers to orders to order_items to shipments) makes one DELETE FROM customers fan out into millions of rows in one transaction, with locks and WAL to match; batch such deletions or soft-delete instead.
  • orphanedRowAction: 'delete' on a relation loaded partially (paginated children) deletes the children that were not loaded.
  • Soft delete does not cascade at the database level; softRemove cascades only with cascade: ['soft-remove'] and only over loaded children.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Creation cascades in the ORM, deletion cascades in the database, RESTRICT by default and CASCADE only where a child has no meaning without its parent. They read the generated FK DDL to verify ON DELETE, and they estimate fan-out before adding a database cascade to a large hierarchy.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on ORM cascade remove and finding orphans created by a bulk job.
  • cascade: true everywhere "to be safe".
  • onDelete: 'CASCADE' from orders to customers direction (deleting an order deletes the customer).
  • Cascade remove on many-to-many.

Interview questions

  1. ORM cascade versus ON DELETE CASCADE: what is the difference and which do you trust? Expected: object-graph, loaded-only, save/remove-only versus database-enforced for every path; trust the database.
  2. What happens to children removed from order.items on save()? Expected: orphanedRowAction; default nullifies the FK.
  3. When would you refuse a database cascade? Expected: deep or large fan-out; when children carry independent value (orders under a customer).

Practical exercise

Model Order to OrderItem with ORM insert cascade and database delete cascade; OrderItem to Product with RESTRICT. Write tests that: create an order with three items in one save; delete the order with delete(id) and assert items are gone; attempt to delete a product that is referenced and assert a 23503 foreign key error. Acceptance criteria: all three tests pass; the SQL log for the create shows one order insert and one batched items insert.

21.11 Subscribers and listeners

Concept

Entity listeners are methods on the entity decorated with @BeforeInsert, @AfterInsert, @BeforeUpdate, @AfterUpdate, @BeforeRemove, @AfterRemove, @BeforeSoftRemove, @AfterSoftRemove, @BeforeRecover, @AfterRecover and @AfterLoad. Subscribers are separate classes implementing EntitySubscriberInterface with the same events plus transaction events, registered with the data source. Both run application code around persistence operations.

Why does it exist?

To attach behaviour to persistence: normalise an email before insert, compute a slug, stamp updatedBy, write an audit row, invalidate a cache. The idea is that the behaviour follows the entity wherever it is saved.

How it works

// Entity listener
@Entity() export class Customer {
  @Column('text') email: string;
  @BeforeInsert() @BeforeUpdate() normaliseEmail() { this.email = this.email.trim().toLowerCase(); }
  @AfterLoad() computeDisplay() { this.display = `${this.email}`; }   // runs for every loaded instance
}

// Subscriber, registered for NestJS by pushing into the data source
@EventSubscriber()
export class OrderAuditSubscriber implements EntitySubscriberInterface<Order> {
  constructor(dataSource: DataSource) { dataSource.subscribers.push(this); }
  listenTo() { return Order; }
  async afterUpdate(event: UpdateEvent<Order>): Promise<void> {
    // event.manager is the transactional manager: this audit row commits or rolls back with the update
    await event.manager.insert(AuditLog, {
      entity: 'order', entityId: event.entity?.id, columns: event.updatedColumns.map((c) => c.propertyName),
    });
  }
}
  1. On save()/remove()/softRemove()/recover(), TypeORM builds "subjects" for every entity in the graph, runs before* listeners and subscriber methods, executes SQL, then runs after*.
  2. @AfterLoad and afterLoad run for every entity hydrated by find* and getMany.
  3. Subscribers get event.manager and event.queryRunner, bound to the current transaction; work done through them is part of it.

The pitfalls, which are the reason most senior engineers avoid them for business logic.

  • They do not run for update(), delete(), upsert(), insert() of plain objects, or query-builder writes. Those paths pass plain values, not entity instances, so @BeforeUpdate never fires; subscribers may receive a partial event with no databaseEntity. An email that is normalised on save() and not on update() is a data quality bug you will find months later.
  • They hide logic. A save() in a service does five things nobody can see from the call site. New team members change a column and break an audit trail.
  • They break with bulk operations. A listener that calls an API per entity turns a 10,000-row save(rows) into 10,000 API calls; an @AfterLoad that formats a field runs 200,000 times for a report.
  • Ordering and errors are subtle. An exception in afterInsert rolls back the insert (good) but is reported as the original operation failing (confusing); listeners on cascaded children run in graph order you did not choose.

Prefer: explicit code in the service (normalise the DTO in a pipe, write the audit row in the same transaction from the service), database triggers for audit trails that must be complete regardless of path, and @BeforeInsert only for pure, cheap, entity-local normalisation that you accept will not cover update().

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A subscriber registered by pushing into dataSource.subscribers after the first query is missed by queries already running; register at module init.
  • afterLoad with select that omits columns sees undefined for them.
  • Subscribers without listenTo() receive events for every entity.
  • A subscriber that makes HTTP calls inside afterInsert runs inside the transaction (Part 20, section 20.8).

Interview questions

  1. Which repository methods trigger @BeforeUpdate and which do not? Expected: save(); not update(), query builder, upsert().
  2. When would you pick a database trigger over a subscriber for auditing? Expected: completeness across all write paths; atomicity; no dependence on the ORM.
  3. What is the risk of @AfterLoad on a hot entity? Expected: runs per hydrated row; CPU on large results.

21.12 Logging and slow-query logging

TypeORM's logging option accepts true (everything), 'all', or an array of 'query' | 'error' | 'warn' | 'info' | 'log' | 'schema' | 'migration'. maxQueryExecutionTime: 500 reports any query over 500 ms through logQuerySlow. The built-in loggers ('advanced-console', 'simple-console', 'file', 'debug') are fine locally; in production, implement the Logger interface and route to your structured logger with parameters redacted or truncated.

// src/database/typeorm.logger.ts
import { Logger as NestLogger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Logger, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class StructuredTypeOrmLogger implements Logger {
  private readonly log = new NestLogger('TypeORM');
  logQuery(query: string, parameters?: unknown[], _qr?: QueryRunner): void {
    if (process.env.LOG_SQL === 'true') this.log.debug({ msg: 'query', query, params: this.redact(parameters) });
  }
  logQueryError(error: string | Error, query: string, parameters?: unknown[]): void {
    this.log.error({ msg: 'query_error', error: String(error), query, params: this.redact(parameters) });
  }
  logQuerySlow(time: number, query: string, parameters?: unknown[]): void {
    this.log.warn({ msg: 'slow_query', durationMs: time, query, params: this.redact(parameters) });
  }
  logSchemaBuild(message: string): void { this.log.log(message); }
  logMigration(message: string): void { this.log.log(message); }
  log(level: 'log' | 'info' | 'warn', message: unknown): void { level === 'warn' ? this.log.warn(message) : this.log.log(message); }
  private redact(params?: unknown[]): unknown[] | undefined {
    return params?.map((p) => (typeof p === 'string' && p.length > 64 ? `${p.slice(0, 64)}...` : p));
  }
}
// DataSource options: logging: ['error', 'warn'], maxQueryExecutionTime: 500, logger: new StructuredTypeOrmLogger()

Sample slow-query log line:

WARN [TypeORM] {"msg":"slow_query","durationMs":1842,"query":"SELECT \"o\".\"id\" ... FROM \"orders\" \"o\" LEFT JOIN \"order_items\" \"item\" ... WHERE \"o\".\"customer_id\" = $1 ORDER BY \"o\".\"created_at\" DESC","params":["c-2f9..."]}

Application-side timing includes pool wait, network and hydration; database-side timing (pg_stat_statements, auto_explain with auto_explain.log_min_duration) shows execution only. When they disagree, the gap is your pool or your hydration. Never log full parameters in production (PII, tokens); never enable 'query' logging at scale (it doubles I/O and leaks data). The application_name connection setting (next section) makes your service identifiable in pg_stat_activity and the server log.

21.13 Connection and pool configuration in NestJS

// src/app.module.ts
TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    type: 'postgres',
    url: config.getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL'),
    applicationName: `orders-api-${config.get('POD_NAME', 'local')}`,   // shows in pg_stat_activity
    autoLoadEntities: true,
    synchronize: false,
    migrationsRun: false,
    logging: ['error', 'warn'],
    maxQueryExecutionTime: 500,
    logger: new StructuredTypeOrmLogger(),
    poolSize: 20,                               // upper bound of connections for this process
    extra: {                                    // passed straight to pg.Pool / pg.Client
      max: 20,
      min: 2,
      idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,                // close idle connections after 30 s
      connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,           // fail fast when the pool is exhausted; default 0 waits forever
      statement_timeout: 10_000,                // server-side cap per statement (ms)
      idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 5_000,
      query_timeout: 15_000,                    // client-side cap, catches a hung socket
    },
    retryAttempts: 5,                           // @nestjs/typeorm: initial connection retries at boot
    retryDelay: 3_000,
  }),
});

Pool sizing arithmetic. PostgreSQL's max_connections (often 100–500) is shared by every pod of every service plus admins and jobs. With 10 pods at max: 20 you already need 200. A pool larger than the number of CPU cores the database has for you rarely helps; 10–20 per pod is typical, and if the product exceeds max_connections you put PgBouncer (transaction pooling) in front and keep the application pools modest. connectionTimeoutMillis must be set: the pg default of 0 waits forever, which turns pool exhaustion into a silent hang instead of an error you can alert on.

Read replicas. TypeORM supports replication: { master: {...}, slaves: [{...}] }; find and query-builder selects go to a replica, writes and anything inside a transaction go to the master; dataSource.createQueryRunner('master') forces the primary for a read that must see the latest commit. Replica lag makes "read your own write" fail (Part 20, section 20.14); route post-write reads to the master.

Health. @nestjs/terminus provides TypeOrmHealthIndicator (pingCheck('database', { timeout: 1500 })) for readiness probes. A pod whose pool is exhausted will fail the ping and be pulled from the load balancer, which is the correct behaviour.

21.14 Performance tips

  • Select only what you need. select: { id: true, name: true } or .select(['p.id', 'p.name']). Wide rows with jsonb or text columns cost network and hydration; a list endpoint that loads product descriptions to show names is paying for bytes it discards.
  • loadRelationIds when you only need foreign keys, not the related rows.
  • Stream large results. createQueryBuilder().stream() returns a readable stream of raw rows (requires pg-query-stream); pair it with a CSV transform for exports instead of getRawMany() on a million rows. Memory stays flat; the connection stays busy for the duration, so use a dedicated pool or run it from a worker.
  • Bulk insert in chunks. insert() with an array of 500–1,000 rows per statement; PostgreSQL's protocol allows 65,535 parameters per statement, so 20 columns means at most ~3,000 rows. save(rows, { chunk: 500 }) for entity graphs, at the cost of one SELECT per chunk.
  • insert().orIgnore() / orUpdate() for idempotent loads; never save() in a loop for the same purpose.
  • Never save() in loops. Collect, then one insert() or one save(array).
  • getRawMany for reports. Hydration is for entities you will mutate.
  • Two-query strategy for wide parents (relationLoadStrategy: 'query') to avoid row multiplication.
  • Query result cache (cache: { type: 'redis', options: {...} } in the data source, then find({ cache: 30_000 }) or .cache('key', 30_000)) for read-heavy lookups that tolerate 30 seconds of staleness; it is a Redis GET per query, not free, and invalidation is by TTL only.
  • Indexes and plans decide everything else. Ten milliseconds saved in the ORM is nothing next to a sequential scan; read the plan (Part 19).

21.15 Sequelize models

Concept

A Sequelize model is a class that describes one table and doubles as the API for querying it. Where TypeORM separates the entity (data) from the repository (behaviour) — the Data Mapper pattern — Sequelize puts both on the same class: Product.findAll() is a static method, and product.save() is an instance method that writes the row it came from. That is the Active Record pattern, and every design difference between the two ORMs follows from it.

There are two ways to declare a model, and a NestJS codebase almost always uses the second:

  • Model.init(attributes, options) — the native Sequelize API. Explicit, no decorators, no reflect-metadata, works in plain JavaScript.
  • sequelize-typescript decorators (@Table, @Column, @HasMany) — a wrapper library that generates the same init call from decorator metadata. This is what @nestjs/sequelize is built on; SequelizeModule.forFeature([Product]) expects decorated classes.

Both produce the identical runtime object. Learn init so you can read the SQL that comes out, then write decorators because that is what the team will use.

Why does it exist?

Because a table has two descriptions that must not drift: the columns PostgreSQL actually has, and the shape your TypeScript code expects. The model is the second one. It tells Sequelize how to build INSERT statements, which attributes map to which columns, how to convert a numeric string into whatever your code wants, and which of the returned values changed since the row was loaded so an UPDATE can list only those columns.

Mental model

Imagine a form template in an office. The template lists every field, its allowed format, its default value, and which fields the clerk stamps automatically (date received, date updated). Model.init is filling in that template once, at office opening. Every later request reuses it. If the template disagrees with the actual filing cabinet, nobody notices until a filing fails.

How it works

flowchart TB
    D["Decorators or Model.init"] --> M["Model class with rawAttributes and options"]
    M --> Q["QueryGenerator: options object to SQL plus bind values"]
    Q --> DI["Postgres dialect and pg driver"]
    DI -->|"parse, bind, execute"| PG["PostgreSQL"]
    PG -->|"rows"| DI
    DI --> H["Instance build: dataValues plus _previousDataValues"]
    H --> S["Service code receives Model instances"]
    S -->|"instance.save"| Q
    Q -.->|"UPDATE lists only changed attributes"| DI
  1. At boot, sequelize.define() / Model.init() / the @Table decorator registers the model on the Sequelize instance under a name.
  2. Attribute definitions become Model.rawAttributes: type, field (the real column name), allowNull, defaultValue, get, set, validate.
  3. A finder call builds an options tree, the dialect's query generator turns it into SQL text with $1-style bind parameters, and pg runs it.
  4. Each returned row becomes an instance: values land in instance.dataValues, and a copy lands in instance._previousDataValues. instance.changed() is the difference between the two. This is how Sequelize knows that product.stock = 4; await product.save() should emit UPDATE products SET stock = $1, updated_at = $2 WHERE id = $3 and not rewrite all twelve columns.
  5. instance.toJSON() returns dataValues plus virtual getters — which is why a model instance serialises cleanly from a NestJS controller, and also why it leaks every column you selected.

Sequelize example

The Model.init form first, because it shows what the decorators generate.

// src/products/product.model.ts (native init style)
import { DataTypes, Model, InferAttributes, InferCreationAttributes, CreationOptional, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class Product extends Model<InferAttributes<Product>, InferCreationAttributes<Product>> {
  declare id: CreationOptional<string>;
  declare sku: string;
  declare name: string;
  declare price: string;          // numeric(12,2) arrives as a string; keep it one
  declare stock: number;
  declare attributes: Record<string, unknown>;
  declare status: 'ACTIVE' | 'ARCHIVED';
  declare version: CreationOptional<number>;
  declare createdAt: CreationOptional<Date>;
  declare updatedAt: CreationOptional<Date>;
  declare deletedAt: CreationOptional<Date | null>;
  declare readonly inStock: boolean;   // VIRTUAL, no column
}

export function initProduct(sequelize: Sequelize): void {
  Product.init(
    {
      id:     { type: DataTypes.UUID, defaultValue: DataTypes.UUIDV4, primaryKey: true },
      sku:    { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false, unique: true },
      name:   { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false },
      price:  { type: DataTypes.DECIMAL(12, 2), allowNull: false },
      stock:  { type: DataTypes.INTEGER, allowNull: false, defaultValue: 0 },
      attributes: { type: DataTypes.JSONB, allowNull: false, defaultValue: {} },
      status: { type: DataTypes.ENUM('ACTIVE', 'ARCHIVED'), allowNull: false, defaultValue: 'ACTIVE' },
      version: { type: DataTypes.INTEGER, allowNull: false, defaultValue: 0 },
      createdAt: DataTypes.DATE,
      updatedAt: DataTypes.DATE,
      deletedAt: DataTypes.DATE,
      inStock: {
        type: DataTypes.VIRTUAL(DataTypes.BOOLEAN, ['stock']),   // declare the columns it reads
        get(this: Product) { return this.getDataValue('stock') > 0; },
      },
    },
    {
      sequelize,
      tableName: 'products',
      underscored: true,   // camelCase attributes map to snake_case columns
      timestamps: true,    // manage created_at / updated_at
      paranoid: true,      // soft delete via deleted_at
      version: true,       // optimistic locking on the version column
    },
  );
}

And the sequelize-typescript form that @nestjs/sequelize consumes. Same table, same SQL.

// src/products/product.model.ts (decorator style)
import {
  Table, Column, Model, DataType, Default, AllowNull, Unique, PrimaryKey,
  CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, DeletedAt, HasMany, BelongsToMany,
} from 'sequelize-typescript';

@Table({ tableName: 'products', underscored: true, timestamps: true, paranoid: true, version: true })
export class Product extends Model<Product> {
  @PrimaryKey @Default(DataType.UUIDV4) @Column(DataType.UUID) id: string;

  @Unique @AllowNull(false) @Column(DataType.TEXT) sku: string;
  @AllowNull(false) @Column(DataType.TEXT) name: string;

  /** DECIMAL comes back as a string from pg. Do not "fix" it with parseFloat. */
  @AllowNull(false) @Column(DataType.DECIMAL(12, 2)) price: string;

  @Default(0) @AllowNull(false) @Column(DataType.INTEGER) stock: number;
  @Default({}) @AllowNull(false) @Column(DataType.JSONB) attributes: Record<string, unknown>;
  @Default('ACTIVE') @Column(DataType.ENUM('ACTIVE', 'ARCHIVED')) status: 'ACTIVE' | 'ARCHIVED';

  @Column({ type: DataType.VIRTUAL(DataType.BOOLEAN, ['stock']), get(this: Product) { return this.getDataValue('stock') > 0; } })
  inStock: boolean;

  @CreatedAt createdAt: Date;
  @UpdatedAt updatedAt: Date;
  @DeletedAt deletedAt: Date | null;

  @HasMany(() => OrderItem, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'orderItems' }) orderItems: OrderItem[];
  @BelongsToMany(() => Tag, { through: 'product_tags', foreignKey: 'productId', otherKey: 'tagId', as: 'tags' }) tags: Tag[];
}

PostgreSQL example

The mapping from DataTypes to real PostgreSQL types is where most schema surprises begin. Sequelize will happily create a column type you did not intend.

DataTypes PostgreSQL column What comes back to Node Notes
STRING character varying(255) string The default 255 is arbitrary; STRING(1000) or TEXT is usually what you want. In PostgreSQL text and varchar perform identically.
TEXT text string Prefer this.
CITEXT citext string Needs CREATE EXTENSION citext. Good for emails.
INTEGER integer number
BIGINT bigint string pg cannot represent 2^53+ safely. Money in cents hits this.
DECIMAL(12,2) numeric(12,2) string The single most common money bug. See section 21.25.
FLOAT / DOUBLE double precision number Never for money.
BOOLEAN boolean boolean
DATE timestamp with time zone Date Sequelize's DATE is a timestamp, not a calendar date.
DATEONLY date string '2026-09-09' No timezone. Correct for birthdays and invoice dates.
UUID uuid string Pair with defaultValue: DataTypes.UUIDV4 or a database gen_random_uuid().
JSON / JSONB json / jsonb parsed object Always JSONB unless you need to preserve key order.
ENUM('A','B') native enum type string Creates enum_products_status. Changing it later is painful; see 21.25.
ARRAY(DataTypes.TEXT) text[] string[] PostgreSQL only.
BLOB bytea Buffer Store files in object storage, not here.
RANGE(DataTypes.DATE) tstzrange [Date, Date] Pairs with exclusion constraints for booking systems.
VIRTUAL no column computed Cannot appear in WHERE or ORDER BY.

underscored: true is the option that makes the model match the DDL written in section 21.1. It converts every attribute name to snake_case for the field, converts the timestamp columns to created_at / updated_at / deleted_at, and — importantly — converts generated foreign keys too, so Order.belongsTo(Customer) produces customer_id rather than customerId. Set it once in define at the root module so no model can forget it:

SequelizeModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    dialect: 'postgres',
    uri: config.getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL'),
    autoLoadModels: true,
    synchronize: false,                                  // never true; see 14.20
    define: { underscored: true, timestamps: true },     // team-wide default
    pool: { max: 20, min: 2, acquire: 10_000, idle: 30_000 },
    logging: (sql, timingMs) => logger.debug({ sql, timingMs }),
    benchmark: true,
  }),
});

Soft delete with paranoid: true. paranoid requires timestamps: true. With it on, instance.destroy() runs UPDATE products SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id = $1, every finder adds AND deleted_at IS NULL, instance.restore() clears it, and destroy({ force: true }) does a real DELETE. To read deleted rows pass paranoid: false in the query options. The trap: a unique constraint does not know about soft deletes. Soft-delete the product with sku = 'ABC-1' and the next INSERT with that SKU fails with 23505 even though no visible row holds it. The fix is a partial unique index that only covers live rows:

-- Replace the plain UNIQUE with a partial index so soft-deleted SKUs can be reused
ALTER TABLE products DROP CONSTRAINT products_sku_key;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX products_sku_live_idx ON products (sku) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

Optimistic locking with version: true. This is the one place Sequelize does more than TypeORM. With version: true, an instance save() or update() emits the check and the increment in one statement:

UPDATE products SET stock = $1, version = $2, updated_at = $3
WHERE id = $4 AND version = $5;

If zero rows match, Sequelize throws OptimisticLockError instead of silently doing nothing. Compare with TypeORM's @VersionColumn, which increments but does not add the WHERE guard (Part 20, section 20.9) — there you must write the conditional UPDATE yourself. Two caveats: the check only applies to instance methods, so Product.update({...}, { where: {...} }) bypasses it entirely, and the column must be NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 in the database or the first update compares against NULL and matches nothing.

const product = await this.productModel.findByPk(id);            // version = 7 loaded
product.stock -= dto.qty;
try {
  await product.save();                                          // ... AND version = 7
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof OptimisticLockError) throw new ConflictException('Product changed, retry');
  throw err;
}

Getters and setters. A column definition may carry get() and set(). Inside them you must use getDataValue / setDataValue; calling this.get('price') from the getter for price recurses until the stack overflows.

@Column({
  type: DataType.BIGINT,                                  // returned as a string by pg
  get(this: Order) {
    const raw = this.getDataValue('totalCents');
    return raw === null ? null : Number(raw);             // safe below 2^53 cents (about 90 trillion)
  },
})
totalCents: number;

@Column({
  type: DataType.CITEXT,
  set(this: Customer, value: string) { this.setDataValue('email', value.trim().toLowerCase()); },
})
email: string;

Setters run on assignment and on Model.create(), but not on Model.update(), bulkCreate with ignoreDuplicates, or raw SQL. Same lesson as TypeORM's @BeforeUpdate (section 21.11): normalisation that must always happen belongs in a validation pipe or a database constraint, not in the model.

defaultScope and why it bites. A defaultScope is a set of query options merged into every finder on that model.

@DefaultScope(() => ({ where: { status: 'ACTIVE' }, attributes: { exclude: ['attributes'] } }))
@Table({ tableName: 'products', underscored: true })
export class Product extends Model<Product> { /* ... */ }

Now Product.findByPk(id) returns null for an archived product, and an admin screen that must show archived products silently shows nothing. Worse, findOrCreate and association mixins inherit it, and an included model brings its own default scope into the join (include: [Product] becomes LEFT JOIN products ON ... AND products.status = 'ACTIVE'), which quietly drops order items whose product was archived. Product.unscoped().findByPk(id) removes it, but only for that call and only for the top-level model — you must call unscoped() on each included model too.

Use defaultScope for things that are never wrong to filter (excluding a password_hash from attributes). Do not use it for business status, and never use it as a security boundary. The failure mode is silence: the query succeeds and returns the wrong rows.

Production scenario

A catalog service with 180,000 products serves GET /products?q=... at 400 requests per second. Two model-level decisions dominate its behaviour. First, price is DECIMAL(12,2) and the service does price * 100 somewhere in a promotions helper; because price is a string, that expression produced NaN for one code path and the endpoint returned "total": null for 0.3% of requests for six weeks before a customer complained. Second, the model had defaultScope: { where: { status: 'ACTIVE' } }, and the reindex job — which reads through the same model — never indexed archived products, so archived products stayed searchable forever because nothing ever deleted them from the search index. Both bugs are model configuration, not query code.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • timestamps: true with a table that has no created_at / updated_at produces column "created_at" does not exist on the first insert. Match the model to the DDL, not the other way round.
  • underscored: true on some models and not others gives you a schema with both customer_id and customerId columns.
  • paranoid: true plus a UNIQUE constraint blocks re-creation of soft-deleted rows; use a partial unique index.
  • paranoid does not cascade: soft-deleting an order leaves its items visible, and ON DELETE CASCADE never fires because no row is deleted.
  • DataTypes.DATE is a timestamp; DataTypes.DATEONLY is the calendar date. Choosing DATE for a birthday introduces timezone shifts at midnight.
  • Virtual fields cannot be used in where, order or group; the SQL has no such column. Sorting by a virtual means sorting in JavaScript after loading everything.
  • A VIRTUAL without its dependency array returns undefined whenever the query used attributes to select a subset.
  • version: true on a column that is nullable makes every update a no-op that throws OptimisticLockError.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the DDL first and make the model describe it, because PostgreSQL enforces and the model only asks. They set underscored and timestamps globally in define so the team cannot drift. They treat DECIMAL and BIGINT as strings all the way to the JSON boundary and convert exactly once, deliberately. They allow defaultScope only for column exclusion, never for row filtering, and they can name the two lines of SQL each model option adds.

Common mistakes

  • parseFloat(product.price) for money.
  • defaultScope for tenant or status filtering, which fails open the moment someone calls unscoped() or joins the model.
  • Relying on setters for normalisation and then using Model.update() everywhere.
  • Leaving DataTypes.STRING (varchar(255)) on a field that will hold longer text.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between Active Record and Data Mapper, and which one is Sequelize? Expected: Active Record puts persistence on the model class; Sequelize is Active Record, TypeORM is (mostly) Data Mapper. Why it matters: it explains why Sequelize models are hard to unit test without a database.
  2. Why does product.price come back as a string, and what should you do about it? Expected: numeric exceeds JavaScript's safe double range; keep it a string or use a decimal library; convert at the boundary.
  3. What exactly does paranoid: true change, and what does it break? Expected: destroy becomes an UPDATE, finders add deleted_at IS NULL; breaks unique constraints and database cascades.
  4. How does Sequelize's version: true differ from TypeORM's @VersionColumn? Expected: Sequelize adds the WHERE version = n guard and throws OptimisticLockError; TypeORM only increments.
  5. Give a concrete way defaultScope can cause a production incident. Expected: silent row filtering on includes and background jobs.

Practical exercise

Take the products DDL from section 21.1 and write both the Model.init and the decorator version of the model against it, with underscored, paranoid and version: true. Then write tests that prove: money round-trips without precision loss, soft delete hides the row from findAll but paranoid: false finds it, re-creating a soft-deleted SKU succeeds once you add the partial unique index, and a concurrent save() on a stale instance throws OptimisticLockError. Acceptance criteria: four passing tests against a real PostgreSQL container, and a query log showing the AND version = $n clause.

21.16 Sequelize associations

Concept

An association tells Sequelize how two models relate so that it can generate joins, generate foreign keys, and attach helper methods to instances. There are four: hasOne, belongsTo, hasMany and belongsToMany. The only structural question is which table holds the foreign key, and the answer decides which side gets which method.

  • belongsTo — this model holds the foreign key. Order.belongsTo(Customer) puts customer_id on orders.
  • hasOne / hasMany — the other model holds the foreign key. Customer.hasMany(Order) also means customer_id lives on orders.
  • belongsToMany — a third table holds both keys. Product.belongsToMany(Tag, { through: 'product_tags' }).

A one-to-many is therefore declared twice, once from each side, and both declarations must agree on the foreign key.

Why does it exist?

Because the join condition, the column names, and the shape of the result are the same every time, and writing them by hand in every query is how mistakes get made. Once an association exists you can say include: ['items'] instead of spelling out LEFT JOIN order_items ON order_items.order_id = orders.id and mapping the flat rows back into a tree.

Mental model

Imagine index cards in a filing box. belongsTo is a card that has another card's number written on it. hasMany is the reverse view: given a customer card, find every order card whose customer number matches. belongsToMany is a separate box of pairings, each slip naming one product and one tag. The physical arrangement never changes; the association is just which direction you are allowed to walk.

Sequelize example

The full association set for our schema, decorator style.

// src/orders/order.model.ts
@Table({ tableName: 'orders', underscored: true, timestamps: true })
export class Order extends Model<Order> {
  @PrimaryKey @Default(DataType.UUIDV4) @Column(DataType.UUID) id: string;

  @ForeignKey(() => Customer) @AllowNull(false) @Column(DataType.UUID) customerId: string;
  @BelongsTo(() => Customer, { foreignKey: 'customerId', as: 'customer' }) customer: Customer;

  @Default('CREATED') @Column(DataType.ENUM('CREATED', 'PAID', 'SHIPPED', 'CANCELLED')) status: string;
  @Default(0) @Column(DataType.BIGINT) totalCents: string;

  @HasMany(() => OrderItem, { foreignKey: 'orderId', as: 'items' }) items: OrderItem[];
}

// src/orders/order-item.model.ts
@Table({ tableName: 'order_items', underscored: true, timestamps: false })
export class OrderItem extends Model<OrderItem> {
  @PrimaryKey @Default(DataType.UUIDV4) @Column(DataType.UUID) id: string;
  @ForeignKey(() => Order) @Column(DataType.UUID) orderId: string;
  @BelongsTo(() => Order, { foreignKey: 'orderId', as: 'order' }) order: Order;
  @ForeignKey(() => Product) @Column(DataType.UUID) productId: string;
  @BelongsTo(() => Product, { foreignKey: 'productId', as: 'product' }) product: Product;
  @Column(DataType.INTEGER) qty: number;
  @Column(DataType.BIGINT) unitPriceCents: string;
}

// src/customers/customer.model.ts
@Table({ tableName: 'customers', underscored: true })
export class Customer extends Model<Customer> {
  @PrimaryKey @Default(DataType.UUIDV4) @Column(DataType.UUID) id: string;
  @Unique @Column(DataType.CITEXT) email: string;
  @HasOne(() => Address, { foreignKey: 'customerId', as: 'address' }) address: Address;
  @HasMany(() => Order, { foreignKey: 'customerId', as: 'orders' }) orders: Order[];
}

Many-to-many needs the through table, and if that table has no created_at you must say so:

@BelongsToMany(() => Tag, {
  through: { model: 'product_tags', timestamps: false },   // the join table has only the two keys
  foreignKey: 'productId',
  otherKey: 'tagId',
  as: 'tags',
})
tags: Tag[];

Aliasing with as, and why it matters more than it looks. The alias is not cosmetic. It becomes:

  • the property name on the result (order.items, not order.orderItems),
  • the name of every generated mixin (order.getItems(), order.addItem(), order.setItems(), order.countItems(), order.createItem()),
  • the key you must use in include, and
  • the table alias in the generated SQL (LEFT JOIN "order_items" AS "items").

If the two sides declare different aliases, or an include names an alias that was not declared, Sequelize throws OrderItem is not associated to Order! at runtime — never at compile time. Two associations between the same pair of models (an order's shippingAddress and billingAddress, both pointing at addresses) are only distinguishable by alias, and forgetting as on one of them makes the second silently overwrite the first in the association registry.

@BelongsTo(() => Address, { foreignKey: 'shippingAddressId', as: 'shippingAddress' }) shippingAddress: Address;
@BelongsTo(() => Address, { foreignKey: 'billingAddressId',  as: 'billingAddress'  }) billingAddress: Address;
// include: [{ association: 'shippingAddress' }, { association: 'billingAddress' }]

How it works

include is Sequelize's relation loader. By default it generates a single query with LEFT OUTER JOINs, selects the joined columns under prefixed aliases, and re-nests them in JavaScript.

const orders = await this.orderModel.findAll({
  where: { customerId },
  include: [{ association: 'items', include: [{ association: 'product', attributes: ['id', 'name'] }] }],
  order: [['createdAt', 'DESC']],
});
SELECT "Order"."id", "Order"."status", "Order"."total_cents" AS "totalCents",
       "items"."id" AS "items.id", "items"."qty" AS "items.qty",
       "items->product"."id" AS "items.product.id", "items->product"."name" AS "items.product.name"
FROM "orders" AS "Order"
LEFT OUTER JOIN "order_items" AS "items" ON "Order"."id" = "items"."order_id"
LEFT OUTER JOIN "products" AS "items->product" ON "items"."product_id" = "items->product"."id"
WHERE "Order"."customer_id" = $1
ORDER BY "Order"."created_at" DESC;

Note the -> separator for nested includes and the dotted output aliases: that is Sequelize's protocol for reconstructing the tree. It de-duplicates parents by primary key, so 20 orders with 5 items each come back as 20 objects — but 100 rows crossed the wire and 100 rows were parsed.

required: true turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

include: [{ association: 'items', required: true }]   // INNER JOIN: orders with no items disappear

The subtle version of this rule: putting a where inside an include sets required: true implicitly. This one line changes the meaning of the endpoint:

// "orders with their cancelled items" -- but actually "only orders that HAVE a cancelled item"
include: [{ association: 'items', where: { status: 'CANCELLED' } }]

// what you probably meant
include: [{ association: 'items', where: { status: 'CANCELLED' }, required: false }]

An order-list endpoint that adds a product-name filter this way starts returning 40 orders instead of 200 and nobody can explain where the rest went. Always write required explicitly when an include carries a where.

The row explosion, and separate: true

A join multiplies rows. Two hasMany includes at the same level multiply against each other, which is the difference between a fast endpoint and an outage.

flowchart TB
    O["20 orders"] --> J1["LEFT JOIN order_items: 10 per order"]
    J1 --> R1["200 rows"]
    R1 --> J2["LEFT JOIN shipments: 20 per order"]
    J2 --> R2["4000 rows returned and parsed"]
    R2 --> N["Sequelize de-duplicates back to 20 orders"]
    N --> W["Wasted: 3980 rows of network, parse and GC"]
    O --> S1["separate true on both"]
    S1 --> Q3["3 queries: 20 orders, 200 items, 400 shipments"]
    Q3 --> N2["620 rows total"]

separate: true is Sequelize's answer, available on hasMany includes only. Instead of joining, it runs the include as its own query:

const orders = await this.orderModel.findAll({
  where: { customerId },
  include: [
    { association: 'items', separate: true },
    { association: 'shipments', separate: true },
  ],
  limit: 20,
});
SELECT ... FROM "orders" AS "Order" WHERE "customer_id" = $1 LIMIT 20
SELECT ... FROM "order_items" AS "OrderItem" WHERE "OrderItem"."order_id" IN ($1,$2,...,$20)
SELECT ... FROM "shipments" AS "Shipment" WHERE "Shipment"."order_id" IN ($1,$2,...,$20)

Three round trips instead of one, but 620 rows instead of 4,000, and no cartesian blow-up as you add includes. It also unlocks limit and order inside the include, which a join cannot express:

{ association: 'items', separate: true, limit: 3, order: [['unitPriceCents', 'DESC']] }

The cost you must know. With separate: true and no limit, Sequelize issues one extra query for the whole parent set, batched with IN. With separate: true and a limit inside the include, it cannot express "top 3 per parent" in one statement, so it issues one query per parent — 20 parents means 20 queries. That is an N+1 you asked for. It is still often the right trade (20 fast indexed queries beat 4,000 rows), but you must see it in the log and decide, not discover it at 400 requests per second. The alternative for "top N per parent" is a raw SQL lateral join or a window function (Part 17, section 17.4).

The limit + include trap and subQuery: false

When you combine limit with a hasMany include, Sequelize does something clever: it wraps the parent table in a subquery so the limit counts parents, not joined rows.

SELECT "Order".*, "items"."id" AS "items.id", ...
FROM (
  SELECT "Order"."id", "Order"."status" FROM "orders" AS "Order"
  WHERE "Order"."customer_id" = $1 ORDER BY "Order"."created_at" DESC LIMIT 20
) AS "Order"
LEFT OUTER JOIN "order_items" AS "items" ON "Order"."id" = "items"."order_id"
ORDER BY "Order"."created_at" DESC;

That is correct: 20 orders with all their items. But the inner subquery only selects columns from orders, so the moment you filter or sort by a joined column you get column "product.name" does not exist. The internet's answer is subQuery: false, and it does remove the error — by removing the subquery:

SELECT ... FROM "orders" AS "Order"
LEFT OUTER JOIN "order_items" AS "items" ON ...
LEFT OUTER JOIN "products" AS "items->product" ON ...
WHERE "Order"."customer_id" = $1 AND "items->product"."name" ILIKE $2
ORDER BY "Order"."created_at" DESC
LIMIT 20;                                  -- 20 JOINED ROWS, not 20 orders

Now LIMIT 20 counts joined rows. Twenty rows might be four orders. The API returns "page 1 of 12" with 4 items on it, the next page overlaps, and pagination is broken in a way that only shows up for orders with many items. This is exactly the TypeORM take + join bug from section 21.5.3, with a different spelling.

The safe patterns, in order of preference:

  1. Paginate the parents alone, then load children separately. findAll({ where, limit, offset }) for orders, then separate: true or a second batched query for items. Predictable counts, predictable SQL.
  2. Filter on a joined column with a WHERE ... IN (subquery) so the join is not needed for the limit: where: { id: { [Op.in]: literal('(SELECT order_id FROM order_items WHERE ...)') } } — parameterise carefully.
  3. subQuery: false only with belongsTo/hasOne includes, where the join cannot multiply rows and LIMIT on joined rows equals LIMIT on parents.
  4. Raw SQL when the query genuinely needs "20 parents ordered by a child aggregate".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • include with attributes: [] on a belongsToMany still selects the through-table row; use through: { attributes: [] } to drop it.
  • A belongsToMany include returns the join row under the through model's name (product.product_tags or your alias); serialising it leaks join metadata into the API response.
  • include plus group produces SQL where the joined columns are not in the GROUP BY; PostgreSQL rejects it with column must appear in the GROUP BY clause.
  • Association mixins (order.getItems()) are lazy and per instance: calling them in a loop is N+1 (section 21.21).
  • hasMany with onDelete: 'CASCADE' in the association options only affects the FK that sync() would create; if the schema came from migrations, the association option is decorative. Check information_schema.referential_constraints for the truth.
  • Self-referencing associations (Category.hasMany(Category, { as: 'children', foreignKey: 'parentId' })) work for one level; recursive trees need a recursive CTE.
  • Two separate: true includes plus a nested separate inside one of them multiply query counts; log and count.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They decide loading strategy per endpoint from the shape of the data: one-to-one and small collections join, large or multiple collections go separate: true, and anything with limit plus a child filter gets written as explicit SQL. They always pass required explicitly. They read the generated SQL for every new include before merging, because include is the single line most likely to turn a 5 ms endpoint into a 5 second one.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a where to an include and not realising it became an INNER JOIN.
  • Reaching for subQuery: false to silence an error, and breaking pagination.
  • Nesting three hasMany includes in one query and blaming PostgreSQL for the latency.
  • Omitting as and then fighting X is not associated to Y!.
  • Trusting association-level onDelete on a migration-managed schema.

Interview questions

  1. Which side of a one-to-many holds the foreign key, and how do hasMany and belongsTo reflect that? Expected: the "many" side; belongsTo is declared on the FK holder.
  2. What SQL does required: true change, and when does Sequelize set it for you? Expected: LEFT to INNER; implicitly whenever the include has a where.
  3. Explain separate: true: what it saves and what it costs. Expected: avoids row multiplication; one extra batched query, or one query per parent when the include has a limit.
  4. Why does limit with a hasMany include produce a subquery, and what breaks when you disable it? Expected: the limit must count parents; subQuery: false makes it count joined rows, breaking pagination.
  5. You must return the 20 newest orders, each with its 3 most expensive items. How? Expected: paginate parents, then separate: true with limit and order (accepting N queries), or one raw SQL statement with ROW_NUMBER() or LATERAL.

Practical exercise

Seed 200 orders, each with 8 items and 3 shipments. Write the endpoint three ways: one query with two joined includes, one query with two separate: true includes, and parent pagination plus manual batched loads. Log rows returned, statements issued and wall time for each. Then add a filter on the product name and observe what subQuery: false does to the returned order count. Acceptance criteria: a table of the three measurements, and a written rule for when your team uses each.

21.17 Sequelize query methods

Concept

Sequelize's query surface is a set of static methods on the model — findAll, findOne, findByPk, findAndCountAll, findOrCreate, create, update, destroy, upsert, bulkCreate, increment, decrement, count, min/max/sum — plus sequelize.query() for raw SQL. Every one of them takes the same options object shape (where, attributes, include, order, group, having, limit, offset, transaction, raw, lock), so learning the options once covers the whole API.

Why does it exist?

Because 80% of the statements a service issues are "select these columns from this table where these conditions hold". Expressing that as a JavaScript object instead of a string means it composes (you can add a condition in an if), it parameterises automatically (no injection), and it maps back to instances. The remaining 20% — reports, upserts, window functions — is what sequelize.query() and literal() are for.

How it works

Every option becomes a clause. where: { status: 'PAID', totalCents: { [Op.gte]: 5000 } } becomes WHERE "status" = $1 AND "total_cents" >= $2. Values always travel as bind parameters; only literal() puts text straight into the SQL, which is why literal() is the one function in this section you must treat as dangerous.

Sequelize example

The finders, with the SQL each produces.

// One row by primary key. SELECT ... FROM "orders" WHERE "id" = $1 LIMIT 1;
const order = await this.orderModel.findByPk(id, { include: [{ association: 'items' }] });

// One row by conditions. Adds LIMIT 1. Returns null (not an exception) when nothing matches.
const latest = await this.orderModel.findOne({ where: { customerId }, order: [['createdAt', 'DESC']] });

// Many rows, only the columns the response needs.
const rows = await this.orderModel.findAll({
  where: { customerId, status: { [Op.in]: ['PAID', 'SHIPPED'] }, createdAt: { [Op.gte]: since } },
  attributes: ['id', 'status', 'totalCents', 'createdAt'],
  order: [['createdAt', 'DESC']],
  limit: 50,
  offset: 0,
});

// Throws NotFoundError instead of returning null; useful in services that always need the row.
const must = await this.orderModel.findByPk(id, { rejectOnEmpty: new NotFoundException('Order not found') });

findAndCountAll and the distinct: true count bug. findAndCountAll runs two statements: your SELECT with LIMIT/OFFSET, and a COUNT. With a hasMany include, the count query joins too, so it counts joined rows:

// WRONG: count is 200 when there are 20 orders with 10 items each
const page = await this.orderModel.findAndCountAll({
  where: { customerId },
  include: [{ association: 'items' }],
  limit: 20,
});
// SELECT count("Order"."id") FROM "orders" LEFT JOIN "order_items" ...   -> 200

// RIGHT
const page2 = await this.orderModel.findAndCountAll({
  where: { customerId },
  include: [{ association: 'items' }],
  distinct: true,     // SELECT count(DISTINCT "Order"."id") ...          -> 20
  limit: 20,
});

The symptom in production is a paginator that says "10 pages" and shows an empty page 3. distinct: true is free to add and correct in every case where a hasMany include exists, so many teams make it a lint rule. Two related notes: with group, findAndCountAll returns count as an array of group counts, not a number; and COUNT(DISTINCT id) over a large join is expensive — for big tables, run the count as its own query without includes, or use an approximate count (Part 17, section 17.2).

findOrCreate and what really happens under concurrency. The method looks atomic. It is not.

const [customer, created] = await this.customerModel.findOrCreate({
  where: { email: dto.email },
  defaults: { email: dto.email, name: dto.name },
});
-- Sequelize opens its own transaction when you do not pass one
BEGIN;
SELECT "id","email" FROM "customers" WHERE "email" = $1 LIMIT 1;   -- not found
INSERT INTO "customers" ("id","email","name") VALUES ($1,$2,$3) RETURNING *;
COMMIT;

Two requests for the same new email arriving 3 ms apart both run the SELECT, both find nothing, and both INSERT. One wins. The other gets 23505 duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customers_email_key". Sequelize catches that specific error and re-runs the SELECT to return the row the winner created, so the caller usually sees success — that recovery is the only reason findOrCreate works at all, and it only works if a unique constraint exists. Without one you get two rows and no error.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as RequestA
    participant B as RequestB
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    A->>PG: BEGIN then SELECT WHERE email = x
    PG-->>A: 0 rows
    B->>PG: BEGIN then SELECT WHERE email = x
    PG-->>B: 0 rows
    A->>PG: INSERT customer x
    PG-->>A: 1 row, COMMIT ok
    B->>PG: INSERT customer x
    PG-->>B: ERROR 23505 unique violation
    Note over B,PG: transaction is now aborted, state 25P02
    B->>PG: ROLLBACK then SELECT WHERE email = x
    PG-->>B: 1 row, the one A created
    Note over A,B: Both callers succeed only because the unique index exists

Now the part that causes incidents: if you pass your own transaction, the failed INSERT aborts your transaction. PostgreSQL marks the whole transaction as failed, and every subsequent statement returns 25P02 current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block — including Sequelize's recovery SELECT. So findOrCreate inside a larger transaction turns a benign race into a hard 500 for the whole request. The workarounds are a savepoint around it, or — better — not using findOrCreate at all:

// Preferred: one atomic statement, no race, no aborted transaction
const [rows] = await this.sequelize.query(
  `INSERT INTO customers (id, email, name) VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), $1, $2)
   ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email
   RETURNING id, email, name, (xmax = 0) AS inserted`,
  { bind: [dto.email, dto.name], type: QueryTypes.SELECT, transaction: t },
);
// DO UPDATE (not DO NOTHING) so RETURNING always yields a row; xmax = 0 tells you if it was an insert

upsert. On PostgreSQL, Model.upsert(values) generates INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (<primary key or unique index>) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING *. Use conflictFields to target a specific unique index when the model has more than one:

await this.productModel.upsert(
  { sku: 'ABC-1', name: 'Widget', price: '19.99', stock: 40 },
  { conflictFields: ['sku'], returning: true },
);

It returns [instance, created], but the created boolean is not reliable across dialects and versions — if the answer matters, use the raw RETURNING (xmax = 0) form above. upsert also updates only the fields you pass, and it does not run instance beforeUpdate hooks (it has its own beforeUpsert/afterUpsert).

bulkCreate with updateOnDuplicate. The bulk loader.

await this.productModel.bulkCreate(rows, {
  updateOnDuplicate: ['name', 'price', 'stock', 'updatedAt'],   // ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET ...
  conflictAttributes: ['sku'],                                  // conflict target other than the PK
  returning: ['id'],
  validate: true,
});

One statement inserts all rows. Two constraints govern how many rows you may pass: PostgreSQL's wire protocol allows 65,535 bind parameters per statement, so 12 columns caps you at about 5,400 rows; and one giant statement holds locks longer. Chunk at 500–1,000 and wrap the chunks in a transaction if the load must be all-or-nothing. Also note ignoreDuplicates: true produces ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and cannot be combined with updateOnDuplicate, and that per-row hooks do not run unless you pass individualHooks: true (which defeats the purpose — see 21.18).

increment and decrement are the atomic ones. This is the pattern that makes stock decrements safe without a lock:

// UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1, updated_at = $2 WHERE id = $3 AND stock >= $1
const [, affected] = await this.productModel.decrement(
  { stock: dto.qty },
  { where: { id: dto.productId, stock: { [Op.gte]: dto.qty } }, transaction: t },
);
if (affected === 0) throw new ConflictException('Insufficient stock');

The arithmetic happens in PostgreSQL under the row lock the UPDATE takes, so two concurrent decrements cannot both read stock = 5 and both write 4. Contrast with the read-modify-write shape (product.stock -= qty; await product.save()), which is a lost update unless version: true is on. Always pair decrement with the guard in the WHERE and check the affected count; the guard is what turns "went negative" into "returned 409".

Operators. Op is imported from sequelize and covers the SQL you need without strings.

import { Op, fn, col, literal, where as sqlWhere } from 'sequelize';

where: {
  status: { [Op.ne]: 'CANCELLED' },
  totalCents: { [Op.between]: [1_000, 50_000] },
  createdAt: { [Op.gte]: since },
  [Op.or]: [{ customerId }, { '$customer.email$': { [Op.iLike]: `%${term}%` } }],  // $nested$ reaches an include
  attributes: { [Op.contains]: { colour: 'red' } },                                 // jsonb @>
  tags: { [Op.overlap]: ['sale', 'new'] },                                          // array &&
}

Op.like is case-sensitive, Op.iLike is PostgreSQL's ILIKE (and cannot use a plain B-tree index unless you index lower(col) or use pg_trgm — Part 19). $association.column$ is how you filter on an included table without writing SQL; it forces the include into the WHERE, which interacts with the subQuery behaviour from section 21.16.

Aggregates, group and having, and the fn/col/literal trio.

const revenue = await this.orderModel.findAll({
  attributes: [
    [fn('date_trunc', 'day', col('created_at')), 'day'],
    [fn('count', col('id')), 'orders'],
    [fn('sum', col('total_cents')), 'revenueCents'],
  ],
  where: { status: 'PAID', createdAt: { [Op.gte]: since } },
  group: [literal('1')],                       // group by the first select expression
  having: literal('count(id) > 10'),
  order: [[literal('1'), 'ASC']],
  raw: true,
});
  • col('created_at') renders a column reference, quoted and unescaped as a value.
  • fn('sum', col('total_cents')) renders sum("total_cents").
  • literal('...') renders the string verbatim into the SQL. It is the only injection hole in the Sequelize API. Never build a literal from request input; if you must (a dynamic sort column), validate it against an allow-list first.
const SORTABLE = new Set(['created_at', 'total_cents', 'status']);
const sort = SORTABLE.has(dto.sort) ? dto.sort : 'created_at';     // allow-list, then literal is safe
order: [[literal(`"${sort}" ${dto.dir === 'asc' ? 'ASC' : 'DESC'} NULLS LAST`)]];

raw: true and what you give up. With raw: true Sequelize skips instance construction and hands you plain objects. You lose: getters and setters, VIRTUAL fields, toJSON(), save(), association nesting (nested include columns arrive as flat 'items.id' keys unless you add nest: true), and hooks. You gain roughly 30–50% less CPU and memory on large result sets, which matters for reports and exports. The rule: raw: true for anything you will serialise or aggregate and never mutate; instances for anything you will save().

sequelize.query: replacements versus bind. Both are safe against injection. They are not the same mechanism.

// replacements: Sequelize escapes the values and splices them into the SQL TEXT before sending
const [a] = await this.sequelize.query(
  `SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE status = :status AND id IN (:ids)`,
  { replacements: { status: 'ACTIVE', ids: productIds }, type: QueryTypes.SELECT },
);

// bind: values travel as real PostgreSQL parameters ($1, $2); the server never sees them as text
const b = await this.sequelize.query(
  `SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE status = $1 AND id = ANY($2::uuid[])`,
  { bind: ['ACTIVE', productIds], type: QueryTypes.SELECT },
);

Prefer bind: parameters are sent out of band, the statement text is identical for every call (so PostgreSQL can reuse the plan and pg_stat_statements groups them into one entry), and there is no escaping code path to get wrong. Use replacements only for the thing bind cannot do — expanding an array into a comma-separated IN list — and note that = ANY($1::uuid[]) covers that case anyway, without a parameter-count limit. Never mix the two in one query. And always set type: QueryTypes.SELECT (or UPDATE, INSERT), otherwise the return shape differs by dialect and you will destructure the wrong thing.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • findAndCountAll without distinct: true over a hasMany include reports joined-row counts.
  • findOrCreate inside a caller-supplied transaction can leave the transaction aborted (25P02).
  • Model.update() returns [affectedCount] on PostgreSQL, and [affectedCount, affectedRows] only when you pass returning: true; code that reads result[1] without it gets undefined.
  • limit with offset on a large table is O(offset); use keyset pagination past a few thousand rows (Part 14, section 14.2).
  • attributes that omit the primary key break include nesting, because Sequelize de-duplicates parents by PK.
  • where on a DECIMAL column with a JavaScript number can lose precision before it reaches the database; pass strings.
