  • Huge Op.in arrays become huge parameter lists and can exceed the 65,535 bind-parameter limit; use = ANY($1::uuid[]) via raw SQL.
  • literal() built from user input is SQL injection, full stop.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know which method issues how many statements and can predict the SQL before running it. They use atomic statements (increment, ON CONFLICT) instead of read-then-write whenever the logic fits. They reach for sequelize.query with bind the moment the options object starts to need literal, because at that point they are writing SQL anyway and would rather write it legibly.

Common mistakes

  • findOrCreate treated as atomic, with no unique constraint behind it.
  • Pagination counts wrong because distinct was omitted.
  • product.stock -= n; save() under concurrency.
  • literal() with interpolated request parameters.
  • raw: true on rows the code then tries to save().

Interview questions

  1. What two statements does findAndCountAll run, and when is the count wrong? Expected: the paged select plus a count; wrong with hasMany includes unless distinct: true.
  2. Walk through findOrCreate under two concurrent requests. Expected: both select, both insert, one gets 23505, Sequelize re-selects; only safe with a unique index; dangerous inside a caller transaction.
  3. replacements versus bind — which and why? Expected: bind uses real server-side parameters, better plan reuse and grouping; replacements splices escaped text.
  4. Why is decrement safer than loading and saving? Expected: arithmetic in the database under the row lock; no lost update.
  5. What do you lose with raw: true? Expected: instances, virtuals, getters, nesting, hooks.

Practical exercise

Write a GET /orders endpoint with filtering, sorting and pagination that returns the correct total count with items included, and a POST /orders/:id/items that decrements stock atomically and returns 409 when insufficient. Prove both with tests: a pagination test asserting the count equals the number of distinct orders, and a concurrency test firing 50 parallel decrements at a product with stock 10 and asserting exactly 10 succeed. Acceptance criteria: both tests pass against real PostgreSQL, and stock is never negative.

21.18 Sequelize hooks

Concept

Hooks are functions Sequelize calls around a persistence operation. They come in three families: instance hooks (beforeValidate, afterValidate, beforeCreate, afterCreate, beforeUpdate, afterUpdate, beforeSave, afterSave, beforeDestroy, afterDestroy, beforeUpsert, afterUpsert), bulk hooks (beforeBulkCreate, afterBulkCreate, beforeBulkUpdate, afterBulkUpdate, beforeBulkDestroy, afterBulkDestroy), and connection hooks (beforeConnect, afterConnect). They can be declared per model or globally on the Sequelize instance.

Why does it exist?

To attach behaviour that must follow the data rather than the call site: normalise an email, compute a search vector, stamp updatedBy, write an audit row, publish an event. Same intent as TypeORM's subscribers (section 21.11), and the same warnings apply, plus one Sequelize-specific improvement: afterCommit.

How it works

// Model-scoped hooks, decorator style
@Table({ tableName: 'customers', underscored: true })
export class Customer extends Model<Customer> {
  @BeforeCreate
  @BeforeUpdate
  static normaliseEmail(instance: Customer): void {
    instance.email = instance.email.trim().toLowerCase();
  }

  @AfterCreate
  static async schedule(instance: Customer, options: CreateOptions): Promise<void> {
    // options.transaction is the transaction the insert ran in, if any
    await AuditLog.create(
      { entity: 'customer', entityId: instance.id, action: 'CREATE' },
      { transaction: options.transaction },     // MUST pass it, or the audit row commits separately
    );
  }
}

Two rules decide whether a hook fires at all:

  1. Instance hooks fire only for instance operations. Model.create(), instance.save(), instance.update(), instance.destroy(). They do not fire for Model.update(), Model.destroy(), Model.bulkCreate() (except beforeBulkCreate), increment/decrement, or sequelize.query().
  2. Bulk hooks fire for the bulk operations, but they receive the options object, not the rows. beforeBulkUpdate(options) sees options.attributes (the values being set) and options.where — it has no idea which rows will match.
@BeforeBulkUpdate
static stampUpdater(options: UpdateOptions & { attributes?: Record<string, unknown> }): void {
  // Works because it mutates the SET clause, not the rows
  if (options.attributes) options.attributes.updatedBy = getCurrentUserId();
}

individualHooks: true bridges the gap: on a bulk update or destroy, Sequelize first SELECTs every matching row, builds instances, and runs the instance hooks per row. It is correct and it is expensive:

// One UPDATE becomes: 1 SELECT of all matching rows + N beforeUpdate + N afterUpdate
await this.orderModel.update({ status: 'CANCELLED' }, { where: { customerId }, individualHooks: true });

For 50,000 matching rows that is 50,000 hook invocations and 50,000 instances in memory in one request. Use it for tens of rows, never for a backfill.

Model hooks versus global hooks. Global hooks run for every model:

sequelize.addHook('beforeFind', (options) => { options.benchmark = true; });
// or in the root module: define: { hooks: { beforeCreate(instance) { /* ... */ } } }

Global hooks are useful for cross-cutting concerns (attaching a tenant filter, timing) and terrible for business logic, because nothing at the call site hints that they exist. Execution order is: global hooks defined on the Sequelize instance run before model hooks of the same name.

afterCommit, and why it is the right place to publish events. A hook running inside a transaction sees data that may never exist. Publishing "OrderPaid" from afterUpdate means the message goes out before COMMIT — and if the transaction rolls back, consumers act on an order that was never paid. transaction.afterCommit() runs only after the commit succeeds.

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as OrdersService
    participant T as Transaction
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    participant K as Kafka
    S->>T: BEGIN
    S->>PG: UPDATE orders SET status = PAID
    PG-->>S: afterUpdate hook fires HERE, still uncommitted
    S->>T: t.afterCommit callback registered
    S->>T: COMMIT
    T->>PG: COMMIT
    PG-->>T: ok
    T->>K: afterCommit runs, publish OrderPaid
    Note over T,K: If COMMIT fails, the callback never runs and nothing is published
    Note over S,K: If the publish fails, the commit already happened. Use an outbox row for real durability.
@AfterUpdate
static publishOnCommit(instance: Order, options: UpdateOptions): void {
  if (!instance.changed('status') || instance.status !== 'PAID') return;
  const publish = () => eventBus.emit('order.paid', { orderId: instance.id });
  // Register on the transaction if there is one; otherwise the write already committed
  options.transaction ? options.transaction.afterCommit(publish) : publish();
}

afterCommit fixes the ordering, not the durability. If the process dies between COMMIT and the publish, the event is lost forever and no retry exists. For anything a downstream system depends on, write an outbox row inside the same transaction and let a relay publish it (Part 27 — Message Queues, and Part 20, section 20.8). afterCommit is right for cache invalidation and best-effort notifications; the outbox is right for money.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A hook that forgets { transaction: options.transaction } writes outside the transaction: the audit row survives a rollback, or deadlocks against the row its own transaction holds.
  • A throwing afterCreate rolls back the insert but surfaces as a confusing error from create().
  • An afterCommit callback that throws cannot undo anything; wrap it in try/catch or you turn a successful commit into a 500.
  • Hooks on beforeFind that mutate options.where silently change every query, including those in background jobs.
  • beforeBulkCreate receives the array; mutating it is how you set defaults for bulk loads, but validation hooks do not run per row unless individualHooks: true.
  • Hooks are not transactional with external systems: an HTTP call inside afterUpdate runs while the row lock is held.
  • Two models whose hooks write to each other create recursion (afterCreate on Order creating an AuditLog whose afterCreate writes an Order).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They allow hooks for pure, local, cheap work: normalising a value, computing a derived column. Everything else goes in the service where it is visible. They never let a hook do I/O to another system except through afterCommit or an outbox. When an audit trail must be complete for every write path — including sequelize.query and a DBA in psql — they use a PostgreSQL trigger, not a hook.

Common mistakes

  • Business logic in hooks, discovered six months later by someone debugging a bulk job that skipped it.
  • Publishing events before commit.
  • individualHooks: true on a migration-scale update.
  • Forgetting to propagate the transaction.

Interview questions

  1. Which operations skip instance hooks? Expected: Model.update/destroy, bulkCreate, increment, raw queries.
  2. What does individualHooks: true cost? Expected: a select of all matching rows plus per-row hooks and instances.
  3. Why is afterCommit better than afterUpdate for publishing, and why is it still not enough? Expected: ordering after commit; no durability, no retry — use an outbox.
  4. When would you use a database trigger instead of a hook? Expected: completeness across all write paths, atomicity, independence from the ORM.

Practical exercise

Add an order.paid event to an existing flow, first from afterUpdate and then via afterCommit plus an outbox table. Write a test that rolls the transaction back and asserts no event was published in the second implementation but was in the first. Acceptance criteria: the outbox version publishes exactly once per commit and survives a process kill between commit and publish.

21.19 Sequelize scopes

Concept

A scope is a named, reusable chunk of query options. defaultScope is applied to every finder on the model (section 21.15); named scopes are opted into with Model.scope('name'); Model.unscoped() removes the default.

@DefaultScope(() => ({ attributes: { exclude: ['internalNotes'] } }))
@Scopes(() => ({
  paid:     { where: { status: 'PAID' } },
  withItems:{ include: [{ association: 'items' }] },
  forCustomer: (customerId: string) => ({ where: { customerId } }),   // parameterised scope
}))
@Table({ tableName: 'orders', underscored: true })
export class Order extends Model<Order> {}

// Usage
await Order.scope('paid', 'withItems').findAll();
await Order.scope({ method: ['forCustomer', customerId] }).findAll();
await Order.unscoped().findByPk(id);         // includes internalNotes

Why does it exist?

To stop the same where fragment being copied into forty call sites and drifting. "Active products", "non-cancelled orders", "this tenant's rows" are genuinely repeated conditions.

How it works and where it fails

Scopes merge. Multiple scopes' where clauses combine with AND, include arrays concatenate, and attributes from a later scope replace an earlier one. The merge rules are the first hazard: two scopes that both constrain status do not produce status IN (...), one wins.

The second hazard is the important one. Scopes for tenant isolation fail silently.

@Scopes(() => ({ tenant: (tenantId: string) => ({ where: { tenantId } }) }))
// ...
await Order.scope({ method: ['tenant', req.tenantId] }).findAll({ where: { status: 'PAID' } });

This works — until someone writes Order.findAll() without the scope in a new endpoint, or a background job, or an admin tool, or inside an include on another model. There is no error, no warning, no failing test. The query returns every tenant's orders and the response looks perfectly normal to whoever wrote it. This is IDOR at the data layer (Part 39, section 39.5), and it is discovered by a customer, not by you.

Scopes are a convenience, not a security boundary. If cross-tenant leakage is a real risk, enforce it where it cannot be forgotten:

-- PostgreSQL row-level security: the database refuses to return other tenants' rows
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY orders_tenant_isolation ON orders
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);
// Set the setting once per request on the pooled connection, inside the transaction
await sequelize.query(`SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)`, { bind: [req.tenantId], transaction: t });

The true third argument makes the setting transaction-local, so a pooled connection cannot carry one tenant's id into another request. Now a forgotten scope returns zero rows instead of everyone's rows: the failure mode flips from silent leak to visible bug. If RLS is too much, the next best thing is a repository wrapper that is the only way to reach the model, with the tenant filter applied inside it and the raw model not exported.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • defaultScope is applied to included models too, silently filtering join results.
  • unscoped() only unscopes the model it is called on, not includes.
  • Scope functions are evaluated at call time; a scope closing over a request value in a singleton service leaks state between requests.
  • Whether the default scope's where reaches Model.update/Model.destroy has varied between versions — never rely on it to prevent a destructive write. Put the condition in the call.
  • Scopes plus raw: true plus includes interact badly; check the SQL.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Scopes for readability, constraints and RLS for safety. They ask "what happens if someone forgets this?" — if the answer is "wrong data is returned and nobody notices", it does not belong in a scope.

Interview questions

  1. How do two scopes with conflicting where keys merge? Expected: one replaces the other; not an OR or IN.
  2. Why are scopes a bad tenant isolation mechanism? Expected: opt-in, silent when forgotten, bypassed by raw queries and includes; use RLS or an enforced repository.
  3. What does unscoped() not do? Expected: it does not unscope included models.

21.20 Sequelize migrations

Concept

sequelize-cli manages an ordered list of migration files and a SequelizeMeta table recording which have run. Each file exports up and down, both receiving a queryInterface (the DDL API) and Sequelize (for DataTypes and literal).

npx sequelize-cli migration:generate --name add-sales-channel-to-orders
npx sequelize-cli db:migrate
npx sequelize-cli db:migrate:status
npx sequelize-cli db:migrate:undo
npx sequelize-cli seed:generate --name demo-products

A .sequelizerc keeps the paths sane in a NestJS project:

// .sequelizerc
const path = require('path');
module.exports = {
  config:         path.resolve('src/database', 'sequelize-cli.config.js'),
  'models-path':  path.resolve('src', 'models'),
  'migrations-path': path.resolve('src/database', 'migrations'),
  'seeders-path': path.resolve('src/database', 'seeders'),
};

How it works

An important difference from TypeORM: sequelize-cli has no migration:generate that diffs models against the database. migration:generate creates an empty skeleton and you write the DDL yourself. That is more typing and considerably less dangerous — there is no tool that can decide on its own to drop a column it does not recognise (section 21.25). The trade is that model and schema drift is entirely your discipline.

The second difference: sequelize-cli does not wrap each migration in a transaction by default. If you want atomicity you write it:

'use strict';
module.exports = {
  async up(queryInterface, Sequelize) {
    await queryInterface.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
      await queryInterface.addColumn(
        'orders', 'sales_channel',
        { type: Sequelize.TEXT, allowNull: true },      // nullable: safe on a live table
        { transaction: t },
      );
      await queryInterface.addConstraint('orders', {
        fields: ['sales_channel'],
        type: 'check',
        name: 'orders_sales_channel_check',
        where: { sales_channel: [null, 'WEB', 'APP', 'POS'] },
        transaction: t,
      });
    });
  },
  async down(queryInterface) {
    await queryInterface.removeColumn('orders', 'sales_channel');
  },
};

The queryInterface API you will actually use: createTable, dropTable, addColumn, removeColumn, changeColumn, renameColumn, addIndex, removeIndex, addConstraint, removeConstraint, bulkInsert, bulkUpdate, bulkDelete, and sequelize.query for anything it cannot express (partial indexes, CREATE EXTENSION, ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE, ON CONFLICT backfills).

Indexes without downtime. A plain CREATE INDEX takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE-blocking SHARE lock and stops writes to the table for the whole build — minutes on a 50 million row table. concurrently: true builds it without blocking writes, at the cost of two table scans and the requirement that it must not run inside a transaction:

async up(queryInterface) {
  // No wrapping transaction here; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY forbids it
  await queryInterface.addIndex('orders', {
    fields: ['status', 'created_at'],
    name: 'orders_status_created_idx',
    concurrently: true,
  });
}

A concurrent build that fails leaves an INVALID index behind; the next run must DROP INDEX IF EXISTS first. Check with SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;.

sync() is not a migration strategy. sequelize.sync() creates missing tables; sync({ alter: true }) diffs models against the schema and issues ALTERs; sync({ force: true }) drops and recreates every table. None of them are versioned, reviewed, ordered or reversible. alter: true in particular will drop a column your models no longer mention, change a type in a way that rewrites the table under an exclusive lock, and drop constraints and indexes it did not create. It is fine for a throwaway local database and a unit test schema. In every environment that holds data someone cares about, synchronize: false in SequelizeModule.forRoot and migrations run from the pipeline (the deployment table in section 21.7 applies unchanged).

21.21 N+1 and lazy getters in Sequelize

Sequelize's N+1 comes from association mixins. Every association generates getX() on the instance, and every call is a query:

// BUG: 1 + N queries
const orders = await this.orderModel.findAll({ where: { customerId } });   // 1
for (const order of orders) {
  const items = await order.getItems();                                    // 1 per order
  total += items.reduce((s, i) => s + Number(i.unitPriceCents) * i.qty, 0);
}
Executing (default): SELECT "id","status" FROM "orders" WHERE "customer_id" = $1;
Executing (default): SELECT "id","qty" FROM "order_items" WHERE "order_id" = $1;   -- o1
Executing (default): SELECT "id","qty" FROM "order_items" WHERE "order_id" = $1;   -- o2
Executing (default): SELECT "id","qty" FROM "order_items" WHERE "order_id" = $1;   -- o3
... 97 more

The signature in the log is the same statement text repeated with different bind values. The same signature appears in pg_stat_statements as one row with calls in the millions and mean_exec_time under a millisecond — high call count with low mean time is N+1 until proven otherwise.

The three fixes mirror section 21.9:

// FIX 1: join (fine for few children per parent)
const a = await this.orderModel.findAll({ where: { customerId }, include: [{ association: 'items' }] });

// FIX 2: separate query (no row multiplication)
const b = await this.orderModel.findAll({ where: { customerId }, include: [{ association: 'items', separate: true }] });

// FIX 3: manual batch, when the children come from elsewhere
const orders = await this.orderModel.findAll({ where: { customerId }, raw: true });
const items = await this.itemModel.findAll({ where: { orderId: { [Op.in]: orders.map((o) => o.id) } }, raw: true });
const byOrder = new Map<string, OrderItem[]>();
for (const i of items) { const list = byOrder.get(i.orderId) ?? []; list.push(i); byOrder.set(i.orderId, list); }

Detecting it automatically. Sequelize's logging option is a function, so counting per request costs three lines plus AsyncLocalStorage:

// src/database/query-counter.ts
export const queryCtx = new AsyncLocalStorage<{ count: number }>();

// In SequelizeModule.forRootAsync options:
logging: (sql: string) => { const s = queryCtx.getStore(); if (s) s.count += 1; },

// In an interceptor: run the handler inside queryCtx.run({ count: 0 }, ...) and log/warn when count > 20

Ship that in staging with a threshold, and N+1 stops reaching production. The mixins are still useful — order.getItems() in a service that handles exactly one order is one clean query — but any mixin call inside a loop is a bug.

21.22 TypeORM vs Sequelize vs raw SQL

Concept

Three ways to talk to PostgreSQL from a NestJS service: a Data Mapper ORM (TypeORM), an Active Record ORM (Sequelize), and SQL text sent through the driver (pg, optionally with a typed query builder such as Kysely). They are not competitors on every axis. Most production systems use two of them, and the interesting question is not "which ORM" but "where is the line between them".

Why does it exist?

Because the shape of the work differs. Writing an order and its items inside a transaction is an object-graph problem, and an ORM is genuinely better at it. Computing "revenue by category per week, ranked, excluding refunds" is a set problem, and SQL is genuinely better at it. Choosing one tool for both means one of the two jobs is done badly.

The comparison

Dimension TypeORM Sequelize Raw SQL (pg, or Kysely for typing)
Type safety Decorators give entity types; find options are typed and select/relations are checked, but query-builder results are any for raw selects and getRawMany<T>() is an unchecked cast. Column-name strings in where fragments are not verified. Weakest of the three. sequelize-typescript types the model, but where/include/attributes are loosely typed, $nested$ paths and literal() are strings, and findAll returns instances typed by the model regardless of the attributes you selected. No types by default: query<T>() is a cast you must earn. With Kysely, the strongest of the three — column names, joins and result shapes are checked against a generated schema type. With zod parsing, runtime-verified as well.
Migrations migration:generate diffs entities against the live schema and writes SQL for you. Powerful and the biggest footgun in the part: the diff is a draft that can drop columns, rewrite tables and create indexes non-concurrently. migrations table, up/down, transaction mode per run. sequelize-cli generates only an empty skeleton; you write queryInterface calls or SQL yourself. Safer by omission, more typing, drift is your discipline. SequelizeMeta table, no wrapping transaction unless you add one. Plain .sql files with a runner (node-pg-migrate, dbmate, sqitch, graphile-migrate, or Kysely's migrator). Full control, zero generation, and you own the versioning table.
Query builder power Strong. createQueryBuilder covers joins, subqueries in SELECT/FROM/WHERE, CASE, locks, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, RETURNING, CTEs via .addCommonTableExpression(). Fragments are still strings once you leave the simple path. Weaker. There is no query builder, only the options object plus fn, col and literal. Anything non-trivial becomes a literal() string, and at that point you have raw SQL with none of the safety. Total. It is SQL. Kysely adds composability and types without giving anything up.
Relation loading relations, leftJoinAndSelect, relationLoadStrategy: 'join' | 'query', eager/lazy. The two-query strategy is a first-class option. include with required, separate: true, nested includes, plus the limit + subQuery behaviour that surprises people. Comparable power, more sharp edges. You write the joins and do the nesting yourself, or run two queries and group in code. More code, no surprises.
Transactions dataSource.transaction(cb), QueryRunner for manual control, savepoints via nesting, isolation levels, pessimistic_read/pessimistic_write. Propagation is manual unless you add a CLS package. sequelize.transaction(cb), savepoints via nesting, isolation levels, LOCK.UPDATE/LOCK.SHARE, and CLS support built in via Sequelize.useCLS(namespace), which makes transaction propagate implicitly. BEGIN/COMMIT on a checked-out client. Explicit, and you must never forget release().
Performance overhead Small per query (tens of microseconds); real cost is hydration of joined results and the statement count it chooses. Similar. Instance construction is slightly heavier; raw: true removes most of it. Lowest. pg returns plain objects; the only cost is your own mapping. For a 50,000-row report the gap is 3–10x in CPU and memory.
Community and maintenance Very widely used and the default in the NestJS docs, but the project has a long history of slow maintenance: it went effectively unmaintained in 2021–2022, was revived by community maintainers, and is still on 0.3.x with no 1.0, a large open-issue backlog and infrequent releases. It works; do not expect fast fixes. Mature and stable on v6, maintained at a modest pace. v7 (@sequelize/core) has been in alpha for a long time with a rewritten TypeScript core and built-in decorators; treat the migration path as a real project, not a version bump. pg is boring, stable and maintained. Kysely and the migration runners are small, active and easy to replace.
Learning curve Steepest. Decorators, metadata, two loading models, cascade semantics, query builder, migration generation. Gentle to start (Active Record reads naturally), then a long tail of behavioural surprises: include semantics, scopes, hooks that do not fire, subQuery. Requires knowing SQL, which every backend engineer needs anyway. Nothing else to learn.
NestJS integration @nestjs/typeorm: forRoot, forFeature, @InjectRepository, TypeOrmHealthIndicator in @nestjs/terminus. First-class. @nestjs/sequelize: forRoot, forFeature, @InjectModel, getModelToken for tests. First-class. A provider wrapping pg.Pool, plus a Kysely instance. Ten lines and no framework coupling.
Testing ergonomics Entities are plain classes and easy to construct; repositories are easy to mock with getRepositoryToken. Integration tests need a real database and a DataSource per suite. Models are the ORM: a model instance cannot exist without a Sequelize instance, so unit tests either mock heavily with getModelToken or use a real database. Active Record makes pure-domain unit testing harder. Trivially mockable at the boundary (one query function), and the honest answer is to test against a real PostgreSQL container either way (Part 40, section 40.2).
Bulk operations insert() with arrays, save(rows, { chunk }), upsert(), orIgnore()/orUpdate(), InsertQueryBuilder. Good. bulkCreate with updateOnDuplicate/ignoreDuplicates, Model.update with a where. Good, with the hook caveats. COPY via pg-copy-streams for hundreds of thousands of rows, INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...). An order of magnitude faster than any ORM path.
JSONB support @Column('jsonb'), and @>/->> operators only through raw fragments in the query builder. Indexing and containment queries are hand-written. DataTypes.JSONB with Op.contains (@>), Op.has, and dotted paths in where. Slightly better ergonomics than TypeORM. Everything PostgreSQL has: jsonb_path_query, jsonb_to_recordset, GIN indexes with jsonb_path_ops, partial expression indexes.
Window functions and CTEs Only via .addCommonTableExpression() or raw fragments in addSelect('ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...)'), and the result is getRawMany. Only via literal(). Effectively raw SQL wearing a costume. Native. This row alone decides most reporting code.
Upserts repository.upsert(values, ['sku']) and .orUpdate() on the insert builder; ON CONFLICT target and RETURNING supported. Model.upsert with conflictFields, bulkCreate with updateOnDuplicate. The created flag is unreliable. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... RETURNING (xmax = 0) AS inserted. Exact, and the only version that tells you truthfully what happened.
Connection pooling control poolSize plus extra passed straight to pg.Pool, so every pg option is reachable, including statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. replication for read replicas. pool: { max, min, acquire, idle, evict } (sequelize-pool, not pg.Pool), plus dialectOptions for driver settings, and replication: { read: [], write: {} }. acquire is the timeout that matters. You own pg.Pool directly: max, idleTimeoutMillis, connectionTimeoutMillis, application_name, and any per-connection SET.
Raw escape hatch manager.query(sql, params), queryRunner.query, entityManager.query inside a transaction. Results are untyped rows. sequelize.query(sql, { bind, type, transaction, model, mapToModel }) — and model: Order will even hydrate instances from raw rows. It is the hatch.

The rows that actually decide it

Maintenance status is a real engineering input, not gossip. TypeORM's history matters because you will hit a bug — the issue tracker has thousands of open ones, some years old — and the question is whether you can work around it in application code. Usually you can, because the escape hatch is manager.query. Sequelize's v6-to-v7 gap matters because a rewritten core with different decorators is a migration you will eventually have to schedule. Neither is a reason to avoid them; both are reasons to keep your data access behind repository classes you own, so that a future migration touches ten files instead of four hundred. That single decision — never call the ORM directly from a controller or a domain service — is worth more than the choice between the two ORMs.

Type safety is where the gap is widest, and it is not close. TypeORM checks that select: { id: true } refers to a real property. Sequelize does not check that attributes: ['totalCents'] matches the model, and it certainly does not narrow the return type to those fields — so order.status compiles and is undefined at runtime. Kysely, by contrast, will not compile a join on a column that does not exist. If your team's pain is "we shipped a query that referenced a renamed column", that is the row to weigh.

Window functions and CTEs is the row that forces the hybrid. Neither ORM can express ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY revenue DESC) without dropping to a string. Once you are writing a string, the ORM adds nothing except an awkward wrapper and an untyped result. Every team that tries hard enough to keep reports "in the ORM" ends up with a 40-line literal() that is harder to read than the SQL it contains.

Performance overhead is the row people over-weight. For a single-row lookup the ORM costs tens of microseconds against roughly 1 ms of database and network time — irrelevant. The cost that matters is structural: how many statements the ORM decided to issue, and how many rows it hydrated. An N+1 costs 100x more than the ORM's per-query overhead ever will. Choose on correctness, ergonomics and escape hatches; the microseconds are noise.

Transactions is where Sequelize has a genuine advantage. Sequelize.useCLS(namespace) makes the current transaction implicit, so a nested service method that calls Order.create() without passing { transaction: t } still joins the transaction. In TypeORM the equivalent requires the transactional EntityManager to be threaded through every call, or a third-party CLS package. This is the most common transaction bug in TypeORM codebases (Part 20, section 20.13), and CLS removes a whole class of it. It also hides the transaction, which cuts both ways.

Decision table

If your situation is... Choose
Existing NestJS codebase already on one of them, working Keep it. Migrating an ORM is a multi-month project with no user-visible benefit.
New service, team knows TypeORM, PostgreSQL, complex object graphs and transactions TypeORM, with raw SQL for reports and a repository layer you own
New service, team knows Sequelize, lots of nested writes across service methods Sequelize with CLS transactions, separate: true discipline, and raw SQL for reports
Read-heavy analytics or reporting service Raw SQL with Kysely or pg plus zod; no ORM
Data pipeline, ETL, bulk loads Raw SQL with COPY; an ORM here is pure overhead
Team is junior-heavy and the schema is simple CRUD Prisma (see 21.24) for the guardrails, or TypeORM if you need Data Mapper semantics
Domain-driven design with aggregates, unit of work and an identity map MikroORM

21.23 When to use an ORM and when raw SQL is better

Concept

The line is not "simple versus complex". It is "is this an object graph I will mutate, or a set I will read?" Writes that change a few related rows inside a transaction are object-graph work: the ORM tracks what changed, generates the right UPDATE, and keeps you honest about the aggregate. Reads that aggregate, rank, window, recurse or bulk-modify are set work: SQL was designed for exactly that, and the ORM can only get in the way.

Mental model

Imagine a workshop. The ORM is the set of power tools on the bench: fast, safe, and perfect for the jobs they were built for. Raw SQL is the hand tools: slower to pick up, but the only thing that fits an odd joint. Nobody argues about which is "better"; a professional has both within reach and knows which one this cut needs.

The decision flow

flowchart TD
    A["New query to write"] --> B{"Does it write data?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C{"Single aggregate: an order plus its items?"}
    C -->|"yes"| D["ORM inside a transaction"]
    C -->|"no"| E{"Bulk: thousands of rows?"}
    E -->|"yes"| F["Raw SQL: COPY, INSERT SELECT, UPDATE FROM VALUES"]
    E -->|"no"| G{"Needs ON CONFLICT, RETURNING, SKIP LOCKED?"}
    G -->|"yes"| H["Raw SQL, or the ORM upsert if it maps cleanly"]
    G -->|"no"| D
    B -->|"no"| I{"Aggregation, ranking, window, recursion?"}
    I -->|"yes"| J["Raw SQL with typed result mapping"]
    I -->|"no"| K{"More than three joins or a joined-column filter with limit?"}
    K -->|"yes"| J
    K -->|"no"| L{"Result is hydrated entities you will mutate?"}
    L -->|"yes"| M["ORM finders with explicit relations"]
    L -->|"no"| N["ORM with raw true, or raw SQL if the shape is odd"]

The hybrid most senior teams land on

Roughly 85% of statements through the ORM, 15% raw, split like this:

ORM for:

  • CRUD on a single aggregate: create an order with its items, update a product, soft-delete a customer.
  • Writes inside a transaction where the object graph matters and the ORM's change tracking earns its keep.
  • Simple list endpoints: filter, sort, paginate, one or two belongsTo includes.
  • Anything a junior will maintain, because the ORM's guardrails (parameter binding, type conversion, relation nesting) prevent whole categories of mistakes.

Raw SQL for:

  • Reports and dashboards. GROUP BY, date_trunc, FILTER (WHERE ...), GROUPING SETS.
  • Window functions. Ranking, running totals, "top 3 per category", LAG/LEAD for diffs.
  • Recursive CTEs. Category trees, org charts, reply threads, graph reachability.
  • Queue claims. UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY run_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10) RETURNING * — no ORM expresses this well, and it is the single most valuable raw query in a backend.
  • Upserts with exact semantics. ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET stock = products.stock + EXCLUDED.stock RETURNING (xmax = 0) AS inserted.
  • Bulk operations. COPY for imports, UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...) for a thousand different updates in one statement, DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... LIMIT 10000) batched deletes.
  • Anything where you already know the plan you want. If you have run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and tuned the query, keep the query.

Here is the queue claim, which no ORM does well, next to the report:

-- src/jobs/sql/claim-jobs.sql
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'RUNNING', claimed_at = now(), claimed_by = $1
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY run_at
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT $2
)
RETURNING id, payload, attempts;
-- src/reports/sql/top-products-per-category.sql
WITH sales AS (
  SELECT p.category_id, p.id AS product_id, p.name,
         sum(oi.qty * oi.unit_price_cents) AS revenue_cents
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders   o ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status IN ('PAID', 'SHIPPED')
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.created_at >= $1
  GROUP BY p.category_id, p.id, p.name
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY revenue_cents DESC) AS rn
  FROM sales
)
SELECT category_id, product_id, name, revenue_cents
FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category_id, rn;

How to keep raw SQL safe

Raw SQL earns its place only if it is as safe as the ORM path. Four rules make it so.

1. Parameters, always. No exceptions, no template literals.

// NEVER. One malicious sort value and the table is gone.
await manager.query(`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = '${status}' ORDER BY ${sort}`);

// ALWAYS: values as parameters; identifiers from an allow-list.
const SORTS = { newest: 'created_at DESC', total: 'total_cents DESC' } as const;
const orderBy = SORTS[dto.sort ?? 'newest'];                       // never interpolate user text
await manager.query(`SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status = $1 ORDER BY ${orderBy} LIMIT $2`, [status, limit]);

Values go in $1. Identifiers (table, column, direction) can never be parameters in SQL, so they must come from a fixed map in your code. If a value list is dynamic, use = ANY($1::uuid[]) rather than building IN ($1,$2,...,$n).

2. Typed result mapping with zod. manager.query<T>() and sequelize.query<T>() are casts: the compiler believes you, and nothing checks the actual rows. One renamed column and every field is undefined at runtime, propagating nulls into the API response. Parse instead of cast.

// src/reports/top-products.query.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

const RowSchema = z.object({
  category_id: z.string().uuid(),
  product_id: z.string().uuid(),
  name: z.string(),
  revenue_cents: z.coerce.number().int(),     // bigint arrives as a string; coerce deliberately
});
export type TopProductRow = z.infer<typeof RowSchema>;

@Injectable()
export class TopProductsQuery {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async run(since: Date): Promise<TopProductRow[]> {
    const rows = await this.ds.query(loadSql('top-products-per-category.sql'), [since]);
    return z.array(RowSchema).parse(rows);     // throws loudly at the boundary, not silently downstream
  }
}

z.coerce.number() is where you decide, once and visibly, that this bigint becomes a JavaScript number — instead of discovering a string in a template three layers up. For money keep it a string or a Decimal and never coerce.

3. Co-locate .sql files. SQL inside a template literal loses syntax highlighting, cannot be pasted into psql, cannot be run through a linter, and produces horrible diffs. Put each statement in a .sql file next to the code that uses it and load it once at startup.

// src/database/load-sql.ts
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';

const cache = new Map<string, string>();
export function loadSql(name: string, dir = join(__dirname, '..', 'reports', 'sql')): string {
  const cached = cache.get(name);
  if (cached) return cached;
  const sql = readFileSync(join(dir, name), 'utf8');   // read once; the file is immutable at runtime
  cache.set(name, sql);
  return sql;
}

Remember to copy **/*.sql in your build step (nest-cli.json compilerOptions.assets, or the Dockerfile) or production will fail at the first report with ENOENT. Now EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on that exact file is a copy-paste, a reviewer reads SQL rather than string concatenation, and a query change shows up as a SQL diff in the pull request.

4. Test raw SQL against a real database. Mocks cannot catch a column rename, a type mismatch, an ambiguous reference or a plan regression. A Testcontainers-backed PostgreSQL, migrations applied, a seeded fixture, and one test per .sql file that asserts the shape and a couple of values is cheap insurance. Add a plan test for the important ones: run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and assert the output does not contain Seq Scan on orders. That test fails the day someone drops the index.

it('claims at most N pending jobs and skips locked rows', async () => {
  await seedJobs(20);
  const [a, b] = await Promise.all([claimJobs('w1', 5), claimJobs('w2', 5)]);   // concurrent workers
  const ids = new Set([...a, ...b].map((j) => j.id));
  expect(ids.size).toBe(10);                       // no job claimed twice
});

Production scenario

An orders service at 800 requests per second: 92% of statements come from TypeORM (order creation, status updates, list endpoints), 8% from eleven .sql files (the queue claim, three reports, a bulk price import, two upserts, a recursive category query, a batched archive delete). The .sql files carry 60% of the database's total CPU time because reports are expensive, and every one of them has a plan test. When the ORM was used for the reports, the same work took 11 minutes and hydrated 2 million entities; the SQL version takes 9 seconds and streams.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged: orders-api p99 has gone from 120 ms to 9 s and the pool is saturated. The cause is a "small" change from the day before: a product-name filter added to the order list endpoint. The developer hit column "product.name" does not exist, found subQuery: false on a forum, and shipped it. LIMIT 20 now counts joined rows, so each request scans and joins far more than before, and pagination loops the client through overlapping pages, tripling traffic. The fix is four lines: paginate the parents with a WHERE id IN (SELECT order_id FROM order_items JOIN products ...) semi-join and load items separately. The lesson is in the review checklist (section 21.26): every include/relations change must show its generated SQL in the pull request.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask: "Will this query's shape ever change with user input, and does it aggregate?" Aggregation means SQL. They refuse to let raw SQL be un-parameterised, untyped or untested, and with those three rules in place they have no ideological problem with it. They keep both paths behind the same repository interface so the caller cannot tell which is which, and so swapping one for the other is a one-file change. And they push back on "let's rewrite everything in X" — the ORM is rarely the reason a system is slow.

Common mistakes

  • Fighting the ORM for a week on a query that is nine lines of SQL.
  • Raw SQL sprinkled through controllers and services, with no parsing and no tests.
  • String-interpolated identifiers "because parameters do not work for column names".
  • Believing raw SQL is unsafe by nature; it is unsafe when concatenated, exactly like any other code.
  • Assuming the ORM is the performance problem before reading a query plan.

Interview questions

  1. Where do you draw the line between ORM and raw SQL, and why there? Expected: object-graph writes versus set-based reads; aggregation, windows, recursion, bulk and queue claims go raw.
  2. How do you make raw SQL as safe as ORM queries? Expected: bound parameters, allow-listed identifiers, runtime schema parsing, co-located files, real-database tests including plan assertions.
  3. Your report takes 11 minutes through the query builder. What do you do first? Expected: get the generated SQL, run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), check row counts and hydration, then rewrite as one statement.
  4. Why is $1 safe when string interpolation is not? Expected: parameters are sent out of band in the extended protocol and are never parsed as SQL; also enables plan reuse and pg_stat_statements grouping.
  5. What is the cost of introducing a second data-access style in one codebase? Expected: two conventions, two testing approaches, drift; mitigate by hiding both behind repositories and a single SQL-file convention.

Practical exercise

Pick the slowest read endpoint in a service you know. Capture the ORM-generated SQL and its EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Rewrite it as a co-located .sql file with bound parameters and a zod row schema, and add an integration test plus a plan assertion. Acceptance criteria: identical results proven by a test comparing both implementations on seeded data, at least a 3x latency improvement, and the raw version behind the same repository method signature as before.

21.24 The wider landscape

TypeORM and Sequelize are not the only options, and for a new NestJS + PostgreSQL service in 2026 they are not automatically the best ones. Four alternatives are worth knowing well enough to argue about.

Prisma. The most polished developer experience in the Node ecosystem. You write a schema.prisma file, run prisma migrate dev, and get a fully typed client where prisma.order.findMany({ include: { items: true } }) returns a type that knows items is present and knows it is absent when you omit it. That result-type narrowing is something neither TypeORM nor Sequelize does, and it eliminates a real class of bug. Migrations are generated from schema diffs with a review step and a shadow database that catches drift. The historical objections — a separate Rust query engine binary that complicated Docker images and Lambda cold starts, and no JOIN-based relation loading (it issued one query per relation) — have both been addressed in recent versions: relation joins are available, and the client has moved toward a TypeScript-native implementation. What remains: the schema lives in Prisma's own DSL rather than TypeScript or SQL, complex SQL still means $queryRaw with Prisma.sql tagged templates, and there is no identity map or unit of work, so aggregate-heavy domain code needs more manual assembly. For a NestJS team that wants strong types, safe migrations and CRUD velocity, and is happy to drop to $queryRaw for reports, Prisma is a strong default. You would choose it over TypeORM when type safety and migration safety matter more than object-graph modelling.

Drizzle. A thin, TypeScript-first layer that reads like SQL. You define tables in TypeScript (pgTable('orders', { id: uuid('id').primaryKey(), ... })), and queries are composed with functions that mirror SQL clauses: db.select().from(orders).where(eq(orders.status, 'PAID')).leftJoin(orderItems, eq(...)). There is no runtime engine to speak of — it generates SQL and hands it to pg — so overhead is close to raw and it runs anywhere, including edge runtimes. drizzle-kit generates SQL migration files from schema diffs, and you commit the SQL. It also offers a relational query API (db.query.orders.findMany({ with: { items: true } })) for the CRUD cases. The trade-offs are honest: no identity map, no change tracking, no cascades, no lifecycle hooks — it is a query builder with a schema, not an ORM. The ecosystem is younger than the others, so you will occasionally be the first person to hit a problem. Choose it over TypeORM when your team is comfortable in SQL, wants end-to-end types with near-zero runtime cost, and does not need aggregate persistence.

Kysely. Not an ORM at all: a type-safe SQL query builder. You supply an interface describing your database (generated from the schema with kysely-codegen), and every query is checked against it — a typo in a column name, a join on the wrong type, or selecting a column you did not include in the result type is a compile error. It supports CTEs, window functions, ON CONFLICT, RETURNING and raw fragments through sql tagged templates that still parameterise correctly. It has a small migration runner. There is no relation loading, no hydration, no change tracking: you write the joins and shape the results. In a hybrid architecture Kysely is the ideal "raw SQL" half — everything section 21.23 asks of raw SQL (parameters, types, testability, composability) comes for free — while TypeORM or Prisma handles the CRUD half. Choose it as a companion rather than a replacement, unless your service is read-heavy enough that CRUD is a rounding error.

MikroORM. The most conceptually complete ORM in TypeScript: a true Data Mapper with an identity map (the same row loaded twice in one context is the same object) and a unit of work (you mutate objects, call flush() once, and it computes the minimal ordered set of statements, including insert ordering across foreign keys). If you have used Doctrine or Hibernate, it will feel immediately familiar. It has a first-class NestJS package with AsyncLocalStorage-based request context — so the entity manager is correctly scoped per request without you threading it — a strong migration system, schema diffing, entity generation from an existing database, and good TypeScript ergonomics. Its downsides are a smaller community than TypeORM or Prisma (fewer Stack Overflow answers at 2 a.m.), a genuinely steeper conceptual curve because you must understand identity maps and flush semantics to avoid surprises, and the fact that unit of work makes the exact SQL less predictable until you learn to read its debug output. Choose it over TypeORM when you are doing domain-driven design with real aggregates (Part 13), when you want transactional write-behind semantics, and when your team can invest in learning it properly.

What would actually move a team off TypeORM. Type safety of query results (Prisma or Kysely), migration safety and a diff you can trust (Prisma or Drizzle), correct request-scoped transaction propagation without threading a manager (MikroORM, or Sequelize's CLS), and a real unit of work for aggregate-heavy domains (MikroORM). What would not: performance benchmarks, GitHub stars, or a blog post. And whichever you pick, keep it behind repository classes you own — that is what makes the next decision cheap.

21.25 Edge cases and failure modes with ORMs

Every item below has cost a real team a real incident. Each one is presented the same way: the symptom you see, the cause underneath, the fix, and how to catch it in code review — because the cheapest place to stop all of these is a pull request.

21.25.1 numeric and decimal arrive as strings

Symptom. An invoice shows total: "19.9919.99". Or NaN. Or a report where every row is null. Tests pass because the fixture used integers.

Cause. PostgreSQL's numeric has arbitrary precision; a JavaScript number is a 64-bit float that cannot represent 0.1 + 0.2 exactly, let alone a 30-digit decimal. pg therefore returns numeric, decimal and bigint as strings, deliberately, and both ORMs pass that through. So product.price * item.qty is '19.99' * 2, which JavaScript coerces to 39.98 and hides the problem, while product.price + shipping is '19.99' + '4.50' = '19.994.50', and Number(order.totalCents) on a bigint past 9,007,199,254,740,991 silently loses the low digits.

Fix. Store money as bigint cents — integers, no rounding questions, exact addition — and keep the string until the JSON boundary. If you must have decimals, use a decimal library and convert deliberately at one place:

import Decimal from 'decimal.js';

// TypeORM: an explicit transformer beats a scattered parseFloat
const decimalTransformer = {
  to: (v: Decimal | null) => (v === null ? null : v.toFixed(2)),
  from: (v: string | null) => (v === null ? null : new Decimal(v)),
};

@Column({ type: 'numeric', precision: 12, scale: 2, transformer: decimalTransformer })
price: Decimal;

// Raw SQL: coerce once, at the parse boundary, and only where it is safe
const Row = z.object({ revenue_cents: z.coerce.number().int() });   // cents fit in a JS number below ~90 trillion

Do not register a global pg type parser that turns every numeric into a float. It "fixes" the symptom everywhere and corrupts money everywhere.

Detect in review. Any arithmetic on a field whose column is numeric, decimal or bigint. Any parseFloat. Any Number(...) on a money field. Any DTO where a money field is typed number but the entity says string.

21.25.2 timestamptz conversion surprises, and Date versus string

Symptom. An order created at 23:40 on 30 September appears in the October report. A birthday shifts by one day for users in Auckland. createdAt comes back as a string in one endpoint and a Date in another.

Cause. Three different type mappings collide.

  • timestamptz (OID 1184) is an absolute instant. pg converts it to a JS Date correctly, and Date is always UTC internally. This one is fine.
  • timestamp without time zone (OID 1114) has no zone. pg parses it as if it were in the Node process's local time. A container running TZ=Europe/Berlin and one running TZ=UTC produce Date objects two hours apart from the identical row. TypeORM's inferred default for a Date property is timestamp without time zone, so this happens by omission.
  • date (OID 1082) is a calendar day. Raw pg gives you a Date at local midnight, which in a negative-offset timezone is the previous day. TypeORM returns '2026-09-09' as a string for @Column('date'), and Sequelize's DATEONLY also returns a string — so the same column is a string in the ORM and a Date in a raw query in the same codebase.

Fix. Always timestamptz for instants, always date for calendar days, and never timestamp without a zone.

@CreateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz', name: 'created_at' }) createdAt: Date;   // TypeORM: state it
@Column({ type: 'date', name: 'invoice_date' }) invoiceDate: string;              // string, not Date
// Sequelize: pin the connection timezone so nothing depends on the container's TZ
SequelizeModule.forRoot({ dialect: 'postgres', timezone: '+00:00', /* ... */ });
// And run every process with TZ=UTC in the Dockerfile / pod spec.

Do all date arithmetic in PostgreSQL where the zone is explicit (date_trunc('day', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Berlin')) rather than in JavaScript. Report boundaries are a business decision about a timezone, not a technical default.

Detect in review. Any @Column({ type: 'timestamp' }) or a Date column with no explicit type. Any migration whose generated SQL says TIMESTAMP instead of TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE. Any new Date() used to build a report boundary without a named timezone.

21.25.3 save() racing under concurrency and silently overwriting

Symptom. A support agent updates an order's address; a webhook updates its status one second later; the address change is gone. No error was logged, both requests returned 200.

Cause. save() is read-modify-write across two round trips. Request A loads the full entity, request B loads the full entity, A writes, B writes — and because Sequelize writes the fields it thinks changed from the state it loaded, and TypeORM's save() writes the fields present on the object, B's write is based on a snapshot taken before A's. This is the classic lost update (Part 20, section 20.2), and the ORM will never tell you it happened.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as AgentRequest
    participant B as WebhookRequest
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    A->>PG: SELECT order 42, status CREATED, address old
    B->>PG: SELECT order 42, status CREATED, address old
    A->>PG: UPDATE order 42 SET address = new
    PG-->>A: 200
    B->>PG: UPDATE order 42 SET status = PAID, address = old
    PG-->>B: 200
    Note over A,B: The new address is gone. Both callers saw success.

Fix. Three options, in order of preference:

  1. Write only what changed, atomically. repository.update(id, { status: 'PAID' }) or Order.update({ status }, { where: { id } }) emits UPDATE ... SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2 and never touches the address column.
  2. Optimistic locking. TypeORM @VersionColumn plus a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE version = $n (TypeORM increments but does not guard — you write the WHERE), or Sequelize's version: true, which does guard and throws OptimisticLockError. Return 409 and let the client retry with fresh data.
  3. Pessimistic lock for short critical sections: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' }, lock: Transaction.LOCK.UPDATE) inside a transaction.

Detect in review. findOne followed by property assignment followed by save(), especially outside a transaction. Any handler that loads a whole entity to change one field.

21.25.4 The findOrCreate race

Symptom. Two customer rows with the same email, or a burst of 500s during a marketing campaign with duplicate key value violates unique constraint in the logs, or — worst — current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block.

Cause. findOrCreate is SELECT then INSERT, not one atomic statement (section 21.17). Without a unique constraint you get duplicates. With one, the loser gets 23505; Sequelize recovers by re-selecting, but if the call ran inside a transaction you supplied, PostgreSQL has already marked that transaction aborted and the recovery SELECT fails too.

Fix. A unique constraint is mandatory. Then replace the pattern with one statement:

INSERT INTO customers (id, email, name) VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), $1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email
RETURNING id, email, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;

DO UPDATE rather than DO NOTHING so RETURNING always yields a row. TypeORM's repository.upsert(values, ['email']) and Sequelize's Model.upsert(values, { conflictFields: ['email'] }) generate the same shape. If you must keep findOrCreate inside a transaction, wrap it in a savepoint (manager.transaction(cb) nested, or SAVEPOINT/ROLLBACK TO) so the failed insert does not poison the outer transaction.

Detect in review. Every findOrCreate: does a unique index cover its where? Is it inside a caller-supplied transaction? Both answers must be checked.

21.25.5 Eager loading row explosion: 20 orders become 4,000 rows

Symptom. An endpoint that returns 20 orders takes 3.4 seconds and the pod's CPU spikes. The database says the query took 180 ms. The gap is Node.

Cause. Two collection joins in one query multiply. 20 orders x 10 items x 20 status-history rows = 4,000 rows on the wire, 4,000 rows parsed by pg, 4,000 objects allocated, then de-duplicated back to 20. The database did the join efficiently; your process did the hydration badly.

Fix. Never join two collections in one query.

// TypeORM: two queries, one per relation level, no multiplication
const orders = await this.orders.find({
  where: { customerId }, relations: { items: true, history: true },
  relationLoadStrategy: 'query', take: 20,
});

// Sequelize
const orders2 = await this.orderModel.findAll({
  where: { customerId }, limit: 20,
  include: [{ association: 'items', separate: true }, { association: 'history', separate: true }],
});

3 queries and 620 rows instead of 1 query and 4,000 rows. Also select fewer columns: a jsonb blob or a text description multiplied 200 times is megabytes of wasted transfer.

Detect in review. Count the hasMany/OneToMany relations in one query. More than one is a red flag. Ask for the row count, not just the query count.

21.25.6 The identity map and stale instances inside a transaction

Symptom. Inside a transaction you run Product.update({ stock: 0 }, { where: { id } }), then read product.stock from an instance you loaded earlier and it still says 5. Or you load the same order twice in one request, mutate one copy, save both, and the second save undoes the first.

Cause. Neither TypeORM nor Sequelize keeps a full identity map, so two loads produce two independent objects with independent snapshots. And a bulk update/increment/raw statement changes the database without touching any in-memory instance. The object in your hand is a photograph, not a live view — and inside a long transaction the photograph gets old fast.

const product = await this.productModel.findByPk(id, { transaction: t });   // stock = 5
await this.productModel.decrement({ stock: 5 }, { where: { id }, transaction: t });
console.log(product.stock);      // still 5: the instance was not notified
await product.save({ transaction: t });   // may write stale values for other changed fields

ORMs that do have an identity map and unit of work (MikroORM, Hibernate-style) have the mirror-image surprise: the same row loaded twice is the same object, so a change in one place appears in another unexpectedly, and nothing is written until flush(), so a raw SELECT in the middle of the transaction does not see your pending changes.

Fix. After any bulk or atomic statement, either await instance.reload({ transaction: t }) / manager.findOne(...) again, or (better) do not keep the instance at all — use RETURNING to get the new state in the same statement:

const [, [updated]] = await this.productModel.decrement(
  { stock: qty }, { where: { id, stock: { [Op.gte]: qty } }, returning: true, transaction: t },
);

Detect in review. Any instance used after a bulk update, increment, upsert or raw query in the same scope. Any function that loads the same entity that its caller already loaded.

21.25.7 migration:generate produces a destructive diff

Symptom. A migration reviewed in ten seconds ("it is generated, it must be right") drops a column, or rewrites a 40 million row table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock during peak traffic.

Cause. TypeORM's generator compares entity metadata to the live schema and emits SQL to make them match. It cannot know intent. A rename looks like "drop one column, add another". A hand-written CHECK constraint that no entity declares looks like "drop this constraint". A column that exists in the database and not in any entity — because another service owns it, or because it was added by a DBA — looks like "drop it". An enum change looks like "create a new type, rewrite the table, drop the old type".

// GENERATED for a rename. This deletes every value in the column.
await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" DROP COLUMN "channel"`);
await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD "sales_channel" text`);

// CORRECT: a rename is metadata-only in PostgreSQL
await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "orders" RENAME COLUMN "channel" TO "sales_channel"`);

Fix. Treat generated migrations as drafts. Read every statement. Convert drop-plus-add into RENAME. Add CONCURRENTLY to index creation and move it out of the transaction. Add lock_timeout before DDL on large tables. Declare hand-written constraints in the entity (@Check(), @Index()) so they stop appearing in the diff. And run migration:generate against a database restored from production structure, not against your local one, so it sees the real schema. Sequelize sidesteps this whole class by not generating diffs at all (section 21.20).

Detect in review. Any migration containing DROP COLUMN, DROP CONSTRAINT, ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE, or CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY. Require the author to state the table's row count and the expected lock duration in the pull request description.

21.25.8 synchronize: true deletes production columns

Symptom. The 07:50 deploy story from section 21.1: two years of merchandising notes gone, discovered at 09:15, four hours to restore, a morning of edits lost.

Cause. synchronize: true (TypeORM) and sync({ alter: true }) (Sequelize) run the destructive diff of 21.25.7 automatically, at boot, with no review. The usual path is a .env left over from local development, or a config factory where the value comes from a variable that is undefined in production and defaults to true.

Fix. Hard-code false, and make the config refuse to start otherwise:

useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => {
  const synchronize = config.get('NODE_ENV') === 'test' && config.get('DB_SYNC') === 'true';
  if (synchronize && config.get('NODE_ENV') !== 'test') throw new Error('synchronize is forbidden outside tests');
  return { type: 'postgres', url: config.getOrThrow('DATABASE_URL'), synchronize, migrationsRun: false /* ... */ };
}

Belt and braces: give the application's database role no DROP privileges. Migrations run as a separate, more privileged role from the pipeline. Then even a mistake cannot delete a column.

Detect in review. Grep for synchronize and sync( in every config file and every test helper on every pull request. It belongs on the CI checklist, not on human memory.

21.25.9 take/limit with a collection join returns fewer parents

Symptom. take: 20 returns 7 orders. The paginator says 10 pages; page 3 is empty; page 2 and page 3 share rows.

Cause. LIMIT applies to result rows. With a joined collection, one parent is many rows, so LIMIT 20 cuts in the middle of a parent's children. TypeORM's find({ take }) handles this by issuing a distinct-ids query first; createQueryBuilder().limit() does not (.take() does). Sequelize handles it by wrapping the parent in a subquery — until you write subQuery: false to make a joined-column filter work, at which point the limit counts joined rows again (section 21.16).

Fix. Separate the pagination from the child loading.

// TypeORM: skip/take (distinct parents) not offset/limit (raw rows)
const page = await this.orders.createQueryBuilder('o')
  .leftJoinAndSelect('o.items', 'i')
  .where('o.customerId = :customerId', { customerId })
  .orderBy('o.createdAt', 'DESC')
  .skip(0).take(20)      // TypeORM issues a distinct-id query, then fetches those parents with their items
  .getMany();

// Or: page the ids first, then load the graph. Always predictable, two queries.
const ids = await this.orders.find({ where: { customerId }, select: { id: true }, order: { createdAt: 'DESC' }, take: 20 });
const full = await this.orders.find({ where: { id: In(ids.map((o) => o.id)) }, relations: { items: true } });

Detect in review. limit/offset on a query builder that joins a collection. subQuery: false anywhere. Any pagination change without a test asserting the returned parent count.

21.25.10 Huge IN (...) lists blow past the parameter limit

Symptom. A nightly job that worked for a year fails with bind message has 70000 parameter formats but 0 parameters, or there is no parameter $65536, or simply gets slower and slower until it times out.

Cause. PostgreSQL's extended protocol allows at most 65,535 bind parameters per statement. In(ids) with 100,000 ids generates IN ($1, $2, ..., $100000). Even below the limit, a 30,000-element IN list produces a statement text of half a megabyte that must be parsed and planned on every call, and it is a unique statement text every time, so pg_stat_statements fills with one-off entries and no plan is reused.

Fix. Use an array parameter, which is a single parameter:

// TypeORM
await this.items.query(`SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ANY($1::uuid[])`, [orderIds]);
// or, staying in the ORM, chunk
for (const chunk of chunked(orderIds, 1000)) await this.items.findBy({ orderId: In(chunk) });

// Sequelize
await this.sequelize.query(`SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ANY($1::uuid[])`,
  { bind: [orderIds], type: QueryTypes.SELECT });

Also handle the empty case: In([]) and Op.in: [] produce SQL that is either invalid or accidentally matches nothing depending on version. Guard with if (ids.length === 0) return []; before the query.

Detect in review. Any In(...) or Op.in fed from an unbounded array. Ask "what is the maximum length of this list in production in two years?"

21.25.11 Connection leaks from an unreleased QueryRunner

Symptom. The service is fine after a deploy and dies four hours later. Requests hang, then fail. SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state shows 20 connections in idle in transaction. Restarting the pod fixes it — for four hours.

Cause. A QueryRunner (TypeORM) or an unmanaged transaction (Sequelize) checked a connection out of the pool and an early return, a thrown exception, or a forgotten branch skipped release(). The pool never gets it back. Each leak permanently removes one connection; after max leaks the pool is empty forever.

flowchart TB
    R["Incoming requests"] --> P["pg pool, max 20"]
    P --> C1["conn 1 to 17: healthy, returned after each query"]
    P --> L["conn 18, 19, 20: leaked by a QueryRunner that threw before release"]
    L --> IDT["State: idle in transaction, forever"]
    C1 --> OK["Requests served"]
    P -->|"pool empty after 20 leaks"| W["New requests wait on acquire"]
    W -->|"acquire timeout"| E["ConnectionAcquireTimeoutError or connection timeout"]
    E --> HC["Readiness probe fails, pod restarts, timer resets"]

Fix. The finally { release() } rule, without exception:

const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
await runner.connect();
await runner.startTransaction('READ COMMITTED');
try {
  await runner.manager.update(Order, id, { status: 'PAID' });
  await runner.manager.insert(Payment, payment);
  await runner.commitTransaction();
} catch (err) {
  await runner.rollbackTransaction();     // safe even if the transaction already failed
  throw err;
} finally {
  await runner.release();                 // ALWAYS. This is the line people forget.
}

Better: use the callback forms (dataSource.transaction(cb), sequelize.transaction(cb)) which cannot leak, and reserve QueryRunner for the rare cases that genuinely need manual control. Add idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 5000 on the database role so PostgreSQL kills leaked sessions even when your code does not.

Detect in review. Every createQueryRunner() must have a finally { release() } in the same function. Every manual sequelize.transaction() (the unmanaged form that returns a transaction object) must have commit/rollback on all paths. Prefer rejecting the manual form entirely.

21.25.12 TimeoutError: connection acquisition timeout under load

Symptom. Under a traffic spike, requests fail with ConnectionAcquireTimeoutError (Sequelize; older versions say TimeoutError: ResourceRequest timed out) or timeout exceeded when trying to connect (pg, from connectionTimeoutMillis). The database itself looks idle: low CPU, few active queries.

Cause. This error means "I could not get a connection from the pool within the timeout". It almost never means the database is down. It means every pooled connection is busy, and it is a symptom whose real causes are, in order of frequency:

  1. A slow query holding connections. 20 connections x one 800 ms query each = 25 requests per second maximum on that path.
  2. N+1, which multiplies the number of connection-seconds each request needs.
  3. A leak (21.25.11): connections gone permanently.
  4. Work inside a transaction that is not database work — an HTTP call, an S3 upload, a sleep — holding a connection for the duration of a network round trip.
  5. A pool that is simply too small for the concurrency, or too large so PostgreSQL is thrashing.

Fix. Do not raise max first; find which of the five it is. pg_stat_activity tells you immediately:

SELECT state, count(*), max(now() - state_change) AS longest
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = current_database() GROUP BY state;

SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS runtime, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' ORDER BY runtime DESC LIMIT 10;

idle in transaction points at a leak or a network call inside a transaction. active with long runtimes points at slow queries. Many short active queries with the same text points at N+1. Then: add the missing index, remove the network call from the transaction, fix the loop, or fix the leak. Set acquire/connectionTimeoutMillis to a few seconds so the failure is fast and alertable instead of a silent hang, and export pool metrics (pool.totalCount, idleCount, waitingCount) to Prometheus so you see saturation before users do.

Detect in review. Any await inside a transaction that is not a database call. Any new query without an index behind its WHERE. Any change to pool size without a stated calculation.

21.25.13 N+1 hidden behind lazy relations and mixins

Symptom. p99 latency grows linearly with page size. Nothing appears in the slow query log because every individual query takes 0.4 ms.

Cause. await order.items on a Promise-typed TypeORM relation, or await order.getItems() in Sequelize, is a query that looks exactly like a property access. In a loop, a map, or a GraphQL resolver, that is one query per parent.

Fix. No Promise-typed relations in new code, no mixin calls inside loops; load explicitly (relations, include, separate: true) or with a request-scoped DataLoader (section 21.9), and ship a per-request query counter in staging.

Detect in review. Any await inside a for/map whose subject is a repository, model or entity property. Any Promise<Something> typed relation.

21.25.14 ORM cascade deletes more than intended

Symptom. Deleting a product deletes three tags that twelve other products used. Or deleting a customer takes 40 seconds, locks the table and produces 2 GB of WAL.

Cause. Two different mechanisms. cascade: ['remove'] on a @ManyToMany removes the related entities, not the join rows — TypeORM does what you literally asked. And an ON DELETE CASCADE chain (customers to orders to order_items to shipments) fans one DELETE out to millions of rows in a single transaction.

Fix. For many-to-many, never cascade remove; to detach associations set product.tags = [] and save, or delete from the join table. For hierarchies, use ON DELETE RESTRICT by default and cascade only where a child has no meaning without its parent. For large fan-outs, batch:

-- Delete children in chunks so locks and WAL stay bounded
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (
  SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 LIMIT 10000
);

Or soft-delete the parent and let a background job reclaim children over time.

Detect in review. Every cascade option: does it include remove, and is the relation many-to-many? Every new FK: what is its ON DELETE, and what is the maximum fan-out? Ask for the row count.

21.25.15 Enum changes

Symptom. A migration adding 'REFUNDED' to an order status enum locks orders for 90 seconds, or fails with ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE cannot run inside a transaction block, or a rollback is impossible because you cannot remove an enum value.

Cause. PostgreSQL native enums are a type, not a constraint. Adding a value is cheap but has transaction restrictions (and on older versions the new value cannot be used in the same transaction that added it). Removing a value requires creating a new type, rewriting every column that uses it, and dropping the old one — a full table rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. TypeORM's generated migration for any enum change does exactly that rewrite, without telling you.

Fix. Prefer text with a CHECK constraint. Adding a value is then ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT plus ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT — no rewrite, no exclusive lock beyond a moment, and fully reversible:

ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_status_check;
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_check
  CHECK (status IN ('CREATED','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED','REFUNDED')) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_status_check;   -- scans without blocking writes

The TypeScript union type gives you the compile-time safety; the CHECK gives you the database-level safety. If you already have native enums, ADD VALUE is fine; just never plan to remove one.

Detect in review. Any migration touching a USER-DEFINED type. Any new @Column({ type: 'enum' }) or DataTypes.ENUM — ask for text plus CHECK instead.

21.25.16 @BeforeUpdate and hooks that do not fire

Symptom. updatedBy is set for changes made through the admin UI and NULL for changes made by the bulk importer. Emails are lowercased sometimes. The audit table has gaps that correlate with background jobs.

Cause. Lifecycle callbacks fire for entity operations only. In TypeORM, @BeforeUpdate runs for save() and not for update(), upsert(), insert() of plain objects, or any query-builder write — those paths send values, never entity instances, so there is nothing to run the hook on. In Sequelize, instance hooks skip Model.update, Model.destroy, bulkCreate, increment/decrement and sequelize.query (section 21.18).

await this.orders.save(order);                                  // @BeforeUpdate runs
await this.orders.update(id, { status: 'PAID' });               // does NOT run
await this.orders.createQueryBuilder().update(Order).set({ status: 'PAID' }).where('id = :id', { id }).execute();  // does NOT run

Fix. Put anything that must always happen where it cannot be skipped:

  • Normalisation: in a class-transformer/class-validator DTO or a NestJS pipe, at the edge.
  • Audit trails and updated_at: a PostgreSQL trigger, which fires for every write path including psql.
  • Derived columns: a generated column (GENERATED ALWAYS AS ... STORED) or a trigger.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN NEW.updated_at = now(); RETURN NEW; END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

Detect in review. Any hook or listener that does something the business depends on. Ask: "which write paths skip this?" If the answer is "bulk imports", it is in the wrong place.

21.26 An ORM code review checklist

Use this as the ORM section of your pull-request template. Most of it is answerable by reading the diff plus the SQL log from a local run.

# Check What a reviewer looks for Why it matters
1 SQL shown The pull request includes the generated SQL for any new or changed query You cannot review what you cannot see; most ORM bugs are visible in one line of SQL
2 Statement count Number of statements per request for the changed endpoint Catches N+1 before it ships
3 Row count Rows returned, not just statements Catches join row explosion, which the statement count hides
4 No loops over the ORM No await repo.* / model.get*() inside for, map, forEach The canonical N+1 shape
5 Collection joins At most one OneToMany/hasMany joined per query; otherwise two-query strategy Cartesian multiplication
6 Pagination correctness skip/take (not offset/limit) with joins; distinct: true on findAndCountAll; no subQuery: false Wrong counts and overlapping pages
7 Explicit required Every Sequelize include with a where states required explicitly A where silently makes it an INNER JOIN
8 Column selection select/attributes present on list endpoints; no jsonb/text blobs fetched to be discarded Network and hydration cost
9 Money and big numbers numeric/bigint handled as strings or cents; no parseFloat; no Number() on large ids Silent financial corruption
10 Timestamps timestamptz for instants, date for calendar days, no bare timestamp, TZ=UTC in the runtime Off-by-one-day and off-by-hours bugs
11 Concurrency on writes No load-mutate-save() on contended rows; atomic update/increment, version column, or explicit lock Lost updates that return 200
12 Transaction scope Every query inside a transaction uses the transactional manager / { transaction: t } / CLS; no HTTP, S3 or queue calls inside Silent non-transactional writes; pool exhaustion
13 QueryRunner release finally { release() } present, or the callback form used Permanent connection leaks
14 Upserts ON CONFLICT with a real unique index behind it; findOrCreate justified and not inside a caller transaction Duplicate rows, aborted transactions
15 IN list bounds Arrays fed to In/Op.in are chunked or converted to = ANY($1::uuid[]); empty array guarded Parameter limit and plan churn
16 Migration reviewed line by line No DROP COLUMN for a rename, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, lock_timeout set, row count stated Data loss and peak-hour locks
17 synchronize / sync false everywhere except test setup; enforced by config, not memory Production column deletion
