18 Cascades ORM cascade for inserts, database ON DELETE for deletes, no cascade remove on many-to-many, fan-out estimated Deleting more than intended
19 Hooks and listeners Nothing business-critical in them; which write paths skip them is stated Gaps in audit trails and normalisation
20 Raw SQL hygiene Bound parameters, allow-listed identifiers, zod-parsed results, co-located .sql, an integration test Injection and silent shape drift
21 Indexes Every new WHERE/ORDER BY/JOIN column has an index, with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) attached The ORM cannot save a sequential scan
22 Scopes and tenancy Tenant isolation enforced by RLS or a mandatory repository, not by an opt-in scope Cross-tenant data leaks fail silently

Senior Checklist — Part 21

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can predict the SQL an ORM call will generate before I run it, and I check the log
  • I can explain what save() does differently from insert(), update() and upsert() in both ORMs
  • I know which relation-loading strategy to use from the shape of the data, and why joining two collections is wrong
  • I can detect N+1 from a query log, from pg_stat_statements, and with a per-request query counter
  • I know which write paths skip lifecycle hooks and where that logic belongs instead
  • I can explain the difference between ORM cascade and ON DELETE CASCADE, and which one I trust
  • I review generated migrations line by line and can name three destructive diffs they produce
  • I would never let synchronize: true or sync({ alter: true }) near data anyone cares about
  • I handle numeric and bigint as strings or cents, and timestamptz with an explicit timezone policy
  • I can size a connection pool from concurrency and query duration, and diagnose an acquire timeout from pg_stat_activity
  • I always release a QueryRunner in finally, or use the callback form
  • I can write the queue claim, the upsert and the top-N-per-group query in raw SQL, safely parameterised and tested
  • I can defend a choice between TypeORM, Sequelize, Prisma, Drizzle, Kysely and MikroORM for a specific team and workload

Part 21 — Key Takeaways

  • The ORM is not the database. Constraints, plans and the SQL log are the truth; entity decorators only describe them.
  • Read the generated SQL. Almost every ORM incident is visible in one statement or one row count before it reaches production.
  • Statement count and row count are the two numbers that matter. N+1 multiplies the first; joined collections multiply the second.
  • Load relations explicitly. eager: true and lazy Promise relations trade a little typing for an unbounded query bill.
  • Writes: prefer one atomic statement (UPDATE ... WHERE, increment, ON CONFLICT) over load-mutate-save(), which loses updates silently.
  • findOrCreate is not atomic; it survives only because of a unique index, and inside a caller's transaction it can abort the whole thing.
  • ORM cascade for creating aggregates, database ON DELETE for deleting them, RESTRICT by default, and estimate the fan-out first.
  • Hooks, listeners and subscribers do not fire for bulk and query-builder writes; anything that must always happen belongs in a pipe, a constraint or a trigger.
  • Generated migrations are drafts. synchronize: true and sync({ alter: true }) are how production columns disappear.
  • numeric and bigint are strings, timestamp without a zone is a bug waiting for a timezone change, and money belongs in bigint cents.
  • A connection acquire timeout means "the pool is exhausted", not "the database is down"; find the slow query, the leak or the network call inside the transaction before raising max.
  • The senior answer is hybrid: the ORM for CRUD and transactional writes, raw SQL for reports, windows, recursion, upserts, bulk work and queue claims — parameterised, zod-parsed, co-located in .sql files and tested against a real database.
  • Keep every ORM call behind repositories you own; that one decision is what makes changing ORMs, or mixing in raw SQL, a small project instead of a rewrite.

Part 22 — Database Scaling

Most backend systems never outgrow one PostgreSQL instance. That sentence surprises people, so let me put numbers on it. A single well-tuned PostgreSQL server on a modern machine (say 32 vCPU, 128 GB RAM, NVMe storage) handles tens of thousands of simple indexed queries per second, several thousand write transactions per second, and multiple terabytes of data. A food-delivery app doing 2,000 orders per minute, a SaaS product with 50,000 tenants, a social feed for a million daily users: all of these fit on one primary with a couple of replicas, provided the schema, indexes and queries are sane.

So why is "database scaling" a whole part of this book? Because the systems that do outgrow one instance fail in ugly, expensive ways, and because most teams reach for the heavy tools (sharding, a new database engine, a rewrite) long before they have exhausted the cheap ones. This part gives you the ladder a senior engineer climbs, rung by rung, and the mechanics of each rung: replication, lag, failover, partitioning, sharding, rebalancing, connection scaling and multi-tenant layouts. Everything is PostgreSQL-specific and wired into NestJS with TypeORM and Sequelize where it matters.

Keep the senior mantra next to you the whole way: Can it timeout? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed? Every rung of the ladder introduces a new way to answer "yes" to one of those.

22.1 The scaling ladder

Concept

The scaling ladder is the ordered list of interventions you try when a database is "slow" or "at capacity". The order matters: each rung is cheaper, safer and more reversible than the one after it, and each rung solves a specific class of problem. Skipping rungs is how teams end up sharding a database whose real problem was a missing index.

 6. Sharding            (split rows across databases; last resort)
 5. Partitioning        (split a huge table inside one database)
 4. Read replicas       (copy the data; route reads away from the primary)
 3. Caching             (do not ask the database at all)
 2. Connection pooling  (stop wasting the database on connection churn)
 1. Queries and indexes (make each request cheap)
 0. Measure             (know which of the above you actually need)

Why does it exist?

Databases become the bottleneck for one of five reasons: individual queries are expensive, there are too many connections, the same data is read over and over, one table is so big that every operation on it hurts, or the write volume exceeds what one machine can absorb. Each reason has a different cure. The ladder exists so you diagnose before you treat.

Without the ladder, engineers guess. The guess is usually "we need to scale horizontally", which is the most expensive guess available.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant whose kitchen cannot keep up. Before you build a second restaurant across town (sharding), you would check whether the chef is cooking each dish in the slowest possible way (bad queries), whether waiters are queuing at the pass instead of batching orders (connections), whether you could pre-cook the ten most popular dishes (caching), whether you could add a second line for cold dishes only (read replicas), and whether the walk-in fridge is so overstuffed that finding anything takes five minutes (a table that needs partitioning). Only when the single kitchen is genuinely at its physical limit do you open a second location, and you accept that the two kitchens will never share a fridge again.

How it works

  1. Measure. Turn on pg_stat_statements. Look at total_exec_time, calls, mean_exec_time and rows. Look at pg_stat_activity for connection counts and wait events. Look at CPU, IOPS, cache hit ratio (pg_stat_database.blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read)). A senior engineer refuses to scale anything before this step.
  2. Queries and indexes. The top ten statements by total time are almost always a handful of missing indexes, SELECT * on wide tables, N+1 loops from an ORM, or unbounded OFFSET pagination. Fixing them commonly buys 5x to 50x. See Part 19 — Indexes and Query Optimization.
  3. Connection pooling. Every PostgreSQL connection is a process with roughly 5 to 10 MB of memory and real CPU cost on connect. 40 pods with a pool of 20 each is 800 connections, which is already past the comfortable zone. PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes thousands of client connections onto tens of server connections. See section 22.9.
  4. Caching. Product pages, user profiles, configuration, permission sets: read a million times, changed once an hour. Redis answers in 0.2 to 1 ms and never touches the database. See Part 26 — Caching.
  5. Read replicas. When reads still dominate after caching, stream a copy of the data to one or more replicas and route read-only traffic there. Reads scale almost linearly with replica count; writes do not scale at all.
  6. Partitioning. When one table reaches hundreds of millions of rows, split it inside the same database by time, range or hash. Queries touch only the relevant partition; old data is dropped by dropping a partition.
  7. Sharding. When writes exceed a single machine, or the dataset exceeds what one machine can store and back up, split rows across independent databases by a shard key. You now own a distributed system.

Rough capacity of one tuned PostgreSQL instance, so you know when you are actually near the edge:

Dimension Comfortable single instance Where pain starts
Simple indexed reads 20,000 to 60,000 QPS CPU saturation, cache miss rate rising
Write transactions 2,000 to 10,000 TPS WAL write throughput, fsync latency, lock contention
Data size 1 to 5 TB Backups, vacuum, index bloat, restore time in hours
Single table 100 to 500 M rows Index size exceeds RAM, vacuum takes hours
Connections 100 to 300 active Memory, context switching, lock manager contention
Replication 2 to 5 streaming replicas Network bandwidth of WAL fan-out

Practical example

An e-commerce order service. p95 latency on GET /orders rose from 40 ms to 900 ms over three months. The team's first proposal was "move orders to a sharded cluster". A senior engineer opened pg_stat_statements and found one query responsible for 71% of total execution time: the order list endpoint filtered by user_id and sorted by created_at DESC, with an index only on user_id. Adding a composite index (user_id, created_at DESC) brought p95 back to 35 ms. Total cost: one migration, twenty minutes.

Production scenario

The decision table below is the one to keep in your head. The symptom column is what you observe; the fix column is the rung to try first.

Symptom you observe Likely cause First fix Next rung if not enough
A few queries dominate pg_stat_statements; CPU high Missing or wrong indexes, bad plans Add or fix indexes, rewrite queries Materialized views, caching
FATAL: too many connections, remaining connection slots are reserved Pool size × pods exceeds max_connections PgBouncer / RDS Proxy, smaller per-pod pools Fewer pods per DB, replicas
Read-heavy, same rows read constantly, cache hit ratio fine but CPU high No application caching Redis cache with TTL and invalidation Read replicas
Read-heavy, working set too large for cache, primary CPU saturated by SELECTs Reads and writes share one machine Read replicas with routed reads More replicas, CQRS read models
One table with hundreds of millions of rows; vacuum runs for hours; queries always filter by date Monolithic huge table Time-range partitioning, drop old partitions Archive to cold storage
Write TPS at the WAL/fsync limit; LWLock:WALWrite waits; primary IOPS maxed Write volume exceeds one machine Batching, async queues, move event/log tables elsewhere Sharding
One tenant or one user dominates load Hot key / hot shard Rate limits, dedicated resources, salting Dedicated shard
Replica lag climbing during backfills Replica cannot replay as fast as primary writes Throttle the writer by lag, bigger replica Logical replication for subsets

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Before touching architecture, a senior engineer asks four questions: What is the actual bottleneck (CPU, IOPS, memory, locks, connections)? Is it reads or writes? Is the load evenly spread or concentrated? What is the cheapest reversible change that addresses exactly that? They refuse to shard on a hunch. They also refuse the opposite mistake: pretending one instance will last forever when the write curve says it will not. The ladder is climbed deliberately, one rung at a time, with a measurement after each.

To a product manager: "We have six levers, ordered from cheap to expensive. We will pull the cheap ones this sprint and measure. If we still need the expensive ones we will plan them properly, because the expensive ones change how every feature is built."

Common mistakes

  • Sharding a database whose problem was three missing indexes.
  • Adding replicas for a write-bound system (replicas do not help writes; they add write cost).
  • Raising max_connections to 2,000 instead of adding a pooler.
  • Caching before measuring, so the cache hides a query that later resurfaces during a cold start.

Interview questions

  1. A team says "our database is slow, we need to shard". What do you ask first? Expected: which queries, which resource is saturated, reads or writes, what does pg_stat_statements show; sharding only helps write or storage limits.
  2. Roughly what can one PostgreSQL instance handle? Expected: tens of thousands of simple QPS, thousands of write TPS, TBs of data, depending on hardware and working set.
  3. Why is connection pooling before caching on the ladder? Expected: it is cheaper, has no invalidation problem, and connection storms cause outages independent of query cost.

22.2 Vertical scaling

Concept

Vertical scaling means running the same database on a bigger machine: more vCPUs, more RAM, faster or more storage. Nothing in the application changes. On AWS RDS it is a change of instance class (say from db.r6g.xlarge to db.r6g.4xlarge) and a change of storage type or provisioned IOPS.

Why does it exist?

Because it is the only scaling technique with zero application complexity. A larger machine raises every ceiling at once: CPU for query execution, RAM for shared_buffers and the OS page cache (which is what makes the working set fit in memory), and IOPS for writes and cache misses. For a large fraction of systems this is the right and final answer.

Mental model

Imagine the restaurant again. Vertical scaling is moving to a building with a bigger kitchen and more burners. Same staff, same menu, same fridge; nothing about how food is cooked changes. It works until you hit the largest building in town.

How it works

  1. RAM determines how much of the data and indexes stay in memory. Rule of thumb: if the working set (rows and index pages touched in a typical hour) fits in RAM, reads are served from memory at microseconds per page; if it does not, every miss is a disk read at 0.1 to 1 ms on NVMe or several ms on network storage.
  2. CPU determines how many concurrent queries execute. PostgreSQL uses one process per connection; a 16 vCPU box comfortably runs 16 to 32 active queries at once. More vCPUs also help parallel query for large scans.
  3. Storage IOPS and throughput determine write rate (every commit is a WAL fsync) and cache-miss read rate. On RDS, gp3 gives a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s, extendable to 16,000 IOPS; io2 goes to 256,000 IOPS at a much higher price.
  4. The change itself on RDS: modify the instance class, choose "apply immediately" or the maintenance window. Single-AZ: a few minutes of downtime. Multi-AZ: the standby is resized first, then a failover of roughly 60 seconds, then the old primary is resized. Applications see connection drops during that minute.

Cost curve, on-demand pricing for a memory-optimised family in one common region, to make the tradeoff concrete:

Instance class vCPU RAM Approx. monthly cost (single-AZ)
db.r6g.large 2 16 GB ~$170
db.r6g.xlarge 4 32 GB ~$340
db.r6g.4xlarge 16 128 GB ~$1,350
db.r6g.16xlarge 64 512 GB ~$5,400
db.r6g.16xlarge Multi-AZ 64 512 GB ~$10,800

Cost doubles as capacity doubles up to the largest class, then there is no next rung. That flat wall is the limit of vertical scaling: after the biggest instance, the only direction is architectural.

Practical example

A ride-booking platform's PostgreSQL primary ran on db.r6g.2xlarge (64 GB). The dataset was 90 GB, the hot working set about 55 GB. Cache hit ratio had dropped to 91%, and pg_stat_activity showed many sessions in IO:DataFileRead. Moving to db.r6g.4xlarge (128 GB) put the whole working set in memory; hit ratio went to 99.6% and p95 latency fell from 120 ms to 18 ms. No code changed. Cost went from ~$680 to ~$1,350 per month, far cheaper than the engineering weeks any other option would need.

PostgreSQL example

After resizing, the memory settings must follow the machine, otherwise the extra RAM sits unused.

-- Check current settings (RDS manages these via parameter groups).
SHOW shared_buffers;          -- typically 25% of RAM
SHOW effective_cache_size;    -- typically 50-75% of RAM; a planner hint, not an allocation
SHOW work_mem;                -- per sort/hash per query node; raise carefully
SHOW maintenance_work_mem;    -- for VACUUM and CREATE INDEX

-- Is the working set in memory? Below 99% on an OLTP system is worth investigating.
SELECT datname,
       round(100.0 * blks_hit / NULLIF(blks_hit + blks_read, 0), 2) AS cache_hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_database
WHERE datname = current_database();

Production scenario

When vertical scaling is the right answer: the working set almost fits in RAM; IOPS is the ceiling and provisioned IOPS solves it; the team is small and cannot operate replicas or shards; the business runway is measured in years and the instance class ladder still has several rungs left.

When it is not: writes are already at the fsync limit on the largest class; the data set is 10 TB and restore-from-backup takes a day; a single machine is a single point of failure and the availability target demands more; the cost curve has crossed what a replica pair would cost.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Resize on Multi-AZ causes a failover; the application must reconnect and retry idempotent work (see section 22.6).
  • Bigger RAM without adjusting shared_buffers and effective_cache_size leaves the planner making choices for a smaller machine.
  • Burstable classes (db.t3, db.t4g) exhaust CPU credits under sustained load and become dramatically slower; never run production primaries on them.
  • Storage cannot be shrunk on RDS; over-provisioning storage is a permanent cost.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

"Buy the bigger box" is not a cop-out; it is usually the most cost-effective engineering decision available, because engineering time is the expensive resource. The senior engineer's job is to know where the wall is (the largest instance class, the write throughput of one machine) and to start the architectural work at least a year before hitting it, not the week after.

Interview questions

  1. When is vertical scaling the wrong answer? Expected: write-bound at the top instance, dataset too large to restore in acceptable time, availability requirements, cost crossover.
  2. What changes after resizing an RDS instance? Expected: memory parameters should be revisited; a Multi-AZ resize causes a failover.

22.3 Read replicas

Concept

A read replica is a second PostgreSQL server that continuously receives the primary's write-ahead log (WAL) and applies it, so it holds a copy of the data that is a little behind the primary. Clients can run SELECT queries on it. They cannot write to it. Adding replicas multiplies read capacity; it does nothing for write capacity.

Why does it exist?

On most OLTP systems, reads outnumber writes by 10:1 to 100:1. Once caching has taken the easy reads, what remains is still mostly reads: order histories, search listings, dashboards, reports. Running those on the primary steals CPU and memory from the writes that only the primary can do. Replicas also give you a warm copy for failover and a place to run heavy analytical queries without hurting production writes.

Mental model

Imagine a busy notary office. Only the head notary (the primary) may stamp new documents. But copies of every stamped document are couriered to three reading rooms (replicas) as soon as they are stamped. Anyone who wants to read a document goes to a reading room. The catch: a document stamped ten seconds ago may not have arrived in the reading room yet. That delay is replication lag, and it is the whole difficulty of using replicas correctly.

How it works

  1. Every change on the primary is first written to the WAL (a sequential log of page changes) before the data files are touched. This is the same log that makes crash recovery possible.
  2. A replica connects to the primary with a replication connection and streams WAL records as they are generated. This is physical (streaming) replication: it copies byte-level page changes, so the replica is an exact binary copy of the primary, same PostgreSQL major version, same everything.
  3. The replica's startup process replays the WAL continuously. Because the replica is running in "recovery" mode while also accepting read-only connections, this is called hot standby.
  4. Logical replication is different: it decodes WAL into row-level changes (insert/update/delete of specific rows in specific tables) and sends them to a subscriber, which applies them as ordinary SQL. It can replicate a subset of tables, cross major versions, and even into a database with a different schema. It is slower and has more caveats (no DDL, sequences are not replicated). Section 22.4 covers both in depth.
  5. The application decides, per query, whether to send it to the primary or a replica. This routing is where the engineering lives.
flowchart LR
    App["NestJS pods"] -->|"writes and consistent reads"| P["Primary PostgreSQL"]
    App -->|"read-only queries"| R1["Replica 1"]
    App -->|"read-only queries"| R2["Replica 2"]
    P -->|"WAL stream"| R1
    P -->|"WAL stream"| R2
    R2 -->|"WAL stream cascading"| R3["Replica 3 for reporting"]

Which reads are safe to send to a replica? The test is: would the user notice if this data were a few seconds old?

Read Safe on replica? Why
Product catalog listing Yes Changes are rare and nobody expects instant consistency
Search results Yes Already eventually consistent
Public user profile Yes Seconds of staleness are invisible
Reports and dashboards Yes Ideal for a dedicated reporting replica
"My orders" list right after placing an order No, or only with a read-your-own-writes guard The user expects to see what they just did
Reading a row to decide a write (inventory check, balance check) No Must be on the primary, inside the transaction, with the right lock
Anything inside a transaction that writes No Transactions are pinned to one connection, and it must be the primary
Auth token lookup after login Risky A token created 200 ms ago may not have replicated

Practical example

A food-delivery app: the restaurant menu page is 60% of all database reads. Menus change a few times a day. Sending menu reads to two replicas removed roughly half the load from the primary and cut primary CPU from 78% to 35%, leaving headroom for the order and payment writes that only the primary can serve.

NestJS example

Routing reads in TypeORM is built in. You declare replication in the DataSource options. TypeORM then sends find* methods and SELECT query builders to a random replica, and everything else (writes, raw query(), anything inside a transaction) to the master.

// src/database/database.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Module({
  imports: [
    TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
      imports: [ConfigModule],
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
        type: 'postgres',
        autoLoadEntities: true,
        replication: {
          // All writes, raw queries and transactions go here.
          master: {
            host: config.getOrThrow('PG_PRIMARY_HOST'),
            port: 5432,
            username: config.getOrThrow('PG_USER'),
            password: config.getOrThrow('PG_PASSWORD'),
            database: config.getOrThrow('PG_DB'),
          },
          // Read-only SELECTs from find* and query builders go to a random slave.
          slaves: [
            { host: config.getOrThrow('PG_REPLICA_1_HOST'), port: 5432,
              username: config.getOrThrow('PG_USER'), password: config.getOrThrow('PG_PASSWORD'),
              database: config.getOrThrow('PG_DB') },
            { host: config.getOrThrow('PG_REPLICA_2_HOST'), port: 5432,
              username: config.getOrThrow('PG_USER'), password: config.getOrThrow('PG_PASSWORD'),
              database: config.getOrThrow('PG_DB') },
          ],
        },
        extra: { max: 10, connectionTimeoutMillis: 3000, statement_timeout: 5000 },
      }),
    }),
  ],
})
export class DatabaseModule {}

The important consequence: with replication configured, a plain repository.findOne() is a replica read. If a service reads a row and then writes based on it, that read must be explicitly forced to the primary.

// src/orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  // Listing is tolerant to a few seconds of staleness: let TypeORM pick a replica.
  async listForUser(userId: string): Promise<Order[]> {
    return this.dataSource.getRepository(Order).find({
      where: { userId },
      order: { createdAt: 'DESC' },
      take: 50,
    });
  }

  // Explicit replica read for a report query built with the query builder.
  async dailyRevenue(day: string): Promise<{ total: string }> {
    const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner('slave'); // force replica
    try {
      return await this.dataSource
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .select('SUM(o.total_cents)', 'total')
        .from(Order, 'o')
        .where('o.created_at::date = :day', { day })
        .setQueryRunner(runner)
        .getRawOne();
    } finally {
      await runner.release(); // always return the connection to the pool
    }
  }

  // Must be fresh: the order was just created and the client is polling for it.
  async getFreshById(orderId: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner('master'); // force primary
    try {
      return await runner.manager.findOne(Order, { where: { id: orderId } });
    } finally {
      await runner.release();
    }
  }
}

Two rules to remember with TypeORM replication: dataSource.query('SELECT ...') always goes to the master, and any operation inside dataSource.transaction(...) or a query runner that has started a transaction is on the master.

Sequelize example

Sequelize has the same idea with read and write in replication. Reads use a round-robin over read hosts; useMaster: true on a query forces the primary.

// src/database/sequelize.provider.ts
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export const sequelize = new Sequelize(process.env.PG_DB!, undefined, undefined, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  replication: {
    write: { host: process.env.PG_PRIMARY_HOST!, username: process.env.PG_USER!, password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD! },
    read: [
      { host: process.env.PG_REPLICA_1_HOST!, username: process.env.PG_USER!, password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD! },
      { host: process.env.PG_REPLICA_2_HOST!, username: process.env.PG_USER!, password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD! },
    ],
  },
  pool: { max: 10, min: 0, idle: 10_000, acquire: 5_000 },
  logging: false,
});

// Usage in a service:
// await Order.findAll({ where: { userId } });                 // replica (round-robin)
// await Order.findByPk(orderId, { useMaster: true });         // primary, fresh read
// await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => { ... });          // everything inside is on the primary

The read-your-own-writes problem

This is the single most common replica bug, so it gets its own walkthrough.

A user taps "Place order". The request writes the order on the primary and returns 201. The mobile app immediately requests GET /orders. That read is routed to a replica which is 300 ms behind. The list does not contain the new order. The user taps "Place order" again. Now there are two orders. Nobody wrote a bug in the ordinary sense; the system simply never promised that a read after a write sees the write.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as NestJS
    participant P as Primary
    participant R as Replica
    C->>A: POST /orders
    A->>P: INSERT order
    P-->>A: committed at LSN 0/5A3F
    A-->>C: 201 Created
    C->>A: GET /orders
    A->>R: SELECT orders
    Note over R: replayed only to LSN 0/5A10
    R-->>A: list without the new order
    A-->>C: 200 stale list

There are four workable solutions, from simplest to most precise.

1. Sticky routing after a write. After any write for a user, route that user's reads to the primary for a short window (say 5 seconds). Implement with a Redis key rw:{userId} with a 5 s TTL set on every write, and a request-scoped decision that checks it.

// src/database/read-routing.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Injectable()
export class ReadRoutingService {
  private static readonly STICKY_SECONDS = 5;

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource, private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  // Call after every write on behalf of a user.
  async markWrote(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.set(`rw:${userId}`, '1', 'EX', ReadRoutingService.STICKY_SECONDS);
  }

  // Choose a query runner: primary if the user wrote recently, replica otherwise.
  async runnerFor(userId: string): Promise<QueryRunner> {
    const recentlyWrote = await this.redis.exists(`rw:${userId}`);
    return this.dataSource.createQueryRunner(recentlyWrote ? 'master' : 'slave');
  }
}

The 5-second window is a guess that is wrong when lag spikes to 30 seconds during a backfill. That is why the next options exist.

2. Session-level consistency by LSN. After a write, ask the primary for its current WAL position and hand that position to the client (in a cookie or response header). On the next read, the replica is asked whether it has replayed at least that far; if not, the read goes to the primary. This is exact, not a guess.

-- On the primary, right after the write commits (same connection or a separate quick call):
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();              -- e.g. 0/5A3F2C10

-- On a replica, before serving a read that must include that write:
SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();          -- e.g. 0/5A3F1000
-- Is the replica caught up to the client's LSN? Positive means still behind.
SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff('0/5A3F2C10', pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()) AS bytes_behind;

3. LSN wait on the replica. Same as option 2, but instead of falling back to the primary, the read handler polls the replica a few times (10 ms apart, up to say 200 ms) until bytes_behind <= 0, then reads. This keeps load off the primary at the cost of a little latency. PostgreSQL 18 introduced a built-in pg_wal_replay_wait() procedure for this; on earlier versions you loop in the application.

4. Route by endpoint intent. Endpoints that are semantically "what did I just do" (GET /orders/:id immediately after creation, the checkout confirmation page) simply always read from the primary. Endpoints that are "browse" read from replicas. This is coarse but trivially correct and is a good default for small teams.

Production scenario

A payments dashboard at 4,000 read RPS and 150 write RPS. Two replicas each take 45% of reads; the primary keeps 10% (the sticky-routed and intent-routed fresh reads) plus all writes. Typical replication lag is 20 to 80 ms; during nightly reconciliation batches it rises to 3 to 8 seconds. The sticky window is 10 seconds and lag is alerted at 5 seconds so someone knows when the guess is about to be wrong. Replica reads p95 at 6 ms; primary writes p95 at 9 ms.

Failure scenario

At 09:12 the on-call is paged: "Duplicate orders spiking." A backfill job started at 09:00 is rewriting a 200-million-row table on the primary and replicas are 40 seconds behind. The mobile app's order-list read is going to a replica, users see no order, they retry. The immediate fix is an environment flag that routes all order reads to the primary; the primary's CPU rises to 70% but the duplicates stop. The long-term fixes are: throttle the backfill by replication lag (Part 23 — Database Migrations shows the script), apply the LSN-based consistency check, and add idempotency keys to POST /orders so a retry cannot create a second order regardless of what the client saw.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale read after write: covered above; assume it will happen and design for it.
  • Replica missing from DNS during a rebuild; the pool keeps failing to connect. Use a replica endpoint (RDS reader endpoint, or a load balancer) rather than hardcoding hosts, and health-check the pool.
  • Query cancelled on replica: ERROR: canceling statement due to conflict with recovery. A long report on the replica held a snapshot; the primary vacuumed rows the replica still needed. Either enable hot_standby_feedback = on (which makes the primary keep those rows, at the cost of bloat) or raise max_standby_streaming_delay on the reporting replica, or move long reports to a dedicated replica where delay is acceptable.
  • Transactions accidentally on a replica: writes fail with cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. Every ORM routes transactions to the master, but hand-built query runners can get this wrong.
  • Pool arithmetic: each pod now has a pool for the primary and for each replica; 40 pods × (10 + 10 + 10) = 1,200 connections. See section 22.9.
  • Replica load imbalance: TypeORM picks a random replica per query and Sequelize round-robins; neither is load-aware. A replica that is slow (running a big report) still gets its share. Put replicas behind a load balancer with health checks if this bites you.
  • Sequences and temporary tables do not exist on a hot standby; code that does SELECT nextval(...) on a replica fails.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Replicas are cheap capacity with a tax: every read now needs a consistency decision. The senior engineer makes that decision explicit in code (a method name like getFreshById, a routing service, an endpoint annotation), never implicit in "whatever the ORM picks". They pair replicas with idempotency on writes, because stale reads cause client retries, and retries without idempotency cause duplicates. They alert on lag before users notice it.

Common mistakes

  • Turning on replication in TypeORM and forgetting that every existing findOne silently became a replica read.
  • Reading a balance from a replica and then writing a debit on the primary. That is a lost update waiting to happen.
  • Assuming lag is always 50 ms because that is what it was during the demo.
  • Running the same pool size against replicas as against the primary without recounting total connections.

Interview questions

  1. How would you route reads to replicas in a NestJS application, and what would you refuse to route? Expected: TypeORM replication config or Sequelize replication; refuse reads that feed a write, reads inside transactions, and read-your-own-writes paths without a guard.
  2. Explain the read-your-own-writes problem and two solutions. Expected: stale replica after a write; sticky routing after write with a TTL, LSN-based check with pg_current_wal_lsn / pg_last_wal_replay_lsn.
  3. What does hot_standby_feedback do and what does it cost? Expected: replica tells the primary which rows it still needs so vacuum does not remove them; cost is bloat on the primary.
  4. Do replicas help write throughput? Expected: no; they add a small cost to the primary (WAL sending) and help only reads and availability.

Practical exercise

Configure a local primary and one replica with Docker (bitnami/postgresql images support POSTGRESQL_REPLICATION_MODE). Wire a NestJS OrdersModule with TypeORM replication. Write a POST /orders followed immediately by GET /orders in a test and observe the stale read with a replica delayed via recovery_min_apply_delay = '2s'. Then implement sticky routing and the LSN check and show both tests pass. Acceptance criteria: the stale-read test reproduces reliably before the fix and passes after; total connection count is documented and below max_connections.

22.4 Replication mechanics

Concept

Replication is the process by which a change made on one PostgreSQL server appears on another. In PostgreSQL every change is described first in the write-ahead log (WAL); replication is, at its core, shipping that log somewhere else and replaying it. The variants differ in what is shipped (raw page changes or decoded row changes), how it is shipped (files or a live stream), and when the primary considers a commit done (before or after the replica has it).

Why does it exist?

Three reasons. Availability: if the primary dies you need a copy that is seconds behind, not a backup that is hours old. Read scaling: a copy can serve queries. Integration: other systems (search indexes, data warehouses, caches) want to know about every change without polling the tables. Each reason pulls toward a slightly different replication mode.

Mental model

Imagine a bookkeeper who writes every transaction in a journal before touching the ledger. Physical replication is photocopying the journal pages and mailing them to a second office that maintains an identical ledger. Streaming replication is a fax line that sends every line as soon as it is written. Logical replication is a clerk reading the journal aloud over the phone in plain words ("customer 42 paid 30 dollars"), so the far office can write it into a differently formatted ledger, or only note the entries it cares about. Synchronous replication is refusing to tell the customer "done" until the far office confirms it has written the line.

How it works

WAL shipping (archive-based). The primary finishes a 16 MB WAL segment file and archive_command copies it to shared storage (S3, NFS). The standby's restore_command fetches segments and replays them. Lag is at least one segment, typically minutes. Today it is mostly used as the backup mechanism (point-in-time recovery) and as a fallback when streaming falls behind.

Streaming replication. The standby opens a replication connection (primary_conninfo) to the primary's WAL sender process and receives WAL records as they are written, at the byte level. Lag is normally milliseconds. This is what RDS read replicas and Multi-AZ standbys use.

Replication slots. A slot is a named bookmark on the primary that says "replica X has consumed WAL up to here; do not delete anything after this point". Without a slot, a replica that disconnects for an hour comes back to find the WAL it needs already recycled, and must be rebuilt from a base backup. With a slot, the primary keeps the WAL. That safety has a sharp edge described in the failure modes below.

Synchronous vs asynchronous. Asynchronous (the default): the primary commits, acknowledges to the client, and streams the WAL whenever it can. A crash between commit and stream loses that transaction on failover. Synchronous: the primary waits for one or more standbys to confirm before acknowledging. The level of confirmation is synchronous_commit: remote_write (standby received and passed to the OS), on (standby fsynced it to disk), remote_apply (standby has replayed it, so a read there sees it). Every step up costs commit latency: on the same availability zone a synchronous commit adds roughly 1 to 3 ms; across regions, 30 to 100 ms.

Quorum commit. synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (replica_a, replica_b, replica_c)' means the commit waits for any two of the three. This keeps a durable copy without a single slow standby stalling every commit.

Logical replication. wal_level = logical makes the primary decode WAL into row changes. A PUBLICATION names the tables; a SUBSCRIPTION on another database connects and applies changes with ordinary inserts, updates and deletes. It works across major versions (the standard zero-downtime upgrade path), can replicate a subset of tables or even filtered rows and columns (PostgreSQL 15+), and the subscriber is a normal writable database. It does not replicate DDL, sequences or large objects, and the initial sync of a big table can take hours.

CDC with Debezium. Change Data Capture uses the same logical decoding (through the pgoutput plugin) but the consumer is Debezium, a Kafka Connect connector. Every row change becomes a Kafka message with before and after images. This is how you feed a search index, a cache invalidator or a data warehouse without dual writes from the application, and it is the mechanism behind the transactional outbox pattern (see Part 27 — Messaging Patterns).

flowchart TB
    W["Client write"] --> WAL["WAL on primary"]
    WAL -->|"streaming, bytes"| S1["Hot standby replica"]
    WAL -->|"archive_command"| ARC["WAL archive S3"]
    WAL -->|"logical decoding pgoutput"| LR["Logical subscriber"]
    WAL -->|"logical decoding pgoutput"| DBZ["Debezium connector"]
    DBZ --> K["Kafka topic per table"]
    K --> ES["Search indexer"]
    K --> DW["Warehouse loader"]

PostgreSQL example

Setting up a publication and inspecting the state of streaming replication.

-- On the primary: allow logical decoding (requires restart) and streaming.
-- postgresql.conf: wal_level = logical, max_wal_senders = 10, max_replication_slots = 10

-- Physical replication slot for a streaming replica (created before the replica connects).
SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('replica_1_slot');

-- Logical replication of only the orders and order_items tables.
CREATE PUBLICATION orders_pub FOR TABLE orders, order_items;

-- On the subscriber database (another server):
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION orders_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=primary.internal dbname=shop user=repl password=...'
  PUBLICATION orders_pub;

-- Who is replicating from me, and how far behind is each?
SELECT client_addr, state, sync_state,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)) AS replay_behind,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- Slots and how much WAL each is holding on disk. Watch this.
SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, wal_status,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained_wal
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Configuring synchronous quorum commit:

-- postgresql.conf on the primary
-- synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (replica_a, replica_b)'
-- synchronous_commit = on

-- Per-transaction override: a non-critical write can skip the wait.
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off;      -- audit log rows: losing one on crash is acceptable
INSERT INTO audit_events (actor_id, action) VALUES ('u_42', 'viewed_invoice');
COMMIT;

Production scenario

A typical production layout on AWS: one primary in AZ-a, a synchronous standby in AZ-b (RDS Multi-AZ does this for you, with the standby not readable), two asynchronous read replicas, and a Debezium connector feeding Kafka. The synchronous standby adds about 2 ms to every commit; write p95 goes from 7 ms to 9 ms and the business gets zero data loss on AZ failure. The read replicas lag 30 to 100 ms in steady state. Debezium lag is usually under a second, but a single 50-million-row UPDATE produces 50 million Kafka messages and the connector spends an hour catching up.

Failure scenario

The replication slot incident. A team created a Debezium connector, then decommissioned it a month later by deleting the Kafka Connect deployment. Nobody dropped the replication slot. The slot's active became false but the primary faithfully kept every WAL segment the dead consumer "might still need". Three weeks later at 03:40 the primary's disk hit 100%, PostgreSQL entered a state where it could not write WAL, and every write in the company failed with PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp". Recovery was SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_slot') followed by a checkpoint, once someone could get a connection. The fix afterwards: an alert on pg_replication_slots where active = false for more than 15 minutes, and max_slot_wal_keep_size = '50GB' (PostgreSQL 13+) so a runaway slot is invalidated instead of filling the disk.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Inactive slot fills the disk: described above. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size, alert on inactive slots and on wal_status = 'unreserved' or 'lost'.
  • Async replica promoted after a crash: transactions acknowledged to clients but not yet streamed are gone. The client received 201 for an order that no longer exists. Only synchronous replication prevents this; otherwise idempotent clients and reconciliation jobs are the mitigation.
  • Synchronous standby down: with synchronous_standby_names naming one standby and no ANY quorum, every commit hangs forever waiting. Always have at least two candidates, or automation that removes the dead one from the list.
  • Logical replication conflicts: a unique violation on the subscriber stops the subscription entirely until a human resolves it (PostgreSQL 15+ can skip a transaction with ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP). Never write to subscriber tables that are also replicated into.
  • Logical replication and sequences: after failing over to a logical subscriber, sequences are at their initial values; you must setval every sequence above the maximum existing id first.
  • Major version mismatch: physical replication requires identical major versions; only logical replication crosses them.
  • Large transactions: logical decoding only sends a transaction after commit (unless streaming of in-progress transactions is enabled, PostgreSQL 14+), so a 2-hour batch job appears as a huge burst at the end.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick the replication mode per requirement, not per fashion: a synchronous standby for durability, asynchronous replicas for read scaling, logical replication for upgrades and selective copies, CDC for integration. They know exactly which transactions can be lost on failover and have written that number down for the business. They treat replication slots as a liability that needs monitoring on day one.

Interview questions

  1. Difference between physical and logical replication? Expected: byte-level page changes vs decoded row changes; physical is an exact copy same version; logical is selective, cross-version, writable subscriber, no DDL.
  2. What is a replication slot and what is the danger? Expected: a bookmark preventing WAL deletion; an abandoned slot fills the disk; mitigate with max_slot_wal_keep_size and alerts.
  3. When would you use synchronous replication and what does it cost? Expected: when losing acknowledged commits is unacceptable; adds a network round trip to every commit and a dependency on the standby's health; quorum commit reduces the risk.
  4. How does Debezium get changes out of PostgreSQL? Expected: logical decoding via pgoutput from a replication slot, publishing before/after row images to Kafka.

22.5 Replication lag

Concept

Replication lag is the delay between a change committing on the primary and that change being visible on a replica. It has two units: bytes (how much WAL the replica has not yet replayed) and time (how old the replica's view is). Both matter. Byte lag tells you about throughput trouble; time lag tells you what users will experience.

Why does it exist?

Lag exists because replication is asynchronous by default and because the replica must do real work to apply changes: write WAL to its disk, replay it into data pages, and possibly wait for its own long-running queries to finish. Anything that makes the primary write faster than the replica can apply, or that pauses replay, creates lag.

Mental model

Imagine subtitles on a live broadcast. The speaker is the primary; the subtitler is the replica. Normally the subtitles trail by a second. When the speaker suddenly talks very fast (a bulk update) the subtitler falls behind. When the subtitler takes a phone call (a long query conflicting with replay) the subtitles freeze while the speaker continues. When nobody is speaking at all, the subtitles look "stuck" at the last line, which is not lag at all, just silence.

How it works

Causes of lag, in the order you should suspect them:

  1. Write bursts on the primary. Bulk updates, backfills, index builds, VACUUM FULL, large deletes. WAL generation jumps from 5 MB/s to 200 MB/s; the replica's single replay process cannot keep up.
  2. Replay conflicts. A long SELECT on the replica holds a snapshot; incoming WAL wants to remove rows that snapshot needs. The replica either cancels the query (after max_standby_streaming_delay, default 30 s) or delays replay. During that delay, lag grows.
  3. Slow replica hardware or storage. A smaller instance class than the primary, or cheaper storage, applies WAL slower than the primary generates it.
  4. Network. Cross-region replicas ride a WAN; bandwidth spikes or partitions cause both byte and time lag.
  5. Replica busy with its own load. CPU starved by the reads you routed there.

Measuring lag:

-- On the primary: per-replica lag in bytes and time (PostgreSQL 10+).
SELECT application_name, state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), sent_lsn)   AS send_lag_bytes,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS replay_lag_bytes,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag                   -- intervals
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- On the replica: how old is my view of the world?
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS time_lag,
       pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() AS received,
       pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()  AS replayed,
       pg_is_in_recovery()       AS is_replica;

A subtlety: now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() grows during idle periods when the primary has committed nothing, because there is nothing new to replay. Compare receive and replay LSNs to distinguish "idle" from "behind": if received = replayed, the replica is caught up regardless of the timestamp.

NestJS example

Expose lag as a metric and use it as a routing signal. This provider polls each replica every two seconds and lets the routing layer avoid replicas that are too far behind.

// src/database/replica-lag.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class ReplicaLagService implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ReplicaLagService.name);
  private lagSeconds = 0;

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  onModuleInit(): void { void this.refresh(); }

  @Interval(2000)
  async refresh(): Promise<void> {
    const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner('slave');
    try {
      const [row] = await runner.query(`
        SELECT CASE WHEN pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() = pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() THEN 0
                    ELSE EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()) END AS lag`);
      this.lagSeconds = Number(row.lag ?? 0);
      if (this.lagSeconds > 5) this.logger.warn(`replica lag ${this.lagSeconds.toFixed(1)}s`);
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.error('lag probe failed', err as Error);
      this.lagSeconds = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY; // treat unknown as unusable
    } finally {
      await runner.release();
    }
  }

  // Routing layer asks this before choosing a replica for a "fresh enough" read.
  replicaAcceptable(maxLagSeconds: number): boolean {
    return this.lagSeconds <= maxLagSeconds;
  }
}

Export lagSeconds as a Prometheus gauge (pg_replica_lag_seconds) and alert at, say, 5 s warning and 30 s critical. If you use RDS, the ReplicaLag CloudWatch metric gives the same number without the probe.

Production scenario

The incident everyone eventually has: "User paid but the order list shows unpaid." The flow is: payment webhook arrives, the worker updates orders.status = 'paid' on the primary, then publishes a push notification "Your payment was received". The user opens the app; GET /orders hits a replica 6 seconds behind because a marketing export is running a huge UPDATE on user_segments. The order shows "awaiting payment". Support tickets follow. The user retries the payment; thanks to the payment provider's idempotency key the second charge is rejected, but the user has now seen a scary screen. The mitigations: route order-status reads for a user who received a status-change notification in the last 30 seconds to the primary; throttle exports by lag; and stop marketing exports from running on the same database as orders at all (a separate reporting replica with max_standby_streaming_delay = -1).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lag looks huge but the primary is idle: timestamp-based lag on a quiet primary; compare LSNs.
  • Lag spikes to minutes during a migration: throttle the migration (Part 23) and pre-warn the on-call.
  • Replica cancels queries: canceling statement due to conflict with recovery. Options: hot_standby_feedback, longer max_standby_streaming_delay, dedicated reporting replica.
  • Lag on the synchronous standby stalls the primary: if synchronous_commit = remote_apply, replay lag on the standby becomes commit latency on the primary.
  • Cascading replicas add lag at each hop.
  • Cache invalidation racing lag: the app invalidates a Redis key on write, the next reader repopulates it from a stale replica, and the stale value now lives in the cache for its full TTL. Repopulate caches from the primary, or delay invalidation by the expected lag.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Lag is not a bug to eliminate; it is a property to bound and to design around. They set a lag budget per read path ("this endpoint tolerates 5 seconds; that one tolerates none") and they make the writers that cause lag (batch jobs, backfills) responsible for staying inside the budget. The most important question they ask of any feature that reads from a replica is: what does the user do when this is stale? If the answer is "retry the write", idempotency is mandatory.

Interview questions

  1. How do you measure replication lag and what is the trap in the timestamp approach? Expected: pg_stat_replication on the primary, pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp on the replica; idle primaries inflate timestamp lag; compare LSNs.
  2. A backfill causes 40 s lag and stale reads. What do you do now and later? Expected: now, route affected reads to the primary and pause or throttle the job; later, lag-aware throttling, LSN-based consistency, idempotent writes.
  3. What causes replay conflicts and how do you handle them on a reporting replica? Expected: vacuum on the primary removing rows a replica query needs; raise max_standby_streaming_delay or use hot_standby_feedback.

22.6 Failover

Concept

Failover is the process of turning a replica into the new primary when the old primary is dead, unreachable or being replaced. It has a database side (promotion, deciding who is primary) and an application side (finding the new primary, reconnecting, dealing with work that was in flight). Both sides must be designed; the database side is often provided by a platform (RDS Multi-AZ, Patroni), the application side is always your responsibility.

Why does it exist?

Machines die. Availability zones lose power. Instance resizes and major version upgrades require a restart. A business that promises 99.95% availability has about 4.4 hours of downtime per year to spend; one unplanned failover with a manual rebuild can spend all of it. Automated failover turns a multi-hour outage into a 30 to 90 second blip.

Mental model

Imagine an air traffic control tower with a duty controller and a shadow controller listening to every radio call. If the duty controller collapses, the shadow takes over; pilots are told to switch frequency. The danger: if the radio link between the two towers merely glitched, both might believe they are in charge and issue conflicting instructions. That is split brain, and it is why failover systems have a third party (a consensus store or a witness) to decide who is really in charge.

How it works

  1. Detection. A health checker (Patroni's loop, RDS's monitoring, a Kubernetes operator) notices the primary is unresponsive for longer than a threshold, typically 10 to 30 seconds. Too short and network hiccups trigger needless failovers; too long and the outage lengthens.
  2. Fencing. The old primary must be prevented from accepting writes even if it comes back. Patroni does this by requiring a leader lease in etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper; a primary that cannot renew its lease demotes itself. Without fencing, two primaries accept writes for the same rows: split brain.
  3. Promotion. The chosen replica runs pg_promote() (or pg_ctl promote), stops replaying WAL, and starts a new timeline. Any transactions the old primary committed but had not streamed are lost (asynchronous) or guaranteed present (synchronous).
  4. Endpoint switch. Clients need to find the new primary. Options: a DNS name updated to the new IP (RDS does this; TTL is 5 seconds), a virtual IP moved by Patroni's callback, an HAProxy or PgBouncer reconfigured, or a Kubernetes Service selector updated by the operator.
  5. Re-pointing other replicas. Remaining replicas must follow the new primary. With pg_rewind the old primary can be turned into a replica without a full rebuild, provided its data directory is intact.
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as NestJS pool
    participant DNS as DB endpoint DNS
    participant P1 as Old primary
    participant P2 as Standby
    participant W as Watchdog
    App->>P1: writes
    P1--xW: health checks fail 3 times
    W->>P1: fence, revoke leader lease
    W->>P2: pg_promote
    P2-->>W: promoted, new timeline
    W->>DNS: point endpoint at P2, TTL 5s
    App->>P1: write fails, connection reset
    App->>DNS: resolve endpoint
    App->>P2: reconnect, retry idempotent work

What the application must do, in order:

  • Detect broken connections quickly. Pool connections to the dead primary are broken sockets. Set TCP keepalives and short connectionTimeoutMillis so a broken connection is discovered in seconds, not after the OS's default 2-hour keepalive.
  • Drain and rebuild the pool. On ECONNRESET, 57P01 admin_shutdown, 25006 read_only_sql_transaction (you are talking to the demoted old primary), evict the connection and reconnect. node-postgres pools remove broken clients on error; make sure your health check exercises a query, not just a socket.
  • Resolve DNS again. Node caches DNS per lookup, not globally, so a new connection will re-resolve. But a long-lived connection never re-resolves; only reconnection picks up the new address. Never pin the IP.
  • Retry idempotent work; do not retry the rest blindly. A SELECT can be retried. An INSERT whose transaction was in flight when the failover hit is in an unknown state: it may have committed on the old primary and been lost, or committed and replicated, or never committed. Only an idempotency key (Part 29 — Idempotency) makes retry safe.
  • Stop background writers for a moment. Workers pounding the endpoint during failover create a retry storm that slows the new primary's warm-up. Use exponential backoff with jitter.

NestJS example

A connection layer that survives failover: keepalive, short connect timeout, health check that detects a read-only (demoted) primary, and a retry wrapper for idempotent operations.

// src/database/typeorm.options.ts
import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';

export const typeOrmOptions = (): TypeOrmModuleOptions => ({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.PG_WRITER_ENDPOINT, // DNS name, never an IP; RDS TTL is 5 s
  port: 5432,
  username: process.env.PG_USER,
  password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD,
  database: process.env.PG_DB,
  autoLoadEntities: true,
  extra: {
    max: 10,
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,   // fail fast while DNS is switching
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,        // recycle idle connections so they re-resolve DNS
    keepAlive: true,
    keepAliveInitialDelayMillis: 10_000,
    statement_timeout: 5_000,
  },
});
// src/database/with-failover-retry.ts
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';

const RETRYABLE = new Set(['57P01', '57P02', '57P03', '08006', '08001', '25006', 'ECONNRESET', 'ECONNREFUSED']);
const logger = new Logger('FailoverRetry');

// Only wrap operations that are idempotent (reads, or writes guarded by an idempotency key).
export async function withFailoverRetry<T>(op: () => Promise<T>, attempts = 4): Promise<T> {
  let delay = 200;
  for (let i = 1; ; i++) {
    try {
      return await op();
    } catch (err) {
      const code = (err as { code?: string }).code ?? '';
      if (!RETRYABLE.has(code) || i === attempts) throw err;
      logger.warn(`retryable db error ${code}, attempt ${i}/${attempts}`);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay + Math.random() * delay)); // jittered backoff
      delay = Math.min(delay * 2, 3_000);
    }
  }
}

A Terminus health indicator that reports "not ready" if the writer endpoint answers but is in recovery, which happens for a few seconds when DNS still points at the demoted node:

// src/health/writer-health.indicator.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthIndicatorService } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class WriterHealthIndicator {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly health: HealthIndicatorService) {}

  async isWritable(key = 'postgres_writer') {
    const indicator = this.health.check(key);
    const [row] = await this.ds.query('SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS ro');
    return row.ro ? indicator.down({ reason: 'endpoint is read-only' }) : indicator.up();
  }
}

Production scenario

RDS Multi-AZ failover, measured across many incidents: detection 10 to 20 s, promotion 15 to 30 s, DNS propagation 5 to 10 s. Total 60 to 90 s during which writes fail. A well-prepared NestJS fleet shows: HTTP 503 for writes for about 70 s (with the client SDKs retrying with backoff), reads continuing from replicas, background workers pausing on backoff, then everything recovering with no manual action. A poorly prepared fleet shows: pods holding dead connections for minutes, workers in a retry storm hammering the new primary, duplicate orders from non-idempotent retries, and one pod stuck in a read-only transaction loop because it cached the old IP.

Patroni on Kubernetes (or a managed operator such as CloudNativePG or Zalando's) gives finer control: leader election via etcd or the Kubernetes API, pg_rewind for the old primary, and a maximum_lag_on_failover setting so a replica far behind is never promoted.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call got paged because writes were failing. Multi-AZ failover had happened after a storage event. By 02:16 the new primary was up and DNS had switched. But the order-placement pods kept failing until 02:41. Root cause: the pods' pool used idleTimeoutMillis: 0 (never recycle) and the OS keepalive default of 7,200 s, so the 10 connections per pod stayed pointed at the dead IP, and the application-level query timeout of 30 s meant each request waited half a minute before erroring. Nobody restarted the pods because the readiness probe only checked that the process was alive. Fixes: keepalive at 10 s, connection timeout 3 s, readiness probe that runs SELECT 1 through the pool, and a runbook step to roll the deployment if failover does not self-heal in two minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Split brain: two primaries accept writes. Only fencing prevents it. Never build a home-made failover script that promotes without fencing.
  • Failover during a transaction: the transaction's outcome is unknown to the client. Design for it with idempotency keys and an outbox; reconcile with a nightly job.
  • Lost transactions on async promotion: acknowledged writes vanish. Decide in advance which tables can tolerate that (audit logs) and which cannot (payments: synchronous).
  • Promoting a lagging replica: minutes of data lost. Set maximum_lag_on_failover (Patroni) or verify lag before manual promotion.
  • DNS TTL ignored: some resolvers and Java-style caches keep an old IP. Node re-resolves on each new connection, but verify it in your runtime.
  • Old primary returns and accepts writes: without fencing or pg_rewind, it diverges. Patroni handles it; hand-rolled setups do not.
  • Connection storm on the new primary: hundreds of pods reconnect at once; PgBouncer in front absorbs it.
  • Replicas orphaned: they were following the old primary's timeline; with recovery_target_timeline = 'latest' they follow the new one, otherwise they stall.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume failover will happen at the worst time and rehearse it: a quarterly game day where the primary is rebooted in staging (and eventually production) and the team watches which pods misbehave. They treat "the application reconnected cleanly" as a feature with tests, not luck. They insist on a pooler or managed proxy so the reconnection storm is absorbed. They know the RPO (how much data can be lost, zero with synchronous) and RTO (how long writes are down, about a minute with automated failover) and have told the business those numbers.

Common mistakes

  • Hardcoding the primary's IP or resolving it once at startup.
  • Retrying every failed write during failover, creating duplicates.
  • A readiness probe that returns 200 while the pool is full of dead sockets.
  • Running the failover script by hand at 3 a.m. and promoting the wrong replica.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through what happens in an RDS Multi-AZ failover and what your NestJS app must do. Expected: detect, promote standby, DNS switch in about a minute; app must detect broken connections, reconnect via DNS, retry only idempotent work, avoid retry storms.
  2. What is split brain and how do Patroni and RDS prevent it? Expected: two writable primaries; leader lease in a consensus store, fencing, only one endpoint.
  3. A transaction was in flight during failover. Did it commit? Expected: unknown; with async replication it may be lost even if it committed; idempotency keys and reconciliation are the answer.
  4. Why should pooled connections have an idle timeout even when traffic is constant? Expected: to re-resolve DNS and rotate away from dead or demoted hosts.

Practical exercise

Run a Patroni cluster locally (the Zalando Patroni repository has a Docker Compose setup with three nodes and etcd). Point a NestJS service at the HAProxy writer port. Under a load generator of 50 writes per second with idempotency keys, kill the primary container. Acceptance criteria: writes resume within 60 seconds without manual action; zero duplicate orders in the table; the metrics dashboard shows the failover window; the old primary rejoins as a replica via pg_rewind.

22.7 Partitioning

Concept

Partitioning splits one logical table into several physical tables (partitions) inside the same database, according to a rule on one or more columns (the partition key). To the application it is still one table called orders; to PostgreSQL it is a parent with children such as orders_2026_08, orders_2026_09. Queries whose WHERE clause constrains the partition key touch only the relevant children. Maintenance (vacuum, index rebuilds, dropping old data) happens per child.

PostgreSQL has supported declarative partitioning since version 10 (PARTITION BY RANGE | LIST | HASH). Before that, people faked it with inheritance and triggers; do not do that today.

Why does it exist?

A single table with 800 million rows hurts in ways that have nothing to do with query plans: autovacuum takes hours and falls behind, so bloat and transaction-id wraparound become real risks; indexes are tens of gigabytes and no longer fit in RAM; deleting last year's rows is a multi-hour DELETE that generates as much WAL as it removes; and a CREATE INDEX is a day-long project. Partitioning turns each of those into an operation on a manageable slice, and turns "delete a year of data" into DROP TABLE orders_2025_01, which takes milliseconds.

Mental model

Imagine a company's paper archive. Instead of one giant filing cabinet with every invoice ever issued, there is one cabinet per month. When the auditor asks for September invoices, you open one cabinet. When retention policy says to shred everything older than seven years, you wheel one cabinet to the shredder. But if the auditor asks for "every invoice to customer 4711 ever", you must open every cabinet: partitioning by month does nothing for that question, and may make it slower.

How it works

  1. Parent table is declared with PARTITION BY and holds no rows itself.
  2. Partitions are created with PARTITION OF parent FOR VALUES .... Each is a real table with its own storage, statistics and indexes.
  3. Routing on insert: PostgreSQL evaluates the partition key of each inserted row and puts it in the matching child. If none matches and there is no DEFAULT partition, the insert fails.
  4. Partition pruning at plan time and execution time: when the query's WHERE clause constrains the partition key with constants or parameters, the planner removes non-matching partitions from the plan entirely. With enable_partition_pruning = on (default), this also works for parameter values known only at execution time (prepared statements, nested loop parameters).
  5. Indexes: an index created on the parent is automatically created on every partition (and on future partitions). Each partition has its own physical index, so each is smaller and cache-friendlier.
  6. Constraints: a primary key or unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key. PostgreSQL cannot enforce uniqueness across partitions otherwise, because each partition's index is separate. This is the constraint that surprises everyone: orders.id alone cannot be the PK if you partition by created_at; the PK becomes (id, created_at).
  7. Attach and detach: an existing table with the right structure can be attached as a partition (ATTACH PARTITION), and a partition can be detached into a standalone table (DETACH PARTITION, with CONCURRENTLY in PostgreSQL 14+ to avoid blocking). This is how you archive: detach, dump to S3, drop.

Range partitioning splits by ordered intervals: dates, ids, amounts. The overwhelmingly common form is time. Partitions must not overlap; gaps are allowed but rows falling in a gap fail to insert.

List partitioning splits by explicit values: region IN ('eu'), status IN ('archived'), tenant_id IN (...) for a handful of giant tenants.

Hash partitioning splits by hash(key) % modulus. It spreads rows evenly across N partitions regardless of value distribution. It is for tables with no natural range and a need to shrink per-partition index size or spread vacuum work, and it is the shape that mirrors hash sharding later. It cannot drop "old" data because every partition holds a slice of every time period.

Time partitioning (range by a timestamp) is the sweet spot: orders by month, events by day, logs by hour. Inserts land in the newest partition; queries are usually "last N days"; retention is "drop partitions older than X".

flowchart TB
    Q["SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-08'"] --> PL["Planner: partition pruning"]
    PL --> P7["orders_2026_07 pruned"]
    PL --> P8["orders_2026_08 pruned"]
    PL --> P9["orders_2026_09 scanned via index"]
    PL --> P10["orders_2026_10 pruned"]
    P9 --> RES["Result rows"]

PostgreSQL example

A time-partitioned orders table with a working primary key, per-partition indexes, a default partition as a safety net, and the queries that prove pruning is happening.

-- Parent. Note the PK includes the partition key: required by PostgreSQL.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           uuid        NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id      uuid        NOT NULL,
  status       text        NOT NULL,
  total_cents  bigint      NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

-- Monthly partitions. Ranges are half-open: FROM inclusive, TO exclusive.
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_08 PARTITION OF orders
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-08-01') TO ('2026-09-01');
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_09 PARTITION OF orders
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_10 PARTITION OF orders
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01');

-- Safety net so an insert with an unexpected date does not fail.
-- Alert if this ever contains rows; it means partition creation fell behind.
CREATE TABLE orders_default PARTITION OF orders DEFAULT;

-- Index on the parent is propagated to every partition, present and future.
CREATE INDEX orders_user_created_idx ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

Verify pruning with EXPLAIN. A pruned partition simply does not appear in the plan.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders
WHERE user_id = '5c0c1a8e-6c4a-4b0a-9a0e-1e1a2b3c4d5e'
  AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days';
Append  (cost=0.56..41.20 rows=12 width=24) (actual time=0.041..0.098 rows=9 loops=1)
  Subplans Removed: 3
  ->  Index Scan using orders_2026_09_user_id_created_at_idx on orders_2026_09
        (cost=0.56..40.80 rows=12 width=24) (actual time=0.039..0.092 rows=9 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((user_id = '5c0c1a8e-...'::uuid) AND (created_at >= (now() - '7 days'::interval)))
        Buffers: shared hit=7
Planning Time: 0.412 ms
Execution Time: 0.131 ms

Subplans Removed: 3 is execution-time pruning: now() is not a constant at plan time, so the planner kept all partitions and the executor dropped the three that could not match. Compare the same query without a created_at condition: every partition is scanned, and the plan shows one index scan per partition plus an Append node. That is the "random access by non-partition key" case where partitioning does not help and adds planning overhead.

Retention and the midnight problem:

-- Retention: drop a month in milliseconds instead of a multi-hour DELETE.
-- Detach first so a running query is not surprised; CONCURRENTLY needs PG 14+.
ALTER TABLE orders DETACH PARTITION orders_2025_08 CONCURRENTLY;
-- Optionally: pg_dump -t orders_2025_08 to S3 before dropping.
DROP TABLE orders_2025_08;

-- Attaching a pre-built partition (e.g. loaded from an archive).
-- A CHECK constraint matching the bounds lets PostgreSQL skip the validation scan.
ALTER TABLE orders_2025_08_restored
  ADD CONSTRAINT bounds CHECK (created_at >= '2025-08-01' AND created_at < '2025-09-01');
ALTER TABLE orders ATTACH PARTITION orders_2025_08_restored
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-08-01') TO ('2025-09-01');

Using pg_partman to automate creation and retention so nobody has to remember to make November's partition:

CREATE EXTENSION pg_partman;

-- Manage 'public.orders' by created_at, one partition per month,
-- always keep 3 future partitions ready.
SELECT partman.create_parent(
  p_parent_table := 'public.orders',
  p_control      := 'created_at',
  p_interval     := '1 month',
  p_premake      := 3
);

-- Retention: drop partitions older than 24 months (set keep_table=false to drop, true to detach only).
UPDATE partman.part_config
SET retention = '24 months', retention_keep_table = false
WHERE parent_table = 'public.orders';

-- Run maintenance hourly with pg_cron (or from a Kubernetes CronJob calling the same procedure).
SELECT cron.schedule('partman-maintenance', '0 * * * *', $$CALL partman.run_maintenance_proc()$$);

Hash partitioning for a table with no natural time dimension, such as a per-user counter table that is updated constantly:

CREATE TABLE user_stats (
  user_id      uuid   NOT NULL,
  orders_count int    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  spent_cents  bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id)             -- partition key is user_id, so this is allowed
) PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);

-- 8 partitions; each holds roughly 1/8 of users. Vacuum runs on 8 smaller tables in parallel.
CREATE TABLE user_stats_p0 PARTITION OF user_stats FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 8, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE user_stats_p1 PARTITION OF user_stats FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 8, REMAINDER 1);
-- ... p2 through p7 in the same shape.

List partitioning where a few tenants are so large they deserve isolation:

CREATE TABLE events (
  tenant_id   text        NOT NULL,
  id          uuid        NOT NULL,
  occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  payload     jsonb       NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id)
) PARTITION BY LIST (tenant_id);

CREATE TABLE events_acme  PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES IN ('acme');      -- the 40% tenant
CREATE TABLE events_globex PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES IN ('globex');   -- the 20% tenant
CREATE TABLE events_rest   PARTITION OF events DEFAULT;                    -- everyone else

TypeORM example

TypeORM does not know about partitions and does not need to: the entity maps to the parent table and PostgreSQL routes rows. Two things must be correct in the entity: the composite primary key, and every query that wants pruning must include the partition key.

// src/orders/order.entity.ts
import { Entity, Column, PrimaryColumn, Index, CreateDateColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'orders' })
@Index('orders_user_created_idx', ['userId', 'createdAt'])
export class Order {
  // Composite PK mirrors the partitioned table: (id, created_at).
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid', { default: () => 'gen_random_uuid()' })
  id!: string;

  @PrimaryColumn({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz', default: () => 'now()' })
  createdAt!: Date;

  @Column('uuid', { name: 'user_id' }) userId!: string;
  @Column('text') status!: string;
  @Column('bigint', { name: 'total_cents' }) totalCents!: string;
}
// src/orders/orders.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository, MoreThanOrEqual } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly repo: Repository<Order>) {}

  // Always bound by created_at so only the relevant partitions are scanned.
  findRecentForUser(userId: string, days = 30): Promise<Order[]> {
    const since = new Date(Date.now() - days * 86_400_000);
    return this.repo.find({
      where: { userId, createdAt: MoreThanOrEqual(since) },
      order: { createdAt: 'DESC' },
      take: 50,
    });
  }

  // Lookup by id alone scans every partition. If the API only has the id,
  // carry the creation date in the public identifier (e.g. UUIDv7) or accept the cost.
