  findById(id: string, createdAt: Date): Promise<Order | null> {
    return this.repo.findOne({ where: { id, createdAt } });
  }
}

Migrations that create partitions belong in raw SQL inside a TypeORM migration; synchronize and migration:generate do not understand PARTITION BY, so never let them touch a partitioned table.

Sequelize example

Same story: model the parent, declare the composite key, and keep synchronize/sync() away from it.

// src/orders/order.model.ts
import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export class Order extends Model {
  declare id: string;
  declare createdAt: Date;
  declare userId: string;
  declare status: string;
  declare totalCents: string;
}

export function initOrder(sequelize: Sequelize): void {
  Order.init(
    {
      id: { type: DataTypes.UUID, primaryKey: true, defaultValue: DataTypes.UUIDV4 },
      createdAt: { type: DataTypes.DATE, primaryKey: true, field: 'created_at', defaultValue: DataTypes.NOW },
      userId: { type: DataTypes.UUID, field: 'user_id', allowNull: false },
      status: { type: DataTypes.STRING, allowNull: false },
      totalCents: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, field: 'total_cents', allowNull: false },
    },
    { sequelize, tableName: 'orders', timestamps: false },
  );
}

Production scenario

An events table for a social product: 40 million rows per day, retention 90 days, so about 3.6 billion rows live at any time. Daily partitions; each is 40 M rows and about 12 GB with indexes. Autovacuum handles a day's partition in under 20 minutes instead of never finishing on the monolithic table. The nightly retention job is DROP TABLE events_2026_06_07, sub-second, versus the old DELETE ... WHERE occurred_at < ... that ran for six hours and generated 200 GB of WAL. Queries for a user's last 7 days of events touch 7 partitions with small indexes, p95 4 ms.

For orders on an e-commerce platform at 3 million orders per month, monthly partitions and a two-year retention in the hot database (older orders detached and moved to a cold "archive" database queried by a separate service) keep the live table at 72 million rows.

When partitioning does not help: a products table with 2 million rows accessed by id and by category; a users table accessed by id and email. Neither has a range dimension in its access pattern. Partitioning them adds planning overhead and per-query Append nodes for no benefit. The signal for partitioning is: the table is huge, and most queries filter on a column you could partition by, and/or retention is by that column.

Failure scenario

The midnight incident. A team partitioned orders by month and created partitions through September by hand. At 00:00:00 on October 1st, every INSERT INTO orders failed with ERROR: no partition of relation "orders" found for row. Checkout was down for 38 minutes until someone created orders_2026_10. There was no default partition and no automation. The fix set: pg_partman with p_premake := 3, an hourly maintenance job, a DEFAULT partition as a net, an alert on SELECT count(*) FROM orders_default > 0, and a synthetic check that inserts and deletes a row dated tomorrow in staging every day.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Partition missing for tomorrow: inserts fail at midnight. Automate creation, keep future partitions pre-made, and add a default partition.
  • Rows in the default partition: they came from a gap or a future date. They also block creating a partition for that range until moved out.
  • Unique constraint not including partition key: ERROR: unique constraint on partitioned table must include all partitioning columns. Design the key first.
  • Foreign keys to a partitioned table: supported from PostgreSQL 12, but the referenced key must include the partition key, so order_items.order_id alone cannot reference orders(id).
  • Updating the partition key moves the row between partitions (supported since PostgreSQL 11) as a delete plus insert; concurrent updates on that row can fail with a serialization error.
  • Too many partitions: thousands of partitions slow down planning (each query considers each partition's metadata) and bloat the catalog. Daily partitions with 2 years of retention is 730 partitions, acceptable; hourly for a year is 8,760 and painful.
  • Cross-partition queries: no created_at predicate means every partition is scanned; a LIMIT 10 ORDER BY created_at DESC still needs a merge across partitions (PostgreSQL's Merge Append handles it, but it is slower than a single index).
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a partitioned parent is not supported directly; create the index ON ONLY the parent, then build it CONCURRENTLY on each partition, then ALTER INDEX ... ATTACH PARTITION. Part 23 shows the recipe.
  • Detach while queries run: plain DETACH takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the parent for a moment; use CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL 14+).
  • Hot latest partition: all inserts and most reads hit one partition; its index pages are contended. That is inherent to time partitioning; it is usually fine because that partition is small and hot in cache. If it is not fine, sub-partition by hash within the day.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Partitioning is a storage-layout decision that leaks into the data model (composite keys) and into every query (the predicate must include the key). So the senior engineer decides on partitioning early for tables that will obviously become huge (events, logs, orders, messages) and designs the primary key and public identifiers accordingly, for example UUIDv7 ids whose timestamp prefix lets you derive the partition from the id. They refuse to partition small or randomly accessed tables. They put partition automation and monitoring in place before the first partition, not after the first midnight outage.

Common mistakes

  • Partitioning users or products because "the table is big", without a range access pattern.
  • Forgetting the partition key in the WHERE clause, so every query scans every partition and is slower than before.
  • Creating partitions by hand and forgetting.
  • Letting TypeORM synchronize: true run against a partitioned table; it will try to "fix" the schema.
  • Using DELETE for retention on a partitioned table instead of DROP or DETACH.

Interview questions

  1. When does partitioning help and when does it hurt? Expected: helps for huge tables with time/range access and retention-by-drop; hurts for random access by non-key columns and with too many partitions.
  2. Why must the primary key include the partition key? Expected: each partition has its own index; uniqueness cannot be enforced across them without a global index, which PostgreSQL does not have.
  3. How does partition pruning work with now() in the query? Expected: plan-time pruning needs constants; execution-time pruning handles runtime values; look for "Subplans Removed" in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
  4. How do you implement 90-day retention on a 3-billion-row table? Expected: daily range partitions, detach/drop partitions older than 90 days, automated with pg_partman or a cron job.
  5. What happens at midnight if the next partition does not exist? Expected: inserts fail; mitigate with pre-created partitions and a default partition.

Practical exercise

Convert an events table with 20 million synthetic rows into daily range partitions using the copy-and-swap technique (create partitioned parent under a new name, copy in batches, rename in one transaction; details in Part 23). Set up pg_partman with 3 days premake and 30 days retention. Acceptance criteria: EXPLAIN on a 7-day query shows only 7 partitions; inserting a row dated 4 days ahead lands in the default partition and triggers your alert query; the retention job drops the oldest partition and its size is freed as shown by pg_total_relation_size.

22.8 Sharding

Concept

Sharding is splitting the rows of a table (usually all the tables of a domain) across several independent databases, each holding a subset of the data. Each database is a shard. A rule, the shard key, decides which shard owns a given row. The application (or a middleware such as Citus) routes each query to the shard that holds the data. Unlike partitioning, the shards do not share a server, a transaction manager, or a query planner. Cross-shard joins, cross-shard transactions and cross-shard uniqueness are not free; they are things you build, badly, yourself.

Sharding is the last rung of the ladder because it is the only rung that changes how every feature is written from then on.

Why does it exist?

One machine has a ceiling on write throughput (WAL fsync, one set of CPUs, one set of disks) and on manageable data size (backup and restore time, vacuum duration). Read replicas cannot raise the write ceiling. Partitioning cannot either, because all partitions live on the same server. When the write curve says you will cross the ceiling within your planning horizon, or when the dataset has become too large to restore in an acceptable time, splitting the data across machines is the remaining option.

Mental model

Imagine a bank that has grown too large for one vault. It opens regional vaults and assigns every customer to exactly one region by the first letter of their surname. A customer's statement is now fast: one vault. But "total deposits across the bank" requires asking every vault and adding up. A transfer between two customers in different regions requires a protocol between two vaults, with all the ways that can half-fail. And when the "S" vault fills up because too many surnames start with S, splitting it means physically moving boxes to a new vault while customers keep depositing. Every one of those problems is what sharding costs.

How it works

  1. Choose the shard key. The column whose value determines the shard. Almost always a tenant or user identifier, because almost all queries in a SaaS or consumer product are scoped to one tenant or user. Section 22.9 is entirely about this choice.
  2. Choose the mapping. Hash: shard = hash(key) % N spreads evenly but makes adding a shard reshuffle almost everything (consistent hashing fixes that; section 22.11). Range: key in [A, M) goes to shard 1; easy to split, prone to hot ranges. Directory: a lookup table tenant_id -> shard stored in a small central database or in Redis; most flexible, adds a lookup per request (cache it), and lets you move a single tenant.
  3. Route every query. The application resolves the shard from the request context (the authenticated tenant, the user id in the path), picks the DataSource for that shard, and runs the query there. Nothing in the request may accidentally use another shard's connection.
  4. Generate globally unique ids. Auto-increment sequences are per shard, so orders.id = 42 would exist on every shard. Use UUIDv7 (time-ordered, generated in the application, index-friendly) or Snowflake-style ids (timestamp + shard id + sequence). Never rely on a shard-local sequence for anything that crosses shards.
  5. Handle cross-shard reads. Fan out to all shards and merge in the application (scatter-gather), or maintain a separate read model (a search index, a warehouse, a CQRS projection) that is fed by CDC from every shard. Reporting never runs against the shards directly.
  6. Avoid cross-shard writes. A transaction that must update two shards is a distributed transaction. PostgreSQL supports two-phase commit (PREPARE TRANSACTION), but it is fragile and slow in practice. Design the domain so that a business transaction lives entirely within one shard, and use sagas with compensation (Part 30) for the rare cases that cannot.
  7. Keep reference data everywhere. Small tables that every shard needs (countries, product categories, feature flags) are copied to every shard, or fetched from a shared service and cached.
flowchart LR
    REQ["Request: tenant t_8842"] --> RES["ShardResolver"]
    RES -->|"lookup directory or hash"| MAP["t_8842 is on shard 2"]
    MAP --> DS2["DataSource shard 2"]
    RES -.-> DS1["DataSource shard 1"]
    RES -.-> DS3["DataSource shard 3"]
    DS2 --> PG2["PostgreSQL shard 2 primary"]
    PG2 --> R2["shard 2 replica"]
    SG["Scatter-gather report"] --> DS1
    SG --> DS2
    SG --> DS3

Citus is the PostgreSQL-native way to shard. It is an extension that turns one PostgreSQL node into a coordinator and others into workers. You declare create_distributed_table('orders', 'tenant_id') and Citus places the table's shards across workers, routes queries that include tenant_id to a single worker, and parallelises queries that do not. Tables co-located on the same distribution column (orders and order_items both on tenant_id) can be joined on the worker. Reference tables are replicated to every worker. It removes most of the application-level routing but keeps the fundamental constraints: transactions and joins across distribution keys are limited, and you must design your schema around one distribution column. It is available managed on Azure (Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL) and self-hosted.

NestJS example

Application-level sharding with one TypeORM DataSource per shard, a ShardResolver that maps a tenant to a shard, and a request-scoped repository accessor. The directory mapping lives in a small control database and is cached in Redis.

// src/sharding/shard.config.ts
export interface ShardConfig { id: number; host: string; replicaHost?: string }

export const shardsFromEnv = (): ShardConfig[] =>
  JSON.parse(process.env.PG_SHARDS_JSON ?? '[]'); // e.g. [{"id":1,"host":"shard1.internal"}, ...]
// src/sharding/shard-datasources.provider.ts
import { Provider } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { shardsFromEnv } from './shard.config';

export const SHARD_DATASOURCES = Symbol('SHARD_DATASOURCES');

// One DataSource per shard, all initialised at boot. Each has its own small pool.
export const shardDataSourcesProvider: Provider = {
  provide: SHARD_DATASOURCES,
  useFactory: async (): Promise<Map<number, DataSource>> => {
    const map = new Map<number, DataSource>();
    for (const shard of shardsFromEnv()) {
      const ds = new DataSource({
        type: 'postgres',
        host: shard.host,
        port: 5432,
        username: process.env.PG_USER,
        password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD,
        database: process.env.PG_DB,
        entities: [__dirname + '/../**/*.entity.js'],
        extra: { max: 5, connectionTimeoutMillis: 3000, statement_timeout: 5000 },
      });
      map.set(shard.id, await ds.initialize());
    }
    return map;
  },
};
// src/sharding/shard-resolver.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { SHARD_DATASOURCES } from './shard-datasources.provider';

@Injectable()
export class ShardResolver {
  constructor(
    @Inject(SHARD_DATASOURCES) private readonly shards: Map<number, DataSource>,
    private readonly redis: Redis,
    private readonly control: DataSource, // small control DB holding tenant -> shard
  ) {}

  // Directory lookup with a cache. Moving a tenant means updating the directory and evicting the key.
  async shardIdFor(tenantId: string): Promise<number> {
    const cached = await this.redis.get(`shard:${tenantId}`);
    if (cached) return Number(cached);
    const [row] = await this.control.query('SELECT shard_id FROM tenant_shards WHERE tenant_id = $1', [tenantId]);
    if (!row) throw new NotFoundException(`tenant ${tenantId} has no shard`);
    await this.redis.set(`shard:${tenantId}`, String(row.shard_id), 'EX', 300);
    return row.shard_id;
  }

  async dataSourceFor(tenantId: string): Promise<DataSource> {
    const id = await this.shardIdFor(tenantId);
    const ds = this.shards.get(id);
    if (!ds) throw new Error(`shard ${id} is not configured on this pod`);
    return ds;
  }

  all(): DataSource[] { return [...this.shards.values()]; } // for scatter-gather and admin jobs only
}
// src/orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ShardResolver } from '../sharding/shard-resolver.service';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { CreateOrderDto } from './dto/create-order.dto';
import { uuidv7 } from 'uuidv7';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly shards: ShardResolver) {}

  async create(tenantId: string, dto: CreateOrderDto): Promise<Order> {
    const ds = await this.shards.dataSourceFor(tenantId);
    // Whole business transaction on one shard: order + items + inventory for this tenant.
    return ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      const order = em.create(Order, { id: uuidv7(), tenantId, status: 'created', totalCents: dto.totalCents });
      await em.save(order);
      await em.query(
        'UPDATE inventory SET reserved = reserved + $1 WHERE tenant_id = $2 AND sku = $3 AND available - reserved >= $1',
        [dto.qty, tenantId, dto.sku],
      );
      return order;
    });
  }

  // Cross-shard report: fan out, merge. Only for admin/reporting paths, never in a user request.
  async countOrdersEverywhere(since: Date): Promise<number> {
    const counts = await Promise.all(
      this.shards.all().map((ds) =>
        ds.query('SELECT count(*)::int AS c FROM orders WHERE created_at >= $1', [since]).then((r) => r[0].c as number),
      ),
    );
    return counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  }
}

The guard rail: every entity carries tenant_id, every query includes it, and the resolver is the only way to obtain a DataSource in request code. A lint rule or a code review checklist enforces that nobody injects a shard DataSource directly.

PostgreSQL example

The control database and a Citus alternative for comparison.

-- Control database: the directory. Tiny, heavily cached, replicated for safety.
CREATE TABLE tenant_shards (
  tenant_id   text PRIMARY KEY,
  shard_id    int  NOT NULL,
  state       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',   -- active | migrating | moved
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- On every shard: the same schema, and every business table carries tenant_id.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY,                  -- UUIDv7 generated by the app: globally unique
  tenant_id   text NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  total_cents bigint NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX orders_tenant_created_idx ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC);
-- Citus: the same domain without application-level routing.
CREATE EXTENSION citus;
SELECT create_distributed_table('orders', 'tenant_id');
SELECT create_distributed_table('order_items', 'tenant_id', colocate_with := 'orders');
SELECT create_reference_table('product_categories');   -- copied to every worker

-- Routed to exactly one worker because tenant_id is present:
SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i USING (tenant_id, id) WHERE o.tenant_id = 't_8842';
-- Runs in parallel across all workers, merged on the coordinator:
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at), sum(total_cents) FROM orders GROUP BY 1;

Production scenario

A B2B SaaS with 30,000 tenants and 25,000 write TPS at peak, well past a single primary. Eight shards, each a primary plus one replica, tenant-to-shard directory in a control database with Redis cache. Each shard runs at about 3,000 write TPS, comfortably in range. The application is a NestJS fleet of 60 pods; each pod holds 8 shard pools of 5 connections plus 8 replica pools of 5, so 80 connections per pod and 4,800 total, which is why PgBouncer sits in front of every shard (section 22.12). Cross-shard reporting is done from a warehouse fed by Debezium from each shard. Global uniqueness for user emails (a user belongs to one tenant, but emails must be unique across the product) is enforced in the control database with a user_emails(email PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id) table written in the same request as the shard write, with a compensating delete if the shard write fails.

Failure scenario

"Why is there an order with id 5100234 on both shard 1 and shard 3?" A team sharded with bigserial ids. Each shard's sequence started at 1. Six months later a support tool that looked up orders by id alone returned the wrong tenant's order. Fixing it required a global backfill to UUIDv7 with dual-written id columns, one of the most expensive migrations the company ever ran. The rule: decide the id strategy before the first shard exists.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cross-shard uniqueness (emails, usernames, coupon codes): needs a global table in a control database, or a deterministic mapping (shard by hash of the unique value itself).
  • Cross-shard transactions: avoid; if unavoidable, saga with compensation and idempotent steps, never a home-made two-phase commit.
  • A tenant outgrows its shard: needs a dedicated shard and a live move (section 22.11).
  • Directory unavailable: with Redis down and the control database slow, no request can be routed. Cache the directory in process memory with a stale-while-revalidate policy; the mapping changes rarely.
  • Misrouted write: a bug writes tenant A's row to shard B. The row is invisible to A and corrupts B's assumptions. Add a CHECK or a trigger on each shard that rejects rows whose tenant_id does not map to this shard (the shard can hold a copy of its own tenant list), and an audit job that scans for strays.
  • Schema drift between shards: migrations must run on every shard in the same order (Part 23 covers this). A shard that missed a migration crashes the pods that reach it.
  • Re-sharding pain: going from 8 to 12 shards with naive hashing moves 2/3 of all rows. Use consistent hashing or a directory from the start.
  • Global secondary indexes do not exist: "find order by external payment reference" must either carry the tenant id or go through a global lookup table.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They delay sharding as long as the ladder allows, because sharding is a one-way door. When they do shard, they shard the whole domain by one key, keep transactions inside a shard, generate ids in the application, build the directory and the migration tooling before the second shard exists, and feed all reporting from CDC rather than from scatter-gather. They evaluate Citus seriously before writing a router by hand. They explain it to the product manager as: "After this, every feature must be designed around the tenant boundary. Cross-tenant features become projects, not tickets."

Common mistakes

  • Sharding by a key that most queries do not include, so every query fans out.
  • Using per-shard sequences for ids.
  • Letting services hold a specific shard's DataSource instead of going through the resolver.
  • Building reporting with scatter-gather in the request path.
  • Sharding the database but not the caches and queues, so a hot tenant still saturates shared Redis.

Interview questions

  1. When would you shard and what would you try first? Expected: only when write throughput or dataset size exceeds one machine after indexes, pooling, caching, replicas, partitioning and write offloading.
  2. How do you keep ids unique across shards? Expected: UUIDv7 or Snowflake generated in the application; never shard-local sequences.
  3. How do you handle a query that needs data from all shards? Expected: scatter-gather for admin paths; CDC-fed read models or a warehouse for reporting; never in the user request path.
  4. What does Citus give you and what does it not solve? Expected: routing, co-located joins, reference tables, rebalancing; does not remove the need for a good distribution key or make cross-key transactions cheap.
  5. How do you enforce a globally unique email in a sharded system? Expected: a global uniqueness table in a control database written in the same request, with compensation.

22.9 Shard keys

Concept

The shard key is the column (or combination) whose value decides which shard a row lives on. It is the most consequential decision in a sharded system, because every query that includes it is cheap and local, and every query that does not is expensive and global. It also decides how evenly data and load are spread, and whether business transactions can stay on one shard.

Why does it exist?

Without a key, there is no deterministic way to know where a row is, and every read becomes a broadcast. The key turns "somewhere in the cluster" into "exactly here".

Mental model

Imagine a library that has to split its collection across four buildings. Split by author's surname and "all books by Tolstoy" is one trip, but "all books about gardening" is four. Split by subject and the reverse is true. Whichever question your visitors ask most is the one your split should make cheap. If one subject is so popular that its building is always crowded while others sit empty, you chose a key with a bad distribution.

How it works

Criteria for choosing, in priority order:

  1. Access pattern alignment. List the top twenty queries by frequency. The key should appear in as many of them as possible, especially in the write path. For a SaaS: tenant_id. For a consumer app: user_id. For a marketplace with buyer and seller: usually buyer_id for orders, and a CDC-fed seller read model, because buyers query far more often than sellers and a row can only live in one place.
  2. Transaction boundaries. A business transaction (place order: order + items + inventory + payment record) must touch only one shard. Every table in that transaction must carry the key.
  3. Cardinality. Many distinct values, so the data can spread across many shards. country (200 values, wildly skewed) is a terrible key; user_id (millions) is a good one.
  4. Distribution. Load and size per key value should be roughly similar, or at least no single value should exceed what one shard can hold. A tenant that is 40% of all traffic breaks any key that lands it on a shared shard (section 22.10).
  5. Stability. The key must not change for a row; moving rows between shards on key change is a migration, not an update. user_id never changes; team_id might, if users move teams.
  6. Availability in the request. The key must be derivable from every request without a global lookup: from the JWT (tenant), from the path (user id), from the resource id itself (UUIDv7 with an embedded shard hint, or a Snowflake id carrying shard bits).

Comparison of common keys:

Key Cardinality Alignment Transaction locality Typical trap
tenant_id (B2B SaaS) Thousands to millions Excellent, every request is tenant-scoped Excellent Whale tenants create hot shards
user_id (consumer) Millions Very good Good, except social features that cross users Celebrity users; cross-user feeds need a read model
order_id (hash) Very high Poor: "my orders" fans out Poor: items and inventory elsewhere Looks even, kills locality
created_at (range) High Good for time queries Poor All writes go to the newest shard: permanently hot
region / country Tiny Good for data residency Good Massive skew; only as a first-level split above another key
product_id High Good for catalog Poor for orders Hot products

Practical example

A ride-booking platform considered driver_id, rider_id and city_id. Rides are written once per trip, then read by both rider and driver, and heavily by city-level dispatch. city_id had 300 values with three cities at 60% of traffic: rejected for skew. driver_id and rider_id each aligned with half the reads. The choice was rider_id for the rides shard key (riders read history far more than drivers do), a CDC-fed driver_rides read model for driver-side history, and a separate Redis-based geo index for dispatch that never touches the shards. Rides are a two-party transaction, which is exactly the kind of case that forces a read model.

PostgreSQL example

Encoding a shard hint into a Snowflake-style id so any service can route from the id alone, without a directory lookup.

-- 64-bit id: 41 bits ms timestamp | 10 bits shard id | 12 bits sequence.
-- Generated in the application, but the layout is documented in the database for tooling.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION shard_of(id bigint) RETURNS int
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT ((id >> 12) & 1023)::int $$;

-- Support tooling can now answer "which shard holds order 7156318204102918145?"
SELECT shard_of(7156318204102918145);   -- 3

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Key derived from mutable data (email, team): rows must move when it changes; avoid.
  • Composite keys (tenant_id, region): more complex routing and more fan-out for tenant-only queries; use only when residency laws require it.
  • Low-cardinality prefix: hashing country + user_id still spreads well, but range-splitting on it creates hot ranges.
  • Key missing from a table: order_items without tenant_id cannot be co-located with orders; every table in the shard must carry the key even if it feels redundant.
  • Key in the JWT but not verified: a client that can choose its own tenant id in a header reads another tenant's shard. The key must come from an authenticated source.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick the key by reading query logs, not by intuition, and they verify the distribution with SELECT key, count(*) and per-key request rates before committing. They design the API so the key is always available (tenant in the token, user id in the path, shard bits in the id). They write down the queries that will not be local and decide, for each, whether it gets a read model or a fan-out.

Interview questions

  1. How do you choose a shard key? Expected: access pattern alignment, transaction locality, cardinality, distribution, stability, availability in the request.
  2. Why is created_at a bad shard key even though it is a great partition key? Expected: all writes go to the newest shard; hot shard forever; partitioning shares a server so hotness is harmless there.
  3. Orders involve a buyer and a seller. Which is the key? Expected: the side with more reads and the write transaction; the other side gets a CDC-fed read model.

22.10 Hot partitions and hot shards

Concept

A hot partition or hot shard is one that receives a disproportionate share of traffic or data, so it saturates while its siblings are idle. The cluster's capacity is then limited by its hottest member, not by the sum. It happens whenever the key's distribution is uneven: one celebrity user, one tenant that is 40% of the business, or a time-based key where "now" is always the busiest value.

Why does it exist?

Real-world distributions are power laws, not uniform. Ten percent of users produce ninety percent of activity; one enterprise customer can be bigger than the next thousand combined; the latest day of a time series gets all the inserts. Any static split of such a distribution will have hot spots.

Mental model

Imagine a supermarket with ten checkouts. If nine are labelled by surname ranges and one is "customers named Smith", the Smith lane has a permanent queue while the others are empty. Adding an eleventh lane for "customers named Jones" does not help the Smiths. You must either split the Smiths across several lanes (salting), give them their own dedicated store (dedicated shard), or stop routing by surname entirely for that group.

How it works

Three flavours, three sets of mitigations.

The celebrity problem (one key value with enormous fan-in: a user with 50 million followers, a viral product). The row itself is hot: every write to it contends on the same page and lock, and every read hits the same shard. Mitigations: cache the hot entity aggressively at the edge and in Redis; move counters out of the row into Redis or a separate counter table with salting (N sub-rows, follower_count_0..N, incremented at random and summed on read); shed non-essential writes (do not update last_seen on every request); rate-limit per key.

The whale tenant (one tenant that is 40% of traffic on a shared shard). Mitigations: a dedicated shard for that tenant, made possible by directory-based routing; that tenant's data is moved live (section 22.11). With hash routing you cannot do this, which is the main argument for directory routing in B2B systems.

The hot latest partition (time-based key: all inserts go to today's partition or the newest range shard). For partitions this is usually fine, because partitions share the server and the latest partition is small and cached. For shards it is fatal: never range-shard by time. If you must split by time for retention, do it as partitions inside each hash shard.

Detecting hotness before users do:

-- Top tenants by write volume on this shard over the last 5 minutes, from an events table.
SELECT tenant_id, count(*) AS writes
FROM order_events
WHERE occurred_at > now() - interval '5 minutes'
GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY writes DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Per-shard load is better read from metrics: per-shard connection count, CPU, TPS.
-- Alert on max(shard_tps) / avg(shard_tps) > 3.
// src/sharding/salted-counter.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

// Spreads increments for a hot key across N sub-keys so no single Redis key (or DB row) is contended.
@Injectable()
export class SaltedCounterService {
  private static readonly SALTS = 16;
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async increment(key: string): Promise<void> {
    const salt = Math.floor(Math.random() * SaltedCounterService.SALTS);
    await this.redis.incr(`${key}:${salt}`);
  }

  async read(key: string): Promise<number> {
    const keys = Array.from({ length: SaltedCounterService.SALTS }, (_, i) => `${key}:${i}`);
    const values = await this.redis.mget(...keys);
    return values.reduce((sum, v) => sum + Number(v ?? 0), 0);
  }
}

Production scenario

A social app with 12 user shards. One creator posts a video that goes viral; 4 million likes in an hour all increment posts.like_count on shard 7. The shard's CPU pins at 100% on lock waits (Lock:tuple and LWLock:BufferContent), and every other user on shard 7 sees 5-second latencies. Mitigation applied in the incident: likes routed to a salted Redis counter with a background job flushing the sum to PostgreSQL every 5 seconds. Long term: like counts never written synchronously to the row; the row stores a value refreshed by the flush job.

A B2B analytics product: tenant acme is 38% of all events. It was moved to a dedicated shard over a weekend using the live-migration procedure in section 22.11. Its p95 improved and, more importantly, the other 4,000 tenants stopped being collateral damage during acme's month-end batch.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Hot key in Redis too: sharding the database does not shard the cache; a single hot Redis key saturates one Redis node. Salt or replicate hot keys (see Part 26 — Caching).
  • Salting breaks exact reads: summing 16 sub-keys is not atomic; a reader may see a total mid-update. Acceptable for counters, not for balances.
  • Dedicated shard becomes a single point of failure for the biggest customer: give it the same HA setup as the shared shards.
  • Rate limiting the hot key hurts the most valuable customer: prefer capacity (dedicated resources) over throttling for whales; prefer throttling for abusive keys.
  • Time-based hot partition and index bloat: the newest partition's B-tree gets constant right-side inserts; it is fine, but monitor for lock contention on the rightmost leaf if you exceed ~10,000 inserts per second on one partition.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume the distribution is skewed and measure it before choosing routing. They pick directory routing in B2B precisely so whales can be isolated. They keep hot counters out of rows. They watch the ratio of the hottest shard to the average and treat a ratio over 3 as a capacity bug.

Interview questions

  1. A single tenant is 40% of traffic and slows everyone else. What do you do? Expected: dedicated shard via directory routing, live move, same HA; short term, rate limits or resource isolation.
  2. A viral post's like counter is melting a shard. Fix it. Expected: move the counter to Redis with salting, flush asynchronously, cache the post.
  3. Why is hash sharding bad for whale tenants? Expected: you cannot choose where a tenant lands; a directory lets you.

22.11 Rebalancing and live data movement

Concept

Rebalancing is moving data between shards while the system keeps serving traffic: adding a shard and giving it a fair share, draining a shard before retiring it, or moving one whale tenant to dedicated hardware. It has two halves: a routing scheme that keeps the amount of data to move small (consistent hashing, or a directory), and a procedure that moves the data without downtime or loss (dual-write, backfill, verify, cut over).

Why does it exist?

Any sharded system that lives long enough must change its shard count. With naive hash(key) % N, changing N from 8 to 9 remaps roughly 8/9 of all keys: almost everything moves, at once. A migration that moves 90% of a multi-terabyte dataset is a multi-week project with enormous risk. Rebalancing techniques exist to move only what must move, and to move it while the business continues.

Mental model

Imagine a ring of 360 mailboxes numbered like degrees on a compass. Each postal worker is assigned a few points on the ring and owns all mailboxes clockwise from their points up to the next worker's point. Hiring a new worker means giving them a few new points on the ring; they take over only the mailboxes between their points and the next existing points. Everybody else's mailboxes stay where they are. That is consistent hashing with virtual nodes. Moving the mail for those few mailboxes while letters keep arriving is the live-migration part.

How it works

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes. Hash each shard's identity to many points on a ring (say 128 virtual nodes per shard). Hash each key to a point; the owner is the first shard point clockwise. Adding a shard adds 128 points and takes over about 1/N of the ring, spread evenly. Removing a shard hands its arcs to the various neighbours. Virtual nodes are what make the split even; with one point per shard the arcs are wildly uneven.

Directory routing makes rebalancing an update to a table: UPDATE tenant_shards SET shard_id = 9 WHERE tenant_id = 'acme' after the data is in place. It is the simplest scheme to reason about and the one to prefer for tenant-keyed systems. Its cost is a lookup per request (cached) and a control database to keep highly available.

Live migration of a key range or tenant, step by step:

  1. Mark migrating. Set the directory state for the tenant to migrating, recording source shard S and target shard T. The resolver keeps routing reads and writes to S.
  2. Enable dual writes. The application (or a trigger plus logical replication) writes every change for the migrating tenant to both S and T. Writes to T are best-effort at this stage; the source of truth is still S. Every write must be idempotent on T (upserts keyed by primary key) because the backfill will overlap with them.
  3. Backfill. Copy the tenant's existing rows from S to T in keyset batches, oldest first, using INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE so that a row updated by a dual write after the backfill read it does not get overwritten with the stale copy (compare an updated_at or version column in the ON CONFLICT clause). Throttle by replica lag and by T's load.
  4. Verify. Row counts per table, checksums of ordered primary keys, spot checks of recently updated rows, and a continuous comparison of dual-write outcomes (a mismatch counter). Do not cut over until the mismatch rate is zero for a sustained period.
  5. Cut over. Briefly block writes for the tenant (a few hundred milliseconds: the resolver returns 503 Retry-After: 1 for that tenant's writes), let in-flight writes to S complete and replicate, flip the directory to T, evict the cache, unblock. Reads and writes now go to T.
  6. Observe with fallback. Keep dual-writing T to S in reverse for a day so an emergency flip back loses nothing. Then stop reverse writes, and after a retention window, delete the tenant's rows from S.
flowchart LR
    A["1 mark migrating"] --> B["2 dual write S and T"]
    B --> C["3 backfill S to T in batches"]
    C --> D["4 verify counts and checksums"]
    D -->|"mismatch"| C
    D -->|"clean"| E["5 short write pause, flip directory to T"]
    E --> F["6 reverse dual write T to S for 24h"]
    F --> G["7 stop reverse, delete from S later"]

With Citus, most of this is citus_rebalance_start() (Citus 11+) which moves shards between workers using logical replication and a brief write lock per shard at the end. With RDS-hosted application sharding you build it yourself or use logical replication (CREATE PUBLICATION ... FOR TABLE orders WHERE (tenant_id = 'acme'), PostgreSQL 15+ row filters) to replace the dual-write and backfill steps with database-level replication, which is often the safer choice.

NestJS example

The resolver from section 22.8 extended with migration states, and a dual-write wrapper.

// src/sharding/tenant-routing.types.ts
export type TenantRoute =
  | { state: 'active'; shardId: number }
  | { state: 'migrating'; shardId: number; targetShardId: number }
  | { state: 'paused' }; // brief window during cutover
// src/sharding/dual-write.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';
import { ShardResolver } from './shard-resolver.service';

@Injectable()
export class DualWriteService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(DualWriteService.name);
  constructor(private readonly shards: ShardResolver) {}

  // Runs the write on the source of truth, then best-effort on the target while migrating.
  async write<T>(tenantId: string, op: (em: EntityManager) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const route = await this.shards.routeFor(tenantId);
    if (route.state === 'paused') {
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException({ message: 'tenant cutover in progress', retryAfterMs: 500 });
    }
    const source: DataSource = this.shards.byId(route.shardId);
    const result = await source.transaction(op);           // source commit is the truth

    if (route.state === 'migrating') {
      const target = this.shards.byId(route.targetShardId);
      try {
        await target.transaction(op);                      // op must be idempotent (upserts)
      } catch (err) {
        this.logger.error(`dual-write to shard ${route.targetShardId} failed for ${tenantId}`, err as Error);
        // Record the mismatch for the verifier; do not fail the user request.
        await this.shards.recordMismatch(tenantId, (err as Error).message);
      }
    }
    return result;
  }
}

The op passed in must be written as an upsert for dual writes to be safe: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET ... WHERE excluded.updated_at > orders.updated_at.

PostgreSQL example

Backfill batch and the verification checksum.

-- One backfill batch: keyset by primary key, idempotent upsert that never regresses newer data.
INSERT INTO orders (id, tenant_id, status, total_cents, created_at, updated_at)
SELECT id, tenant_id, status, total_cents, created_at, updated_at
FROM dblink('source_shard', $$
  SELECT id, tenant_id, status, total_cents, created_at, updated_at
  FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 'acme' AND id > '018f3e1a-0000-7000-8000-000000000000'
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000 $$)
  AS s(id uuid, tenant_id text, status text, total_cents bigint, created_at timestamptz, updated_at timestamptz)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
  SET status = excluded.status, total_cents = excluded.total_cents, updated_at = excluded.updated_at
  WHERE orders.updated_at < excluded.updated_at;

-- Verification: same query on both shards must return identical values.
SELECT count(*), max(updated_at),
       md5(string_agg(id::text || ':' || updated_at::text, ',' ORDER BY id)) AS checksum
FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 'acme';

Production scenario

Moving a 400 GB tenant from a shared shard to a dedicated one: dual writes enabled on Monday; backfill at 5,000 rows per batch with a 50 ms sleep and a pause whenever replica lag exceeds 2 s, completing in about 30 hours; verification clean for 6 hours on Wednesday; cutover Wednesday 23:00 with a 380 ms write pause; reverse dual writes until Thursday 23:00; source rows deleted the following week. Zero user-visible errors beyond a handful of 503 retries absorbed by client SDKs.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Dual write succeeds on source, fails on target: recorded as a mismatch; the backfill or a repair job reconciles. Never fail the user for the target.
  • Backfill overwrites a newer dual write: prevented by the WHERE orders.updated_at < excluded.updated_at guard; requires a monotonic updated_at or version column on every table.
  • Deletes during migration: a delete on the source must also delete on the target; backfill of a row already deleted on the source is harmless only if deletes are dual-written and the backfill reads a snapshot after the delete. Use soft deletes during migration windows if possible.
  • Cutover pause too long: requests time out. Bound it (1 s) and abort the flip if in-flight writes have not drained.
  • Cache holds the old shard: evict shard:{tenant} on flip and keep the cache TTL short during migrations.
  • Sequences and counters on the target: none if you use application-generated ids; if any table still uses a sequence, setval it above the source's max before cutover.
  • Rebalancing under load: backfill competes with production; throttle by target CPU and replica lag, and schedule the heavy part off-peak.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the routing scheme for rebalancing on day one: directory or consistent hashing, never mod N. They treat data movement as a product with tooling: a CLI to start, monitor, verify, cut over and roll back a tenant move, exercised on small tenants first. They prefer database-level logical replication with row filters over application dual writes when the PostgreSQL version allows, because it has fewer ways to lose a write.

Interview questions

  1. Explain consistent hashing and why virtual nodes matter. Expected: points on a ring, clockwise ownership; adding a node moves only 1/N of keys; virtual nodes even out the arcs.
  2. Describe a zero-downtime move of one tenant to a new shard. Expected: mark migrating, dual write, batched idempotent backfill, verify, short pause and directory flip, reverse dual write, cleanup.
  3. How do you stop the backfill from overwriting newer data? Expected: version or updated_at guard in the upsert.

22.12 Connection scaling

Concept

Connection scaling is keeping the number of PostgreSQL connections within what the server handles well, no matter how many application pods, replicas and workers exist. PostgreSQL forks one backend process per connection; each costs memory (5 to 10 MB baseline, more with work_mem in use) and adds contention in shared structures. Beyond a few hundred active connections, throughput goes down, not up. A connection pooler multiplexes many client connections onto few server connections.

Why does it exist?

Because the arithmetic of modern deployments explodes. 40 API pods with a pool of 20, 10 worker pods with a pool of 10, two replicas each receiving read pools, and a few admin tools: 40×20 + 10×10 = 900 connections to the primary alone. Kubernetes autoscaling doubles the pod count during a traffic spike, so at the exact moment the database is busiest it also receives twice as many connections. max_connections is hit, new pods fail with FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections, and the outage is self-inflicted.

Mental model

Imagine a call centre with 50 agents. Without a pooler, every customer keeps a dedicated phone line open all day even when silent, so 900 lines are needed for 900 customers and most agents sit idle waiting for their assigned customer to speak. With a pooler (a switchboard), customers dial in when they have something to say and are connected to any free agent for the duration of the sentence. 50 agents serve 900 customers because customers are silent 95% of the time.

How it works

PgBouncer is the standard pooler. It sits between the application and PostgreSQL. In transaction pooling mode, a client holds a server connection only for the duration of one transaction (for autocommit statements, one statement), then releases it. Typical ratio: 2,000 client connections onto 40 server connections. Costs: session-level features break across transactions (SET without LOCAL, prepared statements before PgBouncer 1.21, advisory locks held across transactions, LISTEN/NOTIFY, temporary tables). Session mode has none of those limitations but only helps by reusing connections across short-lived clients, not by multiplexing.

RDS Proxy is the managed equivalent on AWS. It multiplexes, handles failover more gracefully (it keeps client connections open while the backend switches, often reducing failover impact to a few seconds), and integrates with IAM and Secrets Manager. It "pins" a client to a server connection when session state is detected, which silently removes the multiplexing benefit; watch the DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlySessionPinned metric.

Per-pod pools still exist in front of the pooler: the Node.js pg pool inside each NestJS pod, sized small (5 to 10) because acquiring a connection from PgBouncer is cheap. The application pool's job becomes limiting concurrency per pod, not saving connection setup cost.

Topology: one PgBouncer (or a pair behind a load balancer) per PostgreSQL node, including replicas. PgBouncer is single-threaded; it handles tens of thousands of transactions per second, and multiple instances on the same port with so_reuseport scale it further.

 60 NestJS pods x pool 8  = 480 client connections
          |
          v
   PgBouncer (transaction mode), default_pool_size = 40
          |
          v
   PostgreSQL primary, max_connections = 200 (40 used by pooler + room for admins and replication)

The budget formula the senior engineer keeps handy:

server_connections_needed = sum over poolers (default_pool_size x databases x users) + reserved (superuser, replication, admin)
must be < max_connections, with max_connections itself sized so that
max_connections x work_mem x (average sort/hash nodes per query) fits in RAM after shared_buffers.

NestJS example

Pool settings that fit behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, and the guards that prevent session state leaking.

// src/database/typeorm.options.ts
import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';

export const typeOrmOptions = (): TypeOrmModuleOptions => ({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.PGBOUNCER_HOST,      // pooler, not PostgreSQL directly
  port: 6432,
  username: process.env.PG_USER,
  password: process.env.PG_PASSWORD,
  database: process.env.PG_DB,
  autoLoadEntities: true,
  extra: {
    max: 8,                              // small: PgBouncer does the real pooling
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000,
    idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000,
    statement_timeout: 5_000,            // sent as a startup parameter; PgBouncer passes it through
  },
});

Rules of the road in transaction pooling mode, enforced in code review:

  • Use SET LOCAL inside a transaction, never bare SET (it would leak to the next client that gets the server connection).
  • Take advisory locks and release them within one transaction (pg_advisory_xact_lock), never session-level pg_advisory_lock across statements.
  • Do not rely on LISTEN/NOTIFY through the pooler; open a dedicated direct connection for it.
  • Do not use temporary tables across statements.

PostgreSQL example

-- How many connections, by state and by application, right now?
SELECT application_name, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;

-- Idle-in-transaction connections hold locks and pool slots; kill them past a threshold.
-- Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s' at the database level.
ALTER DATABASE shop SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

-- Headroom check.
SELECT current_setting('max_connections')::int - count(*) AS free_slots FROM pg_stat_activity;

Minimal pgbouncer.ini for a primary:

[databases]
shop = host=primary.internal port=5432 dbname=shop

[pgbouncer]
listen_port = 6432
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 40
max_client_conn = 4000
reserve_pool_size = 5
reserve_pool_timeout = 3
server_idle_timeout = 60
query_wait_timeout = 5       ; clients waiting for a server connection fail fast instead of piling up

Production scenario

Before: 48 pods × pool 20 = 960 connections; max_connections = 1000; autoscale to 70 pods during a campaign caused connection failures across the fleet. After: pool 8 per pod behind two PgBouncer instances with default_pool_size = 50 each; primary sees at most 100 connections plus reserved; 140 pods during the next campaign, no connection errors, and p95 improved by 15% because fewer backends meant less lock manager contention.

Failure scenario

At 11:02 a deploy rolled out a new version. Kubernetes started 40 new pods before terminating the 40 old ones (surge), so for two minutes there were 80 pods × 20 = 1,600 connection attempts against max_connections = 1000. New pods failed readiness on their first query, Kubernetes kept them and retried, old pods were finally terminated, and the fleet recovered after four minutes of partial outage. The pooler would have absorbed this entirely; the interim fix was maxSurge: 10% and a smaller pool; the real fix was PgBouncer.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Pool × replicas × pods exceeding max_connections: recount after every topology change; alert on free slots below 20%.
  • Prepared statements in transaction mode: pg uses unnamed statements by default, but TypeORM or pg with named prepared statements needs PgBouncer 1.21+ with max_prepared_statements set, or errors like prepared statement "s1" does not exist.
  • Session pinning in RDS Proxy: session state silently disables multiplexing; watch the pinned-connection metric.
  • PgBouncer as a single point of failure: run two, behind a load balancer or with DNS round-robin, and health-check them.
  • query_wait_timeout too high: requests queue at the pooler instead of failing fast; latency explodes under overload. Keep it low and let the application's retry handle it.
  • Long transactions monopolise server connections in transaction mode: a 30-second report holds one of the 40 for 30 seconds; run reports through a separate pool with its own limits.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They put a pooler in front of every production PostgreSQL from the start, size the application pool for concurrency rather than connection reuse, and forbid session-level state in application code. They know the connection budget as a number and re-derive it whenever pods, replicas or shards change.

Interview questions

  1. Why does a pooler improve throughput even though it adds a hop? Expected: fewer backends means less memory and contention; multiplexing uses idle time; connection setup avoided.
  2. What breaks in PgBouncer transaction mode? Expected: session SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, temp tables, named prepared statements on older versions.
  3. Size the pools: 60 pods, 2 replicas, primary max_connections 200. Expected: small per-pod pools behind a pooler per node; pooler server pool sized from CPU cores and workload, well under 200 with headroom.

22.13 Write scaling before sharding

Concept

A set of techniques that raise effective write capacity of a single primary without splitting it: batching many small writes into few large ones, moving writes off the request path into queues, separating read models from the write model (CQRS), and moving high-volume low-value writes (events, logs, metrics, audit trails) to a store built for them. Each technique defers sharding, often by years.

Why does it exist?

Most "write-bound" databases are not bound by business writes. They are bound by chatty writes: a row update per page view, an audit row per request, a last_seen touch per API call, an event row per click. Business writes (orders, payments) are a small fraction. Removing or batching the chatter buys back the machine.

Mental model

Imagine a bank teller who must write every coin drop into the ledger by hand. Batching is counting a customer's coins and writing one line. Async queues are putting deposit slips in a tray for a clerk to enter later, in bulk, while the teller serves the next customer. Moving logs elsewhere is putting the visitor sign-in sheet at the door instead of in the ledger.

How it works

  1. Batching. Collect writes for up to N ms or M rows and insert in one statement (INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), ... or COPY). One transaction with 500 rows costs one fsync instead of 500. Throughput per second goes from thousands to hundreds of thousands of rows. Cost: a few milliseconds of latency and the need to handle a partial-batch failure (fall back to per-row inserts to find the bad row).
  2. Async write queues. The request path publishes an event (BullMQ, RabbitMQ, Kafka); a worker consumes and writes in batches. Cost: the write is eventually consistent, and the queue must be durable and the consumer idempotent (Part 30).
  3. CQRS read models. Keep the write model normalised and small; build denormalised read tables (or Elasticsearch, or Redis) from the change stream. Writes get cheaper because they no longer maintain the counters and denormalised columns that reads want. Cost: two models to keep consistent, and read-your-own-writes again.
  4. Move high-write data elsewhere. Click events, request logs, metrics, notification delivery receipts: append-only, huge, queried by time. They belong in ClickHouse, S3 plus Athena, a time-series database, or at least a separate PostgreSQL instance with partitioning. Cost: another system to run, but one designed for that shape.
  5. Delete chatter. UPDATE users SET last_seen = now() on every request is the classic. Write it to Redis and flush hourly, or only update when the previous value is more than 5 minutes old.

NestJS example

A batching writer for an audit trail: buffers rows, flushes every 200 ms or 500 rows, and falls back to single inserts if a batch fails.

// src/audit/audit-batch-writer.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

interface AuditRow { actorId: string; action: string; targetId: string; at: Date }

@Injectable()
export class AuditBatchWriter implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(AuditBatchWriter.name);
  private buffer: AuditRow[] = [];
  private timer?: NodeJS.Timeout;
  private static readonly MAX_ROWS = 500;
  private static readonly MAX_WAIT_MS = 200;

  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  enqueue(row: AuditRow): void {
    this.buffer.push(row);
    if (this.buffer.length >= AuditBatchWriter.MAX_ROWS) void this.flush();
    else if (!this.timer) this.timer = setTimeout(() => void this.flush(), AuditBatchWriter.MAX_WAIT_MS);
  }

  private async flush(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.timer) { clearTimeout(this.timer); this.timer = undefined; }
    const rows = this.buffer; this.buffer = [];
    if (rows.length === 0) return;
    try {
      // One multi-row INSERT: one round trip, one fsync, instead of rows.length of each.
      await this.ds.query(
        `INSERT INTO audit_events (actor_id, action, target_id, occurred_at)
         SELECT * FROM unnest($1::text[], $2::text[], $3::text[], $4::timestamptz[])`,
        [rows.map((r) => r.actorId), rows.map((r) => r.action), rows.map((r) => r.targetId), rows.map((r) => r.at)],
      );
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.error(`batch of ${rows.length} failed; retrying individually`, err as Error);
      for (const r of rows) {
        try {
          await this.ds.query('INSERT INTO audit_events (actor_id, action, target_id, occurred_at) VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4)',
            [r.actorId, r.action, r.targetId, r.at]);
        } catch (single) { this.logger.error('dropping audit row', single as Error); }
      }
    }
  }

  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> { await this.flush(); } // drain on shutdown
}

Rows in the buffer are lost if the pod is killed abruptly; for an audit trail that must be complete, publish to a durable queue instead and batch in the consumer.

Production scenario

A marketplace primary at 9,000 write TPS: 6,500 of them were last_seen touches, session refreshes and click events. Moving click events to Kafka plus ClickHouse, last_seen to Redis with a 10-minute flush, and session refreshes to a sliding TTL in Redis left 1,800 business write TPS on the primary. Sharding was postponed indefinitely.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Batch failure hides one bad row: fall back to per-row to isolate it.
  • Async writes and read-your-own-writes: the user does not see the write immediately; design the UI for it or write synchronously for user-facing state.
  • Queue backlog: the worker falls behind; monitor lag and scale consumers.
  • Buffer lost on crash: batching in memory is at-most-once; use a durable queue when loss is unacceptable.
  • CQRS projection lag: read model minutes behind after a burst; expose freshness to the client.

Interview questions

  1. Primary at 9,000 write TPS. Do you shard? Expected: first classify the writes; move chatter to Redis/queues/columnar stores; batch; usually sharding is unnecessary.
  2. What are the consistency implications of async writes? Expected: eventual visibility, need for idempotent consumers, ordering per key.

22.14 Multi-tenant scaling strategies

Concept

A multi-tenant system serves many customers (tenants) from shared infrastructure. The data layout for tenants decides isolation, cost, operational load and how each of the scaling techniques in this part applies. Three layouts: shared schema with a tenant_id column (optionally enforced with row-level security), one schema per tenant, and one database per tenant.

Why does it exist?

Because the tradeoff between cost efficiency and isolation is real. Ten thousand tiny tenants cannot each have a database; three enterprise customers with compliance demands cannot share a table. Most products end up with a hybrid, and the senior engineer must know what each layout costs at migration time and at scale time.

Mental model

Imagine an office building. Shared schema is an open-plan floor where everyone's desk has a name tag and a rule says "only touch your own desk". Schema per tenant is one room per company on a shared floor with a shared corridor and services. Database per tenant is one building per company. The open plan is cheapest and easiest to rearrange; the buildings are the most private and the most expensive to renovate one by one.

How it works

Layout Isolation Cost per tenant Migrations Noisy neighbour Scaling path Best for
Shared schema + tenant_id (+ RLS) Logical only; one bug leaks data Near zero One migration for everyone; huge tables Shared everything; needs rate limits Partition by tenant list for whales; shard by tenant_id Thousands of small tenants
Schema per tenant Namespace separation, same connection Low; catalog grows N migrations, one per schema; drift risk; hours for 5,000 schemas Shared CPU and pool Move schemas between databases Hundreds of mid-size tenants with custom needs
Database per tenant Strong; separate backups and restore High; pools and connections per DB N migrations across N databases; orchestration required None at the DB level Move databases between servers Tens of large or regulated tenants

Row-level security (RLS) makes the shared-schema layout much safer: a policy on each table ensures every query is filtered by the tenant in the session, even if the developer forgets the WHERE.

CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id text NOT NULL, amount_cents bigint NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now()
);
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;   -- applies to the table owner too

-- The application sets the tenant per transaction; the policy enforces it.
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true))
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true));

-- Per request, inside the transaction (SET LOCAL: safe with PgBouncer transaction mode):
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = 't_8842';
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE created_at > now() - interval '30 days';   -- only t_8842's rows
COMMIT;

The tenant_id index must lead every composite index ((tenant_id, created_at)), otherwise the policy's filter is applied after a broad scan.

NestJS example

A request-scoped tenant context and a query runner wrapper that sets the RLS variable for every transaction.

// src/tenancy/tenant-transaction.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class TenantTransactionService {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  // Every tenant-scoped unit of work goes through here; RLS does the rest.
  async run<T>(tenantId: string, work: (em: EntityManager) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    return this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      // Parameterised via format to avoid injection; set_config with is_local = true equals SET LOCAL.
      await em.query(`SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)`, [tenantId]);
      return work(em);
    });
  }
}

The tenant id comes from the verified JWT (a guard populates it), never from a client-supplied header.

Production scenario

A SaaS with 20,000 tenants: 19,900 on shared-schema with RLS across 4 hash shards keyed by tenant_id; 90 mid-size tenants on their own list partitions inside those shards; 10 enterprise tenants each on a dedicated database with their own backups. One migration pipeline applies each change to 4 shards and 10 dedicated databases in order, with a status table so a failed database can be retried alone. Schema-per-tenant was rejected because a migration across 20,000 schemas took 6 hours and drift between schemas had caused two incidents.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • RLS bypassed by a superuser or table owner without FORCE; connect as a non-owner role.
  • Missing set_config in some code path: with RLS the query returns zero rows rather than leaking, which is the safe failure, but it looks like a data-loss bug. Log the tenant setting on empty results in staging.
  • Migrations across N databases half-applied: tenants on different schema versions; the app must be N-1 compatible (Part 24) and the pipeline resumable.
  • Per-tenant connection pools explode with database-per-tenant: 500 databases × pool 5 = 2,500 connections; use PgBouncer with per-database pools, or a lazy pool that opens on demand.
  • Tenant deletion: shared schema means a big DELETE (do it in batches); database per tenant means DROP DATABASE.
  • Cross-tenant analytics: trivial with shared schema, painful with database per tenant; feed a warehouse by CDC.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start with shared schema plus RLS plus tenant_id-leading indexes, because it is the cheapest to operate and the easiest to shard later by the same key. They add dedicated partitions or databases only for tenants that need isolation for compliance or for load, and they keep the number of distinct layouts to two. They refuse schema-per-tenant at scale unless custom schemas per tenant are the product.

Interview questions

  1. Compare the three multi-tenant layouts for a product expecting 10,000 tenants. Expected: shared schema with RLS by default; dedicated databases for a handful; avoid schema-per-tenant because of migration cost and drift.
  2. How does RLS help and what can still go wrong? Expected: enforces tenant filter at the database; bypassed without FORCE, needs the setting per transaction, needs leading tenant_id indexes.
  3. How would you migrate a shared-schema tenant to its own database? Expected: the live-move procedure from section 22.11.

Senior Checklist — Part 22

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I climb the ladder in order (queries, pooling, cache, replicas, partitioning, sharding) and measure at each rung
  • I can configure TypeORM replication and Sequelize replication and I know which reads I refuse to send to a replica
  • I can solve read-your-own-writes with sticky routing and with an LSN check
  • I can read pg_stat_replication and pg_replication_slots and I alert on lag and on inactive slots
  • I know what my application does during a failover: reconnect via DNS, retry only idempotent work, no retry storm
  • I can design a partitioned table with a correct primary key, automated partition creation and retention by drop
  • I can choose a shard key from query logs and justify it by alignment, cardinality and distribution
  • I can move a tenant between shards with dual writes, idempotent backfill, verification and a sub-second cutover
  • I keep a connection budget and a pooler in front of every PostgreSQL node
  • I remove chatty writes before I consider sharding

Part 22 — Key Takeaways

  • One tuned PostgreSQL instance serves tens of thousands of QPS and terabytes of data; most systems never need more than replicas and partitioning.
  • Diagnose before scaling: pg_stat_statements and pg_stat_activity tell you which rung of the ladder applies.
  • Replicas scale reads only; every replica read needs an explicit consistency decision, and every write needs idempotency because stale reads cause retries.
  • Replication lag is a property to bound, not a bug to eliminate; measure it with LSNs and throttle the jobs that cause it.
  • A replication slot with no consumer will fill your disk; alert on inactive slots and set max_slot_wal_keep_size.
  • Failover is an application feature: DNS endpoints, keepalives, short connect timeouts, readiness that checks writability, retries only for idempotent work.
  • Partition huge tables by the column your queries and retention use; the primary key must include the partition key; automate partition creation before the first midnight.
  • Sharding is a one-way door: shard the whole domain by one key, keep transactions inside a shard, generate ids in the application, feed reporting from CDC.
  • Directory routing lets you isolate whale tenants and move them live; mod N hashing cannot be rebalanced cheaply.
  • Hot keys are a distribution problem: salt counters, cache hot entities, give whales dedicated shards.
  • Pool size times replicas times pods must stay under max_connections; put PgBouncer or RDS Proxy in front of every node and keep application pools small.
  • Before sharding for writes, delete the chatter: batch, queue, move logs and events to a store built for them.
  • Shared schema with tenant_id, RLS and tenant_id-leading indexes is the default multi-tenant layout; dedicated databases are for the few tenants who need them.

Part 23 — Database Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes

A database schema is the one part of a system that cannot be redeployed. Code is stateless: ship a new version, kill the old pods, done. The database carries every row ever written, and every change to its shape must be made in place, while the application keeps reading and writing, while old and new versions of the code run at the same time, and while a single wrong lock can stop the entire business for as long as it takes someone to notice.

This part is about making schema changes boring. It covers migrations as code in TypeORM and Sequelize, where migrations should run, exactly which ALTER TABLE operations are fast and which rewrite terabytes, how to keep a migration from queueing behind a long query and freezing every request, the expand/contract pattern with a complete walkthrough on a users table, batched backfills that do not melt the replicas, why rollback is mostly fiction, and the recipes for renaming, retyping, splitting and shrinking tables without a maintenance window.

The senior mantra applies to every migration: Can it timeout? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed? A migration can do all six, and a migration that partially succeeds is the worst of them.

23.1 Migrations as code

Concept

A migration is a versioned, ordered, executable description of one change to the database schema or data. Migrations live in the repository next to the code that needs them, are reviewed like code, and are applied by a tool that records which ones have already run in a table in the database itself. The database's shape at any moment is the result of applying every migration in order.

Three related but different things get called "migration":

  • Schema migration: changes the structure. ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone_e164 text. Usually fast, sometimes catastrophically slow.
  • Data migration: changes existing rows to fit a new structure or rule. UPDATE users SET phone_e164 = normalize(phone). Never fast on a big table.
  • Backfill: a data migration run in batches, over time, from a worker, with throttling and progress tracking, instead of as one statement. On any table with more than a few million rows, data migrations are backfills.

Why does it exist?

Without migrations as code, schema changes happen by hand in a database console, differ between environments, and nobody can say what the schema looked like last Tuesday. Deploys break because the code expects a column that exists in staging but not in production. A new engineer cannot build a local database that matches production. Migrations solve reproducibility: the same ordered list of changes, applied everywhere, tracked in the database.

Mental model

Imagine a building's renovation log. Every change to the building (a wall removed, a door added) is written as a numbered work order and signed off when done. Anyone can reconstruct the building's current layout by reading the orders in sequence. Nobody knocks out a wall without an order, because next week's electrician needs to know where the wall went. And crucially, once a wall is gone, "undo work order 42" is not a matter of paperwork; you would need to rebuild the wall.

How it works

  1. A developer changes an entity (TypeORM) or model (Sequelize) and generates or writes a migration file with a timestamped name: 1725580800000-AddPhoneE164ToUsers.ts.
  2. The migration has an up function (apply) and a down function (attempt to undo).
  3. The migration runner connects to the database, reads the migrations table (TypeORM's default name; Sequelize's CLI uses SequelizeMeta), finds the files not yet recorded, sorts by timestamp, and runs each up, inserting a row for it.
  4. In PostgreSQL, most DDL is transactional: ALTER TABLE, CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX (the non-concurrent kind), DROP, all roll back if the transaction fails. This is a huge advantage over MySQL. TypeORM runs each migration inside a transaction by default (migrationsTransactionMode: 'all' wraps all pending migrations in one transaction; 'each' wraps each separately; 'none' disables it).
  5. Two statements refuse to run inside a transaction block: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (and DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY), and before PostgreSQL 12, ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE. From PostgreSQL 12, ADD VALUE can run in a transaction but the new enum value cannot be used until that transaction commits. Migrations containing these must run with transactions disabled for that migration.

Forward-only mindset. Write every migration as if down will never be run in production, because on a real database it usually cannot be: a dropped column's data is gone, a backfilled value cannot be un-backfilled, and running down while new code is deployed breaks the new code. down is for local development and for CI checks. Production recovers by writing a new forward migration that repairs the situation. Keep down accurate anyway; it documents intent and it is what lets a developer iterate locally.

migration:generate review discipline. TypeORM can diff entities against the database and emit a migration. The output is a starting point, never a finished migration. It will happily generate ALTER TABLE "users" DROP COLUMN "phone" because you renamed a property, ALTER COLUMN "total" TYPE bigint which rewrites the table, or CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY. Every generated migration is edited by hand and reviewed against the safe-operations table in section 23.3. Generated migrations also tend to include noise (re-creating constraints with different names, altering defaults) whenever entity metadata and the database disagree slightly; delete the noise.

flowchart LR
    E["Entity change in code"] --> G["migration:generate"]
    G --> R["Human edits: CONCURRENTLY, lock_timeout, split unsafe ops"]
    R --> PR["Code review against safety table"]
    PR --> CI["CI: run up on fresh DB, run down, run up again"]
    CI --> J["Migration job before deploy"]
    J --> T["migrations table records the run"]

Practical example

The users table has a free-text phone column with values like +1 (555) 010-2233, 555 010 2233 and 00 44 20 7946 0958. Marketing wants SMS, which needs E.164 format (+15550102233). The change: add phone_e164, normalise every existing row into it, make the application write both, and eventually drop the free-text column. That is one schema migration (add column), one backfill (normalise 30 million rows), one code change per stage, and a final schema migration (drop column), spread over two weeks. Section 23.5 walks through every step of it.

NestJS example

DataSource configuration for migrations, separate from the application's runtime configuration, so the CLI and the migration job have their own entry point.

// src/database/data-source.ts
import 'reflect-metadata';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

// Used by the TypeORM CLI and by the migration job. Never imported by the running app.
export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.PG_HOST,
  port: Number(process.env.PG_PORT ?? 5432),
  username: process.env.PG_MIGRATION_USER,      // a role that owns the tables
  password: process.env.PG_MIGRATION_PASSWORD,
  database: process.env.PG_DB,
  entities: ['dist/**/*.entity.js'],
  migrations: ['dist/database/migrations/*.js'],
  migrationsTableName: 'migrations',
  migrationsTransactionMode: 'each',           // one transaction per migration file
  synchronize: false,                          // never in any environment beyond a scratch DB
  logging: ['migration', 'error'],
});
{
  "scripts": {
    "migration:generate": "typeorm migration:generate -d dist/database/data-source.js -p",
    "migration:run": "typeorm migration:run -d dist/database/data-source.js",
    "migration:run:notx": "typeorm migration:run -d dist/database/data-source.js -t none",
    "migration:show": "typeorm migration:show -d dist/database/data-source.js",
    "migration:revert": "typeorm migration:revert -d dist/database/data-source.js"
  }
}

The -t none (--transaction none) variant is for migrations with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Keep such migrations in their own file, and in the migration body set lock_timeout yourself since there is no surrounding transaction to make it LOCAL.

TypeORM example
