A hand-edited migration for adding the nullable column: transactional, with a lock timeout so it cannot block behind a long query.

// src/database/migrations/1725580800000-AddPhoneE164ToUsers.ts
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class AddPhoneE164ToUsers1725580800000 implements MigrationInterface {
  name = 'AddPhoneE164ToUsers1725580800000';

  public async up(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    // Fail fast instead of queueing behind a long transaction and blocking the app (section 31.4).
    await queryRunner.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`);
    // Nullable, no default: catalog-only change, takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for microseconds.
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "users" ADD COLUMN "phone_e164" text`);
  }

  public async down(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`);
    await queryRunner.query(`ALTER TABLE "users" DROP COLUMN "phone_e164"`);
  }
}

And a non-transactional one for the index, which must run with -t none:

// src/database/migrations/1725581000000-IndexUsersPhoneE164.ts
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class IndexUsersPhoneE1641725581000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  name = 'IndexUsersPhoneE1641725581000000';

  public async up(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    // No transaction here (run with --transaction none), so plain SET, then reset.
    await queryRunner.query(`SET lock_timeout = '3s'`);
    await queryRunner.query(`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS "users_phone_e164_idx" ON "users" ("phone_e164")`);
    await queryRunner.query(`RESET lock_timeout`);
  }

  public async down(queryRunner: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await queryRunner.query(`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS "users_phone_e164_idx"`);
  }
}

If a CONCURRENTLY build fails halfway (lock timeout, cancelled, deadlock), it leaves an invalid index behind that consumes space and slows writes but is never used. The IF NOT EXISTS would then skip re-creating it. Always check for invalid indexes after such a migration and drop them:

SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index_name FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;

Sequelize example

Sequelize migrations use queryInterface; they are plain JavaScript or TypeScript modules run by sequelize-cli or Umzug. They are not wrapped in a transaction automatically; you add one when you want atomicity.

// migrations/20260906120000-add-phone-e164-to-users.ts
import { QueryInterface, DataTypes } from 'sequelize';

export default {
  async up(queryInterface: QueryInterface): Promise<void> {
    await queryInterface.sequelize.transaction(async (transaction) => {
      await queryInterface.sequelize.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`, { transaction });
      await queryInterface.addColumn('users', 'phone_e164', { type: DataTypes.STRING(20), allowNull: true }, { transaction });
    });
  },

  async down(queryInterface: QueryInterface): Promise<void> {
    await queryInterface.sequelize.transaction(async (transaction) => {
      await queryInterface.sequelize.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`, { transaction });
      await queryInterface.removeColumn('users', 'phone_e164', { transaction });
    });
  },
};

For CONCURRENTLY, use queryInterface.sequelize.query(...) outside any transaction; queryInterface.addIndex has a concurrently: true option on PostgreSQL, but the raw statement is clearer to review.

Production scenario

A team of 12 engineers ships 20 to 40 migrations a month to a 1.5 TB database. Their rules: every migration is a separate PR section reviewed by someone who has read section 23.3; generated migrations are always edited; every migration sets lock_timeout; index creation is always CONCURRENTLY in its own file; data changes never run in migrations, only in backfill jobs; and a migration that touches a table over 10 million rows must be tested against last night's production snapshot in a staging environment with timing recorded. Their average migration takes under a second of lock time; their worst in two years took 4 seconds.

Failure scenario

migration:generate produced, among other lines, ALTER TABLE "orders" ALTER COLUMN "total_cents" TYPE bigint because someone changed a TypeScript type from number to string and the column decorator from int to bigint. Nobody noticed in review. In production the statement took an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on orders (300 million rows) and started rewriting the table. Every read and write on orders blocked. Checkout was down for 41 minutes until an on-call engineer found the session with pg_stat_activity, terminated it with pg_terminate_backend, and the transaction rolled back (transactional DDL saved the day; the table was intact). The fix afterwards: the review checklist, snapshot testing for migrations touching big tables, and the type-change recipe in section 23.3.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Migration file with CONCURRENTLY run inside a transaction: ERROR: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block. The migration fails; with 'each' mode the transaction rolls back cleanly; make it its own file and run with -t none.
  • Enum value added and used in the same transaction (PostgreSQL 12+): ERROR: unsafe use of new value "x" of enum type. Split into two migrations.
  • Half-applied migration in 'none' mode: statements 1 and 2 ran, 3 failed; the migrations table has no row; rerunning repeats 1 and 2. Make every statement idempotent (IF NOT EXISTS, IF EXISTS) in non-transactional migrations.
  • Migration table drift between environments: staging has a migration production does not, or the same name with different content. Never edit a migration that has run anywhere; write a new one. Compare SELECT name FROM migrations across environments in CI.
  • Two migrations with the same timestamp from two branches: order becomes arbitrary. Rebase and regenerate the timestamp before merge.
  • Entity and schema disagree after a manual hotfix in production: migration:generate produces a migration to "undo" the hotfix. Record hotfixes as migrations immediately.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat a migration as production code with the highest blast radius in the repository: it runs once, cannot be retried casually, and can lock the whole business. They read every generated line. They separate schema changes (fast, transactional) from data changes (slow, batched, from a worker). They think forward-only and design each migration so that the code deployed before and after it both work (Part 24 — Backward Compatibility).

Common mistakes

  • Trusting migration:generate output.
  • Putting an UPDATE of millions of rows inside a migration, holding a transaction for an hour.
  • Using synchronize: true "only in staging" and then wondering why staging and production diverge.
  • Editing an already-applied migration file.
  • Not setting lock_timeout.

Interview questions

  1. Schema migration, data migration, backfill: what is the difference and where does each run? Expected: structure vs rows vs batched rows; schema in the migration job, data as a batched backfill from a worker.
  2. What cannot run inside a PostgreSQL transaction and how do you handle it in TypeORM? Expected: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, pre-12 ALTER TYPE ADD VALUE; separate file, --transaction none, idempotent statements.
  3. Why "forward-only"? Expected: down cannot restore dropped data and breaks the new code; repair with a new forward migration; keep down for local iteration.
  4. What do you check in a generated migration before merging? Expected: rewrites, missing CONCURRENTLY, dropped columns, implicit NOT NULL, lock timeout, ordering.

23.2 Where migrations run

Concept

A migration must run exactly once, before the code that depends on it, by a process with the right permissions, in a place where a failure is visible and does not take the application down with it. The choice is between running migrations as a distinct step in the deployment pipeline (a CI/CD job, a Kubernetes Job or init container) and running them when the application starts.

Why does it exist?

Because "the app runs migrations on boot" works beautifully with one instance and becomes a race with ten. Ten pods start simultaneously, each sees pending migrations, each tries to run them. TypeORM inserts the migration row after up succeeds, so two pods can both run the same ALTER TABLE; one fails with "column already exists", crashes, restarts, and now you have CrashLoopBackOff on half the fleet in the middle of a deploy, with the schema in a state nobody can describe.

Mental model

Imagine renovating a hotel. You do not let every arriving guest knock out a wall if they notice the renovation is not done. One contractor does the work before the guests arrive, signs the work order, and only then are the doors opened. If the contractor fails, the doors stay closed and someone is called; the guests never see a half-built room.

How it works

Option A: CI/CD job before deploy (recommended). The pipeline builds the image, then runs a one-off container from that same image with the command npm run migration:run, then, only if that succeeds, updates the Deployment. On Kubernetes this is a Job with backoffLimit: 0 (do not auto-retry a failed migration; a human must look) and activeDeadlineSeconds so a hung migration is killed. Helm users put it in a pre-upgrade hook; Argo CD users use a PreSync hook.

Option B: init container. Each pod runs the migration command in an init container before the main container starts. Same race as startup migrations unless the init container takes a lock; the advantage is it needs no separate pipeline step. Acceptable only with an advisory lock, and it still means a migration failure prevents every new pod from starting, which during a failover or scale-up is a bad time to discover it.

Option C: at application startup (migrationsRun: true in TypeORM). Fine for a single-instance development setup. In production, dangerous for the race described above, and because a slow migration delays readiness for every pod, and because the application's database role then needs DDL permissions.

Advisory lock. If you must run migrations from something that may run concurrently, wrap the whole run in a session-level advisory lock so only one runner proceeds and the others wait or skip. This is what tools like Flyway do internally; TypeORM does not.

flowchart LR
    B["Build image"] --> T["Test"]
    T --> M["Migration Job, same image, backoffLimit 0"]
    M -->|"success"| D["Rollout Deployment"]
    M -->|"failure"| S["Stop pipeline, page on-call"]
    D --> V["Verify: migration:show has no pending"]

Permissions. The application role should own nothing and have only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on the tables. A separate migration role owns the tables and runs DDL. This stops a compromised application from altering the schema and stops a well-meaning engineer from running synchronize with production credentials.

Ordering. Migrations run in timestamp order; timestamps come from when the file was created, not merged. Two feature branches can produce files whose order differs from merge order. Rules: regenerate the timestamp on rebase; never have a migration depend on a later one; CI applies all migrations to a fresh database in filename order, so any mis-ordering is caught before production.

Drift detection. Drift is the database's actual schema differing from what the migrations say. It arises from hotfixes in a console, from synchronize in some environment, from failed non-transactional migrations. Detect it in CI by running migration:generate (with --dryrun, or --check on recent TypeORM versions, which exits non-zero when a migration would be generated) against an environment's database after all migrations are applied: any output means drift. Also compare the list of applied migration names between environments.

NestJS example

A small standalone script, packaged in the same image, used by the Kubernetes Job. It uses an advisory lock so that even an accidental concurrent run is safe.

// src/database/run-migrations.ts
import { AppDataSource } from './data-source';

const MIGRATION_LOCK_KEY = 7_236_501; // arbitrary constant, unique per application

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const ds = await AppDataSource.initialize();
  const runner = ds.createQueryRunner();
  await runner.connect();
  try {
    // Session-level advisory lock: held on this connection until released or disconnected.
    const [{ locked }] = await runner.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1) AS locked', [MIGRATION_LOCK_KEY]);
    if (!locked) {
      console.log('another migration runner holds the lock; exiting without changes');
      return;
    }
    const applied = await ds.runMigrations({ transaction: 'each' });
    console.log(`applied ${applied.length} migration(s): ${applied.map((m) => m.name).join(', ') || 'none'}`);
    await runner.query('SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)', [MIGRATION_LOCK_KEY]);
  } finally {
    await runner.release();
    await ds.destroy();
  }
}

main().catch((err) => { console.error('migration failed', err); process.exit(1); });

Note the lock is taken on runner's connection while runMigrations uses the DataSource's own connections; the lock still works because it is a global mutex in PostgreSQL, not tied to the migrating connection. Do not run this through PgBouncer in transaction mode: session-level advisory locks require a stable session. Point the migration job at PostgreSQL directly.

# k8s/migration-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: shop-api-migrate
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0                 # never auto-retry a failed migration
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 1800     # kill a hung migration after 30 minutes
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: registry.internal/shop-api:1.42.0
          command: ["node", "dist/database/run-migrations.js"]
          env:
            - name: PG_HOST
              value: primary.internal      # direct, not PgBouncer
            - name: PG_MIGRATION_USER
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: pg-migrator, key: username } }
            - name: PG_MIGRATION_PASSWORD
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: pg-migrator, key: password } }

PostgreSQL example

Roles and drift checks.

-- Two roles: one owns and migrates, one only uses.
CREATE ROLE shop_migrator LOGIN PASSWORD '...';
CREATE ROLE shop_app      LOGIN PASSWORD '...';

ALTER SCHEMA public OWNER TO shop_migrator;
-- Existing and future tables: app can read/write, cannot alter.
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO shop_app;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO shop_app;
GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO shop_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE shop_migrator IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO shop_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE shop_migrator IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON SEQUENCES TO shop_app;

-- Which migrations has this database seen? Compare across environments in CI.
SELECT id, timestamp, name FROM migrations ORDER BY timestamp;

-- Is a migration runner active right now?
SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS running_for, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE usename = 'shop_migrator';

Production scenario

Deploy pipeline for a 40-pod service: build (4 min), tests (6 min), migration job (typically 2 to 10 s; alerted if over 60 s), rollout with maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 0 (3 min). The migration job runs with the new image against the old code still serving traffic, which is exactly why every migration must be backward compatible with the currently running version (Part 24). Rollback of the code is a normal rollout to the previous image; the schema stays at the new version, which the old code tolerates because of the expand/contract discipline.

Failure scenario

A team ran migrations at startup with 12 replicas. A deploy included CREATE UNIQUE INDEX on a busy table. All 12 pods started, all 12 attempted the index; one won the lock, eleven queued behind it, each holding a connection and blocking readiness. The index took 9 minutes. Kubernetes killed pods on the readiness deadline, restarted them, and each restart re-queued another index attempt. Meanwhile the old pods had been scaled down. Total outage: 34 minutes. Moving migrations to a pre-deploy Job with backoffLimit: 0 and using CONCURRENTLY fixed both halves of the problem.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Migration run twice by two pods: races on DDL, crash loops. Use a Job, or an advisory lock.
  • Job succeeds, rollout fails: schema is ahead of the code. Fine if the migration was backward compatible; disastrous if it dropped a column the old code reads.
  • Job hangs on a lock (section 23.4): activeDeadlineSeconds kills it; the transaction rolls back; the pipeline stops.
  • Job runs through PgBouncer: session advisory lock and SET behave unpredictably in transaction mode; connect directly.
  • Migration role lacks ownership of a table created by hand: must be owner of table. Fix ownership with ALTER TABLE ... OWNER TO shop_migrator.
  • Different migration lists per environment: someone applied a migration in staging that was later renamed; the renamed one is pending in staging and applied in production. Never rename applied migrations.
  • Multiple services sharing one database and one migrations table: their runners collide on the table and on ordering. Give each service its own migrationsTableName, or better, its own schema (section 23.8).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They make the migration step a first-class, visible, separately monitored stage in the pipeline, with its own alert and its own runbook. They give the application role no DDL rights. They ask of every migration: "If this job succeeds and the rollout is then cancelled, is the running code still fine?" If not, the migration is split.

Interview questions

  1. Why not run migrations on application startup? Expected: races between replicas, delayed readiness, DDL permissions in the app, failures hidden in crash loops.
  2. How would you run migrations on Kubernetes? Expected: a Job from the same image, backoffLimit: 0, deadline, before rollout; PreSync hook in Argo CD or pre-upgrade in Helm; direct connection to the primary.
  3. How do you detect schema drift? Expected: generate a migration against each environment in CI and fail on non-empty output; compare applied migration lists.
  4. Two branches created migrations with out-of-order timestamps. What happens and how do you prevent it? Expected: application order differs by environment; regenerate timestamps on rebase; CI applies to a fresh DB.

Practical exercise

Set up a NestJS project with a migrations folder, the run-migrations.ts runner above, and a GitHub Actions workflow that: starts PostgreSQL as a service container, applies all migrations, runs migration:generate --dryrun and fails if any SQL is produced, reverts the last migration and re-applies it, and finally runs the test suite. Acceptance criteria: the workflow fails when you add an entity column without a migration; it fails when a migration's down does not restore the schema; it passes otherwise.

23.3 Locks taken by DDL

Concept

Every DDL statement in PostgreSQL takes a lock on the table it changes. Most take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, the strongest lock, which conflicts with everything including plain SELECT. The question that decides whether a migration is safe is not only which lock it takes but for how long: some operations hold the lock for microseconds while updating the catalog; others hold it while rewriting every row of the table or scanning every row to validate a constraint. A 300-million-row table rewritten under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE is a multi-hour full outage of that table.

Why does it exist?

Locks exist because the catalog and the data files must be consistent: a query planned against the old column layout must not run against the new one. PostgreSQL's designers chose correctness and simplicity; it is the migration author's job to choose operations that need the lock only briefly, and to arrange the long work (rewrites, validations, index builds) so it happens without the strong lock.

Mental model

Imagine changing the sign on a shop door versus rebuilding the shop floor. Both require locking the door for the safety of people inside. Swapping a sign takes ten seconds; nobody minds. Rebuilding the floor with the door locked is a week without customers. The trick is to build the new floor next door while the shop stays open, then swap the sign.

How it works

The lock levels that matter for DDL, weakest to strongest:

Lock mode Taken by Conflicts with
ACCESS SHARE SELECT only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
ROW EXCLUSIVE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE SHARE, SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE, EXCLUSIVE, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, ALTER TABLE ... SET (...) itself and stronger; allows reads and writes
SHARE CREATE INDEX (non-concurrent) writes (ROW EXCLUSIVE) and stronger; allows reads
SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE ADD FOREIGN KEY (on both tables) writes and stronger; allows reads
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE most ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL everything, including SELECT

Now the table you actually need, operation by operation. "Fast" means catalog-only: the lock is held for milliseconds. "Scan" means every row is read while the lock is held. "Rewrite" means every row is copied into a new file while the lock is held.

Operation Lock Duration Safe recipe
ADD COLUMN nullable, no default ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast As is, with lock_timeout
ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <constant> ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast since PostgreSQL 11 (default stored in catalog as attmissingval) As is on PG11+; on PG10 and older: add nullable, backfill, set default
ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <volatile fn> e.g. gen_random_uuid(), clock_timestamp() ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Rewrite Add nullable, set default (applies to new rows only), backfill in batches
ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL with default ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast on PG11+ (non-volatile default) As is on PG11+
ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL without default on non-empty table fails immediately n/a Add nullable, backfill, then NOT NULL via CHECK recipe
ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Scan of whole table ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE); then SET NOT NULL is fast on PG12+ because a valid CHECK proves it; drop the CHECK
ALTER COLUMN ... DROP NOT NULL ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast As is
ALTER COLUMN ... SET DEFAULT / DROP DEFAULT ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast (affects future rows only) As is
ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE binary-compatible (varchar(50) to varchar(100), varchar to text, adding timestamptz precision) ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast As is
ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE other (int to bigint, text to jsonb, varchar(100) to varchar(50)) ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Rewrite plus index rebuilds New column, dual write, backfill, swap (section 23.7)
ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...) ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Scan NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT
ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both tables Scan of referencing table NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on referencing, ROW SHARE on referenced)
ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE / PRIMARY KEY ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Index build under lock CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX (fast)
CREATE INDEX SHARE Full build; blocks writes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (two scans, allows writes, cannot be in a transaction)
DROP INDEX ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast, but waits for running queries using it DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY
DROP COLUMN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast (column marked dropped; space reclaimed on later rewrite) As is, after no code reads it (Part 24)
RENAME COLUMN / RENAME TABLE ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast Fast for the DB, but breaks code instantly; use expand/contract instead
ADD VALUE to enum on the type, not the table Fast Own migration; cannot be used in the same transaction
RENAME VALUE of enum (PG10+) Fast Fast Breaks code that uses the old literal
DROP TABLE / TRUNCATE ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Fast, but waits for all queries Only after all references are gone
VACUUM FULL / CLUSTER ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Rewrite Never on a live table; use pg_repack
ALTER TABLE ... SET LOGGED / UNLOGGED ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Rewrite Avoid on big tables
ATTACH PARTITION with matching CHECK SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on parent, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the child Fast if the CHECK proves the bounds; else scan of the child Add the CHECK first
DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY (PG14+) SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE Fast As is

Three recipes from the table deserve their full SQL.

PostgreSQL example

Adding NOT NULL to a big table without a scan under lock.

-- Step 1: constraint exists but is not checked against existing rows. Fast; ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for ms.
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_phone_e164_not_null
  CHECK (phone_e164 IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;

-- Step 2: validation scans the table under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE: reads and writes continue.
-- On 30 M rows this takes a minute or two and blocks nothing.
ALTER TABLE users VALIDATE CONSTRAINT users_phone_e164_not_null;

-- Step 3 (PostgreSQL 12+): SET NOT NULL notices the valid CHECK and skips its own scan. Fast.
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN phone_e164 SET NOT NULL;

-- Step 4: the CHECK is now redundant.
ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT users_phone_e164_not_null;

Adding a foreign key without blocking writes for the scan.

-- Fast: the constraint applies to new rows immediately, existing rows are unverified.
ALTER TABLE order_items ADD CONSTRAINT order_items_order_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders (id) NOT VALID;

-- The scan; SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on order_items, ROW SHARE on orders. Writes continue.
ALTER TABLE order_items VALIDATE CONSTRAINT order_items_order_fk;

Before VALIDATE, find the orphans that would make it fail, and fix or delete them:

SELECT i.id FROM order_items i LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id WHERE o.id IS NULL LIMIT 100;

Unique constraint without a lock during the index build.

-- Builds without blocking writes. Fails (leaving an invalid index) if duplicates exist; check first.
SELECT email, count(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING count(*) > 1 LIMIT 10;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_uniq ON users (lower(email));

-- Attach the built index as the constraint: catalog-only, fast.
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE USING INDEX users_email_uniq;

Changing a unique constraint (say from (email) to (tenant_id, email)): build the new unique index concurrently, add it as a constraint, then drop the old constraint (which drops its index). Both exist for a moment; that is fine.

Concurrent index on a partitioned table. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the parent is not supported, so:

CREATE INDEX orders_status_idx ON ONLY orders (status);                    -- parent, marked invalid
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_2026_08_status_idx ON orders_2026_08 (status);
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_2026_09_status_idx ON orders_2026_09 (status);
-- repeat for each partition, then attach:
ALTER INDEX orders_status_idx ATTACH PARTITION orders_2026_08_status_idx;
ALTER INDEX orders_status_idx ATTACH PARTITION orders_2026_09_status_idx;
-- once all partitions are attached the parent index becomes valid automatically.

Production scenario

Timings on a 300-million-row orders table (about 120 GB with indexes) on a db.r6g.4xlarge, measured on a snapshot:

Operation Time holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Total time
ADD COLUMN note text 4 ms 4 ms
ADD COLUMN flags int DEFAULT 0 (PG14) 6 ms 6 ms
ADD COLUMN ext_id uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() 2 h 40 min 2 h 40 min
ALTER COLUMN total_cents TYPE bigint 3 h 10 min 3 h 10 min
SET NOT NULL directly 9 min 9 min
CHECK NOT VALID + VALIDATE + SET NOT NULL 5 ms + 0 + 8 ms 11 min (validate, non-blocking)
CREATE INDEX (non-concurrent, blocks writes) n/a, SHARE for 22 min 22 min
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY 0 41 min

The right-hand column is what your calendar shows; the middle column is what your users feel. The whole discipline of this part is moving time from the middle column to the right one.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • DROP INDEX without CONCURRENTLY waits for every running query on the table, and every new query waits behind it (section 23.4).
  • Invalid index after a failed CONCURRENTLY: writes pay for it, reads ignore it; drop it and rebuild.
  • VALIDATE CONSTRAINT fails on a bad row; the constraint remains NOT VALID; fix data, retry.
  • PG11 fast default not applied when the default expression is volatile; check pg_attribute.atthasmissing after the migration to confirm no rewrite happened.
  • Type change on a column with an index rebuilds the index under the same lock; the estimate above includes it.
  • ALTER TABLE on a partitioned parent propagates to every partition; the lock covers all of them.
  • Dropping a column referenced by a view fails; dropping it with CASCADE silently drops the view.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They classify every migration statement as fast, scan or rewrite before writing it, and they never let a scan or rewrite happen under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a table with meaningful traffic. They know the PostgreSQL version in production because the safe list changes with it (fast defaults in 11, NOT NULL via CHECK in 12, DETACH CONCURRENTLY in 14). They test the timing on a snapshot when the table is large.

Interview questions

  1. Which ALTER TABLE operations rewrite the table? Expected: type changes that are not binary-compatible, adding a column with a volatile default, SET LOGGED/UNLOGGED, VACUUM FULL.
  2. How do you add NOT NULL to a 300 M row column without an outage? Expected: CHECK ... NOT VALID, VALIDATE, SET NOT NULL on PG12+, drop the CHECK.
  3. Why CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and what is its cost? Expected: allows writes during the build; takes longer, two scans, cannot be in a transaction, may leave an invalid index.
  4. What lock does ADD FOREIGN KEY take and how do you soften it? Expected: SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both tables during the scan; NOT VALID then VALIDATE.

23.4 lock_timeout and the lock queue

Concept

lock_timeout is a session setting that makes a statement fail if it waits longer than the given time to acquire a lock. For DDL it is the single most important safety setting, because of how PostgreSQL's lock queue works: a request for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE that is waiting behind one long-running SELECT blocks every new query on that table, even plain reads, until it either gets the lock or gives up. A migration with no lock_timeout can turn one slow report into a full outage of a table.

Why does it exist?

Lock requests are queued fairly, in order. If a strong lock request is queued, weaker requests behind it must wait, otherwise the strong request could starve forever. That fairness is correct and also exactly what makes a migration dangerous: it does not matter that ADD COLUMN would take 4 ms; if it has to wait 5 minutes for a report to finish, the application is frozen for 5 minutes.

Mental model

Imagine a single-lane bridge with a rule: vehicles cross in the order they arrived. A wide truck (the migration) arrives and must wait for the bus already on the bridge (the long query). Every car behind the truck waits, even though cars could easily have passed alongside the bus. The truck could have made the same trip at 03:00 in four seconds. lock_timeout is the truck driver's rule: "if I cannot get onto the bridge within three seconds, I pull over and try again later", and the cars flow again.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Long report SELECT
    participant M as Migration ALTER TABLE
    participant A as App queries
    participant PG as PostgreSQL lock manager
    R->>PG: ACCESS SHARE on orders, granted, runs 5 min
    M->>PG: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on orders, queued behind R
    A->>PG: SELECT on orders, ACCESS SHARE
    Note over PG: queued behind M, fairness rule
    A->>PG: INSERT into orders
    Note over PG: queued behind M too
    Note over A: every request on orders hangs
    M-->>PG: lock_timeout 3s expires, ERROR, M leaves the queue
    PG-->>A: queued queries proceed immediately
  1. Set lock_timeout for the migration's session or transaction. Two to five seconds is typical: long enough that the lock is normally obtained, short enough that a queue behind it is barely noticed.
  2. When the timeout fires, the statement fails with ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout (SQLSTATE 55P03). In a transaction, the transaction is aborted and must be rolled back.
  3. The migration runner catches that specific error, waits with backoff (a few seconds, up to a minute), and retries. Retry a bounded number of times, then fail the job and let a human decide.
  4. Combine with statement_timeout for the migration session so a statement that unexpectedly rewrites a table (a wrong assumption about a fast default, say) is killed after a bound instead of running for hours. Note that statement_timeout also covers the lock wait, so set it larger than lock_timeout.
  5. Ask who is blocking. pg_blocking_pids() and pg_stat_activity show the offender; often it is an idle in transaction session from an application bug, which idle_in_transaction_session_timeout should have killed.

PostgreSQL example

-- Inside a migration transaction:
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '30s';      -- must exceed lock_timeout; bounds any accidental rewrite
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN fulfilment_note text;
COMMIT;

-- Who is holding what on orders, and who is waiting?
SELECT a.pid, a.usename, a.state, now() - a.xact_start AS xact_age,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid) AS blocked_by, left(a.query, 60) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity a
JOIN pg_locks l ON l.pid = a.pid
WHERE l.relation = 'orders'::regclass
ORDER BY a.xact_start;

-- Emergency: cancel the blocker (gentle) or terminate it (firm).
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(48213);
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(48213);

TypeORM example

A reusable helper that runs a DDL statement with lock_timeout and a retry loop. Used by migrations for every fast-but-strong-lock statement.

// src/database/migrations/util/ddl.ts
import { QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

const LOCK_TIMEOUT_SQLSTATE = '55P03';

export interface DdlOptions { lockTimeoutMs?: number; statementTimeoutMs?: number; attempts?: number; baseDelayMs?: number }

// Runs one DDL statement in its own transaction with lock_timeout, retrying on lock timeout only.
export async function runDdlWithRetry(qr: QueryRunner, sql: string, opts: DdlOptions = {}): Promise<void> {
  const { lockTimeoutMs = 3000, statementTimeoutMs = 60_000, attempts = 10, baseDelayMs = 2000 } = opts;
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    await qr.query('BEGIN');
    try {
      await qr.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '${lockTimeoutMs}ms'`);
      await qr.query(`SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '${statementTimeoutMs}ms'`);
      await qr.query(sql);
      await qr.query('COMMIT');
      return;
    } catch (err) {
      await qr.query('ROLLBACK');
      const code = (err as { code?: string }).code;
      if (code !== LOCK_TIMEOUT_SQLSTATE || attempt >= attempts) throw err;
      const delay = Math.min(baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1), 60_000) * (0.5 + Math.random());
      console.warn(`lock timeout on attempt ${attempt}/${attempts}; retrying in ${Math.round(delay)}ms: ${sql}`);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
    }
  }
}

This helper manages its own transaction, so migrations using it must run with --transaction none (or migrationsTransactionMode: 'none'), otherwise BEGIN inside TypeORM's transaction produces a warning and the SET LOCAL scope is not what you expect. A clean pattern is: migrations that use the helper are non-transactional by convention, and each statement in them is individually atomic and idempotent.

// src/database/migrations/1725582000000-AddFulfilmentNoteToOrders.ts
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';
import { runDdlWithRetry } from './util/ddl';

export class AddFulfilmentNoteToOrders1725582000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  name = 'AddFulfilmentNoteToOrders1725582000000';

  public async up(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await runDdlWithRetry(qr, `ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS "fulfilment_note" text`);
  }

  public async down(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await runDdlWithRetry(qr, `ALTER TABLE "orders" DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS "fulfilment_note"`);
  }
}

Sequelize example

// migrations/20260906130000-add-fulfilment-note-to-orders.ts
import { QueryInterface } from 'sequelize';

async function ddlWithRetry(qi: QueryInterface, sql: string, attempts = 10): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      await qi.sequelize.transaction(async (transaction) => {
        await qi.sequelize.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`, { transaction });
        await qi.sequelize.query(sql, { transaction });
      });
      return;
    } catch (err) {
      const code = (err as { original?: { code?: string } }).original?.code;
      if (code !== '55P03' || attempt >= attempts) throw err;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2000 * attempt));
    }
  }
}

export default {
  up: (qi: QueryInterface) => ddlWithRetry(qi, `ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS "fulfilment_note" text`),
  down: (qi: QueryInterface) => ddlWithRetry(qi, `ALTER TABLE "orders" DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS "fulfilment_note"`),
};

Production scenario

A migration adds a column to orders at 14:00 on a weekday. A finance analyst is running a 6-minute aggregation on orders from a BI tool. Without lock_timeout: the migration queues, every checkout request hangs for up to 6 minutes, the load balancer's 30-second timeout fires, users see errors, on-call is paged, and by the time someone finds the analyst's query the migration has completed on its own and everything "recovers mysteriously". With lock_timeout = '3s' and the retry loop: the migration fails to get the lock at 14:00:03, the queued checkouts (which waited 3 seconds) proceed, the migration retries at 14:00:07, 14:00:15, 14:00:31, and succeeds at 14:06:10 when the report ends. Total user impact: a few requests 3 seconds slower.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call got paged because p99 > 30s on every endpoint touching users. A nightly migration had started ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN legacy_flags without a lock timeout. An idle in transaction session from a worker that had crashed mid-transaction (and whose connection PgBouncer kept alive) held ACCESS SHARE on users for hours. The migration queued behind it; every login queued behind the migration. Resolution: pg_terminate_backend on the idle session; the migration then completed in 3 ms. Fixes: lock_timeout in every migration, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s' on the database, and an alert on any transaction older than 5 minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • lock_timeout set without LOCAL through a pooler leaks to other clients' sessions; use SET LOCAL inside a transaction, or connect directly for migrations.
  • statement_timeout shorter than lock_timeout: the statement timeout fires first with a different error code and the retry logic does not match; always set statement timeout larger.
  • Retry loop forever: bound attempts; a migration that cannot get a lock in 10 minutes needs a human.
  • Timeout inside a multi-statement transaction aborts everything done so far in that transaction; with 'each' mode the migration is retried as a whole, so it must be idempotent or the retry must start from scratch cleanly.
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and lock timeout: it needs a brief SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE at start and end and waits for existing transactions; a lock timeout during the wait leaves an invalid index to clean up.
  • Lock queue on a partitioned table involves the parent and every partition; the wait is for the slowest of them.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They consider a migration without lock_timeout a bug, in the same category as a network call without a timeout. They know the answer to "what is the longest query that runs on this table?" and they schedule migrations on hot tables outside the windows when reports run. They also fix the root cause on the other side: long transactions and idle-in-transaction sessions are application defects with their own timeouts and alerts.

Common mistakes

  • Believing "it is only ADD COLUMN, it is instant" and skipping the timeout. Instant after the lock is acquired.
  • Retrying on every error, including the "column already exists" that means the previous attempt actually succeeded.
  • Setting lock_timeout globally on the application role, so ordinary application queries fail under lock contention that they would have survived.

Interview questions

  1. Explain how a 4 ms ADD COLUMN caused a 6-minute outage. Expected: queued behind a long query for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; all later queries queued behind it by the fairness rule.
  2. What does lock_timeout do and what value do you use for migrations? Expected: fail the statement if the lock is not acquired in time; 2 to 5 seconds, with retry and backoff.
  3. How do you find and clear what is blocking a migration? Expected: pg_stat_activity with pg_blocking_pids, pg_locks; cancel or terminate the blocker; fix idle-in-transaction at the source.

Practical exercise

On a local database with an orders table of 5 million rows, open one session with BEGIN; SELECT count(*) FROM orders; SELECT pg_sleep(300); and in another run ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN x int without a timeout while a third session runs SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 1 in a loop. Observe the third session freeze. Repeat with SET lock_timeout = '2s' and the retry helper. Acceptance criteria: with the timeout, the reading loop never pauses more than 2 seconds, the migration eventually succeeds after the sleep ends, and the retry log shows the backoff.

23.5 Zero-downtime migrations and the expand/contract pattern

Concept

Expand/contract is the discipline of making every schema change in three phases so that at no moment does any running version of the code find the database in a shape it cannot handle. Expand: add the new thing (column, table, index) alongside the old, without touching the old. Migrate: make the code write to both, backfill existing rows, then move reads and finally writes to the new thing. Contract: once nothing reads or writes the old thing, remove it. Every deploy in between is a normal rolling deploy; every step is reversible until the last.

Why does it exist?

Because a rolling deployment means old and new code run against one database at the same time, and because the schema is changed before the new code is fully out (the migration job runs first). A single migration that renames phone to phone_e164 breaks every old pod the instant it commits and breaks every new pod if it is rolled back. Expand/contract replaces one dangerous step with six boring ones.

Mental model

Imagine replacing a bridge that carries traffic. You do not close it and build a new one in the same spot. You build the new bridge next to it (expand), open both and route some traffic across the new one while checking it holds (migrate), and only when the old bridge carries no traffic do you demolish it (contract). At every moment there is a bridge to drive on, and until demolition you can send everyone back to the old one.

How it works

The walk-through below uses the real change from section 23.1: users.phone (free text) becomes users.phone_e164 (normalised, NOT NULL, indexed), and phone is dropped. Table size: 30 million rows. Every step shows the migration, the code change, and the query that proves the step is done before moving to the next.

users -> add new column -> deploy code (write both, read old) -> backfill in batches
      -> switch reads -> switch writes -> add NOT NULL -> remove old column
flowchart LR
    S0["Step 0 baseline: phone only"] --> S1["Step 1 EXPAND: add phone_e164 nullable"]
    S1 --> S2["Step 2 deploy: write both, read phone"]
    S2 --> S3["Step 3 backfill in batches from a worker"]
    S3 --> S4["Step 4 deploy: read phone_e164 behind a flag"]
    S4 --> S5["Step 5 deploy: stop writing phone, NOT NULL via CHECK"]
    S5 --> S6["Step 6 deploy: entity without phone"]
    S6 --> S7["Step 7 CONTRACT: drop phone"]

Versions of the code are named v1 (baseline) through v5. At each deploy, the previous version and the new version coexist for minutes; the schema at that moment must satisfy both.

Step 0: baseline (v1).

// src/users/user.entity.ts  (v1)
import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' }) id!: string;
  @Column('text', { unique: true }) email!: string;
  @Column('text', { nullable: true }) phone!: string | null;   // free text, e.g. "+1 (555) 010-2233"
}

Step 1: expand the schema. Add the new column, nullable, no default. Fast. Old code (v1) ignores it because TypeORM selects only the columns in the entity and never writes columns it does not know.

// src/database/migrations/1725580800000-AddPhoneE164ToUsers.ts
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class AddPhoneE164ToUsers1725580800000 implements MigrationInterface {
  public async up(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`);
    await qr.query(`ALTER TABLE "users" ADD COLUMN "phone_e164" text`);   // nullable: catalog-only
  }
  public async down(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`);
    await qr.query(`ALTER TABLE "users" DROP COLUMN "phone_e164"`);
  }
}

Verification: the column exists, is nullable, and no rewrite happened.

SELECT column_name, is_nullable, data_type FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'users' AND column_name = 'phone_e164';
-- phone_e164 | YES | text

Step 2: deploy v2, which writes both and reads the old column. The entity gains the new column; every code path that sets phone also sets phone_e164. Reads still use phone. v1 and v2 coexist: v1 writes only phone (leaving phone_e164 null, which the backfill will fix), v2 writes both. Neither breaks.

// src/users/user.entity.ts  (v2)
@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' }) id!: string;
  @Column('text', { unique: true }) email!: string;
  @Column('text', { nullable: true }) phone!: string | null;
  @Column('text', { name: 'phone_e164', nullable: true }) phoneE164!: string | null;  // new, dual-written
}
// src/users/phone-normalizer.ts
import { parsePhoneNumberFromString } from 'libphonenumber-js';

// Returns E.164 ("+15550102233") or null when the input cannot be parsed.
export function toE164(raw: string | null | undefined, defaultCountry: 'US' | 'GB' | 'IN' = 'US'): string | null {
  if (!raw) return null;
  const parsed = parsePhoneNumberFromString(raw, defaultCountry);
  return parsed?.isValid() ? parsed.number : null;
}
// src/users/users.service.ts  (v2: dual write, read old)
import { Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { User } from './user.entity';
import { toE164 } from './phone-normalizer';

@Injectable()
export class UsersService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(User) private readonly users: Repository<User>) {}

  async updatePhone(userId: string, rawPhone: string, country: 'US' | 'GB' | 'IN'): Promise<void> {
    const user = await this.users.findOneBy({ id: userId });
    if (!user) throw new NotFoundException();
    user.phone = rawPhone;                       // old column: still the source of truth
    user.phoneE164 = toE164(rawPhone, country);  // new column: written alongside
    await this.users.save(user);
  }

  async getPhone(userId: string): Promise<string | null> {
    const user = await this.users.findOneBy({ id: userId });
    return user?.phone ?? null;                  // reads still come from the old column
  }
}

Verification: new writes populate both columns.

-- Rows written in the last 10 minutes should all have phone_e164 when phone is parseable.
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE phone_e164 IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL) AS missing_new,
       count(*) AS recent
FROM users WHERE updated_at > now() - interval '10 minutes';

Step 3: backfill. Fill phone_e164 for the 30 million existing rows. Not in a migration: from a worker, in batches, resumable, throttled by replication lag. The full script is in section 23.7; the loop is:

flowchart TB
    A["Read cursor from backfill_progress"] --> B["Replication lag over 2s?"]
    B -->|"yes"| W["Sleep 5s"] --> B
    B -->|"no"| C["SELECT next 2000 ids where phone_e164 IS NULL AND id greater than cursor"]
    C -->|"no rows"| D["Mark done"]
    C -->|"rows"| E["Normalise in app, UPDATE via unnest, one short transaction"]
    E --> F["Save cursor, log progress"]
    F --> G["Sleep 50ms"] --> B

Verification: nothing left to backfill, and a sample comparison passes.

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE phone IS NOT NULL AND phone_e164 IS NULL) AS pending,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE phone_e164 IS NOT NULL) AS filled,
       count(*) AS total
FROM users;
-- pending must be 0 (or equal to the count of unparseable phones, which you handle separately)

-- Unparseable leftovers: decide (null them, fix by hand, or ask the user on next login).
SELECT id, phone FROM users WHERE phone IS NOT NULL AND phone_e164 IS NULL LIMIT 50;

Step 4: deploy v3, which reads the new column behind a flag. Reads switch to phone_e164 when the flag is on; writes still go to both. The flag lets you switch back instantly without a deploy if anything looks wrong.

// src/users/users.service.ts  (v3: read new column when flagged)
async getPhone(userId: string): Promise<string | null> {
  const user = await this.users.findOneBy({ id: userId });
  if (!user) return null;
  if (this.flags.isEnabled('users.read_phone_e164')) {
    // Fall back to the old column for the few rows the backfill could not normalise.
    return user.phoneE164 ?? user.phone;
  }
  return user.phone;
}

Verification: with the flag at 10%, then 50%, then 100%, compare what both paths would return and count mismatches (log a metric phone_read_mismatch_total; it must be zero for a day before step 5).

Step 5: deploy v4, which stops writing the old column, then enforce NOT NULL. v4 writes only phone_e164. v3 and v4 coexist: v3 still writes both, v4 writes one; the old column starts to go stale, which is fine because after step 4 nothing reads it. After v4 is fully out, add the constraint with the CHECK recipe from section 23.3, and the index.

// src/users/users.service.ts  (v4: write only the new column)
async updatePhone(userId: string, rawPhone: string, country: 'US' | 'GB' | 'IN'): Promise<void> {
  const e164 = toE164(rawPhone, country);
  if (!e164) throw new BadRequestException('phone is not a valid number');   // new rule: must be valid
  await this.users.update({ id: userId }, { phoneE164: e164 });
}
// src/database/migrations/1726100000000-UsersPhoneE164NotNull.ts  (run with --transaction none)
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';
import { runDdlWithRetry } from './util/ddl';

export class UsersPhoneE164NotNull1726100000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  public async up(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await runDdlWithRetry(qr, `ALTER TABLE "users" ADD CONSTRAINT "users_phone_e164_nn" CHECK ("phone_e164" IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`);
    await qr.query(`ALTER TABLE "users" VALIDATE CONSTRAINT "users_phone_e164_nn"`);   // non-blocking scan
    await runDdlWithRetry(qr, `ALTER TABLE "users" ALTER COLUMN "phone_e164" SET NOT NULL`);
    await runDdlWithRetry(qr, `ALTER TABLE "users" DROP CONSTRAINT "users_phone_e164_nn"`);
    await qr.query(`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS "users_phone_e164_idx" ON "users" ("phone_e164")`);
  }
  public async down(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS "users_phone_e164_idx"`);
    await runDdlWithRetry(qr, `ALTER TABLE "users" ALTER COLUMN "phone_e164" DROP NOT NULL`);
  }
}

Careful: NOT NULL is only safe once every running version writes phone_e164 on insert. v1 (which never wrote it) must be long gone; v2 onwards writes it. If any insert path in any live version can omit it, the constraint will break that path. This is the "adding NOT NULL and old writers" trap from Part 24.

Verification:

SELECT is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'users' AND column_name = 'phone_e164'; -- NO
SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;  -- must be empty

Step 6: deploy v5, whose entity no longer knows phone. The column still exists in the database; v4 (still knows the column but does not write it) and v5 (does not know it) coexist harmlessly. This deploy must be fully out before the column is dropped, otherwise a v4 pod doing findOneBy will select phone and fail with column "phone" does not exist.

// src/users/user.entity.ts  (v5)
@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' }) id!: string;
  @Column('text', { unique: true }) email!: string;
  @Column('text', { name: 'phone_e164' }) phoneE164!: string;   // phone is gone from the code
}

Verification: no query in the last 24 hours referenced the old column (search pg_stat_statements for phone outside phone_e164), and migration:generate --dryrun shows only the pending DROP COLUMN.

Step 7: contract. Drop the column. Fast. After this, rollback of the code to v4 or earlier is impossible without restoring the column, which is why v5 must have been stable for a while (a week is a common rule) before this runs.

// src/database/migrations/1726700000000-DropUsersPhone.ts
export class DropUsersPhone1726700000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  public async up(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await qr.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'`);
    await qr.query(`ALTER TABLE "users" DROP COLUMN "phone"`);
  }
  public async down(qr: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    // Structure can be restored; the data cannot. This down exists for local development only.
    await qr.query(`ALTER TABLE "users" ADD COLUMN "phone" text`);
  }
}

Total elapsed time for a careful team: about two weeks, five deploys, two migrations that take milliseconds, one migration that scans without blocking, and one backfill that ran for a few hours from a worker. Zero downtime, zero moments where any pod could fail.

Sequelize example

The same step 2 in Sequelize, using a model hook so every write path populates both columns without each caller remembering.

// src/users/user.model.ts (v2)
import { DataTypes, Model, Sequelize } from 'sequelize';
import { toE164 } from './phone-normalizer';

export class User extends Model {
  declare id: string; declare email: string; declare phone: string | null; declare phoneE164: string | null;
}

export function initUser(sequelize: Sequelize): void {
  User.init(
    {
      id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, primaryKey: true, autoIncrement: true },
      email: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false, unique: true },
      phone: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: true },
      phoneE164: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: true, field: 'phone_e164' },
    },
    {
      sequelize, tableName: 'users', timestamps: false,
      hooks: {
        // Dual write: whenever phone changes, derive phone_e164. Runs for create and save.
        beforeSave: (user: User) => {
          if (user.changed('phone')) user.phoneE164 = toE164(user.phone);
        },
      },
    },
  );
}

Hooks do not run for Model.update(...) bulk calls unless individualHooks: true, and never for raw queries. That gap is the argument for a database trigger in section 23.6.

Production scenario

The same pattern applies to every rename, type change, table split and constraint tightening you will ever do. A team that internalises it stops having "migration deploys" at all: every deploy is a rolling deploy, and the schema is always one step ahead of or behind the code in a way both sides tolerate. Their release calendar has no maintenance windows.

Failure scenario

A team skipped step 6 and dropped phone while v4 pods were still serving. v4's entity listed phone; every findOneBy on users failed with column "phone" does not exist; login was down for the 4 minutes it took to finish the rollout of v5, which the on-call had to trigger manually because the deploy pipeline had paused on the migration job's success waiting for a manual approval. The lesson: the contract step is a two-deploy operation (remove from code, then drop), and the drop is its own release, not a tail on the code release.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see a schema change as a sequence of states, and at each state they ask: "which code versions can be running now, and does the schema satisfy each?" They keep the old column until the new path has been in production long enough that they would not want to go back. They put reads behind a flag so switching back is a config change, not a deploy. They resist the urge to compress steps: two weeks of boring is cheaper than an hour of outage.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through renaming a column with zero downtime. Expected: add new column, deploy dual write, backfill, switch reads (flag), stop writing old, deploy entity without old, drop old; at each step both adjacent code versions work.
  2. When is it safe to add NOT NULL to the new column? Expected: after every running version writes it on insert and the backfill is complete; via CHECK NOT VALID + VALIDATE.
  3. Why is dropping the old column two deploys, not one? Expected: the entity must stop referencing it before the column disappears, or old pods fail on select.

23.6 Dual writes

Concept

Dual writing is writing the same fact to two places (two columns, two tables, two databases) during a migration window so that both the old and new representation stay current while existing data is backfilled. It is the "migrate" phase of expand/contract. It is also one of the easiest ways to create subtle inconsistency, so it needs rules.

Why does it exist?

A backfill copies existing rows, but rows keep changing while it runs. Without dual writes, a row updated after the backfill copied it has a stale new column. Dual writes make new changes land in both places; the backfill takes care of the rest; together they converge.

Mental model

Imagine moving your mail to a new address. Forwarding (the backfill) handles letters already in the system. Telling every sender the new address (dual writing) handles new letters. For a while some senders use the old address and some the new; both reach you. Only when everyone has the new address do you cancel the old one.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as UsersService v2
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    C->>S: PATCH /users/42/phone
    S->>S: e164 = toE164 raw
    S->>DB: UPDATE users SET phone=raw, phone_e164=e164 WHERE id=42
    DB-->>S: 1 row
    S-->>C: 204
    Note over S,DB: one statement, one transaction: both columns or neither

The rules:

  1. Same transaction when both targets are in the same database. Two columns of one row, or two tables in one database: write them in one transaction. Then there is no consistency risk at all; the dual write is atomic.
  2. Order and idempotency when the targets are different systems. Old database first (it is the source of truth until cutover), then the new one, best effort. Make the second write idempotent (upsert keyed by primary key with a version or updated_at guard) so retries and backfill overlap are harmless. Record failures of the second write in a mismatch table for a repair job, and never fail the user request because the secondary write failed.
  3. Every write path, not most. Bulk updates, admin scripts, import jobs, ORM bulk methods that skip hooks, raw SQL in a report tool: any path that writes the old column without the new one creates rows the backfill must catch again. Grep for every write to the old column before enabling dual writes. Run the backfill's "pending" query periodically during the window; a non-zero count after the backfill finished means a missed path.
  4. Prefer a trigger when the derivation is pure. If the new value is a deterministic function of the old row (normalise a phone, split a name, compute cents from a decimal), a BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE trigger in PostgreSQL covers every write path, including ones you forgot, with no ordering or partial-failure problem. Its cost: logic in the database that must be removed at contract time, and the derivation must be expressible in SQL or PL/pgSQL.

PostgreSQL example

A trigger version of the dual write for the phone case. The SQL normalisation is deliberately simple (strip non-digits, keep a leading plus, assume a default country code for 10-digit numbers) because true E.164 parsing needs country context; the application's backfill uses the full library and the trigger only keeps new writes from being null until v4 is out.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION normalize_phone_e164(raw text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$
  SELECT CASE
    WHEN raw IS NULL THEN NULL
    WHEN raw ~ '^\+' THEN '+' || regexp_replace(raw, '[^0-9]', '', 'g')
    WHEN length(regexp_replace(raw, '[^0-9]', '', 'g')) = 10 THEN '+1' || regexp_replace(raw, '[^0-9]', '', 'g')
    ELSE NULL
  END
$$;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION users_sync_phone_e164() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  -- Only derive when the app did not already supply a value; the app's parser is better.
  IF NEW.phone_e164 IS NULL OR (TG_OP = 'UPDATE' AND NEW.phone IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.phone) THEN
    NEW.phone_e164 := COALESCE(NEW.phone_e164, normalize_phone_e164(NEW.phone));
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;

CREATE TRIGGER users_phone_e164_sync
BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF phone ON users
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION users_sync_phone_e164();

-- At contract time:
DROP TRIGGER users_phone_e164_sync ON users;
DROP FUNCTION users_sync_phone_e164();

Failure scenario

A team dual-wrote orders.total (numeric) to a new orders.total_cents (bigint) in the service layer. A month later, after cutover, finance found 0.3% of orders with mismatched totals. Cause: a nightly "currency rounding fix" script written years earlier updated total with raw SQL; it never knew about total_cents. The backfill had run before that script's next execution, so the rows it touched afterwards drifted. A trigger would have caught it. The repair was a second backfill comparing the two columns and a permanent consistency check that ran until the old column was dropped.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Partial failure across two databases: source committed, target failed. Record and repair; never roll back the source for a secondary failure.
  • Write ordering across services: two requests update the same row in quick succession; the target receives them out of order. The updated_at guard in the upsert makes the older write a no-op.
  • Hooks bypassed: Model.update, bulkCreate, createQueryBuilder().update(), raw SQL. Audit or use a trigger.
  • Trigger cost: a PL/pgSQL trigger adds tens of microseconds per row; on a table with 10,000 writes per second it is measurable but rarely material.
  • Trigger left behind after the migration silently keeps computing a column nobody uses; put its removal in the contract migration.
  • Dual write to a column with a stricter constraint (NOT NULL, CHECK) fails the whole request when the derivation returns null; keep the new column nullable during the window.

Interview questions

  1. When are dual writes atomic and when are they not? Expected: atomic in one transaction in one database; across systems they are best-effort with idempotent upserts and repair.
  2. Trigger or application code for dual writes? Expected: trigger when the derivation is pure and expressible in SQL, because it covers every write path; application code when it needs external context.
  3. How do you detect a missed write path? Expected: the "pending rows" query stays non-zero after the backfill; a periodic consistency check between old and new.

23.7 Backfill strategies

Concept

A backfill is a data change applied to existing rows in small batches, from a worker process, over time. It replaces the single giant UPDATE that would lock rows for hours, bloat the table, flood the WAL, push replicas minutes behind and hold a transaction open long enough to block vacuum on the whole database.

Why does it exist?

UPDATE users SET phone_e164 = ... on 30 million rows is one transaction. In PostgreSQL an update writes a new row version and leaves the old one for vacuum: 30 million dead tuples, roughly doubling the table's size until vacuum runs, and vacuum cannot remove them until the transaction ends. Every one of those row versions goes into the WAL and to every replica. The statement holds row locks that block concurrent updates to those users for its whole duration. If it fails at row 29 million, everything rolls back and you start over. Batching solves each of those: short transactions, bounded dead tuples per batch that autovacuum handles as you go, throttled WAL, retry from the last cursor.

Mental model

Imagine repainting the lines in a car park that stays open. You do not close the whole car park for a day. You cone off ten spaces, paint them, remove the cones, wait a minute for traffic to settle, and move to the next ten. If it rains, you stop and resume tomorrow from the row you marked. Painting takes longer overall; nobody loses their parking.

How it works

  1. Keyset batches, not offsets. Walk the primary key: WHERE id > $cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT $n. OFFSET gets slower with every batch; keyset is constant time.
  2. Select then update, or update with a subquery. UPDATE users SET ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE id > $1 AND phone_e164 IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 2000) RETURNING id works when the transformation is expressible in SQL. When the transformation needs application logic (a phone library), select the batch, compute in the worker, and update with unnest arrays in one statement.
  3. WHERE id BETWEEN for id ranges when ids are dense integers: UPDATE ... WHERE id BETWEEN 1000001 AND 1002000. Simpler, but sparse ranges (after deletes) produce empty batches; keyset with LIMIT is more robust.
  4. One short transaction per batch. Autocommit each UPDATE. Never wrap the loop in one transaction.
  5. Sleep between batches (20 to 200 ms) to leave room for production traffic and let WAL replicate.
  6. Throttle by replication lag. Before each batch, check the primary's pg_stat_replication; if the slowest replica's replay_lag exceeds a threshold (2 s), sleep and re-check. This is the single most important control; it is what keeps the "user paid but the order shows unpaid" incident from Part 22 from happening during migrations.
  7. Persist progress. Store the cursor in a small table after each batch. A crash, a deploy or a manual stop resumes from the cursor.
  8. Log and expose metrics: rows done, rows per second, estimated remaining, lag observed. A backfill without progress output is a backfill someone will kill at 3 a.m. thinking it is stuck.
  9. Run it from a worker, as a BullMQ job or a Kubernetes Job with the application image, not from the migration runner. It must survive longer than a pipeline step and be stoppable without failing a deploy.
  10. Vacuum afterwards. Autovacuum keeps up with batches, but a manual VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) users at the end refreshes statistics and reclaims what remains. Check bloat with pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup.

NestJS example

A resumable, throttled backfill runnable as a standalone script (node dist/jobs/backfill-phone-e164.js) or wrapped as a BullMQ processor.

// src/jobs/backfill-phone-e164.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { AppModule } from '../app.module';
import { toE164 } from '../users/phone-normalizer';

const JOB = 'users.phone_e164';
const BATCH = 2000;
const SLEEP_MS = 50;
const MAX_LAG_SECONDS = 2;
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function replicaLagSeconds(ds: DataSource): Promise<number> {
  const rows: { lag: string | null }[] = await ds.query(
    `SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM max(replay_lag))::text AS lag FROM pg_stat_replication`);
  return Number(rows[0]?.lag ?? 0);
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const app = await NestFactory.createApplicationContext(AppModule, { logger: ['log', 'warn', 'error'] });
  const ds = app.get(DataSource);
  const log = new Logger('BackfillPhoneE164');
  let stopping = false;
  process.on('SIGTERM', () => { stopping = true; });   // Kubernetes stop: finish the batch, save, exit

  await ds.query(`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS backfill_progress
    (job text PRIMARY KEY, cursor_id bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, done_rows bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
     finished_at timestamptz, updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())`);
  await ds.query(`INSERT INTO backfill_progress (job) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT (job) DO NOTHING`, [JOB]);

  let [{ cursor_id: cursor, done_rows: done }] = await ds.query(
    `SELECT cursor_id, done_rows FROM backfill_progress WHERE job = $1`, [JOB]);
  cursor = BigInt(cursor); done = Number(done);
  const startedAt = Date.now();

  while (!stopping) {
    const lag = await replicaLagSeconds(ds);
    if (lag > MAX_LAG_SECONDS) { log.warn(`replica lag ${lag.toFixed(1)}s, pausing`); await sleep(5000); continue; }

    // Keyset batch: only rows still needing work, strictly after the cursor.
    const batch: { id: string; phone: string | null }[] = await ds.query(
      `SELECT id, phone FROM users WHERE id > $1 AND phone_e164 IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL
       ORDER BY id LIMIT $2`, [cursor.toString(), BATCH]);
    if (batch.length === 0) break;

    const ids: string[] = []; const values: string[] = [];
    for (const row of batch) {
      const e164 = toE164(row.phone);
      if (e164) { ids.push(row.id); values.push(e164); }   // unparseable rows are left for manual review
    }
    if (ids.length > 0) {
      // One short autocommit statement per batch; idempotent thanks to the IS NULL guard.
      await ds.query(
        `UPDATE users AS u SET phone_e164 = v.e164
         FROM unnest($1::bigint[], $2::text[]) AS v(id, e164)
         WHERE u.id = v.id AND u.phone_e164 IS NULL`, [ids, values]);
    }

    cursor = BigInt(batch[batch.length - 1].id);
    done += batch.length;
    await ds.query(`UPDATE backfill_progress SET cursor_id = $2, done_rows = $3, updated_at = now() WHERE job = $1`,
      [JOB, cursor.toString(), done]);

    if (done % (BATCH * 50) === 0) {
      const rate = done / ((Date.now() - startedAt) / 1000);
      log.log(`done=${done} cursor=${cursor} rate=${rate.toFixed(0)}/s lag=${lag.toFixed(1)}s`);
    }
    await sleep(SLEEP_MS);
  }

  if (!stopping) await ds.query(`UPDATE backfill_progress SET finished_at = now() WHERE job = $1`, [JOB]);
  log.log(stopping ? `stopped at cursor ${cursor}; rerun to resume` : `finished: ${done} rows`);
  await app.close();
}

main().catch((err) => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); });

At 2,000 rows per batch and roughly 60 ms per iteration (query, update, sleep), the script processes about 30,000 rows per second in theory and 8,000 to 15,000 in practice on a busy primary: 30 million rows in about an hour, with replicas never more than 2 seconds behind. A single UPDATE would have taken a comparable wall-clock time while blocking those rows and pushing replicas minutes behind.

PostgreSQL example

Pure-SQL variant when the transformation is expressible in SQL, plus the bloat check.

-- One batch. Run in a loop from a script with autocommit; keep the RETURNING max(id) as the next cursor.
WITH batch AS (
  SELECT id FROM users
  WHERE id > 1840000 AND phone_e164 IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 2000
)
UPDATE users u SET phone_e164 = normalize_phone_e164(u.phone)
FROM batch WHERE u.id = batch.id
RETURNING u.id;

-- Bloat and vacuum health during and after the backfill.
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, last_vacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'users';

-- After the backfill.
VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) users;

Make sure the batch query is indexed: with WHERE id > $1 AND phone_e164 IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT n, the primary key index walks forward and skips already-filled rows cheaply as long as filled rows are contiguous behind the cursor, which they are for a keyset backfill. EXPLAIN it before the first run (section 23.12).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Backfill bloats the table and starves autovacuum: batches too large, sleeps too short, or autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay too high for the table. Lower the batch size and raise the sleep; consider ALTER TABLE users SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01) on huge tables so vacuum triggers earlier.
  • Long-running backfill holds back the xmin horizon only if it holds a transaction open; autocommit batches do not. A forgotten BEGIN in the script turns it into the giant transaction you were avoiding.
  • Rows updated by users during the backfill: the phone_e164 IS NULL guard means the backfill never overwrites a dual-written value.
  • Cursor saved before the update commits: with autocommit the order is update then cursor; a crash between them re-does one batch, which is idempotent.
  • Replica lag never drops below the threshold because of unrelated load: the backfill stalls forever; alert on "no progress in 15 minutes".
  • Backfill runs against a replica by mistake (TypeORM replication routes query() to master, but a custom runner may not): the update fails with a read-only error; use createQueryRunner('master') explicitly if in doubt.
  • Unparseable rows: decide the policy up front (null, fix by hand, ask the user); do not let them block NOT NULL indefinitely.
  • Hot rows: a batch that includes a row a user is updating right now waits briefly for the row lock; keep lock_timeout small in the worker too, and retry the batch.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They budget a backfill in three currencies: WAL bytes (replica lag), dead tuples (vacuum), and row locks (user latency). They make it resumable and boring: it should be safe to kill at any moment and restart with one command. They would rather a backfill take a day at zero impact than an hour with a page.

Common mistakes

  • UPDATE in a migration for a big table.
  • OFFSET pagination for batches.
  • One transaction around the whole loop "for atomicity".
  • No progress table, so a crash means starting over, and no progress logs, so someone kills it.
  • No lag throttle, so the read replicas fall minutes behind and users see stale data.

Interview questions

  1. Why not one UPDATE for 30 million rows? Expected: long transaction, dead tuples and bloat, WAL burst and replica lag, row locks, all-or-nothing failure.
  2. Design a resumable, throttled backfill. Expected: keyset batches, short autocommit transactions, sleep, replica lag check, cursor persisted, worker not migration, vacuum after.
  3. How does the backfill avoid overwriting newer dual-written values? Expected: only update rows where the new column is still null, or an updated_at guard.

Practical exercise

Generate 5 million users with messy phone strings. Implement the backfill script above and run it against a primary with one streaming replica configured with recovery_min_apply_delay = '3s'. Acceptance criteria: the script pauses (visible in logs) while lag exceeds 2 s and resumes; killing the script with SIGTERM and restarting continues from the saved cursor without re-updating rows (verify with n_tup_upd deltas in pg_stat_user_tables); n_dead_tup never exceeds 5% of n_live_tup during the run; the pending count reaches zero.

23.8 Rollback and roll-forward

Concept

Rollback of a database migration means returning the schema (and ideally the data) to the state before the migration. For structure-only changes that have not yet been used by data, it is possible. For anything that has changed or removed data, it is usually fiction: a dropped column's values are gone, a backfilled column cannot be "un-backfilled" without losing the writes that happened since, and a down that drops a column the new code just wrote to destroys real user data. The senior stance is roll forward: fix problems with a new migration, keep the old structure around until the new one is proven, and make switching behaviour a configuration change rather than a schema change.

Why does it exist?

Because deploys fail, and the instinct is "just roll back". Code can be rolled back in seconds with no loss. Databases cannot, because time has passed and rows have been written. A team that plans for database rollback the way it plans for code rollback will, one day, run a down migration in production and delete something. Roll-forward thinking replaces that instinct with concrete safety measures taken before the risky step.

Mental model

Imagine a printed newspaper. You can pull tomorrow's edition before it prints (roll back the code). Once today's edition is on the streets, you cannot un-print it; you print a correction tomorrow (roll forward). So you proofread carefully before printing, and you keep the old typesetting plates until the new edition has been out for a while, in case the correction needs them.

How it works

  1. Classify the migration. Additive and unused (a new nullable column, a new table, a new index): reversible; down is safe. Additive and used (the new column has data): reversible only by losing that data. Destructive (drop, type change with narrowing, constraint that rejects existing rows): not reversible without a backup.
  2. Back up before destructive steps. A logical dump of the affected table (pg_dump -t users --data-only is too big for a 30 M row table; instead CREATE TABLE users_phone_backup AS SELECT id, phone FROM users right before DROP COLUMN phone, which is fast and gives you a per-row restore path) or a database snapshot on RDS. Keep it for a defined period, then drop it.
  3. Keep old columns until the new code is proven. The contract step waits a week or more after the last read of the old column. The old column costs a few bytes per row; a broken rollback costs the business.
  4. Flags for behaviour, migrations for structure. Reads switch behind a flag; writes switch behind a flag if practical. Reverting behaviour is then instant and needs no migration.
  5. Code rollback with the schema ahead. After a bad deploy of v3, you roll the code back to v2. The schema is at the v3 level. This works if and only if the migration was backward compatible (the N-1 rule from Part 24). Expand/contract guarantees it.
  6. Roll forward for real problems. The backfill produced wrong values: write a corrective backfill. The new constraint rejects a legitimate case: drop the constraint in a new migration. Never edit the failed migration; add a new one.

PostgreSQL example

-- Right before the destructive contract step: a cheap, per-row recoverable backup.
