CREATE TABLE users_phone_backup_20260921 AS SELECT id, phone FROM users;   -- seconds; no locks beyond ACCESS SHARE
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;

-- If a restore is ever needed (new forward migration, not a down):
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone text;
UPDATE users u SET phone = b.phone FROM users_phone_backup_20260921 b WHERE b.id = u.id;  -- batched in reality

-- Retention: drop the backup after the agreed window.
DROP TABLE users_phone_backup_20260921;

TypeORM's migration:revert runs the last migration's down. Treat it as a development tool; in production wire the pipeline so that revert is a deliberate, approved, separate job that a human runs, never a step that "rollback" automation triggers.

Failure scenario

A deploy failed health checks and the pipeline's automatic rollback ran migration:revert as well as reverting the image. The last migration had added orders.fulfilment_note and the new code had, in the 6 minutes it was live, written 4,000 notes. The down dropped the column; the notes were gone; customer support spent a day asking customers to re-enter delivery instructions. The pipeline now never reverts migrations automatically, and the team's down methods for destructive steps deliberately throw (throw new Error('irreversible: restore from users_phone_backup_20260921')) so nobody can run them by accident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • down for a data migration cannot know which rows were changed since; it either does nothing or destroys new data.
  • Partial rollback across shards: three shards reverted, five not; the app must tolerate both schema states (Part 24).
  • Backup table forgotten for a year, holding personal data past its retention policy; schedule the drop when you create it.
  • Point-in-time restore as a rollback: restores the entire database to before the migration, losing every write since. Only for catastrophes.

Interview questions

  1. Can you roll back a migration in production? Expected: structure-only and unused, yes; anything with data, effectively no; plan for roll-forward, backups before destructive steps, flags for behaviour.
  2. What do you do if a backfill wrote wrong values? Expected: new corrective backfill, not a revert; the old column is still there because contract was not done yet.
  3. Why should down for a DROP COLUMN throw? Expected: it cannot restore data; failing loudly prevents accidental data loss by automation.

23.9 Backward-compatible schema changes: the catalogue

Concept

A schema change is backward compatible when the code version currently running keeps working after the change, and the next code version works before and after it. This section catalogues common changes as safe or unsafe and gives the safe recipe for each unsafe one. The lock behaviour of the statements themselves was covered in section 23.3; this section is about whether the code survives.

Why does it exist?

Because "does this migration lock the table?" and "does this migration break the running pods?" are different questions, and a change can pass one and fail the other. RENAME COLUMN is instant and breaks everything. ADD COLUMN NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 is instant on PG11+ and breaks nothing. A catalogue lets reviewers decide fast.

How it works

Change Safe as one step? Why Safe recipe
Add nullable column Yes Old code ignores it As is
Add column with constant default, nullable or NOT NULL (PG11+) Yes Old inserts get the default As is
Add NOT NULL column without default No Old code inserts without it and fails Add nullable, dual write, backfill, NOT NULL via CHECK once all writers set it
Drop column No Old code selects or writes it Remove from code first, deploy, wait, then drop; back up first
Rename column No Old code uses the old name; new code the new Expand/contract: new column, dual write, backfill, switch, drop
Rename table No Same New table or, simpler, a view with the old name during transition; or keep the name and rename only in code via @Entity({ name })
Change column type, widening compatible (varchar(50) to text, int to bigint in the code's eyes) Type-level yes; lock-level see 23.3 Old code still reads it int to bigint rewrites: new column + backfill + swap
Change column type, narrowing or incompatible (text to jsonb, numeric to int) No Old code writes values the new type rejects New column, dual write, backfill, switch reads, switch writes, drop old
Add index Yes Invisible to code CONCURRENTLY
Drop index Yes for code Invisible to code; watch query plans CONCURRENTLY; check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan first
Add CHECK constraint Depends Rejects old code's writes if they violate it Ensure all live writers comply; NOT VALID + VALIDATE
Add unique constraint Depends Old code may insert duplicates Deduplicate, ensure writers comply, unique index CONCURRENTLY
Change unique constraint columns No Old writers may violate the new one Add new unique index concurrently, then drop the old constraint
Add foreign key Depends Old code may insert orphans Clean orphans, NOT VALID + VALIDATE
Drop foreign key / constraint Yes Loosening never breaks code As is
Add enum value Yes for DB; risky for consumers Old code that switches over the enum may hit an unknown value Add value in its own migration; teach code to tolerate unknown values first (Part 24)
Remove enum value No (and PostgreSQL cannot do it directly) Rows may hold it Stop writing it, migrate rows, recreate the type via new column
Change default Yes Affects only new rows As is
Add table Yes Invisible As is
Drop table No Old code may use it Remove from code, deploy, wait, back up, drop
Split a table No Old code reads the wide table New table, dual write, backfill, switch reads, switch writes, drop moved columns
Add a trigger Depends May reject writes or change values old code relies on Deploy as no-op first, then enable behaviour
Change primary key No Everything depends on it Rarely worth it; add a new unique key and migrate references over months

The recipes for the harder rows:

Renaming a table. The expand/contract on a whole table is heavy. Two lighter options. Option 1: keep the physical name and change only what the code calls it (@Entity({ name: 'legacy_name' })), which is often all anyone wanted. Option 2: create a view with the old name pointing at the renamed table for the transition: ALTER TABLE customers RENAME TO users; CREATE VIEW customers AS SELECT * FROM users; in one transaction. Simple views in PostgreSQL are updatable, so old code's inserts and updates through the view still work. Drop the view after the old code is gone. This is a rare case where a rename is acceptable, because the view keeps the old name alive.

Splitting a table (users into users and user_profiles): create user_profiles(user_id PK REFERENCES users, bio, avatar_url, ...); deploy code that writes profile fields to both places and reads from users; backfill user_profiles from users; switch reads to user_profiles behind a flag; stop writing the columns in users; remove them from the entity; drop them.

Changing a column type (orders.total numeric(12,2) to total_cents bigint): identical to the phone walkthrough with total_cents = round(total * 100) as the derivation, ideally in a trigger since it is pure SQL. Same for int to bigint on a huge table, where the direct ALTER COLUMN TYPE would rewrite for hours: new column, trigger, backfill, swap names in one transaction at the end (section 23.10) so the code's column name never changes.

Adding an enum value. Own migration, ALTER TYPE order_status ADD VALUE IF NOT EXISTS 'partially_refunded', not inside a transaction on PostgreSQL 11 or older, and not used by any statement in the same transaction on 12+. Before writing the new value anywhere, deploy code that handles unknown enum values gracefully, because the old pods will read it. Many teams avoid PostgreSQL enums entirely for evolving sets and use text with a CHECK constraint (which can be replaced with NOT VALID + VALIDATE) or a lookup table.

Changing a unique constraint from (email) to (tenant_id, email): the new one is looser (more rows allowed), so old writers cannot violate it; build the new unique index concurrently, add it as a constraint, drop the old. The reverse direction (tightening) requires deduplication and writer compliance first.

Adding NOT NULL to a big table: section 23.3's CHECK recipe, after every live writer sets the column.

Dropping a column that old pods still read. TypeORM and Sequelize always list columns explicitly in their generated SELECT, so an entity that still declares the column fails the moment the column is gone. Hand-written SELECT * fails differently: it succeeds, and code that reads row.phone gets undefined, which can silently become null in a downstream write. Both are reasons the entity change deploys first.

PostgreSQL example

-- Rename table with a compatibility view, one transaction.
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE customers RENAME TO users;
CREATE VIEW customers AS SELECT * FROM users;     -- updatable: old code keeps working
COMMIT;

-- Later, once no code references customers:
DROP VIEW customers;

-- Enum value: its own migration, outside a transaction on old versions.
ALTER TYPE order_status ADD VALUE IF NOT EXISTS 'partially_refunded';

-- Loosening a unique constraint safely.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_tenant_email_uniq ON users (tenant_id, lower(email));
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_tenant_email_unique UNIQUE USING INDEX users_tenant_email_uniq;
ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT users_email_unique;   -- drops its index too

Edge cases & failure modes

  • View with SELECT * freezes the column list at creation time; adding columns to the table later does not add them to the view. Recreate the view if needed.
  • Enum value added but old pods crash on switch without default: a Part 24 problem, fix the code first.
  • Unique index build fails on duplicates created by a race between the dedupe and the build; add the constraint with writers already enforcing it in code, and retry.
  • Split table and the N+1: reads that used to be one row are now a join; index user_profiles.user_id (it is the PK) and load with relations or a join, not per row.

Interview questions

  1. Is adding a NOT NULL column with a default safe? Expected: yes on PG11+ with a constant default; both for locks and for old writers.
  2. How do you rename a table without breaking old pods? Expected: keep the physical name and change the entity mapping, or rename plus an updatable view with the old name for the transition.
  3. Why is dropping a column dangerous even though it is instant? Expected: old pods select it explicitly via the ORM and fail; SELECT * code silently gets undefined.

23.10 Large table migrations

Concept

Some changes cannot be made in place on a large table without a rewrite: changing int to bigint on the primary key, converting a plain table into a partitioned one, reclaiming space from a bloated table, changing a column's storage or collation. The techniques are: build a new table (or partition) next to the old one, get its data in without blocking, then swap names in a single transaction; use pg_repack for rewrites that keep the same structure; attach pre-built partitions.

Why does it exist?

ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint on 300 million rows: 3 hours of ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Converting orders to a partitioned table: PostgreSQL has no in-place command at all. VACUUM FULL on a bloated 200 GB table: hours of exclusive lock. All three are unacceptable on a live system; all three are routine with the copy-and-swap approach.

Mental model

Imagine replacing the engine of a running bus. You do not stop the bus for a day. You build a second bus with the new engine while the first keeps its route, mirror every ticket sold into the second bus's log, and at the end of the line ask passengers to step across in thirty seconds. The route was never interrupted; the name on the front of the bus stays the same.

How it works

Copy-and-swap.

  1. Create orders_new with the desired structure (bigint id, or PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) with partitions pre-created), without indexes other than the primary key.
  2. Add a trigger on orders that mirrors every insert, update and delete into orders_new (or use logical replication from orders to orders_new on PostgreSQL 15+ with a publication for one table; a trigger is simpler for same-database copies).
  3. Backfill orders_new from orders in keyset batches with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (the trigger already inserted rows changed after the copy started; the conflict clause skips them).
  4. Build the remaining indexes on orders_new with CONCURRENTLY. Nobody is querying it, but concurrent builds avoid a SHARE lock that would block the mirror trigger's writes.
  5. Verify: counts, checksums, and a comparison of rows updated in the last hour.
  6. Swap in one transaction with a lock timeout: ALTER TABLE orders RENAME TO orders_old; ALTER TABLE orders_new RENAME TO orders; plus renaming the sequence and constraints so names match what the code and future migrations expect. Milliseconds.
  7. Drop the mirror trigger (it fires on orders_old now, into nothing), keep orders_old for a retention window, then drop it.

The application never changes: same table name, same columns. The only things to double check are sequence ownership (ALTER SEQUENCE orders_id_seq OWNED BY orders.id and setval above the maximum), foreign keys from other tables (they still point at the old table by OID; they must be re-created against the new one with NOT VALID + VALIDATE before the swap or immediately after), and views that referenced the old table.

pg_repack. An extension plus a command-line tool that rebuilds a table (or an index) online to remove bloat or re-cluster it. It creates a shadow table, mirrors changes with a log table and trigger, copies data, builds indexes, and swaps in a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE at the start and end. pg_repack -d shop -t orders replaces VACUUM FULL orders. It needs free disk space equal to the table plus indexes, and it must not run concurrently with DDL on the same table. It is available on RDS.

Partition attach. To move a big existing table into a partitioned scheme without copying: create the partitioned parent, add a CHECK constraint on the old table matching the partition bounds it will occupy (validated with NOT VALID then VALIDATE, non-blocking), then ATTACH PARTITION (fast because the CHECK proves the bounds), then rename so the parent takes the old table's name. This is the trick for "we have 3 years of orders in one table and want monthly partitions going forward": attach the whole old table as one big partition covering the past, create monthly partitions for the future, and let the old partition age out on your retention schedule.

flowchart LR
    O["orders old structure"] -->|"mirror trigger"| N["orders_new"]
    O -->|"batched INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING"| N
    N --> I["CONCURRENTLY build indexes"]
    I --> V["verify counts and checksums"]
    V --> S["one transaction: rename swap"]
    S --> D["drop trigger, retain orders_old, drop later"]

PostgreSQL example

Converting orders (unpartitioned, 300 M rows) to a partitioned table with the "attach the past as one partition" trick, which avoids copying entirely.

-- 1. New partitioned parent with the same columns; PK must include created_at.
CREATE TABLE orders_partitioned (LIKE orders INCLUDING DEFAULTS INCLUDING GENERATED)
  PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
ALTER TABLE orders_partitioned ADD PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at);

-- 2. Prove the old table's bounds without blocking: NOT VALID + VALIDATE.
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_bounds
  CHECK (created_at >= '2000-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01') NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_bounds;   -- SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, reads and writes continue

-- 3. Future partitions, created ahead.
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_10 PARTITION OF orders_partitioned FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01');
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_11 PARTITION OF orders_partitioned FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-11-01') TO ('2026-12-01');

-- 4. The swap: attach the old table as the "history" partition and take over the name. Milliseconds.
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE orders RENAME TO orders_history;
ALTER TABLE orders_partitioned ATTACH PARTITION orders_history
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2000-01-01') TO ('2026-10-01');       -- fast: the CHECK already proves it
ALTER TABLE orders_partitioned RENAME TO orders;
COMMIT;

-- 5. Indexes on the parent propagate to future partitions; existing indexes on orders_history remain.
CREATE INDEX orders_user_created_idx ON ONLY orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
ALTER INDEX orders_user_created_idx ATTACH PARTITION orders_history_user_id_created_at_idx;  -- reuse the old index
-- then CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on each new partition and attach, as in section 31.3.

Caveats: the old table's primary key was (id); the parent's is (id, created_at). Attaching requires the child to be compatible, and a child with a different PK is allowed (constraints on children may be stricter), but foreign keys from other tables to orders(id) cannot reference a partitioned parent whose key is (id, created_at). Those foreign keys must be dropped and replaced by application-level checks or by including created_at in the referencing tables, which is a schema change of its own. This is the real cost of retro-fitting partitioning, and why Part 22 recommends designing it in early.

Production scenario

int to bigint on events.id (sequence at 1.9 billion, 2.1 billion is the ceiling): copy-and-swap ran as a two-day project. Trigger on Monday, backfill over Monday night at 20,000 rows per second, concurrent index builds Tuesday, verification Tuesday evening, swap Tuesday 23:00 with a 40 ms lock, events_old dropped the following Monday. The application changed nothing except the TypeScript type of id from number to string (bigint comes back as a string from pg), which shipped a week earlier.

Failure scenario

A team converted a 500 GB table with an in-place ALTER COLUMN TYPE, believing it would take "an hour or so" because a 5 GB staging copy took a minute. It held ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for 9 hours. Cancelling it after hour four would have rolled back four hours of rewrite (transactional DDL again), so they let it finish. The product was down for a working day. Copy-and-swap would have made it invisible.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Disk space: copy-and-swap and pg_repack need room for a second copy plus indexes; check pg_database_size against free space first.
  • Sequence ownership after swap: the sequence still belongs to the old table's column; re-own it and setval past the max.
  • Foreign keys to the old table keep pointing at it after rename (they reference OIDs); re-create them against the new table.
  • Mirror trigger and the backfill racing: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING handles inserts; for updates, the backfill must not overwrite a newer mirrored row: copy with ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE ... WHERE excluded.updated_at > target.updated_at, or copy in ascending id order and rely on the trigger for anything after.
  • pg_repack interrupted leaves a repack schema with temporary objects; clean with pg_repack --no-order rerun or drop the leftovers per its documentation.
  • Views, triggers, RLS policies on the old table do not move to the new one; script their re-creation.

Interview questions

  1. Change int to bigint on a 300 M row PK without downtime. Expected: new column or new table, trigger mirror, batched backfill, concurrent indexes, verify, rename swap in one transaction, fix sequence and FKs.
  2. How do you partition an existing huge table? Expected: attach the old table as a history partition using a validated CHECK to avoid the scan, new partitions for the future, rename swap; beware FK implications.
  3. What is pg_repack for? Expected: online rebuild to remove bloat or re-cluster, replacing VACUUM FULL, with brief locks and a full copy on disk.

Practical exercise

Take a 20 M row events table with int id and convert it to bigint id using copy-and-swap while a load generator inserts 500 rows per second and updates 50 rows per second. Acceptance criteria: the load generator sees no errors and no latency spike above 100 ms; after the swap, SELECT max(id) FROM events matches the generator's counter; the sequence continues without gaps larger than the generator's in-flight batch; events_old row count plus generator inserts after the trigger equals the new table's count.

23.11 Migrations across services and shards

Concept

Two situations complicate the single-database story. Shared database: several services (or several deployables of one system) read and write the same tables, so a migration made by one team can break another team's pods. Many databases with the same schema: shards, or a database per tenant, so one logical migration must be applied to N physical databases and the application must survive the window in which some have it and some do not.

Why does it exist?

Because ownership and physical layout do not always match. A shared database is usually a leftover from a monolith that was split by team before it was split by data; it is a known anti-pattern (see Part 11 — Software Architecture) but a common reality. Shards and per-tenant databases are deliberate scaling choices from Part 22 that multiply the migration surface.

Mental model

Imagine several shops sharing one warehouse. If one shop rearranges the shelves overnight, the other shops' staff cannot find anything in the morning. Either one warehouse manager owns the layout and announces changes with notice, or each shop gets its own aisle that nobody else touches. Now imagine a chain with fifty warehouses that must all be rearranged the same way: you need a plan that tracks which warehouses are done, works even when half are done, and can retry the one where the forklift broke.

How it works

Shared database rules.

  1. One owner per table. Write it down. Only the owning service's repository contains migrations for that table. Other services are consumers and may only rely on columns the owner has declared stable.
  2. Separate migration tables and roles per service. Each service uses its own migrationsTableName (migrations_orders, migrations_billing) so runners do not collide, and its own database role with DDL rights only on the schemas it owns. Better still, one PostgreSQL schema per service (orders.*, billing.*) with search_path set per role; cross-service reads happen through views the owner publishes, or through APIs and events.
  3. N-1 compatibility across services, not just across versions of one service. The owner's contract step (dropping a column) must wait until every consumer has stopped using it, which means the owner needs to know its consumers: pg_stat_statements by role, or a grep across repositories, or a deprecation announcement with a date.
  4. Views as contracts. When a consumer needs a table shape the owner wants to change, the owner provides a view with the old shape during the transition, exactly like the rename trick in section 23.9.

Migrations across shards.

  1. Same migration files, applied to every shard, in the same order, by a runner that iterates the shard list and records status per shard. Never a different migration per shard.
  2. Idempotent statements (IF NOT EXISTS, IF EXISTS, NOT VALID guards) so that a rerun on a shard that half-applied is safe.
  3. Status table in the control database: shard_migrations(shard_id, migration_name, applied_at, status, error). The runner skips applied ones, retries failed ones, and reports "12 of 16 shards at version X".
  4. Application tolerates mixed versions, because between the first and last shard the schema differs. Expand/contract already gives you this; the only new rule is that the code deploy waits until all shards are at the required version (the deploy gate checks the status table).
  5. Parallelism with a cap: apply to 4 shards at a time; a lock timeout on one shard does not block the others.
  6. Backfills per shard, each with its own cursor row (backfill_progress keyed by job and shard), throttled by that shard's own replica lag.
flowchart TB
    R["Migration runner"] --> C["Control DB: shard list and status"]
    C --> S1["Shard 1: apply pending"]
    C --> S2["Shard 2: apply pending"]
    C --> S3["Shard 3: lock timeout, retry later"]
    C --> S4["Shard 4: apply pending"]
    S1 --> ST["status table: per shard, per migration"]
    S2 --> ST
    S3 --> ST
    S4 --> ST
    ST --> G["Deploy gate: all shards at version X?"]

NestJS example

A shard-aware runner built on the per-shard DataSource map from Part 22.

// src/database/run-shard-migrations.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { shardsFromEnv } from '../sharding/shard.config';
import { controlDataSource } from './control-data-source';

const PARALLEL = 4;

async function migrateShard(shardId: number, host: string): Promise<void> {
  const ds = new DataSource({
    type: 'postgres', host, port: 5432,
    username: process.env.PG_MIGRATION_USER, password: process.env.PG_MIGRATION_PASSWORD, database: process.env.PG_DB,
    migrations: ['dist/database/migrations/*.js'], migrationsTableName: 'migrations',
  });
  await ds.initialize();
  try {
    const applied = await ds.runMigrations({ transaction: 'each' });
    for (const m of applied) {
      await controlDataSource.query(
        `INSERT INTO shard_migrations (shard_id, migration_name, status, applied_at) VALUES ($1, $2, 'applied', now())
         ON CONFLICT (shard_id, migration_name) DO UPDATE SET status = 'applied', applied_at = now(), error = NULL`,
        [shardId, m.name]);
    }
    console.log(`shard ${shardId}: applied ${applied.length}`);
  } catch (err) {
    await controlDataSource.query(
      `INSERT INTO shard_migrations (shard_id, migration_name, status, error) VALUES ($1, 'pending', 'failed', $2)
       ON CONFLICT (shard_id, migration_name) DO UPDATE SET status = 'failed', error = EXCLUDED.error`,
      [shardId, (err as Error).message]);
    throw err;
  } finally {
    await ds.destroy();
  }
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await controlDataSource.initialize();
  const shards = shardsFromEnv();
  const failures: number[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < shards.length; i += PARALLEL) {
    const results = await Promise.allSettled(shards.slice(i, i + PARALLEL).map((s) => migrateShard(s.id, s.host)));
    results.forEach((r, j) => { if (r.status === 'rejected') failures.push(shards[i + j].id); });
  }
  await controlDataSource.destroy();
  if (failures.length) { console.error(`failed shards: ${failures.join(', ')}; rerun to retry`); process.exit(1); }
}

main().catch((err) => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); });

The deploy pipeline's gate query: SELECT count(DISTINCT shard_id) FROM shard_migrations WHERE migration_name = $1 AND status = 'applied' must equal the shard count before the rollout proceeds.

Production scenario

Sixteen shards, one migration adding a nullable column: the runner finishes in about 20 seconds with 4-way parallelism. A migration with VALIDATE CONSTRAINT on a 100 M row table per shard: about 6 minutes per shard, 25 minutes total, during which the application runs fine on mixed schemas because the constraint was added NOT VALID first (instant everywhere) and validation changes nothing the code can see. A per-shard backfill: 16 cursors, 16 lag throttles, run as 16 Kubernetes Jobs from one template.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shard added mid-migration: the new shard is created from a snapshot at version X while the runner is moving others to X+1; the runner's next pass picks it up because it reads the shard list each time.
  • Two services migrate the same table: one drops a column the other just added a dependency on. Ownership, or separate schemas, is the only cure.
  • Consumer with SELECT * on an owner's table silently gets new columns and loses dropped ones; consumers should select explicit columns or use owner-provided views.
  • Migration table shared by two services with different file sets: each runner sees the other's rows as "unknown migrations" and TypeORM refuses or misorders. Separate table names.
  • Per-tenant databases in the thousands: a migration becomes an hours-long batch; the app must tolerate the mixed state for that long, and the runner must be resumable and rate-limited against the shared host.

Interview questions

  1. Two services share a table. How do you make schema changes safely? Expected: single owner, separate migration tables and roles or schemas, N-1 across services, views as transition contracts, consumer inventory before contract.
  2. How do you run one migration across 16 shards? Expected: same files, idempotent statements, per-shard status in a control DB, bounded parallelism, retry, deploy gate on all-applied, app tolerant of mixed versions.

23.12 Testing migrations

Concept

A migration is tested the way any risky code is tested: for correctness on a fresh database, for reversibility where claimed, for behaviour against realistic data, and, uniquely, for lock time on a production-sized table. The last one is the test most teams skip and the one that would have prevented most migration incidents.

Why does it exist?

Because a migration that works on a 1,000-row development database can hold a lock for hours on 300 million rows, and because a backfill whose query is a sequential scan is fine on a laptop and a disaster in production. Timing does not scale linearly; only a production-like snapshot tells the truth.

Mental model

Imagine testing a bridge design with a toy model. It proves the geometry. It says nothing about whether the real bridge holds real trucks. For that you need a full-size test span, or at least a calculation from the real dimensions.

How it works

  1. Fresh-database test in CI (section 23.2's exercise): apply all migrations from zero, run down for the last one and up again, then generate a migration and assert it is empty. Catches ordering bugs, syntax, and drift between entities and migrations.
  2. Snapshot test for big tables. Restore last night's production snapshot (RDS snapshot to a temporary instance, or a pg_basebackup copy) into an isolated environment. Run the migration with timing. Record the lock hold time per statement, using \timing in psql or by logging clock_timestamp() before and after each statement. Anything over a second under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE goes back to the drawing board. Automate this weekly for the tables in a "big tables" list, and on demand for any migration touching them.
  3. Measure lock behaviour explicitly. In the snapshot environment, start a long SELECT in one session, run the migration in another with lock_timeout, and confirm it fails fast rather than queueing. Confirm the retry loop works.
  4. EXPLAIN the backfill's batch query against the snapshot. It must use the primary key index (or a purpose-built partial index like CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON users (id) WHERE phone_e164 IS NULL); a sequential scan per batch turns a one-hour backfill into a week.
  5. Dry runs. migration:generate --dryrun prints SQL without writing; a wrapper that logs each statement the runner would execute against the target, with the target's PostgreSQL version, catches version-specific traps (fast defaults, ADD VALUE in transaction).
  6. Data assertions after the migration on the snapshot: the verification queries from the walkthrough (pending count, mismatch count, constraint validity, invalid indexes).
  7. Application test against the migrated snapshot with the previous code version, to prove N-1 compatibility; then with the new version.

PostgreSQL example

-- Measure lock hold time of a statement on the snapshot.
\timing on
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';
SELECT clock_timestamp() AS started \gset
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN phone_e164 SET NOT NULL;
SELECT clock_timestamp() - :'started' AS held_for;
ROLLBACK;   -- it is a test

-- EXPLAIN the backfill batch. Must show an Index Scan on the PK (or a partial index), never Seq Scan.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, phone FROM users WHERE id > 1840000 AND phone_e164 IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 2000;
Limit  (cost=0.56..312.40 rows=2000 width=28) (actual time=0.031..3.912 rows=2000 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using users_pkey on users  (cost=0.56..1873201.11 rows=12011200 width=28)
        (actual time=0.029..3.611 rows=2000 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (id > 1840000)
        Filter: ((phone_e164 IS NULL) AND (phone IS NOT NULL))
        Rows Removed by Filter: 41
        Buffers: shared hit=2087
Planning Time: 0.212 ms
Execution Time: 4.101 ms

The Rows Removed by Filter stays small for a keyset backfill because filled rows sit behind the cursor. If it grows large (rows filled by dual writes ahead of the cursor), the partial index makes each batch cheap again.

NestJS example

A Jest test that applies migrations to a disposable database (Testcontainers) and checks both directions plus drift.

// test/migrations.e2e-spec.ts
import { PostgreSqlContainer, StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

describe('migrations', () => {
  let pg: StartedPostgreSqlContainer;
  let ds: DataSource;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    pg = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16').start();
    ds = new DataSource({
      type: 'postgres', url: pg.getConnectionUri(),
      entities: ['src/**/*.entity.ts'], migrations: ['src/database/migrations/*.ts'], synchronize: false,
    });
    await ds.initialize();
  }, 120_000);

  afterAll(async () => { await ds?.destroy(); await pg?.stop(); });

  it('applies all migrations, reverts the last, re-applies, and leaves no drift', async () => {
    await ds.runMigrations({ transaction: 'each' });
    await ds.undoLastMigration({ transaction: 'each' });
    await ds.runMigrations({ transaction: 'each' });
    // Drift check: the schema builder's log must contain no pending up queries.
    const sqlInMemory = await ds.driver.createSchemaBuilder().log();
    expect(sqlInMemory.upQueries.map((q) => q.query)).toEqual([]);
  });

  it('has no invalid indexes after migrations', async () => {
    const rows = await ds.query(`SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS name FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid`);
    expect(rows).toEqual([]);
  });
});

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Snapshot older than the code: a column added yesterday is missing; refresh snapshots nightly and run pending migrations first.
  • Snapshot instance smaller than production: timings are pessimistic, which is the safe direction; but a plan can differ (less RAM changes work_mem decisions). Match the instance class for the big-table tests.
  • Test data too uniform: a generated 30 M rows with sequential ids and no deletes hides sparse-range and bloat behaviour. Prefer real snapshots with personal data masked.
  • CI database is PostgreSQL 16 while production is 13: fast-path rules differ. Pin the CI image to the production major version.

Interview questions

  1. How do you know a migration will not lock a table for an hour? Expected: run it against a production-sized snapshot and measure; classify statements by the lock table; lock_timeout as the safety net.
  2. What do you EXPLAIN before a backfill and what are you looking for? Expected: the batch selection query; index scan on the key, small rows-removed-by-filter, low buffers.
  3. What does a good CI migration job check? Expected: fresh apply, down and up, no drift, no invalid indexes, matching PostgreSQL major version.

23.13 Edge cases, failure modes and the migration safety checklist

The failure modes below are the ones that recur across companies. Each has a one-line cause and the control that prevents it.

  • Migration hangs waiting for a lock and queues every query on the table. Cause: no lock_timeout, a long query or idle-in-transaction session ahead in the queue. Control: lock_timeout with retry; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout; migrations scheduled away from report windows.
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction. Cause: the runner wraps migrations in transactions by default. Control: own file, --transaction none, idempotent statements, invalid-index check afterwards.
  • Half-applied migration. Cause: non-transactional migration failed at statement 3 of 5; the migrations table has no row. Control: every statement idempotent; rerun safe; or keep the migration transactional when no CONCURRENTLY is involved.
  • Migration run twice by two pods. Cause: startup migrations with replicas. Control: pre-deploy Job with backoffLimit: 0; advisory lock as belt-and-braces.
  • Backfill bloats the table and starves autovacuum. Cause: huge batches, no sleep, one giant transaction. Control: small autocommit batches, sleeps, lag throttle, per-table autovacuum tuning, vacuum after.
  • Enum value added and used in the same transaction. Cause: PostgreSQL 12+ allows the ADD VALUE but forbids using it before commit; older versions forbid it in a transaction entirely. Control: own migration for the ADD VALUE; code tolerant to unknown values deployed first.
  • Type change rewrites a 500 GB table for hours. Cause: in-place ALTER COLUMN TYPE. Control: the lock table review; copy-and-swap; snapshot timing test.
  • Old pods crash on a dropped column. Cause: contract before the entity change was fully deployed. Control: remove from code, deploy, wait, then drop; consumer inventory for shared tables.
  • Migration table drift between environments. Cause: edited or renamed applied migrations; hotfixes by hand. Control: never edit applied migrations; drift check in CI; hotfixes recorded as migrations.
  • NOT NULL added while an old writer still omits the column. Cause: constraint before all live versions write the column. Control: the N-1 check before every constraint tightening.
  • Replication slot or WAL explosion during a backfill. Cause: WAL burst faster than replicas or Debezium can consume. Control: lag throttle; watch pg_replication_slots.
  • Foreign keys silently pointing at the old table after a swap. Cause: FKs reference OIDs, not names. Control: re-create FKs with NOT VALID + VALIDATE as part of the swap runbook.

Migration safety checklist

# Check Why
1 Every statement classified: fast, scan, or rewrite (section 23.3) Rewrites and scans under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE are outages
2 lock_timeout set (2 to 5 s) and a retry loop for DDL Prevents the lock queue outage
3 statement_timeout set, larger than lock_timeout Bounds an accidental rewrite
4 Indexes created and dropped with CONCURRENTLY, in their own non-transactional migration Non-concurrent builds block writes; concurrent cannot be in a transaction
5 Invalid-index check after concurrent builds Failed builds leave useless indexes
6 No data changes inside migrations; backfills run from a worker Long transactions, bloat, lag
7 Backfill is keyset-batched, resumable, throttled by replica lag, logs progress Survives crashes and protects replicas
8 Change is backward compatible with the currently running code (N-1) Rolling deploys and code rollback
9 Contract steps (drop, rename, tighten) happen only after the code no longer references the old thing, verified with pg_stat_statements and a waiting period Old pods and forgotten consumers
10 Backup (table copy or snapshot) taken before destructive steps, with a scheduled deletion Roll-forward needs the data
11 down for destructive steps throws instead of destroying data Prevents automated data loss
12 Generated migration reviewed line by line; noise removed migration:generate is a draft
13 Migration run as a pre-deploy Job with backoffLimit: 0, direct to the primary, with a migration role No races, visible failure, least privilege
14 Timing measured on a production-sized snapshot for any table over 10 M rows Only real size tells the truth
15 EXPLAIN on the backfill batch query shows an index scan Sequential scans per batch never finish
16 Enum additions in their own migration; code tolerant of unknown values deployed first Transaction rules and consumer crashes
17 For shared tables: owner identified, consumers inventoried, views provided during transition Cross-service breakage
18 For shards: same files, idempotent statements, per-shard status, deploy gate on all-applied Mixed-version windows
19 Verification query written and run after each step "Done" is a query result, not a feeling
20 Runbook: what to do if the job hangs, fails, or half-applies 3 a.m. decisions made at 3 p.m.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat the checklist as a review gate, not a suggestion. They know that most of the twenty items take a minute each and that skipping any one of them has, somewhere, cost a company a day. They keep a list of the big tables, the PostgreSQL major version in each environment, and the consumers of each shared table, because those three facts decide which recipes apply. When a product manager asks why a "simple rename" takes two weeks, they explain the bridge: the old one carries traffic until the new one is proven, and that is what zero downtime costs.

Senior Checklist — Part 23

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can classify any ALTER TABLE as fast, scan or rewrite and name the safe recipe for the unsafe ones
  • I never run DDL without lock_timeout and I can explain the lock queue outage from memory
  • I can perform a rename or type change with expand/contract across five deploys and two weeks without downtime
  • I can write a keyset, resumable, lag-throttled backfill and prove its batch query uses an index
  • I can add NOT NULL, a foreign key, and a unique constraint to a 300 M row table without blocking writes
  • I run migrations as a pre-deploy Job with a dedicated role, never at application startup with replicas
  • I know why down is for development, and I back up before every destructive step
  • I can convert a huge table to bigint ids or to partitions with copy-and-swap or partition attach
  • I can run one migration across N shards with per-shard status and a deploy gate
  • I test migrations on a production-sized snapshot and measure lock time before they reach production

Part 23 — Key Takeaways

  • Schema migrations are code with the highest blast radius in the repository; review generated migrations line by line.
  • Fast, scan, or rewrite: classify every DDL statement; only fast operations may hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a live table.
  • lock_timeout plus retry is the seat belt: a 4 ms ADD COLUMN without it can freeze a table for the length of the longest running query.
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own non-transactional migration; check for invalid indexes afterwards.
  • NOT NULL, CHECK and foreign keys go on with NOT VALID then VALIDATE; unique constraints ride a concurrently built index.
  • Expand, migrate, contract: add the new, dual-write and backfill, switch reads behind a flag, switch writes, remove the old across separate deploys.
  • Backfills run from a worker in small autocommit keyset batches, throttled by replica lag, with a persisted cursor; never as one UPDATE in a migration.
  • Dual writes are atomic in one transaction; across systems they are best-effort with idempotent upserts; a trigger covers write paths you forgot.
  • Database rollback is mostly fiction: roll forward, keep old columns until the new path is proven, back up before destructive steps, make destructive down methods throw.
  • Copy-and-swap and partition attach turn multi-hour rewrites into millisecond renames; pg_repack replaces VACUUM FULL.
  • Migrations run once, before the rollout, as a Job with a migration role and an advisory lock, never at startup with replicas.
  • Shared tables need an owner and a consumer inventory; shards need idempotent statements, per-shard status and a deploy gate.
  • Measure lock time on a production-sized snapshot; EXPLAIN the backfill query; "done" is a verification query, not a feeling.

Part 24 — Backward Compatibility: APIs, Schemas, Events and Clients

Two questions define this part. How do you change a production database without breaking old application versions? And how do you change an API or an event without breaking old clients? The two questions have the same answer, because they are the same problem: at every moment, more than one version of something is alive, and each version must understand what the others produce.

Old code and new code run side by side during every rolling deployment. A mobile app installed two years ago is still calling your API today. A Kafka consumer that was down for six hours will replay events written by three different producer versions. A Redis cache holds objects serialised by last week's code. A JWT issued by the previous release is presented to the next one. None of these can be "just upgraded"; all of them must be tolerated.

This part gives the rules and the recipes: additive-only changes, the tolerant reader, the N-1 schema rule and its link to expand/contract from Part 23 — Database Migrations, event schema evolution and registry compatibility modes, mobile client realities, contract testing in CI, and a decision table for every kind of change you will be asked to make. The senior mantra applies here as can it return a wrong response?, because the most dangerous incompatibility is not a crash; it is a field that silently means something different.

24.1 Why compatibility matters

Concept

Backward compatibility means a newer version of a producer (server, schema, event publisher) still works with older consumers (clients, pods, subscribers). Forward compatibility means an older consumer can cope with output from a newer producer. In a running system you need both, because deploys are not instantaneous and clients are not under your control.

Why does it exist?

Three facts of production life make compatibility mandatory rather than nice-to-have.

  1. Rolling deployments run mixed versions. A Kubernetes rollout with 40 pods, maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 0, takes several minutes during which pods of version N and N+1 both serve traffic against one database, one Redis, one Kafka. The migration job ran before any N+1 pod started, so the schema is at N+1 while every pod is still N. If a rollout is paused or rolled back, that mixed state can last hours.
  2. Mobile apps live for years. App-store updates are optional; a meaningful fraction of users run versions that are 6 to 24 months old. Every endpoint, field and enum value those versions use is frozen until you are willing to force an upgrade.
  3. Event consumers replay. A consumer that was down for maintenance, crashed, or was rebuilt from scratch will read events written days or weeks ago, by producer versions that no longer exist, mixed with brand-new ones. The topic is a history book; every page must remain readable.

Mental model

Imagine a railway that runs trains from several decades on the same tracks. New track must accept old wheels; new signals must be readable by old drivers; old stations must not confuse new trains. You never close the line to replace everything at once. Every change is made so that whatever is on the tracks right now keeps running, and only later is the oldest stock retired.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant LB as Load balancer
    participant P1 as Pod v1
    participant P2 as Pod v2
    participant DB as PostgreSQL schema v2
    Note over DB: migration job ran first, schema already v2
    LB->>P1: POST /orders
    P1->>DB: INSERT without new column
    DB-->>P1: ok, column nullable or defaulted
    LB->>P2: GET /orders/42
    P2->>DB: SELECT includes new column
    DB-->>P2: ok
    LB->>P1: GET /orders/42
    P1->>DB: SELECT old columns only
    DB-->>P1: ok, ignores new column
    Note over P1,P2: both versions must succeed for minutes or hours

The compatibility window is not a moment; it is a period with a defined start and end, and every artefact that crosses it (rows, cache entries, queued jobs, events, tokens, HTTP responses) must be understood by both ends. Part 22 and Part 23 covered the database mechanics; this part covers the rules that keep the window safe for everything else.

Production scenario

An e-commerce platform deploys 15 times a day across 8 services. Each deploy has a 4-minute mixed-version window. That is an hour a day during which any incompatible change would show up as errors for a fraction of users. The team's rule, enforced in review and CI: every change must be safe if version N+1 is fully deployed, if version N is fully deployed, and if both are half deployed, against the same database, cache and topics. They have not had a deploy-caused incident in two years, not because deploys are rare but because incompatibility is designed out.

Failure scenario

At 11:40 a deploy renamed the JSON field deliveryEta to estimatedDeliveryAt in the order response and shipped a new web client that read the new name. Web users saw an empty ETA for four minutes, which was annoying. The mobile app, which nobody had updated, showed no ETA for three weeks until a new version was approved and, even then, 30% of users had not upgraded a month later. The change was reverted by adding the old field back; it now returns both names indefinitely.

Interview questions

  1. Why is backward compatibility required even for an internal API you control both sides of? Expected: rolling deploys, rollbacks, replayed events, cached data; both sides are never upgraded at the same instant.
  2. What is the difference between backward and forward compatibility? Expected: new producer with old consumer vs old consumer with new producer output; you need both in practice.

24.2 API compatibility and versioning

Concept

An API is compatible with its existing clients when every request they already send still succeeds with the same meaning, and every response they receive still contains every field they rely on, with the same type and semantics. Versioning is the mechanism for offering a different contract to clients that opt in, while keeping the old contract alive for those that do not. Part 14 — REST API Design covered versioning mechanics; this section looks at them through the compatibility lens.

Why does it exist?

Because clients are code you do not deploy. The rule "never break a client" is not idealism; it is the direct consequence of not controlling when the client changes. Versioning exists so that breaking changes can be made somewhere (a new version) without being made to anyone who did not ask.

Mental model

Imagine a bank's paper forms. The bank can add an optional box to a form and old customers who ignore it are fine. The bank cannot remove the "account number" box, rename "amount" to "sum", or change "amount" from dollars to cents, without every customer who memorised the form filling it in wrong. If the bank wants a radically different form, it issues "Form 2" and keeps accepting "Form 1" for years, printing a notice on Form 1 saying when it will stop.

How it works

The rules of additive change, in order of importance:

  1. Add, never remove or rename. New response fields are safe if clients ignore unknown fields (which they must; see the tolerant reader below). New optional request fields are safe with sensible defaults. Removing or renaming a field breaks every reader of it.
  2. Never change a type or a meaning. total from number to string, createdAt from epoch seconds to ISO string, price from net to gross with the same name: each is a break, and the semantic one is the worst because nothing crashes; numbers are just wrong. New meaning gets a new name (totalGross) and the old field keeps its old meaning until sunset.
  3. Loosen validation freely; tighten it only with a version. Accepting a wider range of input breaks nobody. Rejecting input that used to be accepted breaks whoever sent it.
  4. Default new required inputs. If the server needs a new value, it must be able to compute a default when an old client omits it, or the field is not required in this version.
  5. Enum values are additive for producers only. Adding a value to something the server returns breaks strict clients that switch over the enum; adding a value the client may send is safe for the server. Design clients to treat unknown values as "other" (section 24.5).
  6. The tolerant reader. Every consumer, server-side included, ignores fields it does not understand and does not fail on extra data. In NestJS this means ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }) to strip unknown properties, and not forbidNonWhitelisted: true on public endpoints, otherwise a newer client sending a new optional field to an older server gets a 400.
  7. Deprecate with dates and headers. RFC 9745 defines the Deprecation header (a @ followed by a Unix timestamp), RFC 8594 the Sunset header (an HTTP date after which the endpoint may stop working), and Link: <...>; rel="deprecation" points to documentation. Clients and gateways can log and alert on them.
  8. Support N-1 versions at minimum. When v3 ships, v2 keeps working for a published period (six months to two years for mobile-facing APIs); v1 may be sunset. Version negotiation: URI (/v2/orders), header (X-API-Version: 2), or media type (Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json). URI versioning is the most visible and cache-friendly; header versioning keeps URLs stable. Pick one and keep it.
flowchart LR
    C1["Mobile app 2024 calls v1"] --> GW["API Gateway"]
    C2["Web app calls v2"] --> GW
    C3["Partner calls v2"] --> GW
    GW --> A1["v1 controller, Deprecation and Sunset headers"]
    GW --> A2["v2 controller"]
    A1 --> S["Shared OrdersService"]
    A2 --> S

NestJS example

URI versioning with a deprecated v1 and a v2 that changed a field's meaning (net to gross), plus an interceptor that adds deprecation headers to every v1 response.

// src/main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe, VersioningType } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap(): Promise<void> {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.enableVersioning({ type: VersioningType.URI, defaultVersion: '1' });   // /v1/orders, /v2/orders
  app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({
    whitelist: true,                 // tolerant reader: strip unknown properties silently
    forbidNonWhitelisted: false,     // never 400 a client for sending a field we do not know yet
    transform: true,
  }));
  await app.listen(3000);
}
void bootstrap();
// src/orders/dto/order-v1.response.ts and order-v2.response.ts
export class OrderV1Response {
  id!: string;
  status!: string;
  total!: number;            // v1 meaning: net amount in major units, e.g. 42.5. Frozen forever.
  deliveryEta!: string | null;
}

export class OrderV2Response {
  id!: string;
  status!: string;
  totalNetCents!: number;    // new names carry the new meaning; nothing is reused with a different meaning
  totalGrossCents!: number;
  estimatedDeliveryAt!: string | null;
}
// src/orders/orders-v1.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, UseInterceptors } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';
import { OrderV1Response } from './dto/order-v1.response';
import { DeprecationInterceptor } from '../common/deprecation.interceptor';

@Controller({ path: 'orders', version: '1' })
@UseInterceptors(new DeprecationInterceptor({
  deprecatedAt: new Date('2026-06-01T00:00:00Z'),
  sunsetAt: new Date('2027-06-01T00:00:00Z'),
  docs: 'https://developers.shop.example/deprecations/orders-v1',
}))
export class OrdersV1Controller {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get(':id')
  async get(@Param('id') id: string): Promise<OrderV1Response> {
    const o = await this.orders.getById(id);
    return {
      id: o.id, status: o.status,
      total: o.totalNetCents / 100,            // v1 contract preserved exactly
      deliveryEta: o.estimatedDeliveryAt?.toISOString() ?? null,
    };
  }
}
// src/orders/orders-v2.controller.ts
@Controller({ path: 'orders', version: '2' })
export class OrdersV2Controller {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get(':id')
  async get(@Param('id') id: string): Promise<OrderV2Response> {
    const o = await this.orders.getById(id);
    return {
      id: o.id, status: o.status,
      totalNetCents: o.totalNetCents, totalGrossCents: o.totalGrossCents,
      estimatedDeliveryAt: o.estimatedDeliveryAt?.toISOString() ?? null,
    };
  }
}
// src/common/deprecation.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable } from 'rxjs';
import { Response } from 'express';

export interface DeprecationOptions { deprecatedAt: Date; sunsetAt: Date; docs: string }

@Injectable()
export class DeprecationInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly opts: DeprecationOptions) {}

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    // RFC 9745: Deprecation is "@" + Unix seconds. RFC 8594: Sunset is an HTTP-date.
    res.setHeader('Deprecation', `@${Math.floor(this.opts.deprecatedAt.getTime() / 1000)}`);
    res.setHeader('Sunset', this.opts.sunsetAt.toUTCString());
    res.setHeader('Link', `<${this.opts.docs}>; rel="deprecation"`);
    return next.handle();
  }
}

A metric per version (http_requests_total{version="1"}) tells you when v1 traffic has fallen low enough to sunset, and who is still calling it (by API key or user agent) so you can contact them before the date.

Production scenario

A payments API serves 2,000 RPS across v1 (12%), v2 (85%) and v3 (3%, new). v1 has been deprecated for 9 months with a sunset in 3 months; its callers are two partner integrations and mobile versions older than 18 months. The team emailed the partners, added an in-app "please update" banner for old mobile versions, and will return 410 Gone with a JSON body pointing to migration docs after the sunset date. The cost of keeping v1 alive was one controller and a mapping function; the cost of breaking it would have been two partner escalations.

Failure scenario

A "harmless cleanup" changed amount in the refund response from a string ("42.50", a decimal preserved as text to avoid float issues) to a number (42.5). Same name, same value, different JSON type. A partner's strongly typed client (generated from the old OpenAPI file) threw on deserialisation; refunds appeared to fail on their side; they retried; the idempotency key saved the money but their support queue filled up. The lesson: type is part of the contract, and generated clients are strict.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Gateway rewriting versions: an API gateway that maps /v2/* to the backend's /v1/* for "compatibility" hides which version clients really use and breaks when the backend's v1 changes. Version at one layer only.
  • Default version drift: defaultVersion: '1' today, '2' after a config change, and every unversioned caller silently changes contract. Never change the default; require explicit versions from new clients.
  • Response shape depends on a flag: a feature flag that adds fields is additive; a flag that removes or renames is a break behind a switch.
  • Error format changes ({ message } to { error: { code, message } }) are breaking for clients that parse errors; version them like anything else or return both shapes during a transition.
  • Pagination changes (offset to cursor) are breaking; introduce cursor pagination as new parameters and keep offset working, or version.
  • Header case and duplicates: a client that sends X-Api-Version and a server that checks X-API-Version are fine (HTTP headers are case-insensitive), but a proxy that strips unknown headers is not.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat the public contract as a promise with a date. Additive change is the default and is free; anything else needs a version, a deprecation header, a sunset date, a metric showing who is affected, and a communication plan. They refuse to reuse a field name with a new meaning under any circumstances. They ask "which client versions will read this, and what will each do with it?" before approving a response change.

Common mistakes

  • Renaming a field for "consistency".
  • Changing a type "because it was wrong"; it was, and it still must stay until a version ends.
  • forbidNonWhitelisted: true on public endpoints, making the server intolerant of newer clients.
  • Deprecating without a date, so nothing ever gets removed and nothing ever gets migrated.

Interview questions

  1. Which API changes are backward compatible? Expected: add optional fields, add endpoints, loosen validation, add enum values a client may send; not remove, rename, retype, tighten, or change meaning.
  2. How do you deprecate an endpoint properly? Expected: Deprecation and Sunset headers, docs link, per-version metrics, communication, then 410.
  3. A field must change from net to gross. How? Expected: new field name, keep the old with its old meaning, deprecate, remove in a later version.
  4. What is the tolerant reader and how do you implement it in NestJS? Expected: ignore unknown fields; whitelist: true without forbidNonWhitelisted.

Practical exercise

Take an existing GET /orders/:id and introduce v2 with cents-based totals and a renamed ETA field, keeping v1 byte-for-byte identical. Add the deprecation interceptor to v1 and a Prometheus counter by version. Acceptance criteria: a snapshot test of the v1 response fails if any byte changes; v1 responses carry the three headers; the counter distinguishes v1 and v2 traffic; ValidationPipe accepts a v1 request carrying an unknown field.

24.3 Schema compatibility: the N-1 rule

Concept

The N-1 rule: every database schema version must work with the application version currently deployed and with the one about to be deployed, and every application version must work with the schema version before and after its own. Since the migration runs before the rollout, the schema is always one step ahead of the oldest running pod, and if the rollout is reverted, one step ahead of the only running version. The rule is what makes rolling deploys and code rollbacks safe.

Why does it exist?

Because a schema change is applied once, instantly, to a database that many code versions share, while code versions replace each other gradually. There is no way to change schema and code atomically across 40 pods. The only alternative to N-1 compatibility is a maintenance window, and the only alternative to that is an outage.

Mental model

Imagine changing the locks on an office building while people are inside. You cannot swap every lock and hand out new keys at the same instant. So you install locks that accept both the old and the new key, hand out new keys over a week, and only when everyone has the new key do you remove the old key's profile. During the week, both keys work. The N-1 rule is "the lock must accept the previous key and the next key".

How it works

The link to Part 23 is direct: expand/contract is the N-1 rule applied step by step. This section covers the ways code breaks against a schema that is one step ahead or behind, so you can spot them in review.

flowchart LR
    S1["Schema step 1: phone_e164 added"] --- W1["Window: code v1 and v2 both fine"]
    W1 --> S2["Schema step 5: phone_e164 NOT NULL"]
    S2 --- W2["Window: code v4 and v5 both fine, v1 would fail on insert"]
    W2 --> S3["Schema step 7: phone dropped"]
    S3 --- W3["Window: code v5 only, v4 would fail on select"]

Entity mapping and removed columns. TypeORM's find* methods generate SELECT "user"."id", "user"."email", "user"."phone", ... listing every column of the entity. Sequelize does the same with model attributes. If the column has been dropped, every such query fails with column "phone" does not exist. So the entity must lose the column before the column is dropped, which forces the two-deploy contract. A hand-written SELECT * does not fail; it returns a row without the property, and row.phone is undefined. That is worse when the value flows onward (a null written into another table, a notification sent with "undefined").

Entities lagging behind the schema. The reverse case: the schema has a new column the entity does not know. Reads are fine (the column is not selected). Inserts are fine only if the column is nullable or has a default. This is why step 1 of expand/contract adds the column nullable: v1 pods, which do not know it, keep inserting.

Adding NOT NULL with old writers. If the column is NOT NULL without a default and any live version inserts without it, that version's inserts fail. The safe order is: every live version writes the column; then tighten. In a shared-database situation, "every live version" includes other services.

Type changes. Widening (varchar(50) to text) is invisible to code. int to bigint changes what pg returns: JavaScript numbers are safe to 2^53, pg returns bigint columns as strings by default to avoid precision loss, so an entity declared number that becomes bigint starts receiving strings; code doing arithmetic gets "42" + 1 = "421". Change the TypeScript type and the column decorator in the code version before the schema changes.

Renames. Old code uses the old name, new code the new one; no single schema satisfies both. Hence never rename; expand/contract.

Default values as a compatibility tool. A new column with DEFAULT 'pending' lets old inserts succeed and gives the new code a meaningful value to read. Defaults are the schema's version of "default values for new fields" in APIs.

Constraints as breaking changes. A new CHECK or unique constraint that old code can violate is a breaking change for that code, regardless of lock behaviour. Deploy code that complies first; then add the constraint (with NOT VALID + VALIDATE).

TypeORM example

The entity in the middle of the window (code v4 from Part 23): knows both columns, writes only the new one, reads the new one with a fallback. This single entity is compatible with schema steps 1 through 6.

// src/users/user.entity.ts  (v4: compatible with phone present or absent in code, present in DB)
import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('increment', { type: 'bigint' }) id!: string;   // string: bigint arrives as text from pg
  @Column('text', { unique: true }) email!: string;

  // Still declared so SELECTs succeed while the column exists; marked select: false would also work
  // if no code path needs it, and would make the entity tolerant of the column being dropped early.
  @Column('text', { nullable: true, select: false, insert: false, update: false }) phone?: string | null;

  @Column('text', { name: 'phone_e164', nullable: true }) phoneE164!: string | null;
}

select: false plus insert: false and update: false is a useful trick: the column stays mapped for explicit addSelect if ever needed, but ordinary finds no longer list it, so this entity survives the column being dropped. That collapses steps 6 and 7 into one safe deploy in many cases.

Sequelize example

Sequelize selects all model attributes by default; to make a model tolerant of a column that is about to disappear, remove the attribute from the model definition, or use a default scope that excludes it.

// src/users/user.model.ts (transition version)
User.init(
  {
    id: { type: DataTypes.BIGINT, primaryKey: true, autoIncrement: true },
    email: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: false, unique: true },
    phone: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: true },                   // still declared for explicit reads
    phoneE164: { type: DataTypes.TEXT, allowNull: true, field: 'phone_e164' },
  },
  {
    sequelize, tableName: 'users', timestamps: false,
    defaultScope: { attributes: { exclude: ['phone'] } },               // ordinary queries never select phone
  },
);

PostgreSQL example

Finding out whether any live code still touches a column before the contract step.

-- Any statement in the last stats window referencing the old column, excluding the new one.
SELECT calls, left(query, 120)
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE query ~* '\mphone\M' AND query !~* 'phone_e164'
ORDER BY calls DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Reset the counters right after the last old-code deploy so the next check reflects only current code.
SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();

Production scenario

A team's deploy pipeline runs three checks on every PR that contains a migration: (1) the previous release's test suite against the migrated schema, (2) the current release's test suite against the previous schema (that is, without the new migration), and (3) the current suite against the migrated schema. All three must pass. Check (2) is the one people forget, and it is the one that catches "new code assumes the column exists" when a rollout is reverted after the migration ran.

Failure scenario

The "column dropped while old pods run" incident from Part 23 in another shape: a team removed phone from the entity and dropped the column in the same release. The migration job succeeded; the rollout started; for 4 minutes, v4 pods (entity with phone) ran against a schema without it; every user query on those pods failed. The blast radius was 40% of users for 4 minutes. The pipeline now refuses a PR that both removes an entity column and contains a DROP COLUMN.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Rollback after migration: code goes back to N, schema stays at N+1; safe only if N+1 was additive.
  • SELECT * in raw queries silently changes shape; prefer explicit columns in raw SQL that feeds other writes.
  • Enum column with a new value read by old code that maps the enum strictly; handled in section 24.5.
  • JSONB column shape changes are invisible to the schema and entirely a code compatibility issue; version the JSON ({"v": 2, ...}) and read both.
  • Generated columns and triggers added in N+1 may compute values old code did not expect to exist; harmless if old code ignores unknown columns.
  • Per-tenant or per-shard schema at different versions: code must be N-1 compatible for as long as the slowest shard takes.

Interview questions

  1. State the N-1 rule and why it exists. Expected: schema must work with current and next code; code with previous and next schema; because migrations are instant and rollouts are gradual, and rollbacks happen.
  2. Why does dropping a column break an ORM-based service even without SELECT *? Expected: ORMs list entity columns explicitly; the query fails outright.
  3. How do you test N-1 compatibility in CI? Expected: previous code against new schema, new code against previous schema, new against new.

24.4 Event compatibility and schema evolution

Concept

Events (Kafka messages, RabbitMQ messages, webhooks) are contracts with an extra dimension: time. A consumer reads a stream that contains messages from every producer version that ever wrote to it, in order, possibly weeks later. Schema evolution is the set of rules that keeps every message ever written readable by every consumer version that may ever read it.

Why does it exist?

Because topics are durable and consumers are independent. A retention of 7 days (or forever, with compaction) means old messages coexist with new ones. Consumers deploy on their own schedule; some are down for hours; some are rebuilt and replay from the beginning. A producer that changes a field's shape has changed the meaning of history.

Mental model

Imagine a company newsletter archive going back years. A new reader must be able to read the old issues; an old reader who has been away must be able to read the new issues. Adding a new column to the layout is fine. Renaming "Sales" to "Revenue" confuses the old reader; dropping the "Date" line breaks everyone who files issues by date. Whoever changes the layout must think about both readers.

How it works

  1. Envelope with a version. Every event carries metadata separate from its payload: type, version (of the payload schema), id, occurredAt, producer. Consumers dispatch on type and version.
  2. Additive payload changes only. Add optional fields with defaults. Never rename, never remove a field consumers use, never change a type or meaning. New meaning gets a new field name.
  3. Consumers ignore unknown fields. The tolerant reader again. A consumer that validates with a strict schema and rejects extra fields will break the moment a producer adds one.
  4. Upcasters for real changes. When a payload must change shape (v1 to v2), the consumer holds a small function per version step that transforms an old payload into the current shape before the business logic runs. Business logic then sees one shape. Upcasters are pure, chainable (v1 to v2 to v3), and unit-tested against recorded real events.
  5. Schema registry compatibility modes, explained simply. A registry (Confluent Schema Registry with Avro, JSON Schema or Protobuf) stores every version of each topic's schema and refuses to register a new version that violates the configured mode:
    • BACKWARD (the default): a consumer using the new schema can read data written with the old schema. Allowed: delete fields, add fields with defaults. Deployment order: consumers first, then producers.
    • FORWARD: a consumer using the old schema can read data written with the new schema. Allowed: add fields, delete fields that had defaults. Deployment order: producers first, then consumers.
    • FULL: both. Allowed: add or delete optional fields with defaults only. Any deployment order.
    • _TRANSITIVE variants check against all previous versions, not just the latest. Use FULL_TRANSITIVE for topics with long retention or replay; it is the only mode that guarantees any consumer can read any message ever written.
  6. Protobuf and JSON Schema specifics. Protobuf field numbers are the contract; never reuse a number; unknown fields are preserved by default; enums need an UNKNOWN = 0. JSON Schema compatibility depends on additionalProperties; a consumer schema with additionalProperties: false is intolerant.
flowchart LR
    P1["Producer v1 writes OrderPlaced v1"] --> T["Topic order-events, 7 day retention"]
    P2["Producer v2 writes OrderPlaced v2 with new optional field"] --> T
    T --> C1["Consumer old: ignores unknown field"]
    T --> C2["Consumer new: upcaster v1 to v2, then handle"]
    T --> C3["Consumer rebuilt: replays all, upcasts each"]

NestJS example

A typed envelope, an upcaster chain, and a Kafka consumer that dispatches on type and version. The producer only ever publishes the latest version; the consumer accepts all.

// src/events/envelope.ts
export interface EventEnvelope<T = unknown> {
  id: string;            // UUIDv7; also the idempotency key for consumers
  type: string;          // 'order.placed'
  version: number;       // payload schema version
  occurredAt: string;    // ISO 8601
  producer: string;      // 'orders-service@1.42.0'
  payload: T;
}
// src/events/order-placed/order-placed.upcasters.ts
// v1: { orderId, userId, total }            total = net, major units (e.g. 42.5)
// v2: { orderId, userId, totalNetCents, currency }   currency added, cents, still net
// v3: { orderId, userId, totalNetCents, totalGrossCents, currency }

export interface OrderPlacedV3 { orderId: string; userId: string; totalNetCents: number; totalGrossCents: number; currency: string }

type Upcaster = (payload: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>;

// Each step converts exactly one version to the next. Pure, testable against recorded events.
const upcasters: Record<number, Upcaster> = {
  1: (p) => ({ orderId: p.orderId, userId: p.userId, totalNetCents: Math.round(Number(p.total) * 100), currency: 'USD' }),
  2: (p) => ({ ...p, totalGrossCents: p.totalNetCents }),   // gross unknown for old events: best available value, documented
};

export const CURRENT_ORDER_PLACED_VERSION = 3;

export function upcastOrderPlaced(version: number, payload: Record<string, unknown>): OrderPlacedV3 {
  let v = version; let p = payload;
  while (v < CURRENT_ORDER_PLACED_VERSION) {
    const step = upcasters[v];
    if (!step) throw new Error(`no upcaster from order.placed v${v}`);
    p = step(p); v += 1;
  }
  if (v > CURRENT_ORDER_PLACED_VERSION) {
    // A newer producer than this consumer: tolerate, since v3 fields are a subset by the additive rule.
  }
  return p as unknown as OrderPlacedV3;
}
// src/events/order-events.consumer.ts
import { Controller, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { EventPattern, Payload } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { EventEnvelope } from './envelope';
import { upcastOrderPlaced } from './order-placed/order-placed.upcasters';
import { LoyaltyService } from '../loyalty/loyalty.service';

@Controller()
export class OrderEventsConsumer {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderEventsConsumer.name);
  constructor(private readonly loyalty: LoyaltyService) {}

  @EventPattern('order-events')
  async handle(@Payload() envelope: EventEnvelope<Record<string, unknown>>): Promise<void> {
    if (envelope.type !== 'order.placed') return;                      // unknown types are ignored, not errors
    const order = upcastOrderPlaced(envelope.version, envelope.payload);
    await this.loyalty.awardPoints(envelope.id, order.userId, order.totalNetCents);  // idempotent by event id
  }
}

The consumer treats an unknown type as "not for me", never as a failure; a new event type added by a producer must not crash consumers that predate it.

PostgreSQL example

The outbox table (Part 30) that produces these events carries the version so the relay never has to guess, and an archive of consumed events keyed by id gives idempotency.

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  type         text NOT NULL,
  version      int  NOT NULL,
  occurred_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  payload      jsonb NOT NULL,
  published_at timestamptz
);

-- Consumer side: processed event ids for idempotency across redeliveries and replays.
CREATE TABLE consumed_events (
  event_id     uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  consumer     text NOT NULL,
  consumed_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Production scenario

An order-events topic with 7-day retention and 6 consumers owned by 4 teams. Registry mode FULL_TRANSITIVE. Producer changes are additive only; when the totals moved to cents, the producer added totalNetCents alongside total for three months, consumers migrated one by one, and only then did the producer stop writing total (which under FULL required it to have had a default, which it did). A consumer rebuilt from scratch in month two replayed 7 days of mixed messages without error because of the upcaster chain.

Failure scenario

A producer renamed userId to customerId in order.placed. The registry was in NONE mode ("we will be careful"). The loyalty consumer read payload.userId, got undefined, and awarded points to user undefined for 40 minutes; 11,000 events were consumed and acknowledged. Recovery: an upcaster mapping customerId back, a replay from the offset before the deploy with idempotency keyed by event id (which correctly skipped nothing, because the earlier processing had written rows with a null user), and a manual repair of the 11,000 loyalty rows.
