Prevention: two deploys - remove the column from the entity and ship, then drop. Detect with pg_stat_statements before dropping (24.3).

An event replay runs old-schema events through new consumers. A consumer is rebuilt and replays from offset zero. The upcaster for v1 was deleted six months ago "because nobody produces v1 any more" - true, and irrelevant, because the topic still contains v1. Symptom: the rebuild fails immediately and loudly, which is the good case; the bad case is an upcaster that silently produces wrong defaults. Prevention: retain upcasters for retention plus the longest plausible replay, and keep a fixture of one real message per version in the test suite.

Cache poisoning with a new object shape. Covered in 24.6 and 24.8. The distinguishing symptom is that errors persist after the rollout completes, for exactly the TTL, and that the errors do not correlate with pod version. Prevention: versioned key namespaces.

A JWT with a restructured claim is rejected by pods that have not rolled yet. The auth service ships first and starts minting { authz: { roles } } instead of { roles }. Every pod still on the old version returns 401. Symptom: an authentication error rate that climbs as the auth rollout progresses and falls as the API rollout catches up, with a horrible middle where users are logged out at random.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant LB as LoadBalancer
    participant AUTH as AuthServiceV2
    participant P1 as ApiPodV1
    participant P2 as ApiPodV2
    U->>AUTH: POST /login
    AUTH-->>U: token with authz.roles
    U->>LB: GET /orders with token
    LB->>P2: routed to a v2 pod
    P2-->>U: 200 OK
    U->>LB: GET /orders/42 with same token
    LB->>P1: routed to a v1 pod
    P1-->>U: 401, claim roles missing

Prevention: write both claim shapes, read either, retire the old one only after the longest token lifetime has passed (24.6).

A gateway rewrites or pins versions. An API gateway is configured to route /orders to /v1/orders for clients that send no version header. A new deploy adds /v2/orders and someone updates the default to v2 "since v1 is deprecated". Every client that relied on the unversioned path silently changes contract without changing a line of code. The reverse also happens: a gateway strips an unknown header, so your carefully designed version negotiation never reaches the application. Symptom: behaviour that differs between direct calls to the service and calls through the gateway. Prevention: treat gateway routing rules as part of the contract, version them in the same repository, and have a smoke test that calls through the gateway, not around it.

A mobile client caches an old error format. The app persists the last error response to show offline, or a service worker caches a 4xx body. The error format changes from { error: "..." } to { code, message, details }. Old cached errors render as blank dialogs, or the app crashes reading error.error. Symptom: complaints from a small number of users that survive a reinstall-fixes-it support response. Prevention: never cache error bodies; version error envelopes like any other response; keep a stable code field forever.

A "compatible" change that broke a partner because they parsed by position. You add a column to a CSV export, or a field in the middle of a fixed-order JSON array, or an element to an XML sequence. Every consumer using named access is fine. The partner who wrote row[4] now reads the wrong value: their finance import books shipping cost as tax for two weeks before anyone notices. Symptom: no errors at all, and a reconciliation discrepancy discovered by an accountant. Prevention: append-only for positional formats, a documented column order treated as frozen, a header row that consumers are contractually required to use, and a version in the file name (orders_v2_2026-03-01.csv).

Two more worth knowing. A retry storm caused by a compatibility error: an old client gets a 500 from a new pod, retries immediately, hits another new pod, retries again; the error rate multiplies the load exactly when the system is least healthy. Compatibility failures are especially prone to this because they affect a deterministic subset of requests that will never succeed. A partial rollback: a deploy is rolled back for the API but not for the workers, or for one region but not another, leaving a mixed state that was never designed for and can last days.

Senior Checklist — Part 24

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can state the N-1 rule and apply it to a migration plan
  • I can list what version N and N+1 share during a rolling deploy, and check each one
  • I can classify any API change as breaking or not, and name who it breaks
  • I can explain why adding a response enum value breaks mobile clients, and design both sides for unknown values
  • I can version a cache key namespace and a job payload, and write an upcaster
  • I can explain BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL and the deployment order each implies
  • I can set up a CI check that fails a pull request on a breaking OpenAPI diff
  • I can write a consumer-driven contract test and explain what it does not catch
  • I can design a deprecation and sunset timeline with brownouts, and defend the dates
  • I can spot a semantic change that looks additive in a code review
  • I can change a JWT claim structure with no user-visible impact
  • I can explain why a rollback must be safe and what makes it unsafe

Part 24 — Key Takeaways

  • At every moment more than one version is alive: pods, apps, consumers, cached objects, queued jobs, tokens. Compatibility is not politeness, it is the condition for deploying at all.
  • Add, never remove or rename. New meaning gets a new name. total becoming gross is worse than a crash, because nothing crashes.
  • Be a tolerant reader everywhere: ignore unknown fields, handle unknown enum values, treat unknown event and job types as "not mine" rather than fatal.
  • Adding a value to a response enum is a breaking change for strict clients. Gate it by client version, downgrade to a safe older value, and send a label the client can render.
  • The mixed-version window covers everything both versions touch: schema, cache shapes, cache and lock keys, job and event payloads, JWT claims, feature flags, config. Walk the list for every change.
  • Version anything you serialize. A shape version in the cache key and a v in the job payload cost one field each and prevent a whole class of silent corruption.
  • Deploy consumers before producers, and make every rollback safe: the old code must still work against everything the new code has already written.
  • Enforce it in CI. Generate OpenAPI from the code, diff it, fail on the breaking categories, verify consumer contracts, and let the schema registry reject bad event changes before they ship.
  • Mobile and partner clients cannot be upgraded on your schedule. Ship the config endpoint, the unknown-enum fallback and server-driven layout in version 1.0, because you cannot add them later to clients already in the field.
  • Deprecation works when it has a date, per-consumer notification with their own usage numbers, and brownouts. Announcements alone move nobody.
  • Your analytics team is a consumer. Give them versioned views and take away access to the raw tables, and your schema is free again.
  • The checks catch shape, not meaning. Naming discipline and review are the only defence against a field that quietly starts meaning something else.

Part 25 — NoSQL Data Modelling

This book's default datastore is PostgreSQL, and that is a deliberate, defensible default: a relational database with transactions, constraints, joins and a mature ecosystem is the right choice for most backends most of the time. But "most" is not "all", and a senior engineer knows the honest cases where a different store fits better, and how to model data in it — because NoSQL databases are not "PostgreSQL without the annoying parts"; they are different tools with different data models that reward (and demand) a different way of thinking.

This Part covers the main NoSQL families and how to model for each: document databases (MongoDB), key-value and wide-column at scale (DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), time-series (TimescaleDB), and graph (Neo4j concepts). It covers polyglot persistence (using more than one store and keeping them consistent), migrating between NoSQL and PostgreSQL in both directions, and a decision matrix across all of them. The running examples stay in the book's domain: orders, products, trips, metrics.

The honest throughline, consistent with the whole book: do not reach for NoSQL by default or by hype. Reach for it when a specific access pattern or scale requirement makes the relational model a poor fit, understanding what you give up (usually joins, transactions across entities, and flexible ad-hoc queries) for what you gain (usually horizontal scale, a particular access pattern, or a data shape that fits naturally). This Part builds on the SQL-vs-NoSQL decision (Part 61) and Redis (Part 26), going wider and deeper.

25.1 When PostgreSQL is not the right store

25.1.1 The honest cases for NoSQL

Concept

PostgreSQL is an excellent general-purpose database, but there are access patterns and scale points where a specialized store genuinely fits better. The honest cases are specific: extreme write scale beyond what one primary can handle, an access pattern that is always "fetch this one item by key" at massive volume, data whose natural shape is a self-contained document or a time series or a graph of relationships, or a need for a particular consistency/availability tradeoff PostgreSQL does not offer out of the box.

Why does it exist?

Relational databases make tradeoffs: strong consistency, rich queries and joins, and a single primary for writes. Those tradeoffs are perfect for transactional business data and awkward for some workloads — a global write-heavy system that must stay available during a network partition, a stream of billions of time-stamped metrics, a social graph where the interesting queries are "friends of friends". NoSQL databases exist because no single set of tradeoffs is right for every workload; each NoSQL family picks a different point on the tradeoff space to serve a specific shape of problem well.

Mental model

PostgreSQL is a superb all-purpose vehicle — comfortable, capable, handles almost any trip. But if you need to carry thousands of tons across an ocean you want a cargo ship, and if you need to reach a mountain peak you want a helicopter. They are not "better cars"; they are different vehicles for journeys the car is wrong for. NoSQL stores are those specialized vehicles: pick one only when your journey is the kind it is built for, and accept that it cannot do the everyday trips the car does so easily.

How it works — the honest triggers

Consider a specialized store when:
  - Write scale exceeds one primary + sane sharding          -> wide-column (Cassandra), DynamoDB
  - Access is always "get item by key" at massive volume      -> key-value / DynamoDB
  - Data is naturally a self-contained document               -> document DB (MongoDB)
  - Data is high-volume time-stamped events                   -> time-series (TimescaleDB)
  - The query is the relationships ("friends of friends")     -> graph DB (Neo4j)
  - You need multi-region active-active writes                 -> DynamoDB global tables, Cassandra
  - You need sub-millisecond cache-like reads                  -> Redis (Part 26)

Stay with PostgreSQL when:
  - You need transactions across related entities
  - You need joins and flexible ad-hoc queries
  - Your scale fits one primary + read replicas + caching (most apps)
  - Data is relational (it usually is)

The key realization: most applications never cross these thresholds. A well-indexed PostgreSQL with read replicas (see Part 22 — Database Scaling) and a cache (see Part 26 — Caching and Redis) handles very large workloads. The honest cases for NoSQL are real but less common than the hype suggests, and they are driven by a specific requirement, not a general preference.

What you give up

Moving to NoSQL almost always means giving up some of: cross-entity transactions (most NoSQL stores offer limited or single-item transactions), joins (you denormalize or query multiple times instead), flexible ad-hoc queries (NoSQL is modeled around known access patterns, so a new query pattern can require remodeling or a new index), and strong consistency (many offer eventual consistency for availability and scale). You gain horizontal write scale, a natural fit for a particular data shape, or a specific availability guarantee. The tradeoff must be worth it for your specific requirement.

PostgreSQL example

Before reaching for a document store "because the data is flexible", check what PostgreSQL already gives you. A jsonb column stores a document in a binary form, a GIN index makes containment queries fast, and you keep transactions, constraints and joins on the relational columns around it.

-- Product catalog: stable columns are relational, the long tail of attributes is a document.
CREATE TABLE products (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  sku         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        text NOT NULL,
  price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0),
  attributes  jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,       -- {"material":"steel","sterilisable":true,...}
  CHECK (jsonb_typeof(attributes) = 'object')
);

-- jsonb_path_ops is smaller and faster than the default opclass for @> containment.
CREATE INDEX products_attributes_gin ON products USING gin (attributes jsonb_path_ops);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, name FROM products
 WHERE attributes @> '{"material":"steel","sterilisable":true}';
Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (actual time=0.61..2.94 rows=412 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (attributes @> '{"material": "steel", "sterilisable": true}'::jsonb)
  Heap Blocks: exact=380
  Buffers: shared hit=397
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on products_attributes_gin  (actual time=0.55..0.55 rows=412 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (attributes @> '{"material": "steel", "sterilisable": true}'::jsonb)
        Buffers: shared hit=17
Planning Time: 0.12 ms
Execution Time: 3.05 ms

On a 900,000-row catalog that is 3 ms. Heterogeneous attributes, schema flexibility and document-style queries are therefore not by themselves a reason to leave PostgreSQL. The reasons that hold up are about scale, availability topology and access shape, not about JSON.

Production scenario

A food-delivery company runs orders, payments, restaurants and menus on one PostgreSQL primary (32 vCPU, 256 GB RAM) with two read replicas: about 4,000 writes per second at peak and 25,000 reads per second, most reads served by Redis. That is a large business, and it is nowhere near PostgreSQL's limit. The same company does run two non-PostgreSQL stores, each for a stated reason: rider GPS pings (60,000 writes per second, kept for 7 days, read only by rider and time window) go to a wide-column store, and the session and rate-limit state lives in Redis. Everything with money or a foreign key stays relational. That split is what "honest NoSQL" looks like in practice: one or two specialized stores for one or two specific workloads, and the relational core untouched.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 on a Monday a team launched a new "marketplace" product built on a document store chosen in a kickoff meeting because "we might need to scale". By 14:00 the finance team reported that seller payouts did not match orders. The cause: placing an order updated the order document, the seller's balance document and the inventory document in three separate writes, without a transaction, because multi-document transactions had been "too slow in the prototype". A deploy at 11:15 restarted pods mid-request, and 212 orders had been written without the matching balance update. There was no foreign key, no constraint and no transaction to stop it. Reconciliation took two engineers three days. The traffic at launch was 30 orders per minute, a load a single small PostgreSQL instance handles without noticing. The store had been picked for a scale that did not exist, and it cost the one property the domain actually needed: atomic multi-entity writes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • "We will need to scale later": speculative scale is not a requirement; measure current and projected load (see Part 53 — Capacity Estimation and Back-of-the-Envelope Math) before trading away transactions.
  • One hot workload inside an otherwise relational system: move only that workload (for example GPS pings), not the whole domain.
  • Flexible attributes: jsonb plus GIN usually covers it; a separate document store adds a second source of truth.
  • Multi-region active-active writes: this is a genuine trigger; PostgreSQL has no built-in multi-primary conflict resolution, so a store designed for it (DynamoDB global tables, Cassandra) may be justified.
  • Team skills: a store nobody on call understands turns every incident into research; include operational familiarity in the decision.
  • Managed versus self-hosted: a managed NoSQL service removes much of the ops cost; a self-hosted Cassandra cluster adds a lot of it. The same store can be a good or bad choice depending on who runs it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior defaults to PostgreSQL and treats the decision to add or move to a NoSQL store as a significant architectural choice requiring a specific, measured justification (an ADR, Part 61), not a preference or a resume item. They ask: what exact requirement does PostgreSQL fail to meet — write scale past one primary, a specific access pattern at massive volume, a data shape that is genuinely non-relational? They are clear-eyed about what they give up (transactions, joins, query flexibility) and whether the application can tolerate it. They know that most applications never need NoSQL and that premature NoSQL adoption is a common, costly mistake — teams model orders in a document database, then discover they need a transaction across two documents, which the store makes painful. The anti-hype principle of the whole book applies: the simplest store that meets the requirement wins, and that is usually PostgreSQL.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing NoSQL by default or for a resume, without a specific requirement.
  • Underestimating how far PostgreSQL scales with replicas and caching.
  • Not accounting for what you give up (transactions, joins, query flexibility).
  • Picking a NoSQL store before understanding the access patterns it must serve.
  • Modeling inherently relational, transactional data in a document store and then fighting the lack of cross-entity transactions.

Interview questions

  1. When is PostgreSQL not the right store? When a specific requirement — extreme write scale past one primary, a key-only access pattern at massive volume, a naturally non-relational data shape (document, time series, graph), or multi-region active-active writes — exceeds what PostgreSQL plus replicas and caching provides.
  2. What do you typically give up when moving to NoSQL? Cross-entity transactions, joins, flexible ad-hoc queries, and often strong consistency; you gain horizontal scale, a natural data-shape fit, or a specific availability guarantee.
  3. Why is premature NoSQL adoption a common mistake? Most apps never cross the thresholds that justify it; teams lose transactions, joins and query flexibility they later need, for scale they do not have.
  4. How should the decision to adopt NoSQL be made? As a deliberate architectural decision (ADR) justified by a specific, measured requirement PostgreSQL cannot meet, with the tradeoffs explicitly accepted.
  5. "Our product attributes differ per category, so we need MongoDB." How do you respond?
    • Expected answer: Flexible attributes alone do not justify a new store; PostgreSQL jsonb with a GIN index (jsonb_path_ops for containment) serves heterogeneous attributes with transactions and joins intact. Ask what else drives the request: scale, access shape, team experience.
    • Why it matters: "schema flexibility" is the most common and weakest argument for a document store, and accepting it creates a second source of truth.
    • Follow-ups: When would you still choose a document store? How would you validate the shape of a jsonb column? What does a GIN index cost on writes?
  6. Name a workload you would move off PostgreSQL even in a mid-sized company. High-volume, short-lived, key-and-time-addressed telemetry (GPS pings, device metrics at tens of thousands of writes per second) or multi-region active-active writes; the rest of the domain stays relational.

Practical exercise

For three scenarios — a transactional order system at moderate scale, a global IoT system ingesting billions of sensor readings, and a social network whose key queries are relationship traversals — decide for each whether PostgreSQL or a specific NoSQL family fits, and justify with the specific requirement and the tradeoff accepted. Acceptance criteria: you keep the order system on PostgreSQL, choose appropriate specialized stores for the other two, and name what each gives up.

25.2 Document databases (MongoDB)

25.2.1 Document modelling, embedding vs referencing

Concept

A document database like MongoDB stores data as documents — JSON-like objects (BSON) — grouped into collections. Instead of rows across normalized tables joined at query time, a document can hold nested structure, so a related cluster of data lives in one document. The central modeling decision is embedding (nesting related data inside a document) versus referencing (storing a reference to another document, like a foreign key), and it is driven by how the data is accessed.

Why does it exist?

Some data is naturally a self-contained document that is read and written as a whole — a product with its variants and attributes, an event with its payload, a user profile with its settings. Storing and fetching that as one document avoids joins and matches the application's object shape directly. Document databases also have flexible schemas (documents in a collection need not be identical), which suits evolving or heterogeneous data. They exist for data whose natural unit is a document and whose access is document-at-a-time.

Mental model

A relational database is a set of filing cabinets where one entity's data is split across several drawers (tables) and you assemble it by pulling from each (joins). A document database is a set of folders where everything about one entity is in its own folder (document) — the order, its line items, its shipping details, all together — so you grab the whole folder at once. The modeling question is how much to put in each folder: embed related things in the folder (fast to read together, but the folder grows and duplicated data can drift), or keep separate folders with cross-references (no duplication, but you fetch several folders).

How it works — embedding vs referencing

The decision rests on access pattern, cardinality and update behavior:

Embed (nest inside the document) Reference (store an id to another document)
Read together always Yes — one read gets everything No — multiple reads or a lookup
Relationship cardinality One-to-few (an order's line items) One-to-many/large or many-to-many
Updated independently No (embedded data updates with the parent) Yes (referenced doc updates on its own)
Duplication Possible (same data embedded in many docs) None (single source)
Document size Grows with embedded data (size limits apply) Stays bounded 
Order document with EMBEDDED items (read the whole order at once):
{
  "_id": "ord_1001",
  "status": "paid",
  "totalCents": 4299,
  "items": [                          // embedded: fetched with the order, one read
    { "productId": "p1", "name": "Dental Mirror", "quantity": 2, "unitCents": 1000 },
    { "productId": "p2", "name": "Probe", "quantity": 1, "unitCents": 2299 }
  ],
  "shippingAddress": { "line1": "...", "city": "...", "postcode": "..." }  // embedded
}

Product REFERENCED from order items by productId (product updated independently):
{ "_id": "p1", "name": "Dental Mirror", "priceCents": 1000, "category": "tools" }

The rule of thumb: embed data that is read with its parent, has bounded size (one-to-few), and is owned by the parent (line items belong to the order). Reference data that is large, shared, or updated independently (the product catalog, which many orders reference and which changes on its own). Note the deliberate denormalization above: the order item embeds the product name and unitCents as they were at order time, which is correct (an order should record the price paid, not the current price) — a case where duplication is a feature, capturing a point-in-time snapshot.

NestJS example

NestJS integrates with MongoDB via Mongoose (@nestjs/mongoose).

// order.schema.ts -- Mongoose schema with an embedded sub-document
import { Prop, Schema, SchemaFactory } from '@nestjs/mongoose';

@Schema({ _id: false })
class OrderItem {
  @Prop({ required: true }) productId: string;
  @Prop({ required: true }) name: string;          // snapshot at order time (embed)
  @Prop({ required: true }) quantity: number;
  @Prop({ required: true }) unitCents: number;
}

@Schema({ timestamps: true })
export class Order {
  @Prop({ required: true, enum: ['pending', 'paid', 'cancelled'] })
  status: string;
  @Prop({ required: true }) totalCents: number;
  @Prop({ type: [OrderItem], default: [] }) items: OrderItem[];  // embedded array
}
export const OrderSchema = SchemaFactory.createForClass(Order);
// orders.service.ts -- one read returns the order with its embedded items
async findOne(id: string): Promise<Order> {
  const order = await this.orderModel.findById(id).lean();   // no join needed
  if (!order) throw new NotFoundException(`Order ${id} not found`);
  return order;
}

Indexes, transactions and the aggregation pipeline

  • Indexes: document databases index fields (including fields inside embedded documents and arrays) to make queries fast, the same principle as PostgreSQL indexes (Part 19) — a query on an unindexed field scans the collection.
  • Transactions: MongoDB supports multi-document transactions, but they are heavier and more limited than PostgreSQL's; the document model's intent is that a single document is the transactional unit (embedding related data means updating it together is a single-document, atomic operation). Needing frequent multi-document transactions is a sign the data might be relational and belong in PostgreSQL.
  • Aggregation pipeline: MongoDB's way to do analytics-style transformations (grouping, filtering, computing) as a pipeline of stages, analogous to a SQL GROUP BY/aggregate query, for reports and summaries.

Production scenario

An event-logging feature stores each event as a self-contained document with its heterogeneous payload — different event types have different fields, which the flexible schema handles naturally. Events are written once and read individually or queried by indexed fields (type, timestamp, user). Because each event is a complete document read and written as a whole, with no cross-entity transactions needed, a document database fits well and the flexible schema avoids the wide, sparse table a relational model would require for many event types. This is a genuine fit, not a default choice.

Failure scenario

A team modeled orders and products in MongoDB, embedding nothing and referencing heavily, then built a feature that had to atomically decrement inventory and create an order across two documents. MongoDB's multi-document transactions worked but were heavier than expected, and the access pattern (frequent cross-document transactions and ad-hoc joins between orders, products and customers) was exactly what the relational model does best. The data was relational; it had been put in a document store by default. The eventual migration to PostgreSQL (25.6) restored transactions and joins. The lesson: a document database fits document-shaped, document-at-a-time data; relational, transactional data belongs in a relational database.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unbounded embedded arrays: an order with a few items is fine; a document with an ever-growing embedded array hits the document size limit and gets slow; reference instead when the "many" is large.
  • Duplicated embedded data drifting: embedding shared data that changes (the current product price) means updates must touch every copy; embed only snapshots or data owned by the parent.
  • Needing cross-document transactions frequently: a sign the data is relational.
  • Ad-hoc queries the model was not designed for: document models are tuned to known access patterns; a new query may need a new index or a remodel.
  • No schema validation: flexible schema can let bad-shaped documents in; use schema validation to keep data consistent.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior models document data around access patterns: embed one-to-few, read-together, parent-owned data (and point-in-time snapshots) so it is fetched and updated as one atomic document, and reference large, shared, independently-updated data. They treat the single document as the transactional unit and read frequent multi-document transactions as a signal the data may be relational. They index the fields queries use (including inside embedded documents), use schema validation despite the flexible schema, and watch for unbounded embedded arrays. Above all they choose a document database for genuinely document-shaped data, not for relational data by default, because the lack of easy cross-entity transactions and joins punishes relational data put in the wrong store.

Common mistakes

  • Putting relational, transactional data in a document store by default, then fighting for transactions and joins.
  • Embedding large or shared, independently-updated data, causing size limits or drift.
  • Unbounded embedded arrays hitting document size limits.
  • No indexes on queried fields; no schema validation.
  • Modeling without first knowing the access patterns.

Interview questions

  1. Embed vs reference — how do you decide? Embed one-to-few, read-together, parent-owned data (and snapshots) so it is one atomic document; reference large, shared, or independently-updated data to avoid duplication and size limits.
  2. What is the transactional unit in a document database, and what does that imply? The single document; embedding related data makes updating it atomic, and frequent multi-document transactions suggest the data is relational and belongs in PostgreSQL.
  3. When is a document database a genuine fit? For document-shaped, document-at-a-time data with flexible or heterogeneous schema (events, profiles, self-contained entities), accessed as whole documents.
  4. Why is embedding a product's price in an order item sometimes correct? It snapshots the price paid at order time, which is the correct business record; this is deliberate, useful denormalization, not accidental duplication.

Practical exercise

Model an order in MongoDB with embedded line items (snapshotting product name and price at order time) and a referenced customer, implement it with Mongoose in NestJS, index the fields you query, and add schema validation. Then identify an operation that would require a multi-document transaction and reason about whether this data is better suited to MongoDB or PostgreSQL. Acceptance criteria: reads fetch the whole order in one query, items snapshot price correctly, and you can justify the embed/reference choices and the store choice by access pattern.

25.3 Key-value and wide-column at scale (DynamoDB)

25.3.1 Partition keys, single-table design and access patterns

Concept

DynamoDB is a managed key-value and wide-column database built for massive scale and predictable low-latency access by key. Its data model is organized around a partition key (which decides where data is stored and must be in every query) and an optional sort key (which orders items within a partition). You model DynamoDB access-pattern-first: you list the exact queries the application needs, then design the keys so each query is a direct key lookup. This is the opposite of relational modeling, where you model entities and then query flexibly.

Why does it exist?

Some systems need to serve enormous volumes of "get this item by key" or "get these items for this key" with single-digit-millisecond latency, at any scale, with no capacity planning headaches. DynamoDB exists for that: it scales horizontally and transparently by spreading data across partitions by the partition key, so throughput grows with the data. The price is rigidity — you must know your access patterns up front, and queries that do not fit the keys are slow or impossible — which is exactly the tradeoff that buys the scale.

Mental model

Imagine a vast warehouse where every item's shelf is decided by a hash of its key, spread across thousands of aisles (partitions) so no aisle is a bottleneck. To find something, you must know its key — that tells you the exact shelf instantly. Browsing ("find all red items") is not what the warehouse is built for; you would have to walk every aisle. DynamoDB is that warehouse: lightning-fast when you know the key, awkward or impossible for queries that do not use it. You design the keys so every query the business needs is a known-shelf lookup.

How it works — keys and single-table design

  • Partition key: hashes to a partition; determines where the item lives. Every read and write specifies it. Good partition keys spread load evenly (high cardinality); a poor one creates a hot partition (one partition taking disproportionate traffic), a classic DynamoDB problem.
  • Sort key: orders items within a partition, enabling range queries within one partition key ("all orders for this user, newest first", "all events for this device between two times").
  • Single-table design: a DynamoDB-specific practice of storing multiple entity types in one table, using composite key patterns, so that related items share a partition and can be fetched together in one query. It looks strange to a relational eye but is how you avoid joins (which DynamoDB does not do) by pre-arranging related data to be co-located.
Single-table design for a user's orders (one table, multiple entity types):

PK (partition key)      SK (sort key)            attributes
USER#usr_7              PROFILE                   name, email, plan
USER#usr_7              ORDER#2026-01-15#ord_1    status, totalCents
USER#usr_7              ORDER#2026-01-20#ord_2    status, totalCents

Query "get user usr_7's profile and recent orders" = one query:
  PK = "USER#usr_7" AND SK begins_with "ORDER#" (or "PROFILE")
All items for that user share the partition -> fetched together, no join.
  • Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs): because you can only query efficiently by the table's keys, a GSI defines an alternative partition/sort key for a different access pattern (for example, query orders by status instead of by user). You add a GSI for each additional access pattern that does not fit the main keys. GSIs cost extra storage and throughput, so you add them deliberately, one per real access pattern.
  • Capacity modes: on-demand (pay per request, scales automatically, simplest) or provisioned (you set capacity, cheaper at steady predictable load). You choose based on traffic predictability and cost.

Hot partitions

If one partition key gets disproportionate traffic — a single viral product, a celebrity user, a monotonically increasing timestamp key that always writes to the newest partition — that partition becomes a bottleneck even though the table as a whole has capacity. The defenses: choose a high-cardinality partition key that spreads load, add a suffix to spread a hot key across several partitions (write sharding), and avoid sequential keys for high-write workloads. The hot partition is DynamoDB's signature failure mode and must be designed against.

Production scenario

A ride-booking app stores trip history. The dominant access pattern is "get a user's recent trips", so the partition key is the user id and the sort key is the trip timestamp, making that query a single fast partition read ordered by time. A GSI on driver id serves "get a driver's trips". On-demand capacity handles the spiky weekend traffic without planning. Because the access patterns were known and the keys designed for them, every query the app needs is a direct, scalable key lookup, and the system handles enormous volume with predictable low latency — the case DynamoDB is built for.

Failure scenario

A team used DynamoDB with a partition key of status (a low-cardinality field with only a few values). Almost all active orders had status = "pending", so nearly all traffic hit one partition — a hot partition that throttled while the rest of the table sat idle. Worse, a new report needed "orders over $100 across all users", which no key supported, forcing a full table scan that was slow and expensive. The root cause was modeling without access-pattern-first thinking and choosing a low-cardinality partition key. The fixes: a high-cardinality partition key, a GSI for the new access pattern, and, since the workload actually needed flexible ad-hoc queries and joins, a serious reconsideration of whether DynamoDB was the right store at all. The lesson: DynamoDB rewards access-pattern-first design with high-cardinality keys and punishes relational, query-flexible thinking.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Item size: an item is capped at 400 KB including attribute names; an "append every event to the user item" design hits the cap and every write gets more expensive as the item grows (writes are billed per KB of the whole item).
  • Query page size: a single Query returns at most 1 MB of data; a client that ignores LastEvaluatedKey silently shows a truncated list.
  • GSIs are eventually consistent: a write is visible on the base table immediately but on a GSI usually within a second; a "create then list by status" flow can miss the new item.
  • GSI back-pressure: if a GSI is under-provisioned, writes to the base table are throttled too, which surprises teams who only watch the table.
  • Scans: a Scan reads (and bills) the whole table; a 200 GB table scan costs real money and minutes of time. Treat any production Scan as a design bug unless it is a deliberate batch job.
  • Retries and duplicates: the SDK retries throttled requests; an unconditional PutItem retried after a timeout is harmless, but an UpdateItem that increments a counter is not idempotent. Use condition expressions or idempotency tokens (ClientRequestToken on transactions).
  • Sequential keys: a partition key such as the current date sends a whole day's writes to one partition.

25.8 turns this section into running code: the SDK v3 commands, GSIs, transactions and the capacity math.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior models DynamoDB access-pattern-first: write down every query the application needs, then design partition and sort keys and GSIs so each is a direct key lookup, using single-table design to co-locate related items and avoid joins. They choose high-cardinality partition keys to spread load and design against hot partitions (write sharding for hot keys, no sequential keys for high writes). They add a GSI per genuine additional access pattern, mindful of its cost. They choose DynamoDB only when the access patterns are known, stable and key-based at a scale that justifies the rigidity — and they refuse it for workloads that need flexible ad-hoc queries, joins or frequent cross-entity transactions, because those are exactly what DynamoDB sacrifices for scale. The decision is "do our access patterns fit a key-based model at a scale that needs this?", not "is DynamoDB trendy?".

Common mistakes

  • Modeling entities first instead of access patterns first.
  • Low-cardinality or sequential partition keys causing hot partitions.
  • Expecting flexible ad-hoc queries or joins; DynamoDB does neither.
  • Not adding a GSI for an access pattern, forcing full table scans.
  • Choosing DynamoDB for a workload that needs relational flexibility.

Interview questions

  1. How do you model data for DynamoDB? Access-pattern-first: list every query the app needs, then design partition/sort keys and GSIs so each is a direct key lookup, using single-table design to co-locate related items.
  2. What is a hot partition and how do you avoid it? A partition taking disproportionate traffic (from a low-cardinality or sequential key); avoid with high-cardinality keys and write-sharding a hot key across partitions.
  3. What is a GSI and when do you add one? A Global Secondary Index with alternative keys for an access pattern the main keys do not serve; add one per genuine additional access pattern, mindful of its extra cost.
  4. When is DynamoDB the right choice and when is it wrong? Right for known, stable, key-based access patterns at massive scale needing predictable low latency; wrong for workloads needing flexible ad-hoc queries, joins, or frequent cross-entity transactions.

Practical exercise

Design a DynamoDB single-table model for a ride-booking trip history supporting these access patterns: get a user's recent trips, get a specific trip, and get a driver's trips. Specify the partition key, sort key, and any GSI, and explain how each access pattern maps to a key lookup and how you avoid hot partitions. Acceptance criteria: every listed access pattern is a direct key or GSI query (no scans), and the partition key is high-cardinality.

25.4 Wide-column (Cassandra)

25.4.1 Partition keys, clustering columns and the write path

Concept

Cassandra is a wide-column database built for massive write throughput and high availability across many nodes, with no single point of failure and tunable consistency. Data is organized by a partition key (which node stores it) and clustering columns (which order rows within a partition). Like DynamoDB, you model around queries, not entities, and denormalize heavily. Its distinctive strengths are enormous write scale and staying available during node or network failures, with consistency you tune per query.

Why does it exist?

Some workloads write constantly at a scale and availability requirement no single-primary database can meet — global time-series ingestion, activity feeds, messaging, sensor data — and must keep accepting writes even when some nodes or a whole data center are unreachable. Cassandra exists for that: a masterless, horizontally-scaled design where every node can accept writes, data is replicated across nodes and regions, and you tune how many replicas must acknowledge a read or write (consistency vs availability vs latency) per operation. It trades the relational model and strong-by-default consistency for write scale and partition-tolerant availability.

Mental model

Imagine a chain of identical post offices across the world, none of them the "head office" (masterless). You can drop a letter at any one (any node accepts writes), and each letter is copied to several offices (replication) so losing one loses nothing. When you ask for your mail, you can demand confirmation from just one office (fast, maybe slightly stale) or from a majority (slower, more certain) — that is tunable consistency. The design keeps running even if some offices are cut off (availability during partitions), at the cost of not being a single tidy ledger (no joins, eventual consistency unless you pay for more).

How it works — keys, write path and consistency

  • Partition key + clustering columns: the partition key distributes data across nodes; clustering columns order rows within a partition (for example, partition by device id, cluster by timestamp, for "readings for this device ordered by time"). You model each table to serve one query pattern, duplicating data across tables for different patterns.
  • The write path is what makes writes fast: a write goes to an in-memory structure (the memtable) and an append-only commit log, acknowledged quickly; memtables are periodically flushed to immutable disk files (SSTables); because SSTables are immutable, updates and deletes are written as new entries, and a background process (compaction) merges SSTables and removes superseded data. This append-first design gives Cassandra its very high write throughput.
  • Tunable consistency: per query, you choose how many replicas must respond (consistency level) — for example, a write acknowledged by one replica (fast, less durable) versus a quorum (slower, stronger). With reads and writes both at quorum you get strong consistency; at lower levels you trade for latency and availability. This per-query tuning is the practical expression of the CAP tradeoff (see Part 28 — Distributed Systems Fundamentals, 28.4 and 28.10 on quorum).
Time-series table in Cassandra, modeled for one query:
  "get readings for a device, newest first"

  PRIMARY KEY ((device_id), reading_time)   -- partition by device, cluster by time DESC
  -> all of one device's readings on one partition, ordered by time
  -> fast writes (append to memtable + commit log) and fast time-range reads per device

Practical example

Cassandra uses CQL, a SQL-like language. It looks familiar, which is a trap: the PRIMARY KEY is not just uniqueness, it is the physical layout, and the WHERE clause may only use the partition key and a prefix of the clustering columns.

-- CQL: sensor readings, partitioned by device AND day so no partition grows forever.
CREATE TABLE telemetry.readings_by_device (
  device_id   uuid,
  day         date,              -- time bucket: bounds the partition to one day of readings
  reading_at  timestamp,
  temperature double,
  humidity    double,
  PRIMARY KEY ((device_id, day), reading_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (reading_at DESC);

-- Allowed: full partition key, range on the clustering column.
SELECT reading_at, temperature FROM telemetry.readings_by_device
 WHERE device_id = 6f1c2a9e-1d4b-4e0a-9a51-3c7d0b2e8f10 AND day = '2026-11-05'
   AND reading_at > '2026-11-05 08:00:00' LIMIT 500;

-- Rejected without ALLOW FILTERING: no partition key, so every node would be scanned.
-- SELECT * FROM telemetry.readings_by_device WHERE temperature > 40;

A device sending one reading every 10 seconds produces 8,640 rows a day, about 400 KB per partition: comfortably small. Without the day bucket, the same device would accumulate 3 million rows a year in one partition, which slows reads, compaction and repair. 25.9 covers the write and read path, compaction and consistency in depth.

Production scenario

A logistics company ingests GPS pings from 120,000 vehicles every 5 seconds: 24,000 writes per second on average, 60,000 at peak. A 9-node Cassandra cluster across 3 availability zones, replication factor 3, writes at LOCAL_QUORUM with a p99 write latency of about 4 ms. Reads ("where was vehicle X between 10:00 and 10:30") hit one partition and return in under 10 ms. When one node was replaced for a disk failure, writes continued uninterrupted because two of three replicas still acknowledged every write. That is the workload Cassandra exists for: append-heavy, always written by key and time, read by key and time, and required to stay writable through node failures.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: read latency on the "recent alerts" table had jumped from 8 ms to 4 seconds, and some reads were failing with TombstoneOverwhelmingException. The team had modeled alerts as a queue: insert when raised, delete when acknowledged, read "the open alerts for this site". A delete in Cassandra writes a tombstone (a marker), which is only purged after gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default) and a compaction. A busy site had 180,000 tombstones in its partition, and every read scanned them all before finding the 40 live rows. The fix was a remodel: bucket alerts by site and hour, read only the last few buckets, and let old buckets expire by TTL instead of being deleted one by one. The lesson: Cassandra is excellent for append-mostly data and poor as a queue with heavy deletes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unbounded partitions: a partition key without a time bucket grows forever; keep partitions under roughly 100 MB and 100,000 rows.
  • Tombstones: deletes, TTL expiry and writing null all create tombstones; delete-heavy patterns degrade reads.
  • ALLOW FILTERING: makes a query run by scanning; acceptable in a one-off investigation, never in a request path.
  • Lightweight transactions (IF NOT EXISTS): use Paxos, cost about four round trips, and should be rare.
  • Clock skew: Cassandra resolves conflicting writes by timestamp (last write wins); a client with a fast clock silently wins every conflict.
  • Node down during writes: hinted handoff stores the missed writes briefly; a node down longer than the hint window needs a repair.
  • Secondary indexes: local to each node, so a query by a secondary index fans out to every node; model a second table instead.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reaches for Cassandra when the requirement is sustained massive write throughput and high availability across regions with tolerance for node and partition failures — write-heavy, append-mostly workloads like time series, feeds and messaging at scale. They model query-first, one table per access pattern, denormalizing freely, because joins do not exist and ad-hoc queries are not the point. They choose partition keys that spread writes and avoid unbounded partitions (a partition that grows forever becomes a problem). They tune consistency per operation to the business need, understanding they are trading on the CAP tradeoff explicitly. They know Cassandra's operational weight (running a multi-node cluster, compaction tuning) is real, so they adopt it only when the write-scale and availability requirements genuinely justify it over PostgreSQL plus partitioning, or over DynamoDB (which offers similar tradeoffs as a managed service).

Common mistakes

  • Using Cassandra for a workload that does not need its write scale or availability, taking on heavy operations for nothing.
  • Modeling by entity instead of query, then finding queries impossible without a remodel.
  • Partition keys that create hot or unbounded partitions.
  • Expecting strong consistency by default or ad-hoc queries/joins.
  • Ignoring compaction and operational tuning.

Interview questions

  1. What is Cassandra built for? Massive write throughput and high availability across many nodes/regions with tunable consistency and no single point of failure; write-heavy, append-mostly workloads like time series, feeds and messaging at scale.
  2. Explain Cassandra's write path. Writes go to an in-memory memtable and an append-only commit log (fast ack), are flushed to immutable SSTables, and background compaction merges SSTables and removes superseded data; the append-first design gives high write throughput.
  3. What is tunable consistency? Per query you choose how many replicas must respond, trading consistency against latency and availability (quorum reads+writes give strong consistency; lower levels favor availability/latency) — the CAP tradeoff made explicit.
  4. How do you model for Cassandra? Query-first, one table per access pattern, denormalized, with partition keys that spread writes and bounded partition sizes; no joins or ad-hoc queries.

Practical exercise

Design a Cassandra table for storing IoT sensor readings that must support "get a device's readings in a time range, newest first" at high write volume, specifying the partition key and clustering columns, explaining how the write path makes ingestion fast, and choosing a consistency level for writes with justification. Acceptance criteria: the query is a single-partition range read, writes spread across partitions, and partitions do not grow unbounded.

25.5 Time-series and graph databases

25.5.1 Time-series data (TimescaleDB)

Concept

Time-series data is a stream of time-stamped measurements — metrics, sensor readings, prices, events — where the time dimension is central and the volume is high. TimescaleDB is a PostgreSQL extension that optimizes PostgreSQL for this shape by automatically partitioning data by time (into "chunks") and adding time-series features, so you get time-series performance while staying in PostgreSQL with full SQL and joins.

Why does it exist?

Time-series workloads have a distinctive pattern: enormous insert volume (append-only), queries almost always filtered by time range, and a need to age out or down-sample old data. A plain table struggles — inserts slow as it grows, time-range queries scan too much, and deleting old data is expensive (see Part 22 — Database Scaling, 22.7 Partitioning). TimescaleDB exists to make PostgreSQL excel at this: time-based partitioning keeps inserts fast and time-range queries pruned to the relevant chunks, with built-in retention (drop old chunks instantly) and down-sampling (continuous aggregates). You get the time-series optimizations without leaving the relational world.

How it works

TimescaleDB turns a regular table into a hypertable partitioned by time behind the scenes; you write ordinary SQL INSERTs and SELECTs and it routes them to the right time chunks.

-- A hypertable: partitioned by time automatically.
CREATE TABLE metrics (
  time        timestamptz NOT NULL,
  device_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  temperature double precision,
  humidity    double precision
);
SELECT create_hypertable('metrics', 'time');          -- make it a hypertable

-- Time-range queries are pruned to the relevant chunks (fast).
SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS hour, avg(temperature)
  FROM metrics
 WHERE device_id = $1 AND time > now() - interval '7 days'
 GROUP BY hour ORDER BY hour;

-- Retention: drop chunks older than 90 days instantly (not a slow DELETE).
SELECT add_retention_policy('metrics', INTERVAL '90 days');

-- Down-sampling: a continuous aggregate pre-computes hourly rollups.
-- (keeps queries over long ranges cheap by reading aggregates, not raw rows)

The key wins: time-range queries read only the relevant chunks (not the whole table), old data is removed by dropping chunks (instant, versus a week-long DELETE of billions of rows, Part 52), and continuous aggregates pre-compute rollups so dashboards over long ranges are cheap. And because it is PostgreSQL, you keep SQL, joins to your relational data, and one database to operate — the same "stay in PostgreSQL" advantage as pgvector (Part 37).

PostgreSQL example — chunk exclusion, continuous aggregates and compression

The commented "down-sampling" line above is, in real TimescaleDB SQL, a materialized view with the timescaledb.continuous option plus a refresh policy. Here is the full lifecycle for device metrics: one-day chunks, an hourly rollup, compression after a week, and different retention for raw and rolled-up data.

-- One chunk per day suits ~50 million rows/day; the default is 7 days.
SELECT create_hypertable('metrics', 'time', chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '1 day');
CREATE INDEX metrics_device_time_idx ON metrics (device_id, time DESC);

-- Hourly rollup, maintained incrementally by a background job.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW metrics_hourly
WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS bucket,
       device_id,
       avg(temperature) AS avg_temp,
       max(temperature) AS max_temp,
       count(*)         AS samples
  FROM metrics
 GROUP BY bucket, device_id
WITH NO DATA;

SELECT add_continuous_aggregate_policy('metrics_hourly',
  start_offset      => INTERVAL '3 days',    -- re-aggregate late-arriving data up to 3 days back
  end_offset        => INTERVAL '1 hour',    -- leave the still-filling hour alone
  schedule_interval => INTERVAL '30 minutes');

-- Compress chunks older than 7 days: column-wise, grouped per device (often 10x-20x smaller).
ALTER TABLE metrics SET (
  timescaledb.compress,
  timescaledb.compress_segmentby = 'device_id',
  timescaledb.compress_orderby   = 'time DESC');
SELECT add_compression_policy('metrics', INTERVAL '7 days');

-- Raw data for 90 days (the policy added above), rollups for 2 years.
SELECT add_retention_policy('metrics_hourly', INTERVAL '2 years');

The plan for the 7-day query shows why time partitioning matters. Of 90 daily chunks, 83 are excluded before any data is read:

Custom Scan (ChunkAppend) on metrics  (actual time=0.06..38.7 rows=60480 loops=1)
  Order: metrics."time" DESC
  Chunks excluded during startup: 83
  ->  Index Scan using _hyper_1_211_chunk_metrics_device_time_idx on _hyper_1_211_chunk
        (actual time=0.05..4.9 rows=8640 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((device_id = $1) AND ("time" > (now() - '7 days'::interval)))
        Buffers: shared hit=212
  ->  ... 6 more chunk index scans ...
Planning Time: 1.4 ms
Execution Time: 41.3 ms

"Excluded during startup" (rather than at plan time) appears because now() is only known when the query starts; with a literal timestamp the excluded chunks would not appear in the plan at all. A one-year dashboard reads metrics_hourly instead: 8,760 rows per device instead of 3.1 million.

Production scenario

A dental-equipment maker collects telemetry from 40,000 sterilisers: one reading every 10 seconds, about 350 million rows a day at peak season, on one 16 vCPU TimescaleDB instance. Compression brings a day of raw data from 38 GB to 3.1 GB. Device dashboards (last 24 hours, raw) answer in 30-60 ms; fleet reports over a year read the hourly aggregate and answer in under a second. The retention job drops one day-sized chunk each night in about 200 ms. And because it is PostgreSQL, a support engineer joins telemetry to the customers and service_contracts tables in one query.

Failure scenario

At 07:30 on a Tuesday the fleet dashboard showed every device as "offline since 01:00". The continuous aggregate policy had end_offset => INTERVAL '1 minute' and a fleet of devices that buffered readings during a network outage and uploaded them three hours late. The aggregate had already materialized those hours as empty, and the policy's start_offset of 1 hour meant it never looked back far enough to fix them. Raw data was correct; the rollup was not. The fix was to widen start_offset to 3 days (sized from the measured maximum upload delay), run CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate('metrics_hourly', now() - INTERVAL '3 days', now()); once, and alert when late-arrival lag exceeds the window. The lesson: down-sampling is a cache, and a cache must be invalidated for late data.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Late or out-of-order data: size the aggregate refresh window to the real maximum delay.
  • Updates to compressed chunks: supported in recent versions but much slower; design for append-mostly.
  • Chunk interval too small: thousands of tiny chunks inflate planning time; too large and retention is coarse. Aim for a chunk (with indexes) to fit comfortably in memory.
  • Retention on raw data breaking aggregates: keep the aggregate's start_offset well inside the raw retention period, or a refresh would re-aggregate from missing data.
  • High-cardinality tags: a GROUP BY on millions of distinct series is expensive in any time-series store.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reaches for TimescaleDB (or PostgreSQL's native partitioning, Part 22 — Database Scaling) for time-series workloads, because it delivers time-series performance — fast appends, pruned time-range queries, instant retention via chunk drops, cheap rollups — while keeping SQL, joins and one database to operate. They set a retention policy from day one so old data is dropped as chunks rather than deleted row by row, and use continuous aggregates for long-range queries. They consider a dedicated time-series database only when scale or features exceed what TimescaleDB offers, applying the same "stay in PostgreSQL unless a specific requirement forces otherwise" discipline as the rest of this Part. They never store high-volume time-series in a plain unpartitioned table, which degrades as it grows.

Common mistakes

  • Storing high-volume time-series in a plain unpartitioned table, which slows as it grows.
  • Deleting old data with DELETE instead of dropping time chunks (retention policy).
  • No down-sampling, making long-range queries scan all raw rows.
  • Adding a separate time-series database when TimescaleDB in the existing PostgreSQL would do.

Interview questions

  1. What makes time-series data distinctive and why does it need special handling? High append volume, queries filtered by time range, and aging out old data; a plain table slows on inserts, scans too much on range queries, and deletes expensively.
  2. How does TimescaleDB optimize PostgreSQL for time-series? Automatic time-based partitioning (hypertables/chunks) prunes range queries and keeps inserts fast, retention drops old chunks instantly, and continuous aggregates pre-compute rollups — all while keeping SQL and joins.
  3. Why drop chunks instead of deleting rows for retention? Dropping a time chunk is instant metadata work; deleting billions of rows is slow and heavy.

Practical exercise

Create a TimescaleDB hypertable for device metrics, write a time-bucketed average query over the last 7 days, add a 90-day retention policy, and describe how a continuous aggregate would make a 1-year query cheap. Acceptance criteria: the time-range query is pruned to recent chunks, retention drops old chunks rather than deleting rows, and you can explain the down-sampling benefit.

25.5.2 Graph databases (Neo4j concepts)

Concept

A graph database like Neo4j stores data as nodes (entities) and edges (relationships) and is optimized for queries that traverse relationships — "friends of friends", "shortest path", "what is connected to this". When the relationships themselves are the thing you query, and especially when you traverse many hops, a graph database does in one efficient traversal what a relational database does with many expensive self-joins.

Why does it exist?

Relational databases model relationships with foreign keys and resolve them with joins, which is fine for one or two hops but degrades badly for deep traversals — "friends of friends of friends" is three self-joins, and "shortest path between two users" is awful in SQL. Graph databases store relationships as first-class, directly-traversable connections, so a multi-hop traversal follows pointers from node to node rather than computing joins. They exist for workloads where the query is fundamentally about relationships and connectivity: social networks, recommendations, fraud rings, dependency graphs, knowledge graphs.

Mental model

A relational database is a stack of lists (tables) where "who knows whom" is a separate list you cross-reference repeatedly to trace a chain of acquaintances. A graph database is an actual map of people with lines drawn between those who know each other; to find friends of friends you just follow the lines outward two steps. When the question is about the web of connections, having the web drawn directly (the graph) beats reconstructing it from lists each time (joins).

How it works

Nodes and relationships:
  (user:User {name:"Alice"}) -[:FRIEND]-> (user:User {name:"Bob"})
  (Bob) -[:FRIEND]-> (Carol)
  (Alice) -[:BOUGHT]-> (product:Product {name:"Dental Mirror"})

Query (Cypher-style): friends of Alice's friends she is not already friends with
  MATCH (a:User {name:"Alice"})-[:FRIEND]->()-[:FRIEND]->(fof)
  WHERE NOT (a)-[:FRIEND]->(fof) AND a <> fof
  RETURN fof

A traversal follows relationships directly, so a multi-hop query stays efficient as the hops increase, where the equivalent SQL would be an increasingly expensive pile of joins. Graph databases also do connectivity algorithms (shortest path, community detection) natively.

Practical example — Cypher versus a recursive CTE

The real Cypher query for "products bought by friends of friends, which I have not bought", parameterized and limited:

MATCH (me:User {id: $userId})-[:FRIEND]->(:User)-[:FRIEND]->(fof:User)
WHERE fof <> me AND NOT (me)-[:FRIEND]->(fof)
MATCH (fof)-[:BOUGHT]->(p:Product)
WHERE NOT (me)-[:BOUGHT]->(p)
RETURN p.id AS productId, p.name AS name, count(DISTINCT fof) AS buyers
ORDER BY buyers DESC
LIMIT 10;

// Degrees of separation, bounded to 6 hops:
MATCH path = shortestPath((a:User {id: $a})-[:FRIEND*..6]-(b:User {id: $b}))
RETURN length(path) AS hops;

The same in PostgreSQL. Two hops are an ordinary join and perfectly fast with an index on friendships (user_id, friend_id). Variable depth needs a recursive CTE:

-- Everyone within 3 hops of a user, with the shortest distance found.
WITH RECURSIVE reach(user_id, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT f.friend_id, 1, ARRAY[f.user_id, f.friend_id]
    FROM friendships f
   WHERE f.user_id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT f.friend_id, r.depth + 1, r.path || f.friend_id
    FROM reach r
    JOIN friendships f ON f.user_id = r.user_id
   WHERE r.depth < 3
     AND NOT f.friend_id = ANY (r.path)          -- avoid cycles
)
SELECT user_id, min(depth) AS distance
  FROM reach
 GROUP BY user_id;

The CTE is correct, but look at the fan-out: with 200 friends each, depth 1 is 200 rows, depth 2 is 40,000 and depth 3 is 8 million intermediate rows, each one an index lookup and a path array copy. On a 30-million-edge table this took 9 seconds in testing; the equivalent bounded traversal in a graph database followed adjacency pointers and returned in about 150 ms. At depth 2 both were under 20 ms. That is the honest boundary: depth 1-2 stays in PostgreSQL, deep or variable-depth traversal over large graphs is where a graph database earns its keep.

Production scenario

A payments company detects fraud rings: accounts that share devices, cards or addresses with known fraudulent accounts within 4 hops. The source of truth stays in PostgreSQL; account, device and card relationships are streamed into a graph database by CDC (25.6), a few seconds behind. A risk check at checkout runs a bounded traversal (*..4, capped at 5,000 visited nodes) in 20-60 ms and returns a risk score. Nothing is written to the graph by the application directly, so it can be rebuilt from PostgreSQL at any time.

Failure scenario

A recommendation endpoint ran an unbounded variable-length match, -[:FRIEND*]-, written during a hackathon against a 5,000-user test graph. In production a few "super-connector" accounts (a brand account with 2 million followers modeled as friends) made a single query explore most of the graph. At 19:05, during an evening peak, heap usage on the graph database hit its limit, garbage-collection pauses stalled every query, and the recommendations widget timed out site-wide. The fixes: always bound path length (*..3), cap results, exclude or down-weight super-nodes, and set a query timeout. Deep traversal is powerful precisely because it can touch a lot of the graph; bound it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Super-nodes (one node with millions of edges) dominate traversal cost; model them differently or exclude them.
  • Unbounded variable-length paths can explode; always set a maximum depth and a timeout.
  • Graph as a second source of truth: keep it derived and rebuildable from the relational store.
  • Cycles in SQL recursion: without a path check, a recursive CTE loops until depth limits stop it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reaches for a graph database only when relationship traversal is the core query pattern and the traversals are deep — social connections, recommendations through connections, fraud-ring detection, dependency analysis — where a relational model's self-joins become unworkable. For one- or two-hop relationships, PostgreSQL's joins are perfectly fine and simpler, so they do not add a graph database for ordinary foreign-key relationships. They weigh the operational cost of a specialized store (and often keeping it in sync with a relational source of truth, polyglot persistence, 25.6) against the query benefit. The test is "is the question fundamentally about the web of connections, traversed many hops?" — if not, PostgreSQL stays.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a graph database for ordinary one/two-hop relationships PostgreSQL joins handle fine.
  • Not recognizing a genuine deep-traversal workload and suffering slow self-join queries in SQL.
  • Ignoring the sync cost of keeping a graph store consistent with a relational source.

Interview questions

  1. When is a graph database the right tool? When the core queries traverse relationships deeply (friends of friends, shortest path, connectivity), where relational self-joins become unworkable; not for ordinary one/two-hop relationships.
  2. Why are deep traversals faster in a graph database than in SQL? Relationships are stored as directly traversable connections, so a multi-hop query follows pointers node to node, versus SQL computing an expensive join per hop.
  3. Should you use a graph database for foreign-key relationships? No — one/two-hop relationships are well served by PostgreSQL joins; reserve graph databases for genuinely deep, connectivity-centric queries.

Practical exercise

Model a small social graph (users with FRIEND relationships and BOUGHT relationships to products) and write the traversal for "friend-of-friend product recommendations". Then write the equivalent in SQL with self-joins and compare how each scales as the traversal deepens. Acceptance criteria: you can articulate at what traversal depth the graph approach clearly wins and why one/two-hop cases do not justify a graph database.

25.6 Polyglot persistence, migration and the decision matrix

25.6.1 Using multiple stores and choosing among them

Concept

Polyglot persistence is using more than one type of datastore in one system, each for what it does best — PostgreSQL for transactional data, Redis for caching, a search index for search, a time-series store for metrics. It is powerful but adds the cost of operating each store and, crucially, keeping them consistent with the source of truth. This section covers that, migrating between NoSQL and PostgreSQL in both directions, and the decision matrix across all the stores.

Why does it exist?

No single store is best at everything, so a system with diverse needs — transactions, search, caching, analytics, time-series — may genuinely benefit from specialized stores for each. Polyglot persistence exists to let each workload use the right tool. But it exists in tension with simplicity: every additional store is another system to run, secure, back up, monitor and keep in sync, so it is adopted deliberately, not casually.

How it works — keeping stores consistent

The hard part of polyglot persistence is that derived stores (a search index, a cache, a vector store, an analytics warehouse) must stay consistent with the source of truth. The reliable patterns are the ones from earlier in the book:

  • Outbox (see Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency, 29.10 The transactional outbox): a change to the source database writes an event in the same transaction, and a worker propagates it to the other store, so the propagation cannot be lost.
  • CDC (Change Data Capture, see Part 38 — Data Engineering for Backend Engineers, 38.2): the database's change log streams to the other stores.
  • Both make the derived stores eventually consistent with the source, which you must design the application to tolerate (the search index is a second behind, the cache may be briefly stale, Part 26).

The source of truth is one store (usually PostgreSQL for transactional data); the others are derived and kept in sync. Treating two stores as both authoritative for the same data is a recipe for divergence and is avoided.

PostgreSQL (source of truth)
    |  outbox / CDC (Part 29, Part 38)
    +--> search index   (Part 33)
    +--> vector store    (Part 37)  [pgvector avoids this by living in PG]
    +--> cache (Redis)   (Part 26)
    +--> analytics warehouse (Part 38)
Each derived store is eventually consistent; the app tolerates the lag.

How it works — migrating between NoSQL and PostgreSQL

Migrations go both ways, for real reasons:

  • NoSQL to PostgreSQL happens when a team discovers they need transactions, joins or query flexibility they gave up — the common "we modeled relational data in a document store by default" realization (25.2). The migration re-normalizes documents into relational tables, often via a dual-write or backfill-and-cutover (Part 81 on large migrations).
  • PostgreSQL to NoSQL happens when a specific workload genuinely outgrows the relational model — write scale past a single primary, or an access pattern that fits a key-value model at massive scale. The migration denormalizes into the target's access-pattern-first model.

Both are large migrations with the usual pitfalls (Part 81): they fail when underestimated, so they use incremental strategies, dual writes or CDC-based sync, backfills, and reconciliation to verify nothing was lost. The reasons must be specific; migrating stores is expensive and risky, so it is justified by a concrete requirement, not a preference.

The decision matrix

Store Best for Key strength Key tradeoff
PostgreSQL Transactional, relational data (the default) Transactions, joins, constraints, flexible queries Single primary for writes; scale past it needs work
MongoDB Document-shaped, document-at-a-time data Flexible schema, natural document fit Weaker cross-entity transactions; not for relational data
DynamoDB Known key-based access at massive scale Predictable low latency, transparent scale Rigid (access-pattern-first); no joins/ad-hoc queries
Cassandra Huge write volume, high availability across regions Write scale, availability, tunable consistency Query-first modeling, eventual consistency, ops weight
Redis Caching, ephemeral/low-latency state Sub-millisecond reads In-memory, not the source of truth (Part 26)
TimescaleDB High-volume time-series Time partitioning, retention, rollups, stays in PG Still one PostgreSQL (very large scale needs more)
Neo4j Deep relationship traversal Fast multi-hop traversal, graph algorithms Specialized; overkill for one/two-hop relationships 
Default: PostgreSQL. Move or add a store only for a specific, measured requirement:
  need a document-at-a-time flexible-schema fit      -> MongoDB
  need key-based access at massive scale              -> DynamoDB
  need huge write volume + multi-region availability  -> Cassandra
  need sub-ms cache                                   -> Redis
  need high-volume time-series                        -> TimescaleDB (stays in PG)
  need deep relationship traversal                    -> Neo4j

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior defaults to PostgreSQL and adds a second store only for a specific, measured requirement it cannot meet, treating each additional store as a permanent operational tax — another system to run, secure, back up, monitor and, hardest of all, keep in sync with the source of truth via outbox or CDC, with eventual consistency the application must tolerate. They keep one source of truth and make other stores derived, never dual-authoritative. They treat migrating between stores as a serious migration (Part 81) justified by a concrete need, done incrementally with sync and reconciliation. When choosing among stores they match the store to the specific access pattern and scale requirement using the matrix, and they resist polyglot sprawl, because every store added is complexity and cost forever, and the simplest architecture that meets the requirement wins.

Common mistakes

  • Polyglot sprawl: adding stores without a specific requirement, multiplying operational cost.
  • Treating two stores as both authoritative for the same data, causing divergence.
  • Not keeping derived stores in sync via outbox/CDC, so they drift from the source.
  • Not designing the application to tolerate the eventual consistency of derived stores.
  • Migrating stores without a concrete reason, or without incremental sync and reconciliation (Part 81).

Interview questions

  1. What is polyglot persistence and what is its main cost? Using multiple specialized datastores, each for what it does best; the main cost is operating each store and keeping derived stores consistent with the source of truth (outbox/CDC), with eventual consistency to tolerate.
  2. How do you keep a derived store (search index, cache, vector store) consistent with PostgreSQL? Propagate changes via the outbox pattern or CDC so the derived store is eventually consistent; keep one source of truth and the others derived.
  3. Why do teams migrate from NoSQL to PostgreSQL? They discover they need transactions, joins or query flexibility they gave up — commonly after modeling relational data in a document store by default.
  4. How do you choose among PostgreSQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, TimescaleDB and Neo4j? Default to PostgreSQL; move or add a store only for a specific requirement — document fit (MongoDB), key-based massive scale (DynamoDB), huge write volume and availability (Cassandra), time-series (TimescaleDB), deep traversal (Neo4j) — accepting each one's tradeoffs and operational cost.

Practical exercise

For a system with transactional orders, product search, a request cache, high-volume device metrics, and a recommendation feature based on connections, assign each need to a store from the matrix, identify which stores are derived and how you would keep them in sync with the source of truth, and write a short justification resisting any store you do not actually need. Acceptance criteria: PostgreSQL remains the transactional source of truth, derived stores have a stated sync mechanism (outbox/CDC) and eventual-consistency tolerance, and each specialized store is justified by a specific requirement.

25.7 MongoDB in practice: indexes, transactions, aggregation and validation

25.2 decided when a document model fits and how to choose embedding versus referencing. This section is the day-two view: wiring MongoDB into NestJS properly, indexing it so queries do not scan, using transactions only where they belong, running reports with the aggregation pipeline, and putting a schema back on a "schemaless" store.

25.7.1 Connecting and indexing

Concept

A MongoDB query without a matching index performs a collection scan (COLLSCAN): it reads every document, exactly like a sequential scan in PostgreSQL (see Part 19 — Database Indexing). Indexes in MongoDB are B-trees over one or more fields, including fields inside embedded documents and arrays. The design rules are close to PostgreSQL's, with one memorable heuristic for compound indexes: ESR — Equality, Sort, Range.

Why does it exist?

Document stores are usually adopted for read-heavy, document-at-a-time access. That only stays fast if every common query is an index lookup. Teams that treat "flexible schema" as "no design needed" meet the collection scan at the first busy day.

Mental model

Imagine a library sorted by author, then title, then year. Asking "books by Rao, newest first" is instant: walk to Rao, read backwards. Asking "books from 2019 by Rao" is fast too.
