Asking "all books from 2019" means walking the whole library, because year is the last sort key. ESR is the rule for ordering the shelf: things you ask for exactly first, then the order you want results in, then the ranges.

How it works

  1. The query planner looks for indexes whose prefix matches the query's equality fields.
  2. If the index order also matches the sort, results stream in order (no in-memory SORT stage, which is capped at 100 MB of memory).
  3. Range predicates ($gte, $lt, $in over many values) go last, because after a range the index order no longer helps sorting.
  4. explain('executionStats') reports the winning plan and how many keys and documents were examined.

NestJS example

// app.module.ts -- connection from config; majority write and read concerns in the URI
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { MongooseModule } from '@nestjs/mongoose';
import { Order, OrderSchema } from './orders/order.schema';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true }),
    MongooseModule.forRootAsync({
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
        // e.g. mongodb://.../shop?replicaSet=rs0&w=majority&readConcernLevel=majority
        uri: config.getOrThrow<string>('MONGO_URI'),
        maxPoolSize: 50,                  // per pod; 20 pods x 50 = 1,000 connections
        serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000,   // fail fast instead of hanging requests
        autoIndex: false,                 // build indexes in a migration, not on boot
      }),
    }),
    MongooseModule.forFeature([{ name: Order.name, schema: OrderSchema }]),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}
// order.schema.ts (continued from 62.2) -- indexes declared next to the schema
OrderSchema.index({ customerId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 });   // ESR: equality, equality, sort
OrderSchema.index(
  { createdAt: 1 },
  { partialFilterExpression: { status: 'pending' } },             // only pending orders are indexed
);
OrderSchema.index({ 'items.productId': 1 });                      // multikey index on an array field

// A separate collection for checkout sessions: documents expire automatically.
CheckoutSessionSchema.index({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 60 * 60 * 24 });
// orders.service.ts -- the query the index was designed for, plus an explain in a test
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectModel(Order.name) private readonly orders: Model<Order>) {}

  recentForCustomer(customerId: string, status: string) {
    return this.orders
      .find({ customerId, status })
      .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
      .limit(20)
      .lean();                                   // plain objects, no hydration cost
  }

  explainRecent(customerId: string, status: string) {
    return this.orders.find({ customerId, status }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20)
      .explain('executionStats');
  }
}

With autoIndex: false, indexes are created by a deploy step (await this.orders.syncIndexes() in a migration script, or createIndexes in mongosh), because building an index on a 50-million-document collection at application startup turns every deploy into a long index build.

Reading the explain output, and the PostgreSQL twin

The explain output reads much like EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Before the index:

winningPlan: { stage: "SORT", inputStage: { stage: "COLLSCAN" } }
executionStats: { nReturned: 20, executionTimeMillis: 1840,
                  totalKeysExamined: 0, totalDocsExamined: 4210993 }

After the ESR index:

winningPlan: { stage: "LIMIT", inputStage: { stage: "FETCH",
               inputStage: { stage: "IXSCAN", indexName: "customerId_1_status_1_createdAt_-1" } } }
executionStats: { nReturned: 20, executionTimeMillis: 1,
                  totalKeysExamined: 20, totalDocsExamined: 20 }

The healthy ratio is the same as in PostgreSQL: totalDocsExamined close to nReturned. The PostgreSQL twin is CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at DESC);, and the reasoning about column order is identical.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 on a sale day, writes to the products collection began failing with BSONObjectTooLarge. The product document embedded its reviews in an array, a reasonable choice when products had 20 reviews. The bestselling handpiece had 61,000 reviews and its document had reached the 16 MB document limit. Long before failing, it had been hurting: every product-page read fetched 14 MB, and every new review rewrote the whole document. p99 for the product page had crept from 40 ms to 900 ms over three months and nobody connected it to one document. The fix: move reviews to their own collection referenced by productId, indexed { productId: 1, createdAt: -1 }, and keep only a summary (reviewCount, avgRating, the 3 latest reviews) embedded. The rule from 25.2 applies with a number attached: embed one-to-few, and "few" must have a hard upper bound.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • 16 MB document limit and growing arrays: cap embedded arrays ($push with $slice) or move them out.
  • Multikey index limits: a compound index can include at most one array field.
  • Index build on a busy primary consumes I/O; build off-peak and watch replication lag.
  • $regex without an anchored prefix cannot use an index efficiently; use a text or search index.
  • Too many indexes: every index slows every write; 5-8 per collection is plenty for most.
  • Connection pools: maxPoolSize times pod count must stay under what the cluster tier allows.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior writes down the query shapes first, then designs compound indexes with ESR, verifies each with explain('executionStats'), and builds indexes in a deploy step rather than at boot. They put a hard number on every embedded array. They treat the document store with the same discipline as PostgreSQL: the store is schemaless, the application is not.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on autoIndex in production, so deploys trigger index builds.
  • Compound indexes in the wrong order (range before sort), producing an in-memory SORT stage.
  • Embedding unbounded arrays.
  • Never running explain, so a COLLSCAN ships unnoticed.

Interview questions

  1. What is the ESR rule?
    • Expected answer: In a compound index put Equality fields first, then the Sort fields, then Range fields, so the index serves both filtering and ordering.
    • Why it matters: a wrong order forces an in-memory sort or scans far more keys.
    • Follow-ups: Where does $in go? How do you confirm the plan? What does totalKeysExamined versus nReturned tell you?
  2. Why turn off autoIndex in production? Index builds at startup make deploys slow and unpredictable on large collections; indexes belong in a controlled migration.
  3. How would you find a missing index in MongoDB? Profiler or slow query log, then explain('executionStats') looking for COLLSCAN and a high docs-examined to returned ratio.

Practical exercise

Load 1 million orders into a local replica set, run recentForCustomer with explain('executionStats') before and after creating the ESR index, then try the index with the fields in a different order. Acceptance criteria: the final plan is IXSCAN with no SORT stage and totalDocsExamined equals nReturned.

25.7.2 Transactions, write concern and read concern

Concept

In MongoDB a single-document write is always atomic. Multi-document transactions (on replica sets and sharded clusters) give all-or-nothing writes across documents and collections. Write concern says how many replicas must acknowledge a write; read concern says how durable the data you read must be.

Why does it exist?

Even well-modeled document data sometimes needs to change two documents together: an order and an inventory counter. Without a transaction, a crash between the two writes leaves them inconsistent. And with replication, a write acknowledged only by the primary can be lost when that primary fails over before replicating, which is why durable systems use w: 'majority'.

Mental model

Imagine signing a contract. Single-document atomicity is one signature on one page: it is either signed or not. A multi-document transaction is a notary collecting signatures on several pages and stamping them all at once. Write concern majority is filing copies in most branch offices before saying "done", so losing one office loses nothing.

How it works

  1. The service starts a session and runs the callback inside withTransaction.
  2. Every operation passes { session }; MongoDB holds the changes in a snapshot.
  3. On commit, all changes become visible at once. A thrown error aborts them.
  4. withTransaction retries the whole callback on TransientTransactionError (for example a write conflict) and retries the commit on UnknownTransactionCommitResult, so the callback must be safe to re-run.
  5. Transactions are limited to 60 seconds by default (transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds) and hold their changes in memory; keep them small.

NestJS example

// place-order.service.ts -- order and stock decrement atomically
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectConnection, InjectModel } from '@nestjs/mongoose';
import { Connection, Model } from 'mongoose';

@Injectable()
export class PlaceOrderService {
  constructor(
    @InjectConnection() private readonly connection: Connection,
    @InjectModel(Order.name) private readonly orders: Model<Order>,
    @InjectModel(Stock.name) private readonly stock: Model<Stock>,
  ) {}

  async place(dto: PlaceOrderDto): Promise<string> {
    const session = await this.connection.startSession();
    try {
      let orderId = '';
      await session.withTransaction(async () => {          // may run more than once: no side effects inside
        for (const item of dto.items) {
          const res = await this.stock.updateOne(
            { sku: item.sku, available: { $gte: item.quantity } },   // guard: never go negative
            { $inc: { available: -item.quantity } },
            { session },
          );
          if (res.modifiedCount === 0) throw new ConflictException(`Out of stock: ${item.sku}`);
        }
        const [order] = await this.orders.create(
          [{ customerId: dto.customerId, status: 'pending', items: dto.items, idempotencyKey: dto.idempotencyKey }],
          { session },                                    // create() needs the array form with a session
        );
        orderId = String(order._id);
      }, { writeConcern: { w: 'majority' }, readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' } });
      return orderId;
    } finally {
      await session.endSession();
    }
  }
}

Two details matter. The emails, Kafka messages and HTTP calls happen after the transaction commits (or via an outbox collection written inside it), because the callback may run twice. And a unique index on idempotencyKey turns a client retry into a duplicate-key error you can map to "return the existing order" (see Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency).

Production scenario

A marketplace places about 150 orders per second at peak with this transaction. p50 is 12 ms and p99 35 ms with a 3-node replica set in one region and w: 'majority'. Write conflicts on a hot SKU during a flash sale cause about 2% of transactions to retry inside withTransaction, invisible to users. The same flow in PostgreSQL would be one BEGIN ... COMMIT with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (see Part 20 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control); the cost is comparable at this scale. The design question is not "can MongoDB do transactions" (it can) but whether most writes need them. If they do, the data is probably relational.

Failure scenario

After a primary failover at 03:05, customers complained that orders confirmed on screen had vanished. The service used the driver default w: 1 for years: the primary acknowledged 37 orders that had not reached a secondary, then crashed; the new primary never had them, and when the old primary rejoined its unreplicated writes were rolled back. The fix was w=majority in the connection string and readConcernLevel=majority for reads that drive decisions. Since MongoDB 5.0 the default write concern is majority, but older clusters and explicit w: 1 overrides are still common. Check what yours actually uses.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Standalone servers do not support transactions; local development needs a single-node replica set.
  • Long transactions abort at 60 seconds and pressure the cache; batch large jobs instead.
  • Reading from secondaries (readPreference: 'secondaryPreferred') returns stale data; never for read-your-own-write flows.
  • Side effects inside withTransaction run once per retry.
  • Sharded transactions across shards cost a two-phase commit; keep transactional data on one shard key where possible.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior makes the single document the default transactional unit, uses multi-document transactions for the few flows that need them, and treats "most writes need a transaction" as evidence for PostgreSQL. They insist on w: 'majority' for anything with money, keep side effects out of retried callbacks, and pair transactions with idempotency keys.

Common mistakes

  • Using w: 1 for business data.
  • Calling external services inside withTransaction.
  • Forgetting to pass { session } to one operation, which then runs outside the transaction.
  • Long-running transactions over thousands of documents.

Interview questions

  1. What happens to a write acknowledged with w: 1 when the primary fails before replicating? It is rolled back when the old primary rejoins; the client was told "success" for data that no longer exists. Use w: 'majority'.
  2. Why must a withTransaction callback be idempotent? The driver retries it on transient errors, so any side effect inside it can happen twice.
  3. When would you choose a single-document atomic update over a transaction? Whenever the data that must change together can live in one document: findOneAndUpdate with a guard is atomic, faster and cannot partially fail.

Practical exercise

Run a single-node replica set, implement place() above, and fire 200 concurrent orders for a SKU with 50 units. Acceptance criteria: exactly 50 orders succeed, stock ends at 0 (never negative), and a repeated request with the same idempotency key does not create a second order.

25.7.3 The aggregation pipeline and schema validation

Concept

The aggregation pipeline is MongoDB's query language for reports: a list of stages ($match, $group, $sort, $lookup, $project) that each transform the stream of documents, the way WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY and JOIN do in SQL. Schema validation ($jsonSchema) makes the server reject documents that do not match a declared shape.

Why does it exist?

Reports need grouping and totals, not single documents. And a flexible schema without any validation lets one buggy deploy write totalCents: "42.99" as a string into millions of documents. Validation at the database is the last line of defence, independent of any one service's code.

Mental model

Imagine an assembly line: the first station throws away parts you do not need ($match), the next sorts parts into bins ($group), the next orders the bins ($sort). Put the filtering station first, or every later station handles the whole warehouse.

How it works

  1. Put $match (and $sort on indexed fields) at the start, where it can use indexes.
  2. $unwind turns one document with an array into one document per array element.
  3. Each stage is limited to 100 MB of memory unless it may spill to disk (allowDiskUse, on by default since MongoDB 6.0).
  4. $lookup is a left outer join to another collection; it is fine for small enrichment, slow as a general join.

NestJS example

// sales-report.service.ts -- top 10 products by revenue in a period
async topProducts(from: Date, to: Date) {
  return this.orders.aggregate<{ productId: string; name: string; units: number; revenueCents: number }>([
    { $match: { status: 'paid', createdAt: { $gte: from, $lt: to } } },   // uses an index on status+createdAt
    { $unwind: '$items' },
    { $group: {
        _id: '$items.productId',
        units: { $sum: '$items.quantity' },
        revenueCents: { $sum: { $multiply: ['$items.quantity', '$items.unitCents'] } },
    } },
    { $sort: { revenueCents: -1 } },
    { $limit: 10 },
    { $lookup: { from: 'products', localField: '_id', foreignField: '_id', as: 'product' } }, // only 10 lookups
    { $unwind: '$product' },
    { $project: { _id: 0, productId: '$_id', name: '$product.name', units: 1, revenueCents: 1 } },
  ]);
}
[ { productId: "p_88", name: "LED Curing Light", units: 1840, revenueCents: 91908000 },
  { productId: "p_12", name: "Ultrasonic Scaler", units: 702,  revenueCents: 63180000 }, ... ]
// migrations/2026-11-05-orders-validator.ts -- enforce the shape at the server
export async function up(connection: Connection) {
  await connection.db!.command({
    collMod: 'orders',
    validator: { $jsonSchema: {
      bsonType: 'object',
      required: ['customerId', 'status', 'totalCents', 'items'],
      properties: {
        status: { enum: ['pending', 'paid', 'cancelled'] },
        totalCents: { bsonType: ['int', 'long'], minimum: 0 },
        items: { bsonType: 'array', maxItems: 200 },               // a hard bound on the embedded array
      },
    } },
    validationLevel: 'moderate',   // existing invalid docs can still be updated; new writes are checked
    validationAction: 'error',
  });
}

Production scenario

The monthly sales report over 9 million paid orders ran in 4.2 seconds once $match used a { status: 1, createdAt: 1 } index, against 41 seconds when $match came after an $unwind. Reports run against a hidden analytics secondary so they never compete with checkout. At larger scale the same report moves to a warehouse fed by CDC (see Part 38 — Data Engineering for Backend Engineers).

Failure scenario

A release changed the price serializer and wrote totalCents as a decimal string for 6 hours: 310,000 orders. Revenue dashboards built with $sum silently ignored strings and under-reported the day by 18%. Finance found it two days later. The validator above would have rejected the first bad write with a clear error in the deploy's smoke test. After the cleanup the team added validators to every collection that carries money.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • $match late in the pipeline cannot use indexes.
  • $lookup against large collections behaves like a nested loop; denormalize or precompute.
  • $sum over mixed types ignores non-numeric values silently.
  • validationLevel: 'strict' on an old collection can block updates to legacy documents; start with moderate.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior uses the pipeline for operational reports, moves heavy analytics to a warehouse, puts filtering first, and validates every collection that matters at the server, because "schemaless" only moves the schema into every reader's assumptions.

Common mistakes

  • Using $lookup as a general join and recreating a relational model badly.
  • No server-side validation on money fields.
  • Running heavy reports on the primary.

Interview questions

  1. How do you make an aggregation fast? Filter and sort early on indexed fields, reduce documents before $unwind and $lookup, project only needed fields, and run heavy reports on a secondary or warehouse.
  2. Why add $jsonSchema validation to a schemaless database? Application code changes and has bugs; the server-side validator protects every writer at once, especially for money and status fields.
  3. When does a growing number of $lookup stages suggest a different store? When most reports need joins across many collections, the data is relational and PostgreSQL would serve it with less effort.

Practical exercise

Write the top-products report, measure it with $match first and last, then add the validator and try to insert an order with totalCents: "10.00". Acceptance criteria: the first version is at least 5x faster on 1 million orders, and the invalid insert is rejected with a validation error.

25.8 DynamoDB in practice: single-table design, GSIs, transactions and capacity

25.3 explained the DynamoDB mindset. This section builds a real table for an e-commerce order domain with the AWS SDK v3 inside NestJS, then does the capacity arithmetic and shows the hot-partition failure up close. The trip-history worked example in 25.11 applies the same method to a second domain.

25.8.1 From access patterns to keys

Concept

In DynamoDB the access-pattern list is the schema. You write every read and write the application performs, then choose a partition key (PK), a sort key (SK) and a few Global Secondary Indexes so that each pattern is one GetItem or one Query. Two techniques make one table serve many patterns: GSI overloading (one generic GSI whose key attributes mean different things for different item types) and sparse GSIs (only items that carry the GSI key attribute appear in the index).

Why does it exist?

DynamoDB has no joins and no query planner. A pattern that does not map to a key becomes a Scan, which reads and bills the whole table. Designing keys from the access list is the only way to keep every request at single-digit milliseconds no matter how large the table grows.

Mental model

Imagine a warehouse where every box must be labelled before it goes on a shelf, and the label is the only way to find it again. You decide the labels by asking the pickers, before opening day, exactly which questions they will ask. A GSI is a second set of labels on the same boxes, printed for a different team of pickers.

How it works — the access-pattern table

# Access pattern Operation Key condition
1 Get customer profile GetItem PK = CUST#<id>, SK = PROFILE
2 Customer's orders, newest first, 20 per page Query PK = CUST#<id>, SK begins_with ORDER#, ScanIndexForward = false
3 Get one order with its items Query PK = ORDER#<id> (header META + ITEM#<sku> rows)
4 Pending orders older than 30 minutes (ops alert) Query on GSI1 GSI1PK = PENDING#<shard>, GSI1SK < <iso time>
5 Order by payment-provider id (webhooks) Query on GSI2 GSI2PK = PAY#<paymentId> 
PK              SK                                GSI1PK        GSI1SK                 GSI2PK
CUST#c_7        PROFILE                           -             -                      -
CUST#c_7        ORDER#2026-11-05T09:12:44Z#o_91   -             -                      -
ORDER#o_91      META                              PENDING#3     2026-11-05T09:12:44Z   PAY#pi_3Px
ORDER#o_91      ITEM#SKU-123                      -             -                      -
ORDER#o_91      ITEM#SKU-456                      -             -                      -

Three choices to notice. The order summary is duplicated under the customer partition (pattern 2) and the full order lives under its own partition (pattern 3): denormalization is the price of no joins. GSI1 is sparse: only pending order headers carry GSI1PK, and the attribute is removed when the order is paid, so the index stays tiny. And GSI1 is write-sharded (PENDING#0 to PENDING#9), because a single PENDING key would put every new order on one partition.

NestJS example

// dynamo.provider.ts -- one DocumentClient for the app
import { DynamoDBClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';

export const DYNAMO = Symbol('DYNAMO');
export const dynamoProvider = {
  provide: DYNAMO,
  useFactory: () =>
    DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(
      new DynamoDBClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION, maxAttempts: 4 }),   // SDK retries throttles with backoff
      { marshallOptions: { removeUndefinedValues: true } },
    ),
};
// orders.dynamo-repository.ts -- patterns 2 and 3, with real pagination
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, QueryCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersDynamoRepository {
  private readonly table = process.env.ORDERS_TABLE!;
  constructor(@Inject(DYNAMO) private readonly db: DynamoDBDocumentClient) {}

  async customerOrders(customerId: string, cursor?: string) {
    const out = await this.db.send(new QueryCommand({
      TableName: this.table,
      KeyConditionExpression: 'PK = :pk AND begins_with(SK, :prefix)',
      ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':pk': `CUST#${customerId}`, ':prefix': 'ORDER#' },
      ScanIndexForward: false,                       // newest first: SK starts with an ISO timestamp
      Limit: 20,
      ExclusiveStartKey: cursor ? JSON.parse(Buffer.from(cursor, 'base64url').toString()) : undefined,
    }));
    return {
      items: out.Items ?? [],
      nextCursor: out.LastEvaluatedKey             // absent on the last page
        ? Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(out.LastEvaluatedKey)).toString('base64url')
        : null,
    };
  }

  async orderWithItems(orderId: string) {
    const out = await this.db.send(new QueryCommand({
      TableName: this.table,
      KeyConditionExpression: 'PK = :pk',
      ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':pk': `ORDER#${orderId}` },
      ConsistentRead: true,                          // read-your-write after checkout (2x the read cost)
    }));
    const header = out.Items?.find((i) => i.SK === 'META');
    return header ? { ...header, items: out.Items!.filter((i) => i.SK.startsWith('ITEM#')) } : null;
  }
}

LastEvaluatedKey is the cursor. A Query returns at most 1 MB per call, so even without Limit a large partition comes back in pages, and code that ignores the cursor silently truncates. ConsistentRead works on the base table only; GSIs are always eventually consistent.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Filter expressions run after the read: a FilterExpression that discards 95% of a page still bills the full page.
  • Duplicated summaries drift: updating order status must update both the ORDER# header and the CUST# summary, in one transaction (25.8.2) or via Streams.
  • Opaque cursors: encode LastEvaluatedKey, never expose raw keys that leak other customers' ids.
  • A new access pattern: needs a new GSI (built online, with a backfill phase you must wait for) or a new item type written by a backfill job.

25.8.2 Transactions, capacity and hot partitions

Concept

TransactWriteItems writes up to 100 items atomically, with conditions. Capacity is measured in units: 1 WCU is one write per second of an item up to 1 KB; 1 RCU is one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent ones. Transactions cost double. Each physical partition serves at most about 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU and holds about 10 GB.

Why does it exist?

Single-item writes are atomic, but placing an order touches the order header, its items, the customer summary and stock. Without a transaction a crash leaves half an order. And without the capacity arithmetic you cannot predict either your bill or the point where one key starts to throttle.

Mental model

Imagine a toll road with many booths (partitions). The road's total capacity is enormous, but each booth processes at most 1,000 cars a second. If every car is labelled for booth 7, booth 7 jams while the others are empty. Adding lanes to the road (more table capacity) does not help; you must spread the labels.

How it works

  1. Conditions (ConditionExpression) make writes safe: attribute_not_exists(PK) for "create only", available >= :qty for stock.
  2. If any condition in a transaction fails, nothing is written and the error lists which item failed.
  3. ClientRequestToken makes a transaction idempotent for 10 minutes: a retried request with the same token does not apply twice.
  4. On-demand mode bills per request and absorbs spikes up to double the previous peak instantly; provisioned mode bills per hour for set capacity, with auto scaling that reacts in minutes, not seconds.
  5. Adaptive capacity moves throughput toward hot partitions and can isolate a hot item, but nothing lets one partition key exceed about 1,000 WCU.

NestJS example

// place-order.dynamo.ts -- order, items, customer summary and stock in one transaction
import { TransactWriteCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import { TransactionCanceledException } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';

async placeOrder(o: NewOrder, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const now = new Date().toISOString();
  try {
    await this.db.send(new TransactWriteCommand({
      ClientRequestToken: idempotencyKey,               // same key within 10 minutes = no double order
      TransactItems: [
        { Put: { TableName: this.table, ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(PK)',
            Item: { PK: `ORDER#${o.id}`, SK: 'META', status: 'pending', totalCents: o.totalCents,
                    GSI1PK: `PENDING#${shardOf(o.id, 10)}`, GSI1SK: now, GSI2PK: `PAY#${o.paymentId}` } } },
        { Put: { TableName: this.table,
            Item: { PK: `CUST#${o.customerId}`, SK: `ORDER#${now}#${o.id}`, status: 'pending', totalCents: o.totalCents } } },
        ...o.items.map((i) => ({ Put: { TableName: this.table,
            Item: { PK: `ORDER#${o.id}`, SK: `ITEM#${i.sku}`, quantity: i.quantity, unitCents: i.unitCents } } })),
        ...o.items.map((i) => ({ Update: { TableName: this.table,
            Key: { PK: `STOCK#${i.sku}`, SK: 'STOCK' },
            UpdateExpression: 'SET available = available - :q',
            ConditionExpression: 'available >= :q',      // never oversell
            ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':q': i.quantity } } })),
      ],
    }));
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof TransactionCanceledException) {
      // CancellationReasons is index-aligned with TransactItems: find which condition failed
      throw new ConflictException({ reasons: err.CancellationReasons?.map((r) => r.Code) });
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

shardOf is a stable hash of the order id modulo 10; the ops job that lists pending orders runs ten Query calls in parallel (PENDING#0 to PENDING#9) and merges them. That is the read-side cost of write sharding.

Production scenario — the capacity arithmetic

A peak of 800 orders per second, each with 3 items averaging 1.4 KB:

Writes per order: 1 header + 1 summary + 3 items + 3 stock updates = 8 items
Each item 1.4 KB -> rounds up to 2 WCU      (stock rows are tiny: 1 WCU)
Per order: (5 x 2) + (3 x 1) = 13 WCU, doubled for a transaction = 26 WCU
Peak: 800 x 26 = 20,800 WCU/s    Average (200 orders/s): 5,200 WCU/s

Monthly cost at the average (us-east-1 list prices at time of writing; check the pricing page):
  On-demand:   5,200 x 2.63M s = 13.7 billion write units x $0.625 per million  ~= $8,550
  Provisioned: sized for peak with auto scaling, mean ~9,000 WCU x 730 h x $0.00065 ~= $4,270

On-demand costs about twice as much here but needs no capacity planning. Teams commonly launch on on-demand, learn the traffic shape for a few months, then switch steady tables to provisioned with auto scaling. Notice also what drives the bill: item size rounded up per KB, and the transaction multiplier. Trimming the summary item from 1.4 KB to 0.9 KB saves 1 WCU per order on that item alone.

Failure scenario

At 00:00:05 on 11 November, the start of a flash sale, checkout error rates went from 0.1% to 34%. CloudWatch showed the table at 18% of its capacity, yet ProvisionedThroughputExceededException was firing constantly. The culprit was a "units sold" counter for the sale banner: every order did UpdateItem ... ADD sold :q on the single item PK = SALE#2026-11-11. All 2,600 orders per second hit one partition key, far beyond its ~1,000 WCU ceiling, and because the counter update was inside the checkout transaction, the whole transaction failed. The SDK's retries tripled the load on that key. Mitigation at 00:09: remove the counter from the transaction (the banner could be a few seconds stale). Permanent fix: 20 sharded counter items (SALE#2026-11-11#0..19) updated asynchronously from DynamoDB Streams and summed on read with one BatchGetCommand. Lesson: table-level capacity tells you nothing about a single key. Look at the CloudWatch Contributor Insights "most throttled keys" report, and never put a global counter on the write path.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GSI throttling back-pressures the base table: an under-provisioned GSI throttles writes to the table itself.
  • Transactions conflict with concurrent writes to the same item and fail with TransactionConflict; retry with jitter.
  • Limits: 100 items and 4 MB per transaction, 400 KB per item, 25 items per BatchWriteItem, 100 keys per BatchGetItem; batch calls return UnprocessedItems / UnprocessedKeys that you must retry.
  • TTL deletes are not immediate (typically within a few days of expiry); filter expired items on read.
  • Streams keep records for 24 hours; a consumer down longer than that loses changes.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior does the capacity arithmetic before launch, per key and not just per table. They keep transactions for the flows that truly need atomicity, use conditions and ClientRequestToken for idempotency, move counters and aggregates off the hot path to Streams consumers, and watch throttling per key. They pick on-demand to learn and provisioned to save, and they write down the access patterns so the next engineer knows which ones the table does not support.

Common mistakes

  • Treating table capacity as the limit and ignoring the per-key ceiling.
  • Global counters or "latest" items updated by every request.
  • Ignoring UnprocessedItems from batch writes.
  • Large items written often: cost scales with whole-item size on every update.

Interview questions

  1. Your table uses 18% of its capacity but you see throttling. Why?
    • Expected answer: A hot partition key: one key is taking more than a partition can serve (~1,000 WCU / 3,000 RCU). Find it with Contributor Insights, then shard the key, cache or move the write off the hot path.
    • Why it matters: it is the signature DynamoDB incident, and adding capacity does not fix it.
    • Follow-ups: How do you read a write-sharded key? What does adaptive capacity do and not do? Can a GSI cause it?
  2. How many WCU does a transactional write of a 2.5 KB item cost? 3 WCU for the size, doubled for the transaction: 6 WCU.
  3. How do you make TransactWriteItems safe to retry? Pass a ClientRequestToken (idempotent for 10 minutes) and use conditions such as attribute_not_exists(PK) so a duplicate cannot apply twice.
  4. What is a sparse GSI and why is it useful? An index on an attribute only some items have; only those items appear, so "pending orders" stays a small, cheap index.

Practical exercise

Create the table and GSIs with DynamoDB Local, implement patterns 1-5 and placeOrder, then load-test a global counter and the sharded version. Acceptance criteria: no pattern uses Scan, a duplicate placeOrder with the same token creates one order, stock never goes negative, and the sharded counter sustains a write rate the single counter cannot.

25.9 Cassandra in practice: write path, read path, compaction and consistency

Concept

25.4 introduced Cassandra's model and its tombstone trap. Running it well means understanding three mechanisms: how a write becomes durable, how a read finds data across many immutable files, and how replication and consistency levels decide what "acknowledged" means.

How it works — write and read paths

flowchart LR
  W["Write"] --> CL["Commit log append"]
  W --> MT["Memtable in memory"]
  MT -->|"flush when full"| SS["Immutable SSTable"]
  SS -->|"background"| CP["Compaction merges SSTables"]
  R["Read"] --> MT
  R --> BF["Bloom filter per SSTable"]
  BF -->|"maybe present"| PI["Partition index"]
  PI --> DATA["SSTable data"]
  DATA --> MERGE["Merge by timestamp"]
  MT --> MERGE
  1. A write is appended to the commit log (sequential, fast) and applied to the memtable; that is all a write costs, which is why Cassandra writes are cheap.
  2. Full memtables flush to immutable SSTables.
  3. A read checks the memtable, then each SSTable's Bloom filter (a compact structure that says "definitely not here" or "maybe here"), then the partition index, then the data, and merges versions by write timestamp.
  4. The more SSTables a partition is spread over, the slower the read; compaction merges them and drops overwritten data and expired tombstones.
Compaction strategy How it works Use when
SizeTiered (STCS, default) Merges SSTables of similar size Write-heavy, few reads, mixed data
Leveled (LCS) Keeps data in levels with few overlaps Read-heavy, updates to the same rows
TimeWindow (TWCS) One SSTable per time window, dropped whole when expired Time-series with TTL, append-only

Consistency: with replication factor RF per data center, a write at LOCAL_QUORUM waits for floor(RF/2) + 1 local replicas. If read replicas R plus write replicas W exceed RF (2 + 2 > 3), every read overlaps the latest write: strong consistency within the data center, while still tolerating one node down.

NestJS example

-- CQL: keyspace replicated 3x in each of two data centers; TWCS for TTL'd telemetry
CREATE KEYSPACE telemetry
  WITH replication = {'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy', 'eu_west': 3, 'ap_south': 3};

ALTER TABLE telemetry.readings_by_device
  WITH compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
                     'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS', 'compaction_window_size': 1}
   AND default_time_to_live = 2592000;   -- 30 days; whole SSTables expire together under TWCS
// cassandra.provider.ts + readings.repository.ts -- prepared statements, explicit consistency
import { Injectable, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Client, types } from 'cassandra-driver';

@Injectable()
export class ReadingsRepository implements OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly client = new Client({
    contactPoints: process.env.CASSANDRA_HOSTS!.split(','),
    localDataCenter: 'eu_west',                       // route to local replicas only
    keyspace: 'telemetry',
  });

  async insert(r: { deviceId: string; at: Date; temperature: number }) {
    const day = r.at.toISOString().slice(0, 10);       // the time bucket in the partition key
    await this.client.execute(
      'INSERT INTO readings_by_device (device_id, day, reading_at, temperature) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)',
      [r.deviceId, day, r.at, r.temperature],
      { prepare: true, consistency: types.consistencies.localQuorum },
    );
  }

  async lastHour(deviceId: string) {
    const since = new Date(Date.now() - 3_600_000);
    const res = await this.client.execute(
      'SELECT reading_at, temperature FROM readings_by_device WHERE device_id = ? AND day = ? AND reading_at > ?',
      [deviceId, since.toISOString().slice(0, 10), since],   // an hour spanning midnight needs two buckets
      { prepare: true, consistency: types.consistencies.localQuorum },
    );
    return res.rows;
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown() { await this.client.shutdown(); }
}

Production scenario

The 9-node GPS cluster from 25.4 runs TWCS with daily windows and a 30-day TTL: each day's SSTables expire as whole files, so compaction does almost no work on old data and disk stays flat at about 1.8 TB per node. Monitoring watches pending compactions, SSTables per read (p99 under 4), dropped mutations and tombstones scanned per read.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Repairs: replicas drift after node outages; run incremental repair within gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default), or deleted data can reappear.
  • Mixing TTLs or updating old rows under TWCS keeps old windows alive.
  • QUORUM across regions adds 80-150 ms per request; prefer LOCAL_QUORUM.
  • Batches across many partitions are not a performance feature; they load the coordinator.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior picks the compaction strategy from the data's shape, bounds partitions with time buckets, uses LOCAL_QUORUM with RF 3 as the default, and treats repair, compaction and tombstones as ongoing operational work, budgeted before adoption. If no one can own that work, a managed alternative (DynamoDB, or a managed Cassandra service) is the honest choice.

Interview questions

  1. Why are Cassandra writes cheap and reads sometimes expensive? A write is a commit-log append plus a memtable insert; a read may merge many SSTables, which Bloom filters and compaction keep in check.
  2. With RF 3, which consistency levels give read-your-writes in one data center? LOCAL_QUORUM for both reads and writes (2 + 2 > 3), or ONE writes with ALL reads (fragile).
  3. Which compaction strategy for TTL'd time-series, and why? TWCS: data of one time window lives together and expires as whole SSTables, avoiding tombstone-heavy merges.

Practical exercise

Run a 3-node cluster locally, create the keyspace and table, write 1 million readings with the repository, stop one node and keep writing at LOCAL_QUORUM. Acceptance criteria: writes continue with one node down, reads return the latest data, and nodetool tablestats shows SSTables per read staying low after compaction.

25.10 Polyglot persistence and store migrations in practice

Concept

25.6 set the rule: one source of truth, every other store derived and eventually consistent. In practice that means three pieces of code you must own: a relay that propagates changes idempotently, a reconciliation job that proves the stores agree, and a migration playbook for the day you move a workload between stores.

How it works — an idempotent outbox relay

The order service writes the order and an outbox row in one PostgreSQL transaction (see Part 29 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency, 29.10). A relay reads the outbox and writes a read model into DynamoDB. Because the relay can crash and resend, and events can arrive out of order, every write carries the source row's version and is conditional on being newer.

// outbox-relay.service.ts -- PostgreSQL outbox -> DynamoDB read model, safe to replay
@Injectable()
export class OutboxRelay {
  constructor(
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    @Inject(DYNAMO) private readonly db: DynamoDBDocumentClient,
  ) {}

  @Interval(500)
  async drain() {
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
      const rows: OutboxRow[] = await em.query(
        `SELECT id, aggregate_id, version, payload FROM outbox
          WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 100
          FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`,                       // several relay pods never take the same rows
      );
      for (const r of rows) {
        try {
          await this.db.send(new PutCommand({
            TableName: 'order_read_model',
            Item: { PK: `ORDER#${r.aggregate_id}`, SK: 'META', version: r.version, ...r.payload },
            ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(PK) OR version < :v',   // older or duplicate events lose
            ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':v': r.version },
          }));
        } catch (e) {
          if (!(e instanceof ConditionalCheckFailedException)) throw e;          // stale event: ignore, still mark done
        }
        await em.query('UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = $1', [r.id]);
      }
    });
  }
}

The same shape works for MongoDB (updateOne({ _id, version: { $lt: v } }, { $set: ... }, { upsert: true }), with a duplicate-key error on upsert meaning "a newer version exists") and for OpenSearch (version_type: 'external' with the source version). At larger scale, CDC from the PostgreSQL WAL replaces the polling relay (see Part 38 — Data Engineering for Backend Engineers).

A nightly reconciliation job samples or scans ids updated in the last day from PostgreSQL, fetches the same ids from the derived store with BatchGetCommand, compares version, and re-enqueues mismatches. Without it, a bug in the relay is discovered by customers.

How it works — the operational cost of each extra store

Store added Typical monthly infra (small production) Ongoing people cost New failure modes
Redis (managed) $200-800 Low Stale cache, eviction, failover blips
OpenSearch (managed, 3 nodes) $1,000-3,000 Medium: mappings, reindexing, shard sizing Index lag, mapping explosions
MongoDB Atlas (M40-class replica set) $1,500-3,000 Medium Schema drift, index builds, failover
DynamoDB (on-demand) Pay per request; $100s to $10,000s Low ops, high design effort Hot keys, GSI lag, missing access patterns
Cassandra (self-hosted, 6-9 nodes) $4,000-10,000 High: repair, compaction, upgrades Tombstones, repair debt, node replacement

The infrastructure line is the small part. Each store also needs backups and restore drills (see Part 49 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery), access control, monitoring dashboards, a runbook and on-call knowledge. A useful rule: a new store must save more than one engineer's time per year, or it is a cost, not an optimisation.

How it works — migrating between stores

flowchart LR
  P1["1 Dual write or CDC to new store"] --> P2["2 Backfill history"]
  P2 --> P3["3 Reconcile counts and versions"]
  P3 --> P4["4 Shadow reads compare results"]
  P4 --> P5["5 Cut reads over behind a flag"]
  P5 --> P6["6 Cut writes over"]
  P6 --> P7["7 Keep old store as fallback, then retire"]
  1. Start propagation first, then backfill, so nothing written during the backfill is missed. Prefer CDC or an outbox over application dual writes, which can partially fail (see Part 29).
  2. Backfill with idempotent, versioned writes so the backfill and live changes can overlap safely.
  3. Reconcile counts per day and versions per id.
  4. Shadow reads: serve from the old store, query the new one too, log differences.
  5. Cut reads, then writes, behind flags that can flip back in seconds (see Part 81 — Large-Scale Migrations and Legacy Modernization).
  6. Keep the old store warm for a rollback window before retiring it.

Failure scenario

A team moved order history from MongoDB to PostgreSQL. They started the backfill on Monday and turned on dual writes on Wednesday, intending to "catch up the gap later". The gap job ran with a timezone bug and skipped 6 hours of updates. Reconciliation was "count rows per day", which matched, because the orders existed; their statuses did not. After the read cutover, 4,100 customers saw paid orders as pending, and 300 paid twice. The rollback flag worked in 2 minutes, but the cleanup took a week. The fixes they adopted: propagation before backfill, versions in every row, reconciliation that compares versions and not just counts, and a day of shadow reads before any cutover.

Interview questions

  1. How do you keep a derived store correct when events can be duplicated or reordered? Carry the source version and make every write conditional on being newer; add a reconciliation job that compares versions.
  2. Why start propagation before the backfill when migrating? So changes made during the backfill are captured; versioned writes let backfill and live changes overlap without regressions.
  3. What does adding a store cost beyond the bill? Backups and restore drills, security, monitoring, runbooks, on-call skills, and a new class of consistency bugs.

Practical exercise

Implement the relay against DynamoDB Local, then replay the same outbox rows twice and in reverse order. Acceptance criteria: the read model ends with the newest version of every order, and a reconciliation script reports zero mismatches.

25.11 Worked example: ride-booking trip history in DynamoDB versus PostgreSQL

We model the same feature twice, honestly, and decide.

25.11.1 Requirements and access patterns

  • 2 million trips per day, peaking at 150 trip completions per second on Friday evenings.
  • Each trip is written about 4 times (requested, accepted, started, completed) and is about 2 KB.
  • Retention: 3 years online, about 2.2 billion trips, about 4.4 TB of trip data.
  • Rider app opens history often: 800 history reads per second on average, 3,000 at peak.
# Access pattern Volume Consistency need
A1 Rider's trips, newest first, 20 per page Very high A trip may appear a second late
A2 Trip by id (receipt, support) High Read-your-write after completion
A3 Driver's trips for one day (earnings) Medium Eventual is fine
A4 Rider's single active trip; at most one at a time High Strong: must prevent two active trips
A5 (later) Finance: fares by city per day Nightly batch Eventual is fine

25.11.2 The DynamoDB design

Item PK SK GSI1PK / GSI1SK GSI2PK / GSI2SK
Trip TRIP#<id> TRIP RIDER#<riderId> / <requestedAt>#<id> DRIVER#<driverId> / <requestedAt>
Active-trip lock RIDER#<riderId> ACTIVE - -
  • A2 is a GetItem on the base table with ConsistentRead: true.
  • A1 is a Query on GSI1, newest first; GSI1 projects only summary attributes (INCLUDE: pickup and drop labels, fare, status), so each history item in the index is about 0.4 KB and a 20-item page costs 2 read units.
  • A3 is a Query on GSI2 with GSI2SK BETWEEN :dayStart AND :dayEnd.
  • A4 is enforced by a conditional write in a transaction:
// request-trip.ts -- create a trip and claim the rider's single active slot atomically
await this.db.send(new TransactWriteCommand({
  ClientRequestToken: dto.idempotencyKey,
  TransactItems: [
    { Put: { TableName: 'trips',
        Item: { PK: `RIDER#${dto.riderId}`, SK: 'ACTIVE', tripId },
        ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(PK)' } },          // fails if a trip is already active
    { Put: { TableName: 'trips',
        Item: { PK: `TRIP#${tripId}`, SK: 'TRIP', status: 'requested', riderId: dto.riderId,
                cityCode: dto.cityCode, requestedAt: now,
                GSI1PK: `RIDER#${dto.riderId}`, GSI1SK: `${now}#${tripId}` } } },
  ],
}));
// On completion: Update the trip (status, fare, GSI2 keys) and Delete the ACTIVE item in one transaction.

Hot partitions: riders and drivers are high-cardinality keys and no single rider writes more than a few times per minute. GSI eventual consistency is acceptable for A1 and A3 by the requirements table.

25.11.3 The PostgreSQL design

CREATE TABLE trips (
  id            uuid        NOT NULL,
  rider_id      uuid        NOT NULL,
  driver_id     uuid,
  city_code     text        NOT NULL,
  status        text        NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('requested','accepted','in_progress','completed','cancelled')),
  requested_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  completed_at  timestamptz,
  fare_cents    integer     CHECK (fare_cents >= 0),
  currency      char(3)     NOT NULL,
  route         jsonb,                                    -- pickup/drop labels and coordinates
  PRIMARY KEY (id, requested_at)                          -- must include the partition key
) PARTITION BY RANGE (requested_at);

CREATE TABLE trips_2026_11 PARTITION OF trips
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-11-01') TO ('2026-12-01');        -- created ahead by a scheduled job

CREATE INDEX trips_rider_history ON trips (rider_id, requested_at DESC, id DESC);   -- A1 keyset
CREATE INDEX trips_driver_day    ON trips (driver_id, requested_at);               -- A3

-- A4: a unique index on a partitioned table must include requested_at, which would not
-- enforce "one active trip per rider". So the invariant lives in a small unpartitioned table.
CREATE TABLE active_trips (
  rider_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id  uuid NOT NULL
);

A1 is a keyset query (see Part 14 — API Design (REST first), 14.5 Pagination), bounded to the last 13 months for the default screen so old partitions are pruned:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, fare_cents, requested_at, route->>'dropLabel' AS drop_label
  FROM trips
 WHERE rider_id = $1
   AND requested_at > now() - interval '13 months'
   AND (requested_at, id) < ($2, $3)
 ORDER BY requested_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20;
Limit  (actual time=0.09..0.61 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Merge Append  (actual time=0.09..0.59 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: trips.requested_at DESC, trips.id DESC
        Subplans Removed: 23
        ->  Index Scan using trips_2026_11_rider_id_requested_at_id_idx on trips_2026_11
              (actual time=0.03..0.11 rows=6 loops=1)
              Index Cond: ((rider_id = $1) AND (requested_at > (now() - '13 mons'::interval)))
              Filter: (ROW(requested_at, id) < ROW($2, $3))
              Buffers: shared hit=9
        ->  ... 13 more partition index scans, most returning 0-3 rows ...
Planning Time: 0.84 ms
Execution Time: 0.72 ms

Under a millisecond, with 23 of 37 partitions removed at startup. Without the time bound, every partition's index is probed: still about 2 ms, but it grows with every month of retention. (The row comparison appearing as a Filter rather than in the Index Cond is common on partitioned indexes and is cheap here because the leading columns already narrow the scan to one rider.)

// trip.entity.ts + history query in TypeORM
@Entity('trips')
@Index('trips_rider_history', ['riderId', 'requestedAt', 'id'])
export class Trip {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @PrimaryColumn({ name: 'requested_at', type: 'timestamptz' }) requestedAt: Date;
  @Column({ name: 'rider_id', type: 'uuid' }) riderId: string;
  @Column({ name: 'driver_id', type: 'uuid', nullable: true }) driverId: string | null;
  @Column({ name: 'city_code' }) cityCode: string;
  @Column() status: string;
  @Column({ name: 'fare_cents', type: 'integer', nullable: true }) fareCents: number | null;
  @Column({ type: 'jsonb', nullable: true }) route: Record<string, unknown> | null;
}

history(riderId: string, cursor?: { at: Date; id: string }) {
  const qb = this.trips.createQueryBuilder('t')
    .where('t.riderId = :riderId', { riderId })
    .andWhere("t.requestedAt > now() - interval '13 months'")
    .orderBy('t.requestedAt', 'DESC').addOrderBy('t.id', 'DESC')
    .limit(20);
  if (cursor) qb.andWhere('(t.requestedAt, t.id) < (:at, :id)', cursor);
  return qb.getMany();
}

(The partitioned table itself is created by a migration, not by TypeORM synchronization, which does not understand PARTITION BY.)

25.11.4 Cost, operations and the new access pattern

DynamoDB PostgreSQL
Storage (4.4 TB + indexes) ~$1,100 base table + ~$550 for two projected GSIs ~$600 for gp3 storage on primary, same again per replica
Compute / requests ~$600 writes + ~$500 reads (on-demand) Primary + 1 replica, 8 vCPU / 64 GB each: ~$1,800
Rough monthly total ~$2,800 ~$3,000
A1 latency p99 ~8-10 ms ~5 ms on a warm replica
Ops burden Very low; capacity per key, GSI lag Partitions, vacuum, upgrades, failover
Multi-region active-active Global tables Not built in
Joins to payments, refunds, support No; duplicate data or call another service Yes, one query

At this scale the bills are similar (list prices at time of writing, approximate). The difference is the shape of future work. Then finance asks for A5: fares by city per day.

  • PostgreSQL: one query on a replica, GROUP BY city_code, date_trunc('day', completed_at), pruned to yesterday's partition; if it becomes frequent, an index or a rollup table. Hours of work.
  • DynamoDB: a new GSI keyed CITY#<code>#<day> is possible (Bengaluru's 300,000 trips a day are only about 3.5 writes per second on that key, well within limits), but every existing trip must be rewritten to carry the new attribute: 2.2 billion updates, about $2,750 in write units and days of throttled backfill. The better answer is not a GSI at all: export to S3 with the managed table export or Streams, and run the report in a warehouse (see Part 38 — Data Engineering for Backend Engineers). That is a second system for a question PostgreSQL answers in place.

Failure scenario

In the DynamoDB version, at 21:40 on launch day support tickets arrived: "my trip disappeared". Riders finishing a trip were sent to the history screen, which reads GSI1. The GSI lagged the base table by 300-900 ms under load, so the just-completed trip was missing on first render. The data was fine; the read path ignored the consistency column of the requirements table. The fix: after completion the app opens the receipt with A2 (a strongly consistent GetItem on the base table) and prepends that trip to the history list locally.

25.11.5 Decision

Requirement PostgreSQL MongoDB DynamoDB Cassandra Redis TimescaleDB
A1-A4 at this scale Yes Yes Yes Yes, with more ops Cache only Overkill
One-active-trip invariant Yes (table + PK) Yes (unique index) Yes (conditional transaction) Lightweight transaction, costly No Yes
Ad-hoc finance and support queries Strong Moderate (aggregation) Weak (export needed) Weak No Strong
Multi-region active-active Weak Moderate Strong (global tables) Strong Weak Weak
Ops burden for a 6-person team Moderate Moderate Low High Low Moderate

Choice for most teams: PostgreSQL, with a Redis cache in front of A1 for the first page. Trip history joins with payments and support, and new questions arrive every quarter. Choose DynamoDB when the company is AWS-first, needs active-active writes across regions, has stable access patterns, and already exports data to a warehouse for analytics. Write the decision as an ADR (see Part 61 — Architecture Decision Framework) listing A1-A5, so the next access pattern is evaluated against the same table.

Interview questions

  1. Model rider trip history in DynamoDB. How do you enforce one active trip per rider? A conditional Put of RIDER#<id>/ACTIVE with attribute_not_exists(PK) inside the transaction that creates the trip; delete it on completion.
  2. Why can't a unique index on a partitioned PostgreSQL table enforce it? Unique indexes on partitioned tables must include the partition key, so uniqueness is only per partition; use a separate unpartitioned table or a constraint on the current partition only.
  3. What happens in each design when finance needs a new query? PostgreSQL: a query or index. DynamoDB: a GSI plus a backfill of every item, or an export to a warehouse.
  4. Why is the history list sometimes missing a just-finished trip in DynamoDB? GSIs are eventually consistent; read the base table for read-your-write paths.

Practical exercise

Build both designs, load 10 million synthetic trips for 200,000 riders, and implement A1-A4. Acceptance criteria: A1 returns 20 trips in under 10 ms p99 in both, a second concurrent trip request for the same rider fails in both, and you write a one-page ADR that chooses one store for your stated context and lists what A5 would cost in each.

Senior Checklist — Part 25

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can state the honest cases for NoSQL, and show when PostgreSQL jsonb already covers a "document" need
  • I can model documents with the right embed-vs-reference choices and bound every embedded array
  • I can design MongoDB compound indexes with ESR and verify them with explain('executionStats')
  • I can use MongoDB transactions with withTransaction, w: 'majority' and idempotent callbacks
  • I can build a DynamoDB single-table design from an access-pattern table, with sparse and sharded GSIs
  • I can do DynamoDB capacity arithmetic per key, and diagnose a hot partition
  • I can explain Cassandra's write and read paths, compaction strategies, tombstones and LOCAL_QUORUM
  • I can use TimescaleDB hypertables, continuous aggregates, compression and retention
  • I can recognise a deep-traversal workload that justifies a graph database
  • I can keep derived stores correct with versioned, idempotent propagation and reconciliation
  • I can plan a store migration: propagate, backfill, reconcile, shadow-read, cut over, roll back
  • I can model the same feature in DynamoDB and PostgreSQL and defend the choice in an ADR

Part 25 — Key Takeaways

  • PostgreSQL is the right default; leave it only for a specific, measured requirement, and remember that jsonb with GIN already covers most "flexible schema" arguments.
  • Document stores reward document-shaped data: embed bounded, parent-owned data, reference shared data, and validate the schema at the server anyway.
  • In MongoDB, design compound indexes with ESR, use w: 'majority', and treat frequent multi-document transactions as a sign the data is relational.
  • In DynamoDB the access-pattern table is the schema: every pattern is a GetItem or Query, and any Scan in a request path is a design bug.
  • DynamoDB capacity is per key as well as per table: about 1,000 WCU and 3,000 RCU per partition, so global counters and low-cardinality keys throttle no matter how much capacity you buy.
  • Cassandra writes are cheap appends and reads merge SSTables; bound partitions with time buckets, pick compaction by data shape, and avoid delete-heavy patterns that breed tombstones.
  • Time-series belongs in time-partitioned storage with retention by dropping chunks and rollups that are refreshed for late data.
  • Graph databases earn their place for deep, variable-depth traversals; one or two hops are ordinary SQL joins.
  • Keep exactly one source of truth; propagate with versioned, idempotent writes and prove consistency with reconciliation.
  • Every extra store is a permanent tax in backups, security, monitoring and on-call skill; count it before adding one.
  • Migrate between stores by propagating first, backfilling, reconciling versions, shadow-reading, and cutting over behind a flag you can flip back.
  • For trip history at 2 million trips a day, both DynamoDB and PostgreSQL work; the decision turns on future queries, joins and multi-region needs, not raw scale.
